the two exponentials have equal chessboard seminorms, and
\eqref{eq:qcd2-small-cell} bounds the extended source too.
To apply the multiple-cell inequality, first bound each
individual seminorm in this way and then multiply the bounds.
Thus each cell may use its own matrix $S$: each individual
fold is compared with its meson fold by one global symmetry.

Choose $q\ge0$ least such that $\sqrt3L^{-q}<d$, and set
$\eta=L^{-q}/(16n)$. Then
\[
 \eta^{-1}\le16\sqrt3Ln(1+d^{-1}).
\]
First suppose $L^{K-q}\ge16n$. Split each $f_i$ by the
product hat partition at mesh $\eta$. There are at most
$(2R/\eta+3)^3$ pieces for each entry. Each is supported in
a cube of side $2\eta$, its supremum norm does not increase,
and its sharp norm increases by at most $1+80M/\eta$.
Fix one piece from each entry. In each coordinate a piece
forbids at most $4\eta L^K+1$ positions for a wall of a
board whose cells have $\Delta=L^{K-q}$ sites on a side.
The $n$ pieces forbid at most $\Delta/4+n<\Delta$
positions. Choose walls at the remaining half-integral
positions. They are at distance at least $\eta$ from all
pieces. The diameter of a cell is less than $d$, so no
cell contains pieces from two different entries.

For the chosen pieces, let $s_i$ be the corresponding meson
source before its symplectic transformation, and let
$\Lambda(z)=\sum_i\lambda^{\mathfrak b}(z_is_i)$.
The extended generating function is entire, and the
chessboard estimate gives, on each coordinate face indexed
by $A\subset\{1,\ldots,n\}$,
\[
 \left|e^{-\Lambda(z)}\frac{Z^{\mathrm{ext}}(z)}{Z}\right|
 \le\exp\left(|A|c_V+
       \sum_{i\in A}\mathscr C_K(\operatorname{supp}s_i;\eta)\right),
  \qquad |z_i|<\frac{2\varrho_{\lambda_i}}{
                                      \|f_i\chi_i\|_{\lambda_i}}.
\]
Here $\varrho_0=\varrho$, $\varrho_M=\varrho_J$ for $M\ne0$,
and $b^3\le1$. Since every term of $\Lambda$ depends on
one variable, its mixed derivative in all $n\ge2$ variables
vanishes. The logarithmic derivative formula, as in the proof
of \cite[Thm. F]{QCDM1}, is
\[
 \partial_{[n]}\log Z^{\mathrm{ext}}(0)
 =\sum_\pi(-1)^{|\pi|-1}(|\pi|-1)!
       \prod_{A\in\pi}\partial_A
           \left(e^{-\Lambda}Z^{\mathrm{ext}}/Z\right)(0).
\]
The sum of the absolute combinatorial coefficients is at
most $2^nn!$. Writing $G=e^{-\Lambda}Z^{\mathrm{ext}}/Z$,
Cauchy's estimate on smaller coordinate circles, followed by
the limit as their radii increase to the displayed radii, gives
\[
 |\partial_AG(0)|\le
 \exp\left(|A|c_V+
       \sum_{i\in A}\mathscr C_K(\operatorname{supp}s_i;\eta)\right)
 \prod_{i\in A}\frac{\|f_i\chi_i\|_{\lambda_i}}
                            {2\varrho_{\lambda_i}}.
\]
In the product over a partition, each index occurs exactly
once. Hence both the source counts and the inverse Cauchy
radii have the same total cost for every partition.
The refined source count of that theorem gives
\[
 \mathscr C_K(\operatorname{supp}s_i;\eta)
    \le216C_{\mathscr C}(1+\log_L(1/\eta))+C,
\]
because the support has diameter bounded by a fixed
multiple of $\eta$. Hence its exponential contributes
at most $C^n\eta^{-np/2}$.

Summing over the pieces and restoring the original test
functions therefore gives
\[
 |S_n^T(\mathcal X)|\le n!
 \left[\frac{Ce^{c_V}}{\varrho_{\min}}
       (2R/\eta+3)^3(1+80M/\eta)\eta^{-p/2}\right]^n
       \prod_i\|f_i\|_{\lambda_i}.
\]
Here $\varrho_{\min}=\min(\varrho,\varrho_J)$.
The three powers of $\eta^{-1}$ count the pieces, one
comes from their sharp norms, and $p/2$ comes from the
source-energy count. Since $\eta^{-1}\le Cn(1+d^{-1})$,
the right-hand side is at most
\[
 \left[C'(1+R)^3(1+d^{-1})^{4+p/2}\right]^n
       n!\,n^{(4+p/2)n}\prod_i\|f_i\|_{\lambda_i}.
\]
Applying $n^n\le e^nn!$ gives the factorial exponent
$1+(4+p/2)=5+p/2$ in \eqref{eq:qcd2-extended-bound}.

If $L^{K-q}<16n$, then
$a^{-1}<16\sqrt3Ln(1+d^{-1})$. The Pfaffian identity
above and $\|\widehat D_U^{-1}\|\le m_0^{-1}$ give
\[
 |Z_U[M]|\le\det D_U\,
                \exp\left(\frac{\|M\|_1}{2m_0}\right).
\]
For the source of the extended tuple,
$M(v)=-a\sum_i z_if_i(x_v)\lambda_i$; the doubled fibre
has $16N_f$ components and there are $48$ chambers per
site. Thus the fermion contribution is bounded by
$384N_fm_-^{-1}\sum_x\|\sum_i z_if_i(x)\lambda_i\|$.
The action contribution is bounded by
$2a^{-1}\sum_p|w(p)|$.
A radius-$R$ support has at most $27a^{-3}(1+R)^3$ sites
and $81a^{-3}(1+R)^3$ plaquettes. Since $a\le1$,
both costs are bounded by
\[
 B_a(R)=C(1+N_f/m_-)(1+R)^3a^{-4}
\]
times the appropriate test-function norm. Set
$r_i=(B_a(R)\|f_i\|_{\lambda_i})^{-1}$, omitting zero
test functions. On the face $A$, the normalized generating
function has modulus at most $e^{|A|}$ for $|z_i|\le r_i$.
Cauchy's estimate and the cumulant partition formula give
\[
 |S_n^T(\mathcal X)|\le
          2^nn!e^nB_a(R)^n\prod_i\|f_i\|_{\lambda_i}.
\]
Use $a^{-1}<Cn(1+d^{-1})$ and $n^{4n}\le e^{4n}(n!)^4$
to obtain
\[
 |S_n^T(\mathcal X)|
 \le[C(1+N_f/m_-)(1+R)^3(1+d^{-1})^4]^n
                         (n!)^5\prod_i\|f_i\|_{\lambda_i}.
\]
This is bounded by the claimed estimate. Multilinearity
and \cref{C-401-19} give arbitrary labels.

Finally the expectation of any fixed local Grassmann
polynomial converges along the tori defining a state,
as proved in \cite[Prop. 2.5]{QCDM1}. A cumulant is a polynomial in finitely
many such expectations. Passing to the limit proves the
same estimate in the infinite-volume state.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Bilinears on disjoint supports}

The separation loss in \cref{C-401-48} grows with the number
of insertions. For scalar bilinears it can be reduced to one
factor, and removed altogether at orders at least four.
The reason is that the logarithm of the conditional Pfaffian
has a summable remainder after degree three. We control the
first three degrees by meson source energies, subtract them,
and apply the chessboard estimate to the resulting function.

\begin{theorem}[The bound on disjoint supports]\label{C-401-60}
Let $n\ge2$, and let $f_1,\ldots,f_n$ be bounded real
functions with pairwise disjoint supports, each contained
in a ball of radius $R$. For $\lambda_i\in\mathscr S$,
\[
 |S_n^T((\lambda_i,f_i)_i)|
 \le B_D(R)^n(n!)^{4+p/2}
          \prod_i\|\lambda_i\|\,\|f_i\|_\infty
 \qquad(n\ge4).
\]
For $n=2,3$, if two of the supports are at distance at
least $d>0$, the same bound holds with the additional
factor $(1+d^{-1})^3$. The constants are independent of
the cutoff and volume. The bounds hold on the tori,
in their fixed-cutoff infinite-volume limits, and in
the extended continuum limits of \cref{C-401-49}.
For the latter, take the Lipschitz test functions used
to define those limits.
\end{theorem}

We prove the estimate using the gauge marginal $\nu_K$ and
write $\mathsf E$ for its expectation. Let
$\mathsf H_1$ be the one-species, one-flavour space of
antiperiodic fields with spin and colour, and put
\[
 G=\mathsf G_+,\qquad \mathsf G_-=G^*,\qquad
 N_4=\operatorname{Tr}(GG^*)^2,\qquad
 \widehat G=\sum_{h=\pm}P_h\otimes\mathsf G_h.
\]
Multiplication by a site function acts on all the chambers
over that site. The norm of a matrix-valued site function
is its supremum norm. Define
\[
 R_U(\mathbb M)=Z_U[-a\mathbb M]/Z_U[0],\qquad
 W_U^{(q)}(\mathbb M)=-\frac1{2q}
                  \operatorname{Tr}(\widehat G\mathbb M)^q.
\]

\begin{lemma}[The Pfaffian at one configuration]\label{C-401-51}
The operator $G$ is accretive and
\[
 \|G\|\le\mathsf m^{-1},\qquad
 N_4\le3\|G^2\|_2^2.
\]
For $\|\mathbb M\|\le\mathsf m/2$,
\[
 R_U(\mathbb M)^2=\det(1-\widehat G\mathbb M),\qquad
 |R_U(\mathbb M)|=
       \exp\operatorname{Re}\sum_{q\ge1}W_U^{(q)}(\mathbb M),
 \qquad
 \left|\sum_{q\ge4}W_U^{(q)}(\mathbb M)\right|
       \le N_f\|\mathbb M\|^4N_4.
\]
The trilinear form
$\operatorname{Tr}(\mathsf G_hu\mathsf G_hv\mathsf G_hw)$
is symmetric in the scalar site functions $u,v,w$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The real part of $D_+[U]+m_0$ is at least $m_0$.
Its inverse is accretive, since, with
$v=(D_+[U]+m_0)^{-1}u$,
$\operatorname{Re}\langle u,Gu\rangle
=a\operatorname{Re}\langle(D_+[U]+m_0)v,v\rangle\ge0$.
Write $G=X+iY$, with $X\ge0$ and $X,Y$ Hermitian, and set
$S=X^2+Y^2$, $K=i[X,Y]$. Cyclicity gives
\[
 N_4=\operatorname{Tr}S^2+\operatorname{Tr}K^2,\qquad
 \|G^2\|_2^2=\operatorname{Tr}S^2-\operatorname{Tr}K^2.
\]
Moreover
\[
 \operatorname{Tr}K^2
 =2\operatorname{Tr}X^2Y^2-2\|X^{1/2}YX^{1/2}\|_2^2
 \le\tfrac12\operatorname{Tr}S^2,
\]
where the last inequality follows from
$\operatorname{Tr}(X^2-Y^2)^2\ge0$.
This proves the factor three.

The Pfaffian identity is \cref{C-401-16} with source
$-a\mathbb M$. Since $\|\widehat G\mathbb M\|\le1/2$,
its logarithm is the convergent trace series.
For $q\ge4$, the Schatten inequality gives
\[
 |\operatorname{Tr}A^q|\le\|A\|^{q-4}\|A\|_4^4,\qquad
 \|\widehat G\|_4^4=4N_fN_4.
\]
Summing $\sum_{q\ge4}2^{4-q}/(2q)\le1/4$ proves
the remainder bound. Finally the transpose identity
$\mathsf G_h^{\mathsf T}=C_0^{-1}\mathsf G_hC_0$ in the proof of
\cref{C-401-16}, together with cyclicity, reverses
the order of the three multiplication operators.
Cyclic permutations and reversal generate all permutations.
\end{proof}

For scalar site functions $a,b,c,d$, use the first flavour
and write
\[
 J[a,b,c,d]=
 \begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}_{\!\tau}\otimes E_{11}.
\]
Then $\|J[a,b,c,d]\|\le\max(\|a\|,\|d\|)+
\max(\|b\|,\|c\|)$, and the source conjugation is
$J[a,b,c,d]^\star=J[\bar d,\bar b,\bar c,\bar a]$.
Set
\[
 \mathscr E(J)=E_K(0,J)-E_K(0,0),\qquad
 \overline{\mathscr E}(J)=
 \int_0^{2\pi}\mathscr E(V_\varphi JV_\varphi^{-1})
                  \frac{d\varphi}{2\pi},\qquad
 V_\varphi=e^{i\varphi}e_++e_-.
\]
The bar in $\overline{\mathscr E}$ denotes this average.
For a holomorphic function $F$, write $F^{(q)}(J)$ for
the coefficient of $z^q$ in $F(zJ)$.

\begin{lemma}[The energy coefficients]\label{C-401-52}
For $\|J\|\le\rho_*=2\varrho_J$,
\[
 \left|\frac{Z[0,J]}{Z[0,0]}\right|
 \le e^{\operatorname{Re}\mathscr E(J)+c_V\ell^3},
 \qquad
 \left|\frac{Z[0,J]}{Z[0,0]}\right|
 \le e^{\operatorname{Re}\overline{\mathscr E}(J)+c_V\ell^3},
\]
and
\[
 \sum_{q\ge4}|\mathscr E^{(q)}(J)|
 \le2C_4\ell^3(\|J\|/\rho_*)^4.
\]
The latter bound also holds for $\overline{\mathscr E}$.
Both energies respect $\star$-conjugation. In the Taylor
series of $\overline{\mathscr E}(J[a,b,c,d])$, the degrees
in $b$ and $c$ are equal.
The coefficient of $zw$ in
$\mathscr E(ze_+A+we_-D)$ has modulus at most
$C_{\rm mix}\ell^3$ when $\|A\|,\|D\|\le\rho_*$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The first bound is the partition estimate used in
\cref{C-415-17}. The determinant is unchanged by
$J\mapsto V_\varphi JV_\varphi^{-1}$. Averaging its
logarithmic upper bound gives the second inequality.
Conjugation of the local source energies gives the
reality assertion. Averaging the phase kills every
monomial whose degrees in $b,c$ differ.

At level $j$ the source energy is holomorphic for
$\lambda_j\|J\|<r_M$ and bounded by
$C_{\mathfrak E}e^{-\kappa d_j(X)}$.
The inequality $\rho_*\le r_M/(2L)$ and Cauchy's formula
bound the sum of degrees at least four by
\[
 C_{\mathfrak E}(1-(2L)^{-1})^{-1}(2L)^{-4}
 (\|J\|/\rho_*)^4\sum_{j,X}\lambda_j^4e^{-\kappa d_j(X)}.
\]
Use $\sum_Xe^{-\kappa d_j(X)}\le C_En_jM^{-3}$ and
$\sum_j n_j\lambda_j^4\le L\ell^3/(L-1)$.
The definition of $C_4$ in \cref{C-415-3} gives the claim.
The mixed coefficient is a coefficient of
$E_K^{\rm mix}$; apply \cref{C-415-5} and Cauchy's formula
on the unit bidisc. The phase average preserves each bound.
\end{proof}

Put
\[
\begin{gathered}
\theta_q=\varrho_J^4/192,\\
 \rho_q=\min\{2\varrho_J,(\theta_qN_f)^{1/4}\},\\
 \rho_D=\frac{\varrho_J}{400N_f^4},\\
 c_N=c_V+C_{\rm mix}/8+2C_4,\\
 c_D=c_V+C_{\rm mix}+2C_4.
\end{gathered}
\]
In particular $\rho_q\ge\varrho_J/4$.

\begin{lemma}[A fourth Schatten moment]\label{C-401-53}
At every cutoff and torus side,
$\mathsf E e^{\theta_qN_fN_4}\le e^{c_N\ell^3}$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Set $t=\varrho_J^2/16$ and use the flavour-scalar sources
\[
 J_\varphi=
 \begin{pmatrix}\varrho_Je^{i\varphi}&\sqrt t\\
             -\sqrt t&\varrho_Je^{-i\varphi}\end{pmatrix}
             \otimes1_{N_f},\qquad
 J'=\begin{pmatrix}0&\sqrt t\\\sqrt t&0\end{pmatrix}
             \otimes1_{N_f}.
\]
They are $\star$-real and have norm at most
$5\varrho_J/4<\mathsf m/2$. Their determinant quotients
are positive: they are real by $\star$-conjugation,
nonzero along the segment from zero, and equal to one
at zero. With $G_\varphi=G(1-\varrho_Je^{i\varphi}G)^{-1}$,
Schur complementation gives
\[
 R_U(\widehat J_\varphi)=
 \bigl[|\det(1-\varrho_Je^{i\varphi}G)|^2
                   \det(1+tG_\varphi^*G_\varphi)\bigr]^{N_f},
 \quad
 R_U(\widehat J')=\det(1-tG^*G)^{N_f}.
\]
The circle mean of the first logarithmic determinant is
zero. Since $\varrho_J\|G\|\le1/4$,
\[
 \mathop{\mathrm{avg}}_\varphi\|G_\varphi\|_2^2
 =\sum_{k\ge0}\varrho_J^{2k}\|G^{k+1}\|_2^2
 \ge\|G\|_2^2+\tfrac13\varrho_J^2N_4,\qquad
 \|G_\varphi\|_4^4\le(4/3)^4N_4.
\]
Apply $\log(1+y)\ge y-y^2/2$ and
$\log(1-y)\ge-y-y^2$ for $0\le y\le1/2$.
The terms involving $\|G\|_2^2$ cancel, leaving
\[
 \tfrac12\mathop{\mathrm{avg}}_\varphi
       \log R_U(\widehat J_\varphi)
 +\tfrac12\log R_U(\widehat J')
 \ge\frac{N_ft}{2}
       (\varrho_J^2/3-209t/81)N_4
 \ge\theta_qN_fN_4.
\]
H\"older's inequality for this probability average bounds
the expectation of its exponential by the exponential of
the same average of logarithms of expectations.
Use \cref{C-401-52}. In the averaged energy, all terms of
degrees at most three vanish except half the coefficient
of $y_1y_4$ times $\varrho_J^2$: phase averaging kills
unequal diagonal degrees, and the $y_2y_3$ terms at the
two sources cancel. That remaining term is at most
$C_{\rm mix}\ell^3/8$. Degrees at least four cost
$2C_4\ell^3$. This gives $c_N\ell^3$.
The version of H\"older used here follows from finite
weighted H\"older by Riemann sums; all functions are
continuous on the compact finite-lattice gauge space.
\end{proof}

Define the following coefficients of the averaged energy:
$\mathscr E_h^{(q)}(u)=\mathscr E^{(q)}(e_huE_{11})$,
and let $\mathscr E_{+-}(v,w)$, $\mathscr E_{++-}(u,v,w)$,
$\mathscr E_{--+}(u,v,w)$ be the coefficients of $bc$,
$abc$, $dbc$, respectively, in
$\overline{\mathscr E}(J[a,b,c,d])$ at the indicated
arguments. Thus, for example,
\[
 \mathscr E_{++-}(u,v,w)=
 \overline{\mathscr E}^{(3)}(J[u,v,w,0])
       -\overline{\mathscr E}^{(3)}(J[u,0,0,0]).
\]
Set
\[
 Q_h^{(q)}(u)=-q^{-1}\operatorname{Tr}(\mathsf G_hu)^q
                         -\mathscr E_h^{(q)}(u),\qquad
 Q^{+-}(v,w)=\operatorname{Tr}(GvG^*w)+\mathscr E_{+-}(v,w),
\]
\[
 Q^{++-}(u;v,w)=\operatorname{Tr}(GuGvG^*w)
                                      +\mathscr E_{++-}(u,v,w).
\]

\begin{lemma}[The first three loop coefficients]\label{C-401-54}
For $q=1,2,3$ and complex scalar site functions,
\[
 \mathsf E e^{\operatorname{Re}(\xi Q_h^{(q)}(u))}
       \le e^{(c_V+C_{\rm mix})\ell^3}
 \quad\text{if }|\xi|^{1/q}\|u\|\le2\varrho_J.
\]
Moreover
\[
 \mathsf E e^{\operatorname{Re}(\xi Q^{+-}(v,w))}
       \le e^{c_D\ell^3}
 \quad\text{if }(8|\xi|)^{1/2}\max(\|v\|,\|w\|)\le\rho_q,
\]
and
\[
 \mathsf E e^{\operatorname{Re}(\xi Q^{++-}(u;v,w))}
       \le e^{c_D\ell^3}
 \quad\text{if }(8|\xi|)^{1/3}
       [\|u\|+\max(\|v\|,\|w\|)]\le\rho_q.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For the first bound take $h=+$ and $\xi=1$ by homogeneity.
The function
$F(u)=\log\det(1-Gu)-\mathscr E(e_+uE_{11})$
obeys $\mathsf E e^{2\operatorname{Re}F(e^{i\varphi}u)}
\le e^{(c_V+C_{\rm mix})\ell^3}$.
Indeed the positive determinant squared is the source
$J[u,0,0,\bar u]$, and \cref{C-415-5} controls its mixed
energy. Average $2\operatorname{Re}F(e^{i\varphi}u)$
against $(1+\cos q\varphi)d\varphi/(2\pi)$.
Only its $q$th coefficient survives. Weighted H\"older
gives the assertion. Complex conjugation gives $h=-$.

For real $v,w$, take $J=J[0,v,w,0]$.
The odd traces vanish and the second trace is
$-\operatorname{Tr}(GvG^*w)$. By \cref{C-401-51,C-401-52},
\[
 \mathsf E e^{-Q^{+-}(v,w)-\|J\|^4N_4}
       \le e^{(c_V+2C_4)\ell^3}.
\]
The same is true with $v$ replaced by $-v$.
If $\|J\|\le\rho_q$, Cauchy--Schwarz and
\cref{C-401-53} give both signs of
$Q^{+-}/2$ with bound $e^{c_D\ell^3}$.
For complex $v,w$, the real part of $\xi Q^{+-}(v,w)$
is the sum of four such real bilinear terms. H\"older
with four factors and rescaling both arguments by
$(8|\xi|)^{1/2}$ give the stated radius.

For the third bound first take $v,w$ real and
$\rho=\|u\|+\max(\|v\|,\|w\|)\le\rho_q$.
Use $J_{\varphi,\sigma}=J[e^{i\varphi}u,\sigma v,w,
e^{-i\varphi}\bar u]$ with probability weight
$(1+\sigma\cos\varphi)d\varphi/(4\pi)$ on the circle
times $\{1,-1\}$. In the trace expansion through degree
three, the surviving cyclic words have species
$(+,+,-)$ and $(-,-,+)$. Their sum is
$-\operatorname{Re}\operatorname{Tr}(GuGvG^*w)$.
In the energy the surviving terms are
$\operatorname{Re}\mathscr E_{++-}(u,v,w)$ and the
mixed quadratic diagonal coefficient, bounded by
$C_{\rm mix}\ell^3$. The fourth-order remainders give
$\rho^4N_4$ and $2C_4\ell^3$. Thus
\[
 \mathsf E e^{-\operatorname{Re}Q^{++-}(u;v,w)-\rho^4N_4}
       \le e^{c_D\ell^3}.
\]
Use Cauchy--Schwarz and \cref{C-401-53}, then replace
$u$ by any phase multiple. Splitting each of $v,w$
into real and imaginary parts gives four terms.
H\"older and the rescaling $(8|\xi|)^{1/3}$ prove the claim.
\end{proof}

Choose orthonormal bases of $P_hW$, and write $m_{ss'}$
for the matrix entries of $\mathbb M$, with $h(s)=h$ on
$P_hW$. Each set of indices has size $2N_f$.
Define a polynomial $\Lambda(\mathbb M)$ of degree at
most three by the following rule. Expand
\[
 \sum_{q=1}^3W_U^{(q)}(\mathbb M)=
 -\sum_{q=1}^3\frac1{2q}\sum_{s_1,\ldots,s_q}
 \operatorname{Tr}(\mathsf G_{h(s_1)}m_{s_1s_2}\cdots
                       \mathsf G_{h(s_q)}m_{s_qs_1}).
\]
For words in one species use polarization,
\[
 \operatorname{Tr}(\mathsf G_hu\mathsf G_hv)=
 \tfrac14\{\operatorname{Tr}(\mathsf G_h(u+v))^2
                  -\operatorname{Tr}(\mathsf G_h(u-v))^2\},
\]
\[
 \operatorname{Tr}(\mathsf G_hu\mathsf G_hv\mathsf G_hw)=
 \tfrac1{24}\sum_{\eta,\zeta=\pm1}\eta\zeta
                   \operatorname{Tr}(\mathsf G_h(u+\eta v+\zeta w))^3.
\]
Then replace each $-q^{-1}\operatorname{Tr}(\mathsf G_hu)^q$
by $\mathscr E_h^{(q)}(u)$, each
$\operatorname{Tr}(GuG^*v)$ by $-\mathscr E_{+-}(u,v)$,
and each $\operatorname{Tr}(GuGvG^*w)$ by
$-\mathscr E_{++-}(u,v,w)$.
For the word with two minus species use
$\operatorname{Tr}(G^*uG^*vGw)
=\overline{\operatorname{Tr}(G\bar uG\bar wG^*\bar v)}$
and the conjugate energy. These rules specify every term
and its coefficient; $\Lambda(0)=0$.

\begin{proposition}[The normalized Pfaffian]\label{C-401-55}
For $\|\mathbb M\|\le\rho_D$,
\[
 \mathsf E|R_U(\mathbb M)|
       \le e^{\operatorname{Re}\Lambda(\mathbb M)+c_D\ell^3}.
\]
Its quadratic and cubic counterterms have the form
\[
 \Lambda^{(q)}(\mathbb M)=
 \sum_{\rho}\kappa_\rho\mathscr F_\rho^{(q)}
                           (A_\rho\mathbb M),\qquad q=2,3,
\]
where $\mathscr F_\rho$ is $\mathscr E$ or
$\overline{\mathscr E}$, $A_\rho$ acts pointwise and
linearly, $\|A_\rho M\|\le3\|M\|$, and
\[
 \sum_{\rho:q_\rho=2}|\kappa_\rho|\le4N_f^2,\qquad
 \sum_{\rho:q_\rho=3}|\kappa_\rho|\le\tfrac{52}3N_f^3.
\]
Here $q_\rho$ is the degree of the corresponding term.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The replacement rule writes
$\operatorname{Re}(\sum_{q\le3}W_U^{(q)}-\Lambda)$
as a sum of $R=2+20N_f^2+80N_f^3$ variables covered by
\cref{C-401-54}. There are two linear terms, of coefficient
$1/2$ and argument norm at most $2N_f\|\mathbb M\|$;
$16N_f^2$ same-species quadratic terms, of coefficient
$1/8$ and argument norm at most $2\|\mathbb M\|$;
$4N_f^2$ mixed quadratic terms, of coefficient $1/2$;
$64N_f^3$ same-species cubic terms, of coefficient $1/48$
and argument norm at most $3\|\mathbb M\|$; and
$16N_f^3$ mixed cubic terms, of coefficient $1/2$ and
individual argument norms at most $\|\mathbb M\|$.
Add the remainder $N_f\|\mathbb M\|^4N_4$ and apply
H\"older with $R+1\le103N_f^3$ factors.
The radius $\rho_D$ ensures all the required inequalities:
\[
 103N_f^4\rho_D\le2\varrho_J,\qquad
 (4\cdot103N_f^3)^{1/2}\rho_D\le\rho_q,\qquad
 2(4\cdot103N_f^3)^{1/3}\rho_D\le\rho_q,\qquad
 103N_f^3\rho_D^4\le\theta_q.
\]
The same-species quadratic and cubic conditions are weaker.
Each factor is bounded by $e^{c_D\ell^3}$, proving the claim.

For the energy representation, polarization gives coefficient
sum $\frac18(2)(8N_f^2)+\frac12(4N_f^2)=4N_f^2$
in degree two. In degree three the sum is
$\frac1{48}(4)(16N_f^3)+2\frac12(2)(8N_f^3)
=52N_f^3/3$. The two extra factors in the mixed cubic
terms come from the displayed difference defining
$\mathscr E_{++-}$ and its minus-species counterpart.
Each resulting meson source uses at most three matrix
entries, giving the norm bound on $A_\rho$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[A cell containing several bilinears]\label{C-401-59}
Let $\mathbb M$ be supported in one chessboard cell
$\square$, at distance at least $\delta$ from its walls,
with $\|\mathbb M\|\le\rho_D$. There is a polynomial
$\lambda_\square(\mathbb M)$ of degree at most three such that
\[
 \|e^{\Phi[\mathbb M]}\|_{\rm ch}
 \le\exp\{\operatorname{Re}\lambda_\square(\mathbb M)
       +c_D|\square|+\mathscr C_K(\operatorname{supp}\mathbb M;\delta)\}.
\]
Here $\Phi[\mathbb M]=a\sum_{x,v:x_v=x}\phi[\mathbb M(x)](v)$.
The polynomial is holomorphic in the coefficients of $\mathbb M$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Reflection carries $\mathbb M$ to its reflected argument,
with $M^*=\tau_3M^\dagger\tau_3$ after an odd number of
reflections. Let $\mathbb M_r$ be these images and
$\mathbb M^{\rm ch}=\sum_r\mathbb M_r$.
They have disjoint supports and preserve the supremum norm.
The fold identity and positivity give
\[
 \|e^{\Phi[\mathbb M]}\|_{\rm ch}^{\mathsf N}
       =\mathsf E R_U(\mathbb M^{\rm ch})\ge0.
\]
Define
\[
 \lambda_\square(\mathbb M)=\mathsf N^{-1}
 \left(\sum_{r\ {\rm even}}\Lambda(\mathbb M_r)
       +\sum_{r\ {\rm odd}}\overline{\Lambda(\mathbb M_r)}\right).
\]
The second conjugation makes this holomorphic in the
original coefficients, and preserves its degree.

The linear part of $\Lambda$ is additive. For a term of
degree $q=2,3$ in \cref{C-401-55}, put
$T=2\varrho_J/(3\rho_D)$ and apply the source-energy
almost-additivity estimate of
\cite[Prop.~10.16]{QCDM1} to the sources $tA_\rho\mathbb M_r$,
$|t|\le T$. They lie in the admitted source ball and are
at distances at least $2\delta$. The defect is bounded by
$\mathsf N\mathscr C_K(\operatorname{supp}\mathbb M;\delta)$;
this is the same reflected-support count used in
\eqref{eq:qcd2-small-cell}. Cauchy's estimate in $t$ gives
an additional $T^{-q}$. Consequently
\[
 \left|\Lambda(\mathbb M^{\rm ch})-\sum_r\Lambda(\mathbb M_r)\right|
 \le(4N_f^2T^{-2}+\tfrac{52}3N_f^3T^{-3})
       \mathsf N\mathscr C_K(\operatorname{supp}\mathbb M;\delta)
 \le\mathsf N\mathscr C_K(\operatorname{supp}\mathbb M;\delta).
\]
Combine this with \cref{C-401-55} and take the
$\mathsf N$th root, using $\ell^3/\mathsf N=|\square|$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of \cref{C-401-60}]
First assume $L^K\ge16n$ and put $\eta=(16n)^{-1}$.
Use the hat partition from the proof of \cref{C-401-48}.
Each $f_i$ is a sum of at most $(32nR+3)^3$ pieces
$g_i$, supported in cubes $Q_i$ of side $2\eta$,
with $\|g_i\|_\infty\le\|f_i\|_\infty$.
For each tuple of pieces choose a board of side-one
cells whose walls stay at least $\eta$ from the $Q_i$.
The same forbidden-wall count used there applies.
Several pieces may lie in one cell, but their actual
supports are disjoint.

Put $\rho_i=\rho_D/(\|\lambda_i\|\|g_i\|_\infty)$
and $\mathbb M_{\square,z}=\sum_{Q_i\subset\square}
z_ig_i\lambda_i$. On $|z_i|\le\rho_i$ its norm is at
most $\rho_D$, since at most one $g_i$ is nonzero at
each site. Subtract the polynomial
$\Lambda_0(z)=\sum_\square\lambda_\square(\mathbb M_{\square,z})$
from the logarithm of the generating function and write
\[
 F(z)=e^{-\Lambda_0(z)}
       \omega\left(e^{\sum_i z_i\Phi[\lambda_i](g_i)}\right),
 \qquad F(0)=1.
\]
On a coordinate face indexed by $A$, chessboard positivity
and \cref{C-401-59} give
\[
 |F(z)|\le
 \exp\{|A|c_D^++\sum_{i\in A}\mathscr C_K(Q_i;\eta)\},
 \qquad c_D^+=\max(c_D,0).
\]
The source count obeys
$e^{n\sup_Q\mathscr C_K(Q;\eta)}
\le C_{\rm co}^n(16n)^{np/2}$.
The partition formula for $\partial_{[n]}\log F$ and
Cauchy's estimate, exactly as in \cref{C-401-48}, imply
\[
 |\partial_{[n]}\log F(0)|
 \le2^nn!C_{\rm co}^ne^{nc_D^+}(16n)^{np/2}
                                    \prod_i\rho_i^{-1}.
\]

For $n\ge4$, $\partial_{[n]}\Lambda_0=0$.
For $n=2,3$ it vanishes unless all pieces lie in one
cell. In that case use the energy representation in
\cref{C-401-55}. The mixed source-energy estimate of
\cite[Prop.~10.16]{QCDM1}, with two supports at distance
$d$, bounds each derivative by its Cauchy radii times
the count $\mathscr C_K(Q_1;d)$. Reflection averaging
preserves this bound. The coefficient sums give
\[
 |\partial_{[n]}\Lambda_0(0)|
 \le70N_f^3C_{\rm co}(1+d^{-1})^3\prod_i\rho_i^{-1}.
\]
Here the constants are those of the refined count in
\cite[proof of Thm.~F]{QCDM1}; in particular
$\sup_Q\mathscr C_K(Q;d)\le C_{\rm co}(1+d^{-1})^3$
for the cubes of side $2\eta$.
Sum over at most $(32nR+3)^{3n}$ piece tuples.
The inequalities $n^n\le e^nn!$ and
$32nR+3\le35n(1+R)$ give the stated factorial exponent
$1+3+p/2$.

If $L^K<16n$, use
$|R_U(\mathbb M)|\le\exp(\|\mathbb M\|_1/(2\mathsf m))$.
The trace norm includes $48$ chambers and $16N_f$
internal components, hence the full generating function
is at most $\exp\sum_i|z_i|b_i$, with
\[
 b_i=384N_f\mathsf m^{-1}\|\lambda_i\|
                                    \sum_x|f_i(x)|.
\]
A ball of radius $R$ contains at most
$27a^{-3}(1+R)^3$ sites. Since $a^{-1}<16n$,
\[ b_i\le C N_fm_-^{-1}n^3(1+R)^3
\|\lambda_i\|\|f_i\|_\infty. \]
The same partition formula on $|z_i|\le b_i^{-1}$
gives $2^nn!e^n\prod_i b_i$, bounded by
$B_c(R)^n(n!)^4\prod_i\|\lambda_i\|\|f_i\|_\infty$.
Enlarge $B_D(R)$ to cover both regimes.

At fixed cutoff the local Gaussian functionals converge
along the defining torus sequence, so every cumulant does.
The constants are independent of the side. They therefore
pass to these states and to each extended continuum limit.
The functions and labels are extended by multilinearity;
their supports remain disjoint throughout the limit.
\end{proof}


\subsection{Action densities and bilinears on disjoint supports}

The preceding bound for bilinears subtracts a polynomial
of degree three. Action-density sources require a different
organization. We refine a partition only near four or more
bilinear insertions. A cell with at most three such insertions
can be handled by one symplectic change of variables, after
expanding its tensor of labels in rotated meson tensors.
The remaining cells have size comparable to the lattice
spacing and admit a determinant bound. The resulting sum
over scales is integrable because refinement requires four
nearby bilinear entries.

\begin{theorem}[Mixed tuples on a torus]\label{C-401-85}
Suppose $N_f\ge2$, with the source estimates at intermediate
levels in \cite[Props.~10.15 and 10.18]{QCDM1}.
Let $n\ge2$ and $d>0$. For real Lipschitz test functions
with pairwise disjoint supports on $T_\ell$, two of which
are at distance at least $d$, and labels
$\lambda_i\in\{0\}\cup\mathscr S$,
\[
 |S_n^T((\lambda_i,f_i)_i)|
 \le C_n^{\rm W}(d;g)(1+\ell)^{3n}
       \prod_{i:\lambda_i\ne0}\|\lambda_i\|
       \prod_i\|f_i\|_{\lambda_i}.
\]
The constant is independent of $K,\ell,\mathsf b,\mathsf m$,
the labels and the functions. The estimate passes to
every fixed-torus continuum subsequence for this family.
Here $\|f\|_0=\|f\|_\sharp$ and
$\|f\|_\lambda=\|f\|_\infty$ for $\lambda\ne0$.
One may replace $(1+\ell)^{3n}$ by $4^ne^{nc_V\ell^3}$.
\end{theorem}

The factor depending on $\ell$ is retained in this theorem.
For limits on growing tori we use the estimate at pairwise
separated supports in \cref{C-401-48}.

\subsubsection{At most three bilinear labels}

\begin{lemma}[Rotated meson tensors]\label{C-401-77}
Suppose $N_f\ge2$ and $1\le m\le3$. There are finitely
many $S_r\in G$ and meson basis labels $\Gamma_{r,s}$,
chosen once for each $N_f,m$, such that every tensor of
labels has an expansion
\[
 M_1\otimes\cdots\otimes M_m
 =\sum_r a_r\bigotimes_{s=1}^m
                    S_r\widehat\Gamma_{r,s}S_r^{-1},
 \qquad
 \sum_r|a_r|\le c_{\rm lab}(N_f)\prod_s\|M_s\|.
\]
The same matrix $S_r$ occurs in all factors of each summand.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Let $\Omega(u,v)=u^{\mathsf T}\mathcal Jv$ on $W$.
The map
\[
 \iota(u\wedge v)=v(\mathcal Ju)^{\mathsf T}
                         -u(\mathcal Jv)^{\mathsf T}
\]
identifies $\Lambda^2W$ with $\mathscr S$ and intertwines
the $G_{\mathbb C}$ actions. Indeed
$\mathcal J\iota(u\wedge v)$ is antisymmetric, and
\[
 x^{\mathsf T}\mathcal J\iota(u\wedge v)y
 =\Omega(x,u)\Omega(v,y)-\Omega(x,v)\Omega(u,y).
\]
Nondegeneracy of $\Omega$ makes this an isomorphism to
the alternating forms. The subspace of meson labels
corresponds to $W_\psi\wedge W_\chi$, where $W_\psi$
and $W_\chi$ are the two coordinate Lagrangians. The
associated forms vanish on each Lagrangian separately,
and their mixed blocks are arbitrary.

Choose symplectic bases $p_\alpha,q_\alpha$ in each
species, with $\Omega(q_\alpha,p_\beta)=\delta_{\alpha\beta}$.
There are $N_f$ indices in each species. Write
$P_\alpha=\operatorname{span}(p_\alpha,q_\alpha)$.
Let $V_m$ be the span of the $G_{\mathbb C}$ images
of $(W_\psi\wedge W_\chi)^{\otimes m}$.
The corresponding span for $G$ is the same: it is a
complex subspace invariant under the compact group,
hence under its Lie algebra and its complexification,
and therefore under the connected group $G_{\mathbb C}$.
We prove $V_m=(\Lambda^2W)^{\otimes m}$.

A tensor of basis wedges has a multigraph on the indices
$\alpha$, one edge for each wedge. A loop is
$p_\alpha\wedge q_\alpha$ up to sign. A meson wedge
has one $p$ and one $q$. The symplectic flip
$p_\alpha\mapsto q_\alpha$, $q_\alpha\mapsto-p_\alpha$
fixes a loop and exchanges the two types at every
nonloop edge incident to $\alpha$.

If the nonloop edges form a forest, choose flips from
the root outwards to make every edge a meson wedge.
This puts the tensor in $V_m$.

Suppose two edges join the same distinct indices
$\alpha,\beta$. Under
$\mathrm{SL}(P_\alpha)\times\mathrm{SL}(P_\beta)$,
\[
 (P_\alpha\wedge P_\beta)^{\otimes2}
 \simeq\bigoplus_{A,B\in\{\operatorname{Sym}^2,\Lambda^2\}}
                              A(P_\alpha)\otimes B(P_\beta).
\]
These four irreducible summands are pairwise nonisomorphic.
The meson tensor
$(q_\alpha\wedge p_\beta)\otimes(p_\alpha\wedge q_\beta)$
has nonzero projection on each: at either vertex its
factor is $p\otimes q$ or $q\otimes p$, with nonzero
symmetric and alternating parts. Its orbit therefore
spans this whole space. If a third edge is a loop or
disjoint from these vertices, it is fixed by this
operation, and a flip at an outside endpoint makes it
a meson wedge when necessary. If it has one endpoint
at $\alpha$ or $\beta$ and one at $\gamma$, expand its
transformed endpoint in $p,q$ and use the flip at
$\gamma$ separately in each term. This proves the
claim unless all three edges are parallel.

For a triangle on $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$, regroup the
six factors by vertices. The space is the sum of the
eight pairwise nonisomorphic tensor products of the
symmetric and alternating squares at the vertices.
The meson tensor
\[
 (q_\alpha\wedge p_\beta)\otimes
 (q_\beta\wedge p_\gamma)\otimes
 (q_\gamma\wedge p_\alpha)
\]
has nonzero projection on every summand, so its orbit
spans the space.

It remains to treat three parallel edges between
$\alpha$ and $\beta$. First suppose that the species
of $\beta$ contains an index $\gamma$ distinct from
both. The symplectic transformation
\[
 q_\beta\mapsto q_\beta+p_\gamma,\qquad
 q_\gamma\mapsto q_\gamma+p_\beta
\]
fixes all other basis vectors. Let $x_i\in P_\alpha$
be basis vectors. The tensors
\[
 u_y=(x_1\wedge q_\gamma)\otimes
         (x_2\wedge p_\beta)\otimes(x_3\wedge y),
 \qquad y=p_\beta,q_\beta,
\]
belong to $V_3$ by the double-edge case. Subtracting
$u_{p_\beta}$ from its transform gives the tensor
with all three ends at $\beta$ equal to $p_\beta$.
For $u_{q_\beta}$ the expansion has four terms.
The original term and the two terms with an endpoint
at $\gamma$ are already in $V_3$ by the same case;
the remaining term has ends $(p_\beta,p_\beta,q_\beta)$.
Permuting the tensor factors and flipping at $\beta$
give every choice of the three endpoints.

The only remaining case is $N_f=2$ and $\alpha,\beta$
in the same species. On its four-dimensional space
$W_h=P_\alpha\oplus P_\beta$, wedge product defines
a nondegenerate symmetric form $b$ on $\Lambda^2W_h$.
The invariant bivector
$\omega=p_\alpha\wedge q_\alpha+p_\beta\wedge q_\beta$
has $b(\omega,\omega)=2$. Thus
\[
 \Lambda^2W_h=\mathbb C\omega\oplus Z,\qquad
 Z=\omega^\perp,\qquad \dim Z=5.
\]
The standard exterior-square isogeny identifies the
image of $\mathrm{Sp}(4,\mathbb C)$ on $Z$ with
$\mathrm{SO}(Z,b)$, its kernel being $\{1,-1\}$;
see \cite[\S\S16.2, 18.2, pp.~245--247, 278--279]{FH91}.
The meson wedges span $\mathbb C\omega\oplus U$, where
\[
 U=\operatorname{span}\{q_\alpha\wedge p_\beta,
 q_\beta\wedge p_\alpha,
 p_\alpha\wedge q_\alpha-p_\beta\wedge q_\beta\}.
\]
The first two vectors pair nontrivially with one
another and the third has square $-2$, so $U$ is
nondegenerate. Witt's extension theorem \cite[Thm.~8.3]{EKM08} carries it
to every nondegenerate three-plane in $Z$. The
isometry may be chosen with determinant one by
composing with a reflection in the orthogonal
complement. Consequently a triple in $\Lambda^2W_h$
whose $Z$ components have nonzero Gram determinant
lies in a common translate of
$(\mathbb C\omega\oplus U)^3$. Such triples form a
nonempty Zariski-open set. A linear functional
annihilating $V_3$ vanishes on their tensor products,
and hence, by polynomial continuation, on every
tensor product. This proves the remaining case.

These cases exhaust multigraphs with at most three
edges. The hypothesis $N_f\ge2$ supplies $\gamma$
when the parallel edges join different species; the
four-dimensional argument handles its only other
exception. Finally select a basis of rotated meson
tensors in each degree. Equivalence of norms in
these finite-dimensional tensor spaces gives
$c_{\rm lab}(N_f)$ and the stated coefficient bound.
\end{proof}

\subsubsection{Scales and cell estimates}

Let $p_n$ be the least integer with $L^{p_n}\ge16n$,
let $t_n\ge1$ be the least integer with
$A_n:=L^{t_n}\ge2n$, and let $q\ge0$ be the least
integer with $\sqrt3L^{-q}<d$. Put
\begin{equation}\label{C-401-76}
 u_j=L^{-q}A_n^{-j},\qquad v_j=L^{-p_n}u_j.
\end{equation}
Then $u_0\le1$ and
$u_0^{-1}\le\sqrt3L(1+d^{-1})$.
Call the cutoff fine when $u_1\ge2nLa$. In this
case let $j_*$ be the largest integer with
$u_{j_*}\ge2nLa$, so
$2nLa\le u_{j_*}<2nLA_na$.

At mesh $v_j$ use the product hats
$\chi_\alpha^{(j)}(x)=\prod_\mu(1-|x_\mu/v_j-\alpha_\mu|)_+$.
Their enlarged supporting cubes $Q_\alpha^{(j)}$
have side $2v_j(1+2/A_n)$. Their diameter is at most
$4v_j\le u_j/8$, their volume is at least $8v_j^3$,
and at most $27$ of them contain any point. The
refinement coefficients
$c_{\alpha\beta}^{(j)}=\chi_\alpha^{(j)}(v_{j+1}\beta)$
satisfy
\[
 \chi_\alpha^{(j)}=\sum_\beta c_{\alpha\beta}^{(j)}
                         \chi_\beta^{(j+1)},\qquad
 \sum_\alpha c_{\alpha\beta}^{(j)}=1.
\]
They are nonnegative, and a nonzero coefficient
implies $Q_\beta^{(j+1)}\subset Q_\alpha^{(j)}$.
The refinement identity is linear interpolation on
each axis. For containment use
$v_j+v_{j+1}(1+2/A_n)\le v_j(1+2/A_n)$.

For a cell side $u=L^ia\le1$, $i\ge1$, choose
$k(u)=i+n'$ if $u\le\sigma_0(g)$, where $n'$ is
least with $L^{3n'}\ge\ell_g(u)$, and choose
$k(u)=K$ otherwise. The constants $\ell_g,\sigma_0$
are those preceding \cref{C-415-21}. The level choice
in its proof gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:qcd2-mixed-level}
 \begin{gathered}
 u\le\lambda_{k(u)}\le\frac L{\sigma_0(g)}
                              u\ell_g(u)^{1/3},\\
 (C+2+C_P(1+\log x_{k(u)}))
                         \frac{u^3}{\lambda_{k(u)}^3}\le c_V,\\
 \log_L\frac{\lambda_{k(u)}}u
 \le1+\log_L\frac1{\sigma_0(g)}
                         +\frac{\log\ell_g(u)}{3\log L}.
 \end{gathered}
\end{equation}
For completeness, in the first case
$\lambda_{k(u)}<Lu\ell_g(u)^{1/3}\le(4L)^{-1}$,
so the level exists. Also
$x_k\le X_g/u+\bar B$ and
$1+\log x_k\le\ell_g(u)\le L^{3n'}$.
In the other case $\lambda_K=1<u/\sigma_0(g)$,
$u\le1$, and $x_K\le X_g$. These observations give
all three inequalities.

\begin{lemma}[Refining a chessboard]\label{C-401-78}
Let every wall of a board $\mathbb B$ be a wall of
$\mathbb B'$. For even elements $G_{\square'}$ in
the finer cells inside a cell $\square$,
\[
 \left\|\prod_{\square'\subset\square}G_{\square'}
                          \right\|_{{\rm ch},\mathbb B}
 \le\prod_{\square'\subset\square}
                               \|G_{\square'}\|_{{\rm ch},\mathbb B'}.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
On even elements, two parallel reflections compose
to a translation by twice the displacement of their
planes. Therefore reflection in a coarse wall is
the copy map along the intervening fine cells:
an odd row of fine reflections has the same action.
The fold on $\mathbb B$ is consequently a product
of fine-cell copies of the $G_{\square'}$.
Apply the chessboard inequality on $\mathbb B'$.
Every original fine cell occurs once in each of
the $\mathsf N$ coarse copies, giving the product
of its seminorms to power $\mathsf N$. Taking the
$\mathsf N$th root proves the claim.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[A cell at the chosen level]\label{C-401-79}
Let $s\in\mathcal P_{k(u)}^\#$ be supported in a
cell of side $u$, at distance at least $\delta\le u$
from its walls. For $S\in G$,
\[
 \|\alpha_SG_s\|_{\rm ch}
 \le e^{\operatorname{Re}\lambda_{k(u)}^{\mathfrak b}(s)
                  +c_V+\mathscr C_{k(u)}(\operatorname{supp}s;\delta)},
\]
where
\begin{align*}
 \mathscr C_{k(u)}(\operatorname{supp}s;\delta)
 &\le C_{\mathscr C}^\flat[1+(u/\delta)^3]\\
 &\quad+64C_{\mathscr C}(1+\sqrt3u/\delta)^3
 \left[2+\log_L\frac{u}{\sigma_0(g)\delta}
                        +\frac{\log\ell_g(u)}{3\log L}\right].
\end{align*}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The symplectic substitution preserves the seminorm,
as in \cref{C-401-48}. Apply the intermediate-level
cell estimate of \cite[Prop.~10.18(iii)]{QCDM1}
and \eqref{eq:qcd2-mixed-level}. In the counting
term, levels with $\lambda_j\le\delta$ contribute
at most $C_{\mathscr C}^\flat[1+(u/\delta)^3]$ by
the count in part (ii) of that proposition.
At the other levels the enlarged cube count is
at most $64(1+\sqrt3u/\delta)^3$. There are at most
$1+\log_L(\lambda_{k(u)}/\delta)$ such levels;
the last bound in \eqref{eq:qcd2-mixed-level}
gives the result.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[A cell near the lattice scale]\label{C-401-80}
Let $\square$ have side $u=L^ia\le1$, $i\ge1$,
and put $k=k(u)$, $t_k=r_J/(2\lambda_k)$.
If $M(x)\in\mathscr S$ vanishes outside its sites,
$\|M\|_\infty\le t_k$, and $w$ vanishes near its
walls, then
\begin{align*}
 \|e^{O(w)+\Phi[M]}\|_{\rm ch}
 \le\exp\bigg[&\frac2a\sum_{p:x(p)\in\square}|w(x(p))|
              +192N_f\log2\,(u/a)^3+c_V\\
 &+27C_{\mathfrak E}C_{\rm cnt}C_{\rm sh}
                            \bigl(256k+1536(u/a)^3\bigr)\bigg].
\end{align*}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Fold the two sources into all $\mathsf N$ cells.
Reflection preserves $\|M\|_\infty$, so the folded
source has the same bound. Since each plaquette
action lies in $[0,2]$, the action-density factor
costs the first term times $\mathsf N$.

Let $S'$ be the union of the reflected sets of sites,
let $P$ project onto their chambers, and put $T=P\mathsf G_+P$.
The Pfaffian identity in \cref{C-401-51} and the
singular-value determinant inequality give
\[
 |R_U(M^{\rm ch})|^2
       \le\prod_{\sigma}(1+t_k\sigma)^{4N_f},
 \qquad
 |R_U(M^{\rm ch})|\le2^{N_fd'}
                         \det(1+t_k^2T^*T)^{N_f}.
\]
Here $\sigma$ runs over the singular values of $T$,
$d'\le192\mathsf N(u/a)^3$, and the second inequality
uses $(1+x)^2\le2(1+x^2)$.
The determinant is the positive conditional quotient
for the meson source
$J'=t_k1_{S'}(e_{+-}-e_{-+})\otimes1_{N_f}$.
It belongs to $\mathcal P_k^\#$.

The partition bound at level $k$ costs at most
$\mathsf Nc_V$ by \eqref{eq:qcd2-mixed-level}.
For its energy increment, the polymer filing in the
proof of \cref{C-415-20} gives
\[
 |E_k(0,J')-E_k(0,0)|
 \le C_{\mathfrak E}C_{\rm cnt}C_{\rm sh}
                        \sum_{j\le k}\#_j^+(S').
\]
The reflected support count is at most $27\mathsf N$
times the count for one cell. That count is at most
$256[1+6(u/\lambda_j)^3]$, and
$\sum_{j\ge1}(u/\lambda_j)^3\le(u/a)^3$.
Combine these inequalities and take the
$\mathsf N$th root.
\end{proof}

\subsubsection{A partition stopped at four nearby bilinears}

Write $I_B=\{i:\lambda_i\ne0\}$, $I_0=[n]\setminus I_B$,
and $n_B=|I_B|$, $n_0=|I_0|$. Refine the hats as follows.
At stage $j<j_*$, an entry is refined precisely when
its cube lies within distance $2u_j$ of the cubes of
at least four bilinear entries, counting itself if
it is bilinear. Entries that have already stopped
keep their cubes. All remaining entries stop at $j_*$.
A history records the successive nodes. Its weight
is the product of the coefficients $c_{\alpha\beta}^{(j)}$
used in its refinements. A final configuration is
$F=(j_i,\alpha_i)_{i\le n}$; write
$Q_i=Q_{\alpha_i}^{(j_i)}$, $\chi_i=\chi_{\alpha_i}^{(j_i)}$
and $\mathcal X_F=((\lambda_i,f_i\chi_i))_i$.

\begin{lemma}[The stopped partition]\label{C-401-81}
At a fine cutoff,
\[
 S_n^T(\mathcal X)=\sum_H W(H)S_n^T(\mathcal X_{F(H)}),
 \qquad \sum_{H:F(H)=F}W(H)\le1.
\]
The cubes in each history are nested. Discard final
configurations with a zero entry. If $j_i\ge1$, there
are four bilinear entries $l$, with $j_l\ge j_i-1$,
such that
\[
 |y-y'|\le\tfrac52A_nu_{j_i}\qquad(y\in Q_i, y'\in Q_l).
\]
In particular, for $i\in I_0$,
\[
 \sup_{Q_i}|f_i|\le\tfrac52A_nu_{j_i}\operatorname{Lip}f_i,
 \qquad
 \|f_i\chi_i\|_\sharp\le C_\sharp\|f_i\|_\sharp,
 \quad C_\sharp=1+5A_nL^{p_n}+80ML^{p_n}/u_0.
\]
If $j_i<j_*$, at most three final bilinear cubes meet
$Q_i^{[2u_{j_i}]}$, and no final cube with
$j_l\ge j_i+2$ meets $Q_i^{[\sqrt3u_{j_i}]}$.
Here $Q^{[r]}$ is the closed $r$-neighbourhood of $Q$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Multilinearity and the hat refinement identity give
the expansion. The sum of the weights of all chains
ending at one specified node is one, by induction
from $\sum_\alpha c_{\alpha\beta}^{(j)}=1$.
The admissible histories are a subset of these
chains, so their weight sum is at most one.

If $i$ was refined from $j=j_i-1$, at least four
bilinear cubes met $Q_i(j)^{[2u_j]}$. None of these
entries could have stopped at $j'<j$. Indeed that
earlier cube would then have all four cubes within
$2u_{j'}$, since
$\operatorname{diam}(Q_i(j)^{[2u_j]})\le(33/8)u_j
\le2u_{j'}$. It would have been refined, a contradiction.
Thus all four cubes at stage $j$ have diameter at
most $u_j/8$. Their final subcubes are within
$(2+1/4)u_j\le(5/2)A_nu_{j_i}$ of one another as
asserted. For an action-density entry choose a point
in the support of any of these nonzero bilinear
pieces. At that point $f_i=0$, since the original
supports are disjoint. The Lipschitz estimate follows.
Together with $\operatorname{Lip}\chi_i\le2/v_{j_i}$
it bounds the derivative of $f_i\chi_i$. At $j_i=0$
use its supremum norm instead; the two estimates
give $C_\sharp$.

When $i$ stops before $j_*$, the count of nearby
bilinear cubes is at most three. Nestedness preserves
that assertion for the final cubes. If a cube of
level $j_l\ge j_i+2$ met $Q_i^{[\sqrt3u_{j_i}]}$,
its refinement at $j_l-1$ would supply four
bilinear cubes within
\[
 \sqrt3u_{j_i}+\frac{17}{8}u_{j_l-1}
 \le\left(\sqrt3+\frac{17}{8A_n}\right)u_{j_i}
 \le2u_{j_i}
\]
of $Q_i$. This contradicts its stopping rule.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Boards for the stopped pieces]\label{C-401-82}
For each final configuration there are nested boards
$\mathbb B_j$, of cell side $u_j$, such that $Q_i$
is at distance at least $v_{j_i}$ from the walls of
$\mathbb B_{j_i}$. Let $\mathcal T$ be the maximal
cells among those containing the $Q_i$ at their own
levels. They are disjoint and cover all pieces.
If $\square\in\mathcal T$ has level $j<j_*$, it
contains at most three bilinear entries, and each
entry in it has level $j$ or $j+1$. A maximal cell
of level $j_*$ contains only entries of that level.
Every piece in a maximal cell of level $j$ is at
distance at least $v_{j+1}$ from its walls. Every
maximal cell has diameter less than $d$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Choose wall offsets from the finest board upwards.
Once the offset at level $j+1$ is chosen, nestedness
leaves $A_n$ offsets at level $j$, spaced by $u_{j+1}$.
A cube of level $j$ excludes an interval of length
at most $5v_j$ if its distance from the wall is to
be at least $v_j$. Thus all $n$ cubes exclude at
most $5A_n/16+n<A_n$ offsets. At level $j_*$ the
offsets are spaced by $a$, and the same count is
$\frac5{16}u_{j_*}/a+n<u_{j_*}/a$, since
$u_{j_*}\ge2nLa$. Choose the three coordinates
independently. The sides are odd powers of $L$
in lattice units and divide the torus with an even
number of cells, so these are admitted boards.

Cells of these nested boards are either nested or
disjoint. A maximal cell of level $j$ cannot contain
an entry of smaller level, by maximality. It cannot
contain an entry of level at least $j+2$, by the
last assertion of \cref{C-401-81}. That assertion
also limits its bilinear entries to three when
$j<j_*$. Walls of its board remain walls of the
finer boards, giving the distance statement.
Finally its diameter is at most $\sqrt3u_0<d$.
\end{proof}

\subsubsection{Summing the scales}

For $y\in T_\ell^n$, let $r_i(y)$ be the distance
to the third nearest other bilinear point when
$i\in I_B$, and to the fourth nearest bilinear
point when $i\in I_0$. Set $r_i=\infty$ if there
are too few points, and $m_i(y)=\min(u_0,r_i(y))$.
By \cref{C-401-81}, every final configuration with
nonzero pieces satisfies
\[
 m_i(y)\le\tfrac52A_nu_{j_i}\qquad
                           (y\in\prod_lQ_l).
\]

\begin{lemma}[Products of distances]\label{C-401-83}
For nonnegative exponents $\alpha_e$ on the unordered
pairs of $[m]$, suppose that, for every $W\subset[m]$
with $|W|\ge2$,
\[
 S(W):=\sum_{e\subset W}\alpha_e
                         \le3(|W|-1)-\theta,
 \qquad 0<\theta\le1.
\]
Put $\bar\alpha=\sum_e\alpha_e$. For $0<\sigma\le1$,
\[
 \int_{T_\ell^m}\prod_e
        \min(\sigma,|y_u-y_v|)^{-\alpha_e}\,dy
 \le I_m(\theta,\bar\alpha)\sigma^{-\bar\alpha}
                                      (1+\ell)^{3m},
\]
where, if $B_m$ is the number of partitions of $[m]$,
\[
 I_m(\theta,A)=2^A(5m^3)^m mB_m^m
                   \left(1+\sum_{H\ge1}H^m2^{-\theta(H-1)}\right).
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
At dyadic scale $\sigma2^{-h}$, connect points closer
than this distance and let $\mathcal P_h$ be the
partition into connected components. These partitions
refine and are eventually singletons outside a null
set. A block has diameter at most
$(|W|-1)\sigma2^{-h}$. If $h_e$ is the last level
where the endpoints of $e$ share a block, their
distance is at least $\sigma2^{-h_e-1}$. Set $h_e=-1$
if they already lie in different blocks of $\mathcal P_0$;
then their distance is at least $\sigma$, and $d_e=\sigma$.
Consequently the integrand is bounded by
\[
 2^{\bar\alpha}\sigma^{-\bar\alpha}
       2^{\sum_{h\ge1}\sum_{W\in\mathcal P_h}S(W)}.
\]

Fix a sequence of partitions. Represent each block
by its least element. When a block at level $h$
splits into $c_W$ children, its $c_W-1$ new
representatives lie in balls of radius
$(m-1)\sigma2^{-h}$ about the old representative.
Integrate the representatives of $\mathcal P_0$
over the torus and these new representatives over
their balls. The volume of the corresponding
configuration set is at most
\[
 (5m^3)^m(1+\ell)^{3m}
      2^{-3\sum_{h\ge1}\sum_{W\in\mathcal P_h}(|W|-1)}.
\]
Here $\sigma\le1$ and the telescoping identity
$\sum_hh(|\mathcal P_{h+1}|-|\mathcal P_h|)
=\sum_{h\ge1}(m-|\mathcal P_h|)$ were used.
Multiplication by the integrand leaves a factor
at most $2^{-\theta N}$, where $N$ counts the
positive levels whose partition is not discrete.

A strictly refining chain has at most $m$ distinct
partitions, and there are at most $mB_m^m$ such
chains. If its last change is at level $H$, there
are at most $H^m$ choices of the earlier change
levels and $N\ge H-1$. Summing proves the estimate.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[The sum over stopped configurations]\label{C-401-84}
Let $\mathfrak F$ be the final configurations with
nonzero pieces, $P\ge0$, and $b_B,b_0>0$. Then
\[
 \sum_{F\in\mathfrak F}
   \prod_{i\in I_B}b_Bu_{j_i}\ell_g(u_{j_i})^P
   \prod_{i\in I_0}b_0\ell_g(u_{j_i})^P
 \le b_B^{n_B}b_0^{n_0}J_n(P;g)u_0^{-4n}(1+\ell)^{3n},
\]
where $J_n(P;g)$ is finite and independent of the
cutoff and torus side.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For an entry put $g_i=1$ on $I_B$, $g_i=0$ on $I_0$,
and $\psi_i(j)=b_i u_j^{g_i}\ell_g(u_j)^P$.
Divide by $|Q_i|\ge8L^{-3p_n}u_{j_i}^3$ and integrate
over the cubes of a configuration. Using the preceding
bound on $m_i$ and the overlap count $27$, the whole
sum is at most $\int\prod_i\Phi_i(y)\,dy$, where
\[
 \Phi_i(y)=\frac{27}{8}L^{3p_n}
      \sum_{j:u_j\ge x_i}\psi_i(j)u_j^{-3},
 \qquad x_i=\frac{2m_i(y)}{5A_n}.
\]
Going to the next coarser scale decreases each
summand by at least $A_n^{-2}\le1/2$; also $\ell_g$
decreases. Thus
\[
 \Phi_i(y)\le\frac{27}{4}L^{3p_n}b_i
                           x_i^{g_i-3}\ell_g(x_i)^P
                \le b_i K_n(P;g)m_i(y)^{g_i-3-\epsilon},
 \qquad \epsilon=\frac1{8n}.
\]
One may take
\[
 K_n(P;g)=\frac{27}{4}L^{3p_n}(5A_n/2)^3
 (1+\log(5A_n/2))^P(1+\log(X_g+\bar B))^P C_{P,n},
\]
where $C_{P,n}=\sup_{t\ge0}(1+t)^Pe^{-t/(8n)}$.
This follows from
$\ell_g(u/c)\le(1+\log c)\ell_g(u)$ and
$\ell_g(u)\le(1+\log(X_g+\bar B))(1+\log(1/u))$.

First integrate the action-density coordinates with
the bilinear coordinates fixed. If $n_B<4$, all
$m_i=u_0$ and the result follows directly. Otherwise
bound $m_i^{-3-\epsilon}$ by the sum, over four-element
sets $T\subset I_B$, of
$\min(u_0,\max_{l\in T}|y_i-y_l|)^{-3-\epsilon}$.
Choose a diameter pair $e_T=\{u,v\}$ in $T$, of
distance $D_T$. The maximum is at least
$\max(|y_i-y_u|,D_T/2)$. Radial integration gives
\[
 \int_{T_\ell}m_i(y)^{-3-\epsilon}\,dy_i
 \le321n^4\left[\ell^3u_0^{-3-\epsilon}
            +\sum_{e\subset I_B}d_e^{-\epsilon}\right],
 \qquad d_e=\min(u_0,|y_u-y_v|).
\]
Indeed the radial bound for one set is
$\ell^3u_0^{-3-\epsilon}+(8\pi/3+8\pi/\epsilon)
d_{e_T}^{-\epsilon}$, and each pair belongs to at
most $n^2$ such four-element sets. Expanding the
product of the $n_0$ integrals gives at most
$(2n^2)^{n_0}$ terms. Each has a factor
$(\ell^3u_0^{-3-\epsilon})^a$ and $n_0-a$ pair
factors of exponent $\epsilon$.

For a bilinear coordinate, its three nearest
bilinear neighbours give
\[
 m_i^{-2-\epsilon}\le
 \sum_{N_i:\,|N_i|=3}\prod_{l\in N_i}
                         d_{\{i,l\}}^{-(2+\epsilon)/3}.
\]
There are at most $n^3$ choices at each coordinate.
In any resulting distance product, a subset of
$w\ge2$ bilinear indices carries total exponent
at most
\[
 \frac{2+\epsilon}{3}w\min(3,w-1)+n\epsilon.
\]
For $w=2$ this is at most $5/2$; for $w=3$ at most
$11/2$; and for $w\ge4$ at most
$2w+1/4\le3(w-1)-1/2$.
Thus \cref{C-401-83} applies with $\theta=1/2$.
The total exponent is at most $3n$, and including
the factors $u_0^{-(3+\epsilon)a}$ raises it to
at most $4n$. Collecting the finite choices gives
the assertion, for example with
\[
 J_n(P;g)=K_n(P;g)^n(642n^6)^n
                    \max_{1\le m\le n}I_m(1/2,3n).
\]
\end{proof}

\subsubsection{Proof of the mixed estimate}

\begin{proof}[Proof of \cref{C-401-85}]
If any entry is zero, the cumulant vanishes. If the cutoff is
coarse, $a^{-1}<2nLA_n/u_0$. At each configuration
the singular-value determinant estimate gives
\[
 |R_U(\textstyle\sum_{i\in I_B}z_if_i\lambda_i)|
 \le\exp\left(384N_f\mathsf m^{-1}
           \sum_{i\in I_B}|z_i|\|\lambda_i\|
                                      \sum_x|f_i(x)|\right).
\]
Combine this with
$|e^{O(w)}|\le\exp(2a^{-1}\sum_p|w(x(p))|)$.
There are $(\ell/a)^3$ sites and $3(\ell/a)^3$
plaquettes. Cauchy's estimate on the polydisc where
each exponent is at most one and the partition
formula therefore bound the cumulant by
\[
 C_n^{\rm c}(d)\ell^{3n}
         \prod_{i\in I_B}\|\lambda_i\|
         \prod_i\|f_i\|_{\lambda_i},
\]
where
\[
 C_n^{\rm c}(d)=2^nn!
 \left[e(6+384N_f/m_-)
       (2\sqrt3nL^2A_n(1+d^{-1}))^4\right]^n.
\]

For a fine cutoff use \cref{C-401-81,C-401-82}.
Call a maximal cell early if its level is less
than $j_*$, and final otherwise. In each early
cell apply \cref{C-401-77} to its at most three
bilinear labels. Multilinearity expands the
cumulant into terms in which all these labels
are mesons conjugated by one $S_\square$.
The sum of the absolute coefficients is at most
$c_{\rm lab}(N_f)^n$ times the product of the norms
of the labels in early cells. Keep the original
labels in final cells.

Fix one term in this expansion. For an entry in
a cell $\square$, put
\[
 \rho_i=
 \begin{cases}
 r_J/(2\lambda_{k(u_\square)}\|f_i\|_\infty),
                  &i\in I_B,\ \square\text{ early},\\
 r_J/(2\lambda_{k(u_{j_*})}\|\lambda_i\|\|f_i\|_\infty),
                  &i\in I_B,\ \square\text{ final},\\
 2\varrho/(C_\sharp\|f_i\|_\sharp),&i\in I_0.
 \end{cases}
\]
For $|z_i|<\rho_i$, the source in an early cell
belongs to $\mathcal P_{k(u_\square)}^\#$.
Disjoint supports make the source supremum norm
a maximum. The same is true of the sharp norm
for a sum of Lipschitz functions with disjoint
supports: on a segment joining distinct supports,
their two distances to their boundaries add to
at most the segment length. Thus the Lipschitz
constant is at most the largest one. The bound
in \cref{C-401-81} then gives the required sharp
norm bound $2\varrho$.

Subtract from the logarithm of the generating
function the sum $\Lambda(z)$ of the early-cell
energies $\lambda_{k(u_\square)}^{\mathfrak b}$.
It is holomorphic on this polydisc. Its derivative
in all $n$ variables vanishes, since every cell
has diameter less than $d$ and therefore cannot
contain both distinguished separated entries.
Let $F(z)$ be the normalized generating function
multiplied by $e^{-\Lambda(z)}$, so $F(0)=1$.

Apply the ordinary chessboard inequality on
$\mathbb B_0$, then \cref{C-401-78} whenever a cell
is replaced by finer cells. This ends at the
maximal cells. In an early cell apply
\cref{C-401-79} with
$\delta=v_{j+1}=u_\square/(A_nL^{p_n})$.
In a final cell the matrix source has norm at
most $r_J/(2\lambda_{k(u_{j_*})})$. Its
action-density source satisfies
$|w|\le\varrho u_{j_*}$: use the vanishing estimate
in \cref{C-401-81}, $j_*=j_i\ge1$,
$40M\operatorname{Lip}f_i\le\|f_i\|_\sharp$, and
$C_\sharp\ge5A_n$. Hence \cref{C-401-80} applies.
It follows, on a coordinate face indexed by $B$, that
\[
 |F(z)|\le\prod_{\square:\square\text{ contains an entry of }B}
                         e^{K_\square},
\]
where
\[
 K_\square=c_V+c_A+p_A\log\ell_g(u_\square)
       \quad\hbox{in an early cell},\qquad
 K_\square=c_V+c_L+p_L\log\ell_g(u_{j_*})
       \quad\hbox{in a final cell}.
\]
All these numbers are nonnegative. Their constants
are given below. The final-cell bound uses
$u_{j_*}/a<2nLA_n$ and
\[
 k(u_{j_*})\le1+\log_L(2nLA_n/\sigma_0(g))
                   +\frac{\log\ell_g(u_{j_*})}{3\log L}.
\]

Cauchy's estimate bounds $\partial_BF(0)$ by
the same product times $\prod_{i\in B}\rho_i^{-1}$.
In a partition of $[n]$, a cell containing
$n_\square$ entries occurs in at most $n_\square$
blocks. Thus the partition formula and the
vanishing derivative of $\Lambda$ give
\[
 |S_n^T(\mathcal X_{F,r})|
        \le2^nn!\prod_i e^{K_{\square(i)}}\rho_i^{-1}.
\]
Now $u_{j_i}\le u_{\square(i)}\le A_nu_{j_i}$,
and \eqref{eq:qcd2-mixed-level} shows that each
bilinear factor on the right is at most
\[
 b_Bu_{j_i}\ell_g(u_{j_i})^P\|f_i\|_\infty,
 \quad b_B=\frac{2LA_ne^{c_V+c_*}}{r_J\sigma_0(g)},
\]
with an additional $\|\lambda_i\|$ in a final cell.
Each action-density factor is at most
$b_0\ell_g(u_{j_i})^P\|f_i\|_\sharp$, where
$b_0=C_\sharp e^{c_V+c_*}/(2\varrho)$,
$c_* =\max(c_A,c_L)$ and $P=\max(p_A,p_L)+1/3$.

Sum the tensor coefficients and the stopped
configurations, using \cref{C-401-84}. This gives
the theorem with the larger of $C_n^{\rm c}(d)$ and
\[
 C_n^{\rm f}(d;g)=2^nn!c_{\rm lab}(N_f)^n
 \max(b_B,b_0,1)^nJ_n(P;g)
                    (\sqrt3L(1+d^{-1}))^{4n}.
\]
The constants used above can be taken to be
\begin{align*}
 c_A={}&C_{\mathscr C}^\flat[1+(A_nL^{p_n})^3]
 +64C_{\mathscr C}(1+\sqrt3A_nL^{p_n})^3
                 [2+\log_L(A_nL^{p_n}/\sigma_0(g))],\\
 p_A={}&64C_{\mathscr C}(1+\sqrt3A_nL^{p_n})^3/(3\log L),\\
 c_L={}&6\varrho(2nLA_n)^4+192N_f\log2\,(2nLA_n)^3\\
 &+27C_{\mathfrak E}C_{\rm cnt}C_{\rm sh}
       [256(1+\log_L(2nLA_n/\sigma_0(g)))+1536(2nLA_n)^3],\\
 p_L={}&256\cdot27C_{\mathfrak E}C_{\rm cnt}C_{\rm sh}/(3\log L).
\end{align*}
They are formed after the existing source constants
and impose no further restriction on them.
The alternative volume factor follows from
$(1+\ell)^3\le4e^{\ell^3}\le4e^{c_V\ell^3}$.
At fixed $\ell$, every bound is uniform in the
cutoff and passes to a convergent subsequence.
\end{proof}


\begin{proposition}[The enlarged limits]\label{C-401-49}
Let $S$ be a volume-first limit of \cite{QCDM1}, with a
fixed defining sequence. There is a subsequence along
which all extended truncated functions of orders $n\ge2$ converge on
pairwise disjoint $C_c^1$ supports. Their limits
$S^{\mathrm{ext}}$ restrict to $S$ on meson tuples and
satisfy \eqref{eq:qcd2-extended-bound}.

They are symmetric, translation invariant, invariant
under simultaneous conjugation of the labels by
$G_{\mathbb C}$.
At fixed labels, these truncated functions determine
distributions of locally finite order away from the diagonals.
The centered functional $\sigma^{\mathrm{ext}}$, obtained
by the moment--cumulant formula with one-point functions
zero, is reflection positive at every coordinate plane,
with the involution $M\mapsto M^*$. It defines a separable reflection Hilbert space
$\mathcal H^{\mathrm{ext}}$. Time translation gives a
strongly continuous self-adjoint contraction semigroup
$e^{-tH}$, $H\ge0$; spatial translations give a strongly
continuous unitary representation with generators
$P_1,P_2$ commuting strongly with $H$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Fix finitely many pairwise disjoint closed supports,
each in a bounded ball. The uniform bound makes the
truncated functions equicontinuous in the product of
the indicated norms. Enumerate rational unions of
closed cubes, a countable dense family of $C_c^1$
functions on these supports, and the finite label
basis. A diagonal subsequence makes every corresponding
truncated function converge. Equicontinuity extends
the convergence to every tuple, and multilinearity
extends the labels to $\mathscr S$. The original
meson functions converge along the given defining
sequence, so their limits remain $S$.

Symmetry and $G_{\mathbb C}$-invariance are exact at
every cutoff. They pass to the limit. Lattice
translations approximate every real translation;
the estimate and translation continuity in $C^1$
give translation invariance. For a positive-side
tuple, replace each field by its lattice field minus
its expectation. The reflection sends this centered
field to the centered field with label $M^*$ and
reflected conjugate test function. Every reflection
form is therefore the finite sum of products of
truncated functions specified by the centered
moment--cumulant formula. Approximate a coordinate
plane by bond planes. The supports stay a positive
distance from the planes, and the reflected test
functions converge in their insertion norms. Lattice
reflection positivity and the bound pass the form
inequality to the limit.

On a product of open sets with disjoint closures,
the bound makes the limiting truncated functional continuous in
the $C^1$ norms. The Schwartz kernel theorem gives
a distribution there. Uniqueness makes these local
distributions agree on intersections, so they define
one distribution off the diagonals.

On finite linear combinations of positive-time tuples,
define the positive semidefinite form by
\[
 \langle\mathcal X,\mathcal Y\rangle
    =\sigma^{\mathrm{ext}}(\theta_3\mathcal X^*\cdot\mathcal Y).
\]
We first check that time translation descends to its quotient.
Write $T_t\mathcal X=\tau_{te_3}\mathcal X$, $t\ge0$.
Translation invariance and $\theta_3\tau_{te_3}
=\tau_{-te_3}\theta_3$ give
\[
 \langle T_sv,T_tv\rangle=\langle v,T_{s+t}v\rangle,
 \qquad \|T_tv\|^2=\langle v,T_{2t}v\rangle.
\]
For a fixed $v$, these correlations are bounded uniformly
for $s,t\ge0$. Indeed, each is a finite sum of products of
truncated correlations; the support radii stay fixed, the
separations within each tuple stay fixed, and the reflected
tuple stays a positive distance from the translated tuple.

Fix $t>0$ and put $a_k=\|T_{kt}v\|^2$. Cauchy--Schwarz
for the semidefinite form gives
\[
 a_k^2=|\langle T_{(k-1)t}v,T_{(k+1)t}v\rangle|^2
                 \le a_{k-1}a_{k+1}\qquad(k\ge1).
\]
If $a_0=0$, this implies $a_1=0$. If $a_0>0$ and
$a_1>a_0$, all subsequent terms are positive and the
ratios $a_{k+1}/a_k$ are nondecreasing. They are then
bounded below by $a_1/a_0>1$, contrary to boundedness.
Thus $\|T_tv\|\le\|v\|$. In particular null vectors
remain null, so $T_t$ defines a contraction on the quotient
and its completion $\mathcal H^{\mathrm{ext}}$.
The empty tuple gives the unit vector $\Omega$.

Translation is symmetric for the form, so each bounded
operator $T_t$ is self-adjoint. The semigroup law is the
translation law on tuples. In particular
\[
 \langle v,T_tv\rangle=\|T_{t/2}v\|^2\ge0.
\]
This is also the reflection form at the intervening plane.
For a vector represented by finitely many tuples,
\[
 \|T_tv-v\|^2
 =\langle v,T_{2t}v\rangle
       -2\operatorname{Re}\langle v,T_tv\rangle+\|v\|^2
       \longrightarrow0
       \quad(t\downarrow0),
\]
by continuity in the translated test functions. Contraction
extends strong continuity to the completion. The spectral
theorem for a strongly continuous self-adjoint contraction
semigroup now gives $T_t=e^{-tH}$ with $H\ge0$.

Spatial translations preserve the form and have
inverses. They extend to strongly continuous unitary
operators, and their commutation with the semigroup
on tuples gives strong commutation of the generators.
For separability, use the positive-time members of the
countable family used for extraction, and take finite
linear combinations with rational real and imaginary
coefficients. Any positive-time tuple can be approximated
by such tuples with supports in fixed closed sets that
remain separated and stay away from the reflection plane.
Its squared reflection-norm error is a finite combination
of moments, each a polynomial in continuous truncated
functions. The error therefore tends to zero, proving
density of this countable set.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[The internal group on the enlarged space]
\label{C-401-46}
The map $[X]\mapsto[X]$ embeds the mesonic space
$\mathcal H(S)$ isometrically into $\mathcal H^{\mathrm{ext}}$
and intertwines time and spatial translations. Moreover
\[
 V(S)[\mathcal X]=[S\mathcal X S^{-1}],\qquad S\in G,
\]
is a strongly continuous unitary representation. It fixes
$\Omega$, commutes with $H,P_1,P_2$, and is trivial on
$(-1,-1)$. Let $\Sigma_3$ be $1$ on the $\psi$ components
and $-1$ on the $\chi$ components. The generator $Q$ defined by
\[
 V(e^{i\varphi\Sigma_3},e^{i\varphi\Sigma_3})=e^{-i\varphi Q}
\]
has spectrum in $2\mathbb Z$. The mesonic space lies in
$\ker Q$, and both eigenspaces $Q=2$ and $Q=-2$ are
nonzero. Charge conjugation $V(J,J)$ exchanges them.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The two centered functionals agree on meson tuples,
so the displayed embedding preserves inner products.
Both translations act on the functions and are
therefore intertwined. For $S\in G$,
$(SMS^{-1})^*=SM^*S^{-1}$. Invariance of
$\sigma^{\mathrm{ext}}$ proves that $V(S)$ preserves
the form and its null space. Its inverse is $V(S^{-1})$.
For a fixed tuple the orbit lies in a finite-dimensional
span of label tuples and depends continuously on $S$;
this proves strong continuity. The stated commutations
hold on tuples and hence on the completion.

The central element $(-1,-1)$ is the identity on all
quadratic labels. Setting $\varphi=\pi$ therefore
gives $e^{-i\pi Q}=1$, so the spectral theorem places
the spectrum of $Q$ in $2\mathbb Z$. Every meson
is neutral, and the mesonic space lies in its kernel.

To see that the charge-two space is nonzero, choose
the meson $N_f^{-1/2}\sum_f\bar\psi_{+,f}\psi_{-,f}$.
Its matrix is $\tau_+\otimes t_1$,
$\tau_+=(\tau_1+i\tau_2)/2$, a linear combination of
$\Gamma_{1,1}$ and $\Gamma_{2,1}$.
The leading two-point formula of
\cite[Prop. 11.1]{QCDM1}
has a positive definite leading coefficient on this
two-dimensional span. At a pair of reflected small
positive test functions its relative error tends to
zero as their scale tends to zero. Thus the associated
one-field vector has positive norm. The element of
$G$ equal to $J\otimes1$ on the plus half
and to the identity on the minus half sends this
meson to a nonzero multiple of
$\sum_f\psi_{+,f}^{\mathsf T}C_0^{-1}\psi_{-,f}$.
Its image under $V(S)$ has the same positive norm
and charge two. Finally $J\Sigma_3J^{-1}=-\Sigma_3$,
so $V(J,J)QV(J,J)^{-1}=-Q$. This gives the nonzero
charge-minus-two space as well.
\end{proof}

\section{Energy in the charged sectors}
\label{sec:qcd2-charged-energy}

The estimate needed in the continuum has constant one.
A direct propagator estimate initially gives a constant
depending on the cutoff. Reflection positivity removes
that constant before the cutoff is taken to zero.

\subsection{A sharp decay rate on the chamber lattice}

In this subsection lattice spacing is one. Let
\[
 L_\rho=\frac12\sum_{s=1}^3t_s(1-\widehat R_s)
                      \quad\hbox{on }\ell^2(W_3),
 \qquad E=\{g:ge_1=\pm e_3\},
\]
where $\widehat R_s$ is right multiplication by the
within-site chamber reflection $w_s$. The kernel of
$L_\rho$ consists of the constants; let $\lambda_\rho>0$
be its first positive eigenvalue. These are the
within-site operator and its gap used in
\cite[Section 5]{QCDM1}.
There are $16$ elements in $E$ and $48$ in $W_3$.
Define
\begin{equation}\label{C-400-3}
 \begin{split}
 h(k)&=-\lambda_{\min}(L_\rho-k1_E),\qquad
 k(\alpha)=\tfrac32(\cosh\alpha-1)+3\sinh\alpha,\\
 e(\alpha)&=h(k(\alpha)),\quad
 0\le\alpha\le\operatorname{artanh}(1/2),\qquad
 \mu(m_0)=\sup\{\alpha:e(\alpha)<m_0\}.
 \end{split}
\end{equation}

\begin{lemma}[Directional decay]\label{C-400-11}\label{C-400-12}
If $\varphi(v)=\phi((x_v)_3)$ is real and bounded, with increments of modulus
at most $\alpha\le\operatorname{artanh}(1/2)$, then
\[
 \operatorname{Re}(e^\varphi D_Ue^{-\varphi})
                                      \ge m_0-e(\alpha).
\]
If two sets of sites $A,B$ are at separation at least
$d$ in their third coordinates, then, for
$0\le\alpha<\mu(m_0)$,
\[
 \|1_AD_U^{-1}1_B\|
       \le(m_0-e(\alpha))^{-1}e^{-\alpha d}.
\]
The estimates are uniform in $U$. Moreover
$\mu(x)/x\to1$ as $x\downarrow0$, and consequently
$a^{-1}\mu(a\mathsf m)\to\mathsf m$ uniformly for
$\mathsf m$ in compact subsets of $(0,\infty)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Write $R_sf(v)=U(v,v\cdot s)f(v\cdot s)$. This is a
self-adjoint unitary involution. Conjugation changes
the coefficient of the $s$th hop to
$t_s(\tfrac12-\gamma(u_s(v)))e^{-w_s(v)}$, where
$w_s(v)=\varphi(v\cdot s)-\varphi(v)$ and
$w_s(v\cdot s)=-w_s(v)$. Its Hermitian part is
$B_sR_s$, with
\[
 B_s(v)=t_s\bigl(\tfrac12\cosh w_s(v)
                         +\gamma(u_s(v))\sinh w_s(v)\bigr).
\]
The matrix $B_s$ commutes with $R_s$. For $s=1,2,3$,
$w_s=0$, since the hop stays at the same site.
For $s=0$, it vanishes outside $E$. Its two eigenvalues
are $3(\frac12\cosh w\pm\sinh w)$, nonnegative in
the stated interval. Hence
\[
 \operatorname{Re}(e^\varphi D_Ue^{-\varphi})
 =m_0+L_\rho+(\tfrac32-B_0)+B_0(1-R_0)
 \ge m_0+L_\rho-k(\alpha)1_E.
\]
This proves the first estimate.

Choose $\phi(s)=\alpha\min\{\operatorname{dist}(s,B_3),d\}$,
where $B_3$ is the set of third coordinates of $B$.
The weight is zero on $B$ and $\alpha d$ on $A$.
The first estimate makes the conjugated inverse
bounded by $(m_0-e(\alpha))^{-1}$, proving decay.

Let $u$ be the constant unit vector in $\ell^2(W_3)$.
There are $16$ moving chambers among the $48$ chambers,
so $\langle u,1_Eu\rangle=16/48=1/3$. Moreover
\[
 \|(1-|u\rangle\langle u|)1_Eu\|^2
       =\langle u,1_Eu\rangle-|\langle u,1_Eu\rangle|^2
       =\tfrac13-\tfrac19=\tfrac29.
\]
Writing a vector as $cu+v$, $v\perp u$, and using
$L_\rho\ge\lambda_\rho$ on $u^\perp$, gives, for
$0\le k<3\lambda_\rho/2$,
\[
 \frac{k}{3}\le h(k)\le
        \frac{k}{3}+\frac{2k^2}{9\lambda_\rho-6k}.
\]
Indeed the lower bound uses the trial vector $u$.
For the upper bound the quadratic form is bounded
below by $-(k/3+\delta)\|(c,v)\|^2$ when
\[
 \begin{pmatrix}
 \delta&-\sqrt2k/3\\
 -\sqrt2k/3&\lambda_\rho-2k/3+\delta
 \end{pmatrix}\ge0;
 \qquad\delta=\frac{2k^2}{9\lambda_\rho-6k}
\]
satisfies this condition. Since $k(\alpha)=3\alpha+O(\alpha^2)$,
we have $e(\alpha)=\alpha+O(\alpha^2)$.
Inversion at zero gives $\mu(x)=x+O(x^2)$ and the
claimed uniform limit.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Reflection positivity fixes the prefactor]
\label{C-400-17}
Let $T$ be symmetric on a vector space with a positive
semidefinite Hermitian form. If
$\langle v,T^{2k}v\rangle\le C\lambda^{2k}$ for all
$k\ge0$, where $0<\lambda\le1$, then
\[
 \langle v,T^{2k}v\rangle\le\lambda^{2k}\langle v,v\rangle,
 \qquad |\langle v,T^kv\rangle|
                   \le\lambda^k\langle v,v\rangle.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Put $a_k=\langle T^kv,T^kv\rangle$. Cauchy--Schwarz
gives $a_k^2\le a_{k-1}a_{k+1}$. If one $a_k$ with
$k\ge1$ vanishes, this inequality forces all such
$a_k$ to vanish. Otherwise the ratios $a_{k+1}/a_k$
are nondecreasing. A ratio larger than $\lambda^2$
would contradict $a_k\le C\lambda^{2k}$ at large
$k$. Thus $a_k\le\lambda^{2k}a_0$. A final
Cauchy--Schwarz inequality gives the second assertion.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[The lattice charged estimate]\label{C-400-6}
Fix $m_0>0$ and an infinite-volume torus-limit state
$\omega_\nu$. Let $\Theta$ be reflection in $x_3=1/2$
and let $\tau$ be translation by $e_3$. For an even
local element $F$ supported in $x_3\ge1$, form its
reflection class $[F]$. Translation induces a positive
self-adjoint contraction $T$ on the resulting Hilbert
space.

Let $\mathcal F=\{+,-\}\times\{1,\ldots,N_f\}$.
The weight of a monomial is
$n_f=\#\psi_f-\#\bar\psi_f$ and
$|n|_1=\sum_f|n_f|$. If $F$ has weight $n$, then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:qcd2-lattice-charged}
 0\le\omega_\nu(\tau^kF\,\Theta F)
       \le e^{-\mu(m_0)|n|_1k}\,
                           \omega_\nu(F\,\Theta F),\qquad k\ge0.
\end{equation}
If the conditional Gaussian expectation
$h_F(U)=\langle F\rangle_U$ vanishes at every $U$,
the same estimate holds with $2$ in place of $|n|_1$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The fixed-spacing states of \cite{QCDM1} are translation
invariant and reflection positive at coordinate planes
through sites and through links. Thus the form
$\langle[G],[F]\rangle=\omega_\nu(F\Theta G)$ is
positive, and $\Theta\tau=\tau^{-1}\Theta$ makes
translation symmetric. Wick's determinant formula
and $\|D_U^{-1}\|\le m_0^{-1}$ bound
$|\omega_\nu(\tau^kF\Theta F)|$ uniformly in $k$,
with a constant depending on $F,m_0$. Apply
\cref{C-400-17} with $\lambda=1$ to obtain a
contraction on the quotient. Positivity follows
from reflection through $x_3=1$, since
$\Theta F=\Theta_1(\tau F)$ and
$\omega_\nu(\tau F\Theta_1\tau F)\ge0$.

For clarity, consider a pair of monomials of total
degree $2p$. Wick's formula is a sum of at most $p!$
products of $p$ propagators. A propagator pairs only
a quark with an antiquark of the same species.
If the monomial on the positive side has weight $n$,
let $c_f^+$ and $c_f^-$ count its quarks and antiquarks
of species $f$ that are paired across the separation.
Each pairing confined to this side removes one quark
and one antiquark of the same species. Therefore
\[
 c_f^+-c_f^-=n_f,\qquad c_f^++c_f^-\ge|n_f|.
\]
Summing over species shows that at least $|n|_1$
propagators cross. Between the supports of
$\Theta F$ and $\tau^{2k}F$, their separation in
the third coordinate is at least $2k+1$.
By \cref{C-400-11}, for every $\alpha<\mu(m_0)$,
\[
 \omega_\nu(\tau^{2k}F\Theta F)
       \le C(F,\alpha)e^{-\alpha|n|_1(2k+1)}.
\]
The finite sum over the monomials only changes
$C(F,\alpha)$. Applying \cref{C-400-17} removes
this constant. Let $\alpha\uparrow\mu(m_0)$ to
obtain \eqref{eq:qcd2-lattice-charged}. This removal is
performed at each fixed cutoff. The preliminary constant
may depend on the cutoff; the final estimate depends
on $F$ only through its squared reflection norm, which
can subsequently pass to the continuum limit.

For the last assertion subtract the product of the
two conditional Gaussian expectations in Wick's
formula. The permutations preserving both sets
of factors cancel. Every remaining permutation
crosses the separation at least twice: if each
monomial is neutral, one crossing in each direction
is required; otherwise its even nonzero charge
already requires at least two crossings. Since
$h_F=0$, the subtracted product vanishes. This gives
$C(F,\alpha)e^{-2\alpha(2k+1)}$ and the same
argument proves the asserted bound.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Passing the estimate to the enlarged limit}

Let $\mathcal H_n^{\mathrm{ext}}$ be the closed span
of positive-time tuples of total weight $n$. A
quadratic label has quark number $0$ or $\pm2$,
and every label is a sum of weight vectors.
For an irreducible representation $\pi$ of $G$,
write $|\pi|$ for the largest $\ell^1$ norm of
one of its maximal-torus weights. This is the
$\ell^1$ norm of its highest weight: the weights
lie in the convex hull of its signed-permutation
Weyl orbit.

The three estimates below distinguish three notions of
charge. The weight $n=(n_f)_{f\in\mathcal F}$ records,
for each species, the number of $\psi_f$ factors minus
the number of $\bar\psi_f$ factors. On its weight space,
the maximal torus acts by $V(z)v=z^{-n}v$. Taking every
phase equal gives the quark number
\[
 q=\sum_{f\in\mathcal F}n_f,\qquad
 \{Q=q\}=\mathop{\bigoplus}_{\sum_fn_f=q}
                              \mathcal H_n^{\mathrm{ext}}.
\]
Thus quark number retains only the sum of the species
charges. A meson $\bar\psi_{+,f}\psi_{-,f}$ has quark
number zero but weight of $\ell^1$ norm two. The weight
estimate below therefore gives a positive lower bound
on such weight spaces within the quark-number-zero sector.

The $\pi$-isotypic space is the closed span of all
copies of the irreducible representation $\pi$.
It contains the whole multiplet, and may include
vectors of weight zero. Since $H$ commutes with $G$,
a spectral subspace of $H$ in this space contains
whole copies of $\pi$. Applying the weight estimate
to a highest-weight vector therefore bounds the
energy throughout the multiplet. This is stronger
than applying the weight estimate separately to its
zero-weight vectors.


\begin{theorem}[Energy and internal charges]\label{C-400-34}
Let $S^{\mathrm{ext}}$ be an extended volume-first
limit and let $\mathsf m$ be a limit point of the
rescaled mass parameters
$\mathsf m_j=a_j^{-1}m_{0,j}\in[m_-,m_+]$
along its defining sequence.
Then
\[
 H|_{\mathcal H_n^{\mathrm{ext}}}\ge|n|_1\mathsf m,
 \qquad
 H|_{\mathcal H_\pi^{\mathrm{ext}}}\ge|\pi|\mathsf m,
 \qquad
 H|_{\{Q=q\}}\ge|q|\mathsf m.
\]
Only even $|n|_1$ and even quark numbers occur.
Every nontrivial representation that occurs has
$|\pi|\ge2$. In particular,
\[
 H\ge2\mathsf m\quad\hbox{on }\bigl((\mathcal H^{\mathrm{ext}})^G\bigr)^\perp,
 \qquad \ker H\subset(\mathcal H^{\mathrm{ext}})^G.
\]
The spectral projection onto $\ker H$ vanishes on
every nonzero-weight space. The charge-two and
charge-minus-two spaces are nonzero.
\end{theorem}

The gap $2\mathsf m$ here is on the complement of the
$G$-invariant vectors. In the invariant sector these
estimates give only $H\ge0$. Since the vacuum vector
is invariant and has energy zero, the conclusion is
\[
 \mathbb C\Omega\subset\ker H
                     \subset(\mathcal H^{\mathrm{ext}})^G.
\]
Neither uniqueness of the vacuum nor a positive gap
above it within the invariant sector follows from
this theorem.


\begin{proof}
Pass to a subsequence with $\mathsf m_j\to\mathsf m$.
For a finite combination of positive-time tuples
$\mathcal X=\sum_i\zeta_i\mathcal X_i$, with
$\mathcal X_i=((\lambda_{ir},f_{ir}))_r$, put
\[
 F_j=\sum_i\zeta_i\prod_r
     \left(\Phi_j[\lambda_{ir}](f_{ir})
                 -\omega_{\nu_j}(\Phi_j[\lambda_{ir}](f_{ir}))\right).
\]
Here $\Phi_j[0](f)$ means the action-density insertion.
The moment--cumulant formula expresses the correlations
of these centered polynomials using only blocks of at
least two insertions. Thus only the truncated functions
already known to converge occur; convergence of the
individual one-point functions is unnecessary.
If $\mathcal X$ has weight $n$, then $F_j$ has
weight $n$: the mean of a nonzero-weight field
vanishes by the torus symmetry, and subtraction
does not change a zero weight.

For large $j$ the support lies above the bond plane
$x_3=a_j/2$. Fix $t$ in $\bigcup_kL^{-k}\mathbb N$.
Then $t/a_j$ is an integer for all large $j$, and
\cref{C-400-6} gives
\[
 \omega_{\nu_j}(\tau^{t/a_j}F_j\Theta_{a_j/2}F_j)
 \le e^{-|n|_1t\mu(a_j\mathsf m_j)/a_j}
                 \omega_{\nu_j}(F_j\Theta_{a_j/2}F_j).
\]
Reflection in $a_j/2$ differs from reflection in zero
by a translation of size $a_j$. For $C_c^1$ functions
that translation tends to the identity in both
$\|\cdot\|_\infty$ and $\|\cdot\|_\sharp$;
in the latter case use uniform continuity of the
gradient. The supports remain separated. Hence
\eqref{eq:qcd2-extended-bound}, multilinearity and
the moment--cumulant formula let both sides pass
to the limit. The limiting rate is $\mathsf m$
by \cref{C-400-11}, and
\[
 \langle[\mathcal X],e^{-tH}[\mathcal X]\rangle
       \le e^{-|n|_1\mathsf mt}\|[\mathcal X]\|^2.
\]
Strong continuity extends this from the dense set
of times to all $t\ge0$.

The maximal-torus projections
$\int z^nV(z)\,dz$ have ranges
$\mathcal H_n^{\mathrm{ext}}$; they are orthogonal,
sum to the identity and commute with $H$.
The Laplace transform inequality forces the
spectral measure of $H$ on each such space to
be supported in $[|n|_1\mathsf m,\infty)$.
Indeed positive mass on $[0,c]$ with
$c<|n|_1\mathsf m$ would contradict the inequality
as $t\to\infty$.

Every spectral projection of $H$ commutes with $G$.
If the isotypic subspace of $\pi$ had a nonzero
spectral part below $|\pi|\mathsf m$, that part
would contain a copy of $\pi$, hence a vector of
its highest weight. This contradicts the weight
estimate. An even monomial has
$|n|_1\equiv\sum_fn_f\equiv0\pmod2$.
The highest weight of any occurring representation
is an occurring weight, so its norm is even and
is at least two unless the representation is
trivial. Compact-group decomposition proves the
estimate on the complement of the invariant
vectors. The charge estimate follows by summing
weight spaces and using $|n|_1\ge|\sum_fn_f|$.
The conclusions about the kernel follow from
