We isolate the terms of second order which remain after
subtracting the two vacuum energies. The expansion uses
five parameters: the gauge fluctuation, the old fermion
terms, the gauge potential, the mass term, and the
difference of the old scalar terms. Their respective
weights are $1,2,1,2,1$.

\begin{lemma}[The deformed potential]\label{C-416-11}
Use the restarted flows of \cref{C-416-9} at a level
$t\le k<t'$ and $|\zeta|\le\rho'$. All expressions in
this lemma are evaluated at the trivial background on
the infinite lattice. Write
\[
 \mathbf N_\natural^{{\rm F},(j)}
       =\mathbf N^{{\rm F},(j)}-\mathbf c_j^{\rm F},\qquad
 \Delta^{(j)}=(\mathbf G^{(j)}-\mathbf G^{{\rm W},(j)})
                         +(F_0^{(j)}-F_0^{{\rm W},(j)}),
\]
where $\mathbf c_j^{\rm F}$ is $b_j^F$ times the
level-$j$ action. Then
$E_0^{(j)}=E_0^{{\rm W},(j)}+
\mathbf N_\natural^{{\rm F},(j)}+\Delta^{(j)}$.
Let $\mathcal V^{\rm N}$ and $\mathcal V^\delta$ be the
variations of the last two families from the background
$\mathsf U$ to the field $\mathsf U'(B)$ of the step.
Let $\mathcal V_x^{0,\rm W}$ be the gauge potential at
$(\mathsf t_k,x)$ plus the variations of the old gauge
activities. Define
\begin{align*}
 \mathcal V(z)={}&z_3\mathcal V_{x'_k}^{0,\rm W}(B)
       +\mathcal V^{\rm N}(z_1B)+z_5\mathcal V^\delta(z_1B)\\
       &+\mathcal V_k^{\rm F}(z_1B)
        +z_2\mathcal V^{\rm old}_{\ge2}(z_1B)
        +z_4\mathcal V^s(z_1B),\qquad z\in\mathbb C^5.
\end{align*}
The remaining arguments are the fermion variables of
the step. At $z=(1,1,1,1,1)$ this is its full potential.

Put $c'_\diamond=c_{\rm cl}/6$ and $\delta_k=\delta(\mathsf t_k)$.
Choose
\[
 r'_1=\min\left\{
 \frac{c'_\diamond}{C_Vh_F^2\mathsf C_{\mathcal A}\delta_k},
 \frac{\beta_0}{2\mathsf C_{\mathcal A}\delta_k},
 \frac{c'_{\diamond}a_{\rm an}}{c_hK_{\rm old}\mathsf C_{\mathcal A}\delta_k},
 \frac{\mathsf s^\star\alpha_0}{(1+\beta_s)\delta_k},
 \frac{\varepsilon_{\mathfrak h}}{\mathsf C_{\mathcal A}\delta_k},
 \frac{\min\{1,\delta(\gamma^{-2})\}}{\delta_k}\right\}.
\]
The radii $r'_2,r'_3,r'_4$ are the old-fermion, gauge
and mass radii of the second-order step expansion in
\cite[\S8]{QCDM1}, with $c'_\diamond$ in place of its
cluster allowance. Set
\[
 C_\Delta=3K_\Lambda\mathsf C_{\mathcal A}\mathsf s^\star C_w
                      +4(2\bar B+9)/\sigma_\star,
 \qquad r'_5=\frac{c'_\diamond}{C_\Delta\phi(\mathsf t_k)}.
\]
There is a constant $C_{\rm pd}$, formed from the
displayed constants, such that
\[
 (r'_i)^{-1}\le C_{\rm pd}\phi(\mathsf t_k)^{w_i},
 \qquad w=(1,2,1,2,1).
\]
Assume $C_{\rm pd}\phi(\mathsf t_k)\le1/2$.
Then $r'_i\ge2$. On $|z_i|\le r'_i$, the scalar and
fermion parts of the potential each have norm at most
$3c'_\diamond$. The vacuum density $\hat e(z)$ of its
cluster expansion is holomorphic and its Taylor
coefficients satisfy
\[
 |\hat e_n|\le2K_Mc_{\rm cl}\prod_i(r'_i)^{-n_i}.
\]
Write $\hat e_k^{\rm W}(x)$ for the gauge cluster density
and $\mathsf e_k^{\rm t}(x)$ for the test contribution.
With $g_k$ as in \cref{C-416-10},
\begin{align*}
 e_{k+1}(\zeta)-e_{k+1}^{\rm W}(\zeta)
 ={}&e_{k+1}^{\rm F,0}+g_k(x'_k)-g_k(x_k^{\rm W})
       +\mathsf e_k^{\rm t}(x'_k)-\mathsf e_k^{\rm t}(x_k^{\rm W})\\
   &+\hat e(1,1,1,1,1)-\hat e_k^{\rm W}(x_k^{\rm W}),
 \qquad \hat e(0,0,1,0,0)=\hat e_k^{\rm W}(x'_k).
\end{align*}
Here and below $x_k^{\rm W}=x_k^{\rm W}(\zeta)$ when
the argument is omitted. The coefficients $\hat e_n$
vanish if $n_1=0,n_5\ge1$, and also for
$n=e_1,e_1+e_5,e_1+e_3$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The identities for the scalar arrays follow by separating
the fermion normalization and its extracted action term.
The remaining gauge normalization and extraction terms
are formed at the calibrations and agree in the two flows.
The potential identity follows from the exact step.

The radius bounds use
$\delta_k\le A_1\phi(\mathsf t_k)$,
\[
 \sum_{j\le k}C_7L^{(k+1-j)/4}\epsilon_j^\psi
            \le C_7C_2S_\omega\phi(\mathsf t_k)^2,
 \qquad |s'_k|\le2\bar B_M\phi(\mathsf t_k)^2.
\]
Thus $C_{\rm pd}$ can be taken as the maximum of one
and the coefficients obtained by substituting these
three bounds into the inverse radii. It depends only
on the constants up to $\gamma$.
The first, second, third and fourth usual vertices are
bounded by $c'_\diamond$ on these discs, just as in the
second-order expansion of \cite[\S8]{QCDM1}.

For the two additional scalar variations, put
$\delta_\flat=\max\{1,|z_1|\}\delta_k$.
The last radius condition gives
$\delta_\flat\le\min\{1,\delta(\gamma^{-2})\}$.
Since $\delta$ decreases continuously to zero, choose
$\mathsf t_\flat\in[\gamma^{-2},\mathsf t_k]$ with
$\delta(\mathsf t_\flat)=\delta_\flat$.
The background-variation estimate of the step applies
there: the fourth and fifth radius conditions give
\[
 (1+\beta_s)\delta(\mathsf t_\flat)/\alpha_0
                \le\mathsf s^\star,
 \qquad \mathsf C_{\mathcal A}\delta(\mathsf t_\flat)
                \le\varepsilon_{\mathfrak h}.
\]
The other geometric conditions hold at every
$\mathsf t_\flat\ge\gamma^{-2}$.
For the explicit normalization families this estimate
is $\mathsf s_a(\mathsf t_\flat)K_{\rm old}$, where
$\mathsf s_a(x)=c_h\delta(x)/a_{\rm an}$.
The third radius condition bounds it by $c'_\diamond$.

The difference of the fluctuation families contributes
at most
\[3K_\Lambda\mathsf C_{\mathcal A}\mathsf s^\star C_w
\phi(\mathsf t_k),\]using
$\sum_{j\le k}L^{-(k-j)}\le3/2$.
For the Gaussian families, write
$\tau_i=x_i/\mathsf t_i$. Their total variation is
holomorphic on $|\tau_i-1|<\sigma_\star$ and bounded
there by $\mathsf s_a(\mathsf t_\flat)K_{\rm old}\le1$.
Both flows are in the half-radius polydisc. Their common
jump cancels when they are subtracted; hence
$|x'_i-x_i^{\rm W}|\le2\bar B+9$.
Cauchy's estimate and
$\sum_{i<k}\mathsf t_i^{-1}\le2\phi(\mathsf t_k)^2$
give the remaining bound
$4(2\bar B+9)\phi(\mathsf t_k)^2/\sigma_\star$.
These two contributions prove
$\|\mathcal V^\delta(z_1B)\|\le C_\Delta\phi(\mathsf t_k)$.
The $r'_5$ condition completes the potential bound.
The cluster theorem and Cauchy's estimate now give
the stated bound on $\hat e_n$.

The vacuum energy is the sum of its gauge normalization,
fermion normalization, Gaussian, test and cluster parts.
The first is common to the two flows and cancels.
This proves the vacuum-energy identity. At
$z=(0,0,1,0,0)$ the Grassmann integral factors and
equals one, giving the gauge identity.

Finally $\mathcal V^{\rm N},\mathcal V^\delta$ and
$\mathcal V_k^{\rm F}$ vanish at $B=0$. Thus no term
with $n_1=0,n_5\ge1$ occurs. With $z_2=z_3=z_4=0$,
the substitution $B\mapsto-B$ changes $z_1$ to $-z_1$
and preserves the Gaussian, tests and integration domain.
This removes $e_1$ and $e_1+e_5$. The coefficient
$e_1+e_3$ is linear in the first derivative in $B$
of $\mathcal V^{\rm N}+\mathcal V_k^{\rm F}$.
The remaining integrand is invariant under constant
colour rotations. Averaging that derivative over these
rotations gives zero, since the adjoint representation
has no invariant vector. This removes $e_1+e_3$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[The scalar contraction of a total]\label{C-416-19}
At the trivial pair let $\mu$ be the normalized Berezin
Gaussian with covariance $\Gamma_k(\mathbf1)^{-1}$.
Let $\mathcal G=LM\mathbb Z^3$ act in level-$k$ units.
Choose a cube $\Lambda$ of $L^3$ level-$k$ cells and
let $B_R$ be its $R^3$ translates with indices in
$\{0,\ldots,R-1\}^3$. For a formal even total $P$
with no scalar part, put
\[
 (\mathcal J_k[P])_0
      =\lim_{R\to\infty}(R^3M^3)^{-1}\mu(P_{B_R}),
\]
when the limit exists. The subscript restricts monomials
to places in $B_R$, and $P$ is read at $\Psi_k=W$.

Suppose $v_Y$ are even local vertices, independent of
the gauge fluctuation, which vanish at $W=0$, commute
with $\mathcal G$ and satisfy
\[
 S_v=\sup_\square\sum_{Y\supset\square}
                 e^{(\kappa-1)d_k(Y)}\|v_Y\|<\infty.
\]
Let $\bar v$ be the total of their parts in $W$ alone,
and $a^v(X)$ the coefficient of $z$ in the step expansion
at potential $zv$. Then $\|a^v\|\le K_MS_v$, and
\[
 M^{-3}\sum_{X\text{ filed at }c}a^v(X)_0
 =M^{-3}\sum_{Y\text{ filed in }\Lambda}\mu(v_Y)_0
 =(\mathcal J_k[\bar v])_0.
\]
In particular the limit exists and is bounded by $K_MS_v$.
For the old totals $P_j$ of the second-order step,
\[
 |(\mathcal J_k[\sum_{j\le k}P_j])_0|
       \le K_Mc_\psi\sum_{j\le k}
                     C_7L^{(k+1-j)/4}\|P_j\|_j.
\]
The same estimate holds with the norms of any representing
families in place of $\|P_j\|_j$.

The scalar contractions of the mass total
$\mathsf S_1(\mathsf H_{0,k}\Psi_k)$ and of the
second-order total $\mathscr T_k$ also exist. For the
latter, the contribution of a slice $A_i$, $i<k$, is
the slice mean of the density per level-$(k+1)$ site of
\[
 \operatorname{Tr}\bigl((\delta_{A_i}^2\mathbb D_k)_{AA}
                                      \Gamma_k^{-1}\bigr)
 -\tfrac12\operatorname{Tr}
       \bigl[((\delta_{A_i}\mathbb D_k)_{AA}\Gamma_k^{-1})^2\bigr].
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The linear coefficient of the cluster expansion has the
maps used in the identity of totals in
\cite[\S8]{QCDM1}. If $Y^\sharp$ is the enlargement
of $Y$ to the next level, these maps satisfy
\[
 a^v(X)=\sum_{Y:Y^\sharp\subset X}\mathcal L_{X,Y}(v_Y),
 \qquad
 \sum_{X\supset Y^\sharp}\mathcal L_{X,Y}(v_Y)=\mu(v_Y),
\]
and
$\sum_{X\supset Y^\sharp}\|\mathcal L_{X,Y}(v_Y)\|
\le K_EC_Ew_Y(v_Y)$.
The weights $w_Y$ are summable over polymers filed at
a fixed cell. Indeed their input rate is at most
$(1-2\delta_{\rm w})\kappa\le\kappa-1$; the remaining
exponential factors are those of the cluster count.
The count and Cauchy's estimate give $\|a^v\|\le K_MS_v$.

The group $\mathcal G$ acts freely on pairs $(X,Y)$
with $Y^\sharp\subset X$. Each orbit has exactly one
representative with $X$ filed at $c$, and exactly one
with $Y$ filed in $\Lambda$. Translation covariance
makes $\mathcal L_{X,Y}(v_Y)_0$ constant on an orbit.
The preceding absolute bound allows these two sums
over orbit representatives to be equated. This proves
the first equality.

It remains to identify the limit without dropping
boundary terms. Putting generators outside $B_R$ equal
to zero does not increase their norm. Gram's inequality
then gives
\[
 \left|\mu(\bar v_{B_R})-
            \sum_{Y\text{ filed in }B_R}\mu(v_Y)_0\right|
       \le2\sum_{Y\in\mathcal Y_R}\|v_Y\|,
\]
where $\mathcal Y_R$ consists of polymers meeting both
$B_R$ and its complement. A polymer meeting the $n$th
cell layer from the boundary has $d_k(Y)>n-2$.
There are at most $6(RL)^2$ cells in each layer, so
\[
 \sum_{Y\in\mathcal Y_R}\|v_Y\|
 \le6(RL)^2 e^{2(\kappa-1)}S_v
                         \sum_{n\ge0}e^{-(\kappa-1)n}=O(R^2).
\]
The interior sum is $R^3$ times the sum filed in
$\Lambda$. Division by $R^3M^3$ proves the limit.

Apply this argument to the old-activity variation at
$B=0$. Every term contains a $W$ leg, since it is the
old total at $\mathsf H_k\Psi_{k+1}+W$ minus that at
$\mathsf H_k\Psi_{k+1}$. Its vertex norm is at most
$c_\psi\sum_j C_7L^{(k+1-j)/4}\|F^{(j)}\|_j$,
and its part in $W$ alone is $\sum_jP_j$. The resulting
scalar contraction is linear and reads only these
totals. Taking representatives whose norms decrease
to $\|P_j\|_j$ gives the quotient-norm estimate.
The mass vertex is treated in the same way, using
$\mathsf H_{0,k}\mathsf H_k=\mathsf H_{0,k+1}$.
The identity
$\mathscr T_k=\sum_{j\le k}T^{(j)}
 -L^{-k}G_k\mathsf S_1(\mathsf H_{0,k}\Psi_k)$
therefore gives its scalar contraction.

For its value, apply Wick's rule in $B_R$ to the
quadratic and quartic fermion terms of each slice.
The square of the single trace vanishes: the free
covariance is scalar in colour and the first vertex
has colour trace zero. The other contractions are
the two traces displayed above. Their kernels decay
exponentially in the distances among their places.
After division by $R^3M^3$, replacing the finite-box
sums by a sum with one place in $\Lambda$ costs
$O(R^{-1})$. Their limits are the stated trace densities.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[A row bound for the quadratic term]\label{C-416-20}
At the trivial configuration of a weak datum let
$u=\mathsf t_k^{-1/2}B$ be the unscaled fluctuation
on the nonpivot bonds. Let $Q$ be the symmetric kernel
of the quadratic term in
\[
 \log\det\Gamma_k(\mathsf U'(u))
       +\sum_{j\le k}\sum_X
             \mathbf N_\natural^{{\rm F},(j)}(X;\mathsf U'(u)),
\]
so the term is $\sum_{i,j}Q(i,j)u_i u_j$, where
$i=(b,a)$ includes the colour coordinate. Then
\[
 \sup_i\sum_j|Q(i,j)|\le C_{\rm ker},
\]
uniformly in the torus, level and fine mass. One may take
\begin{align*}
 \delta_\star&=\min\left\{
  \frac{\mathsf s^\star\alpha_0}{1+\beta_s},
  \frac{\varepsilon_{\mathfrak h}}{\mathsf C_{\mathcal A}},
  1,\delta(\gamma^{-2})\right\},\qquad
 S_D=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z^3}e^{-2\alpha_DM(|n|_\infty-1)_+},\\
 C_{\rm ker}&=
  \frac{36C_Vh_F^2}{\beta_0}
 +\frac{144S_DC_D^2C_V^2h_F^4}{\Gamma_F^4}
 +\frac{36C_Ec_hK_{\rm old}}
              {a_{\rm an}\mathsf C_{\mathcal A}^2\delta_\star}.
\end{align*}
Here $C_D,\alpha_D$ are the free covariance bounds,
$\Gamma_F$ is its Grassmann weight, and $C_E=4096$
is the polymer-count constant. Thus $C_{\rm ker}$ is
formed from constants up to $\gamma$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
We first record a Cauchy estimate which controls a whole
row. If $f$ is holomorphic and bounded by $M$ on
$\{|u_i|<r\}$, then
\[
 \sum_j|\partial_i\partial_jf(0)|\le4M/r^2.
\]
Indeed apply the two-variable estimate to
$f(se_i+tv)$ on $|s|,|t|<r/2$, choosing $|v_j|=1$
so that the terms $v_j\partial_i\partial_jf(0)$ have
the same phase. A polymer reading the bond $b$ contains
the cell of one of its endpoints. Its sum is therefore
bounded by two sums over polymers containing a fixed cell.

Put the external fermion variables equal to zero in
$\mathcal V_k^{\rm F}(Y;u)$ and call the result
$\mathfrak v_Y(u)$. With $V=\sum_Y\mathfrak v_Y$ and
$\mu$ the free Berezin Gaussian, the exact step gives
\[
 \det\Gamma_k(\mathsf U'(u))/\det\Gamma_k(\mathbf1)
                  =\mu(e^{V(u)}).
\]
The localized variations $\mathcal V^{\rm N}(Y;u)$
sum to the change in the old normalization array for
small real $u$. Gauge invariance permits the chart
background to be replaced by $\mathsf U'(u)$.
Holomorphy extends this identity near zero. Thus
$Q=Q^{\rm F}+Q^{\rm N}$, from
$\log\mu(e^V)$ and $\sum_Y\mathcal V^{\rm N}(Y;u)$.
As $V(0)=0$, their fermion part through order two is
\[
 \mu(V_1)+\mu(V_2)
            +\tfrac12\{\mu(V_1^2)-\mu(V_1)^2\}.
\]

Let $v_Y$ be the supremum of the vertex norm for
$\sup_b|u(b)|\le\beta_0$. Then
\[
 \sum_{Y\supset\square}e^{\kappa d_k(Y)}v_Y
                                      \le C_Vh_F^2\beta_0.
\]
The substitution removing external variables contracts
the norm, and Gram's inequality bounds $|\mu(F)|$ by
$\|F\|$. The coordinate polydisc of radius
$r_F=\beta_0/3$ lies in this domain, since the three
Pauli matrices have norm one. The row estimate applied
to $\mu(\mathfrak v_Y(u))$, with the factor $1/2$
from its quadratic kernel and the two endpoint cells,
bounds the rows of $\mu(V_2)$ by
$4C_Vh_F^2\beta_0/r_F^2=36C_Vh_F^2/\beta_0$.

For quadratic elements $F,F'$ supported in $Y,Y'$, Wick's
rule and covariance decay give
\[
 |\mu(F;F')|\le
 2C_D^2\Gamma_F^{-4}e^{-2\alpha_D\operatorname{dist}_k(Y,Y')}
                                     \|F\|\|F'\|.
\]
Write $x_{Y,i}=\partial_i\mathfrak v_Y(0)$ and choose
phases $v_j$ in the row as before. Cauchy's estimate
bounds both $\|x_{Y,i}\|$ and
$\|\sum_jv_jx_{Y,j}\|$ by $v_Y/r_F$.
File $Y'$ at a cell nearest to $Y$. The covariance sum
over such cells is at most $\#Y S_D$, and
$\#Y\le8(d_k(Y)+1)\le8e^{\kappa d_k(Y)}$.
Summing first over $Y'$ and then over the two endpoint
cells of $Y$ gives
\[
 \sum_j|\mu(\partial_iV_1;\partial_jV_1)|
 \le\frac{32S_DC_D^2(C_Vh_F^2\beta_0)^2}
                {\Gamma_F^4r_F^2}.
\]
Half this quantity is the quadratic-kernel bound,
giving the second term of $C_{\rm ker}$.

For $Q^{\rm N}$ choose $\mathsf t_\star\ge\gamma^{-2}$
with $\delta(\mathsf t_\star)=\delta_\star$. The radius
and background conditions checked in \cref{C-416-11}
apply at this value. Each normalization variation is
holomorphic for $|u(b)|<\mathsf C_{\mathcal A}\delta_\star$
and bounded by
\[
 \frac{c_h\delta_\star K_{\rm old}}{a_{\rm an}}
                    e^{-(1-2\delta_{\rm w})\kappa d_k(Y)}.
\]
Use the coordinate radius
$r_N=\mathsf C_{\mathcal A}\delta_\star/3$.
The row Cauchy estimate, the two endpoint cells and
the quadratic factor $1/2$ give the last term of
$C_{\rm ker}$, since the polymer sum at this rate
is at most $C_E$. Adding the three estimates proves
the assertion.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The terms of second order}

For an operator $X(U)$ of the fermion tower, or for $X(U)=D[U]+m_0$, write
$\mathbb E_i\langle\delta^2\log\det X\rangle$ for
the density per level-$(k+1)$ site of the quadratic
term of its logarithmic determinant, averaged over
the slice $A_i$ at coefficient $x'_i$. This notation
also applies to $X=D+m_0$. The densities are justified
below by their absolutely convergent kernels.

\begin{lemma}[The scalar coefficients]\label{C-416-12}
In the setting of \cref{C-416-11}, put
$c_k^F=\sum_{j\le k}L^{-(k-j)}b_j^F$. Then
\begin{align*}
 \hat e_{2e_1}
   &=\mathbb E_k\langle\delta^2\log\det\mathcal K_{k+1}\rangle
               -3(L^3-1)c_k^F/x'_k+\mathfrak t_k,
       &|\mathfrak t_k|&\le C_{\chi0}\phi(\mathsf t_k)^4,\\
 \hat e_{e_2}+\hat e_{e_4}
   &=(\mathcal J_k[\mathscr T_k])_0+\mathfrak r_k,
       &|\mathfrak r_k|&\le C_{\rm rem}\phi_\sharp(\mathsf t_k)^3,\\
 \sum_{|n|_w\ge3}|\hat e_n|
   &\le C_{\rm w3}\phi(\mathsf t_k)^3.
\end{align*}
The constants may be chosen as
\begin{align*}
 C_{\rm w3}&=2K_Mc_{\rm cl}C_{\rm pd}^3
                           \sum_{w\ge3}(w+1)^5 2^{3-w},\\
 C_{\chi0}&=6K_Mc_{\rm cl}C_{\rm pd}^2
                          +24L^3C_{\rm ker}C_EK_{\rm cp},\\
 C_{\rm rem}&=2K_Mc_\psi C_7C_3S_\omega
       +12(4/3)^{3/2}K_Mc'_\psi c_{\mathsf S}h_F^2
                                                   C_\rho S_3^\sharp.
\end{align*}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For $2e_1$ only $\mathcal V^{\rm N}(z_1B)$ and
$\mathcal V_k^{\rm F}(z_1B)$ remain. These vertices
depend on the fine masses and the calibration, but
not on the running coefficients. Let
$\hat e_{2e_1}(x)$ denote this coefficient with Gaussian
coefficient $x$. Set
\[
 \vartheta(x)=\mathbb E_k^x
       \langle\delta^2\log\det\mathcal K_{k+1}\rangle
                            -3(L^3-1)c_k^F/x=\vartheta_1/x.
\]
We first compare these quantities for real
$|x-x_k|\le r_xx_k$, where $x\ge3\mathsf t_k/4$.

Take tori whose sides $N$, in level-$(k+1)$ units,
tend to infinity. Terms on polymers which do not wrap
around the torus agree with the infinite-lattice terms.
The exponential polymer norm bounds the contribution
of all other polymers, per site, by
\[
 4M^{-3}K_Mc_{\rm cl}(r'_1)^{-2}
                                  e^{-\kappa(N/(2M)-2)}.
\]
To see the count, file each infinite-lattice polymer
at one of its cells. Each nonwrapping torus polymer
has exactly one copy filed in a fixed fundamental
domain. A wrapping polymer, or one too large to fit,
has size at least $N/(2M)-2$. Summing the norm at
the $N^3/M^3$ cells gives the displayed bound after
division by $N^3$.

On each torus the exact fermion integral and the
determinant identities of the tower telescope the
normalization terms. The scalar quotient whose
logarithm is being expanded is
\[
 \nu_{\mathbb T}(e^{f_{\mathbb T}(z_1B)}),\qquad
 f_{\mathbb T}(B)=
 \log\frac{\det\mathcal K_{k+1}[\mathsf U'(B)]}
               {\det\mathcal K_{k+1}[\mathbf1]}
                  -\sum_{j\le k}b_j^FL^jA(\mathsf U'(B)),
\]
where $\nu_{\mathbb T}$ is the normalized gauge
Gaussian with the tests. The first variation vanishes
by constant colour invariance. Thus its quadratic
coefficient is the mean of the quadratic form
$Q_{\mathbb T}(A_k)$ obtained from $f_{\mathbb T}$.
The second derivative of the chart contributes through
the vanished first variation and hence gives zero.

Without the tests the curvature covariance is
$L^{-k}x^{-1}\mathcal C_{(k+1)}\otimes1$.
The kernels of the logarithmic determinant decay
exponentially; those of the action have finite range.
Periodization and dominated convergence therefore give
the infinite-lattice mean $\vartheta(x)$, as detailed
in \cref{C-416-13}. Here
$\tau_{k+1}(\mathcal C_{(k+1)})=2(L^3-1)$,
which accounts for the action coefficient.
The comparison of tested and untested second moments
costs at most
$C_EK_{\rm cp}x^{-1}
 e^{-\gamma_{\rm tail}\mathfrak b(\mathsf t_k)^2/2}$
per matrix entry. The row bound of \cref{C-416-20}
and the at most $9L^3$ bond-colour coordinates per
next-level site give
\[
 |\hat e_{2e_1}(x)-\vartheta(x)|
 \le12L^3C_{\rm ker}C_EK_{\rm cp}\phi(\mathsf t_k)^2
                  e^{-\gamma_{\rm tail}\mathfrak b(\mathsf t_k)^2/2}.
\]

The difference is holomorphic on $|x-x_k|<r_xx_k$.
The coefficient bound and the real estimate at $x_k$
bound it on this disc by $C_{\chi0}\phi(\mathsf t_k)^2$.
On the real diameter it has the preceding exponential
gain. The two-constants estimate used in the
second-order expansion of \cite[\S8]{QCDM1}, with
harmonic-measure lower bound $c_{\rm hm}$ on the
two-thirds disc, gives
\[
 |\hat e_{2e_1}(x)-\vartheta(x)|
 \le C_{\chi0}\phi(\mathsf t_k)^2
 e^{-c_{\rm hm}\gamma_{\rm tail}\mathfrak b(\mathsf t_k)^2/2}
 \le C_{\chi0}\phi(\mathsf t_k)^4.
\]
The last inequality is the imposed Gaussian-tail
ceiling. It applies at $x=x'_k$.

For $e_2$, the gauge fluctuation is absent. The identity
of scalar totals in \cref{C-416-19} gives
$\hat e_{e_2}=(\mathcal J_k[\sum_{j\le k}E_{\ge2}^{(j)}])_0$.
For $e_4$ it gives
$\hat e_{e_4}=-L^{-k}s'_k\sigma_k$, where
$\sigma_k=(\mathcal J_k[\mathsf S_1(\mathsf H_{0,k}\Psi_k)])_0$
and
$|L^{-k}\sigma_k|\le12K_Mc'_\psi c_{\mathsf S}h_F^2$.
Use the identities of totals
\[
 E_{\ge2}^{(j)}=T^{(j)}+R^{(j)},\qquad
 \sum_{j\le k}T^{(j)}=\mathscr T_k
            +L^{-k}G_k(x')\mathsf S_1(\mathsf H_{0,k}\Psi_k).
\]
The remainder totals have vanishing quadratic cell
sums and representatives of norm at most
$2C_3\phi(\mathsf t_{j-1})^3$.
Their scalar contraction is bounded by the first
term of $C_{\rm rem}\phi_\sharp(\mathsf t_k)^3$.
The mass remainder is bounded using
\[
 |s'_k-G_k(x')|\le(4/3)^{3/2}C_\rho S_3^\sharp
                                     \phi_\sharp(\mathsf t_k)^3.
\]
This proves the second estimate.

Finally there are at most $(w+1)^5$ multi-indices of
weight $w$. The coefficient bound of \cref{C-416-11}
and $C_{\rm pd}\phi(\mathsf t_k)\le1/2$ sum to
the stated $C_{\rm w3}$ bound.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Transport through the fermion tower]\label{C-416-13}
For an operator $X$ commuting at the trivial background
with translations of $L^m\mathbb Z^3$, $m\ge i+1$,
let $\mathfrak M_i[X]$ be $n_m$ times the density per
level-$m$ site of the slice-$i$ mean of its quadratic
logarithmic determinant. This quantity does not change
on passing to a coarser common period. At the relabelled
datum,
\begin{align*}
 n_{k+1}(\mathcal J_k[\mathscr T_k])_0
       &=\sum_{i<k}\mathfrak M_i[\Gamma_k],\\
 \mathfrak M_i[\mathcal K_{n+1}]
       &=\mathfrak M_i[\mathcal K_n]+\mathfrak M_i[\Gamma_n],
       &\mathfrak M_i[\mathcal K_1]&=\mathfrak M_i[\Gamma_0],\\
 \mathfrak M_i[D+m_0]
       &=\mathfrak M_i[\mathcal K_n]+\mathfrak M_i[\mathbb D_n],\\
 \mathfrak M_i[D+m_0]
       &=-\tfrac32(L^ix_i)^{-1}n_{i+1}
                   \tau_{i+1}(\mathcal C_{(i+1)}\widehat W_{m_0}).
\end{align*}
The identities hold whenever their displayed levels
exist in the tower. Moreover
\[
 \left|\sum_{i<n}\mathfrak M_i[\mathbb D_n]\right|
          \le n_n C'_M C_{\mathscr T}/\mathsf t_n,
\]
where
\begin{align*}
 C_M&=\nu_0^2C_{\rm el}c_z+(b_F(1-L^{-1}))^{-1},
       &C'_M&=2(C_M+2C_M^2),\\
 C_{\mathscr T}&=C_7C_Th_F^4+4c_{\mathsf S}h_F^2B_F,
       &c_z&=\sup_{s\ge1}s^{-1}
                    \sum_{|z|_\infty\le s}(1+|z|)^{-2}.
\end{align*}
Here $\nu_0=48$ is the number of chamber places per site.
The last sum is the full contraction of $\mathscr T_n$
with $\mathbb D_n(\mathbf1)^{-1}$, multiplied by $n_n$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For a slice $i<k$, the linear block average of level
$k$ is zero. Its second-order displacement is a colour
vector quadratic in the slice and has zero mean.
Consequently the slice derivatives of
$\Gamma_k=(\mathbb D_k)_{AA}+\theta q_{k+1}^+q_{k+1}$
in the Wick contraction agree with those of
$(\mathbb D_k)_{AA}$. The first trace vanishes by its
colour trace. The two surviving contractions in
\cref{C-416-19} are therefore the quadratic
logarithmic determinant of $\Gamma_k$. This proves
the first identity.

On every compatible torus the Schur-complement identities
give, up to constants independent of the field,
\[
 \log\det\mathcal K_{n+1}
       =\log\det\mathcal K_n+\log\det\Gamma_n,
 \qquad
 \log\det(D+m_0)
       =\log\det\mathcal K_n+\log\det\mathbb D_n,
\]
and $\Gamma_0=\mathcal K_1$.
We justify the passage of their quadratic terms to
infinite-lattice densities. At the fixed positive bare
mass, the free inverse $G_{m_0}$, the tower inverses
and their first two field derivatives have exponentially
decaying kernels. For the remaining coarse covariance,
the exact identity is
\[
 \mathbb D_n(\mathbf1)^{-1}
                  =T_nG_{m_0}T_n^*+\theta_n^{-1}.
\]
It holds as a bounded-operator identity on $\ell^2$:
multiply it on either side by
$\mathbb D_n=\theta_n-\theta_n^2T_n\mathcal K_n^{-1}T_n^*$,
using $\mathcal K_n=D+m_0+\theta_nT_n^*T_n$.
The products reduce to the identity. Since $T_n$ is
block-local, this also proves exponential decay of
this inverse at the fixed mass.

For any of these operators, the coefficient kernel of
\[
 Q_X(A)=\operatorname{Tr}(X^{-1}\delta_A^2X)
                   -\tfrac12\operatorname{Tr}((X^{-1}\delta_AX)^2)
\]
has the form $q_X(b,a;b',a')=\sum_v y(v;b,a;b',a')$,
with
$|y|\le Ce^{-c(|x_v-x_b|+|x_v-x_{b'}|)}$.
It is covariant under the common period. If $\Lambda_m$
contains the bonds starting in one level-$m$ block,
the slice mean per block is the absolutely convergent sum
\[
 d_\infty[X]=L^{-i}x_i^{-1}
       \sum_{b\in\Lambda_m}\sum_{b',a}
                    q_X(b,a;b',a)C_\infty(b,b').
\]
The torus kernels are signed periodizations of the same
kernels. Terms winding around a torus of side $H$
have total coefficient sum at most $CH^3e^{-cH/2}$.
The nonwinding terms give the displayed sum with the
periodic covariance $C_{\mathbb T}$. These covariances
are uniformly bounded and converge pointwise to
$C_\infty$. Dominated convergence proves convergence
of their densities. The determinant identities therefore
pass to $\mathfrak M_i=n_md_\infty$.

The free determinant has quadratic term
$-\tfrac12\sum_c\langle dA^c,\widehat W_{m_0}dA^c\rangle$.
The slice curvature covariance is
$L^{-i}x_i^{-1}\mathcal C_{(i+1)}$ in each of the
three colours. This gives the fourth identity and its sign.

For the final bound, the entries of $T_n$ have norm
at most $L^{-2n}$ and there are $\nu_0L^{3n}$ fine
places in a block. The bound
$|G_{m_0}(v,v')|\le C_{\rm el}(1+|x_v-x_{v'}|)^{-2}$
gives, uniformly in $m_0>0$,
\[
 |(T_nG_{m_0}T_n^*)(v,v')|
       \le L^{-4n}(\nu_0L^{3n})(\nu_0C_{\rm el}c_zL^n)
       =\nu_0^2C_{\rm el}c_z.
\]
Thus the coarse covariance entries are bounded by $C_M$.
A full contraction of a product of unit fibre vectors
is bounded by $C_M$ in degree two and by $2C_M^2$
in degree four. It vanishes unless the barred and
unbarred degrees agree.

File representatives of $T^{(j)}$ in the level-$n$
cells and read them at level $n$ through the background
maps. The contribution to one cell has norm at most
$C_7L^{(n-j)/4}C_Th_F^4/\mathsf t_{j-1}$.
The mass term in the identity of $\mathscr T_n$ contributes
at most $4c_{\mathsf S}h_F^2B_F/\mathsf t_n$.
Since
$\sum_{j\le n}L^{(n-j)/4}/\mathsf t_{j-1}\le\mathsf t_n^{-1}$,
their sum in a cell has norm at most
$C_{\mathscr T}/\mathsf t_n$.
Its degree-two and degree-four parts sum to
$\mathscr T_n$. The contraction commutes with cell
translations, and the coefficient sums are absolutely
convergent. Hence the density is $M^{-3}$ times the
contraction in one cell. The preceding covariance
bound proves the last inequality. The same Wick
calculation as for $\Gamma_k$ identifies this contraction
with $\sum_{i<n}\mathfrak M_i[\mathbb D_n]$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[The free coefficient]\label{C-416-16}
The number $I_B$ is finite and positive. There is
$C_{\rm kp}$ depending only on the fixed chamber operator
such that
\[
 |\kappa(l,\mu)|\le C_{\rm kp}N_f,
 \qquad
 \kappa(l,\mu)\longrightarrow\tfrac14N_fI_B
                      \quad(l\to\infty,\ \mu\to0).
\]
The convergence is joint in these two limits.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
We first control the matrices in the definition. The
bound $|s(y)|\le\min\{1,2/|y|\}$ makes the sum over
$n\ne0$ in $M_a$ bounded by
$\pi^{-1-a}((7/3)^3-1)$. Indeed a nonzero coordinate
of $n$ gives a factor $4/(\pi^2n_\nu^2)$ and
$|k_n|\ge\pi$. On the central cube $|s(p_\nu)|\ge2/\pi$.
If $w\perp G(p)$, then
\[
 p^{\mathsf T}\hat B(p)^*w
       =i\prod_\nu\overline{s(p_\nu)}G(p)^*w=0.
\]
Thus the $n=0$ term alone gives
\[
 w^*M_1(p)w\ge(2/\pi)^8|w|^2|p|^{-2},\qquad
 w^*M_2(p)w\ge(2/\pi)^8|w|^2|p|^{-3}.
\]
It follows that
$\|\operatorname{Del}(p)\|\le(\pi/2)^8|p|^2$ and
$\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{Del}M_1)=2$.
The corresponding trace with $M_2$ is positive and
bounded by
\[
 (\pi/2)^8|p|^2
                  \left(3|p|^{-3}+3\pi^{-3}(7/3)^3\right).
\]
This is integrable in three dimensions and proves
$0<I_B<\infty$.

For completeness, $M_1$ is invertible off the coordinate
axes. Its kernel consists of $w$ for which
$\hat B(k_n)^*w$ is parallel to $k_n$ for every $n$.
If two coordinates of $p$ are nonzero, varying one
alias index changes the squared ratio of these
coordinates. The relations
$i\overline{G_\mu(p)}w_\mu=\lambda_n k_{n,\mu}^2$
then force all components of $w$ to vanish. If
$p=p_1e_1\ne0$, only $n_2=n_3=0$ contribute, and
each summand is proportional to $\operatorname{diag}(0,1,1)$.
The kernel is then the span of $G(p)$. In particular,
off the axes the formula for $\operatorname{Del}$ is
\[
 M_1^{-1}-M_1^{-1}G(G^*M_1^{-1}G)^{-1}G^*M_1^{-1}.
\]

We next compute the finite-scale projection. Write
$q=L^l$, $k_n=q^{-1}(p+2\pi n)$ and sum over
$n\in\{-(q-1)/2,\ldots,(q-1)/2\}^3$.
Let $\hat s(k)=(e^{ik_\mu}-1)_\mu$ and
$P^{\rm lat}(k)=1-\hat s(k)\hat s(k)^*/|\hat s(k)|^2$.
The straight-average symbol is diagonal, with
\[
 \hat q_{l,\mu}(k)=q^{-3}\sum_{x\in B^l(0)}e^{ik\cdot x}
                                      \sum_{j=0}^{q-1}e^{ik_\mu j}.
\]
The background curvatures are the image of $G(p)^\perp$
under
\[
 J_p^{(l)}\lambda=
       (|\hat s(k_n)|^{-2}\hat d(k_n)\hat q_l(k_n)^*\lambda)_n.
\]
To verify this, their orthogonal complement is
$d(\ker\mathbf Q_l^s)$. Orthogonality means
$d^*da=(\mathbf Q_l^s)^*\lambda$. The telescoping
identity for a straight average of a gradient gives
$\hat q_{l,\mu}(k)\hat s_\mu(k)=G_\mu(p)\hat A_l(k)$.
Since $\hat A_l(k_0)\ne0$, the right side is transverse
in every alias exactly when $\lambda\perp G(p)$.
Solving for the curvature gives $J_p^{(l)}$.

Put
\[
 M_1^{(l)}(p)=\sum_n\hat q_l(k_n)P^{\rm lat}(k_n)
                       \hat q_l(k_n)^*|\hat s(k_n)|^{-2}.
\]
Then $J_p^{(l)*}J_p^{(l)}=J_p^*M_1^{(l)}J_p$.
The $n=0$ term is positive on $G(p)^\perp$, so the
background projection is
$J_p^{(l)}(J_p^*M_1^{(l)}J_p)^{-1}J_p^{(l)*}$ and has
rank two. Denote its diagonal alias blocks by
$\Pi_{nn}(p)$. They are positive and their traces sum
to two. In particular
\[
 \tau_l(\Pi_l^{\rm tp})=2,\qquad
 \tau_{j+1}(\mathcal C_{(j+1)})=2(L^3-1),
\]
and, for any translation-invariant curvature operator $Y$,
\[
 \tau_l(\Pi_l^{\rm tp}Y)=
       \int\sum_n\operatorname{tr}(\Pi_{nn}(p)Y(k_n))
                                      \frac{d^3p}{(2\pi)^3}.
\]
The geometric sums in $\hat q_l$ give, for each fixed
alias $n$ as $l\to\infty$,
\[
 L^{-l}\hat q_l(k_n)\longrightarrow\omega_n\hat B(p+2\pi n),
 \qquad L^{2l}|\hat s(k_n)|^2\longrightarrow|p+2\pi n|^2,
\]
where $\omega_n$ is a common phase. They also give
\[
 |L^{-l}\hat q_{l,\mu}(k_n)|\le
 \min\{1,\pi/|p_\mu+2\pi n_\mu|\}
       \prod_\nu\min\{1,\pi/|p_\nu+2\pi n_\nu|\},
 \quad L^{2l}|\hat s(k_n)|^2\ge(4/\pi^2)|p+2\pi n|^2.
\]
These bounds follow from
$|\sin(\theta/2)|\ge|\theta|/\pi$ on $[-\pi,\pi]$.

The polarization calculation in \cref{C-403-36} gives
on exact curvatures
\[
 \|\widehat W_{m_0}(k)\|\le C_{\widehat W}N_f|k|^{-1},\qquad
 \|\widehat W_{m_0}(k)-\Upsilon(k;m_0)\|
                    \le C_{\widehat W}N_f(1+|\log|k||),
\]
uniformly for $0\le m_0\le1$. Here
\[
 \Upsilon(k;m)=\frac{N_f}{2\pi}\int_{2m}^\infty
                       \frac{1+4m^2/u^2}{u^2+|k|^2}\,du.
\]
Indeed $\hat\Pi=\hat d^*\widehat W^{\rm f}\hat d$,
and $\hat d$ has lower singular value
$(2/\pi)|k|$ on the transverse space. The remainder
bound for $\hat\Pi$ in \cref{C-403-36}, divided by
this square, gives the second estimate near zero.
The difference between $\hat d^*\hat d$ and
$|k|^2-kk^{\mathsf T}$ is $O(|k|^3)$ and gives the
same bound. Away from zero compactness gives a uniform
bound. Changing bond or plaquette placements conjugates
by diagonal phases and does not change the norm of
the difference from a scalar.
The integral formula shows homogeneity
$\Upsilon(\epsilon k;\epsilon m)=\epsilon^{-1}\Upsilon(k;m)$.
Differentiation in $m$ gives $\partial_m\Upsilon\le0$;
the boundary term is $-4/(4m^2+|k|^2)$ and the
integral term is at most
$8m(4m^2+|k|^2)^{-1}\int_{2m}^\infty u^{-2}\,du$.
Thus $0\le\Upsilon(k;m)\le N_f/(4|k|)$.
The first operator bound follows from the second.

Since $|k_n|\ge L^{-l}\min\{|p|,\pi\}$ and
$\sum_n\operatorname{tr}\Pi_{nn}=2$, the trace formula
gives $|\kappa(l,\mu)|\le C_{\widehat W}c_{\rm mi}N_f$,
where
$c_{\rm mi}=\int(|p|^{-1}+\pi^{-1})\,d^3p/(2\pi)^3$.
For the limit, replace $\widehat W_{L^{-l}\mu}(k_n)$
by $L^l\Upsilon(p+2\pi n;\mu)$. The resulting error
in $\kappa$ is bounded by
\[
 C_{\widehat W}N_f L^{-l}
              \int(3+l\log L+|\log|p||)\frac{d^3p}{(2\pi)^3},
\]
which tends to zero uniformly in $\mu$.
The remaining integrand is
\[
 \tfrac12\operatorname{tr}
    [(J_p^*M_1^{(l)}J_p)^{-1}J_p^*M_\Upsilon^{(l)}J_p],
\]
where $M_\Upsilon^{(l)}$ is $M_1^{(l)}$ with the
factor $\Upsilon(p+2\pi n;\mu)$ in each summand.
The alias bounds give, jointly as $l\to\infty$ and
$\mu\to0$,
\[
 L^{-4l}M_1^{(l)}\longrightarrow M_1,
 \qquad L^{-4l}M_\Upsilon^{(l)}\longrightarrow(N_f/4)M_2.
\]
The phases cancel. The compressed inverse converges
by its proved positivity. The trace is bounded by
$(N_f/2)(|p|^{-1}+\pi^{-1})$. Dominated convergence
therefore gives
$\kappa(l,\mu)\to(N_f/8)\int\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{Del}M_2)
=N_fI_B/4$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Summing the change in the vacuum energy}

\begin{lemma}[The difference of one step]\label{C-416-14}
In the setting of \cref{C-416-11}, put
\[
 v_{k+1}(\zeta)=
  \mathbb E_k\langle\delta^2\log\det\mathcal K_{k+1}\rangle
       +\sum_{i<k}\mathbb E_i\langle\delta^2\log\det\Gamma_k\rangle.
\]
Then
\[
 e_{k+1}(\zeta)-e_{k+1}^{\rm W}(\zeta)
       =e_{k+1}^{\rm F,0}+v_{k+1}(\zeta)
                                +\operatorname{Rem}_{k+1}(\zeta),
 \qquad
 |\operatorname{Rem}_{k+1}(\zeta)|
                         \le C_{\rm vac}\phi_\sharp(\mathsf t_k)^3.
\]
The remainder is holomorphic on $|\zeta|<\rho'$.
One may take
\begin{align*}
 C_{\rm vac}&=C_{\mathfrak g}+C_{\chi0}+C_{\rm rem}
                                           +C_{\rm w3}+C_{\rm eq},\\
 C_{\mathfrak g}&=3(L^3-1)(16(2B_\sharp+6)^2+24C_w),\\
 C_{\rm eq}&=8(2\bar B+9)K_M(K_0^\sharp A_1+4)/r_x.
\end{align*}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Subtract the gauge-only value
$\hat e(0,0,1,0,0)$ from $\hat e(1,1,1,1,1)$.
Among the remaining indices of weight at most two,
the cancellations of \cref{C-416-11} leave precisely
$2e_1,e_2,e_4$. Apply \cref{C-416-12,C-416-13} to
these coefficients. In addition to their remainders,
there remain
\[
 \mathfrak g_k=g_k(x'_k)-g_k(x_k^{\rm W})
                           -3(L^3-1)c_k^F/x'_k
\]
and the differences of the test and gauge cluster
densities at $x'_k,x_k^{\rm W}$.

The two coefficient recursions give
\[
 x_k^{\rm W}-x'_k=c_k^F+\Delta r_k,\qquad
 \Delta r_k=\sum_{j\le k}L^{-(k-j)}
                                    (b_j^r-b_j^{r,\rm W}).
\]
The bounds are $|c_k^F|\le2B_\sharp$ and
$|\Delta r_k|\le6C_w\phi(\mathsf t_k)$.
For $y=(c_k^F+\Delta r_k)/x'_k$ we have $|y|\le1/2$
under the coupling ceilings. Thus
\[
 |\mathfrak g_k|
 \le3(L^3-1)(|y|^2+4|\Delta r_k|/\mathsf t_k)
 \le C_{\mathfrak g}\phi_\sharp(\mathsf t_k)^3.
\]
Here we used $\mathsf t^{-2},\phi(\mathsf t)/\mathsf t
\le\phi_\sharp(\mathsf t)^3$. This is the cancellation
between the extracted fermion coupling and the change
in the Gaussian normalization.

The test and gauge cluster densities are holomorphic
in $|x-x_k^{\rm W}(0)|<r_xx_k^{\rm W}(0)$ and bounded
there by $2K_M\phi(\mathsf t_k)^2$ and
$K_M(K_0^\sharp A_1+2)\phi(\mathsf t_k)$, respectively.
The segment between $x'_k$ and $x_k^{\rm W}$ has length
at most $2\bar B+9$. It stays at distance at least
$r_x\mathsf t_k/8$ from the boundary: $k<t'$ gives
$\mathsf t_k\ge L\gamma^{-2}$, and the ceiling
$24\bar B\gamma^2\le r_x$, with $L\ge13$ and
$\bar B\ge2$, gives
$\mathsf t_k\ge8(2\bar B+9)/r_x$.
Cauchy's estimate therefore bounds their two differences
by $C_{\rm eq}\phi(\mathsf t_k)/\mathsf t_k$.
The remaining three bounds are those of
\cref{C-416-12}. Their sum proves the assertion.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[The derivative of the vacuum-energy difference]
\label{C-416-15}
Suppose $d'\ge\max\{\bar n,d_\natural\}$ and
$C_{\rm pd}\phi(L^{d'+1}\mathsf b_*)\le1/2$.
Then the sums in \cref{C-416-10} satisfy
\[
 c'_{\rm F}(0)-c'_{\rm W}(0)
 =-3\mathsf b_*^{-2}\ell^3L^{2d}
                  \kappa(K-d,L^{-d}\mathsf m)+\mathcal E_d,
\]
where
\[
 \begin{split}
 |\mathcal E_d|\le C_{\mathcal E}\ell^3\bigl[&
 (N_f+1)L^{2d'}\mathsf b_*^{-2}
 +N_fL^d\mathsf b_*^{-3}\\
 &+\mathsf b_*^{-5/2}L^{3d/2}
            (1+d\log L+\log\mathsf b_*)^{9\mathfrak p_0}\bigr].
 \end{split}
\]
One may take
\[
 C_{\mathcal E}=\max\{3C_{\rm kp}+4C'_MC_{\mathscr T}/r_x,
                     9C_{\rm kp}C_{\rm dv},8C_{\rm vac}/r_x\},
 \qquad C_{\rm dv}=24C_w/r_x+6\bar B.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Sum \cref{C-416-14} with weights $n_{k+1}$ over
$t\le k<t'$. The free fermion normalizations are
independent of $\zeta$. Cauchy's estimate gives
\[
 \sum_{t\le k<t'}n_{k+1}|\operatorname{Rem}'_{k+1}(0)|
 \le\frac{8C_{\rm vac}}{r_x}\ell^3\mathsf b_*^{-5/2}L^{3d/2}
                         (1+d\log L+\log\mathsf b_*)^{9\mathfrak p_0}.
\]
This follows by setting $u=K-k$, using
$n_{k+1}=\ell^3L^{3u-3}$ and $1/\rho'=4/(r_x\mathsf b_*)$,
and summing the resulting geometric progression.

By \cref{C-416-13}, the quadratic terms satisfy
\[
 n_{k+1}v_{k+1}
       =\mathfrak M_k[\mathcal K_{k+1}]
                                +\sum_{i<k}\mathfrak M_i[\Gamma_k].
\]
Terms with $i<t$ read only unchanged slice coefficients
and are independent of $\zeta$. For the other terms,
the determinant identities telescope:
\[
 \sum_{t\le i<t'}\left(\mathfrak M_i[\mathcal K_{i+1}]
                   +\sum_{i<k<t'}\mathfrak M_i[\Gamma_k]\right)
   =\sum_{t\le i<t'}
            (\mathfrak M_i[D+m_0]-\mathfrak M_i[\mathbb D_{t'}]).
\]
The coarse-fermion sum is holomorphic and, including
the constant terms $i<t$, is bounded by
$n_{t'}C'_MC_{\mathscr T}/\mathsf t_{t'}$.
Its derivative consequently has modulus at most
$4C'_MC_{\mathscr T}\ell^3L^{2d'}/(r_x\mathsf b_*^2)$.

It remains to differentiate the free polarization term.
Cauchy's estimate in the coefficient recursion gives
\[
 \partial_\zeta x'_i(0)=-L^{K-i}(1+\epsilon_i),\qquad
 |\epsilon_i|\le12C_w/(r_x\mathsf t_i).
\]
Also $x_i^{-2}=\mathsf t_i^{-2}(1+\eta_i)$ with
$|\eta_i|\le3\bar B/\mathsf t_i$. Hence
\[
 \partial_\zeta(1/x'_i)(0)
       =L^{K-i}\mathsf t_i^{-2}(1+\epsilon'_i),
 \qquad |\epsilon'_i|\le C_{\rm dv}/\mathsf t_i.
\]
Since $L^{-i}L^{K-i}\mathsf t_i^{-2}=L^{-K}\mathsf b_*^{-2}$,
the leading part has a coefficient independent of $i$.
Using the projection difference for the curvature slice,
\[
 \sum_{t\le i<t'}n_{i+1}
                  \tau_{i+1}(\mathcal C_{(i+1)}\widehat W_{m_0})
 =2n_tL^t\kappa(t,L^tm_0)
                       -2n_{t'}L^{t'}\kappa(t',L^{t'}m_0).
\]
The first term gives the stated leading term. The
second is bounded by
$3C_{\rm kp}N_f\ell^3L^{2d'}\mathsf b_*^{-2}$.
For the errors $\epsilon'_i$, use
\[
 |n_{i+1}\tau_{i+1}(\mathcal C_{(i+1)}\widehat W_{m_0})|
         \le4C_{\rm kp}N_f\ell^3L^{3(K-i)}L^i.
\]
Their sum is at most
$9C_{\rm kp}C_{\rm dv}N_f\ell^3L^d\mathsf b_*^{-3}$.
These estimates give $C_{\mathcal E}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of \cref{C-416-4}]
Choose $d_2\ge\max\{2,d_\natural\}$ so that, for
every $d\ge d_2$, the following hold:
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 d'\ge\max\{\bar n,d_\natural\},\qquad
 C_{\rm pd}\phi(L^{d'+1}\mathsf b_*)\le1/2,\\
 (2R_{\rm fc}/\bar S)^{1/2}\le\zeta_0\le\rho'/2,\qquad
 2(\rho^{\rm F}(d')+\rho^{\rm W}(d'))\mathsf Q'L^{4d}
                                                        \le L^{7d/4}.
 \end{gathered}
\]
These are conditions on $d$, not further restrictions
on $\gamma$. They hold eventually: the ratio of the
left source radius to $\zeta_0$ is bounded by a
constant times $(1+d)^{1/2}L^{-5d/16+3/2}$, while
the discarded-history exponent decreases quadratically
in $d$ or faster. Here $\mathfrak p_0\ge1$.

The statistic bound $0\le T_d^K\le\mathsf Q'L^{4d}$
and \cref{C-416-8} control the discarded histories.
For the retained histories, \cref{C-416-10} bounds
each error in replacing the mean by $c'_\sharp(0)$ by
\[
 (2R_{\rm fc}\bar S)^{1/2}
       \le C_{\rm conv}\ell^3\mathsf b_*^{-1}
                              (1+d)^{1/2}L^{27d/16},
\]
where $C_{\rm conv}$ may depend on
$1+|\log\mathsf b_*|+\log_+(1/\mathsf m)$.
Apply \cref{C-416-15}. Since $27/16<7/4$,
$3/2<7/4$, and $2d'\le d/4+2$, all the errors,
including their polynomial factors in $d$, are at
most $\mathsf K_{\rm S}L^{7d/4}$ for a fixed constant.
This proves the estimate uniformly for $K>d\ge d_2$.

The bounds and joint limit for $\kappa$ were proved in
\cref{C-416-16}. After division by $L^{2d}$, the
error just proved tends to zero. If
$K\ge K_0(d)$ and $K_0(d)-d\to\infty$, then
$K-d\to\infty$ uniformly over this range and
$L^{-d}\mathsf m\to0$. The joint limit of $\kappa$
therefore gives the asserted uniform limit of the means.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Dependence of the constants]\label{C-416-17}
The free-kernel constants are fixed with the chamber
operator, $L$ and $b_F$. The bounds of the step, the
two scalar histories and their variations are formed
after $h_F$ and before the mass interval. The history
mark and its thresholds precede $\gamma$, whose
additional ceilings are listed in \cref{C-416-2}.
The constants $C_{\rm pd}$ and $C_{\rm ker}$ are
formed after $\gamma$; they impose only an eventual
depth requirement through $d_2$. The relabelling,
discarding constants, $d_2$ and $\mathsf K_{\rm S}$
may depend on the given positive physical mass. Thus
the proof does not assert uniformity of these latter
constants as that mass tends to zero.
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[A finite set of flavour numbers]\label{C-416-18}
For a fixed finite set $F\subset\{1,2,\ldots\}$,
choose each constant free upward to meet its floors
for every $N_f\in F$, and each constant free downward
to meet its ceilings for every $N_f\in F$, in the
original order. All conditions read earlier constants
alone, so this gives a common admissible assignment.
Its gauge constants, label interval, cuts and statistic
$T_d^K$ are the same for every $N_f\in F$.
The mean comparison holds for each of them, with
limit proportional to its own $N_f$ and with its own
eventual depth and error constant.
\end{remark}

\subsection{Recovering the coupling and the flavour number}

The same sequence of gauge-field observables distinguishes
the coupling and the number of fermion flavours. First
invert the pure-gauge mean of $T_d^K$. Its slope has order
$L^{3d}$, so the fermion correction of order $L^{2d}$
still permits recovery of the coupling. Once this label
is known, the normalized correction recovers $N_f$.

\begin{definition}[A common parameter range]\label{C-406-69}
Fix a nonempty finite set
$\mathcal N_f\subset\{1,2,\ldots\}$. Choose the constants
to satisfy both \cref{C-418-2,C-416-2} for each
$N_f\in\mathcal N_f$, retaining all the positive-mass
conditions of the original construction. At each stage
take a constant free upward above all its finitely many
floors, or a constant free downward below all its finitely
many ceilings. Determined constants are evaluated at
each $N_f$. Use common gauge constants and mass interval
$[m_-,m_+]$.

Fix $0<g\le\gamma$, $\ell=2L^m\in\mathfrak L(g)$ and
\[
 J_g=[b_-,b_+]=[g^{-2}+\bar B,X_g-\bar B],\qquad
 X_g=L(g^{-2}+B_\sharp),\qquad
 \mathsf W(g)=J_g\times[m_-,m_+].
\]
Form $T_d^K$ and $d_\natural$ from \cref{C-375-7}
at this interval. We write
$\mu_d^{F,K}[N_f;b,\mathsf m]$, $\mu_d^F[N_f;b,\mathsf m]$
and $\mu_{\rm thr}^F[N_f;b,\mathsf m]$ for the block
and thread laws, making the flavour number explicit.
For $N_f=0$ these denote the corresponding Wilson laws,
which are independent of $\mathsf m$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Compatibility of the estimates]\label{C-406-70}
The choices in \cref{C-406-69} exist. They give one
statistic $T_d^K$ for all the indicated laws, to which
the pure-gauge estimate \cref{C-375-8}, the fermion
variance bound \cref{C-406-58}, the mean comparison
\cref{C-416-4}, and the total-variation convergence
\cref{C-406-68,C-375-24} all apply.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Every additional floor or ceiling in \cref{C-418-2}
reads constants already chosen at its position in the
order. The same holds for the four extra coupling
ceilings and the larger $B_\sharp$ in \cref{C-416-2}.
The second history mark, with dials $(1/2,0,0,c_\star)$
and share $1/2$, is fixed before $\gamma$. It does not
replace the mark used in the cutoff comparison. In
particular that mark's rate $\theta_{\rm tl}$ and its
associated ceiling remain unchanged. Both sets of
thresholds can be imposed on $\gamma$. Finitely many
flavour values therefore give a consistent choice in
the original order, as in \cref{C-416-18}.

The gauge constants, $B_\sharp$, $\bar B$, windows,
admissible sides, mass interval and cuts are common.
Moreover $b_-\ge\gamma^{-2}$ and
\[
 b_+-b_-=(L-1)g^{-2}+(L-3)\bar B>0.
\]
The side condition defining $\mathfrak L(g)$ gives
$MR(b)\le L^m$ for every $b\le L(X_g+\bar B)$;
see \cite[Cor.~118.4]{YMM1}. Hence $J_g$ is an
admissible interval for \cref{C-375-7}.
For any $b\in J_g$, the variance proof may use
$b_\flat=b_-$ and $n=d_\natural$: all its conditions,
$b_\flat\le b$, $MR(b_\flat)\le L^m$ and
$L^nb_\flat\ge\mathsf t_\natural$, hold.
Its cut is precisely
\[
 \{V:\varpi(V)<\bar\varepsilon,
          L^{2(K-d)}\varpi(U_{K-d}(V))
                                      <c_\rho\varepsilon(L^db_-)\}.
\]
On this cut both definitions give $L^KA(U_{K-d}(V))$,
and off it both give zero. The background action is
constant on its gauge orbit. Thus the statistics in
all four estimates agree as Borel functions, not only
almost everywhere for a particular law. The remaining
hypotheses are the constant choices just checked.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[The slope of the pure-gauge mean]\label{C-406-71}
There is $d_{\rm W}\ge d_\natural$, depending only
on the common constants, $g$ and $\ell$, such that
for $K>d\ge d_{\rm W}$ the function
\[
 m_d^K(s)=\mathbb E_{K,s}T_d^K(V_d),\qquad s>0,
\]
is continuously differentiable and satisfies on $J_g$
\[
 2.65s^{-2}N_d\le-(m_d^K)'(s)\le3.35s^{-2}N_d,
 \qquad \operatorname{Var}_{\mu_d^{{\rm W},K}[s]}T_d^K
                                         \le3.62s^{-2}N_d.
\]
Its inverse on $[m_d^K(b_+),m_d^K(b_-)]$ has
Lipschitz constant $b_+^2/(2.65N_d)$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The bare action and $T_d^K$ are bounded at fixed cutoff,
and $T_d^K$ is independent of $s$. Differentiating
$e^{-sO}/\int e^{-sO}dU$ gives
$-(m_d^K)'(s)=\operatorname{Cov}_{K,s}(T_d^K,O)$.
Put $X=\mathbb E_{K,s}(O-\mathbb E_{K,s}O\mid V_d)$.
The tower property gives
\[
 -(m_d^K)'(s)=\mathbb E_{K,s}[(T_d^K-c_s)X]
\]
for the constant $c_s$ in \cref{C-375-8}.
Choose $d_{\rm W}$ large enough that its two errors,
after multiplication by $b_+^2$, are at most $1/10$
and $1/50$. Then
\[
 |\mathbb EX^2-3s^{-2}N_d|\le0.1s^{-2}N_d,
 \qquad \mathbb E|X-(T_d^K-c_s)|^2\le0.02s^{-2}N_d.
\]
Cauchy--Schwarz bounds the covariance error by
$\sqrt{3.1/50}s^{-2}N_d<0.25s^{-2}N_d$.
This gives the two slope bounds. Similarly
\[
 \operatorname{Var}T_d^K
 \le\mathbb E(T_d^K-c_s)^2
 \le(\sqrt{3.1}+\sqrt{1/50})^2s^{-2}N_d
 <3.62s^{-2}N_d.
\]
The slope is bounded away from zero by
$2.65b_+^{-2}N_d$, proving the inverse bound.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[The estimators]\label{C-406-72}
For each $d\ge0$, choose the least $K_d^\sharp>d$
such that the total-variation tail bounds of
\cref{C-406-68} for every $N_f\in\mathcal N_f$ and
of \cref{C-375-24} are at most $L^{-d}$ at depth $d$.
Require also their cutoff thresholds,
$K_d^\sharp\ge L^{4d}$ and
$\lceil K_d^\sharp/1260\rceil\ge d$.
All these requirements persist at larger cutoffs,
so $K_d^\sharp$ exists and $K_d^\sharp\ge2d$.

For $d\ge d_{\rm W}$ put
$T_d^\sharp=T_d^{K_d^\sharp}$ and
$m_d^\sharp=m_d^{K_d^\sharp}$. Let $\pi_d$ be the
nearest-point projection onto the real interval
$[m_d^\sharp(b_+),m_d^\sharp(b_-)]$ and define
\[
 \hat b_d=(m_d^\sharp)^{-1}(\pi_d(T_d^\sharp)).
\]
For the finitely many smaller depths put $\hat b_d=b_-$.
On $\mathcal V_{\rm thr}$ define
\[
 \hat b(V)=\lim_{d\to\infty}\hat b_d(V_d),\qquad
 \Delta_d(V)=L^{-2d}
             (T_d^\sharp(V_d)-m_d^\sharp(\hat b(V))),
 \qquad
 \hat N(V)=-\frac{4\hat b(V)^2}{3\ell^3I_B}
                                    \lim_{d\to\infty}\Delta_d(V).
\]
Where the first limit fails, put $\hat b=b_-$;
where the second fails to exist as a finite real
number, use zero for that limit. Put $\Delta_d=0$
for $d<d_{\rm W}$.

These are Borel functions: $T_d^\sharp$ is Borel,
$m_d^\sharp$ has a continuous inverse, and the
convergence sets of sequences of real Borel functions
are Borel. They depend on the common constants,
$g,\ell$ and $\mathcal N_f$, but not on the unknown
labels $b,\mathsf m$ or the particular $N_f$.
\end{definition}

The definition of $\Delta_d$ uses the limiting estimate
$\hat b$, rather than the depth-$d$ estimate. Substituting
$\hat b_d$ would remove the same mean shift which is
used to recover the flavour number.

\begin{lemma}[The pure-gauge thread limit]\label{C-406-73}
The maps $\operatorname{thr}_K$ which retain all block
fields of depths $d\le K$, and use fixed configurations
after depth $K$, push Wilson's measures to laws
converging weakly to $\mu_{\rm thr}^{\rm W}[b]$ along
the full sequence $K\to\infty$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The coordinates through depth $D$ are the image of
$\mu_D^{{\rm W},K}[b]$ under
$\iota_D(V)=(\mathcal M^{D-d}V)_{d\le D}$.
For a continuous function $\Psi_D$ of these finitely
many coordinates, the difference from its limiting
integral is at most
$2\|\Psi_D\|_\infty\tau_{J_g}(K)$ by
\cref{C-375-24}, since $\Psi_D\circ\iota_D$ is
bounded and Borel. The limit is the corresponding
integral for \cref{C-375-25}. Continuous cylinder
functions form an algebra containing constants and
separating points of the compact product
$\mathcal V_{\rm thr}$. Stone--Weierstrass and mass
one extend convergence to every continuous function.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Parameters as functions of the block fields]
\label{C-406-74}
In the common setting of \cref{C-406-69}, the Borel
functions of \cref{C-406-72} recover
\[
  (\hat b,\hat N)=(b,N_f)
       \quad\mu_{\rm thr}^F[N_f;b,\mathsf m]\text{-almost surely}
\]
for every $N_f\in\mathcal N_f\cup\{0\}$ and
$(b,\mathsf m)\in\mathsf W(g)$.

More precisely, for each positive $N_f$ there are
$d_{\rm F},c_{\rm F}$ such that almost surely
$|\hat b_d(V_d)-b|\le c_{\rm F}L^{-d}$ for all
$d\ge d_0(V)$. Under the pure-gauge law, for every
$\epsilon>0$ this bound can be replaced by
$L^{-(3/2-\epsilon)d}$. In both cases
\[
 \Delta_d\longrightarrow-\tfrac34b^{-2}\ell^3N_fI_B
                                                   \quad\text{almost surely}.
\]
Consequently the laws at distinct pairs $(b,N_f)$
are mutually singular.

At a fixed $b$ and positive $N_f$, the laws at two
masses $m_-\le\mathsf m<\mathsf m'\le m_+$ are
mutually absolutely continuous. Writing these laws
as $P,Q$, for every Borel set $E$,
\[
 Q(E)\le(1+M_g)^3P(E)^{2^{-n_{\rm ch}}},\qquad
 P(E)\le(1+M_g)^3Q(E)^{2^{-n_{\rm ch}}},
\]
with the constants of \cref{C-406-55}.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
At $K=K_d^\sharp$ each block law is within $L^{-d}$
in total variation of its limit. This transfers
probabilities of events; it avoids multiplying a
total-variation error by the growing supremum of
$T_d^\sharp$.

The inverse bound and the contraction property of
$\pi_d$ give, for every block field,
\[
 |\hat b_d-b|\le\frac{b_+^2}{2.65N_d}
                              |T_d^\sharp-m_d^\sharp(b)|.
\]
For positive $N_f$, take $d$ large enough for
\cref{C-406-58,C-416-5}. The variance is at most
$C_vN_d$ and the difference between the fermion mean
and $m_d^\sharp(b)$ is at most $\kappa_+L^{2d}$.
Chebyshev's inequality therefore bounds the event
where the difference from the fermion mean exceeds
$\kappa_+L^{2d}$ by
$C_v\ell^3\kappa_+^{-2}L^{-d}$.
Off this event the inverse inequality gives
$|\hat b_d-b|<c_{\rm F}L^{-d}$ with
$c_{\rm F}=b_+^2\kappa_+\ell^{-3}$. Hence the
limiting block law satisfies
\[
 \mu_d^F(|\hat b_d-b|>c_{\rm F}L^{-d})
                    \le(1+C_v\ell^3\kappa_+^{-2})L^{-d}.
\]
These probabilities are summable. Since the thread
law has these block marginals, Borel--Cantelli gives
the asserted rate and $\hat b=b$ almost surely.

Without fermions the mean is exactly $m_d^\sharp(b)$
and the variance is at most $3.62b^{-2}N_d$.
The same argument gives
\[
 \mu_d^{\rm W}(|\hat b_d-b|>L^{-(3/2-\epsilon)d})
 \le0.52b_+^4b^{-2}\ell^{-3}L^{-2\epsilon d}+L^{-d},
\]
because $3.62/2.65^2<0.52$. Borel--Cantelli for
$\epsilon=1/j$, $j\ge1$, gives the statement for
every positive $\epsilon$ on one event of probability one.

On the event $\hat b=b$, in the fermion model write
\[
 \Delta_d=L^{-2d}(T_d^\sharp-\mathbb E_K^{\rm F}T_d^K)
       +L^{-2d}(\mathbb E_K^{\rm F}T_d^K
                                      -\mathbb E_K^{\rm W}T_d^K).
\]
The second term tends to $-3b^{-2}\ell^3N_fI_B/4$
by \cref{C-416-4}, since $K_d^\sharp\ge2d$.
For each $j\ge1$, Chebyshev and total variation
bound the probability that the first term exceeds
$1/j$ in modulus by
$(j^2C_v\ell^3+1)L^{-d}$.
Borel--Cantelli, followed by a countable intersection
over $j$, makes this term tend to zero almost surely.
For Wilson's law the same proof uses the variance
constant $3.62b^{-2}$ and has no mean shift.
This proves the assertions about $\Delta_d$ and $\hat N$.

Each law therefore assigns mass one to the Borel set
$\{\hat b=b,\hat N=N_f\}$. These sets are disjoint
for different pairs, proving mutual singularity.
For the two-mass assertion, the finite-cutoff
inequalities and their passage to weak limits in
\cref{C-406-11} apply to the Borel maps
$\operatorname{thr}_K$ into the compact metric product.
The full weak convergence of these laws is
\cref{C-406-68}. It identifies the limiting pair
with $P,Q$ and gives both displayed inequalities.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Other realizations of the block fields]
\label{C-406-75}
Let $Y$ be Polish, let $f_K$ be Borel maps from the
cutoff configurations to $Y$, and suppose a continuous
map $\varphi:Y\to\mathcal V_{\rm thr}$ satisfies
$\varphi\circ f_K=\operatorname{thr}_K$.
Every weak limit $P$ of the laws pushed forward by
$f_K$ at $(b,N_f,\mathsf m)$ satisfies
\[
 \varphi_*P=\mu_{\rm thr}^F[N_f;b,\mathsf m].
\]
Limits corresponding to distinct $(b,N_f)$ are
mutually singular on $Y$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
For each bounded continuous $h$ on the thread space,
$h\circ\varphi$ is bounded and continuous on $Y$.
Weak convergence and the factorization give convergence
to its integral against $\varphi_*P$.
The full thread limit is already fixed by
\cref{C-406-68,C-406-73}, so uniqueness of weak
limits proves the identity. The inverse images of
the disjoint full-measure sets in \cref{C-406-74}
then prove singularity.
\end{proof}

\section{The next short-distance coefficient}\label{sec:qcdm2-subleading}

The leading action-density correlation is Gaussian. Its first correction
contains both a pure-gauge term and the fermion polarization. We prove
that their sum has coefficient $(8-2N_f)/(3\pi)$ and control the
remainder uniformly in the volume. The cutoff comparison is needed
to turn the estimate in a finite cutoff window into a continuum law.

\begin{definition}[Test pairs]\label{def:pure-test-pairs}
For \(d>0\) and \(0<\vartheta<1\), let
\(\mathfrak T_{\mathbb R^3}(d;\vartheta)\) consist of the
pairs of nonzero nonnegative Lipschitz functions \(f,h\)
for which there are \(x_f,x_h\in\mathbb R^3\) such that
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \operatorname{supp}f\subset\overline B(x_f,d),\qquad
 \operatorname{supp}h\subset\overline B(x_h,d),\\
 d\le\operatorname{dist}(\operatorname{supp}f,\operatorname{supp}h)
                                                  \le6d,\\
 \int f\ge\vartheta d^3\|f\|_\infty,\qquad
 \int h\ge\vartheta d^3\|h\|_\infty,\\
 \operatorname{Lip}f\le(\vartheta d)^{-1}\|f\|_\infty,\qquad
 \operatorname{Lip}h\le(\vartheta d)^{-1}\|h\|_\infty.
 \end{gathered}
\]
\end{definition}

\subsection{Separated pairs and the short-distance scale}

The next coefficient is measured by two nonnegative functions whose
supports have comparable diameters and separation.
Use \(\mathfrak T_{\mathbb R^3}(d;\vartheta)\) from
\cref{def:pure-test-pairs}.

\begin{definition}[The torus class and the witness depth]\label{C-403-3}
For \(20d\le\ell\), define \(\mathfrak T_{T_\ell}(d;\vartheta)\)
by the same support, separation, integral and Lipschitz conditions
as \(\mathfrak T_{\mathbb R^3}(d;\vartheta)\), with the distance and
integration on \(T_\ell\). Write \(\mathfrak T(d;\vartheta)\) when
the underlying space is specified. For either space put
\[
 \mathfrak f=\|f\|_\infty\|h\|_\infty,\qquad
 \mathcal K_q(f,h)=\iint f(x)h(y)|x-y|^{-q}\,dx\,dy,\qquad
 \mathcal K_{\rm free}=\mathcal K_6 .
\]
Here the torus distance is used in the torus integral.
The constants in the action-density expansion are
\[
 c_2=\frac9{16\pi^2},\qquad
 \mathfrak c_1(N_f)=\frac{8-2N_f}{3\pi}.
\]

For the admitted reference coupling \(g\), put
\[
 X_g=L(g^{-2}+B_\sharp),\qquad
 \mathsf b_-=g^{-2}+\bar B,\qquad
 \mathsf b_+=X_g-\bar B,\qquad
 \bar x_s=L^s(X_g+\bar B).
\]
Retain the witness constant \(\mathsf c_W\ge1\) of the lattice
construction, chosen so that
\(C_W(s):=\mathsf c_W(\log\bar x_s)^{2\mathfrak p_0}>4L^2M\).
The witness depth is
\[
 s(d)=\min\{s\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}:L^sd\ge C_W(s)\}.
\]
The minimum exists since an exponential eventually exceeds the
polynomial in \(s\) on the right. In particular,
\[
 K>s(d)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 a_K<\frac{d}{4L^3M}\le\frac d8.
\]
\end{definition}

For either space, the kernel integral satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{C-403-4}
 10^{-q}\vartheta^2d^{6-q}\mathfrak f
 \le\mathcal K_q(f,h)
 \le(4\pi/3)^2d^{6-q}\mathfrak f.
\end{equation}
Indeed the distance between the supports is at least \(d\), and
their diameters are at most \(2d\), so every distance in the
integral is at most \(10d\). The lower bound uses the two integral
lower bounds. The upper bound uses the support volumes and their
separation. On the torus the balls of radius \(d\) have Euclidean
volume because \(20d\le\ell\). In particular, \(\mathcal K_5(f,h)>0\).

These classes contain smooth pairs for every \(0<\vartheta<1\)
and every allowed \(d\). Indeed, \cite[Lem.~127.5]{YMM1}
constructs a smooth function supported in \(B(2de_3,d)\)
whose pair with its reflection across \(x_3=0\) has the
required bounds. The pair also defines a torus pair when
\(20d\le\ell\), since its supports and their distances fit
in one coordinate ball.

Throughout this section the model is the \(SU(2)\) chamber
model with \(r=1/2\) and \(N_f\ge1\). The positive mass window
and the two conditions on the source construction are those of
\cref{sec:qcdm2-setting}. The additional floor on \(h_F\) and the
ceiling \(\gamma_{\rm e}\) are fixed in \cref{C-403-16}.
All constants below are chosen in that order, before a datum.

\subsection{The next coefficient}

The pure gauge contribution to the next coefficient is
\(8/(3\pi)\). The fermion polarization subtracts
\(2N_f/(3\pi)\). We first keep the cutoff in a polynomial
window, then use cutoff convergence and a comparison of
different tori to remove that restriction.

\begin{proposition}[The expansion at finite cutoff]\label{C-403-13}
Assume the constants of \cref{C-403-16}, including
\eqref{eq:C403-F1}. Let \(0<g\le\gamma_{\rm e}\),
\(0<\vartheta<1\) and \(P>1\).
There are \(C_{\rm lat}\ge1\),
\[
 0<d_{\rm e}\le\min\{d_1,d_{\rm T}\},\qquad
 d_1=\min\{(L\mathsf m_+)^{-2},1/64\},
\]
and a nondecreasing function \(\epsilon_1\) on \((0,d_{\rm e}]\)
tending to zero at zero, such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:C403-finite-expansion}
 \begin{split}
 \bigl|S^T_2((0,f),(0,h))
 &-c_2\mathsf b^{-2}
       [\mathcal K_{\rm free}
          +\mathfrak c_1(N_f)\mathsf b^{-1}\mathcal K_5](f,h)\bigr|\\
 &\le
 \left[\epsilon_1(d)\mathsf b^{-3}d
       +C_{\rm lat}\mathsf b^{-2}\frac{a_K}{d}\right]\mathfrak f .
 \end{split}
\end{equation}
This holds for every datum \((g,\ell,K,\mathsf b,\mathsf m)\),
every \(0<d\le d_{\rm e}\) with
\[
 K>s(d),\qquad L^K\le d^{-P},
\]
and every pair in \(\mathfrak T_{T_\ell}(d;\vartheta)\).
It also holds for \(S^T_2[\nu]\), with
\(\nu\in\mathcal G^{\rm tor}_{K,\beta,m_0}\) and
\((f,h)\in\mathfrak T_{\mathbb R^3}(d;\vartheta)\).
Here \(d_{\rm T}\) is the threshold of \cref{C-403-38}.
The constants and \(\epsilon_1\) depend only on \(g,\vartheta,P\)
and the chosen construction constants.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proposition}[The expansion on a fixed torus]\label{C-403-151}
Assume also the floors and ceilings of \cref{C-418-2}.
Fix \(0<g\le\gamma_{\rm e}\), \(\ell\in\mathfrak L(g)\)
and \(0<\vartheta<1\).
There are \(0<d_2\le\min\{d_1,\ell/20\}\) and a
nondecreasing \(\epsilon_2(d)\to0\) as \(d\to0\), independent
of the label in \(\mathsf W(g)\), such that the following hold
for the continuum limit \(S^{(\ell,\mathsf b,\mathsf m)}\)
of \cref{C-418-8}.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] For \(0<d\le d_2\) and
\((f,h)\in\mathfrak T_{T_\ell}(d;\vartheta)\),
\begin{equation}\label{C-403-152}
 \begin{split}
 \bigl|S_2((0,f),(0,h))
 &-c_2\mathsf b^{-2}
       [\mathcal K_{\rm free}
          +\mathfrak c_1(N_f)\mathsf b^{-1}\mathcal K_5](f,h)\bigr|\\
 &\le\epsilon_2(d)\mathsf b^{-3}d\,\mathfrak f .
 \end{split}
\end{equation}
\item[(b)] Along such pairs with \(d\to0\),
\begin{equation}\label{C-403-153}
 \begin{split}
 \mathsf b^{-2}
  &=\lim\frac{S_2((0,f),(0,h))}
                  {c_2\mathcal K_{\rm free}(f,h)},\\
 \mathfrak c_1(N_f)
  &=\lim\frac{\mathsf b^3S_2((0,f),(0,h))
                      -c_2\mathsf b\mathcal K_{\rm free}(f,h)}
                   {c_2\mathcal K_5(f,h)} .
 \end{split}
\end{equation}
Consequently \(N_f=4-\frac{3\pi}{2}\mathfrak c_1(N_f)\)
is determined by these two-point functions.
\item[(c)] Suppose \(S'\) is another such limit on the same torus
with the same first label \(\mathsf b\) and with \(N'_f\ne N_f\).
Its other admitted constants, reference coupling and mass may
differ. Let \(d'_2,\epsilon'_2\) be its threshold and error.
Then the two-point functions differ at every pair of the class
whenever
\[
 d\le\min\{d_2,d'_2\},\qquad
 \epsilon_2(d)+\epsilon'_2(d)
                  <\frac{3\vartheta^2}{8\pi^3}10^{-5}.
\]
In particular this holds at all sufficiently small \(d\).
\end{enumerate}
The threshold and error here may depend on \(\ell\).
\end{proposition}

\begin{theorem}[The continuum coefficient, uniformly in the volume]
\label{C-403-154}
Assume the hypotheses of \cref{C-403-151}.
Fix \(0<g\le\gamma_{\rm e}\) and \(0<\vartheta<1\).
Let \(d_2^G,\epsilon_2^G\) be the threshold and error there
on the least torus \(T_{\ell_G}\), and let
\(d_{\rm T},\epsilon_{\rm T}\) be those of \cref{C-403-38}.
Set
\[
 d_4=\min\{d_2^G,d_{\rm T}\},\qquad
 \epsilon_4(d)=\epsilon_2^G(d)+\epsilon_{\rm T}(d).
\]
These depend only on \(g,\vartheta\) and the construction
constants; \(\epsilon_4\) is nondecreasing and tends to zero.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] For every \(\ell\in\mathfrak L(g)\), every label
\((\mathsf b,\mathsf m)\in\mathsf W(g)\), \(0<d\le d_4\),
and \((f,h)\in\mathfrak T_{T_\ell}(d;\vartheta)\),
\eqref{C-403-152} holds with \(\epsilon_4\) in place of
\(\epsilon_2\).
For \(C^1\) pairs it therefore holds for every continuum limit
with this label. For all pairs in the class, the lattice
two-point functions converge to this value whenever
\(K_j\to\infty\) and
\((\mathsf b_j,\mathsf m_j)\to(\mathsf b,\mathsf m)\)
on the fixed torus.

\item[(b)] Let \(S\) be a continuum limit on \(\mathbb R^3\)
along growing tori, or a volume-first continuum limit, at \(g\),
with label \((\mathsf b,\mathsf m)\in\mathsf W(g)\).
For \(0<d\le d_4\) and
\((f,h)\in\mathfrak T_{\mathbb R^3}(d;\vartheta)\) of class
\(C^1\),
\begin{equation}\label{C-403-155}
 \begin{split}
 \bigl|S_2((0,f),(0,h))
 &-c_2\mathsf b^{-2}
       [\mathcal K_{\rm free}
          +\mathfrak c_1(N_f)\mathsf b^{-1}\mathcal K_5](f,h)\bigr|\\
 &\le\epsilon_4(d)\mathsf b^{-3}d\,\mathfrak f .
 \end{split}
\end{equation}
Moreover its difference from
\[
 S^{(\ell_G,\mathsf b,\mathsf m)}_2
       ((0,f^{\langle\ell_G\rangle}),
        (0,h^{\langle\ell_G\rangle}))
\]
has modulus at most
\(\epsilon_{\rm T}(d)\mathsf b^{-3}d\,\mathfrak f\).
The superscript denotes periodization after placing the two
supports in one fundamental domain.

\item[(c)] The identities \eqref{C-403-153} hold for \(S\) in
(b) along \(C^1\) test pairs. Thus these two-point functions
determine \(\mathsf b\) and \(N_f\).
If \(S'\) has the same first label and a different number of
flavours, the two-point functions differ on every \(C^1\)
test pair at every \(d\le\min\{d_4,d'_4\}\) satisfying
\[
 \epsilon_4(d)+\epsilon'_4(d)
                  <\frac{3\vartheta^2}{8\pi^3}10^{-5}.
\]

\item[(d)] For the limits in (b) the following two comparisons
hold.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] Choose an admitted pure-theory construction as in
\cref{C-350-3}(c), with blocking factor \(\bar L\), constants
\(B_\sharp^0,\bar B^0\), and ceilings
\(\gamma_{\rm e}^0,\gamma_W^{\rm sd}\).
Use one constant assignment satisfying the numerical hypotheses
of \cite[Prop.~69.1]{YMM1}, and require the full hypotheses of
its history induction \cite[Prop.~69.3 and Thm.~AC]{YMM1}
at every running sequence, radius profile, lattice and step datum
used in the pure comparison. In particular, the running sequences
are admissible and a torus of side \(2\bar L^m\) satisfies
\(M^0R^0(x_K)\le\bar L^m\), with the pure construction
constants; thus \cite[Cor.~69.4]{YMM1} applies.
Let
\[
 0<g_0\le\bar L^{-1/4}
                    \min\{\gamma_{\rm e}^0,\gamma_W^{\rm sd}\}.
\]
Suppose \(S^0\) is a pure-theory limit along growing tori
at \(g_0\), with first-passage labels
\(\bar L^{-K_j}\beta_j\to\mathsf b\).
There are \(d^0>0\) and \(\epsilon^0(d)\to0\), depending only
on \(g_0,\vartheta\) and the admitted extended list of
pure-theory constants, such that
\[
 \begin{split}
 \bigl|S^0_2(f,h)
 &-c_2\mathsf b^{-2}
        [\mathcal K_{\rm free}
                +\tfrac8{3\pi}\mathsf b^{-1}\mathcal K_5](f,h)\bigr|\\
 &\le\epsilon^0(d)\mathsf b^{-3}d\,\mathfrak f
 \end{split}
\]
for \(C^1\) pairs in
\(\mathfrak T_{\mathbb R^3}(d;\vartheta)\), \(d\le d^0\).
Hence \(S_2((0,f),(0,h))\ne S^0_2(f,h)\) whenever
\[
 d\le\min\{d_4,d^0\},\qquad
 \epsilon_4(d)+\epsilon^0(d)
                    <\frac{3\vartheta^2}{8\pi^3}10^{-5}.
\]
Such pure limits exist if
\[
 \mathsf b\in I(g_0)
 =(g_0^{-2}+\bar B^0,\,
          \bar L(g_0^{-2}+B_\sharp^0)-\bar B^0].
\]
In particular, if
\[
 \mathsf b\ge 2\bar B^0+\bar L^{1/2}
        \max\{(\gamma_{\rm e}^0)^{-2},
                         (\gamma_W^{\rm sd})^{-2}\},
\]
one can take \(g_0=(\mathsf b-2\bar B^0)^{-1/2}\).

\item[(ii)] For a \(C^1\) pair in
\(\mathfrak T_{\mathbb R^3}(d;\vartheta)\), \(d\le d_4\), put
\(f_\lambda=f(\cdot/\lambda)\),
\(h_\lambda=h(\cdot/\lambda)\), \(0<\lambda\le1\).
Then
\begin{equation}\label{C-403-156}
 \begin{split}
 \bigl|S_2((0,f_\lambda),(0,h_\lambda))
 &-c_2\mathsf b^{-2}\mathcal K_{\rm free}(f,h)
       -\lambda c_2\mathfrak c_1(N_f)
                    \mathsf b^{-3}\mathcal K_5(f,h)\bigr|\\
 &\le\epsilon_4(\lambda d)\mathsf b^{-3}\lambda d\,\mathfrak f.
 \end{split}
\end{equation}
Thus the quotient by \(\lambda\) after subtraction of the
leading term tends to
\(c_2\mathfrak c_1(N_f)\mathsf b^{-3}\mathcal K_5(f,h)\).
If \(N_f\ne4\), then
\[
 \begin{split}
 |S_2((0,f_\lambda),(0,h_\lambda))
       -S_2((0,f_{\lambda/2}),(0,h_{\lambda/2}))|
 \ge
 \left[\frac{3\vartheta^2}{16\pi^3}10^{-5}
                 -\frac32\epsilon_4(\lambda d)\right]
                    \mathsf b^{-3}\lambda d\,\mathfrak f>0
 \end{split}
\]
whenever
\(\epsilon_4(\lambda d)<\vartheta^2 10^{-5}/(8\pi^3)\).
If \(N_f=4\), \eqref{C-403-156} instead gives an error
\(o(\lambda)\) after subtraction of the leading term.
\end{enumerate}
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

The proofs are in
\cref{sec:proof-C40313,sec:proof-C403151,sec:proof-C403154},
after the source-energy estimates and coefficient calculations.

\subsection{The proof and its estimates}

The proof first replaces the correlation by mixed derivatives of the
source energies, with an error smaller than the desired correction
(\cref{C-403-30}). One complex field scale then separates their terms
of orders four and six from the higher terms (\cref{C-403-33}).
The order-four term is the free
template. The order-six term is a constrained Gaussian coefficient;
comparison of the constrained and unconstrained kernels identifies
its pure-gauge and fermion contributions (\cref{C-403-35}). Finally,
the comparison of two volumes in \cref{C-403-38} and the cutoff
convergence in \cref{C-418-8} give the continuum result, as proved in
\cref{sec:proof-C403154}.

The source-derivative bounds are proved below. The pure-gauge
Gaussian calculations used in the coefficient identification are
in \cref{sec:qcdm2-pure-coefficients}.

\subsection{Histories with no large-field region}

For an action source $(w,0)$, the source enters
the bare density.  The calibrations, tests, history
weights and coordinate maps are those at zero source.
This permits an exact summation of all extensions
of a history before estimating its effective density.

\begin{lemma}\label{C-403-65}
At a datum with the prescribed calibrations, let
$1\le k\le K$ and let $h_\emptyset^{(k)}$
be the sequence of empty outcomes through $k$.
Its regions satisfy
\[
 \Omega_j=\Lambda_j=T_\ell,\qquad
 Z_j=S_j^{\rm pr}=\varnothing,\qquad 1\le j\le k.
\]
Its layers below $k$ are empty and its last
layer is $T_\ell$.  Its generators are exactly
those of $\mathrm{Gr}_k$, and both its coordinates
and its free coordinates are level-$k$ block
fields.  On the domain of its coordinate map,
$\xi_h^{\rm co\prime}(U)=\mathcal M^kU$;
the domain contains $\{\mathfrak w_h\ne0\}$.
It has no outer bonds.  Its evaluation
configurations over a block field $V$ are
the adapted elements of the collared background
over $V$.

For $h\in\mathcal H_{k'}$, $k'\ge k$, the
following are equivalent:
\[
 Z_k(h)=\varnothing,\qquad
 Z_j(h)=\varnothing\ (j\le k),\qquad
 h|_k=h_\emptyset^{(k)}.
\]
For every complex Lipschitz function $w$,
\[
 \sum_{\substack{h\in\mathcal H_K\\Z_k(h)=\varnothing}}
       \operatorname{Ber}\check\tau_h^F[w,0]
                                   (\mathsf X_h^{\rm fr})
 =
       \operatorname{Ber}\check\tau_{h_\emptyset^{(k)}}^F[w,0]
                                   (\mathcal V_k).
\]
Every term here is entire in the finitely many
values of $w$ at bare plaquette barycentres.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Empty sets are admitted outcomes.  Their hulls
and enlargements are empty, so starting from
the empty input region gives
$\Omega_j^c=Z_j=\varnothing$ and hence
$\Lambda_j=T_\ell$ at every successive step.
The prescribed regions lie in
$\Omega_j\setminus\Lambda_j$, so are empty.
It follows that every earlier layer is empty
and all remaining fermion places are at
level $k$.

The determining bonds below $k$ have no
endpoint in the next full region and hence
are absent.  The external fluctuation bonds
are absent for the same reason.  At level
$k$ the determining bonds are all the
bonds of that lattice.  The coordinate
product therefore reduces to $\mathcal V_k$,
and the coordinate map to $\mathcal M^k$.
The support-domain property of the canonical
coordinates gives the stated inclusion.
Every bare bond is an inner bond, leaving
no prescribed outer value in the definition
of the evaluation configurations.

The large-field regions increase with the
level.  Thus $Z_k=\varnothing$ implies
$Z_j=\varnothing$ for $j\le k$.
Conversely the defining formula for each
$Z_j$ contains the enlarged plaquette sets,
fluctuation sets and the three pieces of
its recursive outcome.  If $Z_j$ is empty,
each such set is empty.  The recursion
then starts and ends with empty collar
and rim, so its bond set is empty as well.
The outcome is the empty one.
This proves the equivalences.

Set
\[
 \varsigma_w(U)=
 e^{-A(\beta-a_K^{-1}w,U)}\det(D[U]+m_0).
\]
It is continuous, gauge invariant and
bounded on the compact bare configuration
space.  It is entire in the source values,
uniformly bounded in $U$ on their bounded
sets.  The exact Berezin and coordinate
identities for a history give
\[
 \operatorname{Ber}\check\tau_h^F[w,0]
                  (\mathsf X_h^{\rm fr})
       =\int\mathfrak w_h(U)\varsigma_w(U)\,dU.
\]
The weight is bounded and source independent,
so each term is entire.

The gauge history consistency theorem applies
at the calibration thresholds:
$\mathsf t_j\ge\gamma^{-2}\ge e^{18\mathfrak p_0}$,
$t\mapsto A_0t^{-1/2}(\log t)^{\mathfrak p_0}$
decreases there, and its value at
$\gamma^{-2}$ satisfies
\[
 \varepsilon(\gamma^{-2})
       =A_0\gamma(\log\gamma^{-2})^{\mathfrak p_0}
       \le\min\{\bar\varepsilon/2,\varepsilon_\flat\}.
\]
These are among the history ceilings checked in
\cite[proof of Lem. 82.5]{YMM1}.
Summing the coordinate measures over
all extensions of $h_\emptyset^{(k)}$
therefore gives its block pushforward.
This pushforward preserves total mass.
The equivalences just proved identify the
extensions with $Z_k(h)=\varnothing$,
giving the asserted equality.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Source derivatives and their spatial weights}

The estimates below distinguish the scale of a source from the scale
at which an activity is read.  Write
\[
 a_l=L^la_K,\qquad D_i=\{|\lambda|<\bar\lambda_i\},\qquad
 q_n=\min\{2L^{-n}(1+n\log L)^{2\mathfrak p_0},
                    2^{10/9}L^{-8n/9}\}.
\]
The radii in Lemma~\ref{C-403-33} satisfy
$(\bar\lambda_i/\bar\lambda_{l-1})^2\le q_{i+1-l}<1/4$.
All source derivatives are evaluated at zero source.  A direction
$\mathsf g$ is specified on bare plaquettes; it acts by
$w=z\mathsf g$.  Equivalently, extend these finitely many values to a
Lipschitz function on the torus as in Lemma~\ref{C-403-44}.
For a plaquette $p$, write $\delta_p$ for its coordinate direction.
Linearity gives
$\partial_{\mathsf g}=\sum_p\mathsf g(p)\partial_{\delta_p}$.

\begin{definition}[Weights and source responses]\label{C-403-43}
\begin{enumerate}
\item
Choose $c'\ge18$ so that every polymer $X$ has diameter at most
$c'M(1+d_l(X))/2$ in the units of its level, and put
\[
 \kappa_{\mathrm s}
   =\min\{\kappa/(8c'),\,1/c',\,1/4\},\qquad
 \delta_l(Y;S)=\frac{\operatorname{dist}(Y,S)}{Ma_l}.
\]
Here polymers and cells denote their closed sets of points; distances
on a torus are torus distances.  The diameter assertion follows by
joining the centres of its at most $8(1+d_l(X))$ cubes along a
wall-connected chain: their union has diameter at most
$(8d_l(X)+7+\sqrt3)M\le9M(1+d_l(X))$.

A weight system is a finite family
$\mathscr S=((S_s,\kappa_{(s)}))_s$ of nonempty sets and positive
rates with $\sum_s\kappa_{(s)}\le2\kappa_{\mathrm s}$.  Define
\[
 W_l(Y)=\exp\!\left(\sum_s\kappa_{(s)}\delta_l(Y;S_s)\right),
 \qquad
 \mathcal C_l(\mathscr S)=\sum_cW_l(c)^{-1/2},
\]
where $c$ runs over the cells of level $l$.  A single set $S$ means
rate $\kappa_{\mathrm s}$; two sets mean that rate on each.  The
union of two systems multiplies their weights.

For a family $F$ at level $l$ and $D\subset\mathbb C$, set
\begin{equation}\label{eq:C403-weighted-family}
 \|F\|_{l;D;\mathscr S}
 =\sup_\square\sum_{X\supset\square}e^{\kappa d_l(X)}W_l(X)
   \sup_{\lambda\in D}\sup_P
       \|F(X;P,\cdot;\lambda)\|_{h^{(l)}} .
\end{equation}
The last supremum is over the regular complex pairs on $X$ at
$(\alpha_0,\alpha_1)$.  Thus both suprema inside the sum may use a
different pair and a different $\lambda$ for each polymer.
For the scalar part, local on $X$, also use
\[
 \|F_0\|^{\mathrm{arr}}_{l;D;\mathscr S}
 =\sup_Xe^{(\kappa+1)d_l(X)}W_l(X)
             \sup_{\lambda\in D}\|F_0(X;\lambda)\|_X .
\]
Point $F_0(X)$ equally at the sites of $X$.  This array norm bounds
the pointed norm at rate $\kappa+1$, polymer by polymer.

For a step direction
$\delta=(\delta^{\mathrm p},\delta^{\mathrm o})$, put the weight
$W_{i+1}(Y)$ on each term at $Y$ in its scalar, fermionic and
quadratic-origin norms.  Denote the resulting sizes by
$\epsilon_{V;\mathscr S}$, $\epsilon_{F;\mathscr S}$ and
$\|\cdot\|_{\star;\mathscr S}$.  The distances in these weights are
in the units of the \emph{output} level $i+1$.
For a scalar- or matrix-valued function $c$ on bare sites, set
\[
 \langle c\rangle_{l;D;S}
 =\sup_\square e^{\kappa_{\mathrm s}\delta_l(\square;S)}
       (M^3L^{3l})^{-1}
       \sum_{x\in\square}\sup_{\lambda\in D}|c(x;\lambda)| .
\]
The matrix norm is the operator norm.

If $\mathsf g$ is supported in a closed ball of radius
$r\ge a_K$, define
\[
 e_l[\mathsf g]
 =\|\mathsf g\|_\infty a_l^{-1}
                   \min\{1,(r/a_l)^3\}.
\]
For the separated pair $(f,h)$ at distance scale $\mathsf d\ge a_K$,
write
\[
 \mathfrak f=\|f\|_\infty\|h\|_\infty,\qquad
 e_l[f,h]=\mathfrak f\,a_l^{-2}
                  \min\{1,(\mathsf d/a_l)^{5/2}\},\qquad
 \mathfrak l_l=1+\log^+(a_l/\mathsf d).
\]
Use $r=\mathsf d$ for $f,h$, and $r=a_K$ for $\delta_p$.
The choice $r=\infty$, with $S$ equal to the whole space, imposes
no support restriction and gives weight one and
$e_l[\mathsf g]=\|\mathsf g\|_\infty a_l^{-1}$.

\item
Let $\widetilde E_i[\mathcal V;\mathcal V^{\mathrm o}]$ denote
the activity obtained by the step from level $i$, before removing
its vacuum and mass numbers.  Its three origins are the restriction
of $\mathcal V^{\mathrm o}$ to the tested real fluctuations, the
scalar part $\mathcal V_0$, and $\mathcal V_{\ge2}$.  Include the
Gaussian cluster sum of $\mathcal V^{\mathrm o}$ at threshold
$\infty$; do not include the localised logarithms of the
normalisers, which do not depend on the source.
Assume $\|\mathcal V^{\mathrm o}\|_{\star,\lambda_V}\le w_*/2$.
The tests and Gaussian covariance are those at
$(\mathsf t_i,\xi_i(\lambda))$ in Lemma~\ref{C-403-33}.

At zero source the base point is
$(\mathfrak V_i(\lambda),\mathcal V^{\mathrm q})$.
Write $D\widetilde E_i$ and $D^2\widetilde E_i$ for its first and
second derivatives there.  A direction has a potential component
and a quadratic-origin component, as in
Lemma~\ref{C-403-45}.

\item
The direct source direction $\mathcal V_i^w[\mathsf g]$ is the
variation of
\[
 a_K^{-1}\sum_p\mathsf g(p)
      \bigl[a_p(\mathsf U'(\lambda B))-a_p(\mathsf U)\bigr].
\]
