$\bar\epsilon_V=C_V^\lambda c_\lambda^{-1/2}$,
$\bar\epsilon_F=(C_F^\lambda+C_\eta)c_\lambda^{-1/2}$ and
$p_i=e^{-\gamma_{\mathrm{tail}}\mathfrak b(\mathsf t_i)^2/2}$.
The four scalar vertex families have norms bounded by
\[
 K_P|\lambda|\delta(\mathsf t_i),\quad
 \frac{10}9K_P|\lambda|\delta(\mathsf t_i),\quad
 \frac{10}9K_P|\lambda|\delta(\mathsf t_i),\quad
 c_h\beta_\lambda K_{\mathrm{old}}/a_{\mathrm{an}} .
\]
Their admission sizes satisfy
\[
 \mathsf n^{\mathrm{int}}
      \le\frac{34}9K_P|\lambda|\delta(\mathsf t_i),\qquad
 \mathsf n'\le c_h\beta_\lambda K_{\mathrm{old}}/a_{\mathrm{an}},
 \qquad
 \mathsf n^{\mathrm{int}}+\mathsf n'
              \le\bar\epsilon_V\le c_{\mathrm{cl}}/4=w_*/4 .
\]
They are holomorphic on the field polydisc, the first and
fourth vanish at zero, and the middle two vanish to order
three.  The pointed scalar expansion therefore gives
\begin{equation}\label{C-403-73}
 |\mathbf F^{\mathrm v}(X,P,z;\lambda)|
 \le K_{\mathbf M}^{\mathrm v}
       \left(\frac9{32}K_P^{-1}\mathsf n^{\mathrm{int}}
             +\frac19K_\Lambda^{-1}\mathsf n'+p_i\right)
                   e^{-\kappa_+d_{i+1}(X)}
 \le K_{\mathbf M}^{\mathrm v}(\bar\epsilon_V+p_i)
                   e^{-\kappa_+d_{i+1}(X)}.
\end{equation}
The fermion insertion at a fixed pointer is bounded by
the fermion potential termwise, so its pointed activity
has norm at most
$K'_M\bar\epsilon_Fe^{-\kappa_+d_{i+1}(X)}$.
Summing with
$\sup_\square\sum_{X\supset\square}
 e^{-(\kappa_+-\kappa)d_{i+1}(X)}\le C_E$
gives
$K_M^\bullet(\bar\epsilon_V+\bar\epsilon_F+p_i)$,
where $K_M^\bullet=K_M+C_EK_{\mathbf M}^{\mathrm v}$.
The same bound holds in the array norm because
$\kappa_+\ge\kappa+1$, and on the infinite lattice.
All suprema over $\lambda$ remain inside these sums.

Removing the scalar value at the trivial configuration
costs at most a factor two, for the family and at every
pointer.  Translation covariance under $M\mathbb Z^3$
identifies the value removed on a cube with the sum of
its site values.  Removing the fixed coupling term adds
at most $C_w\phi(x_i)$: the normalised action family has
norm at most one in both norms.
Hence
\[
 \|F^{(i+1)}_0\|_{i+1;D_i}
 \le2K_M^\bullet(C_V^\lambda+C_F^\lambda+C_\eta+2)
                    c_\lambda^{-1/2}+C_w\phi(x_i)\le1 .
\]
This completes the induction.

All expansions converge uniformly with these bounds.
Their summands are jointly holomorphic in
$(\lambda,x',P)$, as are the scalar localisations and
the pointed terms.  The latter can also be formed by
inserting a pointer parameter into the same expansion.
For the scalar pointed terms, the four admitted families
are jointly holomorphic and obey the admission bounds
uniformly, so the scalar pointing theorem applies with
the same extra parameters.
The substitution $(\lambda,B)\mapsto(-\lambda,-B)$
fixes the covariance, tests and quadratic origin and
interchanges the potentials at $\lambda$ and $-\lambda$.
The expansion and its pointing commute with this
orthogonal change of variables.  Thus their outputs
are even in $\lambda$.
At $\lambda=1$ all the covariance, vertex, extraction
and pointing rules coincide with those of the original
step.  Induction proves equality there.

For completeness, we construct the source neighbourhood.
Its relative weight at step $i$ is
\[
 v_i^\lambda=-\lambda^2L^{K-i}w/\xi_i(\lambda),\qquad
 |v_i^\lambda|\le
                  2\lambda_\circ^2\|w\|_\infty/\mathsf b .
\]
The quadratic source origin has norm
$\le C_v^{\mathrm q}\sup|v_i^\lambda|$.
The linear term has size at most
\[2\alpha_0C_{\mathrm{lin}}c_\lambda^{-1/2}\|w\|_\sharp.\]
The higher source vertices and
$\lambda^2\sigma_i(w,0)$ are holomorphic and vanish at
$w=0$.  On a fixed finite datum they are bounded on
$|\lambda|\le\lambda_\circ$, $\|w\|_\sharp<4\varrho$.

Suppose the preceding steps are formed on a source ball
of radius $\varepsilon_i$.  Their activities are uniformly
bounded there by the expansion estimate.
The differences between the next potential and its
zero-source value, and between its quadratic origin and
$\mathcal V^{\mathrm q}$, therefore have a finite bound
$S_i(\lambda_\circ)$.  This includes the old-family
variations, read by their finite-lag estimates.
Schwarz's lemma permits the choice
\[
 \varepsilon_{i+1}
 =\min\left\{\frac{\varepsilon_i}{2},\,
       \frac{\varepsilon_i}{S_i}
                   \min\{c_{\mathrm{cl}}/4,w_*/8\}\right\},
\]
with the second entry omitted if $S_i=0$.
On this smaller ball the potential size is at most
$c_{\mathrm{cl}}/2$ and the quadratic-origin norm at
most $5w_*/64+w_*/8<w_*/4$.
The expansion is thus jointly holomorphic.
Its parity follows as before, including the linear
source term, which is odd in both $\lambda$ and $B$.
Starting with $\varepsilon_0=4\varrho$ proves (1).

It remains to verify the exact identity in (3).
Let $0<\lambda\le1$ be real and let $W$ pass the
output density test.  For $B$ in the calibration box,
$\lambda B$ remains in that box.  The chart at
$\lambda B$ is defined, its fluctuation test equals one,
and its input block field $V_W(\lambda B)$ passes the
input density test.
The vertex sum identities hold at this point.  In the
scaled fluctuation coordinates they read
\begin{align*}
 \sum_Y\mathcal V^{\mathrm g,\lambda}(Y;P_W,B)
  ={}&\mathsf J_W(\lambda B)
       -\frac{\mathsf t_i}{\lambda^2}G_W(\lambda B)
       -\frac{\xi_i(\lambda)}{\lambda^2}
                    [\mathbb F_W(\lambda B)-\mathbb F_W(0)]\\
    &+\frac12(B,\widehat{\mathsf G}_WB)_1
        +\frac{\tau_i(\lambda)}2(B,\mathsf B^\circ B)_1 .
\end{align*}
With $\mathsf A^\circ=\mathsf B^\circ+\widehat{\mathsf G}_W$
and $C^\circ=(\mathsf A^\circ)^{-1}$,
\begin{align*}
 e^{-\frac12(B,\widehat{\mathsf G}_WB)_1
        -\frac{\tau}2(B,\mathsf B^\circ B)_1}\,dB
 ={}&\tau^{-\dim B_i/2}
      \left(\int e^{-\frac12(B_1,\mathsf A^\circ B_1)_1}\,dB_1\right)\\
    &\hspace{12mm}\cdot d\mu_{\tau^{-1}C^\circ}(B)
                                      e^{\mathcal V^{\mathrm q}(B)} .
\end{align*}
Thus the gauge part has precisely the announced Jacobian,
gauge fixing and action weight, including its scalar
Gaussian factor.

The fermion substitution and shift give the fermion
vertex and its normaliser at the same field
$\mathsf U'(\lambda B)$.  The old-family and mass
variations add to the differences between their values
at that field and the background.  The bracket sum
identity ensures this also for the scalar localisation.
At nonzero source the terms of orders one, two and at
least three add to the full source weight on the fibre.
The Gaussian quadratic-origin sum is restored to the
level-$i+1$ scalar activity and energy, including at
nonzero source.  The remaining joined integral is the
exponential of the new activity sum.
Removing the prescribed numbers changes only their
placement in the level-$i+1$ form, and
\[
 \lambda^{-2}L^i\xi_i(\lambda)
   =\lambda^{-2}L^{i+1}\xi_{i+1}(\lambda)+L^{i+1}b_{i+1}.
\]
This proves the one-step identity up to a nonzero
constant independent of field and source.

At level zero the form is
$e^{-A(\beta/\lambda^2-a_K^{-1}w,U)-S_F(U)}$.
Fubini's theorem composes the finite chart integrals.
Each chart lies in the fibre over its output block
field, so all kernels are evaluated at one bare
configuration $U$.  Their Berezin integrals compose
to $T^F_{h_\emptyset}[U]$.  Completing the square at
each step has Berezin Jacobian one and produces
$\theta^{-\dim H_{i+1}}\det\Gamma_i[U]$.
The determinant identity in
Proposition~\ref{C-403-58} gives its value at $\Psi_j=0$;
its hypothesis $m_0\le L^{-j}$ follows from
$m_0=L^{-K}\mathsf m\le L^{-K}/2$.
Integrating the remaining generators gives the original
bare determinant.
Finally the coupling identities telescope to
\eqref{eq:C403-scaled-telescoping}, while the mass
members start at $s_0=\sigma_0=0$.  This proves (3).
\end{proof}

\subsection{The response recursion gives the source derivatives}

The response families need not coincide polymer by polymer
with derivatives of the original flow.  Their sums do coincide
after reading all legs at the current level.  This is the
identity needed for source energies and observables.

\begin{lemma}[Derivatives of the flow]\label{C-403-44}
In the setting of Proposition~\ref{C-403-33-flow}, the
objects of Definition~\ref{C-403-43} at level $l$ are
holomorphic and even on $D_{l-1}$.
The input directions satisfy
$\delta_i[\mathsf g](-\lambda,-B)
 =\delta_i[\mathsf g](\lambda,B)$.
On $|\lambda|<\bar\lambda_j$, for $l\le j$, the following
identities hold.
\begin{enumerate}
\item
For every direction $\mathsf g$,
\[
 \sum_X\left.\partial_z
                   \mathfrak E_l(X;z\mathsf g,0)\right|_{z=0}
       =\sum_X\mathfrak e_l[\mathsf g](X).
\]
The derivative of the field-dependent activities through
level $l$, together with the mass term, is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:C403-first-total}
 \sum_{l'\le l}\sum_X\mathbf P^{(l')}[\mathsf g](X)
       -L^{-l}\mathsf S_1(\lambda^4\mathfrak N_l[\mathsf g]\,\cdot).
\end{equation}
This is an identity of functions of the fields at level $l$,
at backgrounds of real block fields passing the density test,
including the trivial block field.  All formal legs of lower
levels are read at level $l$.
The mass coefficients satisfy
\[
 \lambda^2\partial_{\mathsf g}\sigma_l(x)
  =\lambda^4\mathfrak N_l[\mathsf g](x)
   -\sum_{l'\le l}L^{l-l'}
       (\lambda^4\mathfrak n_{l'}[\mathsf g]
          -\lambda^2\partial_{\mathsf g}\nu_{l'})(y_{l'}(x)).
\]
The direct action-source term stands beside
\eqref{eq:C403-first-total}; its derivative is
$a_K^{-1}\sum_p\mathsf g(p)a_p(\mathsf U)$.

\item
For the pair $(f,h)$,
\[
 \mathsf n_l^\lambda
  =\sum_X\left.\partial_{z_1}\partial_{z_2}
       \mathfrak E_l(X;z_1f+z_2h,0)\right|_{z=0}
  =\sum_X\mathfrak e_l[f,h](X).
\]
The mixed derivative of the field-dependent terms is
$\sum_{l'\le l}\sum_X\mathbf Q^{(l')}[f,h](X)$,
in the same sense as (1).  The mixed derivative of the
direct action-source term is zero.

\item
On $\mathbb Z^3$, in the constant direction $1$,
$\mathfrak n_l^\infty[1]$ and
$\mathfrak N_l^\infty[1]$ are invariant under translations
by $M\mathbb Z^3$ in level-$l$ units.
For the constant-source chain,
\[
 \partial_c\sigma_k^{\mathrm c}(0)
       =\sum_{l\le k}L^{k-l}\partial_c\nu_l^\infty,
 \qquad
 \partial_c\nu_l^\infty
       =-\mathfrak s_l^{-1}
           \sum_{X,p}\operatorname{ord}_0[\mathsf k_{X,p}](y).
\]
In the last expression the kernels are those of
$\widetilde{\mathbf P}^{\infty(l)}[1]$ at $\lambda=1$.
The expression has the same value at every site $y$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The recursion is first justified level by level.
The derivatives of the expansion in Lemma~\ref{C-403-45}
are defined and holomorphic for directions of finite size.
The direct source direction has finite size by
Lemma~\ref{C-403-47}; the old scalar and fermionic
variations have finite size by Lemma~\ref{C-403-46}.
The moments of a quadratic family at a site are bounded
by $4A_\kappa^2h_F^{-2}$ times its fibre norm at the
trivial pair.  Cauchy's estimate on $D_{l-1}$ bounds
their $\lambda^4$ coefficient.
Thus $\mathfrak n_l,\mathfrak N_i$ are finite, as are
their mass-variation directions.
Removing scalar values costs at most another copy of the
norm, and the extracted forms cost at most
$K_\mu^{\mathrm s}-K_\mu$ copies, by the piecewise
mass-extraction estimate.  The coefficient bound
$|\lambda^4a^{[4]}_{X,p}|\le
\sup_{D_{l-1}}|a_{X,p}|$ is sufficient here.
These estimates involve only preceding levels, so they
close a finite induction without using the quantitative
response bounds to be proved later.

All localisations and background walk terms are
holomorphic in $\lambda$; finite differences and moment
extraction are linear operations.  The expansion
commutes with $B\mapsto-B$.  Its input directions at
$(-\lambda,-B)$ equal those at $(\lambda,B)$, because
the direct vertex reads $\lambda B$, the mass direction
has the factor $\lambda^4$, and the preceding families
are even.  Induction proves the asserted holomorphy
and parity.

An arbitrary plaquette direction can be inserted into
the original Lipschitz source flow.  Define
\[
 \varphi_p(x)=\max\{0,1-2\sqrt2\,|x-x(p)|/a_K\},\qquad
 \widehat{\mathsf g}=\sum_p\mathsf g(p)\varphi_p .
\]
Distinct barycentres have distance at least $a_K/\sqrt2$,
so the open supports of these tents are disjoint.
Thus
\[
 \widehat{\mathsf g}(x(p))=\mathsf g(p),\quad
 \|\widehat{\mathsf g}\|_\infty=\|\mathsf g\|_\infty,\quad
 \operatorname{Lip}\widehat{\mathsf g}
           \le2\sqrt2\,a_K^{-1}\|\mathsf g\|_\infty,\quad
 \|z\widehat{\mathsf g}\|_\sharp
           \le80\sqrt2\,Ma_K^{-1}|z|\|\mathsf g\|_\infty .
\]
The source neighbourhood in
Proposition~\ref{C-403-33-flow} therefore admits this
direction.  Differentiating there shows that the actual
source-flow derivatives are holomorphic and even in
$\lambda$.  Since $\lambda_\circ<\bar\lambda_j$ was
arbitrary, this holds on the claimed disc.

We prove (1) by induction on $l$.  The assertion is
empty at level zero.
First, the usual chain rule applies to the cluster
expansion with source-dependent origins.
Indeed, write their joint input as
$\mathcal W(z)=\mathcal W(0)+z\dot{\mathcal W}+z^2R(z)$.
The expansion at
$\mathcal W(0)+t\dot{\mathcal W}+sR(z)$ is holomorphic
in $(t,s,z)$.  On $(t,s)=(z,z^2)$, differentiation at
zero gives $D\widetilde E_i[\dot{\mathcal W}]$.

Second, totals depend only on totals of the directions.
The sum of $\widetilde E_i[\mathcal V;\mathcal V^{\mathrm o}]$
is the logarithm of the joined integral with weight
$e^{\mathcal V^{\mathrm o}}$, tests, and $e^{\mathcal V}$.
The Gaussian cluster sum restores precisely the
normalising denominator of the joined integral.
This sum therefore reads
$\sum_Y(\mathcal V(Y)+\mathcal V^{\mathrm o}(Y))$ alone.
Two inputs with the same total have equal exponentials
of their activity sums.  Their continuous logarithms
agree at the base point, so their difference, a constant
in $2\pi i\mathbb Z$, is zero on the common parameter
disc.  Their first and mixed derivatives agree.
Reading the formal legs at level $i+1$ is a unital
Grassmann-algebra homomorphism which fixes the
fluctuation generators.  It commutes with their Berezin
integral, the exponential and the logarithm.  Thus the
same assertion holds after reading the legs.

The localisations in Definition~\ref{C-403-43} have the
required totals.  In degree zero the bracket
localisation sums to the variation of the scalar array;
its equal shares sum to the original family.
For fermionic terms, the finite differences sum to
the term at full shift, and the terms in the
long-lag decomposition sum to the family at every
shift amplitude.  Consequently the three directions
sum respectively to the direct source variation,
the mass variation, and the variation of the old
family total.
This is first an identity at real $0<\lambda\le1$,
where $\lambda B$ passes the tests, and then on $D_i$
by holomorphy.

At the background of a block field $W$ passing the
output test, the field $\mathsf U'(\lambda B)$ for
real tested fluctuation is, up to the site gauge
factor, the background of its input block field.
That input block field passes its density test.
The same is true at $B=0$.
Joint gauge invariance and the induction hypothesis
therefore identify the derivatives of the actual
field-dependent exponent with the response totals
at both ends of the variation.
It follows that the derivative of the actual step
input has the total of $\delta_i[\mathsf g]$.
The preceding logarithm argument identifies the
total of its new activity derivative with
$\widetilde{\mathbf P}^{(i+1)}[\mathsf g]$.
At the trivial block field this proves the identity
for the scalar source energy.

The mass bookkeeping is exact even though its
extracted coefficients differ from the response
coefficients.  The actual derivative of the new
activity has total
\[
 \mathbf P^{(i+1)}[\mathsf g]
 +L^{-(i+1)}
     \mathsf S_1((\lambda^2\partial_{\mathsf g}\nu_{i+1}
              -\lambda^4\mathfrak n_{i+1}[\mathsf g])\,\cdot).
\]
The mass term has derivative
$-L^{-(i+1)}
\mathsf S_1(\lambda^2\partial_{\mathsf g}\sigma_{i+1}\,\cdot)$,
where
$\partial_{\mathsf g}\sigma_{i+1}
 =L\partial_{\mathsf g}\sigma_i+
       \partial_{\mathsf g}\nu_{i+1}\circ y_{i+1}$.
The terms with $\partial_{\mathsf g}\nu_{i+1}$ cancel.
The term added with $\mathfrak n_{i+1}$ is cancelled
by the recurrence
$\mathfrak N_{i+1}=L\mathfrak N_i+
\mathfrak n_{i+1}\circ y_{i+1}$.
Mass terms carry exactly between levels:
$L^{-l}\mathsf S_1(c\,\cdot)$ becomes
$L^{-i}\mathsf S_1(L^{i-l}c\,\cdot)$ at level $i$.
This proves \eqref{eq:C403-first-total} and the
displayed coefficient identity.
The argument also shows that the total derivative
depends only on the plaquette values of the source,
so any Lipschitz extension gives the same result.

For (2), the direct weight is linear in $w$.
The two-variable chain rule gives the mixed derivative
of the new activity as $D\widetilde E_i$ of the mixed
input derivative, plus
$D^2\widetilde E_i$ of its two first derivatives.
The latter have the totals of $\delta_i[f],\delta_i[h]$.
By induction, the mixed input derivative has the
total of $\sum_{l\le i}\mathcal V_i^{\mathrm{old}}
[\mathbf Q^{(l)}[f,h]]$.
The scalar part at the trivial configuration is
$\mathfrak e_{i+1}[f,h]$.
All mixed derivatives of the mass shifts cancel
between the activity and the carried mass term,
exactly as above.  No mass coefficient is moved
in the mixed response recursion.  This proves (2).

We give the infinite-lattice assertion separately;
translation covariance alone would only give a
cell-periodic moment.
The translations by $ML^{i+1}\mathbb Z^3$ preserve
the cubes at all preceding levels, the shift systems,
the chosen paths, and every localisation rule.
At the trivial configuration they preserve the
structure and tests as well.
For the constant direction, induction therefore
gives covariance of $\delta_i^\infty[1]$,
$\widetilde{\mathbf P}^{\infty(i+1)}[1]$ and
$\mathbf P^{\infty(i+1)}[1]$, including pieces
and units.  The moments and $\mathfrak N^\infty$
have the asserted cell periodicity.
The constant chain itself satisfies
\[
 \sigma_k^{\mathrm c}(c)
       =\sum_{l\le k}L^{k-l}(\nu_l^\infty(c)-\mu_l)
\]
on its source disc.  Differentiation gives the first
formula of (3).

To identify the moment at every site, fix $l$ and
compare increasing tori $T_\ell$ at the same cutoff
and labels.  At $\lambda=1$ form the response
recursion on $T_\ell$ using the infinite-lattice
numbers $\mathfrak n_{l'}^\infty[1]$ in its mass
forms.  They define functions on the torus by
the cell periodicity just proved.
Put the forms at the images of their polymers;
cells may wrap around.  In old variations keep
the infinite-lattice cell sum at the cell, and
file the remainder at its possibly wrapping
polymers.
The proof of (1) applies to this recursion because
the cancellation is valid for any numbers moved.
The derivative expansion at $\lambda=1$ is
admissible on every such torus: its zero-source
potential has size below $c_{\mathrm{cl}}/2$;
using half the parameter radius leaves size
below $c_{\mathrm{cl}}$ and quadratic-origin
norm below $(5/64+1/4)w_*<w_*/2$.
Its direction norms are finite uniformly in
$\ell$ at the finitely many levels considered.
The image of a polymer has no larger size,
and the cell decomposition has the same
long-lag bound.

Let $K_l^{\mathrm{fl},\ell}$ and
$K_l^{\mathrm{rsp},\ell}$ be the quadratic
kernels, read at level $l$ and at the trivial
configuration, of the actual step derivative
and this response total.  The preceding
identity gives
$K_l^{\mathrm{fl},\ell}
 =K_l^{\mathrm{rsp},\ell}$.
The finite-torus mass rule omits pieces of
diameter at least $\ell/4$ and treats wrapping
pieces separately.  Its value differs from
$-\mathfrak s_l^{-1}
 \operatorname{ord}_0K_l^{\mathrm{fl},\ell}(y)$
by a quantity tending to zero.
Indeed, the first omitted polymers have
$d_l\ge\ell_l/(2c'M)-1$, where $\ell_l=\ell/a_l$;
wrapping pieces have
$d_l\ge\ell_l/(2M)-2$.
Cauchy's estimate on the constant-source disc
$|c|<2\varrho$ bounds their derivatives.
Half the kernel-piece decay pays for the
moment sum; the remaining half gives a bound
by a datum-dependent constant times
$e^{-\kappa\ell_l/(4c'M)}$.
The torus comparison for the constant-source
chain also gives
\[
 |\partial_c\nu_l^{(\ell)}(y;0)-\partial_c\nu_l^\infty|
 \le\frac{C'_{\mathrm{tor}}}{\varrho}
       [\phi(x_l)+L\phi(x_{l-1})]
                         e^{-c_{\mathrm t}\ell/(2a_l)} .
\]
This follows by applying Cauchy's estimate to
$\sigma_{l'}^{(\ell)}-\sigma_{l'}^{\mathrm c}$ and
using $\nu_{l'}-\mu_{l'}=
\sigma_{l'}-L\sigma_{l'-1}$.

For a polymer that fits in $T_\ell$, the response
objects, pieces and units are the images of the
infinite-lattice ones.  This follows inductively
from locality of the expansion derivative and
of each shift and walk term; the forms were
chosen to be those images.
At fixed sites their kernels consequently
converge to the infinite-lattice kernel.
The background maps at the trivial configuration
are antiperiodic sums of their infinite-lattice
maps and converge locally, with uniform decay.
The sums over wrapping polymers tend to zero,
bounded by
$e^{-\kappa(\ell_l/(2M)-2)}$ times their uniform
norm.  The off-diagonal kernel bounds dominate
the moment sums.  Therefore
\[
 \operatorname{ord}_0K_l^{\mathrm{rsp},\ell}(y)
        \longrightarrow
          \operatorname{ord}_0K_l^{\mathrm{rsp},\infty}(y).
\]
Combining the limits gives
\[
 \partial_c\nu_l^\infty
  =-\mathfrak s_l^{-1}
        \operatorname{ord}_0K_l^{\mathrm{rsp},\infty}(y)
  =-\mathfrak s_l^{-1}
        \sum_{X,p}\operatorname{ord}_0[\mathsf k_{X,p}](y).
\]
The last sum is absolutely convergent by the
piecewise moment bound.
The left side is independent of $y$, which
proves the final assertion.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Differentiating one expansion}

\begin{lemma}[First and mixed step derivatives]\label{C-403-45}
Let $0\le i<j$, $\lambda\in D_i$ and $D\subset D_i$.
A direction $\delta=(\delta^{\mathrm p},\delta^{\mathrm o})$
consists of a potential on the field polydisc of the step,
with scalar and fermionic local terms, and a scalar
quadratic-origin family defined at every real fluctuation.
Set
\[
 \epsilon(\delta)=\epsilon_V(\delta^{\mathrm p})
             +\epsilon_F(\delta^{\mathrm p})
             +2(c_{\mathrm{cl}}/w_*)
                          \|\delta^{\mathrm o}\|_{\star,\lambda_V}.
\]
The expansion at
$(\mathfrak V_i(\lambda)+t\delta^{\mathrm p},
  \mathcal V^{\mathrm q}+t\delta^{\mathrm o})$
is holomorphic for
$|t|<3c_{\mathrm{cl}}/(4\epsilon(\delta))$.
Its first derivative is linear in $\delta$, and its
mixed derivative is bilinear in the two directions.
For each output polymer $X$,
\begin{align*}
 \|D\widetilde E_i[\delta](X)\|
   &\le\frac32K'_M\epsilon(\delta_X)
                                  e^{-\kappa_+d_{i+1}(X)},\\
 \|D^2\widetilde E_i[\delta_1,\delta_2](X)\|
   &\le8c_{\mathrm{cl}}^{-1}K'_M
         \epsilon(\delta_{1,X})\epsilon(\delta_{2,X})
                                  e^{-\kappa_+d_{i+1}(X)}.
\end{align*}
Here $\delta_X$ restricts both components to input
polymers $Y$ with $Y^\sharp\subset X$.

For weight systems as in Definition~\ref{C-403-43}, put
\[
 \epsilon_{\mathscr S}(\delta)
   =\epsilon_{V;\mathscr S}(\delta^{\mathrm p})
     +\epsilon_{F;\mathscr S}(\delta^{\mathrm p})
     +2(c_{\mathrm{cl}}/w_*)
                           \|\delta^{\mathrm o}\|_{\star;\mathscr S},
\]
with the weights measured at output level $i+1$.
Then
\begin{align*}
 \|D\widetilde E_i[\delta]\|_{i+1;D;\mathscr S}
   &\le\frac32K_M
                  \sup_{\lambda\in D}\epsilon_{\mathscr S}(\delta),\\
 \|D^2\widetilde E_i[\delta_1,\delta_2]\|
                      _{i+1;D;\mathscr S_1\cup\mathscr S_2}
   &\le8c_{\mathrm{cl}}^{-1}K_M
       \sup_{\lambda\in D}\epsilon_{\mathscr S_1}(\delta_1)
       \sup_{\lambda\in D}\epsilon_{\mathscr S_2}(\delta_2).
\end{align*}
The scalar parts obey the same bounds in the array
norm, with $K'_M$ instead of $K_M$.
The derivatives retain holomorphy in all input
parameters, locality on $X$, and joint gauge
invariance when the directions have these properties.
Their scalar parts are then local terms at the
fixed radii $(\alpha_0,\alpha_1)$.
All assertions hold on $\mathbb Z^3$ with the same
constants.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The base potential has size at most
$c_{\mathrm{cl}}/4$ and the quadratic origin has
norm at most $5w_*/64$.
Since $c_{\mathrm{cl}}=w_*$, on the indicated
$t$-disc the perturbed potential has size below
$c_{\mathrm{cl}}$ and the quadratic origin has norm
below
$(5/64+3/8)w_*=29w_*/64<w_*/2$.
Thus both the joined expansion and the quadratic-origin
Gaussian cluster sum exist and are holomorphic.
The same statement holds in several parameters entering
the origins linearly.

Write
$p=e^{-\gamma_{\mathrm{tail}}\mathfrak b(\mathsf t_i)^2/2}$.
The tail ceiling and
$C_\eta c_\lambda^{-1/2}\le c_{\mathrm{cl}}/4$,
$C_\eta\ge16K_M\ge16$, imply
$p\le c_{\mathrm{cl}}/64$.
The joined activity minus its Gaussian part is bounded
at $X$ by
$K'_M(\epsilon_V+\epsilon_F+p)e^{-\kappa_+d_{i+1}(X)}$.
The Gaussian part is bounded by
$K_\Pi\|\mathcal V^{\mathrm q}
                +t\delta^{\mathrm o}\|_{\star,\lambda_V}
 e^{-\kappa_+d_{i+1}(X)}$.
Combining the base sizes and the perturbation size
gives the common bound
\[
 \frac{71}{64}K'_Mc_{\mathrm{cl}}
                                  e^{-\kappa_+d_{i+1}(X)} .
\]
Locality says that the activity at $X$ sees only
$\delta_X$.  Apply Cauchy's estimate on its disc
of radius $3c_{\mathrm{cl}}/(4\epsilon(\delta_X))$.
The factor is $71/48\le3/2$.
For two directions use the bidisc with radii
$3c_{\mathrm{cl}}/(8\epsilon(\delta_{a,X}))$.
The sum of the two perturbation sizes remains below
$3c_{\mathrm{cl}}/4$, and the resulting factor
is $71/9\le8$.
Zero-size directions follow by continuity.
Linearity and bilinearity follow by differentiating
the holomorphic expansion in its linear parameters.

For $Y^\sharp\subset X$, one has
$\operatorname{dist}(Y,S)\ge\operatorname{dist}(X,S)$.
Consequently
\[
 \epsilon(\delta_X)
       \le W_{i+1}(X)^{-1}\epsilon_{\mathscr S}(\delta).
\]
For two directions the weights multiply.
The polymer estimates are uniform in $\lambda$;
take the supremum at each polymer before summing.
The geometric sum
$\sup_\square\sum_{X\supset\square}
 e^{-(\kappa_+-\kappa)d_{i+1}(X)}\le C_E$
gives $K_M=C_EK'_M$ and the asserted family bounds.
Since $\kappa_+\ge\kappa+1$ and a scalar part has
at most its fibre norm, the array bounds follow
without the geometric sum.

The structure, covariances, quadratic origin and
base potential are holomorphic in the pair.
Adjoin the pair variables to the perturbation
parameters in the uniformly convergent expansion.
Its locality shows that it reads only the
restriction of that pair to $X$.
Cauchy integration in the perturbation parameters
preserves both properties.
Gauge covariance of the expansion similarly
passes to its derivatives; in degree zero it
is strict gauge invariance.
These properties and the displayed bounds are
the defining conditions for scalar local terms
at the fixed radii.

On $\mathbb Z^3$, each polymer calculation is
the calculation in a torus into which that
polymer fits.  The scaled-flow induction gives
the same input sizes there, and the proof uses
only local data and uniform polymer sums.
Thus the constants are unchanged.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Taking finite differences inside a term sum}

The long-lag estimates control a sum at one pair.
Moving a supremum inside that sum would lose this estimate.
The following form of Cauchy's formula keeps the sum inside
the supremum when the shift is varied and localised.

\begin{lemma}[Amplitude differences and localisation]
\label{lem:C403-amplitude-differences}
Let $t(\mu;s)$ be terms holomorphic for
$|\mu|<R$ and $|s|<e^{\bar\kappa}$, where $s$ are the
shift parameters of the step from level $i$.
The term \(t(\mu;s)\) is read at the pair obtained by
substituting the shift \(\mu\mathfrak h(s)\); this
substitution is its only dependence on \(\mu,s\).
Each term is filed at $Y_t\in\mathcal D_i$, and depends
on the shift only at bonds of $Y_t$.
All terms use the restrictions of one shift system
on a polymer containing them.
Let $R_t\subset Y_t$ be the cubes containing endpoints
of the bonds used by $t$.
For a set of cubes $\Gamma$, let $\Delta_\Gamma$ be
the finite difference with the other parameters zero;
file it at the enlargement $Y_{t,\Gamma}$ prescribed
by the step.
For nonnegative numbers $w_t$, $1<\rho<R$ and
$r=e^{\bar\kappa}/2$,
\begin{equation}\label{C-403-150}
\begin{split}
 &\sum_{t,\Gamma:\,Y_{t,\Gamma}\supset\square}
       e^{(\kappa-1)d_i(Y_{t,\Gamma})}w_t
          \|\Delta_\Gamma[t(1;\cdot)-t(0;\cdot)]\|\\
 &\hspace{8mm}\le\frac{1.19}{\rho-1}
      \sup_{\square'}\sup_{|\mu|=\rho,\ |s|\le r}
         \sum_{t:\,Y_t\supset\square'}
           e^{(\kappa-1/2)d_i(Y_t)}w_t\|t(\mu;s)\|.
\end{split}
\end{equation}
The same estimate holds for the sums over all terms,
without the conditions involving $\square,\square'$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The term with $\Gamma=\emptyset$ vanishes, since the
shift is zero at $s=0$.
Cauchy's formula on $|\mu|=\rho$ and
$|s_b|=r$ for $b\in\Gamma$ writes the difference as
the angular average of
$t(\rho e^{i\varphi};re^{i\theta_\Gamma},0)$
multiplied by
\[
 (\rho e^{i\varphi}-1)^{-1}
           \prod_{b\in\Gamma}(re^{i\theta_b}-1)^{-1}.
\]
Its norm is at most $(\rho-1)^{-1}(r-1)^{-\#\Gamma}$
times the angular average of $\|t\|$.
The parameter floor
$\bar\kappa\ge(\kappa+2)c_0+\log C_{\mathrm g}+9
\ge\kappa+3$
gives $r-1\ge e^{\bar\kappa-1}$.
The finite difference vanishes unless every wall-connected
component of $\Gamma$ meets $R_t$.

Use one auxiliary probability law for all the terms.
Let $\mu=\rho e^{i\varphi}$ have uniform angle, and
independently let each $s_b$ be zero with probability
$1-p$ and have uniform angle on $|s_b|=r$ with
probability $p=e^{-4}$.
For an admissible $\Gamma$, let $E_\Gamma^t$ be
the event that the support of $s$ meets the union
of $\Gamma$, its wall neighbours and $R_t$ exactly
in $\Gamma$.
On this event the support components meeting $R_t$
are precisely those of $\Gamma$.
The component property of the shift therefore gives
$t(\mu;s)=t(\mu;s1_\Gamma)$.
The events $E_\Gamma^t$ are disjoint, and
\[
 \mathbb P(E_\Gamma^t)
       \ge p^{\#\Gamma}(1-p)^{6\#\Gamma+\#R_t}.
\]
Conditioned on this event, the active angles remain
uniform.  Thus the angular average above equals
the integral over $E_\Gamma^t$ divided by its
probability.

The enlargement estimate gives
\[
 e^{(\kappa-1)d_i(Y_{t,\Gamma})}
  \le e^{(\kappa-1)d_i(Y_t)}
                          e^{(\kappa+2)c_0\#\Gamma}.
\]
Put
\[
 y=e^{(\kappa+2)c_0}(r-1)^{-1},\qquad
 y_1=\frac{y}{p(1-p)^6}.
\]
Since $C_{\mathrm g}y\le e^{-8}$ and
$p(1-p)^6\ge0.0163$,
$C_{\mathrm g}y_1\le0.0206$.
For one term, summing over its disjoint events
therefore bounds its total by
\[
 (\rho-1)^{-1}
     (1-p)^{-\#R_t}e^{(\kappa-1)d_i(Y_t)}
                         w_t\int\|t(\mu;s)\|\,d\mathbb P .
\]
Here $\#R_t\le8(d_i(Y_t)+1)$ and
$(1-p)^{-8}\le e^{0.148}$, so
\[
 (1-p)^{-\#R_t}e^{(\kappa-1)d_i(Y_t)}
       \le e^{0.148}e^{(\kappa-1/2)d_i(Y_t)}.
\]
For terms with $Y_t\supset\square$, sum under
this integral and use the displayed supremum
in \eqref{C-403-150}.

If $\square\notin Y_t$ but
$Y_{t,\Gamma}\supset\square$, the component
of $\Gamma$ reaching $\square$ has some size $q$.
There are at most $C_{\mathrm g}^q$ possible
connected sets of that size containing
$\square$, and at most $q$ choices for its
cube in $R_t\subset Y_t$.
Retain the factor $y_1^q$ in the preceding
event estimate.  The extra count is
\[
 \sum_{q\ge1}q(C_{\mathrm g}y_1)^q\le0.0215 .
\]
Consequently the total factor is at most
$e^{0.148}(1+0.0215)\le1.19$.
For the unrestricted sum there is no extra
count, and $e^{0.148}\le1.19$ suffices.
The proof sums the terms before taking
suprema over the common parameters throughout.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Reading and varying an old response}

The estimate for an old response has three terms.  Terms of
degree at least four, and the field-dependent part of the
quadratic term, gain four powers of the scale ratio.
A difference of quadratic legs gains $2+\alpha$ powers,
where $\alpha=3/4$.  The remaining local quadratic term is
measured by its cell sum.  We keep this last term explicitly
until the moment equation controls it.

Let $1\le l\le i<K$ and $n=i+1-l$.  Use a weight system
$\mathscr S$ and put
\[
 \mathcal N=\min\{M^3L^{3n},\mathcal C_l(\mathscr S)\}.
\]
Assume that a family $F$ at level $l$ has the following
properties.
Its scalar terms are local on the whole regular-pair
core, at $(\alpha_0,\alpha_1)$, and are pointed equally
at their sites.
Its fermionic part is an absolutely convergent sum
$F_{\ge2}(X)=\sum_\sigma F_\sigma(X)$, each summand
filed at a cell of $X$, holomorphic and jointly gauge
invariant on that core.

At the trivial pair, read the quadratic kernels in the
level-$l$ field $\Phi$.  Their units are obtained by
moving diagonal terms from the cell of a summand to
the cell of their site $y$.
Each moved term is a fixed linear combination of
row and column sums at $y$ of the quadratic kernels
of two families $F_1,G$ with the same holomorphy and
invariance, with sum of absolute coefficients at most
two.  The decomposition is $F=F_1+F_2$, with
$F_2=0$ allowed.  Kernels of $G$ may be read at a
second admitted fine mass, provided their background
maps have the same bounds.
Attach each moved term to the summand from which it
is moved.

In the norm of $F_{\ge2}$, sum the norms of its
summands before the polymer sum.
For a summand to which moved terms are attached,
let $\|F_{\sigma,2}^{\mathrm{tr}}(X)\|$ include the
trivial-pair quadratic norms of $F_\sigma(X)$,
$F_1(X)$ and $G(X)$.  The norm
$\|F_2^{\mathrm{tr}}\|_{l;D;\mathscr S}$
uses these quantities.
Write $m_c$ for the sum of the quadratic units
filed at the cell $c$; on a torus include the
seam transport in every piece and write
$m_c^{\mathrm{tor}}$.

For the output we also use the norm
\[
 \|H\|^{\mathrm{out}}_{i+1;D;\mathscr S}
  =\sup_{\lambda\in D}\sup_{Z,P}\sup_{\square\subset Z}
       \sum_{\square\subset Y\subset Z}
        e^{\kappa d_{i+1}(Y)}W_{i+1}(Y)
                  \|H(Y;P|_Y;\lambda)\|_{h^{(i+1)}} .
\]
Here $P$ is one triple in the regular-pair core on
$Z$, whose restrictions are used in the sum.
This norm is bounded by the strong family norm
of Definition~\ref{C-403-43}.

There are two readings.  In reading (R), read at
level $i+1$ with no shift, so the filing level is
$i_{\mathrm f}=i+1$ and its lag is $n_{\mathrm f}=n$.
In variation (V), read at level $i$ in a step
to level $i+1$, so $i_{\mathrm f}=i$ and
$n_{\mathrm f}=n-1$.  Substitute the shift
$\mu\mathfrak h_Y(s;P,B')$, where
$B'=\lambda\mathsf t_i^{-1/2}B$, at every parameter
of the shift polydisc and every amplitude satisfying
\[
 |\mu|c_h\sup|B'|\le\mathsf c_{\mathrm{os}}\alpha_0,
\]
strictly when $n_{\mathrm f}=0$.
In both cases use the weight $W_{i+1}$, and put
$\pi_{\mathrm f}(Y)=(1+\operatorname{diam}_{i_{\mathrm f}}Y/M)^4$.

At
$n_{\mathrm f}\ge n_{\mathrm{lag}}$,
where $n_{\mathrm{lag}}$ is the least integer with
$2(2A_\kappa C_H)^2L^{-n_{\mathrm{lag}}}\le1$,
write the legs first at level $l$, then at the
filing level, using their local and walk terms.
Transport the legs of each quadratic term to the
centre of its cell.
For a summand $\sigma$ of $X$, let $T_{\mathrm b}(\sigma)$
contain its terms of degree at least four and the
difference between its quadratic term and its value
at the trivial pair.
Let $T_{\mathrm c}(\sigma)$ contain its trivial-pair
quadratic terms with at least one difference of legs,
including both copies of each moved piece attached
to the summand.
Let $T_{\mathrm d}(c)$ contain the terms of
$\bar\Phi(z_c)m_c\Phi(z_c)$.
File each term at the hull of its original polymer,
walk sets and transport paths, enlarged by the at
most eight cubes used for its regular gauge.
A cell term is filed at the cube of $c$, enlarged
by the walks of its two legs.

\begin{lemma}[Lag estimates]\label{C-403-46}
There are constants $C_{\mathrm{rd}},C_{\mathrm{mo}}\ge1$,
independent of $h_F$, coupling, field scale, level,
side and source, with the following properties.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(R0)]
Subtract the trivial-pair value of each scalar
term and read it at any level $i+1\le K$,
including $K$.  File it at the hull $Y(X)$,
enlarged by the regular-gauge cube when that
cube is used.  On the whole output core,
\[
 |F_0(X;\rho_XP)-F_0(X;\mathbf1,0)|
 \le C_{\mathrm{rd}}(1+d_l(X))^4L^{-4n}\|F_0(X)\|_X .
\]
The resulting family has strong weighted norm at most
$C_{\mathrm{rd}}\mathcal NL^{-4n}
\|F_0\|^{\mathrm{arr}}_{l;D;\mathscr S}$.
For $D\subset D_i$, its scalar variation has size
\[
 \epsilon_{V;\mathscr S}(\mathcal V_i^{\mathrm{old}}[F_0])
 \le2s_\lambda C_{\mathrm{rd}}\mathcal NL^{-4n}
                       \|F_0\|^{\mathrm{arr}}_{l;D;\mathscr S},
 \qquad s_\lambda=c_h\beta_\lambda/a_{\mathrm{an}},
\]
at rate $(1-2\delta_{\mathrm w})\kappa\ge\lambda_V$.

\item[(T)]
At $n_{\mathrm f}\ge n_{\mathrm{lag}}$, at one
pair and at either weight $h_F$ or $C_Hh_F$
on the filing-level generators,
\begin{align*}
 \sum_{t\in T_{\mathrm b}(\sigma)}
    e^{\kappa d_{i_{\mathrm f}}(Y_t)}
        \pi_{\mathrm f}(Y_t)\|t\|
 &\le C_{\mathrm{rd}}L^{-4n}
        e^{\kappa d_l(X)/2}\|F_\sigma(X)\|,\\
 \sum_{t\in T_{\mathrm c}(\sigma)}
    e^{\kappa d_{i_{\mathrm f}}(Y_t)}
        \pi_{\mathrm f}(Y_t)\|t\|
 &\le C_{\mathrm{rd}}L^{-(2+\alpha)n}
        e^{\kappa d_l(X)/2}\|F_{\sigma,2}^{\mathrm{tr}}(X)\|,\\
 \sum_{t\in T_{\mathrm d}(c)}
    e^{\kappa d_{i_{\mathrm f}}(Y_t)}
        \pi_{\mathrm f}(Y_t)\|t\|
 &\le C_{\mathrm{rd}}L^{-2n}h_F^2\|m_c\|.
\end{align*}
Here $\alpha=3/4$.

\item[(M)]
For every $\lambda\in D$, site $y$ and cell $c$,
\[
 W_l(y)\sum_{X,p}
       \|\operatorname{ord}_0\mathsf k_{X,p}(y)\|_{\mathrm{tr}}
 \le C_{\mathrm{mo}}h_F^{-2}
                         \|F_2^{\mathrm{tr}}\|_{l;D;\mathscr S},
 \qquad
 W_l(c)\|m_c\|_{\mathrm{tr}}
 \le C_{\mathrm{mo}}h_F^{-2}
                         \|F_2^{\mathrm{tr}}\|_{l;D;\mathscr S}.
\]
These estimates apply separately to $F,F_1,G$.
The units also have the first absolute moment
bound
\[
 \sum_{\mathfrak u\text{ at }c}\sum_{y,y'}
   \|\beta_{\mathfrak u}(y,y')\|
     (1+|y-z_c|_l+|y'-z_c|_l)
       \le C_{\mathrm{mo}}h_F^{-2}\varepsilon_{\mathrm f},
\]
where $\varepsilon_{\mathrm f}$ bounds their
unweighted family norms.
Restricting the displayed \(\operatorname{ord}_0\) moment
sum over \(X,p\) to pieces whose
polymer $Z_p$ has $d_l(Z_p)\ge d_*$ gives the
additional factor $e^{-\kappa d_*/2}$.
If the kernels are holomorphic on
$|\lambda|<\bar\lambda$, the same estimates
hold for their $\lambda^4$ moments with
$\bar\lambda^4\sum\|a_{X,p}^{[4]}(y)\|_{\mathrm{tr}}$
in place of the moment sum.

\item[(R2)]
Put
\[
 \mathsf B_{\mathrm R}
  =L^{-4n}\|F_{\ge2}\|_{l;D;\mathscr S}
   +L^{-(2+\alpha)n}\|F_2^{\mathrm{tr}}\|_{l;D;\mathscr S}
   +L^{-2n}h_F^2
                \sup_cW_l(c)\sup_{\lambda\in D}\|m_c\|.
\]
The fermionic family read at level $i+1$ has norm
at most $C_{\mathrm{rd}}\mathcal N\mathsf B_{\mathrm R}$.
For $n\ge n_{\mathrm{lag}}$ this is the
$\|\cdot\|^{\mathrm{out}}$ norm.  For
$n<n_{\mathrm{lag}}$ it is the strong family norm.

\item[(V2)]
For $D\subset D_i$ and \(n_{\mathrm f}\ge n_{\mathrm{lag}}\),
the variation is the sum of
$t(1)-t(0)$ at
$\widetilde\Psi=\Psi_i^{\mathrm{bg}}+W$ and
$t(0)(\widetilde\Psi)-t(0)(\Psi_i^{\mathrm{bg}})$,
followed by the finite differences in the shift
parameters. At every lag the variation has size
\[
 \epsilon_{F;\mathscr S}(\mathcal V_i^{\mathrm{old}}[F_{\ge2}])
       \le c'_\psi C_{\mathrm{rd}}\mathcal N\mathsf B_{\mathrm R}
\]
in the summed norm at rate $\kappa-1$.
When $n_{\mathrm f}\ge n_{\mathrm{lag}}$ one
may replace $c'_\psi$ by $s_\lambda+c_\psi$.

\item[(H)]
The full, reduced and feedback first-response
families and the mixed-response families have
the hypotheses above, with the units specified
in Definition~\ref{C-403-43}.
The families joining cells have them at
$D=\{1\}$, with their polymers as units.
\end{enumerate}
For lags below $n_{\mathrm{lag}}$, no leg expansion is
needed: reading keeps each summand at the hull of its
polymer, and variation uses the direct fermionic
variation.  The constants in the proof cover these
lags as well.
On a torus all cell sums and distances are those of
the torus, with the seam in the transports.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
We give constants, then prove the scalar and fermionic estimates
separately.  All estimates are at one $\lambda\in D$ until the
last supremum is taken.

\emph{Constants and weights.}
Let
\begin{align*}
 C_4&=\sum_{v\in\mathbb Z^3}(1+|v|_\infty)^{-4},&
 c_{\mathrm{ft}}&=\min\{\kappa/(16C_t),1/(48C_t)\},\\
 P_{\mathrm{ft}}&=e(6/(ec_{\mathrm{ft}}))^6,&
 C'&=\sup_x\sum_y e^{-\alpha_Dd(x,y)/2}.
\end{align*}
Thus $u^6\le P_{\mathrm{ft}}e^{c_{\mathrm{ft}}u-1}$ for $u\ge0$.
Use the constants of the localized leg bounds, the regular
gauge construction and scalar localization, and set
\begin{align*}
 C_{\mathrm{ft}}
 &=2^{10}(1+8C_{\mathrm{nb}}M^3A_\kappa)^2(A_\kappa C_H)^8\\
 &\quad{}\times
 \bigl[1+C_{\mathrm{gf}}+\nu+
 C_t\{C_H(\alpha)+4C_H(c_T\epsilon_*+C_QL\alpha_1)\}\bigr]^2,\\
 C_{\mathrm{pt}}
 &=4e^{\kappa/8}e^{\kappa c_0}M^2P_{\mathrm{ft}}C_{\mathrm{ft}}L^4,\\
 C_{\mathrm{gf}}^{(2)}
 &=(6C_{\mathrm{lg}}C_tM/\rho_{\mathrm A})^2
       +(8C_tM/s_Q)^4+L^{4n_{\mathrm{lg}}},\\
 C_{\mathrm{rd}}^0
 &=2C_\Sigma M^3
       (8e\,\mathsf C_{\mathrm{oc}}C_{\mathrm E,2}L^8+8L^{11}),\\
 C_{\mathrm{rd}}^{\mathrm{R0}}
 &=2232e^{1/2}e^{\kappa c_0}C_{\mathrm E,0}C_{\mathrm{gf}}^{(2)},\\
 C_{\mathrm{rd}}^\psi
 &=2^7C_4e^{\kappa/16}L^{4n_{\mathrm{lag}}}C_{\mathrm{pt}},\\
 C_{\mathrm{rd}}
 &=\max\{C_{\mathrm{rd}}^0,C_{\mathrm{rd}}^{\mathrm{R0}},
                                      C_{\mathrm{rd}}^\psi\},\\
 C_{\mathrm{mo}}
 &=2^{14}e^{\kappa/8}A_\kappa^2C'^2M^3(1+3M)(1+c'M).
\end{align*}
Here $\nu=8N_f$, $c_T=64L^2$, $\alpha=3/4$ and
$C_{\mathrm E,0}\le C_{\mathrm E,2}$ are the polymer-counting
constants with counting rate $\kappa_{\mathcal D}=\log9216$.
These constants precede the choice of $h_F$.

Write $d=d_l(X)$.  If $Z\subset X$, the diameter estimate
$\operatorname{diam}_lX\le c'M(1+d)/2$ and the restrictions
$\kappa_{\mathrm s}c'\le\min\{\kappa/8,1\}$ imply
\begin{equation}\label{eq:C403-lag-weights}
 \begin{split}
 W_l(Z)&\le e^{\kappa_{\mathrm s}c'(1+d)}W_l(X),\\
 W_l(X)^{-1/2}
 &\le\min\{e^{\kappa(1+d)/16},e^{(1+d)/2}\}W_l(Z)^{-1/2}.
 \end{split}
\end{equation}
If $Y\supset Z$, distances at the output level decrease
by $L^{-n}$.  Consequently,
\[
 W_{i+1}(Y)\le W_l(Z)^{L^{-n}}
                   \le W_l(Z)W_l(Z)^{-1/2}.
\]
The last inequality uses $L^{-n}\le1/2$.

\emph{The scalar variation.}
Use the scalar localization of the bare array whose only
nonzero member is $G^{(l)}=F_0$, pointed equally at its sites,
with $e_l=0$.  Proposition~\ref{C-403-33-flow} places
$(P,\lambda\mathsf t_i^{-1/2}B)$ in the admitted domain at
$\mathsf t_\flat$.  A localized potential with index
$\mathfrak i$ therefore has bound
\[
 2\mathsf C_\Phi\mathsf s_{\mathfrak a}(\mathsf t_\flat)
       \|f_{\mathfrak i}\|
       e^{-(\bar\kappa-1)\mathfrak m_i(X_{\mathfrak i},Y)},
 \qquad
 \mathsf s_{\mathfrak a}(\mathsf t_\flat)
       =(1+\beta_s)\delta(\mathsf t_\flat)/\alpha_0.
\]
We check the sum of the weighted data in this estimate.

For a narrow index $(l,z)$, which occurs only if $l<i$,
the domain $X'(z)$ is the union of at most eight cubes
about one corner at level $i$.  It has $d_i(X'(z))=0$
and contains at most $8M^3L^{3(n-1)}$ level-$l$ sites.
The scalar localization estimate gives
\[
 \|f_{(l,z)}\|
 \le \mathsf C_{\mathrm{oc}}L^{8-4n}
       \sum_{X_1\ni z}(d_l(X_1)+2)^2
                                \|F_0(X_1,\cdot,z)\|_{X_1}.
\]
In this sum $W_l(z)\le e^{1+d_l(X_1)}W_l(X_1)$.
The unit of decay between $\kappa+1$ and $\kappa$
and the polymer count give
\[
 W_{i+1}(Y)\|f_{(l,z)}\|
 \le e\,\mathsf C_{\mathrm{oc}}C_{\mathrm E,2}L^{8-4n}
          W_l(c(z))^{-1/2}
                         \|F_0\|^{\mathrm{arr}}_{l;D;\mathscr S}.
\]
Either count the sites in $X'(z)$ or use
$\sum_zW_l(c(z))^{-1/2}\le M^3\mathcal C_l(\mathscr S)$.
The total for one narrow domain is bounded by
\[
 \mathsf B_{\mathrm{nr}}
 =8e\,\mathsf C_{\mathrm{oc}}C_{\mathrm E,2}M^3L^8
       \mathcal NL^{-4n}\|F_0\|^{\mathrm{arr}}_{l;D;\mathscr S}.
\]

For a wide index $(l,z,X)$, use
\[
 W_{i+1}(Y)
 \le W_l(X)e^{(1+d)/2}W_l(c)^{-1/2},
 \qquad c\subset X.
\]
The shares of $X$ add to $F_0(X)$.  The remaining decay
pays $e^{d/2}$, while
$W_l(c)^{-1/2}\le\min\{1,\mathcal C_l(\mathscr S)\}\le\mathcal N$.
Thus one wide domain contributes at most
$\mathsf B_{\mathrm{wd}}e^{-\kappa d}$, where
\[
 \mathsf B_{\mathrm{wd}}
   =e^{1/2}\mathcal N\|F_0\|^{\mathrm{arr}}_{l;D;\mathscr S}.
\]
There are no such domains with $d<\max\{2L^{n-2}-2,0\}$.
The localization sum uses
$\varpi_m=L^{3m}e^{-(2L^{m-1}-2)}\le L^{7-4m}$ for $m\ge1$.
Indeed, $7(m-1)\log L\le2L^{m-1}-2$ for $L\ge13$.
It follows that
\begin{align*}
 &W_{i+1}(Y)\sum_{\mathfrak i}\|f_{\mathfrak i}\|
       e^{-(\bar\kappa-1)\mathfrak m_i(X_{\mathfrak i},Y)}\\
 &\quad\le C_\Sigma
          (\mathsf B_{\mathrm{nr}}+L^{11-4n}\mathsf B_{\mathrm{wd}})
             e^{-(1-2\delta_{\mathrm w})\kappa d_i(Y)}\\
 &\quad\le\tfrac12C_{\mathrm{rd}}^0\mathcal NL^{-4n}
          \|F_0\|^{\mathrm{arr}}_{l;D;\mathscr S}
             e^{-(1-2\delta_{\mathrm w})\kappa d_i(Y)} .
\end{align*}
When $l=i$, there are no narrow indices and the same bound
uses only $\mathsf B_{\mathrm{wd}}$.

The localized variation is holomorphic in the amplitude
$\zeta$ of $B'$, vanishes at $\zeta=0$, and is admitted
for $|\zeta|<\mathsf R_i/|\lambda|$, where
$\mathsf R_i=\delta(\mathsf t_\flat)/\delta(\mathsf t_i)>|\lambda|$.
Schwarz's lemma supplies $|\lambda|/\mathsf R_i$.
The remaining scalar prefactor is
\begin{align*}
 2\mathsf C_\Phi\mathsf s_{\mathfrak a}(\mathsf t_\flat)
                   \frac{|\lambda|}{\mathsf R_i}
 &=\frac{3(1+\beta_s)c_h\mathsf C_{\mathcal A}
                     |\lambda|\delta(\mathsf t_i)}{a_{\mathrm{an}}}\\
 &\le3(1+\beta_s)s_\lambda\le3.6s_\lambda.
\end{align*}
We used $2a_{\mathrm{an}}=\mathsf c_{\mathrm{os}}\alpha_0$
and the field-scale bound
$\mathsf C_{\mathcal A}|\lambda|\delta(\mathsf t_i)\le\beta_\lambda$.
The result is $1.8s_\lambda C_{\mathrm{rd}}^0$ times the
displayed array bound.  This proves the scalar variation
with the asserted constant $2C_{\mathrm{rd}}$ and rate.

\emph{The scalar reading.}
Fix $X$, its filing cell $c$, and put $D'=M(1+d)$.
Let $E(\mathbf q)=F_0(X;\mathbf q)$ and let
$\mathbf p_*$ be the pair obtained by reading an output
triple $P$ to $X$.  Reading maps the full output core to
the full core on $X$.
If
$2(C_tD'+M+2)>s_QL^n$, the elementary estimate
$|E(\mathbf p_*)-E(\mathbf1,0)|\le2\|F_0(X)\|_X$ gives
\[
 |E(\mathbf p_*)-E(\mathbf1,0)|
 \le2(8C_tM/s_Q)^4(1+d)^4L^{-4n}\|F_0(X)\|_X.
\]
If this inequality of lengths fails but $n<n_{\mathrm{lg}}$,
the same elementary estimate gives
$2L^{4n_{\mathrm{lg}}}L^{-4n}\|F_0(X)\|_X$.

In the remaining case the regular-gauge cube $Q$
contains the bonds of $X$ and their neighbours.
The at most eight output cubes meeting $Q$ are included
in $Y(X)$.  The regular gauge and its complex continuation
carry $\mathbf p_*$ to a pair $\mathbf q_1$ without changing
$E$.  The radial disc through that pair is
\[
 \zeta\longmapsto
       (e^{i\zeta L^{-l}A_{Q,1}},\zeta J_{Q,1}),
 \qquad
 |\zeta|\le\rho_{\mathrm A}/\beta_2,\qquad
 \beta_2=6C_{\mathrm{lg}}C_tL^{-2n}D'.
\]
It lies in the admitted pair domain.
Subtract $E(\mathbf1,0)$ along this disc to obtain $g(\zeta)$.
Then $|g|\le2\|F_0(X)\|_X$ and $g(0)=0$.
Also $g'(0)=0$: the differential at the trivial pair is
an invariant complex linear form on the Lie-algebra
valued pair, and averaging its argument under constant
$\mathrm{SU}(2)$ conjugations gives zero.
Schwarz's lemma to second order gives
\[
 |g(1)|\le
 2(6C_{\mathrm{lg}}C_tM/\rho_{\mathrm A})^2
       (1+d)^2L^{-4n}\|F_0(X)\|_X .
\]
If $\beta_2>\rho_{\mathrm A}$, the same bound follows
from the elementary estimate instead.
All three cases are bounded by
$2C_{\mathrm{gf}}^{(2)}(1+d)^4L^{-4n}\|F_0(X)\|_X$.
The composition with pair restriction is defined on
the whole output core, also when $i+1=K$.

For the family norm, $d_{i+1}(Y(X))\le c_0+L^{-n}d$.
If $Y(X)$ contains a fixed output cube, $X$ meets one
of at most $9L^{3n}$ old cells, including the possible
regular-gauge enlargement.  Alternatively sum their
weights, giving at most $9\mathcal C_l(\mathscr S)$.
For such a cell $c''$, \eqref{eq:C403-lag-weights} gives
\[
 W_{i+1}(Y(X))
 \le W_l(X)\min\{1,e^{(1+d)/2}W_l(c'')^{-1/2}\}.
\]
Use $(1+d)^4e^{-d/2}\le124$.  The polymer summand is at most
\[
 248e^{1/2}e^{\kappa c_0}C_{\mathrm{gf}}^{(2)}L^{-4n}
 \min\{1,W_l(c'')^{-1/2}\}
 e^{-\kappa(1-L^{-n})d}
                      \|F_0\|^{\mathrm{arr}}_{l;D;\mathscr S}.
\]
Since $\kappa(1-L^{-n})\ge12\kappa/13>
\kappa_{\mathcal D}+2$, its polymer sum is bounded by
$C_{\mathrm E,0}$.  The cell count proves (R0), with
$9\cdot248=2232$ as in $C_{\mathrm{rd}}^{\mathrm{R0}}$.

\emph{Terms from the fermionic reading.}
Suppose first that $n_{\mathrm f}\ge n_{\mathrm{lag}}$.
Expand each leg at level $l$ and then at the filing level,
retaining the local term and every walk term.
The localized leg estimate, including the factors
$e^{|\omega'|}$ and $e^{|\omega|}$ for the two stages
and the positive growth in polymer length, is
\[
 (2A_\kappa C_H)^2L^{-n_{\mathrm f}}h^{(l)}(n').
\]
For a term of degree $2p\ge4$, the definition of
$n_{\mathrm{lag}}$ bounds the product of these estimates by
\[
 (2A_\kappa C_H)^8L^{-4n_{\mathrm f}}2^{-(2p-4)}
\]
times its original coefficient norm.
This proves the four powers of scale for the first part
of $T_{\mathrm b}$.

For the quadratic term minus its trivial-pair value,
transport its coefficient and both legs to the centre
of the filing cell.  The regular-gauge estimate for
the coefficient is
$2\mathsf B_E C_{\mathrm{gf}}L^{-2n_{\mathrm f}}D'^2$,
where now
\[
 D'=M(1+d)+9M_w\sum_{\omega'}(|\omega'|+1).
\]
Together with two legs this again gives $L^{-4n_{\mathrm f}}$.
The coefficient is estimated on all pairs, but the
second-stage legs must remain at one pair.
To respect this order, sum the first-stage rows with
their individual suprema before estimating the
coefficient.  There are at most
$8C_{\mathrm{nb}}M^3(1+d)$ first cubes of a row.
Each leg therefore costs at most the additional factor
$(1+8C_{\mathrm{nb}}M^3A_\kappa)(1+d)$.
Its square is included in $C_{\mathrm{ft}}$, and
$(1+d)^2\le e^{\kappa d/11}$ because $\kappa>22$.
The remaining estimates keep one common pair.

For $T_{\mathrm c}$, a transported difference of legs
has the bound
\[
 \bigl[2C_H(\alpha)+4C_H(c_T\epsilon_*+C_QL\alpha_1)\bigr]
                  L^{-(1+\alpha)n_{\mathrm f}}.
\]
In the local and walk decomposition one may use
\[
 5L^{-2n_{\mathrm f}}+
 2A_\kappa\bigl[C_H(\alpha)+4C_H(c_T\epsilon_*+C_QL\alpha_1)\bigr]
                  L^{-(1+\alpha)n_{\mathrm f}} .
\]
The other leg contributes $L^{-n_{\mathrm f}}$.
Transport paths have length at most $C_tD'$; a moved
site term needs at most $3M$ within its cell.
The row and column sums defining moved pieces obey
the double-kernel bound $4A_\kappa^2h_F^{-2}$.
Their coefficients have absolute sum at most two.
Counting the removed and inserted copies therefore gives
\[
 \sum_p e^{\kappa\sum\Delta^+}
        \sum_y\|a_{X,p}(y)\|_{\mathrm{tr}}
 \le16A_\kappa^2h_F^{-2}
                       \|F_{\sigma,2}^{\mathrm{tr}}(X)\|.
\]
Thus these pieces have the same $2+\alpha$ gain.
For $T_{\mathrm d}$ the two legs give directly
\[
 \nu\|m_c\|
       (2A_\kappa C_H^2L^{-n_{\mathrm f}}h_F)^2 .
\]

We include the filing and diameter costs explicitly.
The hull of a term has length at most
$L^{-n_{\mathrm f}}d+\sum\Delta^+$, before its
regular-gauge enlargement.  The latter costs
$e^{\kappa c_0}$.  Transports cost at most
\[
 e^{\kappa(1+d)/8}
         e^{\sum_{\omega'}(|\omega'|+1)/8}.
\]
For all three types of terms, including the cell terms,
\[
 \pi_{\mathrm f}(Y_t)D'^2\le M^2u^6,\qquad
 u=5+2C_t(1+d)+6C_t\sum_{\omega'}(|\omega'|+1)
                         +2\sum_\omega(|\omega|+1).
\]
The rounding error of two per walk is paid by
$6C_t(1-L^{-n_{\mathrm f}})(|\omega'|+1)\ge72/13$.
For a cell term the formula at $d=0$ also covers its
diameter $6+2\sum_\omega(|\omega|+1)$.
The definition of $P_{\mathrm{ft}}$ now gives
\[
 M^2u^6\le M^2P_{\mathrm{ft}}e^{\kappa d/8}
       \prod_{\omega'}e^{(|\omega'|+1)/8}
       \prod_\omega e^{(|\omega|+1)/24}.
\]
The shares of the original polymer decay used here are
$1/13+1/8+1/8$, and, for the coefficient supremum,
another $1/11$.  Their sum is less than $1/2$.
The walk factors use only $1/4$ of a first-stage
walk rate and $1/24$ of a second-stage rate.
Their remaining factor $e^{7/24}$ per leg is absorbed
by the degree sum, since $e^{7/12}<2$.
Consequently the three estimates in (T) hold first
with $C_{\mathrm{pt}}$ on the right.
This constant includes the factor $L^4$ needed to
replace $n_{\mathrm f}\ge n-1$ by $n$.

\emph{Summing the reading and taking variations.}
Lemma~\ref{lem:C403-amplitude-differences} applies
under the sum over the terms just constructed.
In particular, its factor $1.19$ does not interchange
the common-pair supremum with that sum.

For a long-lag reading use $W_{i+1}(Y_t)\le W_l(X)W_l(X)^{-1/2}$
or the corresponding cell inequality.
To replace $W_l(X)^{-1/2}$ by the weight of its filing
cell costs at most $e^{\kappa(1+d)/16}$.
This is paid by the decay still left above.
There are two ways to sum over the cells.
Dropping the requirement that the output contains
a specified cube gives $\mathcal C_l(\mathscr S)$.
Dropping the weights instead, and using the factor
$\pi_{\mathrm f}(Y_t)$, gives at most
$16C_4L^{3n_{\mathrm f}}$.
The resulting constant is
$16C_4e^{\kappa/16}C_{\mathrm{pt}}\mathcal N$,
bounded by $C_{\mathrm{rd}}\mathcal N$.
This proves (R2).  The supremum over $\lambda$ and
the common pair is taken only after the sum over
the output polymers contained in that pair's domain.

For the variation, the shift-amplitude disc has radius
\[
 R=\frac{\mathsf c_{\mathrm{os}}\alpha_0}
             {c_h\sup|B'|}>\frac2{s_\lambda}\ge6.
\]
Holomorphy follows term by term from the localized
legs.  The weight $C_Hh_F$ on the filing-level field
covers both its background contribution of weight
$C_HL^{-1}h_F$ and its fluctuation contribution
of weight $\Gamma_F$.
The sum of the decomposed differences is the
original variation, first at real admitted fields
and then throughout the disc by holomorphy.
For $t(1)-t(0)$, use the amplitude-difference lemma
with weights $W_{i+1}(Y_t)$ and
$\rho=1+s_\lambda^{-1}$.  Its cost is $1.19s_\lambda$.
For
$t(0)(\Psi_i^{\mathrm{bg}}+W)-t(0)(\Psi_i^{\mathrm{bg}})$,
there is no shift-parameter dependence.
The Grassmann substitution estimate uses
\[
 h=C_Hh_F,\quad h_a=C_HL^{-1}h_F,\quad h_b=\Gamma_F,
 \quad h_b'=C_Hh_F(1-L^{-1}).
\]
It costs $h_b/h_b'\le c_\psi$.
The total cost is at most $1.19(s_\lambda+c_\psi)$.
Use the preceding cell count at $n_{\mathrm f}=n-1$.
The inequalities $1.19\le2$ and
$2\cdot16C_4e^{\kappa/16}C_{\mathrm{pt}}\le C_{\mathrm{rd}}$
prove the stronger assertion in (V2).

For a lag below $n_{\mathrm{lag}}$ retain the unexpanded
reading and file it at the hull of its original polymer.
Its least degree is two.  The two legs give
$L^{-2n}\le L^{2n_{\mathrm{lag}}}L^{-4n}$.
The hull uses $e^{\kappa d/13}$; its diameter factor
is bounded by $P_{\mathrm{ft}}e^{\kappa d/8}$.
For the direct variation split the legs into their
background and fluctuation parts and use the same
amplitude-difference lemma.
The fluctuation, amplitude and chain costs are at most
\[
 1.19(c_\psi+s_\lambda+C_G\beta_\lambda)
                         \le1.19c'_\psi .
\]
The amplitude radius here is
$2a_{\mathrm{an}}L^{n_{\mathrm f}}/(c_h\sup|B'|)>2/s_\lambda$.
The remaining chain dependence is paid by the
decay at rate $\kappa$.
The unweighted cell recount is $319$, and hence
the total is at most
$380L^{4n_{\mathrm{lag}}}M^3L^{3n}L^{-4n}$
times $c'_\psi$ and the old norm.
For the weighted count it is at most
\[
 2e^{\kappa/16}e^{1/2}c'_\psi
       \mathcal C_l(\mathscr S)L^{4n_{\mathrm{lag}}}L^{-4n}
\]
times that norm.  If $n_{\mathrm f}\ge1$, the hull
pays the additional weight with half the source
distance decay; if $n_{\mathrm f}=0$, use $e^{-d/2}$.
Both bounds are already included in $C_{\mathrm{rd}}^\psi$.
Thus the same constants cover the short lags.

\emph{Moments and moved terms.}
A kernel piece has support $Z_p\times Z_p$, with
$Z_p\supset X$ and $d_l(Z_p)\le d+\sum\Delta^+$.
For $y\in Z_p$,
$W_l(y)\le W_l(X)e^{\kappa(1+d_l(Z_p))/8}$.
The two localized legs, summed at rate $\kappa/8$
with their walk factors, give the double-kernel bound
$4A_\kappa^2h_F^{-2}$ times the original norm.
For the cell containing $y$, the walk recount is
\[
 (1-e^{-1})\sum_{t\ge0}(2t+5)^3e^{-t}<319.
\]
Including both row and column sums gives
$2552e^{\kappa/8}A_\kappa^2h_F^{-2}
\|F_2^{\mathrm{tr}}\|_{l;D;\mathscr S}$.
The cell sum consists of the original summands,
their removed diagonal pieces and the pieces
inserted at the cells of their sites.
It is bounded by
\[
 (4+5104M^3A_\kappa^2)e^{\kappa/8}h_F^{-2}
                            \|F_2^{\mathrm{tr}}\|_{l;D;\mathscr S}.
\]

For the first absolute moment, the distance within
a summand's support is at most
$c'M(1+d_l(Z_p))/2$.
Use
$1+d_l(Z_p)\le e^d e^{\sum\Delta^+}$.
An inserted site piece is at distance at most $3M/2$
from its cell centre.  The two contributions are
bounded by
\[
 \bigl[36(1+c'M)A_\kappa^2
       +10208A_\kappa^2M^3(1+3M)\bigr]h_F^{-2}
                                                       \varepsilon_{\mathrm f}.
\]
The moved terms of a fixed $X$ also obey
\[
 4C'^2h_F^{-2}
       \bigl(\|F_1(X)\|+\|G(X)\|\bigr)
                             e^{-\alpha_Dd(X,y)/2}.
\]
These estimates are all bounded by the stated
$C_{\mathrm{mo}}$, since $36+10208<2^{14}$.

For the tail $d_l(Z_p)\ge d_*$ use
\[
 1_{\{d_l(Z_p)\ge d_*\}}
 \le e^{-\kappa d_*/2}
         e^{\kappa d/2}e^{\kappa\sum\Delta^+/2}.
\]
Together with the weight already used, the total
rate is at most $5\kappa/8\le\kappa+2$.
The same localized-leg constant and the same
cell recount therefore prove the tail assertion.
Apply Cauchy's formula for the fourth coefficient
on $|\lambda|=r<\bar\lambda$ under this absolutely
convergent sum, and then let $r$ increase to
$\bar\lambda$.  This proves the coefficient version.

\emph{Applicability and the torus.}
The differentiated step functions in
Lemma~\ref{C-403-45} are holomorphic and invariant
on the full core.  Each direct, mass and old
variation has these properties term by term.
The transports are gauge covariant, and the
trivial-pair value is invariant under constant
gauge transformations.
The scalar arrays are pointed by equal shares.
For $P$ and $P_{\mathrm{red}}$, the moved pieces
use $F_1=\widetilde P$, $G=0$, and the row and
column coefficients $1/2,1/2$.
The fourth coefficients are bounded by the
Cauchy estimate just proved.
For $P_{\mathrm{rsp}}$, use
$F_1=\widetilde P_{\mathrm{rsp}}$, $G=0$;
there is no order-four subtraction, by
Lemma~\ref{C-403-48}.
The families $Q$ and $R$ move no diagonal terms.
The degree assertions in that lemma use only the
first two parts of its proof, and do not depend
on the applicability clause proved here.
The families joining cells have the same
termwise invariance and locality.
This proves (H).

On a torus, retain the seam in every transport
and use the torus distance in every count.
The terms with no leg difference then give
$m_c^{\mathrm{tor}}$, as required.
For an infinite-lattice scalar variation each
localization index fits in a sufficiently large
torus; its definition and its bounds agree there.
Passing back index by index, and using the
absolute bounds proved above, gives the same
variation on the infinite lattice.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The direct source and mass directions}

The direct source estimate counts the plaquettes in its
support.  The mass estimate uses the mean of its coefficient
over a cell.  Both estimates retain this spatial information
through localization.

\begin{lemma}\label{C-403-47}
Let $0\le i<j$, $\lambda\in D_i$ and
$s_\lambda=c_h\beta_\lambda/a_{\mathrm{an}}\le1/3$.
Let $C_{\mathrm{cf}}$ be the completed-field constant
of the first step, and put
\begin{align*}
 a_{\mathrm{src}}
 &=\max\{\alpha_0^2,2^{13}\mathsf c_{\mathrm{os}}
                                      \alpha_0C_{\mathrm{cf}}/c_h\},\\
 A_{\mathrm{src}}
 &=3a_{\mathrm{src}}(1+2M^3c_{\mathrm{cl}}/w_*),&
 C_{\mathrm{src}}&=3^5C_\Sigma M^3A_{\mathrm{src}}.
\end{align*}
Then:
\begin{enumerate}
\item For a bare plaquette $p$,
\[
 \epsilon(\mathcal V_i^w[\delta_p])
       \le A_{\mathrm{src}}s_\lambda a_K^3a_i^{-4}.
\]
If $i\ge1$, its terms are the finite differences in
the shift parameters, filed at polymers $Y$ containing
the cube set $X(p)$, with $d_i(X(p))=0$.
If $i=0$, it is one term at the cubes containing a
corner of $p$, again with $d_0(X(p))=0$.
\item Let $\mathsf g$ be supported on plaquettes whose
barycentres lie in a closed ball of radius $r\ge a_K$,
and let the nonempty closed set $S$ contain these
barycentres and lie in that ball.  Then
\[
 \epsilon_S(\mathcal V_i^w[\mathsf g])
             \le C_{\mathrm{src}}s_\lambda e_i[\mathsf g].
\]
This also holds at $r=\infty$, with $S$ the entire
torus or $\mathbb R^3$.
\item Let $\varkappa$ be a function on the bare sites
with scalar values or values in the matrices on
\(\mathbb C^2_{\rm s}\otimes\mathbb C^2_\tau
                  \otimes\mathbb C^{N_f}\),
acting trivially on colour. For a matrix coefficient use its
operator norm in the weighted cell mean
$\langle\varkappa\rangle_{i;\{\lambda\};S}$.
For every nonempty $S$,
\[
 \epsilon_S(\mathcal V_i^{\mathrm s}[\varkappa])
 \le C_{\mathrm{mn}}c'_\psi c_{\mathsf S}h_F^2
                      \langle\varkappa\rangle_{i;\{\lambda\};S},
 \qquad C_{\mathrm{mn}}=37.
\]
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The weight in the level-$i$ action is
$\beta_i-a_K^{-1}w$.  Its direction at $\delta_p$
therefore has sign $+$ and is obtained from
\[
 a_K^{-1}\bigl[a_p(\mathsf U'(\mu\lambda B))
                                      -a_p(\mathsf U)\bigr]
\]
by taking its terms of orders $1$, $2$ and at least
$3$ in $\mu$, at $\mu=1$.  The first and third terms
belong to the scalar potential; the quadratic term
belongs to the quadratic origin.
Write $\mathcal A=\lambda\mathsf t_i^{-1/2}B$.
On the step polydisc,
$\sup|\mathcal A|<\beta_\lambda\le\beta_0/2$.

Suppose first that $i\ge1$.  On $X(p)$, the function
$f_p=a_K^{-1}a_p$ is local on the regular-pair core
and satisfies
\[
 \|f_p\|_{X(p)}
       \le\tfrac12\alpha_0^2a_K^{-1}L^{-4i}
       =\tfrac12\alpha_0^2a_K^3a_i^{-4}.
\]
Its localization is the finite difference
$\psi_Y(\mu)$ at the polymers $Y\supset X(p)$.
The sum of these differences is $f_p$ at the shifted
background minus $f_p$ at the background.
For $|\mu|\le2$ the shift remains admitted, and its
term radius is
\[
 \varrho_{\mathrm t}
   =\frac{\mathsf c_{\mathrm{os}}\alpha_0}{2c_h\beta_\lambda}
   =s_\lambda^{-1}\ge3.
\]
The localized function is holomorphic near this disc,
vanishes at $\mu=0$, and obeys
\[
 |\psi_Y(\mu)|
 \le\alpha_0^2s_\lambda a_K^3a_i^{-4}
       e^{-(\bar\kappa-1)\mathfrak m_i(X(p),Y)}.
\]
Cauchy's estimate on $|\mu|=2$ bounds the linear,
quadratic and remaining terms at $\mu=1$ by,
respectively, $1/2$, $1/4$ and $1/4$ of this expression.
The quadratic coefficient is a quadratic form in
$\mathcal A$, defined at all fluctuations.

The cubes of $X(p)$ have a common corner.  Starting
there, add the other cubes of $Y$ in wall-connected
order; one edge for each added cube extends an edge
tree meeting all cubes.  Thus
$d_i(Y)\le\mathfrak m_i(X(p),Y)$.
Since $\bar\kappa\ge\kappa+3$ and
$\lambda_V\le(1-2\delta_{\mathrm w})\kappa$, the
localization decay pays the factor $e^{\lambda_Vd_i(Y)}$.

At $i=0$ there is no shift system.  The field is
$e^{iB'}\mathsf U$, where $B'$ is the completed
fluctuation.  Its pivot values depend only on the
pair and fluctuation in $X(p)$ when their pivot
bond belongs to $X(p)$.  The entire expression
therefore belongs to this one set.
For $|\mu|\le2$, the completed-field estimate gives
\[
 \sup|B'(\mu\mathcal A)|\le
       \varepsilon_{B'}:=4C_{\mathrm{cf}}\beta_\lambda\le1.
\]
The four factors $Z_s$ of the original plaquette
have norm at most $2$; their perturbed versions
have norm at most $2e^{\varepsilon_{B'}}$ and
$|Z'_s-Z_s|\le2(e^{\varepsilon_{B'}}-1)$.
For the inverse factors use
$U^{-1}=JU^TJ^{-1}$, with $J$ unitary, since
$\det U=1$.
Telescoping the product of four factors gives
\[
 |\partial(e^{iB'}\mathsf U)(p)-\partial\mathsf U(p)|
 \le64e^{3\varepsilon_{B'}}(e^{\varepsilon_{B'}}-1)
 \le2^{12}\varepsilon_{B'}.
\]
As $a_p=1-\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}\partial U(p)$,
the function $\psi(\mu)$ above obeys
\begin{align*}
 |\psi(\mu)|
 &\le2^{14}C_{\mathrm{cf}}\beta_\lambda a_K^{-1}\\
 &=2^{13}(\mathsf c_{\mathrm{os}}\alpha_0C_{\mathrm{cf}}/c_h)
                                 s_\lambda a_K^{-1}\\
 &\le a_{\mathrm{src}}s_\lambda a_K^3a_0^{-4}.
\end{align*}
It vanishes at zero.  The same Cauchy estimate gives
the three fractions $1/2,1/4,1/4$.

At every level the two scalar parts, after the decay
weight is inserted, cost at most
$3a_{\mathrm{src}}s_\lambda a_K^3a_i^{-4}/4$.
If $\mathcal Q_Y$ is the quadratic part, its bound
on the field polydisc of radius $r_{\mathrm f}\ge1$
gives at real fluctuations
\[
 |\mathcal Q_Y(B)|
 \le M^3\sup|\mathcal Q_Y|
                     \left(1+M^{-3}\sum_b|B(b)|^2\right).
\]
Its origin norm therefore costs at most $M^3$
times the supremum.  Combining the potential
and origin norms gives
\[
 \epsilon(\mathcal V_i^w[\delta_p])
 \le a_{\mathrm{src}}s_\lambda a_K^3a_i^{-4}
             \left(\frac34+\frac{M^3c_{\mathrm{cl}}}{2w_*}\right),
\]
which proves the first assertion.

For the second, the set $X(p)$ contains the square
of $p$, hence its barycentre.  Every polymer carrying
this plaquette contribution meets $S$, so its source
weight is $1$.
There are at most
$3(2r/a_K+1)^3\le81(r/a_K)^3$
bare plaquettes with barycentre in the ball, and
at most $12M^3L^{3i}$ plaquettes have a prescribed
set $X(p)$.  At $i\ge1$, sum the localized terms
using the scalar localization estimate, with data
\[
 b_{i,X}=a_{\mathrm{src}}s_\lambda a_K^3a_i^{-4}
                         \sum_{p:X(p)=X}|\mathsf g(p)|.
\]
These data vanish unless $d_i(X)=0$.  The sum is
bounded by
$C_\Sigma\sup_Xb_{i,X}
e^{-(1-2\delta_{\mathrm w})\kappa d_i(Y)}$.
At $i=0$ the same estimate holds directly, since
the terms have size zero and $C_\Sigma\ge1$.
The two plaquette counts and
\[
 a_K^3a_i^{-4}
       \min\{M^3L^{3i},(r/a_K)^3\}
 \le M^3a_i^{-1}
                    \min\{1,(r/a_i)^3\}
\]
give $\sup_Xb_{i,X}\le81M^3a_{\mathrm{src}}
s_\lambda e_i[\mathsf g]$.
Use the preceding potential and origin factors
to obtain the bound with $C_{\mathrm{src}}$.
For $r=\infty$ only the count per set is needed.

Finally consider the mass direction.  The usual
mass-variation proof is linear in its coefficient
at each place $v$.  Before counting which cubes
its walks reach, a place contributes its operator
norm times
$L^{-i}\nu(C_HL^{-i}h_F)^2$.
There are $\nu_PM^3L^{3i}$ places per cube and
$c_{\mathsf S}=M^3\nu_P\nu C_H^2$.
Thus the constant coefficient in that estimate
can be replaced by the mean of $|\varkappa|$
over the bare sites of the cube.
The part with a fluctuation leg costs at most
$c_\psi c_{\mathsf S}h_F^2/2$ before its walks
are counted.  The change from $\mathsf U$ to
$\mathsf U'$ costs at most
$C_G\beta_\lambda c_{\mathsf S}h_F^2$.
A matrix coefficient has trace norm at most
$\nu$ times its operator norm, so the same
constants apply.

At $i=0$ the variation is explicitly
\[
 -\sum_v\bigl[
   \bar\psi^{\mathrm{bg}}(v)\varkappa(x_v)W(v)
  +\bar W(v)\varkappa(x_v)\psi^{\mathrm{bg}}(v)
  +\bar W(v)\varkappa(x_v)W(v)\bigr],
 \qquad
 \psi^{\mathrm{bg}}=H_0(\mathsf U)\Psi_1.
\]
There is no change-of-background part and no walk
for the identity image of $W$; the same estimate
applies place by place.

The terms originating in a cube $c$ are summable
at rate $\kappa+2$.  If their polymer also contains
a cube $\square$, lowering the rate to $\kappa$
gives $e^{-2\operatorname{dist}(c,\square)/M}$.
The sum of these factors over $c$ is at most $37$.
For the source weight,
\[
 e^{\kappa_{\mathrm s}\delta_{i+1}(Y;S)}
 \le e^{\kappa_{\mathrm s}\sqrt3/L}
                        e^{\kappa_{\mathrm s}\delta_i(c;S)}
 \le2e^{\kappa_{\mathrm s}\delta_i(c;S)} .
\]
The weighted mean over $c$ is bounded by
$\langle\varkappa\rangle_{i;\{\lambda\};S}$.
Consequently
\begin{align*}
 \epsilon_S(\mathcal V_i^{\mathrm s}[\varkappa])
 &\le2\left(\frac{37}{2}c_\psi+C_G\beta_\lambda\right)
       c_{\mathsf S}h_F^2\langle\varkappa\rangle_{i;\{\lambda\};S}\\
 &\le37c'_\psi c_{\mathsf S}h_F^2
                              \langle\varkappa\rangle_{i;\{\lambda\};S}.
\end{align*}
\end{proof}

\subsection{Orders at zero field scale}

Here the order of a function means its joint Taylor
order at $\lambda=0$ and at the trivial pair, in
$\lambda$ and the coordinates of that pair, at fixed
fluctuation $B$.  In particular, the fluctuation enters
the members as $\lambda B$.

\begin{lemma}\label{C-403-48}
The response families have the following orders.
\begin{enumerate}
\item The scalar parts of
$\delta_i[\mathsf g]$, $\widetilde{\mathbf P}^{(i+1)}[\mathsf g]$,
$\widetilde{\mathbf P}^{\mathrm{red},(i+1)}[\mathsf g]$,
$\mathbf P^{(i+1)}[\mathsf g]$ and
$\mathbf P^{\mathrm{red},(i+1)}[\mathsf g]$
have order at least $2$; their parts with fermion
legs have order at least $3$.
The member
$\mathcal V_i^{\mathrm s}[\lambda^4\mathfrak N_i[\mathsf g]]$
has order at least $4$, and the parts with legs of
its image under $D\widetilde E_i$ have order at least $5$.
The scalar parts of
$\mathbf P^{\mathrm{rsp},(i+1)}[\mathsf g]$,
$\widetilde{\mathbf Q}^{(i+1)}[f,h]$ and
$\mathbf Q^{(i+1)}[f,h]$ have order at least $4$,
and their parts with legs have order at least $5$.
\item The integrated response families, including
the numbers $\mathfrak e_{i+1}$, are even in $\lambda$.
The members $\delta_i[\mathsf g]$ are invariant under
$(\lambda,B)\mapsto(-\lambda,-B)$.
All these families and members vanish at $\lambda=0$
at every pair.  The numbers $\mathfrak n_i[\mathsf g]$
and $\mathfrak N_i[\mathsf g]$ are independent of $\lambda$.
At the trivial pair, the parts with legs of
$\widetilde{\mathbf P}$ and
$\widetilde{\mathbf P}^{\mathrm{red}}$
start at order $\lambda^4$; those of
$\mathbf P^{\mathrm{rsp}}$ and
$\widetilde{\mathbf Q}$ start at order $\lambda^6$.
The values $\mathfrak e_{i+1}[f,h](X)$ start at order
$\lambda^4$.  Hence $\mathsf n_j^\lambda$ is
holomorphic, even and of order at least $\lambda^4$.
\item One has
$\mathfrak n_l[\mathsf g]=\mathfrak n_l^{\mathrm{red}}[\mathsf g]$.
Let $F$ be either $\mathbf P^{(l)}[\mathsf g]$
or $\mathbf P^{\mathrm{red},(l)}[\mathsf g]$,
$1\le l\le j$, with its prescribed units.
Write $a_{X,p}(z;\lambda)$ for the moments of its
pre-extraction kernels and $a_{X,p}^{[4]}(z)$
for their fourth coefficients.
The latter coefficients agree in the full and
reduced systems.  The cell sum is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:C403-cell-moment}
 m_c=\sum_{z\in c}\left[
   \sum_{X,p}a_{X,p}(z;\lambda)
  -\mathfrak s_l^{-1}\sum_yA_l(y,z)
             \lambda^4\sum_{X,p}'a_{X,p}^{[4]}(z)\right].
\end{equation}
The prime denotes the pieces read by the extraction rule.
On $\mathbb Z^3$, $m_c$ has order at least $\lambda^6$.
On a torus write $m_c=m_c^{(6)}+\lambda^4m_c^{[4]}$,
where $m_c^{(6)}$ is even and has order at least $6$.
Put
\[
 c_{\mathrm{def}}=\min\{4c_{\mathrm t},\kappa/(8c'M)\},
 \qquad
 C_{\mathrm{def}}=M^3C_{\mathrm{mo}}
                                  (c_b^{-2}C_A+e^{\kappa/2}).
\]
For weights of one or two sets and $\lambda\in D_{l-1}$,
\begin{align*}
 h_F^2W_l(c)|\lambda|^4\|m_c^{[4]}\|
 &\le C_{\mathrm{def}}e^{-c_{\mathrm{def}}\ell_G/a_l}
      \left(\frac{|\lambda|}{\bar\lambda_{l-1}}\right)^4
                             \|F_2^{\mathrm{tr}}\|_{l;D_{l-1};\mathscr S},\\
 h_F^2W_l(c)\sup_{D_{l-1}}\|m_c^{(6)}\|
 &\le2C_{\mathrm{mo}}\|F_2^{\mathrm{tr}}\|_{l;D_{l-1};\mathscr S}.
\end{align*}
The cell sums of $\mathbf P^{\mathrm{rsp},(l)}[\mathsf g]$
and $\mathbf Q^{(l)}[f,h]$ have no extraction forms
and have order at least $\lambda^6$ on both lattices.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
We prove the orders, parity and equality of fourth
moments together by induction.  At level zero there
are no response families and $\mathfrak N_0=0$.
Every potential member vanishes at $\lambda=0$
and depends on $\lambda$ and $B$ through $\lambda B$
and $\lambda^2$; it therefore has joint order at least one.
The direct weight direction has order at least two,
since $a_p(\mathbf1)=0$ and
$a_p=\tfrac12\det(\partial U(p)-\mathbf1)$
is quadratic in $\partial U(p)-\mathbf1$.
Each of its three amplitude parts retains this
joint order.  So do the finite differences used
to localize it: each partial shift is the original
background when $\lambda B=0$.
At level zero the completed-field formula gives
the same conclusion.

The mass direction has order at least four
because of its factor $\lambda^4$.
Some of its terms linear in $W$ have exactly
that order, so one cannot claim order five
before integration.
Its part of degree two in the new generators
vanishes when $\mathsf U'=\mathsf U$, by
$H_{0,i}(\mathsf U)H_i(\mathsf U)=H_{0,i+1}(\mathsf U)$,
and hence has order at least five.
The parts linear in $W$ have Gaussian mean zero;
to contribute after expansion they require another
member with a $W$ leg, of order at least one.
The $\bar WW$ part has degree zero in the new
generators, and requires another member with
legs to contribute to their positive-degree part.
Thus the parts with legs of the image under
$D\widetilde E_i$ have order at least five.

To justify this order count through the expansion,
use its derivative formulas from
Lemma~\ref{C-403-45}.
They are sums of Gaussian means of the direction,
or the two directions, multiplied by potential
members.  The Gaussian covariances and quadratic
origin are holomorphic near $\lambda=0$ and the
trivial pair; the tests depend on the fluctuation.
The derivative bounds give uniform convergence
on a smaller polydisc in $\lambda$ and the pair.
Taylor coefficients therefore pass through the
integrals and sums.  A product whose factors
have orders $k_1,k_2,\ldots$ has no coefficient
below their sum.  A scalar direction can produce
legs only in the presence of another member
with legs, of order at least one.

Old-family variation also preserves joint order.
Its maps of the pair and $\lambda B$ send zero
and the trivial pair to the trivial pair, and its
finite differences are linear combinations of
these compositions.  Removing a scalar value
at the trivial pair preserves the orders.
The induction hypothesis now proves the first
response orders in the first assertion.

The full and reduced systems differ, before
extraction, by
\begin{align*}
 \widetilde{\mathbf P}^{\mathrm{rsp},(i+1)}[\mathsf g]
 =D\widetilde E_i\biggl[
   \mathcal V_i^{\mathrm s}[\lambda^4\mathfrak N_i[\mathsf g]]
   +\sum_{l\le i}\mathcal V_i^{\mathrm{old}}
                  [\mathbf P^{\mathrm{rsp},(l)}[\mathsf g]]
                         \biggr].
\end{align*}
This equality holds polymer by polymer with the
specified units.  At preceding levels the full
and reduced fourth moments agree, so their forms
agree.  Their remaining units differ by the
kernel difference minus its diagonal moment
at the original cell, and the differences of
the moved pieces at their destination cells.
The piece rule and variation are linear in these
units.  The induction hypothesis and the
mass-direction count above therefore give
orders at least four and five for the scalar
and fermionic parts of this difference.

The expansion commutes with $B\mapsto-B$.
Direct directions depend on $\lambda B$;
the mass coefficient is $\lambda^4\mathfrak N_i$;
old variations of even families have the same
simultaneous symmetry.
Thus their integrated families are even in
$\lambda$.  At the trivial pair, joint order
is order in $\lambda$.  The fermionic feedback
part, of order at least five and even, starts
at order six.  Its fourth moments vanish.
Hence the full and reduced fourth moments
agree at level $i+1$, as do their extraction forms.
Removing the scalar value then gives the claimed
orders of $\mathbf P^{\mathrm{rsp},(i+1)}$.
The form added to $\mathbf P$ itself has order
four and does not change its asserted lower orders.

The new contribution to $\widetilde{\mathbf Q}$
is $D^2\widetilde E_i[\delta_i[f],\delta_i[h]]$.
Each direction has order at least two.
A term with legs uses a direction's part with
legs or a further member with legs, and so
has order at least five.
The old $\mathbf Q$ variations preserve the
inductive orders.  This proves the first assertion
and the equality of fourth moments.

At $\lambda=0$ the fine field equals its
background, so the direct weight direction
vanishes.  The mass direction vanishes by its
factor, and old variations vanish by the
induction hypothesis at every pair, including
their zero-shift differences involving $W$.
Linearity and bilinearity of the expansion
derivatives then show that all new response
families vanish there.
The extraction numbers are fourth Taylor
coefficients and do not depend on $\lambda$.
Parity upgrades the joint orders at the
trivial pair from three to four and from
five to six.  The scalar mixed values have
order at least four, and their absolutely
convergent sum is $\mathsf n_j^\lambda$.
This proves the second assertion.

It remains to establish the cell formula and
the torus bounds.  The units at the original
cell consist of a kernel minus its diagonal
moment and have total moment zero.
The moved piece at $z$ contributes
$a_{X,p}(z;\lambda)$ at the cell of $z$.
The extraction form contributes
$-\mathfrak s_l^{-1}A_l(y,z)
\lambda^4a_{X,p}^{[4]}(z)$ at $y$.
Summing gives \eqref{eq:C403-cell-moment}.
On $\mathbb Z^3$ every piece is read and
$\sum_yA_l(y,z)=\mathfrak s_l$.
The cell sum is consequently the sum of
$a_{X,p}(z;\lambda)-\lambda^4a_{X,p}^{[4]}(z)$,
which starts at order six.

On the torus its fourth coefficient is
\begin{align*}
 m_c^{[4]}=\sum_{z\in c}\biggl[
 &\sum_{X,p}'\left(1-\mathfrak s_l^{-1}\sum_yA_l(y,z)\right)
                                      a_{X,p}^{[4]}(z)\\
 &+\sum_{X,p}''a_{X,p}^{[4]}(z)\biggr].
\end{align*}
The double prime denotes the omitted pieces
whose original polymer has diameter at least
$\ell_G/4$.  Pieces whose expanded polymer
wraps around the torus remain in the first sum.
The matrix map
$\Lambda_zN=N-\mathfrak s_l^{-1}\sum_yA_l(y,z)N$
satisfies
\[
 \|\Lambda_zN\|
       \le c_b^{-2}C_Ae^{-4c_{\mathrm t}\ell_G/a_l}\|N\|.
\]
Cauchy's formula for the fourth coefficient
and the moment bound of Lemma~\ref{C-403-46}
give, at each site,
\[
 h_F^2W_l(z)|\lambda|^4
       \left\|\sum_{X,p}'a_{X,p}^{[4]}(z)\right\|
 \le \left(\frac{|\lambda|}{\bar\lambda_{l-1}}\right)^4
           C_{\mathrm{mo}}\|F_2^{\mathrm{tr}}\|_{l;D_{l-1};\mathscr S}.
\]
For an omitted piece its expanded polymer has
\[
 d_l(Z_p)\ge t_G:=\frac{\ell_G}{2c'Ma_l}-1.
\]
Apply the tail version of the same moment bound
before Cauchy's formula.  It gives the extra factor
\[
 e^{-\kappa t_G/2}
   =e^{\kappa/2}e^{-\kappa\ell_G/(4c'Ma_l)}
   \le e^{\kappa/2}e^{-2c_{\mathrm{def}}\ell_G/a_l}.
\]
If $t_G<0$, this factor exceeds one and the
ordinary moment bound gives the same inequality.
