There are $M^3$ sites in $c$, and
$W_l(z)\ge W_l(c)$.  Summing proves the first
torus estimate.
The moment estimate for $m_c$ and Cauchy's
bound $|\lambda|^4\|m_c^{[4]}\|
\le\sup_{D_{l-1}}\|m_c\|$ prove the second.

The feedback families have no forms, since
the full and reduced forms agree.
Their moments are the differences of the
two sets of moments, whose fourth coefficients
agree.  They therefore start at order six.
The $\mathbf Q$ families have only their
scalar values removed; their fermionic
parts at the trivial pair already start at
order six.  This proves the final assertion.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The fourth moment and its accumulated mass}

The reduced response controls the extracted fourth
coefficient.  The full response is needed to compare
its accumulation with the constant-source mass chain.
That comparison bounds the constant part before the
Lipschitz variation of a test function is estimated.

Let $c_{\mathrm{def}},C_{\mathrm{def}}$ be as in
Lemma~\ref{C-403-48}, and set
\begin{align*}
 S_{\mathrm{tor}}
 &=3C_{\mathrm{def}}\sum_{n\ge1}
              L^{2n}q_n^2e^{-2Mc_{\mathrm{def}}L^n},\\
 S_\diamond
 &=\sum_{n\ge1}
   \bigl(L^{n/2}q_n+3L^{(2-\alpha)n}q_n^2+3L^{5n/2}q_n^3\bigr)
        +S_{\mathrm{tor}},\\
 K_{\mathfrak n}&=3c_{\mathsf S}c_b^{-2}C_{\mathrm{mo}}.
\end{align*}
These sums converge.  Indeed, $q_n\le2^{10/9}L^{-8n/9}$
gives exponents $-7n/18$, $-19n/36$ and $-n/6$
in the three ordinary sums; in the torus sum
$L^{2n}q_n^2\le4(1+n\log L)^{4\mathfrak p_0}$.

Choose $C_{\mathcal C}\ge8M^3$ to satisfy, for
$n=i+1-l\ge0$ and the directions and sets of
Lemma~\ref{C-403-47},
\begin{align}
 e_l[\mathsf g]\min\{M^3L^{3n},\mathcal C_l(S)\}
 &\le C_{\mathcal C}L^{4n}e_{i+1}[\mathsf g],
       \label{eq:C403-count-first}\\
 e_l[f,h]\min\{M^3L^{3n},\mathcal C_l(S_f,S_h)\}
 &\le C_{\mathcal C}L^{9n/2}e_{i+1}[f,h].
       \label{eq:C403-count-mixed}
\end{align}
Require also
$\mathcal C_l(S)\le C_{\mathcal C}(1+r/a_l)^3$
for $S$ in a radius-$r$ ball, and
\[
 \mathcal C'_l:=
 \sum_\square e^{-\kappa_{\mathrm s}
                (\delta_l(\square;S_f)+\delta_l(\square;S_h))}
 \le
 \begin{cases}
 C_{\mathcal C},&a_l\ge\mathsf d,\\
 C_{\mathcal C}(\mathsf d/a_l)^3
 e^{-\kappa_{\mathrm s}\mathsf d/(2Ma_l)},
                                      &a_l<\mathsf d.
 \end{cases}
\]
These conditions are simultaneous on every torus and
on $\mathbb Z^3$; their verification is included below.
They require only a constant depending on
$M,\kappa_{\mathrm s}$.
Finally put
\[
 \theta=3K_\mu^{\mathrm s}K_MC_{\mathrm{rd}}C_{\mathcal C}
       (1+2C_{\mathrm{mo}})S_\diamond(2s_\lambda+c'_\psi)
       \le\frac12.
\]
The last inequality is one of the parameter choices
in the field-scale construction: the $c'_\psi$ term
is at most $1/4$ after choosing $h_F$, and the
$2s_\lambda$ term is at most $1/4$ after choosing
$c_\lambda$.

\begin{lemma}\label{C-403-49}
For $1\le i\le j$ the following estimates hold.
\begin{enumerate}
\item The reduced response and its pre-extraction
version satisfy
\[
 \|\mathbf P^{\mathrm{red},(i)}[\mathsf g]\|_{i;D_{i-1};S}
 \le A^{\mathrm{red}}e_i[\mathsf g],
 \qquad
 A^{\mathrm{red}}=6K_\mu^{\mathrm s}K_MC_{\mathrm{src}}L^4.
\]
This holds in the scalar array norm and in the
fermionic norm that sums the individual summands
at each polymer, including each extraction form
at its own polymer.
\item At each level-$i$ site $y$,
\[
 |\mathfrak n_i[\mathsf g](y)|
 \le K_{\mathfrak n}(c_{\mathsf S}h_F^2)^{-1}
       A^{\mathrm{red}}\bar\lambda_{i-1}^{-4}
       e_i[\mathsf g]e^{-\kappa_{\mathrm s}\delta_i(y;S)} .
\]
Here and below matrix absolute values are operator norms.
\item Define
\[
 C_{\mathrm{fb}}
 =43LC_{\mathrm{mn}}K_{\mathfrak n}K_\mu^{\mathrm s}
                         K_Mc'_\psi S_\diamond .
\]
Use $\rho$ from \eqref{C-403-50}; the parameter choice
$(\rho\bar\lambda_K)^2\ge2$ implies
$C_{\mathrm{fb}}\bar\lambda_i^{-2}\le1/2$.
In the constant direction on $\mathbb Z^3$,
\[
 |\mathfrak N_i^\infty[1](x)|
      \le\frac{A_c}{\mathsf b\mathsf t_i},\qquad
 A_c=2\left(
       \frac{\bar B_M}{4\varrho}\sup_{\bar I(g)}\mathsf b+C_r
                                      \right).
\]
The finite number $C_r$ is specified in the proof.
The function is invariant under the level-$i$
translations by $M\mathbb Z^3$.
\item On the least torus, for any representative
$\hat x$ of a bare site $x$,
\[
 |\mathfrak N_i[1](x)-\mathfrak N_i^\infty[1](\hat x)|
       \le\frac{C_{\mathrm{wr}}^{\mathfrak N}}{\mathsf b\mathsf t_i}.
\]
The constant is given below and depends on $g$
and the fixed constants.
\item For a direction of the test pair, on $D_i$,
\[
 c_{\mathsf S}h_F^2|\lambda|^4
       \langle\mathfrak N_i[f]\rangle_{i;\{\lambda\};S_f}
 \le A_{\mathfrak N}e_i[f]\mathfrak l_i^{4\mathfrak p_0+1}.
\]
The same holds for $h$; $A_{\mathfrak N}$ depends
on $g,\vartheta$ and the fixed constants.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\emph{The spatial counts.}
Cells have spacing $Ma_l$.
Summing their exponential distance weights from
a radius-$r$ ball gives
$\mathcal C_l(S)\le C(1+r/a_l)^3$.
On a torus, the weight of a cell is at most the
sum of weights of its translates in $\mathbb R^3$
relative to one representative of the ball.
Thus the same constant works on every torus.
For \eqref{eq:C403-count-first}, if
$a_l\le a_{i+1}\le r$, the size
ratio is $L^n$ and the geometric count is
at most $M^3L^{3n}$.
If $r\le a_l$, the ratio is $L^{4n}$
and the weighted count is at most $8C$.
If $a_l<r<a_{i+1}$, the ratio is
$L^n(a_{i+1}/r)^3$ and the count is at
most $8C(r/a_l)^3$.
At $r=\infty$ the first case applies.

For the pair, if $a_l\ge\mathsf d$,
the size ratio is $L^{9n/2}$ and the count
is at most $8C$.
If $a_l<\mathsf d$, the ratio is at
most
$L^{2n}+L^{9n/2}(a_l/\mathsf d)^{5/2}$.
The distance between the supports is at least
$\mathsf d$.  Split the two-set weight in half:
one half gives
$e^{\sqrt3\kappa_{\mathrm s}/4}
e^{-\kappa_{\mathrm s}\mathsf d/(4Ma_l)}$;
the other sums about $S_f$ to at most a
constant times $(\mathsf d/a_l)^3$.
The boundedness of
$t^5e^{-\kappa_{\mathrm s}t/(4M)}$ proves
\eqref{eq:C403-count-mixed}; when
$a_{i+1}\le\mathsf d$, use also
$L^{2n}\le(\mathsf d/a_l)^2$.
For $\mathcal C'_l$, the corresponding split
gives $e^{-\kappa_{\mathrm s}\mathsf d/(2Ma_l)}$,
and a remaining cell count at most
$16C(\mathsf d/a_l)^3$.
For $a_l\ge\mathsf d$ its count is
at most $8C$.
Taking the largest of these constants proves
all requirements on $C_{\mathcal C}$.

\emph{The reduced response.}
Proceed by induction on $i$ on either lattice.
There is no family at level zero.
The direction at the step from $i$ is
\[
 \mathcal V_i^w[\mathsf g]
       +\sum_{1\le l\le i}
          \mathcal V_i^{\mathrm{old}}
                    [\mathbf P^{\mathrm{red},(l)}[\mathsf g]].
\]
The direct term gives at most
$\tfrac32K_MC_{\mathrm{src}}L^4e_{i+1}[\mathsf g]$
after applying $D\widetilde E_i$, by
Lemmas~\ref{C-403-45} and \ref{C-403-47}.

For an old family $F=\mathbf P^{\mathrm{red},(l)}[\mathsf g]$,
put $n=i+1-l$.  It is holomorphic on $D_{l-1}$.
By Lemma~\ref{C-403-48}, it is even and vanishes
at zero; at the trivial pair its fermionic
summands, including its forms, start at order four.
Schwarz's lemma, applied separately to each
polymer and summand and using
$(\bar\lambda_i/\bar\lambda_{l-1})^2\le q_n$, gives
\begin{align*}
 \|F_0\|^{\mathrm{arr}}_{l;D_i;S},
 \ \|F_{\ge2}\|_{l;D_i;S}
       &\le q_nA^{\mathrm{red}}e_l[\mathsf g],\\
 \|F_2^{\mathrm{tr}}\|_{l;D_i;S}
       &\le3q_n^2A^{\mathrm{red}}e_l[\mathsf g].
\end{align*}
For the second line, the pre-extraction summand
is counted again as $F_1$ when its moved pieces
are attached; the forms are counted once.
The two inductive norms bound their sum by
$2A^{\mathrm{red}}e_l$, hence by the
displayed factor three.

The order-six cell remainder gains $q_n^3$.
The torus fourth-coefficient defect gains
$q_n^2e^{-c_{\mathrm{def}}\ell_G/a_l}
\le q_n^2e^{-2Mc_{\mathrm{def}}L^n}$.
Thus
\[
 h_F^2\sup_cW_l(c)\sup_{D_i}\|m_c\|
 \le
 \bigl(6C_{\mathrm{mo}}q_n^3
       +3C_{\mathrm{def}}q_n^2e^{-2Mc_{\mathrm{def}}L^n}\bigr)
                          A^{\mathrm{red}}e_l[\mathsf g].
\]
On $\mathbb Z^3$ omit the second term.
The lag estimates and \eqref{eq:C403-count-first}
therefore give
\begin{align*}
 \epsilon_S(\mathcal V_i^{\mathrm{old}}[F])
 \le{}&C_{\mathrm{rd}}C_{\mathcal C}L^{4n}
 \bigl[(2s_\lambda+c'_\psi)L^{-4n}q_n
       +3c'_\psi L^{-(2+\alpha)n}q_n^2\\
 &\qquad+c'_\psi L^{-2n}
       (6C_{\mathrm{mo}}q_n^3
           +3C_{\mathrm{def}}q_n^2e^{-2Mc_{\mathrm{def}}L^n})\bigr]
                  A^{\mathrm{red}}e_{i+1}[\mathsf g].
\end{align*}
Summing over $l$ is bounded by
$\theta A^{\mathrm{red}}e_{i+1}/
(3K_\mu^{\mathrm s}K_M)$.
Here $q_n\le L^{n/2}q_n$ and
$L^{2n}q_n^3\le L^{5n/2}q_n^3$, so all terms
are included in $S_\diamond$.
The derivative estimate now gives
\[
 \|\widetilde{\mathbf P}^{\mathrm{red},(i+1)}[\mathsf g]\|
 \le\left(\tfrac32K_MC_{\mathrm{src}}L^4
       +\frac{\theta}{2K_\mu^{\mathrm s}}A^{\mathrm{red}}\right)
                                      e_{i+1}[\mathsf g].
\]

Removing the scalar value doubles its array norm
at most.  The extraction forms add at most
$K_\mu^{\mathrm s}-K_\mu$ times the pre-extraction
norm, with the supremum on $D_i$ taken at each form.
To see this in the required order, a form satisfies
\[
 \sup_{D_i}\|P_{z;X,p}\|
 \le c_b^{-2}c_{\mathsf S}M^{-3}h_F^2
                          \bar\lambda_i^4\|a_{X,p}^{[4]}(z)\|.
\]
Apply the piecewise form estimate to the fourth
coefficient of each original polymer.
Its pieces use a rule independent of $\lambda$;
$W_{i+1}(Z_p)\le W_{i+1}(X)$ since $Z_p\supset X$;
and Cauchy's estimate bounds
$\bar\lambda_i^4$ times that coefficient by the
original polymer norm on $D_i$.
This proves the stated form factor without
interchanging a supremum and a sum.
The total extraction factor is at most
$\max\{2,1+K_\mu^{\mathrm s}-K_\mu\}\le2K_\mu^{\mathrm s}$.
With $\theta\le1/2$ and the definition of
$A^{\mathrm{red}}$, the induction closes.

\emph{The fourth coefficient at a site.}
It is the fourth coefficient of
$-\mathfrak s_i^{-1}\sum_{X,p}'a_{X,p}(y;\lambda)$
in the reduced system, by Lemma~\ref{C-403-48}.
The moment estimate and the bound just proved give
\[
 W_i(y)\sum_{X,p}\|a_{X,p}(y;\lambda)\|_{\mathrm{tr}}
       \le3C_{\mathrm{mo}}h_F^{-2}
                              A^{\mathrm{red}}e_i[\mathsf g].
\]
The restricted sum is holomorphic on $D_{i-1}$.
Apply Cauchy's formula there and use
$\mathfrak s_i^{-1}\le c_b^{-2}$ and
operator norm at most trace norm.
This proves the second assertion.

\emph{The constant part.}
Put $\hat{\mathsf n}_i=(\mathsf b\mathsf t_i)^{-1}$,
so $L^{i-l}\hat{\mathsf n}_l=\hat{\mathsf n}_i$, and set
\[
 \|\mathfrak N\|_{*,i}
   =\max_{l\le i}\sup_x
          \frac{|\mathfrak N_l^\infty[1](x)|}{\hat{\mathsf n}_l}.
\]
The site supremum has only finitely many translation
classes at each level.
The constant-source identity of
Lemma~\ref{C-403-44} gives
\begin{align*}
 \mathfrak N_i^\infty[1](x)
 &=\partial_c\sigma_i^{\mathrm c}(0)
       -\sum_{l\le i}L^{i-l}r_l(y_l(x)),\\
 r_l(y)&=\partial_c\nu_l^\infty-\mathfrak n_l^\infty[1](y).
\end{align*}
Let $m_l(\lambda;y)$ be $-\mathfrak s_l^{-1}$
times the moment of
$\widetilde{\mathbf P}^{\infty(l)}[1]$ at $y$.
It is even and starts at order four,
$m_l(1;y)=\partial_c\nu_l^\infty$, and its fourth
coefficient is $\mathfrak n_l^\infty[1](y)$.
Thus $r_l$ is its tail of orders at least six
at $\lambda=1$.  Cauchy's formula gives
\[
 |r_l(y)|\le\frac87\bar\lambda_{l-1}^{-6}
                             \sup_{D_{l-1}}|m_l(\cdot;y)|,
\]
using $\bar\lambda_{l-1}^{-2}\le1/8$.
The constant chain is holomorphic on $|c|<8\varrho$
and satisfies
$|s_i+\sigma_i^{\mathrm c}(c)|\le2\bar B_M/\mathsf t_i$.
Hence
$|\partial_c\sigma_i^{\mathrm c}(0)|
\le\bar B_M/(4\varrho\mathsf t_i)$.

Separate the moment and its tail into their reduced
and feedback parts.
For the reduced part the preceding estimate gives
\[
 \sup_{D_{l-1}}|m_l^{\mathrm{red}}|
 \le K_{\mathfrak n}(c_{\mathsf S}h_F^2)^{-1}
                                  A^{\mathrm{red}}a_l^{-1}.
\]
Since $a_l^{-1}/\hat{\mathsf n}_l=\mathsf t_l^2$,
$\mathsf t_l\le2x_l\le2x_{l-1}$ and
$\bar\lambda_{l-1}^{-2}
=c_\lambda(\log x_{l-1})^{2\mathfrak p_0}/(2x_{l-1})$,
\[
 \frac{L^{i-l}|r_l^{\mathrm{red}}|}{\hat{\mathsf n}_i}
 \le\frac47K_{\mathfrak n}(c_{\mathsf S}h_F^2)^{-1}
    A^{\mathrm{red}}c_\lambda^3
                    \frac{(\log x_{l-1})^{6\mathfrak p_0}}{x_{l-1}}.
\]
Here $x_{l-1}\ge L^{i+1-l}x_i/2$ and
$x_i\ge e^{18\mathfrak p_0}$.
The function $(\log x)^{6\mathfrak p_0}/x$
decreases for $x\ge e^{6\mathfrak p_0}$.
The geometric series obtained by substituting
$L^{i+1-l}x_i/2$ is uniformly bounded.
Let $C_r$ be any bound for the sum of the
displayed right sides; it depends only on
the constants listed in the statement.

Run the feedback response on its own discs.
At step $k-1$ its driving member is
$\mathcal V_{k-1}^{\mathrm s}
[\lambda^4\mathfrak N_{k-1}^\infty[1]]$.
Relative to $e_k[1]=a_k^{-1}$,
its derivative image is bounded by
\[
 \mathfrak d_k=
 \frac32K_MC_{\mathrm{mn}}c'_\psi c_{\mathsf S}h_F^2
 L\,\frac{25}{4}c_\lambda^{-2}
 (\log x_{k-1})^{-4\mathfrak p_0}\|\mathfrak N\|_{*,k-1}.
\]
Indeed,
$\hat{\mathsf n}_{k-1}a_k=L/\mathsf t_{k-1}^2$
and
$\bar\lambda_{k-1}^4
\le(25/4)\mathsf t_{k-1}^2c_\lambda^{-2}
(\log x_{k-1})^{-4\mathfrak p_0}$.
The quantity $\mathfrak d_k$ is nondecreasing in $k$.

For the old feedback families the scalar and
fermionic norms gain $q_n$ on a smaller disc.
Their trivial-pair quadratic norms and cell sums
gain $q_n^3$, since their order is at least six.
With the moved-piece convention, the former
cost at most $2q_n^3$ and the latter at most
$2C_{\mathrm{mo}}q_n^3$ times the old response norm.
These are bounded by the terms used in the
reduced induction.  Thus the total old-family
factor is at most $\theta/(2K_\mu^{\mathrm s})$.
No forms are extracted from a feedback family;
removing the scalar value costs at most two.
If $R_k$ is its larger family or scalar-array
norm divided by $e_k[1]$, then
\[
 R_k\le2\mathfrak d_k+\theta\max_{k'<k}R_{k'},
 \qquad R_k\le4\mathfrak d_k.
\]
The pre-extraction norm is at most
$\mathfrak d_k+\tfrac12\theta\max_{k'<k}R_{k'}
\le2\mathfrak d_k$.
Its quadratic norm with attached moved pieces
is therefore at most $4\mathfrak d_ke_k[1]$.

Apply the moment estimate and Cauchy's tail bound
once more.  Since
$(8/7)\cdot4\cdot(3/2)\cdot(25/4)=300/7\le43$
and
\[
 \bar\lambda_{l-1}^{-6}\mathsf t_l^2
       c_\lambda^{-2}(\log x_{l-1})^{-4\mathfrak p_0}
       \le\bar\lambda_{l-1}^{-2},
\]
one obtains
\[
 \frac{L^{i-l}|r_l^{\mathrm{rsp}}|}{\hat{\mathsf n}_i}
 \le43LC_{\mathrm{mn}}K_{\mathfrak n}K_Mc'_\psi
                 \bar\lambda_{l-1}^{-2}\|\mathfrak N\|_{*,l-1}.
\]
Use
$\bar\lambda_{l-1}^{-2}\le
q_{i+1-l}\bar\lambda_i^{-2}$,
$\sum q_n\le S_\diamond$ and $K_\mu^{\mathrm s}\ge1$.
The sum is at most
$C_{\mathrm{fb}}\bar\lambda_i^{-2}\|\mathfrak N\|_{*,i}
\le\frac12\|\mathfrak N\|_{*,i}$.
Therefore
\[
 \|\mathfrak N\|_{*,i}
 \le\frac{\bar B_M\mathsf b}{4\varrho}
           +C_r+\frac12\|\mathfrak N\|_{*,i},
\]
which proves the constant-direction estimate.

\emph{The torus in the constant direction.}
At a nonwrapping level-$l$ polymer $X$, subtract
from $\widetilde{\mathbf P}^{\mathrm{red},(l)}[1](X)$
the infinite-lattice pre-extraction family in
the corresponding local coordinates.
Denote this difference by $\Delta^{(l)}(X)$.
We prove inductively that its scalar part has
joint order at least four and its fermionic
part has joint order at least five.
It is even, so its quadratic part at the
trivial pair starts at order six.

The zero-source field-scale steps have the same
local structure on these two polymers:
the gauge-fixing operators, gauge vertices,
scalar localization, normalizers, shift system
and fermion objects are carried to each other
by the local coordinate identification.
The common coefficients are $\xi_i(\lambda)$,
$\tau_i(\lambda)$ and $\lambda^2s_i$.
The extraction uses the same infinite-lattice
numbers.  Induction gives the same assertion
for their old zero-source families.
The direct constant source is also local and
compatible with this identification.
Thus $\Delta^{(1)}=0$ on nonwrapping polymers.

At a later level, an old contribution filed at
a nonwrapping polymer receives no term from
a wrapping original polymer.  Its difference
from the infinite-lattice reading has precisely
three parts:
\begin{enumerate}
\item the preceding difference
$\Delta^{(l')}(X')$ with its scalar value removed;
\item the negative of the extraction forms of
pieces that fit locally but whose original
polymer has diameter at least $\ell_G/4$,
so the torus rule omits them;
\item the difference of the cell terms,
$\bar\Phi(z_c)(m_c-m_c^\infty)\Phi(z_c)$.
\end{enumerate}
The first has the inductive orders; removing
a constant has no effect on its variation.
In the second, forms used by both rules agree:
the induction gives equality of the fourth
coefficients of their nonwrapping pieces.
In the third,
\[
 m_c-m_c^\infty
      =\lambda^4m_c^{[4]}+(m_c^{(6)}-m_c^\infty).
\]
Apart from terms of order at least six, the
last two parts are bilinears
$\lambda^4\bar\Psi K\Psi$ with $K$ independent
of $\lambda$ and the fluctuation.
Their variation with no $W$ leg vanishes at
$\lambda=0$, hence has order at least five.
Terms linear in $W$ have zero Gaussian mean
and require another member of positive order
to contribute after expansion.
Terms with two $W$ legs have degree zero in
the new generators and require an additional
member with legs to contribute to their
positive-degree part.
Thus their derivative images have scalar
order at least four and fermionic order
at least five.
This closes the induction for $\Delta^{(l)}$.

Consequently the fourth moments agree for
pieces whose original and expanded polymers
both fit in the torus.  The difference
$\mathfrak n_l[1](y)-\mathfrak n_l^\infty[1](\hat y)$
is $-\mathfrak s_l^{-1}$ times the difference
of two sums: the torus pieces retained by
extraction whose expanded polymer wraps,
and the infinite-lattice pieces whose
expanded polymer does not fit or whose
original polymer has diameter at least
$\ell_G/4$.
In either sum,
\[
 d_l(Z_p)\ge t'_G:=\frac{\ell_G}{2c'Ma_l}-2.
\]
The wrapping estimate is
$d_l(Z_p)\ge\ell_G/(2Ma_l)-2$;
the large-diameter estimate is stronger
than $t'_G$.  Here $c'\ge2$.
The tail moment bound and Cauchy's formula
for the fourth coefficient give
\[
 |\mathfrak n_l[1](y)-\mathfrak n_l^\infty[1](\hat y)|
 \le2e^\kappa K_{\mathfrak n}(c_{\mathsf S}h_F^2)^{-1}
       A^{\mathrm{red}}\bar\lambda_{l-1}^{-4}a_l^{-1}
                    e^{-2c_{\mathrm{def}}\ell_G/a_l}.
\]
For $t'_G<0$ use the ordinary moment estimate;
the displayed tail factor before its simplification
then exceeds one.

Now
\[
 \bar\lambda_{l-1}^{-4}a_l^{-1}
 \le4c_\lambda^2L^{-2}
             (\log x_{l-1})^{4\mathfrak p_0}\hat{\mathsf n}_l,
 \qquad x_{l-1}\le2\mathsf bL^{K-l+1}.
\]
Sum with factors $L^{i-l}$.
The identity $L^{i-l}\hat{\mathsf n}_l=\hat{\mathsf n}_i$
gives the asserted torus estimate with
\begin{align*}
 C_{\mathrm{wr}}^{\mathfrak N}
 ={}&8e^\kappa K_{\mathfrak n}(c_{\mathsf S}h_F^2)^{-1}
          A^{\mathrm{red}}c_\lambda^2L^{-2}\\
 &{}\times\sup_{\mathsf b\in\bar I(g)}
       \sum_{u\ge0}
       \bigl(\log(2\mathsf bL^{u+1})\bigr)^{4\mathfrak p_0}
                            e^{-2c_{\mathrm{def}}\ell_GL^u}.
\end{align*}
This is finite.  The translation periods of the
infinite-lattice constant-direction response
divide the torus periods, so its value is
independent of the chosen representative $\hat x$.

\emph{A direction of the test pair.}
Linearity and $1=\sum_p\delta_p$ give the exact
identity, at every bare site $x$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:C403-localized-mass}
 \mathfrak N_i[f](x)
 =f(x)\mathfrak N_i[1](x)
 +\sum_{1\le l\le i}L^{i-l}\sum_p
       (f(x(p))-f(x))\mathfrak n_l[\delta_p](y_l(x)).
\end{equation}
First suppose $a_i\le\mathsf d$.
Then $e_i[f]=\|f\|_\infty a_i^{-1}$
and $\mathfrak l_i=1$.
The constant-direction estimates bound the first
term by
$(A_c+C_{\mathrm{wr}}^{\mathfrak N})\|f\|_\infty
\hat{\mathsf n}_i$.
Moreover
$\bar\lambda_i^4\hat{\mathsf n}_i
\le(25/4)c_\lambda^{-2}a_i^{-1}$.

For the second term use
$|f(x(p))-f(x)|\le
\|f\|_\infty|x(p)-x|/(\vartheta\mathsf d)$,
with the torus distance.
The direction $\delta_p$ is supported in the
radius-$a_K$ ball $S_p$ about $x(p)$, and
$e_l[\delta_p]=a_K^3a_l^{-4}$.
Since
$\delta_l(y_l(x);S_p)\ge|x(p)-x|/(Ma_l)-3$,
the site estimate gives
\begin{align*}
 &\sum_p|x(p)-x|\,|\mathfrak n_l[\delta_p](y_l(x))|\\
 &\quad\le C_{\mathrm{Lip}}M^4K_{\mathfrak n}
       (c_{\mathsf S}h_F^2)^{-1}A^{\mathrm{red}}
                                    \bar\lambda_{l-1}^{-4},
 \qquad C_{\mathrm{Lip}}=78\pi e\,\kappa_{\mathrm s}^{-4}.
\end{align*}
For completeness, the barycentres form three
translates of $a_K\mathbb Z^3$.  Choose representatives
that realize each torus distance and set
$\kappa_l=\kappa_{\mathrm s}/(Ma_l)\le1/(4a_K)$.
On one translate their radial sum is at most
\[
 a_K^{-3}e^{1/4}\int_{\mathbb R^3}
          (|z|+a_K)e^{-\kappa_l|z|}\,dz
       \le26\pi e^{1/4}a_K^{-3}\kappa_l^{-4}.
\]
The three translates and $e^{3\kappa_{\mathrm s}}\le e^{3/4}$
give $C_{\mathrm{Lip}}$.

Multiply \eqref{eq:C403-localized-mass} by
$c_{\mathsf S}h_F^2\bar\lambda_i^4$ and use
\[
 \sum_{l\le i}L^{i-l}
       (\bar\lambda_i/\bar\lambda_{l-1})^4
       \le\sum_{n\ge1}L^{n-1}q_n^2\le S_\diamond .
\]
Since $\mathsf d\ge a_i$, this yields
\[
 c_{\mathsf S}h_F^2\bar\lambda_i^4|\mathfrak N_i[f](x)|
       \le B_fe_i[f],
\]
where
\[
 B_f=\frac{25}{4}c_\lambda^{-2}c_{\mathsf S}h_F^2
                 (A_c+C_{\mathrm{wr}}^{\mathfrak N})
       +\frac{C_{\mathrm{Lip}}M^4K_{\mathfrak n}
                       A^{\mathrm{red}}S_\diamond}{\vartheta}.
\]

This estimate also has the required spatial decay.
If $\Delta_x=\operatorname{dist}(x,S_f)/(Ma_i)\ge1$,
then $f(x)=0$.  Apply the site estimate directly
to the direction $f$, using
$e_l[f]=L^{i-l}e_i[f]$ and
$\delta_l(y_l(x);S_f)\ge L^{i-l}\Delta_x-\sqrt3$.
It gives
\begin{align*}
 c_{\mathsf S}h_F^2\bar\lambda_i^4|\mathfrak N_i[f](x)|
 &\le2K_{\mathfrak n}A^{\mathrm{red}}e_i[f]
       \sum_{u\ge0}L^{2u}q_{u+1}^2e^{-\kappa_{\mathrm s}L^u\Delta_x}\\
 &\le2K_{\mathfrak n}A^{\mathrm{red}}\Sigma_{\mathrm w}
                          e_i[f]e^{-\kappa_{\mathrm s}\Delta_x},
\end{align*}
where
\[
 \Sigma_{\mathrm w}
   =\sum_{u\ge0}L^{2u}q_{u+1}^2
                              e^{-\kappa_{\mathrm s}(L^u-1)}<\infty.
\]
For $\Delta_x<1$, use $e^{\kappa_{\mathrm s}}\le2$.
Thus, with
$B'_f=2(B_f+K_{\mathfrak n}A^{\mathrm{red}}\Sigma_{\mathrm w})$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:C403-mass-spatial-bound}
 c_{\mathsf S}h_F^2\bar\lambda_i^4|\mathfrak N_i[f](x)|
 \le B'_fe_i[f]\,
         e^{-\kappa_{\mathrm s}\operatorname{dist}(x,S_f)/(Ma_i)}
 \qquad(a_i\le\mathsf d).
\end{equation}
On each level-$i$ cube the exponential pays the
source weight of its mean.  This proves the
assertion at these levels.

Now suppose $a_i>\mathsf d$.
Let $l_{\mathsf d}$ be the last level with
$a_{l_{\mathsf d}}\le\mathsf d$ and put
$n_{\mathsf d}=i-l_{\mathsf d}\ge1$.
This level exists because $\mathsf d\ge a_K$.
Then
\[
 e_i[f]=\|f\|_\infty\mathsf d^3a_i^{-4},
 \qquad
 \mathfrak N_i[f]
 =L^{n_{\mathsf d}}\mathfrak N_{l_{\mathsf d}}[f]
       +\sum_{l_{\mathsf d}<l\le i}
                         L^{i-l}\mathfrak n_l[f]\circ y_l.
\]
Also
$1+n_{\mathsf d}\log L\le(1+\log L)\mathfrak l_i$
and $n_{\mathsf d}-1\le\mathfrak l_i-1$.

For $l<i$ and $x$ in a level-$i$ cube $\square$,
\[
 e^{\kappa_{\mathrm s}\delta_i(\square;S_f)}
 e^{-\kappa_{\mathrm s}\operatorname{dist}(x,S_f)/(Ma_l)}
 \le
 e^{-\kappa_{\mathrm s}\operatorname{dist}(x,S_f)/(2Ma_l)} .
\]
The mean of the right side over $\square$ is at most
$C_{\mathcal C}L^{-3(i-l)}(1+\mathsf d/a_l)^3$.
This follows by counting the $M^3L^{3l}$ bare sites
in each level-$l$ cell and summing its distance
weight, then dividing by $M^3L^{3i}$.

For the first term use
\eqref{eq:C403-mass-spatial-bound} at $l_{\mathsf d}$
and
$|\lambda|^4\le q_{n_{\mathsf d}}^2
\bar\lambda_{l_{\mathsf d}}^4$ on $D_i$.
If $l_{\mathsf d}=0$, this term vanishes.
Otherwise its weighted mean is at most
\[
 8C_{\mathcal C}L^{2n_{\mathsf d}}q_{n_{\mathsf d}}^2
             B'_fe_i[f]
 \le32C_{\mathcal C}(1+\log L)^{4\mathfrak p_0}
                  B'_f\mathfrak l_i^{4\mathfrak p_0}e_i[f].
\]
We used
$L^{2n}q_n^2\le4(1+n\log L)^{4\mathfrak p_0}$
and
$(1+\mathsf d/a_{l_{\mathsf d}})^3
\le8(\mathsf d/a_{l_{\mathsf d}})^3$.

For each $l_{\mathsf d}<l<i$, the site estimate,
$e_l[f]=L^{4(i-l)}e_i[f]$,
the preceding mean bound and
$|\lambda|^4\le q_{i+1-l}^2\bar\lambda_{l-1}^4$
give at most
\[
 16C_{\mathcal C}K_{\mathfrak n}A^{\mathrm{red}}
             L^{2(i-l)}q_{i+1-l}^2e_i[f]
 \le64C_{\mathcal C}K_{\mathfrak n}A^{\mathrm{red}}L^{-2}
       (1+\log L)^{4\mathfrak p_0}
                         \mathfrak l_i^{4\mathfrak p_0}e_i[f].
\]
There are at most $\mathfrak l_i-1$ such levels.
The level $l=i$ contributes at most
$2K_{\mathfrak n}A^{\mathrm{red}}q_1^2e_i[f]
\le K_{\mathfrak n}A^{\mathrm{red}}e_i[f]$.
Adding these bounds proves the final assertion with
\[
 A_{\mathfrak N}
 =64C_{\mathcal C}(1+\log L)^{4\mathfrak p_0}
                (B'_f+K_{\mathfrak n}A^{\mathrm{red}}).
\]
It also bounds $B'_f$.  The proof for $h$ is identical.
\end{proof}

\subsection{First and mixed responses}

\begin{lemma}[First responses]\label{C-403-51}
Put
\[
 A^{\mathrm{rsp}}=6K_\mu^{\mathrm s}K_MC_{\mathrm{mn}}
                               c'_\psi A_{\mathfrak N}L^4,
 \qquad
 A_{\mathbf P}=A^{\mathrm{red}}+A^{\mathrm{rsp}},
 \qquad
 A'_{\mathbf P}=C_{\mathrm{src}}+C_{\mathrm{mn}}A_{\mathfrak N}
                                                    +A_{\mathbf P}.
\]
For $1\le i\le j$,
\begin{align*}
 \|\mathbf P^{\mathrm{rsp},(i)}[f]\|_{i;D_{i-1};S_f}
 &\le A^{\mathrm{rsp}}e_i[f]\mathfrak l_i^{4\mathfrak p_0+1},\\
 \|\mathbf P^{(i)}[f]\|_{i;D_{i-1};S_f}
 &\le A_{\mathbf P}e_i[f]\mathfrak l_i^{4\mathfrak p_0+1}.
\end{align*}
The latter bound also holds for the pre-extraction family.
These estimates hold in the scalar array norm and
in the fermionic norm summing the individual
summands, with each form at its own polymer.
For $0\le i<j$,
\[
 \epsilon_{S_f}(\delta_i[f])
       \le A'_{\mathbf P}e_i[f]\mathfrak l_i^{4\mathfrak p_0+1}
                  \quad\hbox{on }D_i.
\]
The same estimates hold for $h$.
The families $\mathbf P^{(l)}[f]$, $l\le i$,
read together at level $i\le K$, have norm at most
\[
 \bigl(1+C_{\mathrm{rd}}C_{\mathcal C}
                  (1+2C_{\mathrm{mo}})S_\diamond\bigr)
             A_{\mathbf P}e_i[f]\mathfrak l_i^{4\mathfrak p_0+1}
\]
in $\|\cdot\|^{\mathrm{out}}_{i;D_{i-1};S_f}$.
Their scalar parts have the same bound in the
strong family norm on the full level-$i$ cores.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The feedback recursion is driven by
$\mathcal V_i^{\mathrm s}[\lambda^4\mathfrak N_i[f]]$.
It has no extraction forms.  Its units are the
differences of the full and reduced units:
the kernel minus its moment at the original cell,
and the moved pieces at the cells of their sites.
Thus the old variations split term by term into
reduced and feedback variations.
At level one the feedback vanishes because
$\mathfrak N_0=0$.

For the induction, let $R_l$ be the larger of the
feedback family norm and its scalar array norm,
divided by $e_l[f]\mathfrak l_l^{4\mathfrak p_0+1}$.
Lemmas~\ref{C-403-47} and \ref{C-403-49} give
\[
 \epsilon_{S_f}
       (\mathcal V_i^{\mathrm s}[\lambda^4\mathfrak N_i[f]])
 \le C_{\mathrm{mn}}c'_\psi A_{\mathfrak N}L^4
                e_{i+1}[f]\mathfrak l_{i+1}^{4\mathfrak p_0+1}.
\]
For an old feedback family of lag $n=i+1-l$,
Schwarz's lemma gives factors $q_n$ in its scalar
array and fermionic norms, $2q_n^3$ in its
trivial-pair quadratic norm with attached pieces,
and $2C_{\mathrm{mo}}q_n^3$ in its cell sum.
The latter two use order six and the absence of
forms, on both the torus and $\mathbb Z^3$.
The lag estimate and spatial count therefore
bound the sum of old variations by
\[
 \frac{\theta}{3K_\mu^{\mathrm s}K_M}
       \max_{l\le i}R_l\,
                 e_{i+1}[f]\mathfrak l_{i+1}^{4\mathfrak p_0+1}.
\]
Indeed, $2q_n^3\le3q_n^2$ and
$2C_{\mathrm{mo}}\le3(1+2C_{\mathrm{mo}})$,
so this is the same summable bracket as in
the reduced induction.
The derivative image has bound
\[
 \left(\tfrac32K_MC_{\mathrm{mn}}c'_\psi A_{\mathfrak N}L^4
       +\frac{\theta}{2K_\mu^{\mathrm s}}\max_{l\le i}R_l\right)
                     e_{i+1}[f]\mathfrak l_{i+1}^{4\mathfrak p_0+1}.
\]
Removing the scalar value doubles the norm at most.
It follows that
$R_{i+1}\le A^{\mathrm{rsp}}/(2K_\mu^{\mathrm s})
 +(\theta/K_\mu^{\mathrm s})\max_{l\le i}R_l
\le A^{\mathrm{rsp}}$.
The pre-extraction bound is half this bound.
Adding the reduced response proves the first
two estimates.

For $\delta_i[f]$, the direct term costs
$C_{\mathrm{src}}e_i[f]$.
Its mass term costs at most
$A^{\mathrm{rsp}}e_i[f]\mathfrak l_i^{4\mathfrak p_0+1}/
(6K_\mu^{\mathrm s}K_ML^4)$.
The old full families have
$\|F_2^{\mathrm{tr}}\|\le3A_{\mathbf P}
e_l[f]\mathfrak l_l^{4\mathfrak p_0+1}$.
Their cell sums are those of
Lemma~\ref{C-403-48}, including the torus defect.
The reduced-family summation therefore bounds
their total by
$A_{\mathbf P}e_i[f]\mathfrak l_i^{4\mathfrak p_0+1}/6$,
using $e_{i+1}\le e_i$ and
$K_\mu^{\mathrm s}K_M\ge1$.
The mass term is also at most one sixth of this
size.  These bounds imply the assertion for
$A'_{\mathbf P}$.

For the readings at level $i$, the family with
$l=i$ already has the required strong norm.
For $l<i$, put $n=i-l$ and apply
Lemma~\ref{C-403-46} on $D_{i-1}$.
The scalar family vanishes at the trivial pair,
so (R0) is its actual reading on the full core,
including at $i=K$.
The fermionic terms use the common-pair norm
for long lags and the strong norm for short lags.
Their combined bound is
\begin{align*}
 C_{\mathrm{rd}}C_{\mathcal C}
 \bigl[2q_n+3L^{(2-\alpha)n}q_n^2
 +L^{2n}(6C_{\mathrm{mo}}q_n^3
               +3C_{\mathrm{def}}q_n^2e^{-2Mc_{\mathrm{def}}L^n})\bigr]
             A_{\mathbf P}e_i[f]\mathfrak l_i^{4\mathfrak p_0+1}.
\end{align*}
Its sum is bounded by the asserted factor
$C_{\mathrm{rd}}C_{\mathcal C}(1+2C_{\mathrm{mo}})S_\diamond$.
The scalar contribution alone is bounded by
$C_{\mathrm{rd}}C_{\mathcal C}q_n$ times the size,
in the strong norm.  This proves the final
assertion without moving a pair supremum
inside the long-lag fermionic sum.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Mixed responses]\label{C-403-52}
Set
\[
 C_{\mathfrak l}=\sup_{t\ge1}
                   t^{-7/2}(1+\log t)^{8\mathfrak p_0+2},
 \qquad
 A_{\mathbf Q}=32c_{\mathrm{cl}}^{-1}K_M
                            (A'_{\mathbf P})^2C_{\mathfrak l}L^{9/2}.
\]
For $1\le i\le j$,
\[
 \|\mathbf Q^{(i)}[f,h]\|_{i;D_{i-1};S_f,S_h}
                \le A_{\mathbf Q}e_i[f,h].
\]
The same holds before extraction and in the
scalar array norm.
For $0\le i<j$, on $D_i$,
\[
 \epsilon_{S_f,S_h}\left(
       \sum_{1\le l\le i}\mathcal V_i^{\mathrm{old}}
                                  [\mathbf Q^{(l)}[f,h]]\right)
 \le\frac{\theta}{3K_\mu^{\mathrm s}K_M}
                       A_{\mathbf Q}e_{i+1}[f,h]
 \le A_{\mathbf Q}e_i[f,h].
\]
The sum is zero at $i=0$.
The families with $l\le i$, read at level $i\le K$,
have together norm at most
\[
 \bigl(1+C_{\mathrm{rd}}C_{\mathcal C}
                    (1+2C_{\mathrm{mo}})S_\diamond\bigr)
                         A_{\mathbf Q}e_i[f,h]
\]
in $\|\cdot\|^{\mathrm{out}}_{i;D_{i-1};S_f,S_h}$.
The scalar parts obey the same bound in the
strong norm on the full cores.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The new mixed term is the second derivative
of the step in the two first-response directions.
Lemmas~\ref{C-403-45} and \ref{C-403-51} bound it by
\[
 8c_{\mathrm{cl}}^{-1}K_M(A'_{\mathbf P})^2
             e_i[f]e_i[h]\mathfrak l_i^{8\mathfrak p_0+2}.
\]
If $a_i\le\mathsf d$, the product of
sizes is $e_i[f,h]$ and $\mathfrak l_i=1$.
If $a_i>\mathsf d$, set $t=a_i/\mathsf d$.
Its ratio to $e_i[f,h]$ is
$t^{-7/2}(1+\log t)^{8\mathfrak p_0+2}\le C_{\mathfrak l}$.
In either case the new term is at most
$8c_{\mathrm{cl}}^{-1}K_M(A'_{\mathbf P})^2
C_{\mathfrak l}L^{9/2}e_{i+1}[f,h]$.

For an old mixed family at lag $n=i+1-l$,
its scalar and fermionic norms gain $q_n$
on $D_i$.  Its trivial-pair quadratic norm
gains $q_n^3$, and its cell sum gains
$C_{\mathrm{mo}}q_n^3$, since it has no forms
and starts at order six there.
The spatial count is now
$\mathcal Ne_l[f,h]\le
C_{\mathcal C}L^{9n/2}e_{i+1}[f,h]$.
The sum of its old variations is bounded by
\begin{align*}
 C_{\mathrm{rd}}C_{\mathcal C}
 \sum_{n\ge1}
 \bigl[(2s_\lambda+c'_\psi)L^{n/2}q_n
       +c'_\psi L^{(5/2-\alpha)n}q_n^3
       +c'_\psi C_{\mathrm{mo}}L^{5n/2}q_n^3\bigr]
                                     A_{\mathbf Q}e_{i+1}[f,h].
\end{align*}
Here
$L^{(5/2-\alpha)n}q_n^3
=(L^{n/2}q_n)L^{(2-\alpha)n}q_n^2
\le L^{(2-\alpha)n}q_n^2$,
because $L^{n/2}q_n\le2^{10/9}L^{-7n/18}\le1$.
Thus this is at most
$\theta A_{\mathbf Q}e_{i+1}/
(3K_\mu^{\mathrm s}K_M)$.
It proves the old-direction estimate as well.

Apply the step derivative estimate and remove
the scalar value, at cost at most two.
The induction closes because
\[
 \|\mathbf Q^{(i+1)}[f,h]\|
 \le2\left(8c_{\mathrm{cl}}^{-1}K_M(A'_{\mathbf P})^2
       C_{\mathfrak l}L^{9/2}
       +\frac{\theta}{2K_\mu^{\mathrm s}}A_{\mathbf Q}\right)
                                      e_{i+1}[f,h]
 \le(\tfrac12+\theta)A_{\mathbf Q}e_{i+1}[f,h].
\]
The pre-extraction norm is at most half the
middle expression, and the same argument
uses scalar array norms throughout.

For the total reading, the term $l=i$ is
already bounded.  For $l<i$, the lag estimate
and the same Schwarz factors give
\[
 C_{\mathrm{rd}}C_{\mathcal C}
       [2L^{n/2}q_n+L^{(5/2-\alpha)n}q_n^3
                           +C_{\mathrm{mo}}L^{5n/2}q_n^3]
                         A_{\mathbf Q}e_i[f,h].
\]
Its sum has the stated bound.  The scalar
part has only the first term with coefficient
one, in the strong norm on the full core;
the fermionic part uses the common-pair norm.
The scalar estimate includes the top level.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Sums of response families]\label{C-403-53}
Let $G$ be a level-$i$ family and let $S$ be
a nonempty set in a closed ball of radius $r\ge a_K$.
Then
\[
 \sum_{X'}\sup_{\lambda\in D}\|G(X')\|
 \le e^{\kappa/16}C_{\mathcal C}
            (1+r/a_i)^3\|G\|_{i;D;S}.
\]
For the two supports of a test pair,
\[
 \sum_{X'}\sup_{\lambda\in D}\|G(X')\|
 \le e^{\kappa/8}\mathcal C'_i\|G\|_{i;D;S_f,S_h}.
\]
The norms on the left include the individual
pair suprema.
For one pair $P$ on a polymer $Z$, the analogous
bound for
$\sup_{\lambda\in D}\sum_{X'\subset Z}
\|G(X';P|_{X'},\cdot;\lambda)\|_{h^{(i)}}$
holds with $\|\cdot\|^{\mathrm{out}}$ on the right.

For $1\le i\le j$, on $D_{i-1}$,
\begin{align*}
 \left|\sum_{X'}\mathfrak e_i[f](X')\right|
 &\le C_{\mathfrak e,1}\|f\|_\infty a_i^{-1}
       (\mathsf d/a_i)^3\mathfrak l_i^{4\mathfrak p_0+1},\\
 \left|\sum_{X'}\mathfrak e_i[f,h](X')\right|
 &\le C_{\mathfrak e,2}\mathsf n_0(X;a_i)
 \begin{cases}
 (\mathsf d/a_i)^{5/2},&a_i\ge\mathsf d,\\
 (\mathsf d/a_i)^3
       e^{-\kappa_{\mathrm s}\mathsf d/(2Ma_i)},
                                      &a_i<\mathsf d,
 \end{cases}
\end{align*}
where
$C_{\mathfrak e,1}=8e^{\kappa/16}C_{\mathcal C}A_{\mathbf P}$
and
$C_{\mathfrak e,2}=e^{\kappa/8}C_{\mathcal C}A_{\mathbf Q}$.
On $D_i$ the second sum is $\mathsf n_i^\lambda$,
so it has the same bounds there.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Overcount the polymer sum by
$\sum_\square\sum_{X'\supset\square}$.
For $X'\supset\square$, the diameter estimate gives
\[
 \delta_i(X';S)\ge\delta_i(\square;S)
                                  -\tfrac12c'(1+d_i(X')).
\]
Hence its inverse weight is bounded by
$e^{\kappa/16}e^{\kappa d_i(X')/16}
e^{-\kappa_{\mathrm s}\delta_i(\square;S)}$.
The family norm pays the polymer factor and
the remaining cube sum is bounded by
$C_{\mathcal C}(1+r/a_i)^3$.
Two source weights give instead
$e^{\kappa/8}e^{\kappa d_i(X')/8}$ and
the cube sum $\mathcal C'_i$.
For the common-pair assertion do this count
at fixed $\lambda,Z,P$, using only the
restrictions of $P$, then take the suprema.

A scalar value at the trivial pair is
bounded by its family's norm.
Apply the first part to the pre-extraction
families in Lemmas~\ref{C-403-51} and \ref{C-403-52}.
Use
\[
 e_i[f](1+\mathsf d/a_i)^3
       \le8\|f\|_\infty a_i^{-1}
                                      (\mathsf d/a_i)^3
\]
and
$e_i[f,h]=\mathsf n_0(X;a_i)
\min\{1,(\mathsf d/a_i)^{5/2}\}$.
The bounds on $\mathcal C'_i$ give the two
mixed cases.  The identity with
$\mathsf n_i^\lambda$ is the total-family
identity of Lemma~\ref{C-403-44} on $D_i$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Responses joining different cells}

Use the board and sources of
Definition~\ref{C-403-43-linking}, and let
$n_{\mathfrak J}=\#\mathfrak J\le16$.
We work at $\lambda=1$ throughout this subsection.
The decay between different cells will absorb
the growth of the source sizes under reading.

Define, in this order,
\begin{align*}
 C_r^D&=\frac{71}{64}\left(\frac{4r}{3}\right)^r,
                                      &&1\le r\le16,\\
 C_{\mathrm v}
 &=\max\{1,2s_\lambda+c'_\psi\}C_{\mathrm{rd}}(3+C_{\mathrm{mo}}),\\
 T_{\mathrm x}
 &=\frac{2[39\log L+\log(12K_MC_{\mathrm v}M^3)]}{L-1}.
\end{align*}
Let $C_{\mathcal C}^{\mathrm B}$ bound the cube count
\[
 \sum_\square e^{-\kappa_{\mathrm B}\delta_l(\square;S)}
       \le C_{\mathcal C}^{\mathrm B}(1+r_S/a_l)^3
\]
for every $S$ in a radius-$r_S$ ball, $r_S\ge a_K$.
Put
\[
 C_{\mathrm{sup}}^{\mathrm x}
    =\sup_{t\ge0}(1+t)^3e^{-c_1t/2},\qquad
 m_{\mathrm x}=\min\{m\ge0:c_1\ell_GL^m/4\ge T_{\mathrm x}\}.
\]
For a one-cell block set
$A'_{\{\mathsf g\}}=A'_{\mathbf P}$ and
$A'_{\{f_c,h_c\}}=A_{\mathbf Q}$.
For sets $\mathsf J$ joining cells define inductively
$A'_{\mathsf J}=A_{\mathsf J}$, where
\begin{align*}
 A_{\mathsf J}
 &=4K_Me^{c_E}C_{\mathfrak l}^8L^{36}
       \sum_{\substack{\pi\in\operatorname{Part}(\mathsf J)\\\#\pi\ge2}}
       C_{\#\pi}^D c_{\mathrm{cl}}^{1-\#\pi}
                                  \prod_{b\in\pi}A'_b,\\
 A_{n_{\mathfrak J}}^{\mathrm x}
 &=4e^{\kappa/8}C_{\mathcal C}^{\mathrm B}C_{\mathrm{sup}}^{\mathrm x}
       \max_{\substack{\mathsf J\text{ joins cells}\\
                       \#\mathsf J\le n_{\mathfrak J}}}A_{\mathsf J}.
\end{align*}
Only the numbers of cells carrying one or two
directions enter $A_{\mathsf J}$.
The constants through $T_{\mathrm x}$ are chosen
after $c_\lambda,\rho$ and before $\gamma_{\mathrm e}$.
The number $m_{\mathrm x}$ is chosen after $g$.
The constants $A_{\mathsf J}$ are chosen after
$A'_{\mathbf P},A_{\mathbf Q}$ and depend on
$g,\vartheta$ and the fixed constants.
None depends on the cutoff, $\mathsf b,\mathsf m$,
the distance scale or the positions of the sources,
and none enters an earlier parameter choice.

\begin{lemma}\label{C-403-61}
For every $\mathsf J\subset\mathfrak J$ joining cells:
\begin{enumerate}
\item At every $l\le K$,
\[
 \left.\partial_{\mathsf J}\sum_X
          \mathfrak E_l(X;w,0)\right|_{w=0}
       =\sum_X\mathfrak e_l[\mathsf J](X),
 \qquad
 \left.\partial_{\mathsf J}E_k(w,0)\right|_{w=0}
       =\sum_{l\le k}\sum_X\mathfrak e_l[\mathsf J](X).
\]
The derivative of the field-dependent total at
level $l$, including the accumulated mass member,
is the sum of the $\mathbf R^{(l')}[\mathsf J]$,
$l'\le l$, read at that level.
This is an identity of functions at the backgrounds
of real block fields passing the density test,
with values in the level-$l$ Grassmann algebra.
\item For $1\le i\le K-m_{\mathrm x}$,
\[
 \|\mathbf R^{(i)}[\mathsf J]\|_{i;\mathsf J}
       \le A_{\mathsf J}\varsigma_i^{\mathrm x}
                                      \widehat e_i[\mathsf J].
\]
The same bound holds before removing its scalar
value, and
$\epsilon_{\mathsf J}(\delta_{i-1}[\mathsf J])
\le A_{\mathsf J}\varsigma_i^{\mathrm x}\widehat e_i[\mathsf J]$.
\item For the same $i$,
\[
 \sum_{l\le i}\sum_X|\mathfrak e_l[\mathsf J](X)|
       \le A_{n_{\mathfrak J}}^{\mathrm x}
       e^{-c_{\mathrm x}D_{\mathrm x}/a_i}\widehat e_i[\mathsf J].
\]
The same bound holds for the families
$\mathbf R^{(l)}[\mathsf J]$, $l\le i$, read at
level $i$, evaluated at restrictions of one regular
complex pair on any level-$i$ polymer $Z$, and
summed over their polymers contained in $Z$
in the Grassmann norm at $h^{(i)}$.
The whole torus is allowed as $Z$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The source-neighbourhood construction in
Proposition~\ref{C-403-33-flow} at $\lambda=1$
makes all steps through $K$ holomorphic for
$\|w\|_\sharp<\varepsilon_K(1)$.
On the finite torus, $w=\sum_sz_s\mathsf g_s$
belongs to this neighbourhood for small $z$.
Thus all the derivatives in the statement exist.

\emph{Derivatives of the totals.}
Induct on the level, simultaneously for all
sets of directions.
There is no activity or mass response at level zero.
At each step the source enters through the
weight members, linear in $w$, and through
variation of the field-dependent total.
The calibration, tests, backgrounds, vertices
and covariance structure are independent of $w$.
For every block $b$ of a partition, the derivative
of the potential and quadratic origin therefore
has the total of $\delta_i[b]$.
For a singleton this is the first-response
identity; for a pair in one cell it is the
mixed-response identity.  For a block joining
cells it is the level induction hypothesis.
Higher derivatives of the direct weight vanish.

Including its Gaussian part, the sum of the
step activities is the logarithm of the
Gaussian integral of
$e^{\mathcal V^{\mathrm o}}\chi_i e^{\mathcal V}$.
It depends on the potential and origin through
their totals alone.
For two systems of at most sixteen directions
with equal totals, their expansions on a
common parameter polydisc are continuous
logarithms of the same exponential.
They agree at zero, so their difference,
which lies in $2\pi i\mathbb Z$, is zero.
Their mixed derivatives agree.
The chain rule in the distinct source variables
is the sum over partitions of $\mathsf J$.
It follows that
\[
 \left.\partial_{\mathsf J}
       \sum_X\widetilde E^{(i+1)}(X;w,0)\right|_{w=0}
       =\sum_X\widetilde{\mathbf R}^{(i+1)}[\mathsf J](X).
\]
The mass extraction moves a local bilinear
from the activity into the mass member and
does not change their field-dependent total.
Evaluation of the scalar part at the trivial
configuration is linear, so its derivative
is the sum of $\mathfrak e_{i+1}[\mathsf J]$.
Subtracting this value and carrying the
preceding total to level $i+1$ proves the
first assertion.

\emph{A step derivative of order at most sixteen.}
For directions $\delta_1,\ldots,\delta_r$,
use the polydisc
\[
 |t_a|<\frac{3c_{\mathrm{cl}}}{4r\epsilon(\delta_a)}.
\]
Zero-size directions are handled by their
vanishing derivative or by a limiting radius.
Its total perturbation size is less than
$3c_{\mathrm{cl}}/4$.
The potential size is less than
$c_{\mathrm{cl}}/4+3c_{\mathrm{cl}}/4$ and
the origin norm less than
$(5/64+3/8)w_*<w_*/2$.
Thus the expansion is admitted and holomorphic.
The potential part, twice the tail and the
Gaussian origin give the polymer bound
\[
 \left(\frac14+\frac1{32}+\frac5{64}+\frac34\right)
       c_{\mathrm{cl}}K'_Me^{-\kappa_+d_{i+1}(X)}
       =\frac{71}{64}c_{\mathrm{cl}}K'_Me^{-\kappa_+d_{i+1}(X)}.
\]
The tail bound used here is
$c_\lambda^{-1/2}\le c_{\mathrm{cl}}/64$.
Cauchy's formula and locality give
\[
 \|D^r\widetilde E_i[\delta_1,\ldots,\delta_r](X)\|
 \le C_r^D c_{\mathrm{cl}}^{1-r}K'_M
       \prod_a\epsilon(\delta_{a,X})
                              e^{-\kappa_+d_{i+1}(X)} .
\]
When $\mathsf J$ is the disjoint union of
$\mathsf J_a$, the local directions satisfy
$\epsilon(\delta_{a,X})\le
(w_{i+1}^{\mathsf J_a}(X))^{-1}
\epsilon_{\mathsf J_a}(\delta_a)$.
The weights multiply to $w_{i+1}^{\mathsf J}$.
The decay excess $\kappa_+-\kappa\ge2c_E+1$
permits the polymer sum, with $K_M=C_EK'_M$,
and retains the scalar array rate $\kappa+1$.
Consequently
\begin{equation}\label{eq:C403-link-step-derivative}
 \|D^r\widetilde E_i[\delta_1,\ldots,\delta_r]\|_{i+1;\mathsf J}
 \le C_r^D c_{\mathrm{cl}}^{1-r}K_M
                         \prod_a\epsilon_{\mathsf J_a}(\delta_a).
\end{equation}
The cases $r=1,2$ give $71/48\le3/2$ and
$71/9\le8$, consistently with the earlier estimates.

\emph{Reading an old family.}
Each member of $\widetilde{\mathbf R}^{(l)}$
is a Cauchy integral of step activities with
holomorphic, jointly gauge-invariant inputs.
It therefore has those properties on the full
core.  Its scalar part is local and pointed
by equal shares.  Its units are its polymers;
no diagonal terms are moved.
Thus Lemma~\ref{C-403-46} applies with $F_1=G=0$.
Its cell sums are bounded by
$C_{\mathrm{mo}}h_F^{-2}\|F\|_{l;\mathsf J}$,
including the torus cell sums.
The total source weight rate is
$\#\mathsf J\,\kappa_{\mathrm B}\le2\kappa_{\mathrm s}$.
For $n=i+1-l\ge1$, discard the decay factors
$L^{-4n},L^{-(2+\alpha)n},L^{-2n}\le1$
in the lag estimate and use the count $M^3L^{3n}$.
It gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:C403-link-old-variation}
 \epsilon_{\mathsf J}
          (\mathcal V_i^{\mathrm{old}}[\mathbf R^{(l)}[\mathsf J]])
 \le C_{\mathrm v}M^3L^{3n}
                          \|\mathbf R^{(l)}[\mathsf J]\|_{l;\mathsf J}.
\end{equation}
The reading itself has the same bound in
$\|\cdot\|^{\mathrm{pair}}_{i+1;\mathsf J}$:
the scalar value is zero at the trivial pair,
so (R0) gives its reading even on the top core;
the fermionic bracket costs at most
$2+C_{\mathrm{mo}}$ times the old norm.

\emph{The source sizes.}
The first-response size changes by at most
$L^{4n}$, the mixed one by at most $L^{9n/2}$,
and $\mathfrak l_l\le\mathfrak l_{i+1}$.
There are at most eight cells.  Hence
\[
 \widehat e_l[\mathsf J]\le
                    L^{36n}\widehat e_{i+1}[\mathsf J].
\]
For a partition $\pi$ of $\mathsf J$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:C403-link-size-products}
 \prod_{\substack{b\in\pi\\b\text{ in one cell}}}\widehat e_i[b]\,
 \prod_{\substack{b\in\pi\\b\text{ joins cells}}}\widehat e_{i+1}[b]
 \le C_{\mathfrak l}^8L^{36}\widehat e_{i+1}[\mathsf J].
\end{equation}
Indeed, a cell whose sources lie in one block
costs at most $L^{9/2}$.
If its two sources lie in different blocks,
the product estimate in Lemma~\ref{C-403-52}
costs at most $C_{\mathfrak l}L^{9/2}$
when both blocks lie in one cell,
$C_{\mathfrak l}L^4$ when only one does,
and $C_{\mathfrak l}$ when both join cells.

\emph{New terms joining cells.}
Induct on $\#\mathsf J$.  In a partition with
at least two blocks, every block joining cells
is smaller than $\mathsf J$.
A one-cell block has its direction bounded
by $A'_b\widehat e_i[b]$, by the first- and
mixed-response estimates.
A smaller block joining cells has bound
$A'_b\varsigma_{i+1}^{\mathrm x}\widehat e_{i+1}[b]$.
If such a block occurs, retain its factor
$\varsigma_{i+1}^{\mathrm x}$ and discard
the same factors from the other blocks.
Equations~\eqref{eq:C403-link-step-derivative}
and \eqref{eq:C403-link-size-products} then give
\[
 C_{\#\pi}^Dc_{\mathrm{cl}}^{1-\#\pi}K_M
       \prod_{b\in\pi}A'_b\,
       \varsigma_{i+1}^{\mathrm x}C_{\mathfrak l}^8L^{36}
                                      \widehat e_{i+1}[\mathsf J].
\]

If every block lies within one cell, the inputs
have rate $\kappa_{\mathrm s}$ at each support,
whereas the output asks only for
$\kappa_{\mathrm B}=\kappa_{\mathrm s}/8$.
The unused weight is
\[
 \exp\!\left[-\frac78\kappa_{\mathrm s}
                         \sum_{s\in\mathsf J}\delta_{i+1}(X;S_s)\right].
\]
Two of these supports lie in different cells.
Their distances from $X$ add to at least
$D_{\mathrm x}-\operatorname{diam}X$.
By the choices of $\eta_{\mathrm x}$ and $c_1$,
this unused weight is at most
\[
 \varsigma_{i+1}^{\mathrm x}e^{c_E(1+d_{i+1}(X))}.
\]
One $c_E$ of the decay excess pays the polymer
factor, another pays the polymer count, and
the remaining unit keeps the scalar array rate.
The preceding new-term bound therefore holds
with the additional factor $e^{c_E}$.
Sum over the partitions with at least two blocks.
By the definition of $A_{\mathsf J}$ their
total is at most
$A_{\mathsf J}\varsigma_{i+1}^{\mathrm x}
\widehat e_{i+1}[\mathsf J]/4$.

\emph{Induction over the levels.}
For $i<K-m_{\mathrm x}$ put
\[
 v_l=\frac{\|\mathbf R^{(l)}[\mathsf J]\|_{l;\mathsf J}}
             {\varsigma_l^{\mathrm x}\widehat e_l[\mathsf J]},
 \qquad
 t=\frac{c_1D_{\mathrm x}}{a_{i+1}}\ge T_{\mathrm x}.
\]
The inequality for $t$ uses
$D_{\mathrm x}\ge\ell_G/4$ and
$a_{i+1}\le L^{-m_{\mathrm x}}$.
Since
$\varsigma_l^{\mathrm x}
=\varsigma_{i+1}^{\mathrm x}e^{-t(L^n-1)}$,
the old-direction estimate is
\[
 \epsilon_{\mathsf J}(\delta_i[\mathsf J])
 \le C_{\mathrm v}M^3
       \sum_{n=1}^i L^{39n}e^{-t(L^n-1)}v_{i+1-n}\,
              \varsigma_{i+1}^{\mathrm x}\widehat e_{i+1}[\mathsf J].
\]
Use $L^n-1\ge n(L-1)$ and
$x=L^{39}e^{-t(L-1)}$.
The definition of $T_{\mathrm x}$ implies
$x\le L^{-39}(12K_MC_{\mathrm v}M^3)^{-2}$.
Thus the sum of the kernel is at most
$2x\le(6K_MC_{\mathrm v}M^3)^{-1}$.
Apply \eqref{eq:C403-link-step-derivative} at
$r=1$ to the old direction and remove the
scalar value at cost two.
The result is
\[
 v_{i+1}\le
 2\left(\frac32K_MC_{\mathrm v}M^3
        \sum_{n=1}^iL^{39n}e^{-t(L^n-1)}v_{i+1-n}
             +\frac14A_{\mathsf J}\right)
 \le\frac12\max_{l\le i}v_l+\frac12A_{\mathsf J}.
\]
The sum is empty at $i=0$, so induction gives
$v_l\le A_{\mathsf J}$.
Before removing the scalar value the norm is
at most half this bound, and the old-direction
bound is at most this size divided by $6K_M$.
This proves the second assertion.
The same finite recursive estimates, without
the contraction restriction on $i$, show that
all families needed for the total identities
through $K$ have finite size.

\emph{Summing the families.}
For $X\supset\square$,
$w_i^{\mathsf J}(\square)\le
e^{\kappa(1+d_i(X))/8}w_i^{\mathsf J}(X)$.
The polymer decay pays the factor depending
on $d_i(X)$.  Keep any one support in the
remaining cube count to obtain
\[
 \sum_X\sup\|G(X)\|
 \le e^{\kappa/8}C_{\mathcal C}^{\mathrm B}
                       (1+\mathsf d/a_i)^3\|G\|_{i;\mathsf J}.
\]
The same proof at fixed $Z,P$ gives the
common-pair version of this bound.
Since $\mathsf d<D_{\mathrm x}$,
\[
 (1+\mathsf d/a_l)^3(\varsigma_l^{\mathrm x})^{1/2}
       \le C_{\mathrm{sup}}^{\mathrm x}.
\]
Apply this to the scalar values of the
pre-extraction families.
Their sum over levels is bounded by
\[
 e^{\kappa/8}C_{\mathcal C}^{\mathrm B}C_{\mathrm{sup}}^{\mathrm x}
 A_{\mathsf J}\sum_{l\le i}
       e^{-c_{\mathrm x}D_{\mathrm x}/a_l}\widehat e_l[\mathsf J].
\]
The level-$i$ term dominates this sum up to
a factor two:
\[
 \sum_{m\ge1}L^{36m}e^{-(t_i/2)(L^m-1)}\le1,\qquad
 t_i=c_1D_{\mathrm x}/a_i\ge T_{\mathrm x}.
\]
Indeed,
$L^{36}e^{-T_{\mathrm x}(L-1)/2}
=L^{-3}(12K_MC_{\mathrm v}M^3)^{-1}\le1/12$.

For the read families use
\eqref{eq:C403-link-old-variation} without
the variation, at lag $i-l$, and the same
kernel estimate with exponent $39$.
Together with the level-$i$ family their
common-pair norm is at most
$(1+(6K_M)^{-1})A_{\mathsf J}
\varsigma_i^{\mathrm x}\widehat e_i[\mathsf J]$,
hence at most twice that size without the
parenthesized factor.
The fixed-pair polymer count just proved and
the bound by $C_{\mathrm{sup}}^{\mathrm x}$
give the final assertion, with the stated
$A_{n_{\mathfrak J}}^{\mathrm x}$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Consequences of the complex field scale}

For the fixed test pair $X=(f,h)$ put
\begin{equation}\label{C-403-29}
 \mathfrak f=\|f\|_\infty\|h\|_\infty,\qquad
 \mathsf n_m(X;\mathsf d)=\mathsf b^{-m}\mathsf d^{m-2}\mathfrak f,
 \qquad
 \mathsf l=\max\{1,\log(2\mathsf b/\mathsf d)\}.
\end{equation}
The cases $m=2$ and $m=3$ are the scales of
the leading and next covariance coefficients.

\begin{proposition}[One complex field scale]\label{C-403-33}
Assume $g\le\gamma_{\mathrm e}$ and the parameter
choices of Remark~\ref{C-403-16}.
For every datum on the least torus, the flow
with no large-field region has the complex
field-scale construction of
Proposition~\ref{C-403-33-flow}.
Every gauge fluctuation is multiplied by
$\lambda$, the fermion fluctuations are unchanged,
and the level-$j$ action has weight
\[
 \lambda^{-2}\bigl(L^j\xi_j(\lambda)-\lambda^2a_K^{-1}w\bigr),
 \qquad
 \xi_j(\lambda)=L^{-j}\beta
                      +\lambda^2(x_j-L^{-j}\beta).
\]
The mass member is multiplied by $\lambda^2$.
Each step removes the original gauge-action
coefficient and $\lambda^2$ times its original
mass increment, as well as its vacuum and
source energies at $\lambda$.
There are radii $\bar\lambda_j>1$ and
$0<\rho\le1/2$ with
\[
 \bar\lambda_j^{-2}\le
       c_\lambda(\log x_j)^{2\mathfrak p_0}\frac{a_j}{\mathsf b},
 \qquad
 (\rho\bar\lambda_j)^2\ge2 .
\]
They depend on the datum only through the
specified running coefficients.
\begin{enumerate}
\item The zero-source energies and activities
are even and holomorphic for $|\lambda|<\bar\lambda_j$.
For each $1\le\lambda_\circ<\bar\lambda_j$ they
extend holomorphically in $(\lambda,w)$ for
$|\lambda|\le\lambda_\circ$ and
$\|w\|_\sharp<\varepsilon_j(\lambda_\circ)$,
with some positive radius.
At $\lambda=1$ the construction agrees with the
original source flow, including at every source
in its admitted polydisc.
At $\lambda=0$ the gauge field is its background
and the fermion steps are Gaussian Berezin integrals.
\item Let
\[
 \mathsf n_j^\lambda=
 \left.\partial_{z_1}\partial_{z_2}
       \sum_{X'}\mathfrak E_j(X';z_1f+z_2h,0)\right|_{z=0},
 \qquad
 \mathsf n_j^\lambda=\sum_{m\ge0}\mathsf n_{j,[2m]}\lambda^{2m}.
\]
For $0\le m\le4$ and $0\le p\le3$,
\begin{align*}
 \sum_{j=1}^K|\mathsf n_{j,[2m]}|
 &\le C_m^{\mathrm{ii}}\mathsf l^{2m\mathfrak p_0}
                                      \mathsf n_m(X;\mathsf d),\\
 \left|\sum_{j=1}^K\left(
        \mathsf n_j^1-\sum_{m=0}^p\mathsf n_{j,[2m]}\right)\right|
 &\le C_p^{\mathrm{ii}}\mathsf l^{2(p+1)\mathfrak p_0}
                                      \mathsf n_{p+1}(X;\mathsf d).
\end{align*}
One may choose the same constant at index $k$
for the coefficient and remainder estimates
that use that index.
\item On $|\lambda|<\bar\lambda_j$,
\[
 |\mathsf n_j^\lambda|\le
 C_{\mathrm{iii}}\mathsf n_0(X;a_j)
 \begin{cases}
 (\mathsf d/a_j)^{5/2},&a_j\ge\mathsf d,\\
 (\mathsf d/a_j)^3e^{-\kappa_{\mathrm s}\mathsf d/(2Ma_j)},
                                                &a_j<\mathsf d.
 \end{cases}
\]
The first source derivative is at most
\[
 C_{\mathrm{iii}}\|f\|_\infty a_j^{-1}
                (\mathsf d/a_j)^3\mathfrak l_j^{4\mathfrak p_0+1}.
\]
If $a_j\ge\mathsf d$, it is also at most
$C_{\mathrm{iii}}\|f\|_\infty a_j^{-1}
(\mathsf d/a_j)^{11/4}$.
The same holds for $h$.

The first and mixed derivatives of the
field-dependent total, including the mass
member, are respectively
\[
 \sum_{l\le j}\sum_{X'}\mathbf P^{(l)}[f](X')
          -L^{-j}\mathsf S_1(\lambda^4\mathfrak N_j[f]\,\cdot),
 \qquad
 \sum_{l\le j}\sum_{X'}\mathbf Q^{(l)}[f,h](X'),
\]
read at level $j$ as total functions.
The action-weight member is kept separately.
On $D_{j-1}$ their activity families have
weighted read norms at most
\[
 C_{\mathrm{iii}}e_j[f]\mathfrak l_j^{4\mathfrak p_0+1},
 \qquad C_{\mathrm{iii}}e_j[f,h],
\]
respectively.  Scalar terms use the strong
norm on the full core.  Short-lag fermionic
terms use the strong norm; long-lag terms
use the norm with a common pair for the sum.
On $D_j$,
\[
 c_{\mathsf S}h_F^2|\lambda|^4
          \langle\mathfrak N_j[f]\rangle_{j;\{\lambda\};S_f}
 \le C_{\mathrm{iii}}e_j[f]\mathfrak l_j^{4\mathfrak p_0+1}.
\]
All these response families are even and vanish
at $\lambda=0$.  At the trivial configuration
their first and mixed fermionic parts start
at orders four and six, respectively.
\end{enumerate}
The constants depend on $g,\vartheta$ and the
fixed construction constants.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Proposition~\ref{C-403-33-flow} proves the
field-scale construction and its agreement
with the source flow.
Lemmas~\ref{C-403-44}, \ref{C-403-48},
\ref{C-403-49}, \ref{C-403-51}, \ref{C-403-52}
and \ref{C-403-53} give the total identities,
orders, moment estimates, read norms and
source-energy estimates in the third assertion.
Their proofs preserve the distinction between
the strong scalar norm and the common-pair
fermionic norm at long lags.
Increase $C_{\mathrm{iii}}$ by
$\sup_{t\ge1}t^{-1/4}(1+\log t)^{4\mathfrak p_0+1}$
to obtain the first-derivative exponent $11/4$.

For an even holomorphic function $H$ bounded
by $\mathsf B$ on $|\lambda|<\bar\lambda_j$,
Cauchy's formula gives
\[
 |H_{[2m]}|\le\mathsf B\bar\lambda_j^{-2m},\qquad
 \left|H(1)-\sum_{m=0}^pH_{[2m]}\right|
 \le\frac{\mathsf B\bar\lambda_j^{-2p-2}}
                                    {1-\bar\lambda_j^{-2}}.
\]
Here $\bar\lambda_j^{-2}\le\rho^2/2\le1/8$.
For $a_j\ge\mathsf d$, the contribution to
the coefficient of order $2m$ is at most
\[
 C_{\mathrm{iii}}c_\lambda^m
      (\log x_j)^{2m\mathfrak p_0}
      \mathsf b^{-m}\mathsf d^{5/2}a_j^{m-9/2}\mathfrak f .
\]
In this range $\log x_j\le\mathsf l$.
For $m\le4$, the exponent $m-9/2$ is negative,
so the geometric sum begins at the scale
$a_j\asymp\mathsf d$ and is bounded by
a constant times
$\mathsf l^{2m\mathfrak p_0}\mathsf n_m(X;\mathsf d)$.

For $a_j<\mathsf d$, put $t=\mathsf d/a_j$.
The bound is the same target size times
a constant times
\[
 (1+\log t)^{2m\mathfrak p_0}
                     t^{5-m}e^{-\kappa_{\mathrm s}t/(2M)}.
\]
We used
$\log x_j\le\mathsf l(1+\log(\mathsf d/a_j))$.
The possible $t$ are one number in $(1,L]$
times successive powers of $L$, so this
sum is uniformly finite.
For the remainder use the same calculation
with $m=p+1\le4$ and the additional factor
$(1-\bar\lambda_j^{-2})^{-1}\le8/7$.
Take at each index the larger of the
coefficient and remainder constants.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[The scalar specialization]\label{C-403-54}
The same field-scale argument applies to the
pure gauge steps calibrated at the places
$\mathsf t_i$ in \eqref{C-403-42}.
Omit the fermion vertex, fermion normalizer,
mass member and all terms with fermion legs.
The remaining terms satisfy the potential,
origin and scalar-family bounds of
Proposition~\ref{C-403-33-flow}.
The extraction moments vanish, and the
first-response recursion is its reduced
recursion.

Lemmas~\ref{C-403-45}--\ref{C-403-53} then
use only (R0) and the scalar variation in
Lemma~\ref{C-403-46}.
For first derivatives the lag factor is
$L^{4n}L^{-4n}q_n=q_n$.
For mixed derivatives it is
$L^{9n/2}L^{-4n}q_n=L^{n/2}q_n$.
Both are summable, and no accumulated-mass
logarithm occurs.
Thus their proofs give the same first and
mixed bounds with $1$ replacing
$\mathfrak l_i$; one may retain
$A_{\mathbf P},A'_{\mathbf P},A_{\mathbf Q}$
as upper bounds for the constants.
For $a_j\ge\mathsf d$, on
$|\lambda|<\bar\lambda_j$, this gives
\[
 |\mathsf n_j^\lambda|
       \le C_{\mathfrak e,2}\mathsf n_0(X;a_j)
                                      (\mathsf d/a_j)^{5/2},
 \qquad
 \left|\left.\partial_z\sum_{X'}\mathfrak E_j(X';zf,0)
                                              \right|_{z=0}\right|
       \le C_{\mathfrak e,1}\|f\|_\infty a_j^{-1}
                                      (\mathsf d/a_j)^3.
\]
\end{remark}

\subsection{The fermion polarization}
\label{sec:qcdm2-polarization}

The quadratic part of the fermion determinant controls the leading
change in the mean block action.  We define it on the infinite lattice,
including at bare mass zero.  The estimate below separates its
continuum singularity from a local quadratic term and a remainder.
Throughout this subsection the lattice spacing is one and
\(0\le m_0\le1\).

\begin{lemma}\label{C-403-32}
Let \(G=(D_+[1]+m_0)^{-1}\) denote the free kernel on
\(\mathbb Z^3\), for one flavour.  If \(U=1\) off finitely many
bonds, set
\[
 \psi^F(U)=-2\log\left|\det\bigl(1+G(D_+[U]-D_+[1])\bigr)\right|.
\]
The determinant is a finite determinant and is nonzero, also when
\(m_0=0\).  Near \(U=1\), \(\psi^F\) is real analytic, has no
linear term, and has quadratic part
\begin{equation}\label{eq:qcdm2-polarization-definition}
 \psi^F_2(A)
 =2\operatorname{Re}\left\{
  \frac12\operatorname{Tr}(G\mathbb V_1G\mathbb V_1)
       -\operatorname{Tr}(G\mathbb V_2)\right\}
 =\frac12\sum_{c=1}^3(A^c,\Pi A^c).
\end{equation}
Here \(\mathbb V_j\) is the term of degree \(j\) in
\(D_+[e^{iA}]-D_+[1]\).  The kernel \(\Pi\) is real, symmetric
and translation invariant, and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:qcdm2-polarization-decay}
 |\Pi(b,b')|\le C(1+|b_--b'_-|)^{-4},\qquad
 \Pi\,\mathrm d\chi=0
\end{equation}
for every bounded complex function \(\chi\).  The constant is
uniform in \(m_0\).
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The free estimates of \cite[\S6]{QCDM1} give
\[
 \|\widehat G(p)\|\le C|p|^{-1},\qquad
 |G(v,w)|\le C(1+|x_v-x_w|)^{-2}.
\]
The symbol is integrable, and its inverse Fourier transform is
continuous in \(m_0\), including at zero.  Both inverse identities
hold on vectors of finite support.  Write
\(\mathbb V=D_+[U]-D_+[1]\).  This operator is supported on the
places over the endpoints of the finitely many altered bonds, so
\(\det(1+G\mathbb V)=\det(1+\mathbb VG)\) is finite dimensional.
The other spin block gives its complex conjugate.

To check nonvanishing, suppose that
\(w+\mathbb VGw=0\), with \(w\ne0\) supported on these places.
Then \(v=Gw\) belongs to \(\ell^2\), since it decays as
\((1+|x|)^{-2}\), and
\((D_+[U]+m_0)v=0\).  The real part of this equation gives
\[
 0=\langle v,(\Delta[U]+m_0)v\rangle.
\]
For the chamber operator this forces the component orthogonal to
the chamber constants to vanish, and the remaining site field to
be covariantly constant.  Its norm is constant; membership in
\(\ell^2\) therefore forces \(v=0\), a contradiction.  On any
fixed finite set of links the squared modulus of the determinant is thus a positive
continuous function of the compact link variables.  Its logarithm
is smooth and is analytic near \(1\).

Expanding \(\log\det(1+G\mathbb V)\) gives
\eqref{eq:qcdm2-polarization-definition}.  Its linear term vanishes
because the free operator is scalar in colour and
\(\operatorname{tr}\sigma_c=0\).  Constant colour rotations imply
that the quadratic colour tensor is a multiple of
\(\delta_{cc'}\).  Taking its real part gives the real symmetric
kernel \(\Pi\).

Gauge invariance can be checked without an infinite determinant.
Put \(A_1=D_+[1]+m_0\), \(B=D_+[U]+m_0\), and let \(u-1\)
have finite support.  The identity
\[
 1+G(uBu^{-1}-A_1)
 =[1+G(u-1)A_1]u^{-1}\,
       u[1+G(B-A_1)]u^{-1}
\]
is an identity between products of finite-rank perturbations of
the identity.  The first two factors have determinant one, since
\[
 \det[1+G(u-1)A_1]
 =\det[1+(u-1)A_1G]=\det u=1.
\]
Thus \(\psi^F(U^u)=\psi^F(U)\).  Comparing quadratic terms under
\(u=e^{-i\chi}\) proves \(\Pi\mathrm d\chi=0\) for finitely
supported \(\chi\).

The second-order vertex is diagonal in the bond index.  The term
with two first-order vertices contains two free propagators
between the endpoints of the two bonds.  Their decay gives
\eqref{eq:qcdm2-polarization-decay}.  Translation invariance follows
from that of the free operator.  For bounded \(\chi\), replace it
by its restriction to a ball of radius \(R\) and use
\[
 \sum_{|b'_--b_-|\ge R-1}(1+|b_--b'_-|)^{-4}\longrightarrow0.
\]
The row sum is absolutely convergent, so the identity extends to
bounded \(\chi\), and hence to plane waves.
\end{proof}

Define, with the value at \(m=0\) understood by continuity,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:qcdm2-upsilon}
 \Upsilon(k;m)
 =\frac{N_f}{2\pi}\left[
 \frac{2m}{|k|^2}
 +\frac{|k|^2-4m^2}{|k|^3}\arctan\frac{|k|}{2m}\right]
 =\frac{N_f}{2\pi}\int_{2m}^{\infty}
       \frac{1+4m^2/\mu^2}{\mu^2+|k|^2}\,d\mu.
\end{equation}
In particular, \(\Upsilon(k;0)=N_f/(4|k|)\).

\begin{lemma}\label{C-403-36}
Place bond variables at their midpoints, so that
\[
 A_\mu(y)=e^{ik\cdot(y+e_\mu/2)}\alpha_\mu,\qquad
 (\Pi A)_\mu(y)=e^{ik\cdot(y+e_\mu/2)}
                    (\widehat\Pi(k;m_0)\alpha)_\mu.
\]
There are constants \(c^{\mathrm{vp}}\in\mathbb R\) and \(C\),
depending only on the chamber operator, such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:qcdm2-polarization-asymptotic}
 \begin{split}
 &\left|\widehat\Pi_{\mu\nu}(k;m_0)
 -( |k|^2\delta_{\mu\nu}-k_\mu k_\nu)
       \bigl(c^{\mathrm{vp}}+N_f^{-1}\Upsilon(k;m_0)\bigr)\right|\\
 &\hspace{15mm}\le C|k|^2\left[
 (|k|+m_0)(1+|\log|k||)+\frac{m_0}{|k|+m_0}\right]
 \end{split}
\end{equation}
for \(0<|k|\le\pi\) and \(0\le m_0\le1\).  Away from
\(k=0\), \(\widehat\Pi\) is uniformly bounded and continuous in
\((k,m_0)\).
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Write \(\langle p\rangle=|p|+m_0\),
\(p_\pm=p\pm k/2\), and \(\widehat k_\mu=2\sin(k_\mu/2)\).
We use \(\int_p\) for normalized Lebesgue integration over either
the momentum torus or \(\mathbb R^3\), as specified.  All constants
in this proof depend only on the chamber operator.

\emph{Symmetry and the light component.}
The decay in \eqref{eq:qcdm2-polarization-decay} gives an absolutely
convergent Fourier series, uniformly in \(m_0\).  The same equation,
applied to plane waves, gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:qcdm2-polarization-Ward}
 \widehat\Pi(k;m_0)\widehat k=0.
\end{equation}
The cubic isometries act on midpoint variables by their linear
parts.  Improper isometries exchange the two spin blocks, which
enter the determinant symmetrically.  Thus
\(\widehat\Pi(tk)=t\widehat\Pi(k)t^{\mathsf T}\) for
\(t\in W_3\); in particular \(\widehat\Pi\) is even and real
symmetric.  Uniform boundedness settles the claimed estimate
when \(|k|\ge\delta/2\), for any fixed small \(\delta>0\).

Let \(\Pi_0\) project onto the chamber constants and put
\(\Pi_1=1-\Pi_0\).  On the positive spin block set
\[
 H=\Pi_1(D_++m_0)\Pi_1,\quad
 X=\Pi_0D_+\Pi_1,\quad X'=\Pi_1D_+\Pi_0,\quad
 S=\Pi_0(D_++m_0)\Pi_0-XH^{-1}X'.
\]
The chamber gap gives \(\operatorname{Re}H\ge\lambda_\rho+m_0\).
The triangular factorization
\[
 D_++m_0=(1+XH^{-1})(S\oplus H)(1+H^{-1}X')
\]
splits the relative determinant into its \(S\) and \(H\)
determinants.  Indeed, at a finitely supported link perturbation
all relative factors are finite-rank perturbations of the identity.
The two triangular relative factors have determinant one.  Both
remaining determinants are gauge invariant, since \(\Pi_1\)
commutes with gauge transformations.  Their quadratic kernels give
\(\Pi=\Pi^S+\Pi^{\mathrm h}\).

At \(U=1\), \(\widehat D_+(p)\) is a trigonometric polynomial.
Consequently \(H(p)^{-1}\) is analytic on a complex strip of width
\(\min\{1,\lambda_\rho/(2C)\}\), with norm at most
\(2/\lambda_\rho\).  Its mass derivative has norm at most
\(4/\lambda_\rho^2\).  The heavy kernel and its required momentum
and mass derivatives are therefore bounded.  The free kernel of
\(S^{-1}\), being a compression of the full propagator, is bounded
by \(C(1+|x-y|)^{-2}\).  These bounds justify the determinant
splitting also at \(m_0=0\), by dominated convergence in its
quadratic coefficients.

For \(|p|\le4\delta\), the Schur complement has the expansion
\begin{equation}\label{eq:qcdm2-light-symbol}
 \widehat S(p)=m_0+i\sigma\cdot p+K_2(p)+K_3(p,m_0),
\end{equation}
where \(K_2\) is quadratic and independent of \(m_0\), and
\[
 |K_3|\le C|p|^2\langle p\rangle,quad
 |\partial_p^\alpha K_3|\le C\langle p\rangle^{3-|\alpha|}
       \ (|\alpha|\le4),\quad
 |\partial_{m_0}\partial_p^\alpha K_3|
       \le C\langle p\rangle^{2-|\alpha|}
       \ (|\alpha|\le3).
\]
To see the mass dependence explicitly, write \(H=H_\circ+m_0\)
and let \(X_1,X'_1\) be the linear terms of \(X,X'\) at zero.
Then
\[
 K_2=\frac r2|p|^2-X_1H_\circ(0)^{-1}X'_1.
\]
The remaining Schur terms are cubic in \(p\), or contain
\(H^{-1}-H_\circ^{-1}=-m_0H^{-1}H_\circ^{-1}\) between
\(X,X'=O(|p|)\).  This proves all the displayed bounds by Taylor's
formula.

The first vertex of \(S[e^{iA}]\), at mean fermion momentum \(q\)
and gauge momentum \(k\), has the form
\[
 v_\mu(q,k)=i\sigma_\mu+v^{(1)}_\mu(q,k)
                              +v^{(2)}_\mu(q,k;m_0).
\]
Here \(v^{(1)}\) is linear in \((q,k)\) and independent of mass,
and, for \(|\alpha|\le3\),
\[
 |\partial^\alpha v^{(2)}|
  \le C(|q|+|k|+m_0)^{2-|\alpha|},\qquad
 |\partial_{m_0}\partial^\alpha v^{(2)}|
  \le C(|q|+|k|+m_0)^{1-|\alpha|}.
\]
In fact each mass-dependent first variation of the Schur term
contains \(X\) or \(X'\); hence
\(\partial_{m_0}v=O(|q|+|k|)\), and the bounds follow by Taylor
expansion at \((q,k,m_0)=0\).  The second vertex
\(w_{\mu\nu}(q,k)\) and the derivatives used below are smooth and
bounded.  Formula \eqref{eq:qcdm2-polarization-definition} now writes
the light contribution as
\[
 \widehat\Pi^S(k)=\int_{[-\pi,\pi]^3} B(p,k)\,\frac{dp}{(2\pi)^3}
                         +T(k).
\]
The integrand \(B\) is the trace, with the normalization in that
formula, of
\[\widehat S(p_-)^{-1}v_\mu(p,k)
  \widehat S(p_+)^{-1}v_\nu(p,-k).\]
The term \(T\) contains one propagator and the second vertex,
with the sign of \(-\operatorname{Tr}(G\mathbb V_2)\).

\emph{Parity and the expansion at zero momentum.}
On the two spin blocks an operator and its adjoint occur together.
Their Hermitian parts multiply \(\tau_0\) and their anti-Hermitian
parts multiply \(\tau_3\).  Inversion shows that \(m_0,K_2,v^{(1)}\)
have the former parity and \(i\sigma\cdot p,i\sigma_\mu\) the
latter.  A trace with an odd number of \(\tau_3\) factors vanishes.

Put \(G^c(p)=(m_0+i\sigma\cdot p)^{-1}\).  For small \(\delta\),
the Neumann expansion of \eqref{eq:qcdm2-light-symbol} gives
\[
 \widehat S^{-1}=G^c+G^{(1)}+G^{(2)},\qquad
 G^{(1)}=-G^cK_2G^c,
\]
\[
 G^{(2)}=G^cK_2G^c(K_2+K_3)\widehat S^{-1}
                              -G^cK_3\widehat S^{-1}.
\]
For \(|\alpha|\le3\), these three terms satisfy bounds of degrees
\(-1-|\alpha|,-|\alpha|,1-|\alpha|\), respectively, in
\(\langle p\rangle\).  A mass derivative lowers each degree by
one.  The first two terms are homogeneous in \((p,m_0)\) of degrees
\(-1,0\).

Choose a radial smooth \(\chi\), equal to one on
\(|p|\le\delta\) and zero on \(|p|\ge2\delta\).  On the support
of \(\chi(p_-)\chi(p_+)\), expand
\[
 B=B^c+B^{(1)}+B^{(2)}.
\]
The term \(B^c\) uses \(G^c\) and the constant vertices;
\(B^{(1)}\) uses exactly one \(G^{(1)}\) or \(v^{(1)}\).
They are homogeneous of degrees \(-2,-1\) in \((p,k,m_0)\).
Every term of \(B^{(2)}\) has total degree at least zero, with
each of its propagator factors of degree at least \(-1\).
Parity gives \(B^{(1)}(p,k;0)=0\).  Every surviving term at
positive mass contains \(m_0/(p^2+m_0^2)\), so
\(B^{(1)}=O(m_0|p|^{-2})\) at infinity, with one additional
inverse power for each momentum derivative.

For differentiation of these integrals, separate the points
\(p_-=0\) and \(p_+=0\) by cutoffs
\(\zeta(p_-/|k|),\zeta(p_+/|k|)\), where \(\zeta=1\) on
the ball of radius \(1/4\) and zero outside radius \(1/3\).
On the first piece use \(p_-\) as variable, so derivatives fall
on the other factor; do the converse on the second piece.
The remaining piece stays away from both singularities.
Derivatives of order \(j\) of these cutoffs cost \(C_j|k|^{-j}\)
on shells of volume \(O(|k|^3)\).  On those shells all momenta
are comparable to \(|k|\).  In particular the cutoff terms from
three derivatives of \(B^{(2)}\) are bounded.

\emph{The continuum term.}
For one flavour the continuum kernel is
\[
 -2\int_p\operatorname{tr}_4[\gamma_\mu G^c_4(p)
                  \gamma_\nu G^c_4(p+k)],
 \qquad G^c_4(p)=(m_0+i\gamma\cdot p)^{-1}.
\]
The factor two is the colour trace.
The two spin blocks cancel the parity-odd trace.  With
\(\gamma_\mu=\sigma_\mu\otimes\tau_3\), the continuum trace is
\[
 \operatorname{tr}_4[
 \gamma_\mu(-i\not p+m_0)\gamma_\nu(-i(\not p+\not k)+m_0)]
 =4[-p_\mu(p+k)_\nu-p_\nu(p+k)_\mu
                +\delta_{\mu\nu}(p\cdot(p+k)+m_0^2)].
\]
Feynman parametrization, \(p=l-xk\), gives
\(\Delta=m_0^2+x(1-x)|k|^2\).  The rotational average of the
numerator is
\[
 \delta_{\mu\nu}(l^2/3+\Delta)
               +2x(1-x)(k_\mu k_\nu-|k|^2\delta_{\mu\nu}).
\]
The first term divided by \((l^2+\Delta)^2\) is
\(\partial_l\cdot[l/(3(l^2+\Delta))]\).  To handle it by
absolutely convergent integrals, subtract the same loop at mass
\(M>m_0\).  Its boundary flux through \(|l|=R\) is
\[
 \frac{4\pi}3R^3
 [(R^2+\Delta_{m_0})^{-1}-(R^2+\Delta_M)^{-1}]
 \longrightarrow0.
\]
The remaining integral uses
\(\int_l(l^2+\Delta)^{-2}=(8\pi\sqrt\Delta)^{-1}\)
and equals
\[
 (|k|^2\delta-kk^{\mathsf T})
        [\Upsilon(k;m_0)-\Upsilon(k;M)]/N_f.
\]
This also proves \eqref{eq:qcdm2-upsilon} by elementary integration.
Third momentum derivatives of the mass-\(M\) loop are
\(O(M^{-2})\), by homogeneity.  Letting \(M\to\infty\) shows
that third momentum derivatives and \(\partial_{m_0}\partial_k^2\)
of the continuum loop agree with those of
\((|k|^2\delta-kk^{\mathsf T})\Upsilon/N_f\).
Consequently
\[
 R_c=\int_p\chi(p_-)\chi(p_+)B^c
                    -( |k|^2\delta-kk^{\mathsf T})\Upsilon/N_f
\]
is \(C^2\) and satisfies
\( |\partial_k^3R_c|+|\partial_{m_0}\partial_k^2R_c|\le C\).
Indeed, these derivatives are integrals of
\([\chi(p_-)\chi(p_+)-1]B^c\), away from both singularities.

\emph{The first correction and the remainder.}
Define the absolutely convergent integral on \(\mathbb R^3\)
\[
 F(k;m_0)=\int_p\left[
 \tfrac12\{B^{(1)}(p,k)+B^{(1)}(p,-k)\}-B^{(1)}(p,0)\right].
\]
It is even, homogeneous of degree two, and vanishes when either
\(k=0\) or \(m_0=0\).  Its mass derivative is homogeneous of
degree one and bounded for \(|k|=1\), \(0\le m_0\le1\).
Thus \(|F|\le Cm_0|k|\) when \(m_0\le|k|\).
For \(|k|\le m_0\), use
\(F(k;m_0)=m_0^2F(k/m_0;1)\); the function on the right is
even and \(C^2\), and vanishes at zero.  Hence
\begin{equation}\label{eq:qcdm2-polarization-first-remainder}
 |F(k;m_0)|\le C|k|^2\frac{m_0}{|k|+m_0}.
\end{equation}
Writing \(\Phi_1=\int_p\chi(p_-)\chi(p_+)B^{(1)}\), the
difference \(R_1=\Phi_1-\Phi_1(0)-F\) is an integral away from
the singularities and has derivatives through order three
bounded by \(Cm_0\).

For \(R_2=\int_p\chi(p_-)\chi(p_+)B^{(2)}\), consider a term
of total degree \(n\ge0\), whose factor at \(p_-\) has degree
\(n_-\ge-1\).  In \(|p_-|\le|k|/4\), three derivatives give
at most
\[
 C\langle p_-\rangle^{n_-}
          (|k|+m_0)^{n-n_--3}.
\]
Its integral is bounded.  The same holds near \(p_+=0\) and
on the remaining region \(|p|\le|k|\).  On
\(|k|\le|p|\le2\delta\), the bound is
\(C\langle p\rangle^{n-3}\), whose integral is at most
\(C(1+|\log|k||)\).  Including the cutoff terms gives
\[
 |\partial_k^3R_2(k)|\le C(1+|\log|k||),\qquad
 |\partial_{m_0}\partial_k^2R_2(0;m_0)|
                   \le C(1+|\log m_0|).
\]
In particular \(R_2\) is \(C^2\).  The complementary integral
\(\Pi^{\mathrm{out}}=\int_p[1-\chi(p_-)\chi(p_+)]B\)
is smooth with bounded derivatives.  In \(T\), momentum
derivatives fall on the second vertex, and a mass derivative
costs at most \(C\langle p\rangle^{-2}\), which is integrable.
The heavy term has already been bounded.

\emph{The quadratic local term.}
Collect these terms as
\[
 \widehat\Pi=(|k|^2\delta-kk^{\mathsf T})\Upsilon/N_f+F+Q,
\quad
 Q=R_c+\Phi_1(0)+R_1+R_2+\Pi^{\mathrm{out}}+T+\widehat\Pi^{\mathrm h}.
\]
The function \(Q\) is even and \(C^2\), with
\[
 |\partial_k^3Q(k;m_0)|\le C(1+|\log|k||),\qquad
 |\partial_k^2Q(0;m_0)-\partial_k^2Q(0;0)|
                   \le Cm_0(1+|\log m_0|).
\]
For the last bound integrate the mass derivative from zero.
Its value at zero is justified as follows.  At a fixed
\(k\ne0\), dominated convergence gives continuity in mass of
the second derivatives.  The third-derivative estimate bounds
the difference between those derivatives at \(k\) and at zero
by \(2C|k|(1+|\log|k||)\), uniformly in mass.  This extends
continuity to \(k=0\).

The Ward identity along every ray gives \(Q(0;m_0)=0\).
Taylor's formula therefore yields
\[
 Q(k;m_0)=\tfrac12\partial_k^2Q(0;m_0)[k,k]
                  +O(|k|^3(1+|\log|k||)).
\]
At mass zero, \(F=0\) and \(\Upsilon=N_f/(4|k|)\).
Since \(\widehat k-k=O(|k|^3)\), the Ward identity forces the
homogeneous quadratic matrix
\(T_2(k)=\tfrac12\partial_k^2Q(0;0)[k,k]\) to satisfy
\(T_2(k)k=0\).  A cubic-invariant symmetric quadratic matrix has
the form
\[
 \alpha|k|^2I+\beta kk^{\mathsf T}
                        +\gamma\operatorname{diag}(k_1^2,k_2^2,k_3^2).
\]
Its product with \(k\) vanishes only when
\(\gamma=0\), \(\beta=-\alpha\).  Thus
\(T_2(k)=c^{\mathrm{vp}}(|k|^2I-kk^{\mathsf T})\).
Combining this with the bounds for \(F\) and \(Q\), and using
\[
 m_0(1+|\log m_0|)
 \le2(|k|+m_0)(1+|\log|k||)
 \quad (|k|,m_0\le1),
\]
proves \eqref{eq:qcdm2-polarization-asymptotic}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The determinant in the second covariance coefficient}

The finite-dimensional Laplace formula is \cref{C-403-31}.



\begin{lemma}[The constrained determinant]\label{lem:C403-block-determinant}
On the bare torus with a flat block constraint
$\mathcal M^nU=1$, $n\ge1$, put
\[
 \mathcal K_n[U;m_0]
       =D[U]+m_0+\mathfrak a_nR_n(U)^*R_n(U),
 \qquad 0\le m_0\le1.
\]
For one flavour let $\mathcal K_{n,+}$ be its
restriction to the $e_+$ block and define, near
the trivial configuration,
\[
 \psi^{(\le n)}(U)
 =-2\operatorname{Re}
       \bigl[\log\det\mathcal K_{n,+}[U;m_0]
                       -\log\det\mathcal K_{n,+}[1;m_0]\bigr].
\]
This function is real analytic, vanishes at $1$
and has zero linear part.
If $G_n=\mathcal K_{n,+}[1;m_0]^{-1}$ and
$\mathbb V_j^{(n)}$ is the degree-$j$ part of
$\mathcal K_{n,+}[e^{iA};m_0]-\mathcal K_{n,+}[1;m_0]$,
then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:C403-block-polarization}
 \psi_2^{(\le n)}(A)
 =2\operatorname{Re}\left\{
     \tfrac12\operatorname{Tr}
         (G_n\mathbb V_1^{(n)}G_n\mathbb V_1^{(n)})
       -\operatorname{Tr}(G_n\mathbb V_2^{(n)})\right\}
 =\tfrac12\sum_{c=1}^3(A^c,\Pi^{(\le n)}A^c).
\end{equation}
The kernel is real and symmetric and annihilates
exact forms.

In the setting of Lemma~\ref{C-403-31}, multiplying
the density by $e^{-N_f\psi_{\mathcal K}}$, with
$\psi_{\mathcal K}=\psi^F$ of Lemma~\ref{C-403-32}
or $\psi^{(\le n)}$, leaves $\zeta_0$ unchanged
and changes $\zeta_2$ by
\[
             -N_f\langle X_{1,0};X_{2,0};\psi_{\mathcal K,2}\rangle.
\]
There is no quadratic term in $N_f$ and no
contribution from $\psi_{\mathcal K,3}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The averaging operators are real analytic
near the trivial configuration.
Their entries are finite sums of transports,
with the normalization in $R_n$.
At positive mass $\mathcal K_n$ is invertible.
At zero mass its inverse at the trivial
configuration is the antiperiodic image sum
of the exponentially decaying constrained
free kernel.  It is therefore invertible
there as well, and invertibility persists
in a neighbourhood.
The operator commutes with $e_\pm$; at real
configurations its $e_-$ block is the adjoint
of its $e_+$ block.  Thus
$\det\mathcal K_n=|\det\mathcal K_{n,+}|^{2N_f}$.
This proves analyticity of the stated logarithm.

The expansion of $\log\det(\mathcal K_{n,+}[1]+\mathbb V)$
gives \eqref{eq:C403-block-polarization}.
At the trivial configuration the inverse acts
as the identity on colour.  Every term of
the first variation has one colour matrix
$\sigma_c$, including the first variations
of the averaging transports.
Its trace vanishes because
$\operatorname{tr}\sigma_c=0$.
Constant colour rotations force the quadratic
colour tensor to be a multiple of
$\delta_{cc'}$.

Gauge covariance gives
$R_n(U^u)=u|_{\mathbb T^{(n)}}R_n(U)\mathsf u^{-1}$
and
$\mathcal K_n[U^u;m_0]
=\mathsf u\mathcal K_n[U;m_0]\mathsf u^{-1}$.
For $u=e^{-i\chi}$, the logarithmic field
changes by $A\mapsto A+\mathrm d\chi+O(2)$.
Comparison of quadratic terms, with no
