linear term present, proves
$\psi_2^{(\le n)}(A+\mathrm d\chi)=\psi_2^{(\le n)}(A)$.
Its polarized form gives
$\Pi^{(\le n)}\mathrm d\chi=0$.

Finally, in any smooth chart
$A=A_{(1)}+A_{(2)}+\cdots$, the quadratic
part of the logarithmic determinant is
$\psi_{\mathcal K,2}(A_{(1)})$:
the potential contribution
$\psi_{\mathcal K,1}(A_{(2)})$ vanishes.
In the Laplace formula $W_1$ is unchanged
and $W_2$ gains $N_f\psi_{\mathcal K,2}$.
The latter occurs exactly once and linearly
in $\zeta_2$, proving the final assertion.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[The fermionic covariance coefficient]
\label{lem:C403-fermionic-covariance-coefficient}
In one colour let
$C(p,q)=\langle F_pF_q\rangle_0$ and
$\mathsf Y(p;b)=\langle F_pA_b\rangle_0$
be the infinite-lattice free curvature and
curvature-potential covariances.
Then
\[
 (\mathsf Y\Pi\mathsf Y^{\mathsf T})(p,q)
   =\sum_{b,b'}\mathsf Y(p;b)\Pi(b,b')\mathsf Y(q;b')
\]
is absolutely convergent, and put
\[
 \mathsf B_1^F(p,q;m_0)
       =-3C(p,q)(\mathsf Y\Pi\mathsf Y^{\mathsf T})(p,q).
\]
The second covariance coefficient of the
Dirichlet box theory with its determinant
relative to the infinite-lattice free operator
has the iterated limit
\begin{align*}
 &\lim_{n\to\infty}\lim_{\beta\to\infty}
 \beta^3\left[
   \langle a_{p+o_n};a_{q+o_n}\rangle_{n,\beta,m_0}
       -\beta^{-2}\mathsf B_0^{[n]}(p+o_n,q+o_n)\right]\\
 &\qquad=\mathsf B_1^{\mathrm{lat}}(p,q)
                                      +N_f\mathsf B_1^F(p,q;m_0).
\end{align*}
Here the box configurations equal $1$ outside
their free bonds, their density is proportional to
$e^{-\beta S(U)}e^{-N_f\psi^F(U)}$, and $o_n$
places the two fixed plaquettes in the interior.

For the flat block constraint at depth $n$ on
a torus of bare side $N$, write
\[
\begin{gathered}
A_{(1)}=\sum_{i<n}A_i,\\
 C_N^{(n)}(p,q)=\langle(\mathrm dA_{(1)})_p
                              (\mathrm dA_{(1)})_q\rangle_0
                         =(\Pi_0^{\mathrm{tp}}-\Pi_n^{\mathrm{tp}})(p,q),
 \\
 \mathsf Y^{(n)}(p;b)=\langle(\mathrm dA_{(1)})_p A_{(1),b}\rangle_0 .
\end{gathered}
\]
The covariance is the projection onto
$\mathsf{Fl}_n$.  The determinant changes
the second Laplace coefficient by
$N_f\mathsf B_N^{F,(n)}$, where
\[
 \mathsf B_N^{F,(n)}(p,q;m_0)
   =-3C_N^{(n)}(p,q)
       (\mathsf Y^{(n)}\Pi^{(\le n)}
                              \mathsf Y^{(n)\mathsf T})(p,q).
\]
Each $\mathsf Y^{(n)}(p;\cdot)$ is a potential
of $C_N^{(n)}(\cdot,p)$ whose sum over bonds
in each direction is zero.  In this formula
it may be replaced by any potential with
these properties.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
We first check that the determinant-weighted
box law has the stated Laplace interpretation.
By Lemma~\ref{C-403-32}, its determinant ratio
is a positive continuous function of finitely
many compact links.  It is bounded above
and below by positive constants and is gauge
invariant.
The axial-gauge localization for the pure
box measure therefore applies with each of
$1,a_p,a_q,a_pa_q$ multiplied by this ratio.
Outside a fixed small window it gives an
$O(e^{-c\beta})$ error for fixed box and mass.
Inside, the density is
$e^{-\beta\phi-\Theta-N_f\psi^F}$, where
\[
 \phi(A)=S(e^{iA})+\frac1{2\tau_{\mathrm{gf}}}\|\mathrm d^*A\|^2.
\]
Its Hessian is
$\mathrm d^*\mathrm d+
\tau_{\mathrm{gf}}^{-1}\mathrm d\mathrm d^*$,
positive definite on the box forms.
The determinant logarithm is smooth there.
Lemma~\ref{C-403-31} and
Lemma~\ref{lem:C403-block-determinant}
thus apply, with the same pure-gauge leading
coefficient.

The leading plaquette term is
$a_p^{[2]}=\tfrac12\sum_c(F_p^c)^2$.
For one colour the connected Wick contractions
in
\[
 \left\langle\tfrac12F_p^2;\tfrac12F_q^2;
                                  \tfrac12(A,\Pi A)\right\rangle_0
\]
join one $F_p$ to one $F_q$ in four ways,
and join the other two to the two $A$ factors
in two ways.  There are eight contractions,
each contributing
$C(p,q)(\mathsf Y\Pi\mathsf Y^{\mathsf T})(p,q)$.
The prefactor is $1/8$, and three colours
give the factor three.
The same count on a finite box, with its free
bonds, yields
\begin{align*}
 \beta^3\bigl[
   \langle a_p;a_q\rangle_{n,\beta,m_0}
                         -\beta^{-2}\mathsf B_0^{[n]}(p,q)\bigr]
 ={}&\mathsf B_1^{[n]}(p,q;\tau_{\mathrm{gf}})\\
 &-3N_fC^{[n]}(p,q)
            (\mathsf Y^{[n]}\Pi\mathsf Y^{[n]\mathsf T})(p,q)
       +O(\beta^{-1}).
\end{align*}
The left side is independent of the
gauge-fixing parameter, so take
$\tau_{\mathrm{gf}}=1$.

The pure box kernels, after translating by
$o_n$, converge to their infinite-lattice
kernels, as does the pure coefficient
$\mathsf B_1^{[n]}$ to $\mathsf B_1^{\mathrm{lat}}$.
They obey uniformly
$|\mathsf Y^{[n]}(p+o_n;b+o_n)|
\le c_0\langle x_p-b_-\rangle^{-2}$,
where $\langle z\rangle=\max\{1,|z|\}$;
set the term to zero if a bond is outside
the free bonds of the box.
Together with the polarization decay, this
bounds the double-sum summand by
\[
 c_0^2C_\Pi^{\mathbb Z}
 \langle x_p-b_-\rangle^{-2}
 \langle b_--b'_-\rangle^{-4}
 \langle b'_--x_q\rangle^{-2}.
\]
This majorant is summable.
Indeed, first convolve the last two factors:
their sum is at most
$C\langle b_--x_q\rangle^{-2}
(1+\log\langle b_--x_q\rangle)$,
hence at most
$C\langle b_--x_q\rangle^{-3/2}$.
Its product with the first factor is
summable since $2+3/2>3$.
Dominated convergence proves both absolute
convergence of the infinite-lattice sum and
the asserted outer limit.
Gauge independence follows from the Ward
identity $\Pi\,\mathrm d=0$.

For the block constraint, the independent
slices have curvature covariances
$\mathcal C_{(i+1)}$ in each colour.
Their sum is
$\Pi_0^{\mathrm{tp}}-\Pi_n^{\mathrm{tp}}$,
which is the projection onto $\mathsf{Fl}_n$.
The covariance applied to $\mathrm d^*\delta_p$
is $\mathsf Y^{(n)}(p;\cdot)$.
It belongs to
$T_n=\ker\mathbf Q_n^{\mathrm{lin}}$, and
its coboundary is $C_N^{(n)}(\cdot,p)$.

Every $A\in T_n$ has zero sum in each bond
direction.  To see this, sum
$\mathbf Q_n^{\mathrm{lin}}A
=\mathbf Q_n^{\mathrm s}A-\mathrm d\bar n_nA=0$
over the coarse bonds in that direction.
The coboundary sums to zero, while the
straight-path average sums to
$L^{-2n}\sum_xA_\mu(x)$:
each bare bond belongs to $L^n$ of its
straight paths.
The same Wick calculation therefore gives
the displayed constrained coefficient.
Two potentials with the same curvature
and these zero sums differ by a closed
one-form with zero periods, hence an exact
form.  The constrained Ward identity
annihilates their difference.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[The continuum polarization profile]\label{C-403-12}
Use four-component Dirac matrices
$\gamma_\mu=\sigma_\mu\otimes\tau_3$ and colour
generators with $\operatorname{tr}(\sigma_c\sigma_d)
=2\delta_{cd}$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item The gauge-invariant quadratic part of the
continuum fermion determinant has transverse
kernel $(k^2\delta_{\mu\nu}-k_\mu k_\nu)\Upsilon(k;m)$,
up to a local transverse term
$c(k^2\delta_{\mu\nu}-k_\mu k_\nu)$, where
\begin{align*}
 \Upsilon(k;m)
  &=\frac{N_f}{2\pi}
     \left[\frac{2m}{k^2}
       +\frac{k^2-4m^2}{|k|^3}
                           \arctan\frac{|k|}{2m}\right]\\
  &=\frac{N_f}{2\pi}\int_{2m}^\infty
           \frac{1+4m^2/\mu^2}{\mu^2+k^2}\,d\mu .
\end{align*}
It is positive for $k\ne0$,
$\Upsilon(k;0)=N_f/(4|k|)$, and
$\Upsilon(0;m)=N_f/(3\pi m)$ for $m>0$.
For $m/|k|\to0$,
\[
 \Upsilon(k;m)
 =\frac{N_f}{4|k|}
     -\frac{N_fm^2}{|k|^3}
     +\frac{16N_fm^3}{3\pi|k|^4}
     +O(m^5|k|^{-6}).
\]
\item Set
\[
 \mathcal F(s)=
 \begin{cases}
  [1-(1+s)e^{-2s}]/s,&s>0,\\
  1,&s=0.
 \end{cases}
\]
In the formal continuum perturbative expansion of
the action-density covariance, the term linear in
$N_f$ at order $\mathsf b^{-3}$,
away from coincident points, is
\[
 -\frac{3N_f}{8\pi^3}\mathsf b^{-3}
                         |x|^{-5}\mathcal F(m|x|).
\]
The function $\mathcal F$ decreases from one to zero,
is positive, and satisfies
\[
 \mathcal F(s)=1-\tfrac23s^2+\tfrac23s^3+O(s^4),
 \qquad
 \mathcal F(s)=s^{-1}+O(e^{-2s})\quad(s\to\infty).
\]
At $m=0$ this coefficient is
$-(N_f/4)\mathfrak k|x|^{-5}$, where
$\mathfrak k=3/(2\pi^3)$.
In the same formal expansion, the term quadratic in $N_f$ at order
$\mathsf b^{-4}$ and $m=0$ is
$3(\pi^2+8)N_f^2|x|^{-4}/(256\pi^4)$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The determinant expansion gives
\[
 \Pi_{\mu\nu}(k)
   =-2N_f\int_p
       \operatorname{tr}_4[\gamma_\mu G_m(p)
                                  \gamma_\nu G_m(p+k)].
\]
Traces with three gamma matrices vanish because
$\operatorname{tr}\tau_3=0$, so there is no
parity-odd term. The numerator trace is
\[
 4[-p_\mu(p+k)_\nu-p_\nu(p+k)_\mu
                    +\delta_{\mu\nu}(p\cdot(p+k)+m^2)].
\]
Introduce a Feynman parameter and put
$p=l-xk$, $\Delta=m^2+x(1-x)k^2$.
After angular averaging, the expression inside
the factor four is
\[
 \delta_{\mu\nu}(l^2/3+\Delta)
          +2x(1-x)(k_\mu k_\nu-k^2\delta_{\mu\nu}).
\]
Divided by $(l^2+\Delta)^2$, its first term
is the divergence
$\delta_{\mu\nu}\partial_l\cdot
 [l/(3(l^2+\Delta))]$.
A gauge-invariant regularization removes this
constant; on the lattice it is cancelled by
the tadpole.
Since
$\int_l(l^2+\Delta)^{-2}=(8\pi\sqrt\Delta)^{-1}$,
the remaining term gives
$\Upsilon=(2N_f/\pi)\int_0^1
 x(1-x)(m^2+x(1-x)k^2)^{-1/2}\,dx$.
Elementary integration yields the first formula.
For the second use
\[
 |k|^{-1}\arctan\frac{|k|}{2m}
      =\int_{2m}^\infty\frac{d\mu}{\mu^2+k^2},
 \quad
 \frac{k^2-4m^2}{k^2(\mu^2+k^2)}
   =-\frac{4m^2}{\mu^2k^2}
          +\frac{1+4m^2/\mu^2}{\mu^2+k^2}.
\]
The integral of $4m^2/\mu^2$ is $2m$.
The limits and expansion follow from these
formulas, proving (a).

For (b), write the curvature covariance as
$G=\mathsf b^{-1}G^0-\mathsf b^{-2}G^1
+\mathsf b^{-3}G^2+\cdots$, with
$\hat G^j=(\delta-\hat k\hat k)\Upsilon^j$.
Away from zero, $G^0=\mathbb K_3$.
Wick's formula with three colours gives the
coefficient $-3\operatorname{tr}(\mathbb K_3G^1)$.
The spectral representation reads
\[
 \frac{\Upsilon}{k^2}
   =\frac{N_f}{2\pi}\int_{2m}^\infty
      (1+4m^2/\mu^2)\mu^{-2}
         \left[\frac1{k^2}-\frac1{k^2+\mu^2}\right]d\mu .
\]
The bracket transforms to
$(1-e^{-\mu r})/(4\pi r)$, $r=|x|$.
For $Y=e^{-\mu r}/(4\pi r)$,
\[
 -\Delta Y=-\mu^2Y,\qquad
 \partial_i\partial_jY
  =Y[\hat x_i\hat x_j(\mu^2+3\mu/r+3/r^2)
                    -\delta_{ij}(\mu/r+1/r^2)]
\]
away from zero.
Use
$( -\Delta\delta+\partial\partial)(4\pi r)^{-1}
=\mathbb K_3$,
$\operatorname{tr}\mathbb K_3=0$, and
$\operatorname{tr}(\mathbb K_3\hat x\hat x^{\mathsf T})
=2/(4\pi r^3)$.
The contraction is
\[
 \operatorname{tr}\left[
  \mathbb K_3(-\Delta\delta+\partial\partial)
                   ((4\pi r)^{-1}-Y)\right]
  =\frac6{16\pi^2r^6}\mathsf h(\mu r),
 \quad
 \mathsf h(t)=1-e^{-t}(1+t+t^2/3).
\]
Thus the coefficient is
$-3N_f r^{-5}/(8\pi^3)$ times
\[
 \frac32\int_{2s}^\infty
           (1+4s^2/t^2)t^{-2}\mathsf h(t)\,dt,
 \qquad s=mr.
\]
Primitives for $\mathsf h(t)/t^2$ and
$\mathsf h(t)/t^4$ are
$-(1-e^{-t}(1+t/3))/t$ and
$-(1-e^{-t}(1+t))/(3t^3)$.
The integral before multiplication by $3/2$
is
$2[1-(1+s)e^{-2s}]/(3s)$.
This gives $\mathcal F$.
Since $(s\mathcal F(s))''=-4se^{-2s}\le0$
and $s\mathcal F(s)\to0$ at zero,
$\mathcal F$ is decreasing.
Positivity and the two expansions follow
from its explicit expression.
Its large-mass coefficient equals the first
correction in
$c_2(\mathsf b+N_f/(3\pi m))^{-2}r^{-6}$,
since $2c_2/(3\pi)=3/(8\pi^3)$.

At $m=0$, the transforms of $|k|^{-3}$ and
$|k|^{-4}$, up to the irrelevant constant in
the first, are $-(2\pi^2)^{-1}\log r$ and
$-r/(8\pi)$. Hence
\[
 G^1=\frac{N_f}{4\pi^2r^2}\hat x\hat x^{\mathsf T},
 \qquad
 G^2=\frac{N_f^2}{128\pi r}
                         (\delta+\hat x\hat x^{\mathsf T}).
\]
The coefficient
$\frac32[2\operatorname{tr}(\mathbb K_3G^2)
                 +\operatorname{tr}(G^1G^1)]$
is $3(\pi^2+8)N_f^2r^{-4}/(256\pi^4)$.

These Gaussian expressions give the stated
coefficients of the continuum expansion.
Indeed, a connected graph with $n_x,n_0\ge2$
legs at the two observables, fermion loops
with $j_i$ legs, ghost loops with $g_i$ legs,
and gauge vertices with $v_i\ge3$ legs
has order $\mathsf b^{-e}$, where
\[
 e=\tfrac12(n_x+n_0+\sum_i j_i+\sum_i g_i)
                         +\sum_i(v_i/2-1).
\]
One-legged fermion and ghost loops vanish by
their colour traces. With $l$ fermion loops,
$e\ge2+l$, with equality only for two legs
at each observable, no ghost or gauge vertex,
and two legs at each fermion loop.
The loops then lie in the two gauge lines
joining the observables. For $l=1,2$ these
are precisely the Gaussian insertions computed
above.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[The fermionic coefficient in physical units]
\label{prop:C403-polarization-position}
Let $(f,h)\in\mathfrak T_{\mathbb R^3}(\mathsf d;\vartheta)$,
$8a\le\mathsf d$, and $\mathsf m\ge0$ with
$\mathsf m\mathsf d\le1$.
The fermionic part of the second covariance
coefficient on $a\mathbb Z^3$ satisfies
\begin{align*}
 &a\mathsf b^{-3}\sum_{p,q}
       f(ax(p))h(ax(q))\,N_f\mathsf B_1^F(p,q;a\mathsf m)\\
 &\quad=-\frac{3N_f}{8\pi^3}\mathsf b^{-3}
       \iint f(x)h(y)|x-y|^{-5}
                         \mathcal F(\mathsf m|x-y|)\,dx\,dy
                 +\epsilon_{\mathrm{vp}},
\end{align*}
where $p,q$ and their barycentres $x(p),x(q)$
are in the unit lattice, and $\mathcal F$
is the continuum polarization profile.
More precisely,
\[
 \epsilon_{\mathrm{vp}}
   =-2c_2c^{\mathrm{vp}}N_fa\mathsf b^{-3}
                          \mathcal K_{\mathrm{free}}(f,h)
          +\epsilon'_{\mathrm{vp}},
\]
and both errors obey
\[
 |\epsilon'_{\mathrm{vp}}|,\ |\epsilon_{\mathrm{vp}}|
 \le C_{\mathrm{vp}}\mathsf b^{-3}
          [a\log(\mathsf d/a)+a]\|f\|_\infty\|h\|_\infty.
\]
The constant depends on the lattice fermion
operator, its parameter $r$, $N_f$ and $\vartheta$.
The local polarization constant therefore
changes the coupling label by
$N_fc^{\mathrm{vp}}a$, which tends to zero.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Put $\mathsf r=\mathsf d/a\ge8$ and
$m_0=a\mathsf m\le1/8$.
We use the notation $F,Q,R_2,B^{(1)},B^{(2)}$
from the proof of Lemma~\ref{C-403-36}.
In Feynman gauge write
\[
 \mathsf B_1^F(p,q;m_0)
       =-3\Pi_\infty(p,q)X(p,q),\qquad
 X(p,q)=(\alpha_p,\Pi\alpha_q),\qquad
 \alpha_p=\mathrm d^*\Delta^{-1}\delta_p .
\]
The expression is gauge independent by
Lemma~\ref{lem:C403-fermionic-covariance-coefficient}.
Use the dual direction $\lambda(p)$ of a
plaquette and put its coordinate at its
barycentre.  The orientation signs in the
curvature covariance and $X$ cancel in
their product.
For variables at bond midpoints and
plaquette barycentres, set
\[
 \hat k_\mu=2\sin(k_\mu/2),\qquad
 \widehat{\mathrm d}(k)\alpha=i\hat k\times\alpha,\qquad
 \varpi(k)=\frac{\hat k\hat k^{\mathsf T}}{\hat k^2}.
\]
The matrix $\widehat{\mathrm d}$ is Hermitian,
$\widehat{\mathrm d}\hat k=0$ and
$\widehat{\mathrm d}^{\,2}
=\hat k^2I-\hat k\hat k^{\mathsf T}$.
Thus the symbols of $\Pi_\infty$ and $X$
are $I-\varpi$ and
$\widehat{\mathrm d}\widehat\Pi\widehat{\mathrm d}/\hat k^4$.
The corresponding kernel includes the phase
$e^{ik\cdot(x(p)-x(q))}$; with the midpoint
conventions its integrand is periodic.
Write $\rho=|x(p)-x(q)|$ for $p\ne q$.

\emph{Four derivatives of the remainder.}
Choose a smooth radial $\chi_0$ equal to one
on $|k|\le\delta/8$ and zero on $|k|\ge\delta/4$.
Set
\begin{align*}
 R(k;m_0)
 &=\widehat\Pi(k;m_0)
      -(\hat k^2I-\hat k\hat k^{\mathsf T})
               (c^{\mathrm{vp}}+\chi_0(k)N_f^{-1}\Upsilon(k;m_0)),\\
 \mathsf w(k)
 &=(|k|+m_0)(1+|\log|k||)+\frac{m_0}{|k|+m_0}.
\end{align*}
We claim that for $|\alpha|\le4$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:C403-polarization-derivatives-four}
 |\partial_k^\alpha R(k;m_0)|
 \le C|k|^{2-|\alpha|}\mathsf w(k)
                      \quad(0<|k|\le\delta/8),
\end{equation}
with uniformly bounded derivatives away from
that ball.

First, the spectral integral for $\Upsilon$
gives
\[
 |\partial_k^\alpha\Upsilon(k;m)|
       \le C_\alpha N_f(|k|+m)^{-1-|\alpha|}.
\]
Indeed, the spectral factor $1+4m^2/\mu^2$
is at most two for $\mu\ge2m$ and
$|\partial_k^\alpha(\mu^2+k^2)^{-1}|
\le C_\alpha(\mu^2+k^2)^{-1-|\alpha|/2}$.
Its integral over $[2m,\infty)$ is bounded
by both $C_\alpha|k|^{-1-|\alpha|}$
and $C_\alpha m^{-1-|\alpha|}$.

Away from $k=0$, split the loop integral
into neighbourhoods of $p=\pm k/2$ and
their complement.  In each neighbourhood
use the variable of the singular propagator.
The $k$ derivatives then fall on the
other factors, smooth at a distance bounded
below from their singularity.
The one remaining singular factor is at
most $C|p_\mp|^{-1}$ and is integrable.
The free inverse derivative estimate, analytic
vertices and analytic heavy term give
uniform bounds through order four.
This proves the away-from-zero assertion.

Near zero, the decomposition in the proof
of Lemma~\ref{C-403-36} reads
\[
 R=\mathsf D(c^{\mathrm{vp}}+N_f^{-1}\Upsilon)
       +F+\widetilde Q
       +\tfrac12[\partial_k^2Q(0;m_0)-\partial_k^2Q(0;0)][k,k],
\]
where
$\mathsf D=(k^2I-kk^{\mathsf T})
             -(\hat k^2I-\hat k\hat k^{\mathsf T})$
and
$\widetilde Q=Q-\tfrac12\partial_k^2Q(0;m_0)[k,k]$.
The analytic matrix $\mathsf D$ vanishes to
order four.  The first term therefore has
derivatives bounded by $C|k|^{3-|\alpha|}$.

For $F$, differentiate its symmetrized
$B^{(1)}$ integral also in $m_0$.
Its local singularities have degree at
least $-2$.  At infinity the differentiated
integrand is $O(k^2|p|^{-4})$ at order zero,
$O(|k||p|^{-4})$ at order one in $k$,
and $O(|p|^{-2-|\alpha|})$ thereafter.
The same partition around the two singular
points shows that
$\partial_k^\alpha\partial_{m_0}F$ is
homogeneous of degree $1-|\alpha|$ and
uniformly bounded on $|k|=1$, $0\le m_0\le1$.
Since $F(k;0)=0$, integration in the mass gives
$|\partial_k^\alpha F|\le Cm_0|k|^{1-|\alpha|}$
when $m_0\le|k|$.
When $|k|\le m_0$, use
$F(k;m_0)=m_0^2F(k/m_0;1)$.
The last function is $C^4$ on the unit ball,
vanishes at zero with its first derivative,
and is even.  Hence in this range
$|\partial_k^\alpha F|\le C|k|^{2-|\alpha|}$.
Together,
\[
 |\partial_k^\alpha F(k;m_0)|
       \le C|k|^{2-|\alpha|}\frac{m_0}{|k|+m_0}.
\]

For $\widetilde Q$, extend the propagator
and vertex estimates in that proof to four
derivatives.  The analytic remainders used
there have four bounded derivatives.
For a term of total degree $n\ge0$ in $B^{(2)}$,
the two regions $|p_\mp|\le|k|/4$ and the
remaining part of $|p|\le|k|$ contribute at
most $C|k|^3(|k|+m_0)^{n-4}$ to
$\partial_k^4R_2$.
The region $|k|\le|p|\le2\delta$ contributes
$C\int (|p|+m_0)^{n-4}\,d^3p$.
Derivatives falling on the cutoffs cost at
most $C|k|^{-1}$.
Thus $|\partial_k^4R_2|\le C|k|^{-1}$.
The other terms $R_c,R_1,\Pi^{\mathrm{out}},T$
and the heavy term have bounded fourth
derivatives: their integrands are smooth
on their supports and have integrable
$O(|p|^{-6})$ tails after differentiation.
The constant $\Phi_1(0)$ is independent of $k$.
Together with the third-derivative bound
already proved, this gives
\[
 |\partial_k^\alpha Q(k;m_0)|
       \le C|k|^{3-|\alpha|}(1+|\log|k||),
                      \qquad |\alpha|=3,4.
\]
The function $\widetilde Q$ and its first
two derivatives vanish at zero.
Taylor's formula along the segment to $k$
and
$\int_0^1(1+|\log(t|k|)|)\,dt
\le2(1+|\log|k||)$
give the same estimate for
$\partial_k^\alpha\widetilde Q$ at every
$|\alpha|\le4$.
Finally the coefficients of the last
quadratic term are bounded by
$Cm_0(1+|\log m_0|)
\le2C(|k|+m_0)(1+|\log|k||)$.
These four estimates prove
\eqref{eq:C403-polarization-derivatives-four}.

\emph{Position-space kernels.}
The matrix identity
$\widehat{\mathrm d}
(\hat k^2I-\hat k\hat k^{\mathsf T})
\widehat{\mathrm d}
=\hat k^4(I-\varpi)$ gives
\[
 X=c^{\mathrm{vp}}\Pi_\infty+N_f^{-1}X_\Upsilon+X_R.
\]
The last two kernels have symbols
$\chi_0\Upsilon(I-\varpi)$ and
$\widehat\sigma_R=
\widehat{\mathrm d}R\widehat{\mathrm d}/\hat k^4$.

We use the following shell estimate.
If $\widehat\sigma$ is supported near zero
and
$|\partial^\alpha\widehat\sigma(k)|
\le A|k|^{-|\alpha|}\omega(|k|)$ for
$|\alpha|\le4$, decompose it into shells
$|k|\asymp2^{-j}$.
Four integrations by parts on each shell
bound its kernel by
\[
 CA\sum_{j\ge0}2^{-3j}\omega_j
                         \min\{1,2^{4j}|u|^{-4}\},
\]
where $\omega_j$ is the supremum on the shell.
For $|u|\ge1$, this gives respectively
\begin{align*}
 &CA[|u|^{-4}(1+\log|u|)^2
                     +m_0|u|^{-3}(1+\log|u|)]
       &&\text{if }\omega(t)=(t+m_0)(1+|\log t|),\\
 &CAm_0|u|^{-2}
       &&\text{if }\omega(t)=m_0/(t+m_0),\\
 &CA|u|^{-4}(1+\log|u|)
       &&\text{if }\omega(t)=t.
\end{align*}
For the second estimate use
$m_0/(t+m_0)\le\min\{1,m_0/t\}$.

The lattice curvature kernel satisfies
\[
 |\Pi_\infty(p,q)
       -\mathbb K_3(x(p)-x(q))_{\lambda(p)\lambda(q)}|
 \le C'_{\mathrm{lat}}\rho^{-5},
 \qquad
 \mathbb K_3(u)=\frac{3\hat u\hat u^{\mathsf T}-I}{4\pi|u|^3}.
\]
In particular $|\Pi_\infty(p,q)|\le C\rho^{-3}$.
Let $\mathcal G_1(u;m)$ be the continuum
inverse Fourier transform of
$\Upsilon(k;m)(I-kk^{\mathsf T}/k^2)$.
The same shell argument over all integer
shells, with three integrations by parts
for the kernel and four for its gradient,
gives
\[
 |\mathcal G_1(u;m)|\le CN_f|u|^{-2},\qquad
 |\nabla\mathcal G_1(u;m)|\le CN_f|u|^{-3}.
\]
These are uniform in the mass.
Homogeneity gives
$\mathcal G_1(u;m_0)=a^2\mathcal G_1(au;\mathsf m)$.

The difference between the symbol of
$X_\Upsilon$ and this continuum symbol is
\[
 \chi_0\Upsilon(\varpi^0-\varpi)
       +(\chi_0-1)\Upsilon(I-\varpi^0),
 \qquad \varpi^0=kk^{\mathsf T}/k^2.
\]
Since $\varpi-\varpi^0$ has symbol order two,
the first term has derivatives bounded by
$CN_f|k|^{1-|\alpha|}$.
Its kernel is at most
$CN_f\rho^{-4}(1+\log\rho)$.
The second vanishes near zero and has
four integrable derivatives at infinity,
so its kernel is at most $CN_f\rho^{-4}$.
It follows, for $\rho\ge1$, that
\[
 |X_\Upsilon(p,q)-\mathcal G_1(x(p)-x(q);m_0)_{\lambda(p)\lambda(q)}|
       \le CN_f\rho^{-3},\qquad
 |X_\Upsilon(p,q)|\le CN_f\rho^{-2}.
\]

By \eqref{eq:C403-polarization-derivatives-four},
$|\partial^\alpha\widehat\sigma_R|
\le C|k|^{-|\alpha|}\mathsf w(k)$ near zero.
After removing a smaller ball its derivatives
through order four are bounded; include
the midpoint phase before integration by
parts on the torus, so boundary terms cancel.
The shell bounds give
\begin{align*}
 |X_R(p,q)|
 &\le C[\rho^{-4}(1+\log\rho)^2
       +m_0\rho^{-3}(1+\log\rho)+m_0\rho^{-2}]\\
 &\le C[\rho^{-3}(1+\log\rho)+m_0\rho^{-2}].
\end{align*}

\emph{The plaquette sums.}
There are at most $81\mathsf r^3$ plaquettes
in either source support.
For a contributing pair,
$\mathsf r\le\rho\le10\mathsf r$.
The preceding kernel estimates give, entry
by entry in the two dual directions,
\[
 N_f\Pi_\infty X
 =N_fc^{\mathrm{vp}}\Pi_\infty^2
       +\mathbb K_3\mathcal G_1+\mathsf E+N_f\Pi_\infty X_R,
\]
where
$|\mathsf E|\le CN_f\rho^{-6}$ and
$|N_f\Pi_\infty X_R|
\le CN_f[\rho^{-6}(1+\log\rho)+m_0\rho^{-5}]$.
Thus
\begin{align*}
 &a\mathsf b^{-3}\sum_{p,q}
       f(ax(p))h(ax(q))N_f\mathsf B_1^F(p,q;m_0)\\
 &\qquad=-3N_fc^{\mathrm{vp}}a\mathsf b^{-3}\Sigma_2
          -3a\mathsf b^{-3}\Sigma_F+\mathsf E',
\end{align*}
where $\Sigma_2$ is the sum with kernel
$\Pi_\infty(p,q)^2$, $\Sigma_F$ uses
$(\mathbb K_3)_{\lambda(p)\lambda(q)}
(\mathcal G_1)_{\lambda(p)\lambda(q)}$, and
\[
 |\mathsf E'|\le CN_f\mathsf b^{-3}
       [a+a\log(\mathsf d/a)+a\mathsf m\mathsf d]\mathfrak f.
\]
The last term is at most $a$ by hypothesis.

We spell out the Riemann-sum error.
Suppose on $\mathsf d/2\le|u|\le11\mathsf d$
that $|\kappa(u)|\le A\mathsf d^{-n}$
and $|\nabla\kappa(u)|\le A\mathsf d^{-n-1}$.
For fixed dual directions, the product
cubes of side $a$ about the two barycentres
tile $\mathbb R^6$.  At most
$(2\mathsf r+3)^6$ meet the source support.
On each the function
$f(x)h(y)\kappa(x-y)$ has Lipschitz constant
at most $3A\vartheta^{-1}\mathsf d^{-n-1}\mathfrak f$.
Summing its error from the centre gives
\begin{align*}
 \left|a^6\!\!\sum_{\lambda(p)=\lambda,\lambda(q)=\lambda'}
 f(ax(p))h(ax(q))\kappa(ax(p)-ax(q))
       -\iint f(x)h(y)\kappa(x-y)\,dx\,dy\right|\\
 \le CA\vartheta^{-1}(a/\mathsf d)\mathsf d^{6-n}\mathfrak f .
\end{align*}

For $\Sigma_2$, take $n=6$ and use
$\mathbb K_3(u)=a^3\mathbb K_3(au)$ and
$\operatorname{tr}\mathbb K_3(u)^2
=3/(8\pi^2)|u|^{-6}$.
The lattice-square error is $O(\rho^{-8})$.
Consequently
\[
 \Sigma_2=\frac3{8\pi^2}\mathcal K_{\mathrm{free}}(f,h)
                   +O(\vartheta^{-1}a/\mathsf d+\mathsf r^{-2})\mathfrak f.
\]
Since $3\cdot3/(8\pi^2)=2c_2$, this gives
the stated term containing $c^{\mathrm{vp}}$,
with error at most
$CN_f\vartheta^{-1}(a/\mathsf d)a\mathsf b^{-3}\mathfrak f$.

For $\Sigma_F$, use $n=5$,
$(\mathbb K_3\mathcal G_1)(u;m_0)
=a^5(\mathbb K_3\mathcal G_1)(au;\mathsf m)$
and the continuum identity
\[
 -3\operatorname{tr}(\mathbb K_3\mathcal G_1)(u;\mathsf m)
       =-\frac{3N_f}{8\pi^3}|u|^{-5}\mathcal F(\mathsf m|u|).
\]
The Riemann-sum error is at most
$CN_f\vartheta^{-1}a\mathsf b^{-3}\mathfrak f$.
Adding these errors to $\mathsf E'$ gives
the asserted bound for $\epsilon'_{\mathrm{vp}}$.
The term containing $c^{\mathrm{vp}}$ is itself
at most $Ca\mathsf b^{-3}\mathfrak f$ by the
free-kernel test-pair bound, so the same
form of estimate holds for $\epsilon_{\mathrm{vp}}$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The leading covariance coefficient}

Fix a datum $(g,\ell_G,K,\mathsf b,\mathsf m)$ on the
least torus, with $g\le\gamma_{\mathrm e}$, and
$(f,h)\in\mathfrak T_{T_{\ell_G}}(\mathsf d;\vartheta)$,
where $\vartheta\in(0,1)$ and $8a_K\le\mathsf d\le1$.
Write $\mathfrak f=\|f\|_\infty\|h\|_\infty$.
For $0\le i<K$, let $B_i$ be the unscaled
$\mathfrak{su}(2)$-valued fluctuation on the positively
oriented non-pivot bonds $\mathfrak X_i^+$.
Let $\mu_i$ be the centred Gaussian measure with covariance
$\mathsf t_i^{-1}(\mathsf A_i^{\rm cv})^{-1}\otimes1$,
and let $\chi_i$ be the product of the bond tests at
the calibration $\mathsf t_i$. Put
\[
 \mu_i^\chi=\frac{\chi_i\mu_i}{\int\chi_i\,d\mu_i},
 \qquad \mu=\bigotimes_{i<K}\mu_i,\qquad
 \mu^\chi=\bigotimes_{i<K}\mu_i^\chi.
\]
The curvature response of the $i$th chart is
$\mathsf T_i^{\rm cv}
 =\mathsf H_i^{\rm cv}\mathsf C_{\mathbf1,\mathbb R}$,
acting separately on the three colour components.
At a bare plaquette $p$, set
\[
 \Theta_p=\sum_{i<K}(\mathsf T_i^{\rm cv}B_i)(p),
 \qquad
 \mathcal O^\Theta(u)
   =\frac1{2a_K}\sum_pu(x(p))|\Theta_p|^2.
\]

\begin{proposition}[The coefficient of order four]\label{C-403-55}
Let $\mathsf n_{j,[4]}$ be the coefficient of
$\lambda^4$ in the mixed jet of \cref{C-403-33}.
Then
\begin{enumerate}
\item
\[
 \sum_{j\le K}\mathsf n_{j,[4]}
   =\operatorname{Cov}_{\mu^\chi}
                   (\mathcal O^\Theta(f),\mathcal O^\Theta(h)).
\]
This number depends only on the lattice, $\mathsf b$,
the test pair, and the thresholds
$\delta(\mathsf t_i)=
 A_1\mathsf t_i^{-1/2}(\log\mathsf t_i)^{\mathfrak p_0}$.
It reads the member, $r$, and $N_f$ only through
the previously chosen constants, and is independent of
$m_0,x_i,s_i,b_i$.
\item
\[
 \operatorname{Cov}_{\mu}
                   (\mathcal O^\Theta(f),\mathcal O^\Theta(h))
       =\frac32\mathsf b^{-2}
                    \mathcal K[C^{\rm fl}_{K,0}](f,h).
\]
The difference between this covariance and the tested
covariance in (a) has absolute value at most
$C_\chi\mathsf b^{-2}\mathsf d^3\mathfrak f$.
\item With $C_{\rm ord}=3C_{\rm tm}+C_\chi$ and
$X_g=L(g^{-2}+B_\sharp)\ge\mathsf b$,
\begin{align*}
 \left|\sum_{j\le K}\mathsf n_{j,[4]}
       -c_2\mathsf b^{-2}\mathcal K_{\rm free}(f,h)\right|
 &\le\mathsf b^{-2}
       \left[\frac{3C_{\rm tm}}{2\vartheta}
                      \frac{a_K}{\mathsf d}
                       +C_{\rm ord}\mathsf d^3\right]\mathfrak f\\
 &\le\left[
      C_{\rm ord}X_g\mathsf d^2\,\mathsf b^{-3}\mathsf d
      +\frac{3C_{\rm tm}}{2\vartheta}
                     \mathsf b^{-2}\frac{a_K}{\mathsf d}
          \right]\mathfrak f .
\end{align*}
\item The assertions hold at every lattice translate of
$(f,h)$, with the same constants and the same
$\mathcal K_{\rm free}(f,h)$, hence also after the
translation average of \cref{C-403-30}.
The conditions $\mathsf d\le\mathsf d_{\mathrm e}$ and
$K>s(\mathsf d)$ in \cref{C-403-13} imply
$\mathsf d<1$ and $8a_K\le\mathsf d$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proposition}

Here $C_{\rm tm}$ is the constant of the curvature-template
comparison \cite[Prop.\ 121.2]{YMM1}. The remaining
constants can be chosen explicitly:
\begin{align*}
 C_\chi&=\frac{841}{4}
  \left(12C_\Theta K_{\chi,2}S^{\rm lv}_3
       +18K_{\chi,2}^2(S^{\rm lv}_3)^2
       +9K_{\chi,4}S^{\rm lv}_6\right),\\
 S^{\rm lv}_q&=\sum_{k\ge1}L^{qk}
           e^{-\frac12c_{\rm tl}k^2(\log L)^2},
       \quad q=3,6,\qquad
 c_{\rm tl}=\tfrac12\gamma_{\rm tail}A_1^2,\\
 K_{\chi,2}&=\max\{(C_{\rm tp}^{\rm row})^2C_EK_{\rm cp},
                         \sqrt3\,C_{\rm sm}C_{\rm tp}\},\\
 K_{\chi,4}&=\max\{(C_{\rm tp}^{\rm row})^4C_EK_{\rm cp}^{(4)},
     C_{\rm sm}(\sqrt{105}+6\sqrt3+9C_{\rm sm})C_{\rm tp}^2\},\\
 C_\Theta&=1+3C_{\rm lat}^{\natural}+C_{\rm tp}^{\rm bg},
 \qquad
 C_{\rm sm}=\tau_*^{1/2}(1+\tau_*^{1/2})e^{\tau_*},
 \qquad \tau_*=N_{\mathsf H}^3K_M .
\end{align*}
The constants $C_{\rm tp},C_{\rm tp}^{\rm row},
C_{\rm tp}^{\rm bg}$ are those of the slice estimates
\cite[Prop.\ 120.6]{YMM1}; $C_{\rm lat}^{\natural}$
is the absolute constant in the free-kernel estimate
\cite[(2245)]{YMM1}.
The test-tail rate is $\gamma_{\rm tail}=2(LM)^{-3}$,
$K_M=C_EK'_M$, and $K_{\rm cp}$ is the one-step
tested-covariance constant. The fourth-order constant
$K_{\rm cp}^{(4)}$ is specified below.
Both series converge because their exponents are
quadratic in $k$ with negative leading coefficient.
These constants are chosen after $A_1,K_M,K_{\rm cp}$.
They impose no additional condition on an earlier
constant and are independent of $g,\vartheta,P,K$,
the side, $\mathsf b,\mathsf m$, and the test pair.

\begin{lemma}[One level under its test]\label{C-403-56}
In the setting of \cref{C-403-55}, set
\[
 p_i=\exp[-\tfrac12\gamma_{\rm tail}
                              \mathfrak b(\mathsf t_i)^2].
\]
Uniformly in the torus, the following hold for $0\le i<K$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item Both $\mu_i$ and $\mu_i^\chi$ have zero odd moments.
For non-pivot bonds $b,b'$ and colours $c,c'$,
\[
 \left|\mathsf E_{\mu_i^\chi}B_i^c(b)B_i^{c'}(b')
           -\mathsf E_{\mu_i}B_i^c(b)B_i^{c'}(b')\right|
       \le C_EK_{\rm cp}\mathsf t_i^{-1}p_i.
\]
\item For four bonds and colours, repetitions allowed,
\[
 \left|\kappa^{\mu_i^\chi}
          (B_i^{c_1}(b_1),\ldots,B_i^{c_4}(b_4))\right|
        \le C_EK_{\rm cp}^{(4)}\mathsf t_i^{-2}p_i,
\]
where
\[
 K_{\rm cp}^{(4)}
   =16K_P^\Pi\mathsf C_{\rm ex}((L+2)M)^3
                                e^{4\lambda_1}M^6w_*^{-4}.
\]
The corresponding Gaussian cumulant is zero.
\item If $N_{i+1}^\square$ is the number of cubes at
level $i+1$ and $\tau_i^\chi=N_{i+1}^\square K_Mp_i$,
then
\[
 \int\chi_i\,d\mu_i\ge e^{-\tau_i^\chi}.
\]
Every real polynomial $P$ in $B_i$ satisfies
\[
 |\mathsf E_{\mu_i^\chi}P-\mathsf E_{\mu_i}P|
 \le ((\tau_i^\chi)^{1/2}+\tau_i^\chi)
                   e^{\tau_i^\chi}
                     (\mathsf E_{\mu_i}P^2)^{1/2}.
\]
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
At the trivial pair, $x_i=\mathsf t_i$, and zero
quadratic potential, the one-step tested comparison
has normalized measures $\mu_i^\chi$ and $\mu_i$.
Its unscaled fluctuation is
$B_i=\mathsf t_i^{-1/2}B$.
The Gaussian and the bond tests are even; their
odd moments therefore vanish. The one-step covariance
comparison gives (a), after discarding its exponential
decay factor.

For (b), introduce four distinct complex parameters,
even if some bonds or colours coincide:
\[
 S(\sigma)=\sum_{r=1}^4\sigma_rB_i^{c_r}(b_r).
\]
Place each summand on the cube containing its bond,
or on the two-cube polymer containing its endpoints.
These polymers have size zero. The one-step expansion
admits these complex Borel functions as one quadratic
origin: the name of that class does not require the
function to be quadratic. Since
\[
 |B(b)|\le\tfrac12M^{3/2}(1+M^{-3}|B(b)|^2),
\]
the norm of the $r$th summand is at most
$\tfrac12|\sigma_r|\mathsf t_i^{-1/2}M^{3/2}$.
Thus, on the polydisc
\[
 |\sigma_r|<\rho_0,\qquad
 \rho_0=\tfrac12w_*\mathsf t_i^{1/2}M^{-3/2},
\]
each summand has norm at most $w_*/4$.
There are at most four summands on any polymer,
so their family has norm at most $w_*$.
The expansion applies with this single origin and
with no potential origin.

The difference
\[
 \log\int\chi_i e^{S(\sigma)}d\mu_i
             -\log\int e^{S(\sigma)}d\mu_i
\]
is the sum of the activities marked by a failed
large-field test. Each is holomorphic on the polydisc
and bounded by
\[
 K_P^\Pi p_*e^{-\kappa_+d_{i+1}(X)},\qquad
 p_*=\mathsf C_{\rm ex}((L+2)M)^3e^{4\lambda_1}p_i .
\]
This estimate is independent of the norm of the
origin. The second logarithm is a quadratic polynomial
in $\sigma$, so it has no coefficient of
$\sigma_1\sigma_2\sigma_3\sigma_4$.
That coefficient in the first logarithm is the
fourth cumulant; its normalization contributes
only a constant.

Locality forces a contributing polymer to contain
all four bonds. Cauchy's estimate on radii
$\rho<\rho_0$, followed by $\rho\uparrow\rho_0$,
bounds its coefficient by
\[
 K_P^\Pi p_*\rho_0^{-4}e^{-\kappa_+d_{i+1}(X)},
 \qquad \rho_0^{-4}=16M^6w_*^{-4}\mathsf t_i^{-2}.
\]
Summing polymers containing the cube of $b_1$
costs $C_E$. This gives (b).

At zero potential, the scalar activities of the
test logarithm have norm at most $K_Mp_i$.
Their sum is therefore bounded by
$N_{i+1}^\square K_Mp_i=\tau_i^\chi$.
Consequently
\[
 \int\chi_i\,d\mu_i\ge e^{-\tau_i^\chi},
 \qquad
 \int(1-\chi_i)\,d\mu_i
      \le1-e^{-\tau_i^\chi}\le\tau_i^\chi .
\]
Finally,
\[
 \mathsf E_{\mu_i^\chi}P-\mathsf E_{\mu_i}P
  =\frac{\mathsf E_{\mu_i}[(\chi_i-1)P]
       +\mathsf E_{\mu_i}[P]\int(1-\chi_i)\,d\mu_i}
          {\int\chi_i\,d\mu_i}.
\]
Cauchy--Schwarz and $(1-\chi_i)^2\le1-\chi_i$
bound the first numerator term by
$(\tau_i^\chi)^{1/2}(\mathsf E_{\mu_i}P^2)^{1/2}$.
The second is at most
$\tau_i^\chi(\mathsf E_{\mu_i}P^2)^{1/2}$.
The lower bound for the denominator proves (c).
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of \cref{C-403-55}]
\par\medskip\noindent\emph{The exact covariance at a real field scale.}\quad 
Let $0<\lambda\le1$ and
$w=z_1f+z_2h$ in the source neighbourhood of
\cref{C-403-33-flow}. Evaluate the level-$K$ form
at block field $\mathbf1$ and $\Psi_K=0$.
Its logarithm is the sum of its source energies
and a source-independent number.
Indeed, the gauge action vanishes at $\mathbf1$;
the mass and fermion terms have fermion degree two;
and the scalar value of each remaining activity
has already been removed as its source energy.
By \cref{C-403-44}, its mixed derivative is
$\sum_{j\le K}\mathsf n_j^\lambda$.

The exact chart identity in \cref{C-403-33-flow}
expresses the same form as
\[
 \mathfrak z_\lambda
  \int_{\mathsf{Bx}}\rho^{[\lambda]}(B)
           \exp\left(a_K^{-1}\sum_pw(x(p))
                               a_p(U_\lambda(B))\right)dB,
 \qquad
 \mathsf{Bx}=\prod_{i<K}\{\chi_i=1\}.
\]
Here $U_\lambda(B)$ is the composite chart over
$\mathbf1$ with fluctuations $\lambda B_i$,
and $\mathfrak z_\lambda\ne0$ is independent of $w$.
The density is the product of the Wilson factor
$e^{-\beta A(U_\lambda)/\lambda^2}$,
the gauge fixings and Jacobians, the chart elimination
factors $z_i^{\rm el}$, and the fermion factor.
All depend on $B,\lambda$ but not on $w$.
All density tests equal one on $\mathsf{Bx}$:
the final field $\mathbf1$ passes its test, and
descending through a chart with a passing fluctuation
preserves the density test. The fluctuation
$\lambda B_i$ passes whenever $B_i$ does.

The fermion tower is formed at the single bare
configuration $U=U_\lambda(B)$. Its exact determinant
identity gives
\[
 \mathcal Z_F(U)
 =\prod_{i<K}\theta^{-\dim H_{i+1}}\det\Gamma_i[U]
 =\frac{\det(D[U]+m_0)}{\det\mathbb D_K[U]},
 \qquad \theta=b_F.
\]
For real links it is nonzero because
$\operatorname{Re}\Gamma_i[U]>0$.
The level-$K$ form has the logarithm supplied by
the flow, so its integral at $w=0$ is also nonzero.
Define its normalized weight $\mu^{[\lambda]}$
on $\mathsf{Bx}$ and put
\[
 O^{[\lambda]}(u)
       =a_K^{-1}\sum_pu(x(p))a_p(U_\lambda(B)).
\]
Differentiating the logarithm gives the exact identity
\begin{equation}\label{eq:C403-real-scale-covariance}
 \sum_{j\le K}\mathsf n_j^\lambda
   =\operatorname{Cov}_{\mu^{[\lambda]}}
                 (O^{[\lambda]}(f),O^{[\lambda]}(h)).
\end{equation}

\par\medskip\noindent\emph{The derivative of the composite chart.}\quad 
Let $U_\lambda^{(i)}$ be the level-$i$ background
obtained from the fluctuations $\lambda B_{i'}$,
$i\le i'<K$, over $\mathbf1$.
Thus $U_\lambda^{(K)}=\mathbf1$ and
$U_\lambda^{(0)}=U_\lambda(B)$.
The chart expresses $U_\lambda^{(i)}$ as a gauge
transform of
$e^{i\mathcal A(\lambda B_i;U_\lambda^{(i+1)})}
 U_\lambda^{(i+1)}$.
The shift $\mathcal A$ and the site gauge factor
are holomorphic, and equal $0$ and $\mathbf1$
at zero fluctuation.
If $\mathfrak y_i$ is the first derivative at zero,
the site gauge factor contributes an exact form.
The first derivative of the shift has curvature
$\mathsf T_i^{\rm cv}B_i$. Consequently
\[
 d\mathfrak y_i
    =d\mathfrak y_{i+1}+\mathsf T_i^{\rm cv}B_i,
 \qquad \mathfrak y_K=0,\qquad d\mathfrak y_0=\Theta.
\]
At a plaquette the chart therefore has logarithm
$\lambda\Theta_p+O(\lambda^2)$.
Since $a_p=1-\cos|Y_p|
=\tfrac12|Y_p|^2+O(|Y_p|^4)$,
\[
 \lambda^{-2}O^{[\lambda]}(u)
                    \longrightarrow\mathcal O^\Theta(u).
\]
This convergence is uniform on the closure of
$\mathsf{Bx}$. To see the required uniformity, keep
the finite datum fixed. The zero fluctuation and
trivial pair lie in the interiors of all chart
domains. There are finitely many levels and the
closure of $\mathsf{Bx}$ is compact.
Hence all composed charts are holomorphic for
$|\lambda|<2\lambda_{\rm h}$ with one
datum-dependent $\lambda_{\rm h}>0$, and continuous
on $|\lambda|\le\lambda_{\rm h}$ times that compact
set. Cauchy's formula gives uniform Taylor remainders.

\par\medskip\noindent\emph{The limiting weight.}\quad 
The same argument applies to the gauge fixings,
Jacobian factors, and fermion tower.
The latter is holomorphic near $\mathbf1$, since
its finitely many matrix inverses exist there.
Its value $\mathcal Z_F(\mathbf1)$ is nonzero.
The elimination factor of the $i$th chart tends
uniformly to $L^{9\#\Gamma_{i+1}^{\rm b}}$:
at the trivial field every pivot coefficient is
$L^{-3}\mathrm{id}$.
Writing the gauge-fixing and Jacobian remainders
as $\mathcal V_i^{\rm G},\mathcal V_i^{\rm J}$,
we have, uniformly on this compact set,
\[
 \frac{\beta}{\lambda^2}A(U_\lambda)
                      \longrightarrow\frac\beta2|\Theta|^2,
 \quad
 \hat{\mathsf G}_i\longrightarrow
                 \hat{\mathsf G}_{\mathbf1,\mathbb R}\otimes1,
 \quad
 \mathcal V_i^{\rm G},\mathcal V_i^{\rm J}\longrightarrow0.
\]
The density limit is the product Gaussian $\mu$.
Here is the required orthogonality calculation.
The range of $\mathsf T_i^{\rm cv}$ is the
$i$th curvature slice
$\mathsf{Bg}_i\cap\mathsf{Fl}_{i+1}$.
The background condition follows from the curvature
response. The fluctuation condition follows from
\[
 Q_{i+1}^{\rm pl}\mathsf H_i^{\rm cv}
                \mathsf C_{\mathbf1,\mathbb R}B
 =\mathsf Wd\mathsf C_{\mathbf1,\mathbb R}B
 =d\mathbf Q^s\mathsf C_{\mathbf1,\mathbb R}B
 =d(\mathbf Q^{\rm lin}+d\mathsf k_i)
                    \mathsf C_{\mathbf1,\mathbb R}B=0.
\]
The slices are orthogonal
\cite[Lem.\ 120.1]{YMM1}. With $\eta_i=L^{-i}$,
\[
 |\Theta|^2
   =\sum_{i<K}\eta_i
         (B_i,(\mathsf B_i^{\rm cv}\otimes1)B_i)_1.
\]
Since $\beta\eta_i=\mathsf t_i$ and
$\mathsf A_i^{\rm cv}
 =\mathsf B_i^{\rm cv}+\hat{\mathsf G}_{\mathbf1,\mathbb R}$,
the limiting Wilson and gauge-fixing exponents add to
$\sum_{i<K}\tfrac12\mathsf t_i
 (B_i,(\mathsf A_i^{\rm cv}\otimes1)B_i)_1$.

More explicitly, put
\begin{align*}
 R_\lambda={}&-\frac\beta{\lambda^2}A(U_\lambda)
   +\sum_{i<K}\left(\mathcal V_i^{\rm G}
                      +\mathcal V_i^{\rm J}
       +\tfrac12\mathsf t_i
          (B_i,(\mathsf A_i^{\rm cv}\otimes1-\hat{\mathsf G}_i)B_i)_1
             \right)\\
 &+\sum_{i<K}\log
       \frac{z_i^{\rm el}}{L^{9\#\Gamma_{i+1}^{\rm b}}}
       +\log\frac{\mathcal Z_F(U_\lambda)}
                        {\mathcal Z_F(\mathbf1)}.
\end{align*}
The last logarithm is the branch vanishing at zero.
For sufficiently small $\lambda$ it is defined
uniformly on the compact set. We have
$\sup|R_\lambda|\to0$ and
\[
 \mu^{[\lambda]}
       =\frac{e^{R_\lambda}\mu^\chi}
                          {\int e^{R_\lambda}\,d\mu^\chi}.
\]
Divide \eqref{eq:C403-real-scale-covariance} by
$\lambda^4$. The uniform observable and density
limits identify the limit with the covariance in
(a). The zero coefficients of lower order and
holomorphy in \cref{C-403-33} identify the same
limit with $\sum_j\mathsf n_{j,[4]}$.
Its stated parameter dependence follows directly
from the resulting tested Gaussian formula.

\par\medskip\noindent\emph{Removing the Gaussian tests.}\quad 
The covariance of the $i$th curvature slice is
\[
 \mathsf E_\mu[
  (\mathsf T_i^{\rm cv}B_i)^c(p)
  (\mathsf T_i^{\rm cv}B_i)^{c'}(q)]
 =\delta_{cc'}\mathsf t_i^{-1}L^{-i}
                                  \mathcal C_{(i+1)}(p,q)
 =\delta_{cc'}\beta^{-1}\mathcal C_{(i+1)}(p,q).
\]
The slices are independent and
$\sum_{i<K}\mathcal C_{(i+1)}=C^{\rm fl}_{K,0}$
\cite[(2227)]{YMM1}.
Wick's formula, with three colours, now gives
\[
 \operatorname{Cov}_{\mu}
             (\mathcal O^\Theta(f),\mathcal O^\Theta(h))
 =\frac32a_K^{-2}\beta^{-2}
                 \sum_{p,q}f(x(p))h(x(q))C^{\rm fl}_{K,0}(p,q)^2
 =\frac32\mathsf b^{-2}\mathcal K[C^{\rm fl}_{K,0}](f,h).
\]

For the tested covariance, write
$\Theta_i=\mathsf T_i^{\rm cv}B_i$ and
\[
 \delta S_i^{cc'}(p,q)
      =(\mathsf E_{\mu_i^\chi}-\mathsf E_{\mu_i})
                            [\Theta_i^c(p)\Theta_i^{c'}(q)],
 \qquad \delta S=\sum_i\delta S_i.
\]
Let $\kappa_i$ denote the tested joint cumulant of
$\Theta_i^c(p),\Theta_i^c(p),\Theta_i^{c'}(q),
\Theta_i^{c'}(q)$. Independence between levels
and the zero odd moments give
\begin{align*}
 &\operatorname{Cov}_{\mu^\chi}(\mathcal O^\Theta(f),\mathcal O^\Theta(h))
       -\operatorname{Cov}_{\mu}(\mathcal O^\Theta(f),\mathcal O^\Theta(h))\\
 &=\frac1{4a_K^2}\sum_{p,q}f(x(p))h(x(q))
       \sum_{c,c'}\left[
         \sum_i\kappa_i
       +4\delta_{cc'}\beta^{-1}C^{\rm fl}_{K,0}(p,q)
                                      \delta S^{cc'}(p,q)
       +2(\delta S^{cc'}(p,q))^2\right].
\end{align*}

We estimate these terms separately according to
the side at level $i$.
If $i=0$, or if $\ell_GL^{K-i}\ge N_{\mathsf H}$,
the row bound in \cite[Prop.\ 120.6]{YMM1} is
\[
 \sum_b|\mathsf T_i^{\rm cv}(p,b)|
                         \le C_{\rm tp}^{\rm row}L^{-2i}.
\]
Multilinearity and \cref{C-403-56}(a),(b) imply
\begin{align*}
 |\delta S_i^{cc'}(p,q)|
  &\le(C_{\rm tp}^{\rm row})^2 C_EK_{\rm cp}
                              \beta^{-1}L^{-3i}p_i,\\
 |\kappa_i|
  &\le(C_{\rm tp}^{\rm row})^4 C_EK_{\rm cp}^{(4)}
                              \beta^{-2}L^{-6i}p_i .
\end{align*}

In the remaining case $i\ge1$ and
$N_{i+1}^\square<N_{\mathsf H}^3$.
Thus $\tau_i^\chi\le\tau_*p_i$ and
\[
 \epsilon_i=((\tau_i^\chi)^{1/2}+\tau_i^\chi)e^{\tau_i^\chi}
                         \le C_{\rm sm}\sqrt{p_i}.
\]
For $X=\Theta_i^c(p)$ and $Y=\Theta_i^{c'}(q)$,
the Gaussian slice estimate gives variances at most
$V_i=\beta^{-1}C_{\rm tp}L^{-3i}$.
Wick's formula gives
\[
 \mathsf E_\mu X^4\le3V_i^2,\quad
 \mathsf E_\mu X^2Y^2\le3V_i^2,\quad
 \mathsf E_\mu X^4Y^4\le105V_i^4.
\]
Part (c) of \cref{C-403-56}, first at $XY$
and then at $X^2,Y^2$, yields
\[
 |\delta S_i|\le\sqrt3\,\epsilon_iV_i,\qquad
 \mathsf E_{\mu_i^\chi}X^2
       \le(1+\sqrt3\,\epsilon_i)\mathsf E_{\mu_i}X^2.
\]
Use the identity
\begin{align*}
 \kappa_i={}&(\mathsf E_{\mu_i^\chi}-\mathsf E_{\mu_i})X^2Y^2\\
 &-(\mathsf E_{\mu_i^\chi}X^2\mathsf E_{\mu_i^\chi}Y^2
                       -\mathsf E_{\mu_i}X^2\mathsf E_{\mu_i}Y^2)\\
 &-2((\mathsf E_{\mu_i^\chi}XY)^2-(\mathsf E_{\mu_i}XY)^2).
\end{align*}
The three lines are bounded respectively by
$\sqrt{105}\epsilon_iV_i^2$,
$\sqrt3\,\epsilon_i(2+\sqrt3\,\epsilon_i)V_i^2$,
and $2\sqrt3\,\epsilon_i(2+\sqrt3\,\epsilon_i)V_i^2$.
Both side cases therefore give the uniform bounds
\[
 |\delta S_i|\le K_{\chi,2}\beta^{-1}L^{-3i}\sqrt{p_i},
 \qquad
 |\kappa_i|\le K_{\chi,4}\beta^{-2}L^{-6i}\sqrt{p_i}.
\]

Put $k=K-i\ge1$. Since
$\mathsf t_i=\mathsf bL^k$, $\mathsf b\ge g^{-2}\ge4$,
and $\mathfrak p_0\ge1$,
\[
 \sqrt{p_i}
       \le e^{-\frac12c_{\rm tl}k^2(\log L)^2}.
\]
Hence
\[
 \sum_{i<K}L^{-3i}\sqrt{p_i}\le a_K^3S^{\rm lv}_3,
 \qquad
 \sum_{i<K}L^{-6i}\sqrt{p_i}\le a_K^6S^{\rm lv}_6.
\]
On the supports of $f,h$, the physical separation
is at least $\mathsf d$. The free-kernel and background
estimates, with the slice telescope, give
\[
 |C^{\rm fl}_{K,0}(p,q)|
                    \le C_\Theta a_K^3\mathsf d^{-3}.
\]
Each support contains at most
$3(2\mathsf d/a_K+1)^3
 \le29(\mathsf d/a_K)^3$ plaquette barycentres:
there are three translates of a lattice of spacing
$a_K$, and $8a_K\le\mathsf d$.
Substitution into the covariance difference gives
\begin{align*}
 |\operatorname{Cov}_{\mu^\chi}-\operatorname{Cov}_{\mu}|
 &\le\frac{841}{4}a_K^{-2}(\mathsf d/a_K)^6
          \mathfrak f\,\beta^{-2}a_K^6\\
 &\quad\cdot
   [9K_{\chi,4}S^{\rm lv}_6
       +12C_\Theta K_{\chi,2}S^{\rm lv}_3\mathsf d^{-3}
       +18K_{\chi,2}^2(S^{\rm lv}_3)^2]\\
 &\le C_\chi\mathsf b^{-2}\mathsf d^3\mathfrak f .
\end{align*}
In the last step use $a_K\beta=\mathsf b$ and
$\mathsf d\le1$. This proves (b).

\par\medskip\noindent\emph{The continuum template.}\quad 
Apply \cite[Prop.\ 121.2]{YMM1} to the fluctuation
template with $n=K$ and $a_{K-n}=1\ge\mathsf d$.
The hypotheses are $8a_K\le\mathsf d$,
$20\mathsf d\le\ell_G$, and the prescribed test-pair
condition, all of which hold on the least torus.
It gives
\[
 \left|\mathcal K[C^{\rm fl}_{K,0}](f,h)
           -\frac3{8\pi^2}\mathcal K_{\rm free}(f,h)\right|
 \le C_{\rm tm}
     \left[\frac{a_K}{\vartheta\mathsf d}
                   +(\mathsf d/\ell_G)^3+\mathsf d^3\right]\mathfrak f
 \le C_{\rm tm}
      \left[\frac{a_K}{\vartheta\mathsf d}+2\mathsf d^3\right]\mathfrak f .
\]
Combine this with (a),(b) and
$c_2=\frac32\frac3{8\pi^2}$.
The second bound in (c) uses
$\mathsf b^{-2}\mathsf d^3
 \le X_g\mathsf d^2\mathsf b^{-3}\mathsf d$.

All hypotheses and estimates are invariant under
lattice translations. The continuum template is
translation invariant as well, proving (d)'s first
assertion. At the data of \cref{C-403-13},
$\mathsf d\le\mathsf d_{\mathrm e}
\le\mathsf d_0(g,\vartheta)\le1/200$.
The definition of the stopping scale gives
\[
 \mathsf d=\check{\mathsf d}\,
          L^{K-s(\mathsf d)}a_K,\qquad
 \check{\mathsf d}>4L^2M.
\]
Since $K>s(\mathsf d)$, this implies
$\mathsf d>4L^3Ma_K\ge8a_K$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The block constraint and the fermion loop}

All quantities in this subsection are in bare lattice
units. We compare the operator under a flat block
constraint with the infinite-lattice operator at the
same bare mass. The first step is to compute the
two derivatives of the composite fermion average.

\begin{lemma}[The composite average and its current]
\label{C-403-57}
Let $n\ge1$, on $\mathbb Z^3$ or on the bare torus
at cutoff $K\ge n$. For a bare site $x$, let
$y_0(x)=x$, and let $y_{m+1}(x)$ be the site whose
level-$(m+1)$ block contains $y_m(x)$.
For a bond $b$, let $m_x(b)$ be the least $m\ge0$
such that both endpoints of $b$ lie in
$B^{m+1}(y_{m+1}(x))$. Set $m_x(b)=\infty$ if there
is no such level, considering only levels at most
$K$ on a torus, and set $L^{-\infty}=0$.
Write $|x-b|=|x-b_-|_\infty$.

Let $a$ be a real one-form and $U=e^{ia\sigma_3}$.
For $w$ at level $m+1$ and $z\in B(w)$, denote by
$\bar s_m(w,z)$ and $\mathrm{Var}_m(w,z)$ the mean
and variance of $(\mathbf Q_m^sa)(\Gamma)$ over
$\Gamma\in\mathcal G(w,z)$. Put
$\kappa_m(w)=L^{-3}\sum_{z\in B(w)}\bar s_m(w,z)$.
Then the following hold.
\begin{enumerate}
\item The matrix $R_n(U)$ is diagonal in the
eigenbasis of $\sigma_3$. For $x\in B^n(y)$ its
entries at eigenvalues $1$ and $-1$ are
$L^{-3n/2}\upsilon_x\iota^*$ and
$L^{-3n/2}\bar\upsilon_x\iota^*$, respectively.
The function $\upsilon_x$ is real analytic near
$a=0$, and, for $x,x'\in B^n(y)$,
\begin{align*}
 \bar\upsilon_x\upsilon_{x'}
   ={}&1+i(\tilde\phi(x')-\tilde\phi(x))
           +\mathsf p(x)+\mathsf p(x')\\
     &-\tfrac12(\tilde\phi(x')-\tilde\phi(x))^2
           +O(|a|^3),
\end{align*}
where
\begin{align*}
 \tilde\phi(x)
   &=\sum_{m<n}
      [\bar s_m(y_{m+1}(x),y_m(x))-\kappa_m(y_{m+1}(x))]
       =\sum_bJ_x(b)a(b),\\
 \mathsf p(x)
   &=-\frac12\sum_{m<n}
       \left[\mathrm{Var}_m(y_{m+1}(x),y_m(x))
        -L^{-3}\sum_{z\in B(y_{m+1}(x))}
                          \mathrm{Var}_m(y_{m+1}(x),z)\right]\\
   &=\sum_{b,b'}\mathsf p_x(b,b')a(b)a(b').
\end{align*}
The phase of $\upsilon_x$ is
$\bar n_n(y)+\tilde\phi(x)+O(|a|^3)$, where
$\bar n_n$ is linear in $a$ and constant within
each level-$n$ block.
\item With $C_J=20L^2$,
\begin{align*}
 |J_x(b)|
   &\le5L^{-2m_x(b)}
       \le C_J(1+|x-b|)^{-2},\\
 |\mathsf p_x(b,b')|
   &\le9L^{-4\max\{m_x(b),m_x(b')\}}\\
   &\le C_J^2(1+|x-b|)^{-2}(1+|x-b'|)^{-2}.
\end{align*}
These coefficients vanish unless both endpoints
of each displayed bond lie in $B^n(y_n(x))$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Constant gauge transformations $e^{i\theta\sigma_3}$
fix $U$, so gauge covariance shows that they fix
$\mathcal M^mU$. Near the identity it therefore
has the form $e^{ia_m\sigma_3}$.
Conjugation by $i\sigma_1$ replaces $a$ by $-a$,
so $a_m$ is odd. Analyticity and the derivative of
the block average give
$a_m=\mathbf Q_m^{\rm lin}a+O(|a|^3)$.
At one step,
$\mathbf Q^{\rm lin}=\mathbf Q^s-d\mathsf k$ and
$\mathbf Q^{\rm lin}d\theta=d(\theta|)$.
Since $\mathbf Q_{m+1}^s=\mathbf Q^s\mathbf Q_m^s$,
induction yields
\[
 \mathbf Q_m^{\rm lin}
       =\mathbf Q_m^s-d\bar n_m,\qquad
 \bar n_0=0,\qquad
 \bar n_{m+1}
       =\mathsf k_m\mathbf Q_m^s+\bar n_m|_{m+1}.
\]
Here $\mathsf k_m\mathbf Q_m^sa=\kappa_m$.

For one step at $V=e^{ia_m\sigma_3}$, let
$\bar a$ and $\mathrm{var}$ be the path mean and
variance of $a_m(\Gamma)$. The eigenvalue-$1$
entry of its transport average $S(V;w,z)$ is
\[
 e^{i\bar a}(1-\tfrac12\mathrm{var}+O(|a|^3)).
\]
Its determinant is $1-\mathrm{var}+O(|a|^4)$;
the normalization has square
$1-L^{-3}\sum_{z\in B(w)}\mathrm{var}(w,z)+O(|a|^4)$.
The other eigenvalue gives the complex conjugate.
Along a path from $w$ to $z$,
\[
 (\mathbf Q_m^{\rm lin}a)(\Gamma)
   =(\mathbf Q_m^sa)(\Gamma)-\bar n_m(z)+\bar n_m(w).
\]
The last two terms are path independent. Thus
$\mathrm{var}=\mathrm{Var}_m(w,z)+O(|a|^4)$ and
$\bar a=\bar s_m(w,z)-\bar n_m(z)+\bar n_m(w)
 +O(|a|^3)$.

The composite average is the product of these
normalized one-step entries:
\[
 R_n(U)(y,x)
    =L^{-3n/2}\prod_{m<n}
       q(\mathcal M^mU;y_{m+1}(x),y_m(x))\,\iota^*.
\]
Its eigenvalue-$1$ entry consequently has the form
$\upsilon_x=e^{i\phi_1(x)}(1+\mathsf p(x))+O(|a|^3)$,
where
\[
 \phi_1(x)
  =\sum_{m<n}[\bar s_m(y_{m+1},y_m)
                    -\bar n_m(y_m)+\bar n_m(y_{m+1})].
\]
Substitute
$\bar n_m(y_{m+1})
 =\bar n_{m+1}(y_{m+1})-\kappa_m(y_{m+1})$.
The sum telescopes to
$\phi_1(x)=\bar n_n(y)+\tilde\phi(x)$.
For $x,x'$ in the same block the first term
cancels. Expanding
$e^{i(\phi_1(x')-\phi_1(x))}
 (1+\mathsf p(x))(1+\mathsf p(x'))$
proves (a).

For (b), a bare bond has coefficient at most
$L^{-3m}L^m=L^{-2m}$ in the straight average
of a level-$m$ bond. It can occur only if the
block containing its base point is incident to
that level-$m$ bond. A shortest contour inside
$B(w)$ has at most two bonds incident to that
site. The coefficients of a bare bond in
$\bar s_m$, in $\kappa_m$, and in the difference
of two contour sums are therefore at most
$2L^{-2m}$, $2L^{-2m}$, and $4L^{-2m}$.
They vanish unless both endpoints lie in
$B^{m+1}(w)$.
The $m$th contribution to $J_x(b)$ is thus at
most $4L^{-2m}$ and vanishes for $m<m_x(b)$.
Since $L\ge13$,
\[
 |J_x(b)|\le\frac{4L^{-2m_x(b)}}{1-L^{-2}}
                                  \le5L^{-2m_x(b)}.
\]

The variance is the mean, over pairs of paths,
of half the square of their difference.
Its quadratic kernel is at most $8L^{-4m}$.
The $m$th contribution to $\mathsf p_x(b,b')$
obeys the same bound and vanishes below
$\bar m=\max\{m_x(b),m_x(b')\}$. Hence
\[
 |\mathsf p_x(b,b')|
       \le\frac{8L^{-4\bar m}}{1-L^{-4}}
       \le9L^{-4\bar m}
       \le9L^{-2m_x(b)}L^{-2m_x(b')}.
\]
If $m_x(b)<\infty$, $x$ and $b$ lie in a cube
of side $L^{m_x(b)+1}$. Thus
$L^{-2m_x(b)}
 \le4L^2(1+|x-b|)^{-2}$.
Finally $m_x(b)\le n-1$ exactly when the endpoints
of $b$ lie in $B^n(y_n(x))$. This proves the
support assertion and both spatial bounds.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[The fermion operator under a flat block constraint]
\label{C-403-58}
There is $C_\Pi$, depending only on the member,
$r,L,b_F$, with the following properties for $n\ge1$.
Part (a) holds for $m_0>0$, and (b)--(d) for
$0\le m_0\le L^{-n}$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item On the history with no large-field region,
at cutoff $K\ge n$ and every $\mathrm{SU}(2)$
configuration,
\[
 \prod_{i<n}\theta^{-\dim H_{i+1}}\det\Gamma_i[U]
    =\theta_n^{-\dim H_n}\det\mathcal K_n[U;m_0],
 \qquad \theta=b_F,\quad \theta_n=L^n\mathfrak a_n.
\]
The prefactor is independent of $U$.
\item On one colour and one flavour in the range
of $e_+$, put $\mathcal K=\mathcal K_n[\mathbf1;m_0]$.
Let $\mathbb V_j^{\rm D}$ be the term of order
$j$ in $a$ in $D_+[e^{ia}]$. Write
$1_{\rm bl}(x,x')$ for the indicator that $x,x'$
belong to one level-$n$ block, and set
\begin{align*}
 \mathbb V_1^{\rm R}(x,x')
 &=i\mathfrak a_nL^{-3n}1_{\rm bl}(x,x')
          (\tilde\phi(x')-\tilde\phi(x))\iota\iota^*,\\
 \mathbb V_2^{\rm R}(x,x')
 &=\mathfrak a_nL^{-3n}1_{\rm bl}(x,x')
       [\mathsf p(x)+\mathsf p(x')
           -\tfrac12(\tilde\phi(x')-\tilde\phi(x))^2]\iota\iota^*,
 \qquad
 \mathbb V_j=\mathbb V_j^{\rm D}+\mathbb V_j^{\rm R}.
\end{align*}
On a torus, $\Pi^{(\le n)}$ is eight times the
real part of the kernel of
\[
 \tfrac12\operatorname{Tr}
       [\mathcal K^{-1}\mathbb V_1\mathcal K^{-1}\mathbb V_1]
            -\operatorname{Tr}[\mathcal K^{-1}\mathbb V_2].
\]
This formula defines $\Pi^{(\le n)}$ on $\mathbb Z^3$.
The unconstrained $\Pi$ is given by the same
formula with $\mathcal K^{-1}$ replaced by $G_1$
and $\mathbb V_j$ by $\mathbb V_j^{\rm D}$.
\item On $\mathbb Z^3$, with $|b-b'|$ the
distance between bond base points,
\begin{align*}
 |\Pi(b,b')-\Pi^{(\le n)}(b,b')|
 &\le C_\Pi(L^n+|b-b'|)^{-2}(1+|b-b'|)^{-2},\\
 |\Pi^{(\le n)}(b,b')|
 &\le C_\Pi(1+|b-b'|)^{-4}
                   e^{-\delta_f|b-b'|/(2L^n)},\\
 |\Pi(b,b')|&\le C_\Pi(1+|b-b'|)^{-4}.
\end{align*}
Both kernels annihilate $d\chi$ for bounded
$\chi$ and annihilate constant one-forms.
The kernel $\Pi$ is translation invariant,
and $\Pi^{(\le n)}$ is invariant under
$L^n\mathbb Z^3$.
With $b=\langle x,x+e_\mu\rangle$ and
$b'=\langle x+u,x+u+e_\nu\rangle$,
\[
 \Pi_{\mu\nu}(u)=\Pi_{\mu\nu}(e_\mu-e_\nu-u),
 \quad
 \sum_u\Pi_{\mu\nu}(u)=0,\qquad
 |\hat\Pi_{\mu\nu}(k)|\le C_\Pi|k|,
 \quad k\in[-\pi,\pi]^3 .
\]
\item On a bare torus of side
$N=\ell L^K\ge16L^n$,
\[
 \Pi_N^{(\le n)}(b,b')
  =\sum_{z\in N\mathbb Z^3}
      \Pi^{(\le n)}(\tilde b,\tilde b'+z)
          +\mathcal E_N(b,b'),
 \qquad
 |\mathcal E_N(b,b')|
        \le C_\Pi L^{4n}e^{-\delta_fN/(2L^n)}.
\]
Here $\tilde b,\tilde b'$ are lifts to $\mathbb Z^3$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
\par\medskip\noindent\emph{The determinant identity.}\quad 
The empty history has
$\mathcal K_n=D[U]+m_0+\mathfrak a_nR_n^*R_n$.
The exact Schur-complement identities of the
fermion tower give
$\Gamma_0=\mathcal K_1$ and
$\det\Gamma_j=\det c_j\det\mathcal K_{j+1}/\det\mathcal K_j$.
They hold at every real configuration when
$m_0>0$, where all the inverses exist.
The determinant product thus telescopes to
$\det\mathcal K_n\prod_{1\le j<n}\det c_j$.

The operator $P=Lq_{j+1}^+q_{j+1}$ is idempotent,
with rank $\dim H_{j+1}$, and
\[
 c_j=\theta_j(1-P)+(\theta_j+\theta/L)P.
\]
It follows that
$\det c_j=\theta_j^{\dim H_j-\dim H_{j+1}}
 (\theta_j+\theta/L)^{\dim H_{j+1}}$
is field independent.
For $n=1$, the normalized product is
$\theta^{-\dim H_1}=\theta_1^{-\dim H_1}$.
The recursion
$\theta_{n+1}^{-1}
 =\theta^{-1}+(L\theta_n)^{-1}$
implies $\theta_n+\theta/L=\theta\theta_n/\theta_{n+1}$.
Multiplying the $n$th prefactor by
$\theta^{-\dim H_{n+1}}\det c_n$
therefore gives $\theta_{n+1}^{-\dim H_{n+1}}$.
This proves (a).

\par\medskip\noindent\emph{The quadratic determinant.}\quad 
At $A=a\sigma_3$, both $D_+[U]$ and $R_n(U)$
are diagonal in colour, and their two colour
blocks are obtained by replacing $a$ with $-a$.
If $\ell(a)$ is the logarithm of the determinant
of the eigenvalue-$1$ block, the two-colour
logarithm is $\ell(a)+\ell(-a)$.
The determinant convention in
\cref{lem:C403-block-determinant} gives
\[
 \tfrac12(a,\Pi^{(\le n)}a)
                      =-4\operatorname{Re}\ell_2(a).
\]
By \cref{C-403-57}, the first two terms of
$\mathfrak a_nR_n^*R_n$ are precisely the
displayed $\mathbb V_1^{\rm R},\mathbb V_2^{\rm R}$.
The logarithmic determinant expansion is
\[
 \ell_2
  =\operatorname{Tr}[\mathcal K^{-1}\mathbb V_2]
      -\tfrac12\operatorname{Tr}
                    [\mathcal K^{-1}\mathbb V_1
                     \mathcal K^{-1}\mathbb V_1].
\]
This proves (b), including its factor eight.
Removing the block term gives the formula for $\Pi$.

\par\medskip\noindent\emph{Comparison of the propagators.}\quad 
Put $G=G_1$ on one colour block. The resolvent
identity gives
\[
 \delta G=G-\mathcal K^{-1}
     =G\,\mathfrak a_nL^{-3n}
                         \iota1_{\rm bl}\iota^*\mathcal K^{-1}.
\]
The elementary and constrained inverse estimates give
\[
 |G(v,v')|\le C_{\rm el}(1+|x_v-x_{v'}|)^{-2},\quad
 |\mathcal K^{-1}(v,v')|
 \le C_{\rm fr}(1+|x_v-x_{v'}|)^{-2}
                         e^{-\delta_f|x_v-x_{v'}|/L^n}.
\]
They apply also at $m_0=0$ under the block
constraint. For a level-$n$ block $B$,
\[
 \sum_{z\in B}(1+|u-z|)^{-2}
       \le CL^{3n}(L^n+\operatorname{dist}(u,B))^{-2}.
\]
There are $O(1+t^2)$ blocks at distances between
$tL^n$ and $(t+1)L^n$ from a point.
Using $\mathfrak a_n\le b_FL^{-n}$ in the
resolvent identity yields
\begin{align*}
 |\delta G(v,v')|
 &\le Cb_FL^{2n}\sum_B
       (L^n+\operatorname{dist}(x_v,B))^{-2}
       (L^n+\operatorname{dist}(B,x_{v'}))^{-2}
                        e^{-\delta_f\operatorname{dist}(B,x_{v'})/L^n}\\
 &\le C(L^n+|x_v-x_{v'}|)^{-2}.
\end{align*}

The quadratic form for $\Pi-\Pi^{(\le n)}$
is eight times the real part of
$\Theta_1+\cdots+\Theta_5$, where
\begin{align*}
 \Theta_1&=\tfrac12\operatorname{Tr}
                  [\delta G\mathbb V_1^{\rm D}G\mathbb V_1^{\rm D}]
          +\tfrac12\operatorname{Tr}
                  [\mathcal K^{-1}\mathbb V_1^{\rm D}
                                      \delta G\mathbb V_1^{\rm D}],\\
 \Theta_2&=-\operatorname{Tr}[\delta G\mathbb V_2^{\rm D}],\\
 \Theta_3&=-\operatorname{Tr}
             [\mathcal K^{-1}\mathbb V_1^{\rm R}
                         \mathcal K^{-1}\mathbb V_1^{\rm D}],\\
 \Theta_4&=-\tfrac12\operatorname{Tr}
             [\mathcal K^{-1}\mathbb V_1^{\rm R}
                         \mathcal K^{-1}\mathbb V_1^{\rm R}],\\
 \Theta_5&=\operatorname{Tr}[\mathcal K^{-1}\mathbb V_2^{\rm R}].
\end{align*}
The $D_+$ vertex at $b$ acts only over its
endpoints and has norm at most
$c_{\rm hop}=3(1+r)$.
An average vertex at $b$ is supported on the
block $B_b$ containing it and carries the
currents and quadratic kernels of \cref{C-403-57}.
Writing $x=b-b'$, the first two terms satisfy
\[
 |\Theta_1(b,b')|
    \le C(L^n+|x|)^{-2}(1+|x|)^{-2},\qquad
 \Theta_2(b,b')=0\ (b\ne b'),\qquad
 |\Theta_2(b,b)|\le CL^{-2n}.
\]
For the mixed term use
\[
 \sum_{u\in B_b}(1+|b'-u|)^{-2}(1+|u-b|)^{-2}
                         \le C(1+|x|)^{-1},
 \qquad
 \sum_{u\in B}|\mathcal K^{-1}(u,v)|\le CL^n.
\]
They give
\[
 |\Theta_3(b,b')|
    \le CL^{-3n}(1+|x|)^{-1}
                         e^{-\delta_f(|x|-2L^n)_+/L^n}.
\]

Each vertex in $\Theta_4$ is a difference of
currents at its two endpoints.
When two currents are joined by a propagator,
the corresponding term is bounded by
\begin{align*}
 &CL^{-8n}L^{4n}C_J^2
       \sum_{u,u'}(1+|u-b|)^{-2}
                   (1+|u-u'|)^{-2}(1+|u'-b'|)^{-2}\\
 &\hspace{25mm}\le
        CL^{-4n}\left(1+\log^+
                          \frac{L^n}{1+|x|}\right).
\end{align*}
The other terms are at most
$CL^{-8n}(C_JL^n)^2(CL^n)^2$.
All carry the factor
$e^{-\delta_f\operatorname{dist}(B_b,B_{b'})/L^n}$.
Finally $\Theta_5$ vanishes unless $B_b=B_{b'}$.
In that case
$\sum_u|\mathsf p_u(b,b')|
 \le CC_J^2(1+|x|)^{-1}$,
and the current products obey the same bound,
so $|\Theta_5|\le CL^{-3n}(1+|x|)^{-1}$.

For $|x|\le L^n$, these estimates are bounded
by $CL^{-2n}(1+|x|)^{-2}$.
For the logarithm, use
$s^2(1+\log(1/s))\le1$ for $0<s\le1$,
with $s=(1+|x|)/L^n$; the short transition
interval is absorbed into the same constant.
For $|x|>L^n$, exponential decay and the
boundedness of $t^4e^{-\delta_ft}$ give
$C|x|^{-4}$. This proves the difference estimate.
Applying the same estimates with constrained
propagators throughout retains
$e^{-\delta_f|x|/(2L^n)}$ and gives the bound
for $\Pi^{(\le n)}$. The elementary inverse
estimate gives the stated bound for $\Pi$.

\par\medskip\noindent\emph{Gauge identities and symmetries.}\quad 
For finitely supported $\chi$, gauge covariance
gives first derivative $-i[\chi,\mathcal K]$
at $d\chi$ and mixed derivative
$-i[\chi,\mathbb V_1(a)]$ at $(a,d\chi)$.
Substitution into the trace formula and cyclicity
cancel the bilinear form at $(a,d\chi)$.
The same argument applies with $G^{-1}$.
The sums are justified by finite support and
the kernel bounds just proved.

To extend to bounded $\chi$, cut it off by
$\eta_R(y)=\eta(y/R)$, equal to one for
$|y|\le R$ and zero for $|y|\ge2R$.
At finitely supported $a$, the error is at most
\[
 CR^{-2}\sup_{R\le|y|\le2R}|\chi(y)|
                 +CR^{-1}\sup|d\chi|.
\]
This tends to zero both for bounded $\chi$
and for $\chi(y)=\mathsf c\cdot y$.
The latter proves annihilation of constant
one-forms, hence zero sums in each direction.

The block operators, contour families, and their
derivatives commute with translations in
$L^n\mathbb Z^3$. Thus
$J_{u+z}(b+z)=J_u(b)$ and the corresponding identity
holds for $\mathsf p_u$, proving the claimed
translation covariance of $\Pi^{(\le n)}$.
Without the block term there is full translation
invariance. Point reflection exchanges $e_+$ and
$e_-$, whose determinants are complex conjugates.
The real fermion action is invariant under it.
Keeping the orientations of the reflected bonds
gives
$\Pi_{\mu\nu}(u)=\Pi_{\mu\nu}(e_\mu-e_\nu-u)$.
With $c=(e_\mu-e_\nu)/2$, the zero sum implies
\[
 e^{-ik\cdot c}\hat\Pi_{\mu\nu}(k)
   =\sum_u\Pi_{\mu\nu}(u)
                  [\cos(k\cdot(u-c))-1].
\]
Its absolute value is at most
$\sum_u|\Pi_{\mu\nu}(u)|
       \min\{|k|^2|u-c|^2,2\}\le C|k|$.
This finishes (c).

\par\medskip\noindent\emph{The torus comparison.}\quad 
The constrained inverse on antiperiodic sections
is the signed image sum of its infinite-lattice
kernel. The averages and their derivatives are
block local and agree on the two lattices.
In a trace with two propagators, the terms whose
image displacements add to zero have sign one,
since the signs form a character. They give the
periodized infinite-lattice loop. In a trace with
one propagator the vertex lies in one block;
only its zero image does not wind, and, since
$N\ge16L^n$, only one periodized vertex contributes.

Every remaining term winds. Its propagators have
total length $l\ge N-4L^n\ge3N/4$.
Split their exponential factor as
\[
 e^{-\delta_fl/L^n}
       \le e^{-\delta_fN/(2L^n)}
                         e^{-\delta_fl/(3L^n)}.
\]
The remaining image sums are bounded uniformly
because $N\ge16L^n$.
At most four block point sums cost $L^{12n}$.
Two average vertices contribute
$\mathfrak a_n^2L^{-6n}\le b_F^2L^{-8n}$;
their currents and quadratic kernels are bounded
by $5$ and $9$.
Thus these terms cost at most $CL^{4n}$,
and terms with fewer average vertices cost less.
The bound in (d) follows.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Curvature covariances under a flat block constraint]
\label{C-403-59}
Let $n\ge1$ and $c_g=\delta_{\rm tp}L/4$,
with the slice constants of
\cite[Prop.\ 120.6]{YMM1} chosen as functions of $L$.
There is $C_g$, depending only on $L$, such that
the following hold. Distances between plaquettes
are distances between their barycentres.
\begin{enumerate}
\item On a bare torus $\Lambda_N$ at cutoff
$K\ge n$, put
\[
 C_N^{(n)}=\Pi_0^{\rm tp}-\Pi_n^{\rm tp}
             =\sum_{j\le n}\mathcal C_{(j)},\qquad
 S_N^{(n)}=\Pi_n^{\rm tp}.
\]
The first is the orthogonal projection onto
$\mathsf{Fl}_n$, and
\[
 |C_N^{(n)}(p,q)|
       \le C_g(1+|p-q|)^{-3}e^{-c_g|p-q|/L^n},
 \qquad
 |S_N^{(n)}(p,q)|\le C_{\rm tp}L^{-3n}.
\]
\item On tori of bare sides $N_s=L^sN$,
the kernels $C_{N_s}^{(n)}$ and $\Pi_0^{\rm tp}$
converge pointwise to $C_\infty^{(n)}$ and
$\Pi_{0,\infty}^{\rm tp}$.
The latter is the orthogonal projection onto
closed two-forms in $\ell^2(\mathbb Z^3)$ and
has bound $C_g(1+|p-q|)^{-3}$.
The former obeys (a), is invariant under
$L^n\mathbb Z^3$, and satisfies
\[
 C_N^{(n)}(p,q)
     =\sum_{z\in N\mathbb Z^3}
                C_\infty^{(n)}(\tilde p,\tilde q+z).
\]
The kernel
$S_\infty^{(n)}=\Pi_{0,\infty}^{\rm tp}-C_\infty^{(n)}$
satisfies
$|S_\infty^{(n)}(p,q)|\le C_g(L^n+|p-q|)^{-3}$.
The columns of both kernels are closed.
\item Let $\mathsf g=d^*\Delta^{-1}$ on
two-forms of $\mathbb Z^3$, and set
\[
 \alpha_p=\mathsf g\delta_p,\qquad
 \beta_p=\mathsf gS_\infty^{(n)}(\cdot,p),\qquad
 \alpha_p^{(n)}=\alpha_p-\beta_p .
\]
Then $d\alpha_p=\Pi_{0,\infty}^{\rm tp}(\cdot,p)$
and $d\alpha_p^{(n)}=C_\infty^{(n)}(\cdot,p)$.
For $j=0,1,2$, the $j$th differences of
$\alpha_p$ obey
$|\nabla^j\alpha_p(b)|
 \le C_g(1+|b-p|)^{-2-j}$, and
\[
 |\beta_p(b)|\le
  C_g(L^n+|b-p|)^{-2}
                  (1+\log^+(|b-p|/L^n)).
\]
\item There is a potential $\alpha_p^{\rm loc}$
with
\[
 d\alpha_p^{\rm loc}=C_\infty^{(n)}(\cdot,p),\qquad
 |\alpha_p^{\rm loc}(b)|
       \le C_gL^{2n}e^{-c_g|b-p|/(8L^n)}.
\]
It is covariant under simultaneous translation
by $L^n\mathbb Z^3$, and
$\alpha_p^{\rm loc}-\alpha_p^{(n)}=d\chi_p$
for a bounded function $\chi_p$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
In bare units the slice estimate is
\[
 |\mathcal C_{(j)}(p,q)|
   \le C_{\rm tp}L^{-3(j-1)}
          e^{-\delta_{\rm tp}r_\infty/L^{j-1}},
 \qquad r_\infty\ge |p-q|/\sqrt3 .
\]
For $r_\infty\ge1$, write $t_i=r_\infty/L^i$.
For $i\le n-1$,
\[
 L^{-3i}e^{-\delta_{\rm tp}t_i}
 \le r_\infty^{-3}t_i^3e^{-\delta_{\rm tp}t_i/2}
             e^{-\delta_{\rm tp}r_\infty/(2L^{n-1})}.
\]
The sum of $t_i^3e^{-\delta_{\rm tp}t_i/2}$
along the geometric sequence is bounded by
a constant depending on $L$.
For $r_\infty<1$, the slice sum is at most
$2C_{\rm tp}$. Summing the telescope proves
the first bound in (a), since
$\delta_{\rm tp}L/(2\sqrt3)\ge c_g$.
The background bound in
\cite[Prop.\ 120.6]{YMM1} gives the second.

An exact form on $\Lambda_{N_{s+1}}$ which is
$N_s$-periodic is exact on $\Lambda_{N_s}$:
average any potential over the translates.
The plaquette average commutes with these
translations. Thus the $N_s$-periodic part of
$\mathsf{Fl}_n(\Lambda_{N_{s+1}})$ is exactly
$\mathsf{Fl}_n(\Lambda_{N_s})$.
Its projection commutes with translations,
and the two inner products on periodic forms
differ only by $L^3$.
Consequently
\[
 C_{N_s}^{(n)}(p,q)
   =\sum_{z\in N_s\mathbb Z^3/N_{s+1}\mathbb Z^3}
                  C_{N_{s+1}}^{(n)}(\tilde p,\tilde q+z).
\]
If $|\tilde p-\tilde q|\le N_s/3$, all nonzero
images have distance at least $2N_s/3$.
Part (a) bounds the successive difference by
$C_gL^3e^{-c_gN_s/(2L^n)}$, a summable sequence.
This proves existence of $C_\infty^{(n)}$.
The same identity and dominated convergence
give its periodization formula and symmetries.

The Fourier formula for $\Pi_0^{\rm tp}$ is a
Riemann sum of a bounded symbol continuous
away from zero. Its limit is the projection
onto closed $\ell^2$ two-forms.
The symbol is smooth away from zero and its
derivative of order $j$ is bounded by $C|k|^{-j}$.
The dyadic Fourier estimate therefore gives
decay $(1+|p-q|)^{-3}$.
The limit of (a) gives
$|S_\infty^{(n)}|\le C_{\rm tp}L^{-3n}$;
subtracting its two kernels also gives
$|S_\infty^{(n)}|\le C(1+|p-q|)^{-3}$.
Together these yield the stated bound.
Closedness passes to the pointwise limit,
since $d$ has finite range.

The symbols of $\mathsf g$ and of its $j$th
differences have degrees $j-1$ near zero.
The same dyadic estimate gives decay
$(1+|\cdot|)^{-2-j}$.
Moreover $d\mathsf g=dd^*\Delta^{-1}$ has the
symbol of the projection onto closed two-forms,
giving the assertion about $\alpha_p$.
For a closed form $F$ bounded by
$C(L^n+|\cdot-p|)^{-3}$, absolute convergence
allows
$d\mathsf gF=F-d^*\Delta^{-1}dF=F$.
Apply this to $S_\infty^{(n)}(\cdot,p)$.

For completeness, put $t=|b-p|$.
When $t\le2L^n$,
\[
 |\beta_p(b)|
 \le C\sum_{|u-p|\le3L^n}(1+|b-u|)^{-2}L^{-3n}
       +C\sum_{|u-p|>3L^n}|u-p|^{-5}
 \le CL^{-2n}.
\]
When $t>2L^n$, points with $|u-p|\le t/2$
contribute at most
$Ct^{-2}\sum_{|v|\le t/2}(L^n+|v|)^{-3}
\le Ct^{-2}(1+\log(t/L^n))$.
The remaining points contribute at most
\[
 Ct^{-3}\sum_{|u-b|\le2t}(1+|b-u|)^{-2}
                  +C\sum_{|u-b|>2t}|u-b|^{-5}
 \le Ct^{-2}.
\]
This proves (c).

For (d), put $F=C_\infty^{(n)}(\cdot,p)$ and
write $x=(x_\perp,x_3)$.
Choose the axial potential
$\alpha_3^{\rm ax}=0$ and
$\alpha_i^{\rm ax}(x)=\pm\sum_{t\ge x_3}F_{i3}(x_\perp,t)$,
$i=1,2$, with the sign fixed by the convention
for $d$. Then $d\alpha^{\rm ax}=F$ on the
$i3$ plaquettes. Closedness and decay give
the same identity on the $12$ plaquettes.
As $x_3\to-\infty$, its first two components
tend to a closed one-form
$\varphi_i(x_\perp)$ on $\mathbb Z^2$.
Its line sums are independent of the transverse
line by closedness, and tend to zero as the
line goes to infinity. They therefore vanish.
Hence
\[
 \chi(x_\perp)
    =\sum_{t<0}\varphi_1(x_\perp+te_1)
    =-\sum_{t\ge0}\varphi_1(x_\perp+te_1),
 \qquad d_\perp\chi=\varphi .
\]
If $p_3$ is the third coordinate of the base
point of $p$, define
\[
 \alpha_p^{\rm loc}
       =\alpha^{\rm ax}-d(\chi(x_\perp)1[x_3<p_3]).
\]
Its curvature remains $F$.
Above the plane $x_3=p_3$, its first two
components are forward sums of $F$; below
that plane they are the opposite backward sums.
In each case all summands are at least as
far from $p$ as $x$.
Its third component is zero except on bonds
crossing that plane, where it equals $\chi$,
computed using the ray pointing away from
$p_\perp$. The exponential bound in (b)
therefore gives
$C_gL^{2n}e^{-c_g|b-p|/(8L^n)}$.
This construction commutes with the required
translations.
The difference $\alpha_p^{\rm loc}-\alpha_p^{(n)}$
is closed on $\mathbb Z^3$, so is $d\chi_p$.
Define $\chi_p$ by integrating from a site
beside $p$ along coordinate paths.
The bounds just proved and those in (c)
bound these path sums uniformly in the endpoint.
Thus $\chi_p$ is bounded.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Removing the flat block constraint from the fermion loop]
\label{C-403-60}
There are $C_F<\infty$ and
$c_F=\min\{c_g/48,\delta_f/12\}$, depending only
on the member, $r,L,b_F$, with the following
property. Let $n\ge1$, $0\le m_0\le L^{-n}$,
and $\mathsf r\ge1$.
Let $\Lambda_N$ be a bare torus at cutoff
$K\ge n$, with $N\ge\max\{16L^n,30\mathsf r\}$.
Let $S_1,S_2$ each lie in a closed ball of
radius $\mathsf r$, with their mutual distance
between $\mathsf r$ and $6\mathsf r$.
Suppose $w_1,w_2$ are real plaquette functions
supported, through their barycentres, in $S_1,S_2$.
Choose lifts $\tilde w_1,\tilde w_2$ supported
in lifts of those sets at the same distance.
Then
\begin{align*}
 &\left|\sum_{p,q}w_1(p)w_2(q)\mathsf B_N^{F,(n)}(p,q;m_0)
       -\sum_{p,q}\tilde w_1(p)\tilde w_2(q)
                                  \mathsf B_1^F(p,q;m_0)\right|\\
 &\quad\le C_F\left[
      \left(\frac{\mathsf r}{L^n}\right)^2
                      (1+\log\mathsf r+n\log L)
       +\mathsf r^5L^{14n}e^{-c_FN/L^n}\right]
          \mathsf r\,\|w_1\|_\infty\|w_2\|_\infty .
\end{align*}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
There are at most $(C\mathsf r^3)^2$ contributing
pairs. For each pair put
$\rho=|\tilde p-\tilde q|$; the support assumptions
give $\mathsf r\le\rho\le10\mathsf r\le N/3$.
In Feynman gauge on $\mathbb Z^3$,
$\langle A_bA_{b'}\rangle_0=\Delta^{-1}(b,b')$,
so the curvature covariance is
$\Pi_{0,\infty}^{\rm tp}$ and its potential
is $\alpha_p$. By
\cref{lem:C403-fermionic-covariance-coefficient},
\[
 \mathsf B_1^F(\tilde p,\tilde q)
    =-3\Pi_{0,\infty}^{\rm tp}(\tilde p,\tilde q)X,
 \qquad X=(\alpha_{\tilde p},\Pi\alpha_{\tilde q}).
\]
On the torus use
\[
 \alpha_p^{\rm per}
    =\sum_{z\in N\mathbb Z^3}\alpha_{\tilde p}^{\rm loc}(\cdot+z)
                              -\mathsf c_p ,
\]
where $\mathsf c_p$ is the constant one-form
making its sum in each bond direction zero.
It is a potential of $C_N^{(n)}(\cdot,p)$, so
the same coefficient formula gives
\[
 \mathsf B_N^{F,(n)}(p,q)
    =-3C_N^{(n)}(p,q)
                (\alpha_p^{\rm per},
                          \Pi_N^{(\le n)}\alpha_q^{\rm per}).
\]

\par\medskip\noindent\emph{The infinite-lattice comparison.}\quad 
The Ward identity and reflection symmetry improve
the decay of $\Pi\alpha_q$.
For $b=\langle x,x+e_\mu\rangle$, put
$g_\nu(u)=\alpha_{q,\nu}(x+u)$ and
$c=(e_\mu-e_\nu)/2$.
Part (c) of \cref{C-403-58} yields
\[
 (\Pi\alpha_q)(b)
  =\frac12\sum_{\nu,u}\Pi_{\mu\nu}(u)
       [g_\nu(u)+g_\nu(2c-u)-g_\nu(0)-g_\nu(2c)].
\]
If $R=|x-q|\ge8$ and $|u|\le R/2$, the bracket
is at most $C(1+|u|)^2R^{-4}$ by the second
difference estimate of \cref{C-403-59}.
For $|u|>R/2$, use
$|\Pi_{\mu\nu}(u)|\le C|u|^{-4}$ and
$|g_\nu(u)|\le C(1+|x+u-q|)^{-2}$.
Summing the two regions gives
\[
 |(\Pi\alpha_q)(b)|\le C(1+|b-q|)^{-3},
 \qquad
 |X|\le C\rho^{-2}(1+\log\rho).
\]

Write the difference of the constrained and
unconstrained loop pairings as
\begin{align*}
 D:={}&(\alpha_{\tilde p}^{(n)},
                   \Pi^{(\le n)}\alpha_{\tilde q}^{(n)})-X\\
  ={}&(\alpha_{\tilde p}^{(n)},
                       (\Pi^{(\le n)}-\Pi)\alpha_{\tilde q}^{(n)})
       -(\beta_{\tilde p},\Pi\alpha_{\tilde q})
       -(\Pi\alpha_{\tilde p},\beta_{\tilde q})
       +(\beta_{\tilde p},\Pi\beta_{\tilde q}).
\end{align*}
By \cref{C-403-59},
\[
 |\alpha_p^{(n)}(b)|
 \le C(1+|b-p|)^{-2}
                          (1+\log^+(|b-p|/L^n)).
\]
Convolving this estimate with the difference
kernel of \cref{C-403-58}, splitting the sums
at distance $L^n$, bounds the first term by
$CL^{-2n}(1+\log^+(L^n/\rho))$.
Up to that distance the two potential factors
have power $-2$; beyond it the difference
kernel has power $-4$.
The second and third terms are bounded by
\[
 C\sum_b(L^n+|b-\tilde p|)^{-2}
       (1+\log^+(|b-\tilde p|/L^n))
                          (1+|b-\tilde q|)^{-3}
 \le CL^{-2n}(1+n\log L)
\]
and the same estimate with the points exchanged.

For the last term, Plancherel and
$|\hat\Pi(k)|\le C|k|$ combine with
the $C|k|^{-1}$ symbol bound for $\mathsf g$.
It is at most
\[
 C\prod_{u\in\{\tilde p,\tilde q\}}
 \left(\sum_{v,v'}
   |S_\infty^{(n)}(v,u)|\,
       \kappa(v-v')\,|S_\infty^{(n)}(v',u)|\right)^{1/2},
 \qquad \kappa(v)\le C(1+|v|)^{-2}.
\]
The bound
$|S_\infty^{(n)}(v,u)|\le C(L^n+|v-u|)^{-3}$
makes this at most $CL^{-2n}$.
Thus
$|D|\le CL^{-2n}(1+n\log L)$.
As $C_\infty^{(n)}
=\Pi_{0,\infty}^{\rm tp}-S_\infty^{(n)}$,
\begin{align*}
 &|C_\infty^{(n)}(\tilde p,\tilde q)(X+D)
                 -\Pi_{0,\infty}^{\rm tp}(\tilde p,\tilde q)X|\\
 &\quad\le|\Pi_{0,\infty}^{\rm tp}|\,|D|
                    +|S_\infty^{(n)}|(|X|+|D|)\\
 &\quad\le C\rho^{-3}L^{-2n}
                              (1+\log\rho+n\log L).
\end{align*}
For the last inequality use
$|S_\infty^{(n)}|\le C(L^n+\rho)^{-3}$ and
$\rho L^{2n}\le(L^n+\rho)^3$.

\par\medskip\noindent\emph{The torus comparison.}\quad 
All nonzero periodized images of the curvature
kernel have distance at least $2N/3$, so
\[
 |C_N^{(n)}(p,q)-C_\infty^{(n)}(\tilde p,\tilde q)|
                          \le Ce^{-c_gN/(2L^n)} .
\]
By \cref{C-403-58}(d), the fermion loop kernel
is the periodization of $\Pi^{(\le n)}$ plus
$\mathcal E_N$.
The periodized kernel annihilates constant
one-forms. Absolute convergence, translation
covariance, and the definition of $\mathsf c_p$
therefore give
\begin{align*}
 (\alpha_p^{\rm per},\Pi_N^{(\le n)}\alpha_q^{\rm per})
   ={}&\sum_{z\in N\mathbb Z^3}
      (\alpha_{\tilde p}^{\rm loc},
                     \Pi^{(\le n)}\alpha_{\tilde q+z}^{\rm loc})\\
     &+(\alpha_p^{\rm per},\mathcal E_N\alpha_q^{\rm per}).
\end{align*}
The zero image is $X+D$.
Indeed, $\alpha^{\rm loc}-\alpha^{(n)}$ is the
coboundary of a bounded function, which the
kernel annihilates by \cref{C-403-58}(c).
All these pairings converge absolutely.

Set $\gamma_F=\min\{c_g/8,\delta_f/2\}$.
The exponential bounds in \cref{C-403-58,C-403-59}
bound the term with image $z$ by
$CL^{7n}e^{-\gamma_F|\tilde p-\tilde q-z|/(2L^n)}$.
The nonzero images therefore sum to at most
$CL^{7n}e^{-\gamma_FN/(6L^n)}$.
Also
$\|\alpha_p^{\rm per}\|_1
 \le2\|\alpha_{\tilde p}^{\rm loc}\|_1\le CL^{5n}$,
so
\[
 |(\alpha_p^{\rm per},\mathcal E_N\alpha_q^{\rm per})|
       \le CL^{14n}e^{-\delta_fN/(2L^n)}.
\]
The periodized loop kernel is bounded, giving
$|(\alpha_p^{\rm per},\Pi_N^{(\le n)}
\alpha_q^{\rm per})|\le CL^{14n}$.
Combining the curvature and loop comparisons
bounds their product difference by
\[
 CL^{14n}
   (e^{-c_gN/(2L^n)}
     +e^{-\gamma_FN/(6L^n)}
     +e^{-\delta_fN/(2L^n)})
       \le3CL^{14n}e^{-c_FN/L^n},
\]
because $c_F=\gamma_F/6$.

Finally sum over at most $(C\mathsf r^3)^2$
pairs. The infinite-lattice difference costs
$C\mathsf r^3L^{-2n}
 (1+\log\mathsf r+n\log L)$, and the image
error costs $C\mathsf r^6L^{14n}e^{-c_FN/L^n}$.
These are exactly the two terms in the
claimed estimate.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Removing the flat block constraint from the pure coefficient]
\label{C-403-110}
Let $0<g\le\gamma_{\mathrm e}$, $P>1$, and
$\mathsf d_1=\min\{(L\mathsf m_+)^{-2},1/64\}$.
There is a nondecreasing function
$\epsilon^{\rm pure}:(0,\mathsf d_1]\to[0,\infty)$,
depending on $g,P$ and the constants, and tending
to zero at zero, with the following property.
Let $0<\mathsf d\le\mathsf d_1$,
$K>s(\mathsf d)$, and $L^K\le\mathsf d^{-P}$.
On the least torus put
$N=\ell_GL^K$, $\mathsf r=L^K\mathsf d$, and
let $n$ be the least level with
$L^na_K\ge\mathsf d^{1/2}$.
Let $S_1,S_2,w_1,w_2,\tilde w_1,\tilde w_2$
have the support and lift properties in
\cref{C-403-60}, and put
$\eta=\|w_1\|_\infty\|w_2\|_\infty$.
Then:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\mathsf r\ge4L^3M$ and $2\le n\le K$.
The coefficient of $\beta^{-3}$ in the
Laplace expansion of the covariance of $a_p,a_q$
on $\{\mathcal M^nU=\mathbf1\}$, with action
\[
 F_\kappa=A+\sum_{j<n}\kappa_jG_j(\mathcal M^jU),
                   \qquad \kappa_j>0,
\]
is the chart-independent and strength-independent
coefficient $\mathsf g_2[N,n](p,q)$ of
\cref{C-350-12}.
Write
$\mathsf T[N,n](w)
 =\sum_{p,q}w_1(p)w_2(q)\mathsf g_2[N,n](p,q)$.
\item
\[
 \left|\mathsf T[N,n](w)
       -\sum_{p,q}\tilde w_1(p)\tilde w_2(q)
                                  \mathsf B_1^{\rm lat}(p,q)\right|
