                 \le\epsilon^{\rm pure}(\mathsf d)\mathsf r\eta .
\]
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The definition of the witness depth gives
\[
 \mathsf r\ge L^{s(\mathsf d)+1}\mathsf d
          \ge LC_W(s(\mathsf d))
          \ge L\mathsf c_W\ge4L^3M.
\]
Here $C_W(s)=\mathsf c_W(\log\bar x_s)^{2\mathfrak p_0}$,
$\bar x_s\ge L$, and $\mathsf c_W\ge4L^2M$.
Thus $a_K<\mathsf d<\sqrt{\mathsf d}$, whereas
$L^Ka_K=1$. The least $n$ exists and
\[
 L^na_K\in[\sqrt{\mathsf d},L\sqrt{\mathsf d}),
 \qquad
 L^n\ge\mathsf r\mathsf d^{-1/2}>L^2.
\]
In particular $n\ge3$.

Restricting the QCD constants to the pure parameters
gives an admitted pure choice. In particular,
the QCD floor on $B_\sharp$ dominates the pure
floor, since its added fermion bound is nonnegative.
The pure coupling ceiling included in
$\gamma_{\mathrm e}$ ensures
$\ell_GL\ge C_LM$ and $\ell_G\ge N_{\mathsf H}$.
Hence the side condition for \cref{C-350-12}
holds at every level $1\le t\le K$, including
$t=n$. That proposition proves (a).

The contributing plaquette barycentres have
separation between $\mathsf r$ and $10\mathsf r$.
Their base points have distance at most
$10\mathsf r+2\le N/8$, since
$80\mathsf d+16a_K\le2\le\ell_G$.
Each support has at most $30\mathsf r^3$
plaquette barycentres, so there are at most
$900\mathsf r^6$ pairs.

\par\medskip\noindent\emph{Uniform comparison bounds.}\quad 
Use $\check C_{\rm X},\check C_{\rm R},
\check C'_{\rm W},\check C_\star$ for the
constants in \cref{C-350-11,C-350-7,C-350-14,C-350-15},
respectively. Let $\check\gamma^{\rm tr}$ and
$\check\delta_{\rm tp}$ be their Gaussian and
curvature decay rates, and let $\nu_{\rm W}$
be the side-ratio threshold in \cref{C-350-14}.
Set
\[
 \Upsilon_{\rm X}(x,\mathsf N)
   =\check C_{\rm X}\mathsf N^{36}
        \exp[-\tfrac18\check\gamma^{\rm tr}
                                 \mathfrak b(x)^2],
 \qquad \mathfrak b(x)=A_1(\log x)^{\mathfrak p_0},
 \qquad \mathsf b_*=X_g-\bar B=\mathsf b_+ .
\]
The function decreases in $x$ and increases
in $\mathsf N$.
Choose the least $k_{\rm X}\ge3$ and largest
$\mathsf d_{\rm X}\in(0,L^{-5}]$ for which
\begin{align*}
 \check\gamma^{\rm tr}A_1^2
              (\tfrac{k}{78}\log L)^{2\mathfrak p_0}
 &\ge\max\{80,8\log(10240\ell_G^3)+24k\log L\},
                         &&k\ge k_{\rm X},\\
 \check\gamma^{\rm tr}A_1^2
       \left(\log\frac3{4\sqrt{\mathsf d}}\right)^{2\mathfrak p_0}
 &\ge\max\{80,8\log(10240(\ell_GL)^3)
                         +576P\log(1/\mathsf d)\},
                         &&0<\mathsf d\le\mathsf d_{\rm X}.
\end{align*}
They exist because $2\mathfrak p_0\ge2$.
Put
\[
 \mathsf d_{\rm p}
  =\min\{\mathsf d_1,(\ell_G/(L\nu_{\rm W}))^2,
                             \mathsf d_{\rm X},L^{-k_{\rm X}}\}
\]
and define
\begin{align*}
 \varepsilon^{\rm ch}(\mathsf d)
  ={}&900\check C'_{\rm W}(\ell_GL)^{237}
       \mathsf d^{-5693P}
             e^{-\check\delta_{\rm tp}\ell_G\mathsf d^{-1/2}/48}\\
   &+\Upsilon_{\rm X}
       (\tfrac34\mathsf d^{-1/2},
                         (\ell_G+\mathsf b_*)L\mathsf d^{-24P})\\
   &+\check C_{\rm R}
       (\log(2\mathsf b_*L)+24P\log(1/\mathsf d))^{6\mathfrak p_0}
                                      \mathsf d^{3/4},\\
 \varepsilon^{\rm top}(k)
  ={}&\Upsilon_{\rm X}(L^{k/78},(\ell_G+\mathsf b_*)L^k)
       +2700\check C_\star\ell_G^{19}L^{20}kL^{-k/24}.
\end{align*}
For $0<\mathsf d\le\mathsf d_{\rm p}$ take
\[
 \epsilon^{\rm pure}(\mathsf d)
     =\sup_{0<d'\le\mathsf d}\varepsilon^{\rm ch}(d')
             +\sup_{k>s(\mathsf d)}\varepsilon^{\rm top}(k).
\]

\par\medskip\noindent\emph{A second pure datum.}\quad 
Let
\[
 K'=\max\{K,\lceil24\log_L\mathsf r\rceil\},\quad
 N'=\ell_GL^{K'},\quad
 n_1=K'-\lceil K'/78\rceil .
\]
Use the pure datum with cutoff $K'$ and label
$\mathsf b_*$, whose running couplings are $x'_j$.
This is admitted because $\mathsf b_*$ is in the
pure label window. Put
$\mathsf N'=(\ell_G+\mathsf b_*)L^{K'}$.
Lift the sources to $\Lambda_{N'}$ as in
\cref{C-350-14}, writing them $\breve w_1,\breve w_2$;
if $K'=K$, leave them unchanged.
Their physical support radius there is
$\mathsf d'=\mathsf rL^{-K'}$ and
$8a_{K'}\le\mathsf d'$.
The normalization $\mathsf r\eta$ is unchanged.
Since $\mathsf r\le\mathsf d^{1-P}$,
\[
 \mathsf r^{24}\le L^{K'}
       \le\max\{\mathsf d^{-P},L\mathsf r^{24}\}
       \le L\mathsf d^{-24P}.
\]
Also $s(\mathsf d)\ge k_{\rm X}$, since
$L^s\mathsf d<1\le C_W(s)$ for $s<k_{\rm X}$.
Thus $K'\ge K\ge k_{\rm X}+1\ge4$.

We need $2\le n<n_1\le K'$.
If $K'=K$, write $\lambda_0=\log_L(1/\mathsf d)\ge5$.
Then $K\ge24(K-\lambda_0)$, so
$K\le24\lambda_0/23$. Consequently
\[
 \lceil K/78\rceil
       <24\lambda_0/1794+1
       \le\lambda_0/2-1<K-n .
\]
The last inequality is
$L^{n-K}<L\sqrt{\mathsf d}$.
If $K'>K$, then
$\mathsf r\le L^{K'/24}$ and
$\mathsf d=\mathsf rL^{-K}\ge\mathsf rL^{1-K'}$.
Hence
\[
 L^n<L\mathsf r\mathsf d^{-1/2}
       \le L^{1/2}\mathsf r^{1/2}L^{K'/2}
       \le L^{1/2+25K'/48},
 \quad
 n_1>77K'/78-1\ge\tfrac12+25K'/48 .
\]
This proves the required level ordering.
We also have $L^n\ge\mathsf r$.

\par\medskip\noindent\emph{The five comparisons.}\quad 
First compare the two torus sizes at level $n$.
If $K'>K$, \cref{C-350-14} applies because
\[
 \nu=N/L^n>\ell_G\mathsf d^{-1/2}/L\ge\nu_{\rm W}
\]
and the pair base points lie within $N/8$.
It gives
\[
 |\mathsf T[N,n](w)-\mathsf T[N',n](\breve w)|
   \le900\mathsf r^6\check C'_{\rm W}
                       N'^{237}e^{-\check\delta_{\rm tp}L\nu/48}\eta .
\]
Divide by $\mathsf r\eta$ and use
$\mathsf r^5\le\mathsf d^{-5P}$ and
$N'\le\ell_GL\mathsf d^{-24P}$.
This is the first term of
$\varepsilon^{\rm ch}(\mathsf d)$.
For $K'=K$ the difference is zero.

Second remove the Gaussian tests at level $n$
in the pure progression. Its coefficient is
$\mathsf H^{(n)}[D']=\beta'^3a_{K'}^2\gamma_2^{\rm r}$,
while $\mathsf T[N',n]=\beta'^3a_{K'}^2\gamma_2^\circ$,
with $\beta'=L^{K'}\mathsf b_*$.
By \cref{C-350-6},
\[
 x'_{n-1}\ge\tfrac34\mathsf b_*L^{K'-n+1}
                         >\tfrac34\mathsf d^{-1/2}.
\]
The two conditions of \cref{C-350-11} follow
from $\mathsf d\le\mathsf d_{\rm X}$.
That proposition and \cref{C-350-13} give
\[
 |\mathsf H^{(n)}[D']-\mathsf T[N',n](\breve w)|
                   \le\Upsilon_{\rm X}(x'_{n-1},\mathsf N')\eta .
\]
It is bounded by the second term of
$\varepsilon^{\rm ch}(\mathsf d)\mathsf r\eta$.

Third, the pure tail estimate \cref{C-350-7}
at $n\le n_1$ gives
\[
 |\mathsf H^{(n_1)}[D']-\mathsf H^{(n)}[D']|
  \le\check C_{\rm R}\mathsf l'^{6\mathfrak p_0}
                 (\mathsf r/L^n)^{3/2}\mathsf r\eta .
\]
Here $\mathsf r/L^n\le\sqrt{\mathsf d}$ and
\[
 \mathsf l'=\max\{1,\log(2\mathsf b_*/\mathsf d')\}
       \le\log(2\mathsf b_*L)+24P\log(1/\mathsf d).
\]
This is the third term of
$\varepsilon^{\rm ch}(\mathsf d)\mathsf r\eta$.

Fourth remove the tests at level $n_1$.
Now
$x'_{n_1-1}\ge
 \tfrac34\mathsf b_*L^{\lceil K'/78\rceil+1}
 \ge L^{K'/78}$,
and the conditions of \cref{C-350-11} hold
because $K'\ge k_{\rm X}$.
The cost is at most
$\Upsilon_{\rm X}(L^{K'/78},
                  (\ell_G+\mathsf b_*)L^{K'})\eta$.

Finally use \cref{C-350-15} on the lattice
$(\ell',n_1)$, where
$\ell'=N'/L^{n_1}=\ell_GL^{\lceil K'/78\rceil}$.
It has $\ell'\ge N_{\mathsf H}$ and
$\ell'L\ge C_LM$. Summing its bound over
the at most $900\mathsf r^6$ pairs costs
\[
 2700\check C_\star\mathsf r^6\ell'^{19}
                         n_1L^{-n_1/2}\eta
 \le2700\check C_\star\ell_G^{19}L^{20}
                        K'L^{-K'/24}\mathsf r\eta .
\]
Indeed,
$\mathsf r^5\le L^{5K'/24}$,
$\ell'\le\ell_GL^{K'/78+1}$, and
$n_1>77K'/78-1$, and the resulting exponent is
$5/24+19/78+1/156-1/2=-1/24$.
The last two comparisons cost at most
$\varepsilon^{\rm top}(K')\mathsf r\eta$.
Since $K'>s(\mathsf d)$, adding the five
bounds proves (b) for $\mathsf d\le\mathsf d_{\rm p}$.

\par\medskip\noindent\emph{The modulus.}\quad 
The supremum formula is nondecreasing because
$s(\mathsf d)$ does not increase with $\mathsf d$.
Each term of $\varepsilon^{\rm ch}(\mathsf d)$
tends to zero: its exponential terms dominate
every displayed power of $\mathsf d^{-1}$.
Likewise $\varepsilon^{\rm top}(k)\to0$,
and $s(\mathsf d)\to\infty$.
Thus $\epsilon^{\rm pure}(\mathsf d)\to0$.

For $\mathsf d_{\rm p}<\mathsf d\le\mathsf d_1$,
we have
$K\le K_{\rm p}
 :=\lfloor P\log_L(1/\mathsf d_{\rm p})\rfloor$.
Let $G_{\rm p}$ bound the finitely many
$|\mathsf g_2[\ell_GL^k,t](p,q)|$ with
$1\le t\le k\le K_{\rm p}$ and the
$|\mathsf B_1^{\rm lat}(p,q)|$ at base-point
separation at most $10L^{K_{\rm p}}+2$.
The latter collection is finite modulo
translation. The difference in (b) is at most
$1800G_{\rm p}\mathsf r^6\eta$.
Extend the modulus on this interval by
\[
 \epsilon^{\rm pure}(\mathsf d)
     =\epsilon^{\rm pure}(\mathsf d_{\rm p})
                                  +1800G_{\rm p}L^{5K_{\rm p}} .
\]
This preserves monotonicity and proves the
remaining cases. All these choices precede
the final small-distance ceiling.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Removing tests from the coefficients at the split]
\label{lem:C403-test-removal}
Assume the parameter choices of \cref{C-403-33},
including the floor {\rm(F1)} and the admitted
gauge-background conditions. Let $P>1$ and
$0<\mathsf d\le\mathsf d_1
=\min\{(L\mathsf m_+)^{-2},1/64\}$.
For a datum on the least torus with
$K>s(\mathsf d)$ and $L^K\le\mathsf d^{-P}$,
let $n$ be the least integer with
$L^na_K\ge\sqrt{\mathsf d}$.
For $m=1,2,3$, the coefficient
$\sum_{j\le n}\mathsf n_{j,[2m]}$
differs from the coefficient at order $\lambda^{2m}$
of the Gaussian Laplace expansion under the
flat level-$n$ constraint by at most
\[
 \epsilon_{\rm t}(\mathsf d)
                         \mathsf n_m(X;\mathsf d),
 \qquad \epsilon_{\rm t}(\mathsf d)\longrightarrow0 .
\]
The modulus depends on $g,P$ and the constants,
uniformly in the other parameters of the datum
and the position of the test pair.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\par\medskip\noindent\emph{The exact finite-dimensional integral.}\quad 
At block field $\mathbf1$ and $\Psi_n=0$,
the logarithm of the level-$n$ form has mixed
source derivative $\sum_{j\le n}\mathsf n_j^\lambda$.
The scalar values of all activities have
been removed as source energies.
The exact chart composition of
\cref{C-403-33-flow} expresses the form as a
source-independent nonzero number times the
bare integral on $\{\mathcal M^nU=\mathbf1\}$.
The gauge fluctuations enter as $\lambda B_i$,
$i<n$, with tests at $\mathsf t_i$;
the gauge fixings have coefficients
$\mathsf t_i/\lambda^2$, and the Wilson
weight is $e^{-A(\beta/\lambda^2-a_K^{-1}w,U)}$.
The running action coefficients leave no
counterterm, since
\[
 \lambda^{-2}L^i\xi_i(\lambda)
                   +\sum_{l\le i}L^lb_l
                         =\lambda^{-2}\beta .
\]
By \cref{C-403-58}(a), the fermion factor at
$\Psi_n=0$ is
\[
 \prod_{i<n}\theta^{-\dim H_{i+1}}\det\Gamma_i[U]
     =\theta_n^{-\dim H_n}\det\mathcal K_n[U;m_0].
\]
Thus the field-dependent determinant is exactly
the constrained determinant in
\cref{lem:C403-block-determinant}.
At fixed finite lattice, the Taylor coefficients
are unique. The tested coefficients are therefore
cumulants in the product of the tested Gaussian
measures of the levels $i<n$.

Let $\mu=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mu_i$ and
$\chi=\prod_{i<n}\chi_i$. By \cref{C-403-56},
\[
 \tau_n=\sum_{i<n}N_{i+1}^\square K_M
       e^{-\frac12\gamma_{\rm tail}\mathfrak b(\mathsf t_i)^2}
 \le N^{\rm b}K_M
       e^{-\frac12\gamma_{\rm tail}\mathfrak b(\mathsf t_n)^2},
 \qquad \int\chi\,d\mu\ge e^{-\tau_n}.
\]
Here $N^{\rm b}$ is the number of bare bonds.
For a real polynomial $\mathfrak P$, the same
Cauchy--Schwarz argument as in that lemma gives
\begin{equation}\label{C-403-71}
\begin{split}
 |\mathsf E^\chi\mathfrak P-\mathsf E\mathfrak P|
   &\le(\sqrt{\tau_n}+\tau_n)e^{\tau_n}
                        (\mathsf E\mathfrak P^2)^{1/2},\\
 |\mathsf E^\chi\mathfrak P|
   &\le e^{\tau_n}(\mathsf E\mathfrak P^2)^{1/2}.
\end{split}
\end{equation}
We next obtain polynomial bounds for the
Taylor coefficients to which this is applied.

\par\medskip\noindent\emph{A chain at fixed radii.}\quad 
Start at the trivial triple
$\mathscr P_n=(\mathbf1,0,0)$.
For $1\le i<n$, define $\mathscr P_i$ by
substituting the step shift at fluctuation
$\lambda B_i$ into the restriction of
$\mathscr P_{i+1}$.
All triples have the same radii
$(\alpha_0,\alpha_1)$ and real factor $\mathbf1$.
Here are the domain checks.
The side condition is
$m'<m_{\mathfrak L}(g)+K-i$, with $M=L^{m'}$;
it follows from
$M\check R_i\le L^{m_{\mathfrak L}(g)+K-i-1}$
and $\check R_i\ge1$.
The standing radii satisfy
\[
 \alpha_0<\alpha_1,\quad
 \alpha_1^2\le\mathsf c_\natural\alpha_0,\quad
 \alpha_0+\alpha_1\le a^\star
                               \le\min\{a_{\mathfrak h},a^\sharp\}.
\]
Thus they are admitted one-level substitution
radii over themselves.
At $|\lambda|\le1$ the field polydisc gives
$\sup|\lambda B_i|<\beta_\lambda\le\beta_0/2$.
The standing bound
$c_h\beta_0\le\epsilon_P\le\varepsilon_{\mathfrak h}/2$
places the pair and fluctuation in the shift
domain, and
\[
 \frac{\mathsf c_{\rm os}\alpha_0}
                         {c_h\beta_\lambda}
   =\frac{2a_{\rm an}}{c_h\beta_\lambda}\ge6>1.
\]
The substitution theorem
\cite[Prop.\ 51.15]{YMM1} therefore applies
at amplitude one. Its conclusion uses the
same radii as its hypothesis, so the iteration
loses no radius. Heredity of the cores
\cite[Lem.\ 49.2]{YMM1} permits restrictions
to every polymer and fine cube needed by
the next step.

If $\mathscr A_{i+1}$ is the second member of
$\mathscr P_{i+1}$ and $\mathbf a_i,\mathbf K_i$
are the shift members, the substituted triple
has second member
\[
 (iL^{-i})^{-1}
       \log(e^{iL^{-i}\mathbf a_i}
                              e^{iL^{-i-1}\mathscr A_{i+1}})
\]
and current $L^{-3}J_{i+1}+\mathbf K_i$.
Its pair has first member
$e^{iL^{-i}\mathbf a_i}\mathscr U_{i+1}$.
The fixed real factor and the holomorphic
substitution make the chain holomorphic in
$\lambda$. At level zero there is no shift
system: the bare configuration is
$U^{\rm ch}=e^{iB'}\mathscr U_1$, where $B'$
is the completed field of $\lambda B_0$.
The completed-field bound
$2C_{\rm cf}\beta_0\le
\min\{r_P^\circ,\alpha_1/2\}$ gives
\[
 U^{\rm ch}(b)=e^{iX(b;\lambda)},\qquad
 |X(b;\lambda)|\le\alpha_1,\qquad X(b;0)=0.
\]
The logarithm is holomorphic for $|\lambda|<1$.

\par\medskip\noindent\emph{The chain and the composite chart.}\quad 
The chain just constructed follows the fine
fields of the steps; the composite chart
follows their minimal backgrounds.
Their integrals agree by the triangular
change of variables used in \cref{C-350-13}.
The proof applies at the present calibrations
$\mathsf t_i$: its geometric hypotheses are
the passing tests and regular pair cores,
already checked, and the tests are radial
in each fluctuation.
To specify the change of variables, let
$W_n=\mathbf1$ and
$W_i=V_{W_{i+1}}[\lambda B_i]$ be the composite
block fields. Descending from $\mathfrak v_n=\mathbf1$,
choose real gauge transformations $\mathfrak v_i$
so that the pair of $\mathscr P_i$, at
\[
 \check B_i=\operatorname{Ad}(\mathfrak v_{i+1})B_i,
\]
is the pair of the plain triple over $W_i$
transformed by $\mathfrak v_i$.
The covariance of the shift gives the induction:
the fine field of a step lies in the minimal
orbit over $W_i$, its current is
$L^{-3}J_{i+1}+\mathbf K_i$, and a real gauge
transformation carries that pair to the chosen
minimal background. The transformation
$\mathfrak v_i$ reads only heights at least $i$.
At level zero covariance of the completed
field gives the same conclusion for the
bare configuration.

Every factor of the integrand is invariant
under this simultaneous transformation:
the gauge fixing and the J, G, A potentials
are functions of the regular pair and
fluctuation; the elimination factors depend
on the averaged background; the action and
observables are gauge invariant; and the
fermion factor is the determinant of an
operator conjugated by the gauge action.
The plain triples, their real gauge transforms,
and the substituted triples lie in the cores
where these identities hold.
At a fixed choice of the higher fluctuations,
$B_i\mapsto\check B_i$ is a fixed rotation at
each bond. It preserves the box and Lebesgue
measure. Integrate from the lowest height
upward, holding those rotations fixed at
each integration, as in \cref{C-350-13}.
The two integrals agree for real
$0<\lambda\le1$ and every admitted source.

Their Gaussian coefficients also agree.
Apply the Laplace expansion to either
coordinate system on a product of small
balls $|\lambda B_i(b)|<r$.
The frozen rotations preserve that product,
the integrand, and the Euclidean norm.
The positive quadratic phase from
\cref{C-350-12} therefore remains positive
in the chain coordinates. Uniqueness of
the expansion identifies the Gaussian
cumulants of the chain with the Laplace
coefficients of the composite chart.

\par\medskip\noindent\emph{Uniform bounds for the gauge logarithm.}\quad 
On $|\lambda|\le1$, the two observables are
bounded by a power of $N^{\rm b}$ and $\beta$,
times their test-function norms.
The Wilson terms are polynomials in
$e^{iX(b;\lambda)}$ and its inverse.
They vanish to second order at zero, so
$\lambda^{-2}a_p(U^{\rm ch})$ is holomorphic
and bounded by the maximum principle.
The Wilson logarithm is therefore at most
$C\beta N^{\rm b}$.

At a step, write its scaled fluctuation as
$B=\mathsf t_i^{1/2}B_i$.
The logarithm of its gauge fixing is
$-\tfrac12(B,\hat{\mathsf G}(P)B)_1
 +\sum_Y\mathbb V^{{\rm G},\lambda}(Y)$,
and its Jacobian logarithm is
$\sum_Y\mathbb V^{{\rm J},\lambda}(Y)$.
The row bound for each fine-cube operator
$\hat{\mathsf G}_\square$ gives
\[
 |(B,\hat{\mathsf G}_\square B)_1|
       \le c_{\mathsf G}n_M\mathsf C_{\mathcal A}^2
                                      \mathfrak b(\mathsf t_i)^2,
\]
where $n_M$ is the number of bonds meeting
one closed $M$-cube. Since
\[
 \mathfrak b(\mathsf t_i)^2
   \le A_1^2(2\mathfrak p_0)^{2\mathfrak p_0}\mathsf t_i
   \le A_1^2(2\mathfrak p_0)^{2\mathfrak p_0}\beta ,
\]
the sum of these quadratic terms is at most
$C L^{-3i}\beta N^{\rm b}$.
The J and G vertices obey
\[
 |\mathbb V^{\natural,\lambda}(Y)|
     \le\tfrac{10}{9}K_P\delta(\mathsf t_i)
                       Q_Y(B)e^{-(\kappa+1)d_i(Y)}.
\]
There are at most $8(1+d_i(Y))$ cubes in $Y$,
and
\[
 \delta(\mathsf t_i)Q_Y(B)
 \le\delta(\mathsf t_i)
       +8(1+d_i(Y))M^{-3}n_M\mathsf C_{\mathcal A}^2
                    \delta(\mathsf t_i)\mathfrak b(\mathsf t_i)^2 .
\]
The last scalar factor is at most
$A_1^3(6\mathfrak p_0)^{3\mathfrak p_0}$.
The spare exponential absorbs $1+d_i(Y)$;
the polymer sum and $\sum_{i<n}L^{-3i}\le2$
give a bound $C\beta N^{\rm b}$ for the
gauge fixings and Jacobians, both at
$\lambda$ and at zero.

The elimination factor of a step is the
product of $(\det\mathsf m_c)^{-1}$ over
bonds of the level above.
Its logarithm is
$\mathsf z_c+3\log L$, where
$\mathsf z_c=-\operatorname{Log}\det(L\mathsf m_c)$
and $\mathsf z_c=6\log L$ at the identity.
The local pivot-log bound
\cite[(1392)--(1393)]{YMM1} gives
\[
 |\mathsf z_c-6\log L|\le C_{\mathsf z}a_{\rm nf}.
\]
We check its applicability here. The standing
constant condition supplies
$a=L\max\{\alpha_0,\alpha_1\}\le a_{\rm nf}$.
The frame is $(K,m_{\mathfrak L}(g),(\mathsf t_l))$,
with $\mathsf t_l\ge\mathsf b>\gamma^{-2}>1$,
$\varepsilon(\mathsf t_l),\delta(\mathsf t_l)\le1$,
and $M\check R_l\le L^{m_{\mathfrak L}(g)+K-l-1}$.
At $t=i+1\le n$ this is the empty history,
so each level-$t$ bond is in its regular set.
The pair $(\mathscr U_{i+1},0)$ has decomposition
$(\mathbf1,L^{-1}\mathscr A_{i+1})$ in the
level-$i$ units. Its curvature bound is
$|\partial\mathscr U_{i+1}-\mathbf1|
 <\alpha_0L^{-2(i+1)}$; its form and difference
bounds are exactly those of the core after
the scale factors $L,L^2$; its current is zero.
Restrictions to the double block of $c$
preserve these bounds.
In the local gauge the logarithmic potential
has norm less than $4a/L$. The averaged pivot
matrix has
$E=L^3\mathsf m_c-1$ with
$|E|\le4C_{\rm piv}C_Qa/L\le1/2$.
Thus $|\operatorname{tr}\log(1+E)|\le6|E|$,
and its imaginary part has modulus at most
$\pi/2$; it is the principal determinant
logarithm. One may take
$C_{\mathsf z}=24C_{\rm piv}C_Q/L$.
The elimination map is consequently defined,
$\det(L\mathsf m_c)$ avoids $(-\infty,0]$,
and $\mathsf z_c$ is holomorphic in
$\mathscr U_{i+1}$ throughout this domain.
Thus it is holomorphic in $\lambda$ and
is the logarithm of the actual elimination
factor. There are at most $N^{\rm b}$ bonds
over levels $1,\ldots,n$, so their logarithmic
change is at most $2C_{\mathsf z}a_{\rm nf}N^{\rm b}$.

\par\medskip\noindent\emph{The fermion logarithm and coefficient bounds.}\quad 
Schwarz's lemma applied to
$X(b;\lambda)$ gives
$|X(b;\lambda)|\le\alpha_1|\lambda|$.
Thus, on $|\lambda|<L^{-n}$,
$|X(b;\lambda)|<\alpha_1L^{-n}$.
The real background is $\mathbf1$ and is
regular at every level.
The admitted determinant expansion through
depth $n$ applies because
$0<m_0=L^{-K}\mathsf m\le L^{-K}/2$.
At each $j<n$ it gives
\[
 \log\delta Z_j^{\rm F}(U^{\rm ch})
       -\log\delta Z_j^{\rm F}(\mathbf1)
  =\sum_{Y\in\mathcal D_{j+1}}
                          \mathbf N^{{\rm F},(j+1)}(Y,U^{\rm ch}),
 \qquad
 |\mathbf N^{{\rm F},(j+1)}|
       \le2C_NN_fe^{-(\kappa+1)d_{j+1}(Y)} .
\]
These terms are holomorphic in $X$, hence
in $\lambda$.
Their sum is the logarithmic change of the
entire fermion factor, and is bounded by
$CN_fN^{\rm b}$.
This also proves that the chain integral
is holomorphic near zero.

At order $\lambda^{2m}$ the mixed covariance
coefficient is a finite sum, with coefficients
depending on $m$, of products of at most
$2m+2$ Gaussian means. Each mean contains
at most $2m+2$ Taylor coefficients of the
observables and the logarithm of the integrand.
At order $k\le2m$ those coefficients are
homogeneous fluctuation polynomials of
degree $k$ or $k+2$, the latter coming from
the factor $\lambda^{-2}$ in the action.
Cauchy's estimate on $|\lambda|=L^{-n-1}$
costs
$L^{(n+1)k}\le(L^3N^{\rm b})^{k/3}$.
The preceding bounds therefore control
each coefficient by a power of $N^{\rm b}\beta$
times $(1+\varpi_B)^{2m+2}$, and the appropriate
test-function norm, where
\[
 \varpi_B=
 \max_{i<n,b}
      \frac{\mathsf t_i^{1/2}|B_i(b)|}
                         {\mathsf C_{\mathcal A}\mathfrak b(\mathsf t_i)}.
\]
The rotations preserve these absolute values.
The scaled Gaussian variances are bounded,
so $\mathsf E\varpi_B^{2q}\le C_qN^{\rm b}$.
Apply \eqref{C-403-71} and H\"older to each
factor in the cumulant. The tested and
untested coefficients differ by at most
\[
 C_m^{\rm t}(\sqrt{\tau_n}+\tau_n)
       e^{C_m^{\rm t}\tau_n}
                 (N^{\rm b}\beta)^{c_m^{\rm t}}\mathfrak f.
\]
Finally
$N^{\rm b}\le3\ell_G^3\mathsf d^{-3P}$,
$\beta\le\mathsf b\mathsf d^{-P}$, and
$\mathsf t_n>\mathsf b\mathsf d^{-1/2}/L$.
Since the label window bounds $\mathsf b$
above and below and $\mathfrak p_0\ge1$,
$\tau_n$ tends to zero faster than every
power of $\mathsf d$.
After division by
$\mathsf n_m(X;\mathsf d)
=\mathsf b^{-m}\mathsf d^{m-2}\mathfrak f$,
the displayed bound is a modulus
$\epsilon_{\rm t}(\mathsf d)\to0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Identification of the first three covariance coefficients]
\label{C-403-35}
Assume the constants of \cref{C-403-33},
including {\rm(F1)} and the admitted gauge-background
conditions. Let $g\le\gamma_{\mathrm e}$,
$\vartheta\in(0,1)$, $P>1$, and
$\mathsf d_1=\min\{(L\mathsf m_+)^{-2},1/64\}$.
For every datum on the least torus with
$0<\mathsf d\le\mathsf d_1$,
$K>s(\mathsf d)$, and $L^K\le\mathsf d^{-P}$,
the coefficient $\sum_j\mathsf n_{j,[2m]}$,
$1\le m\le3$, agrees with the order-$\beta^{-m}$
lattice covariance coefficient on $\mathbb Z^3$,
including its factor $\beta^{-m}$ and the
physical observable normalization, up to
\[
 C_m\epsilon'_m(\mathsf d)\mathsf n_m(X;\mathsf d),
 \qquad \epsilon'_m(\mathsf d)\longrightarrow0.
\]
The assertion holds also for the translation
mean of the jets. Its constants and moduli
depend only on $g,\vartheta,P$ and the
chosen constants.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Split at the least $n$ with
$L^na_K\ge\sqrt{\mathsf d}$.
The bounds of \cref{C-403-33}(iii), followed
by Cauchy's estimate for $\lambda$, give
\[
 \sum_{j>n}|\mathsf n_{j,[2m]}|
 \le C\mathsf l^{2m\mathfrak p_0}
        \mathsf b^{-m}\mathsf d^{5/2}
                         (L^{n+1}a_K)^{m-9/2}\mathfrak f
 \le C\mathsf l_+^{6\mathfrak p_0}
                   \mathsf d^{3/4}\mathsf n_m(X;\mathsf d),
\]
where
$\mathsf l_+=\max\{1,\log(2\mathsf b_+/\mathsf d)\}$.
This is a convergent geometric sum for
$m\le3$. By \cref{lem:C403-test-removal},
the levels at most $n$ may be replaced by
the Gaussian Laplace coefficient under the
flat block constraint at cost
$\epsilon_{\rm t}(\mathsf d)\mathsf n_m$.

Put $\mathsf r=\mathsf d/a_K$ and
$N=\ell_G/a_K$ in bare units.
The supports lie in balls of radius
$\mathsf r$, with distance between
$\mathsf r$ and $6\mathsf r$.
By \cref{C-403-110},
$\mathsf r\ge4L^3M$ and $2\le n\le K$.
The scale choice gives
\[
 \mathsf r/L^n\le\sqrt{\mathsf d},\quad
 m_0L^n<L\mathsf m_+\sqrt{\mathsf d}\le1,\quad
 N/L^n>\ell_G\mathsf d^{-1/2}/L\ge16 .
\]
Also $30\mathsf r\le N$ and
\[
 1+\log\mathsf r+n\log L
       \le(1+\log L)(1+2P\log(1/\mathsf d)).
\]
These check all hypotheses for the comparisons
of the preceding subsection.

For $m=1$, both connected coefficients vanish:
two quadratic observables require at least
two gauge lines.
For $m=2$, the determinant contributes nothing
at this order. Wick's formula gives the
bare coefficient
$\tfrac32\sum_{p,q}f(x(p))h(x(q))C_N^{(n)}(p,q)^2$.
On $\mathbb Z^3$ it gives the same expression
with $C_N^{(n)}$ replaced by
$\Pi_{0,\infty}^{\rm tp}$.
By \cref{C-403-59}, their squares differ at
a contributing pair by at most
\[
 C\left(L^{-3n}|p-q|^{-3}
                              +e^{-c_gN/(2L^n)}\right).
\]
There are at most $C\mathsf r^6$ such pairs.
Multiplying by
$\beta^{-2}a_K^{-2}=\mathsf b^{-2}$
therefore bounds the physical difference by
\[
 C\left[\mathsf d^{3/2}
        +\mathsf d^{-6P}
                e^{-c_g\ell_G\mathsf d^{-1/2}/(2L)}\right]
                         \mathsf n_2(X;\mathsf d).
\]

For $m=3$, the determinant formula separates
the coefficient into its pure part and
\[
 N_f\sum_{p,q}f(x(p))h(x(q))
                           \mathsf B_N^{F,(n)}(p,q;m_0).
\]
The infinite-lattice coefficient is the
same sum with the kernels
$\mathsf B_1^{\rm lat}+N_f\mathsf B_1^F$.
We identify the pure part carefully.
The composite chart over $W_n=\mathbf1$
is an adapted chart
$U=\Psi(\mathbf1,(\lambda B_i)_{i<n})$
of $\{\mathcal M^nU=\mathbf1\}$.
By the exact one-step measure identity,
the product of its Jacobian and elimination
factors is a constant times the Haar density
$e^{-\theta(\mathbf1,\cdot)}$ in this chart:
compose the identities and use Fubini.
The densities are continuous, so the
identity holds throughout the chart.
The gauge fixings contribute
\[
 \sum_{i<n}\frac{\mathsf t_i}{\lambda^2}
                          G_i(\mathcal M^iU)
   =\frac\beta{\lambda^2}
          \sum_{i<n}\kappa_iG_i(\mathcal M^iU),
 \qquad \kappa_i=\mathsf t_i/\beta=L^{-i}.
\]
Thus the pure integrand is a constant times
$e^{-(\beta/\lambda^2)F_\kappa(U)
                -\theta(\mathbf1,(\lambda B_i))}$,
with exactly the phase and chart density
of \cref{C-350-12}.
By \cref{C-403-110}(a), its order-three
coefficient is $\mathsf T[N,n](w)$ for
$w_1(p)=f(x(p))$, $w_2(q)=h(x(q))$.
Part (b) of that lemma bounds its difference
from the pure infinite-lattice coefficient
by $\epsilon^{\rm pure}(\mathsf d)\mathsf r\mathfrak f$.
Since
$\beta^{-3}a_K^{-2}\mathsf r=\mathsf b^{-3}\mathsf d$,
its physical size is
$\epsilon^{\rm pure}(\mathsf d)\mathsf n_3$.

The fermion terms are compared at the same
bare mass $m_0$ by \cref{C-403-60}.
Using the checked scale bounds, its error
in physical units is at most
\[
 CN_f\left[
    \mathsf d(1+P\log(1/\mathsf d))
      +L^{14}\mathsf d^{-19P}
                 e^{-c_F\ell_G\mathsf d^{-1/2}/L}\right]\mathsf n_3 .
\]
We can therefore take, after adjusting the
constants $C_m$,
\begin{align*}
 \epsilon'_1(\mathsf d)
  &=\mathsf l_+^{6\mathfrak p_0}\mathsf d^{3/4}
                              +\epsilon_{\rm t}(\mathsf d),\\
 \epsilon'_2(\mathsf d)
  &=\epsilon'_1(\mathsf d)+\mathsf d^{3/2}
       +\mathsf d^{-6P}e^{-c_g\ell_G\mathsf d^{-1/2}/(2L)},\\
 \epsilon'_3(\mathsf d)
  &=\epsilon'_1(\mathsf d)+\epsilon^{\rm pure}(\mathsf d)\\
  &\quad+N_f[
       \mathsf d(1+P\log(1/\mathsf d))
          +L^{14}\mathsf d^{-19P}
                          e^{-c_F\ell_G\mathsf d^{-1/2}/L}].
\end{align*}
Each tends to zero.
The bounds hold at every position of the
test pair. The translations in \cref{C-403-30}
are lattice translations, and the infinite-lattice
coefficient is invariant under them.
Averaging proves the final assertion.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Comparison between torus sizes}

\begin{proposition}[The local covariance is independent of the side to next order]
\label{C-403-38}
Assume the constants of \cref{C-403-33},
including {\rm(F1)} and the admitted gauge-background
conditions, and let $g\le\gamma_{\mathrm e}$,
$\vartheta\in(0,1)$.
Use $\ell_G,\mathsf b_+,\mathsf Q,\mathsf d_{\rm R},
m_*(\mathsf d),\omega_{\rm r}(\mathsf d)$ from
\cref{C-403-30}, and $m_{\rm x}$ from \cref{C-403-61}.
There is $\mathsf d_{\rm T}\in(0,\mathsf d_{\rm R}]$
and a nondecreasing modulus
$\epsilon_{\rm T}(\mathsf d)\to0$ such that
the following holds.

Fix $(g,K,\mathsf b,\mathsf m)$, with
$0<\mathsf d\le\mathsf d_{\rm T}$ and
$K>s(\mathsf d)$.
Let $\nu,\nu'$ each be either a torus measure
at these parameters and a side in $\mathfrak L(g)$,
regarded as a law on periodic configurations of
$a_K\mathbb Z^3$, or a torus-limit state
in $\mathcal G^{\rm tor}_{K,\beta,m_0}$.
For every
$(f,h)\in\mathfrak T_{\mathbb R^3}(\mathsf d;\vartheta)$,
at any position, and $X=((0,f),(0,h))$,
\begin{align*}
 |S_2^T[\nu](X)-S_2^T[\nu'](X)|
 &\le C^{\rm T}[\omega_{\rm r}(\mathsf d)^{1/8}
                                  +\mathsf d]\,\mathsf d\,\mathfrak f\\
 &\le\epsilon_{\rm T}(\mathsf d)
                                  \mathsf b^{-3}\mathsf d\,\mathfrak f.
\end{align*}
For torus measures the tuple is periodized.
The constants and modulus depend on $g,\vartheta$
and the chosen constants, and are independent
of the cutoff, labels, masses, sides, states,
and test pair.

Every pair in
$\mathfrak T_{T_\ell}(\mathsf d;\vartheta)$
is the periodization of such a pair on
$\mathbb R^3$. The values of
$\mathcal K_{\rm free},\mathcal K_5$ and
$\mathfrak f$ agree on the two tori and
on $\mathbb R^3$.
\end{proposition}

We choose $\mathsf d_{\rm T}$ to be the largest
number at most $\mathsf d_{\rm R}$ such that
$m_*(\mathsf d_{\rm T})\ge m_{\rm x}$ and
\[
 2\mathsf Q^2\,96^3\frac{40M}{\varrho\vartheta}
       \mathsf d^{5/2}(1+\log(1/\mathsf d))^{4\mathfrak p_0+1}
          \le1\qquad(0<\mathsf d\le\mathsf d_{\rm T}).
\]
The proof specifies $C^{\rm T}$, after which
we take
\[
 \epsilon_{\rm T}(\mathsf d)
 =\mathsf b_+^3C^{\rm T}
       \sup_{0<d'\le\mathsf d}[\omega_{\rm r}(d')^{1/8}+d'].
\]

\begin{proof}
\par\medskip\noindent\emph{Lifts, placement, and packing.}\quad 
The pair is contained in a ball
$\mathbb B(x_0,5\mathsf d)$.
On a torus this ball has radius less than
$\ell/4$, since $32\mathsf d\le\ell$.
It therefore lifts isometrically to
$\mathbb R^3$.
All template integrals use only distances
at most $10\mathsf d$, so their values
are unchanged by the lift or periodization.

The witness-depth inequality gives
$a_K<\mathsf d/(4L^3M)$.
Choose the board offset $o\in a_K\mathbb Z^3$
with $|x_0-o|_\infty\le a_K/2$.
The pair then lies in $\mathbb B(o,6\mathsf d)$.
Use the same offset and cell zero on every
torus under comparison.
Put
\[
 \delta=a_K\lceil18\mathsf d/a_K\rceil\le19\mathsf d,\quad
 \mathcal T_{\rm cell}
   =\{t\in\delta\mathbb Z^3:
             |t|_\infty\le1/(4\sqrt3)-7\mathsf d\},
 \quad N=\#\mathcal T_{\rm cell}.
\]
The translated pair at $t$ lies in
$\mathbb B(o+t,6\mathsf d)\subset\mathbb B_*$.
The balls containing distinct translated
pairs have mutual distance at least
$18\mathsf d-10\mathsf d\ge\mathsf d$.
Together with the original separation, this
makes all the $f^t,h^t$ supports pairwise disjoint.
Since $\mathsf d\le\mathsf d_{\rm R}\le1/400$,
\[
 N\ge
 \left(2\frac{1/(4\sqrt3)-7\mathsf d}{19\mathsf d}-1\right)^3
                           \ge(96\mathsf d)^{-3}.
\]
Every plaquette with barycentre in
$\mathbb B_*$ has its corners in cell zero:
the cell half-side is
$\ell_G/4-a_K/2>1/4+a_K$.
Thus all the translated observables are
bounded real functions of the links in
the cell algebra.

\par\medskip\noindent\emph{Centre with the least-torus law.}\quad 
Write $\mu_G=\mu_{K,\ell_G,\beta,m_0}$,
$\mu_f=\mu_G(O(f))$, $\mu_h=\mu_G(O(h))$,
and $\sigma=S_2^T[\mu_G](X)$.
Set
\[
 \mathsf X=\frac1N\sum_t[
        (O(f^t)-\mu_f)(O(h^t)-\mu_h)-\sigma],
 \qquad
 \mathsf X_f=\frac1N\sum_t(O(f^t)-\mu_f),
\]
and define $\mathsf X_h$ in the same way.
All are bounded real cell functions.
Translation invariance gives, for every
$\mu_\ell=\mu_{K,\ell,\beta,m_0}$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:C403-centred-covariance}
 S_2^T[\mu_\ell](X)-\sigma
      =\mu_\ell(\mathsf X)
                       -\mu_\ell(\mathsf X_f)\mu_\ell(\mathsf X_h).
\end{equation}

The chessboard inequality applies to the
even cell algebra with antiperiodic fermions:
the sides have an even number of sites,
$\beta\ge0$, $m_0>0$, and the partition
function is positive.
For the board with $N_\ell$ cells, write
\[
 \|Y\|_{{\rm ch},\ell}
    =\left(\frac{\Omega_\ell(\operatorname{Fold}Y)}
                         {Z_\ell}\right)^{1/N_\ell}.
\]
It gives $|\mu_\ell(Y)|\le\|Y\|_{{\rm ch},\ell}$
for $Y=\mathsf X,\mathsf X_f,\mathsf X_h$.

The unnormalized two-volume folded inequality
\cref{C-387-15}(C3)
applies because the boards have the same
odd cell side and the same cell zero, with
$2L^{m-m_{\mathfrak L}(g)}\ge2$ cells in
each direction on $\ell=2L^m$.
As $N_\ell=8(\ell/\ell_G)^3$, it yields
\[
 \|Y\|_{{\rm ch},\ell}
 \le\|Y\|_{{\rm ch},\ell_G}
       \left(\frac{Z_{\ell_G}^{(\ell/\ell_G)^3}}
                         {Z_\ell}\right)^{1/N_\ell}.
\]
The zero-source partition-function estimates are
\[
 Z_{\ell_G}\le e^{E_K(\ell_G)+(C+2)\ell_G^3},
 \qquad
 Z_\ell\ge e^{E_K(\ell)-C_P(1+\log x_K)\ell^3}.
\]
Here $E_K(\ell)=\ell^3\sum_{j\le K}e_jL^{3(K-j)}$
has side-independent coefficients and
$x_K\le L(g^{-2}+B_\sharp)$.
Thus the ratio is at most $e^{c_V\ell^3}$,
with
$c_V=C+2+C_P(1+\log[L(g^{-2}+B_\sharp)])$.
Combining the estimates gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:C403-side-chessboard-reduction}
 |S_2^T[\mu_\ell](X)-\sigma|
 \le e^{c_V\ell_G^3/8}\|\mathsf X\|_{{\rm ch},\ell_G}
       +e^{c_V\ell_G^3/4}
            \|\mathsf X_f\|_{{\rm ch},\ell_G}
            \|\mathsf X_h\|_{{\rm ch},\ell_G}.
\end{equation}

\par\medskip\noindent\emph{The folded generating function.}\quad 
For the eight cells on $T_{\ell_G}$, let
$\theta_c$ and $\mathbb B_*^{(c)}$ be the
reflections and balls of the board in
\cref{C-403-43-linking}.
Put $f_c^t=f^t\circ\theta_c$ and
$h_c^t=h^t\circ\theta_c$.
The cell copies preserve products and real
coefficients and send $a_p$ to $a_{\theta p}$.
Thus $\operatorname{Fold}\mathsf X=\prod_c\mathsf X_c$,
where
$\mathsf X_c=N^{-1}\sum_t[
(O(f_c^t)-\mu_f)(O(h_c^t)-\mu_h)-\sigma]$.

Introduce independent signs $\epsilon_{c,t}$,
sixteen variables $z_{c1},z_{c2}$, and
\[
 F_c=\sum_t\epsilon_{c,t}f_c^t,\quad
 H_c=\sum_t\epsilon_{c,t}h_c^t,\quad
 w_c=z_{c1}F_c+z_{c2}H_c,\quad W=\sum_cw_c .
\]
Let $\mathsf p(w)$ be the degree-one and
degree-two terms of
$\log(Z_K^{\rm sub}[w]/Z_K^{\rm sub}[0])$,
and set
$\mathsf c(w)=E_K(w)-E_K(0)+\mathsf p(w)$.
Its derivatives through order two equal
those of $\log(Z[w]/Z[0])$.
Define
\[
 \mathsf Z^{\rm c}(z)
   =e^{-\sum_c\mathsf c(w_c)}\frac{Z[W]}{Z[0]}
   =\mu_G\!\left(\prod_ce^{O(w_c)-\mathsf c(w_c)}\right).
\]
Let $I$ be the sixteen variables and
$\partial_I=\prod_c\partial_{z_{c1}}\partial_{z_{c2}}|_0$.
Differentiating centres both observables in
each cell and subtracts their covariance.
The torus symmetries identify the means
and covariance with $\mu_f,\mu_h,\sigma$.
Averaging the signs retains only $t=t'$
within each cell. Therefore
\begin{equation}\label{eq:C403-fold-derivative}
 N^{-8}\operatorname{mean}_\epsilon
                   \partial_I\mathsf Z^{\rm c}(0)
       =\mu_G(\operatorname{Fold}\mathsf X)
       =\|\mathsf X\|_{{\rm ch},\ell_G}^{8}.
\end{equation}
With all signs one and $z_{c2}=0$, the
eight derivatives $\prod_c\partial_{z_{c1}}$
give $N^8\|\mathsf X_f\|_{{\rm ch},\ell_G}^8$.
The analogous assertion holds for $h$.

Use the polydisc
\[
 \Delta=\{|z_{c1}|\le\|F_c\|_\circ^{-1},
              |z_{c2}|\le\|H_c\|_\circ^{-1}\},
 \qquad \|u\|_\circ=\|u\|_\sharp/\varrho .
\]
A sum of functions on disjoint supports,
each vanishing on the support boundary,
has sharp norm equal to the largest of
their sharp norms. For points in different
supports, follow the segment between them
to the two boundaries; the sum of the
two travelled distances is at most the
original distance. This proves the
Lipschitz assertion as well as the
supremum assertion.
Consequently
$\|F_c\|_\circ=\|f\|_\circ$,
$\|H_c\|_\circ=\|h\|_\circ$.
On $\Delta$, $W,w_c,\zeta w_c$,
$|\zeta|\le1$, all have sharp norm at most
$\varrho$ and lie in the interior of the
admitted source domain.

The subtracted partition-function bound is
$|Z_K^{\rm sub}[w]/Z_K^{\rm sub}[0]|
\le e^{c_V\ell_G^3}\le\mathsf Q$.
For
$\psi(\zeta)=Z_K^{\rm sub}[\zeta w_c]/
 Z_K^{\rm sub}[0]$,
Cauchy's estimate and $\psi(0)=1$ give
\[
 |\mathsf p(w_c)|
   =|\psi'(0)+\tfrac12(\psi''(0)-\psi'(0)^2)|
                                      \le3\mathsf Q^2 .
\]
Different cell balls have separation at
least $\ell_G/4$.
The separated-source energy estimate thus
gives
$|E_K(W)-\sum_cE_K(w_c)+7E_K(0)|
\le C_{\rm add}$, where
\[
 C_{\rm add}
   =8\sup_{K,S}\mathscr C_K(S;\ell_G/4)<\infty .
\]
Here $S$ ranges over sets in a ball of
radius $1/4$.
The count is finite because its level-$j$
cube count is at most
$(4+1/(2Ma_j))^3$, and
\[
 C_{\mathscr C}\sum_{m\ge0}
       (4+L^m/(2M))^3e^{-\kappa_{\rm E}\ell_GL^m/4}<\infty .
\]
It follows that
\[
 |\mathsf Z^{\rm c}|\le
 C_Z:=\mathsf Qe^{C_{\rm add}+24\mathsf Q^2}
                              \quad\hbox{on }\Delta .
\]

The eight-derivative identity and Cauchy's
estimate give
$\|\mathsf X_f\|_{{\rm ch},\ell_G}
\le C_Z^{1/8}N^{-1}\|f\|_\circ$.
Since
$\|f\|_\sharp\le40M\|f\|_\infty/(\vartheta\mathsf d)$
and $N^{-1}\le(96\mathsf d)^3$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:C403-fold-first-moments}
 \|\mathsf X_f\|_{{\rm ch},\ell_G}
 \|\mathsf X_h\|_{{\rm ch},\ell_G}
 \le C_Z^{1/4}
       \left(\frac{96^3\,40M}{\varrho\vartheta}\right)^2
                                      \mathsf d^4\mathfrak f.
\end{equation}

\par\medskip\noindent\emph{The remainder at the reduction scale.}\quad 
Set $k=K-m_*(\mathsf d)$.
By \cref{C-403-30}, $1\le k<K$, $a_k\ge\mathsf d$,
and $Z[W]=\mathsf A_k[W]+\mathsf B_k[W]$,
with both terms holomorphic.
Split $\mathsf Z^{\rm c}$ accordingly.
On $\Delta$ the remainder bound and
the zero-source floor give
\[
 |e^{-E_K(W)}\mathsf B_k[W]|
          \le\omega_{\rm r}(\mathsf d)M_0,\qquad
 Z_K^{\rm sub}[0]\ge M_0/\mathsf Q .
\]
Hence
$|\mathsf Z_B^{\rm c}|\le\omega_{\rm r}C_Z$.
Cauchy's estimate in sixteen variables gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:C403-fold-remainder}
 |N^{-8}\operatorname{mean}_\epsilon
                 \partial_I\mathsf Z_B^{\rm c}(0)|
          \le\omega_{\rm r}C_Zu_0^8,\qquad
 u_0=N^{-1}\|f\|_\circ\|h\|_\circ
      \le96^3(40M/\varrho)^2\vartheta^{-2}
                                          \mathsf d\mathfrak f .
\end{equation}

\par\medskip\noindent\emph{The retained term and its partitions.}\quad 
Since $0<\mathsf A_k[0]\le Z[0]$, near zero
we may write
\[
 \mathsf Z_A^{\rm c}
       =\frac{\mathsf A_k[0]}{Z[0]}e^{\mathcal L},\qquad
 \mathcal L(z)
       =\log\frac{\mathsf A_k[W]}{\mathsf A_k[0]}
                                 -\sum_c\mathsf c(w_c),
 \qquad \mathcal L(0)=0 .
\]
After taking the sixteen derivatives, sign
averaging keeps the same translation index
for the two directions in each cell.
Thus
\[
 N^{-8}\operatorname{mean}_\epsilon
                   \partial_I\mathsf Z_A^{\rm c}(0)
  =N^{-8}\sum_{(t_c)_c}\frac{\mathsf A_k[0]}{Z[0]}
          \sum_{\pi\in\operatorname{Part}(I)}
                              \prod_{b\in\pi}L_b(t).
\]
Here $L_b(t)$ is the derivative
$\partial_b\mathcal L(0)$ with the directions
$f_c^{t_c},h_c^{t_c}$.
If $b$ lies within one cell, the subtraction
of $\mathsf c(w_c)$ gives
\[
 L_b(t)=-\left.\partial_b
                   \log(1+\mathsf B_k/\mathsf A_k)[w_c]\right|_0 .
\]
It is one of $-\mathsf r_1(f_c^{t_c})$,
$-\mathsf r_1(h_c^{t_c})$,
$-\mathsf r_2(f_c^{t_c},h_c^{t_c})$
from \cref{C-403-30}.
If $b$ joins two or more cells, the
subtraction vanishes. Since
$\mathsf A_k[W]=e^{E_k(W)}\mathsf I_k[W]$,
\[
 L_b(t)
  =\left.\partial_bE_k(W)\right|_0
      +\left.\partial_b
            \log\langle e^{\mathsf T_k(W)}\rangle_k\right|_0 .
\]

\par\medskip\noindent\emph{Derivatives joining different cells.}\quad 
Let $\mathsf J$ be the directions of such
a block $b$.
They belong to a collection of sixteen
directions as in \cref{C-403-43-linking}.
The support balls and scale assumptions
have already been checked, and
$m_*(\mathsf d)\ge m_{\rm x}$ gives
$1\le k\le K-m_{\rm x}$.
Part (c) of \cref{C-403-61}, discarding its
additional separation exponential, yields
\[
 |\partial_bE_k(W)|_0
                  \le A_{16}^{\rm x}\widehat e_k[\mathsf J].
\]
For
$\varphi(z)=\langle e^{\mathsf T_k(W)}\rangle_k$,
we have $\varphi(0)=1$.
For a derivative set $\gamma$, write
$\mathsf T_k[\gamma]=\partial_\gamma\mathsf T_k(W)|_0$.
When $\gamma$ joins cells, its direct
linear source weight vanishes, and
\cref{C-403-61}(a) identifies it with the
sum of the response activities
$\mathbf R^{(l)}[\mathsf J_\gamma]$, $l\le k$,
read at the common background.

The norm estimate applies to that actual
background. If $V$ passes the level-$k$
test and $\mathsf U\in\mathsf{Ev}_k(V)$,
\cref{C-403-66}(a) supplies one regular
pair on the torus whose restrictions
are the pairs used to read every activity.
Part (c) of that lemma bounds the fibre
norm term by term by the corresponding
Grassmann norm at those restrictions.
The summed bound in \cref{C-403-61}(c)
therefore gives
$A_{16}^{\rm x}\widehat e_k[\mathsf J_\gamma]$,
uniformly over $V$.
For $\gamma$ within one cell,
\cref{C-403-30} instead gives
$C_{\rm T}\widehat e_k[\mathsf J_\gamma]$.
Put $C_\star=\max\{1,C_{\rm T},A_{16}^{\rm x}\}$.

The derivatives are even and commute.
They pass under $\langle\cdot\rangle_k$, so
\[
 \partial_\gamma\varphi(0)
   =\left\langle
      \sum_{\rho\in\operatorname{Part}(\gamma)}
                  \prod_{\eta\in\rho}\mathsf T_k[\eta]
                                      \right\rangle_k .
\]
Apply the expectation bound of \cref{C-403-30}
to this one function, and use submultiplicativity
of the fibre norm.
Splitting the pair of a cell into two
blocks costs at most $C_{\mathfrak l}$:
at $a_k\ge\mathsf d$,
\[
 \widehat e_k[\{f_c\}]\widehat e_k[\{h_c\}]
  =e_k[f_c]e_k[h_c]\mathfrak l_k^{8\mathfrak p_0+2}
                         \le C_{\mathfrak l}e_k[f_c,h_c].
\]
There are only eight cells. Hence
\[
 |\partial_\gamma\varphi(0)|
 \le\#\operatorname{Part}(I)\,\mathsf Q_k
             C_\star^{\#\gamma}C_{\mathfrak l}^{8}
                                   \widehat e_k[\mathsf J_\gamma].
\]
The moment-to-cumulant formula is
\[
 \partial_b\log\varphi(0)
   =\sum_{\pi'\in\operatorname{Part}(b)}
       (\#\pi'-1)!(-1)^{\#\pi'-1}
                           \prod_{\gamma\in\pi'}\partial_\gamma\varphi(0).
\]
Using $\mathsf Q_k\ge1$ and the combinatorial
constant $\mathsf k_{16}$ gives
\[
 |L_b(t)|\le C_{\rm lk}\mathsf Q_k^{\#b}
                                      \widehat e_k[\mathsf J],
 \qquad
 C_{\rm lk}
  =A_{16}^{\rm x}
     +\mathsf k_{16}\#\operatorname{Part}(I)^{16}
                          C_\star^{16}C_{\mathfrak l}^{136}.
\]
This bound is uniform in the translation indices.

\par\medskip\noindent\emph{The four possibilities in one cell.}\quad 
Fix a partition $\pi$ of the sixteen variables.
Bound every block joining cells as above,
and assign its factors
$\mathsf Q_k^{\#b}\widehat e_k[\mathsf J]$
to the cells containing its directions.
There are at most eight such blocks.
The remaining factors depend on $t_c$
alone, so their sums separate:
\[
 N^{-8}\sum_{(t_c)}\prod_{b\in\pi}|L_b(t)|
      \le\max\{1,C_{\rm lk}\}^{8}\prod_cv_c .
\]
Set $u_A=\mathsf Q_k^2e_k[f,h]$.
There are four possible forms of $v_c$.

If both directions of $c$ belong to blocks
joining cells, then $v_c\le C_{\mathfrak l}u_A$.
If they form one block within $c$, use
complex numbers $s_t$ of modulus one with
$s_t\mathsf r_2(f_c^t,h_c^t)
=|\mathsf r_2(f_c^t,h_c^t)|$.
Sign averaging gives
\[
 \sum_t|\mathsf r_2(f_c^t,h_c^t)|
   =\operatorname{mean}_\epsilon
      \mathsf r_2\left(\sum_t\epsilon_tf_c^t,
                            \sum_t\epsilon_ts_th_c^t\right).
\]
The disjoint-support norm bound and
\cref{C-403-30} yield
$v_c\le7\omega_{\rm r}\mathsf Q^3u_0$.

If both directions are singleton blocks,
choose phases separately for $\mathsf r_1$.
Linearity and the same norm bound give
\[
 \sum_t|\mathsf r_1(f_c^t)|
                   \le2\omega_{\rm r}\mathsf Q^2\|f\|_\circ,
 \qquad
 v_c\le4\omega_{\rm r}^2\mathsf Q^4u_0.
\]
Finally, if one is a singleton and the
other joins another cell, then
\[
 v_c\le2\omega_{\rm r}\mathsf Q^2
          N^{-1}\|f\|_\circ
                       \mathsf Q_k\widehat e_k[\{h\}],
\]
or the same with $f,h$ exchanged.
Use
$e_k[h]=\|h\|_\infty\mathsf d^3a_k^{-4}$,
$e_k[f,h]=\mathfrak f\mathsf d^{5/2}a_k^{-9/2}$,
$\mathfrak l_k\le1+\log(1/\mathsf d)$,
$a_k\le1$, and $\mathsf Q_k\ge1$.
The ratio of this last bound to $u_A$ is
at most
\[
 2\mathsf Q^2\,96^3\frac{40M}{\varrho\vartheta}
    \mathsf d^{5/2}(1+\log(1/\mathsf d))^{4\mathfrak p_0+1}
 \le1
\]
by the choice of $\mathsf d_{\rm T}$.
All four cases consequently satisfy
\[
 v_c\le v:=C_{\mathfrak l}u_A
                                  +11\omega_{\rm r}\mathsf Q^4u_0.
\]

\par\medskip\noindent\emph{Assembly and passage to states.}\quad 
Summing partitions and using
$\mathsf A_k[0]/Z[0]\le1$ gives
\[
 |N^{-8}\operatorname{mean}_\epsilon
                   \partial_I\mathsf Z_A^{\rm c}(0)|
 \le\#\operatorname{Part}(I)
                   \max\{1,C_{\rm lk}\}^{8}v^8.
\]
Combine this with
\eqref{eq:C403-fold-derivative} and \eqref{eq:C403-fold-remainder}
and $\omega_{\rm r}\le\omega_{\rm r}^{1/8}\le1$:
\[
 \|\mathsf X\|_{{\rm ch},\ell_G}
     \le C_{\mathsf X}
                   [\omega_{\rm r}(\mathsf d)^{1/8}u_0+u_A],
\]
where
\[
 C_{\mathsf X}
   =C_Z^{1/8}
     +\#\operatorname{Part}(I)^{1/8}
           \max\{1,C_{\rm lk}\}(C_{\mathfrak l}+11\mathsf Q^4).
\]
The definition of $m_*(\mathsf d)$ gives
\[
 \mathsf Q_k\le\mathsf d^{-1/8},
 \qquad a_k^{-3}\le\log(1/\mathsf d).
\]
Therefore
$u_A\le\mathfrak f\mathsf d^{9/4}
(\log(1/\mathsf d))^{3/2}\le\mathsf d^2\mathfrak f$.
For the last step, put $u=\log(1/\mathsf d)$.
The ceiling $\mathsf d_{\rm R}\le\mathsf Q^{-8}$
gives $u\ge128$, and $u^{3/2}e^{-u/4}$
decreases on $[6,\infty)$ and is below one
at $128$.

Substitute these bounds and
\eqref{eq:C403-fold-first-moments}
into \eqref{eq:C403-side-chessboard-reduction}.
For every $\ell\in\mathfrak L(g)$,
\[
 |S_2^T[\mu_\ell](X)-\sigma|
       \le\tfrac12C^{\rm T}
          [\omega_{\rm r}(\mathsf d)^{1/8}+\mathsf d]
                                      \mathsf d\mathfrak f ,
\]
where
\begin{align*}
 C^{\rm T}=2\bigg[
 &e^{c_V\ell_G^3/8}C_{\mathsf X}
       \left(1+96^3(40M/\varrho)^2\vartheta^{-2}\right)\\
 &+e^{c_V\ell_G^3/4}C_Z^{1/4}
                 \left(\frac{96^3\,40M}{\varrho\vartheta}\right)^2
                      \bigg].
\end{align*}
Every torus-limit state is a weak limit
of torus measures at these fixed parameters.
The smeared lattice observables are bounded
continuous functions of finitely many links,
so their means and products pass to the limit.
The same bound therefore holds for such
a state in place of $\mu_\ell$.
Joining two states through $\sigma$ gives
the factor two in the stated estimate.
Finally $\mathsf b\le\mathsf b_+$ gives
the estimate with $\epsilon_{\rm T}$.

The ceiling $\mathsf d_{\rm T}$ is positive.
Indeed $m_*(\mathsf d)\ge m_{\rm x}$ is
equivalent to
$8c_V^+(m_{\rm x})\ell_G^3L^{3m_{\rm x}}
\le\log(1/\mathsf d)$, and the other
ceiling inequality holds for all sufficiently
small $\mathsf d$.
The modulus is nondecreasing by construction.
It tends to zero because
$m_*(\mathsf d)\to\infty$ and the expression
for $\omega_{\rm r}$ has a factor
$L^{3m_*}$ multiplied by the exponential
of a negative multiple of
$(\log(\mathsf b_-L^{m_*}))^{2\mathfrak p_0}$,
where $2\mathfrak p_0>1$.
All constants were chosen after the
cell-response and reduction constants and
before the final distance ceiling.
They do not depend on the cutoff exponent
$P$ or on either side.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Proof of the finite-cutoff expansion}
\label{sec:proof-C40313}

\begin{proof}[Proof of \cref{C-403-13}]
Fix \(g,\vartheta,P\). All constants used in this proof have
already been chosen in \cref{C-403-16}.
Put \(d_\natural=\min\{d_1,d_{\rm T}\}\).
The threshold in \cref{C-403-38} satisfies
\[
 d_{\rm T}\le d_{\rm R}\le
 \min\{d_0(g,\vartheta),
                  e^{-8c_V^+(1)\ell_G^3L^3}\},
\]
so the reduction depth \(m_*(d)\) is at least one.
For \(d\le d_\natural\) and \(K>s(d)\) we have
\(a_K<d/8\) and \(\mathsf m d\le1/10\).
Write \(\tau=a_K/d\) and \(\lg u=1+|\log u|\).

\emph{Averaging on the least torus.}
First suppose \(\ell=\ell_G\).
The two supports lie in a ball \(B(x_0,5d)\).
Take
\[
 \delta=a_K\lceil17d/a_K\rceil,\qquad
 n_\delta=\lfloor\ell_G/\delta\rfloor,\qquad
 \mathcal T=\delta\{0,\ldots,n_\delta-1\}^3 .
\]
Here \(17d\le\delta\le18d\). Two distinct translates differ
in some coordinate by \(k\delta\), \(1\le|k|<n_\delta\);
their circular distance in that coordinate is at least
\(\min\{\delta,\ell_G-(n_\delta-1)\delta\}\ge\delta\).
Thus the balls \(B(x_0+t,8d)\), \(t\in\mathcal T\),
are separated by at least \(d\).
Since \(\ell_G\ge2\) and \(d\le1/64\),
\[
 N_\delta:=\#\mathcal T
 \ge\left(\frac{\ell_G}{18d}-1\right)^3
 \ge\left(\frac{\ell_G}{24d}\right)^3.
\]
Apply \cref{C-403-30}(e) to these translates:
\[
 S^T_2((0,f),(0,h))
   =\frac1{N_\delta}\sum_{t\in\mathcal T}
                  \sum_{j\le K}\mathsf n_j^1(t)+R,\qquad
 |R|\le\epsilon_{\rm R}(d)\mathsf b^{-3}d\,\mathfrak f .
\]
The mixed source jet \(\mathsf n_j^\lambda(t)\) is the one in
\cref{C-403-33}. At \(\lambda=1\) its source energy is the
source energy of the original flow, so the finite sum of its
mixed derivatives is the derivative appearing in the reduction.

\emph{The fourth and sixth coefficients.}
Each \(\mathsf n_j^\lambda(t)\) is even and holomorphic in
\(\lambda\), and vanishes to order four at zero. At \(p=3\),
\cref{C-403-33}(ii) gives
\[
 \begin{split}
 \left|\sum_{j\le K}
   [\mathsf n_j^1(t)-\mathsf n_{j,[4]}(t)
                         -\mathsf n_{j,[6]}(t)]\right|
 \le C_3^{\rm ii}\frac d{\mathsf b_-}
       \left(\max\left\{1,\log\frac{2\mathsf b_+}{d}\right\}\right)
                    ^{8\mathfrak p_0}
               \mathsf b^{-3}d\,\mathfrak f .
 \end{split}
\]
The bound is independent of \(t\). By \cref{C-403-55}(c),(d),
the average of the fourth coefficients differs from
\(c_2\mathsf b^{-2}\mathcal K_{\rm free}(f,h)\) by at most
\[
 \left[C_{\rm ord}X_gd^2\mathsf b^{-3}d
           +\frac{3C_{\rm tm}}{2\vartheta}
                        \mathsf b^{-2}\tau\right]\mathfrak f .
\]
The hypothesis \(L^K\le d^{-P}\) is used in
\cref{C-403-35}, with \(m=3\), to identify the sixth
coefficient. Its average differs by at most
\(C_3\epsilon'_3(d)\mathsf b^{-3}d\,\mathfrak f\) from
\[
 \mathsf b^{-3}\mathsf P_1^{\rm lat}(f,h;a_K)
   +a_K\mathsf b^{-3}N_f
        \sum_{p,q}f(x(p))h(x(q))
                       \mathsf B_1^F(p,q;a_K\mathsf m).
\]
The factor \(a_K\) comes from the physical normalization
\(O(f)=a_K^{-1}\sum_pf(x(p))a_p\) and
\(\beta^{-3}=a_K^3\mathsf b^{-3}\).
The determinant part in this formula is precisely the
quadratic fermion loop identified in
\cref{lem:C403-fermionic-covariance-coefficient}.

By \cref{IV-73-73,IV-73-100}, the pure contribution is
\[
 \frac3{2\pi^3}\mathsf b^{-3}\mathcal K_5(f,h)
       +R_{\rm pure},\qquad
 |R_{\rm pure}|\le C_{\rm IV}\vartheta^{-1}
                \tau\lg(1/\tau)\mathsf b^{-3}d\,\mathfrak f.
\]
By \cref{prop:C403-polarization-position}, the fermion
contribution is
\[
 -\frac{3N_f}{8\pi^3}\mathsf b^{-3}
   \iint f(x)h(y)|x-y|^{-5}
                 \mathcal F(\mathsf m|x-y|)\,dx\,dy+R_{\rm vp},
\]
where
\[
 |R_{\rm vp}|\le C_{\rm vp}
                \tau\lg(1/\tau)\mathsf b^{-3}d\,\mathfrak f,
 \qquad
 \mathcal F(s)=\frac{1-(1+s)e^{-2s}}s,\quad \mathcal F(0)=1 .
\]
All its hypotheses hold: \(8a_K\le d\),
\(a_K\mathsf m\le1\) and \(\mathsf m d\le1\).

The mass profile has
\[
 0\le1-\mathcal F(s)\le\frac23s^2,\qquad s\ge0.
\]
The first inequality is \cref{C-403-12}(b).
For the second, the function
\(\varphi(s)=\frac23s^3-s+1-(1+s)e^{-2s}\) satisfies
\(\varphi(0)=\varphi'(0)=0\) and
\(\varphi''(s)=4s(1-e^{-2s})\ge0\).
Using \eqref{C-403-4} at \(q=3\), the error made by replacing
\(\mathcal F\) by one is at most
\[
 \frac{3N_f}{8\pi^3}\frac23\mathsf m^2
       \mathcal K_3(f,h)\mathsf b^{-3}
 \le\frac{4N_f}{9\pi}(\mathsf m_+d)^2
                    \mathsf b^{-3}d\,\mathfrak f .
\]
The two coefficients now add to
\[
 \frac3{2\pi^3}-\frac{3N_f}{8\pi^3}
        =c_2\mathfrak c_1(N_f).
\]

\emph{Combining the errors.}
Put \(C_\diamond=C_{\rm IV}\vartheta^{-1}+C_{\rm vp}\) and
\[
 \begin{split}
 \Sigma_0(d)={}&\epsilon_{\rm R}(d)
   +C_3^{\rm ii}\frac d{\mathsf b_-}
       \left(\max\left\{1,\log\frac{2\mathsf b_+}{d}\right\}\right)
                   ^{8\mathfrak p_0}
   +C_{\rm ord}X_gd^2\\
 &\quad+C_3\epsilon'_3(d)
                  +\frac{4N_f}{9\pi}(\mathsf m_+d)^2 .
 \end{split}
\]
The least-torus error is bounded by
\[
 \left[\Sigma_0(d)\mathsf b^{-3}d
   +C_\diamond\tau\lg(1/\tau)\mathsf b^{-3}d
   +\frac{3C_{\rm tm}}{2\vartheta}\mathsf b^{-2}\tau\right]
                                                           \mathfrak f .
\]
To remove the logarithm from the mesh error, split into two
cases. If \(\lg(1/\tau)\le\mathsf b/d\), its contribution
is at most \(C_\diamond\mathsf b^{-2}\tau\mathfrak f\).
Otherwise \(\tau<e^{1-\mathsf b/d}\).
The function \(u(1-\log u)\) increases on \((0,1]\), and
\(xe^{1-x}\) decreases on \([1,\infty)\). Since
\(\mathsf b\ge\mathsf b_->d\), this gives
\[
 \tau\lg(1/\tau)\le
       \frac{\mathsf b}{d}e^{1-\mathsf b/d}
       \le\eta_{\rm lat}(d)
       :=\frac{\mathsf b_-}{d}e^{1-\mathsf b_-/d}.
\]
Thus in both cases the error is at most
\[
 \left[(\Sigma_0(d)+C_\diamond\eta_{\rm lat}(d))
                                  \mathsf b^{-3}d
      +C_{\rm lat}\mathsf b^{-2}\frac{a_K}{d}\right]\mathfrak f,
 \qquad
 C_{\rm lat}=\max\left\{1,\frac{3C_{\rm tm}}{2\vartheta}
                                      +C_\diamond\right\}.
\]

For another torus, lift the pair to \(\mathbb R^3\) and
periodize it on \(T_{\ell_G}\), as in \cref{C-403-38}.
The supports lie in a ball of radius \(5d<\ell_G/4\), and
\(32d\le\ell_G\), so the distances, integrals, suprema and
Lipschitz bounds are preserved. A path from a support to its
complement first meets its boundary, where the function
vanishes; this also checks the Lipschitz bound across the
period boundary. The same lemma bounds the change in the
two-point function by
\(\epsilon_{\rm T}(d)\mathsf b^{-3}d\,\mathfrak f\).
It gives exactly the same comparison for a torus-limit state
on the infinite lattice.

Finally set
\[
 \Sigma(d)=\Sigma_0(d)+C_\diamond\eta_{\rm lat}(d)
                                      +\epsilon_{\rm T}(d).
\]
Every term tends to zero. The number
\[
 d^*=\sup\{d'\le d_\natural:
                       \Sigma(d)\le1\text{ for }0<d\le d'\}
\]
is positive. Choose \(d_{\rm e}=d^*/2\) and
\(\epsilon_1(d)=\sup_{0<d'\le d}\Sigma(d')\).
These have all the asserted dependencies and prove
\eqref{eq:C403-finite-expansion}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Removing the cutoff on a fixed torus}
\label{sec:proof-C403151}

\begin{proof}[Proof of \cref{C-403-151}]
The finite-cutoff expansion is only available when \(L^K\)
is bounded by a fixed power of \(d^{-1}\).
We choose a cutoff in that range and use the quantitative
cutoff estimate to control the remaining tail.

The constants can be chosen jointly. Choose \(h_F\) after
the constants on the left of \eqref{eq:C403-F1}, then choose
the leg constants. The enlarged free-history constants
precede \(A_0\), and the energy constants precede the final
choice of \(\mathscr C\). The coupling ceilings are imposed
last. Thus the floors and ceilings in \cref{C-418-2} do not
invalidate \cref{C-403-16}.

At \(n=2\), let the rate and cutoff exponent from
\cref{C-418-7}(iii) be
\[
 c^{\rm fs}=\frac{c_\#}{92},\qquad
 P^{\rm fs}=\frac{920}{c_\#},
\]
and write its constants as \(K^{\rm fs}(g,\ell)\) and
\(C^{\rm fs}(g,\ell)\).
Put \(P_\star=P^{\rm fs}+1\) and apply
\cref{C-403-13} with \(P=P_\star+1\).

Choose \(d_W\in(0,1/L]\) so that, for every \(0<d\le d_W\),
\begin{equation}\label{eq:C403-witness-cutoff}
 d^{1-P_\star}\ge
 L\mathsf c_W
       [\log(d^{-P_\star}(X_g+\bar B))]^{2\mathfrak p_0}.
\end{equation}
Such a choice exists: with \(v=\log(1/d)\), the two sides
grow respectively as \(e^{(P_\star-1)v}\) and a polynomial
in \(v\).
Set
\[
 d_2=\min\{d_{\rm e},\ell/20,d_W,L^{-K^{\rm fs}(g,\ell)}\}.
\]
For \(d\le d_2\), choose
\[
 K(d)=\lceil P_\star\log_L(1/d)\rceil .
\]
Then
\[
 d^{-P_\star}\le L^{K(d)}
       <L d^{-P_\star}\le d^{-P},
\]
because \(d\le1/L\). Also \(K(d)>s(d)\). Indeed
\[
 L^{K(d)-1}d\ge L^{-1}d^{1-P_\star},\qquad
 \bar x_{K(d)-1}<d^{-P_\star}(X_g+\bar B),
\]
so \eqref{eq:C403-witness-cutoff} places \(K(d)-1\) in the
set defining \(s(d)\). Finally,
\[
 K(d)\ge
 P^{\rm fs}\max\{0,\log_L(1/d)\}+K^{\rm fs}(g,\ell).
\]
Thus both the finite-cutoff expansion and the cutoff tail
estimate apply at \(K(d)\).

By \cref{C-418-8}, the difference between the continuum
two-point function and the one at this cutoff is at most
\[
 \frac{C^{\rm fs}(g,\ell)}{1-L^{-c^{\rm fs}}}
       d^{c^{\rm fs}P_\star}
                     \|f\|_\sharp\|h\|_\sharp .
\]
For the present class and \(d\le1\),
\[
 \|f\|_\sharp\le
       \frac{1+40M}{\vartheta d}\|f\|_\infty,\qquad
 \|h\|_\sharp\le
       \frac{1+40M}{\vartheta d}\|h\|_\infty .
\]
The mesh term in \cref{C-403-13} is at most
\(C_{\rm lat}\mathsf b^{-2}d^{P_\star-1}\mathfrak f\).
Since \(\mathsf b\le X_g\), their sum is bounded as in
\eqref{C-403-152} with
\[
 \begin{split}
 \epsilon_2(d)={}&\epsilon_1(d)
       +C_{\rm lat}X_gd^{P_\star-2}\\
 &+\frac{(1+40M)^2C^{\rm fs}(g,\ell)X_g^3}
             {\vartheta^2(1-L^{-c^{\rm fs}})}
                         d^{c^{\rm fs}P_\star-3}.
 \end{split}
\]
Both exponents are positive:
\(P_\star-2>0\) and
\(c^{\rm fs}P_\star-3=7+c_\#/92>0\).
This proves (a), including the dependence and monotonicity
of the error.

For (b), the bounds \eqref{C-403-4} give
\[
 \mathcal K_6\ge10^{-6}\vartheta^2\mathfrak f,\qquad
 \mathcal K_5\ge10^{-5}\vartheta^2d\,\mathfrak f .
\]
The error in the first quotient of \eqref{C-403-153} is
therefore at most
\[
 10^6\vartheta^{-2}\mathsf b^{-3}d
       \left[(4\pi/3)^2|\mathfrak c_1(N_f)|
                         +\epsilon_2(d)/c_2\right],
\]
and the error in the second is at most
\[
 \frac{10^5}{c_2\vartheta^2}\epsilon_2(d).
\]
Both tend to zero, uniformly over the test pairs.

For (c), subtract the two expansions. Since distinct
integer flavour numbers satisfy
\[
 c_2|\mathfrak c_1(N_f)-\mathfrak c_1(N'_f)|
                       \ge\frac3{8\pi^3},
\]
the modulus of the difference is at least
\[
 \left[\frac{3\vartheta^2}{8\pi^3}10^{-5}
                -\epsilon_2(d)-\epsilon'_2(d)\right]
                                  \mathsf b^{-3}d\,\mathfrak f.
\]
This is positive under the stated condition.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Changing the volume and identifying the coefficient}
\label{sec:proof-C403154}

\begin{proof}[Proof of \cref{C-403-154}]
\emph{Comparison with the least torus.}
The comparison in \cref{C-403-38} holds for every
\(K>s(d)\); it has no upper bound on \(L^K\).
At any real label \((\mathsf b',\mathsf m')\in\mathsf W(g)\)
it bounds the difference between the two-point function on
any allowed torus, or in any torus-limit lattice state,
and the function on \(T_{\ell_G}\), by
\[
 C^{\rm T}[\omega_{\rm r}(d)^{1/8}+d]\,d\,\mathfrak f
       \le\epsilon_{\rm T}(d)\mathsf b^{-3}d\,\mathfrak f .
\]
In the last inequality \(\mathsf b\) can be any label in
\(\bar I(g)\): the definition of \(\epsilon_{\rm T}\) uses
the upper endpoint \(\mathsf b_+\).
Lift and periodize the pair as in the proof of
\cref{C-403-13}; the functions \(\mathcal K_5,\mathcal K_6\)
and \(\mathfrak f\) are unchanged.

For a fixed torus, let \(K\to\infty\) with the label held
fixed. By \cref{C-418-8}, both lattice functions converge
at these Lipschitz entries. Add the least-torus expansion
from \cref{C-403-151}. This proves (a).
The moving-label convergence and the agreement with
the \(C^1\) continuum limits both follow from \cref{C-418-8}.

For (b), take a sequence defining \(S\), either with sides
tending to infinity or with torus-limit lattice states.
After restricting the sequence, its labels converge to
\((\mathsf b,\mathsf m)\in\mathsf W(g)\).
On \(C^1\) pairs the first two-point function converges to
the defining value of \(S_2\). On the least torus,
\cref{C-418-8} gives convergence along the entire
sequence of labels. Passing to the limit in the comparison
gives
\[
 |S_2((0,f),(0,h))
      -S^{(\ell_G,\mathsf b,\mathsf m)}_2
        ((0,f^{\langle\ell_G\rangle}),
         (0,h^{\langle\ell_G\rangle}))|
 \le\epsilon_{\rm T}(d)\mathsf b^{-3}d\,\mathfrak f .
\]
Adding the least-torus expansion proves \eqref{C-403-155}.
The division estimates and the flavour gap in the proof
of \cref{C-403-151} now prove (c).

\emph{Comparison with the pure theory.}
Use the admitted pure-theory constants of (d)(i).
The pure short-distance estimate and its extension through
all sufficiently deep cutoffs are \cref{C-350-3}(c).
On the least pure torus it gives a threshold \(d'_{\rm e}\)
and an error \(\bar\epsilon'(d)\to0\).
The side comparison \cref{C-350-21} costs at most
\[
 C_2^{\rm T}(g_0)\vartheta^{-1}
                   d^2(\mathsf b')^{-2}\mathfrak f
\]
when \(K\ge3\) and \(a_K\le9d\).
Put
\[
 \mathsf b_+^0=\bar L(g_0^{-2}+\bar B^0),\qquad
 d^0=\min\{d'_{\rm e},1/180,d_\star\},\qquad
 \epsilon^0(d)=\bar\epsilon'(d)
            +C_2^{\rm T}(g_0)\vartheta^{-1}\mathsf b_+^0d,
\]
where \(d_\star\) is the threshold in \cref{C-350-21}.
For each fixed \(d\le d^0\), pass to the defining
first-passage sequence of \(S^0\). Its depths tend to
infinity and its labels \(\mathsf b_j\) tend to
\(\mathsf b\), while \(a_{K_j}/d\to0\).
The pure expansion and the side comparison therefore give
the displayed estimate for \(S^0\).
The coefficient gap from the matter theory is
\[
 c_2|\mathfrak c_1(N_f)-\mathfrak c_1(0)|
       =\frac{3N_f}{8\pi^3}\ge\frac3{8\pi^3}.
\]
The same lower bound \eqref{C-403-4} proves the asserted
inequality of the two-point functions.

The existence assertion at
\(\mathsf b\in I(g_0)\) is \cite[Prop.~92.1]{YMM1}.
For this label, the data \(K,L^K\mathsf b\) are admitted
at every cutoff; taking their sides to infinity and extracting
a subsequence gives a pure growing-torus limit with the same label.
The estimate just proved applies to each such limit.
For the stated explicit choice of \(g_0\), the lower bound
on \(\mathsf b\) gives the required coupling ceiling.
It also gives \(\mathsf b\ge6\bar B^0\), since the admitted
pure constants have
\((\gamma_W^{\rm sd})^{-2}\ge4\bar B^0\).
Now \(g_0^{-2}=\mathsf b-2\bar B^0\), so
\(\mathsf b>g_0^{-2}+\bar B^0\).
For the upper end of \(I(g_0)\), use \(\bar L\ge13\):
\[
 \bar L(g_0^{-2}+B_\sharp^0)-\bar B^0-\mathsf b
  =(\bar L-1)\mathsf b-(2\bar L+1)\bar B^0
                       +\bar L B_\sharp^0\ge0.
\]
This verifies \(\mathsf b\in I(g_0)\).

\emph{Dilations.}
The pair \((f_\lambda,h_\lambda)\) belongs to
\(\mathfrak T_{\mathbb R^3}(\lambda d;\vartheta)\):
the supports and separation scale by \(\lambda\),
the integrals by \(\lambda^3\), the Lipschitz constants by
\(\lambda^{-1}\), and the suprema do not change.
Changing variables gives
\[
 \mathcal K_q(f_\lambda,h_\lambda)
                      =\lambda^{6-q}\mathcal K_q(f,h).
\]
Thus \eqref{C-403-155} is exactly \eqref{C-403-156}.
Divide its remainder by \(\lambda\) to obtain the limit.
Apply that formula at \(\lambda\) and \(\lambda/2\).
Monotonicity of \(\epsilon_4\) bounds the sum of the
remainders by
\(\frac32\epsilon_4(\lambda d)\mathsf b^{-3}
\lambda d\,\mathfrak f\).
If \(N_f\ne4\), then
\[
 \frac12c_2|\mathfrak c_1(N_f)|\mathcal K_5(f,h)
 \ge\frac{3\vartheta^2}{16\pi^3}10^{-5}d\,\mathfrak f,
\]
which proves the strict lower bound in (d)(ii).
At \(N_f=4\) the coefficient vanishes, leaving the
stated remainder estimate.
\end{proof}

\appendix
\section{Comparing two meshes}\label{sec:qcdm2-two-mesh}

We compare the fermion operators reconstructed on two bare lattices at a common block scale. The comparison controls their inverses and the determinant at the start of the restarted flow.

\subsection{Block operators in physical units}

We first record the estimates for the chamber operator
that will be used to compare two meshes. Their constants
do not require a lower bound on the mass.
Fix $r=1/2$, odd $L\ge13$ and $b_F>0$. In units in
which the target block lattice has spacing one, let
$\xi=L^{-j}$ be the bare spacing and $\ell'$ the side.
The spinor norm is $\|f\|^2=\xi^3\sum_v|f(v)|^2$.
Write $f=\iota\varphi+g$, where $\iota$ is the
isometric inclusion of chamber-independent spinors and
$g=\Pi_1f$. Put
\[
 \mathcal N(f)^2=\|\nabla^U\varphi\|^2+\xi^{-2}\|g\|^2,
 \qquad (\nabla_e^U\varphi)(x)
  =\xi^{-1}(U(x,x+\xi e)\varphi(x+\xi e)-\varphi(x)),
\]
with both orientations in the gradient norm.

\begin{lemma}[Energy estimates independent of the mesh]
\label{C-408-8}
Let $\alpha=\xi^{-2}\max_p|\partial U(p)-1|$.
There are constants $c_1',C_{\rm en}>0$, depending
only on the chamber operator, such that
\[
 \begin{split}
 \operatorname{Re}\langle f,D^\xi[U]f\rangle
   &\ge\tfrac12\lambda_\rho\xi^{-1}\|g\|^2
                           +c_\Delta\xi\|\nabla^U\varphi\|^2,\\
 \|D^\xi[U]f\|^2
   &\ge\tfrac12c_1'\mathcal N(f)^2
                      -C_{\rm en}(\alpha+\ell'^{-2})\|f\|^2.
 \end{split}
\]
For $m\ge0$,
$\|(D^\xi[U]+m)f\|\ge\|D^\xi[U]f\|$ and
$\operatorname{Re}(D^\xi[U]+m-\widehat J)
\ge m-\sup|J|$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The first inequality is the chamber coercivity in
\cite[\S5]{QCDM1}, after inserting the powers of
$\xi$ in the norm and difference. The last two
claims follow by expanding the square and using
$\operatorname{Re}D^\xi\ge0$.

For the second inequality at $U=1$, the heavy block
of $\widehat D(p)$ has real part at least
$\lambda_\rho$, its light-heavy couplings are $O(|p|)$,
and its light Schur complement is
$i\gamma\cdot p+O(|p|^2)$. Thus its two block
equations control $|p||\Pi_0f|+|\Pi_1f|$ near zero.
Away from zero the symbol is invertible, and compactness
gives a positive minimum. Equivalently,
\[
 c_1'=\inf_{p\ne0,f\ne0}
 \frac{|\widehat D(p)f|^2}{2\widehat p^2|\Pi_0f|^2+|\Pi_1f|^2}>0,
 \qquad \widehat p^2=\sum_\mu(2-2\cos p_\mu).
\]
Plancherel proves the free bound with coefficient $c_1'$.

Set $R=\min\{\alpha^{-1/2},\ell'/4\}$.
If $R<\xi$, the error in the statement absorbs
$\mathcal N(f)^2\le24\xi^{-2}\|f\|^2$.
Otherwise choose $\sum_i\chi_i^2=1$ subordinate to
cubes of side $2R$, with bounded overlap and
$\operatorname{Lip}\chi_i\le C/R$.
The range-one property gives
$\|[D^\xi,\chi_i]\|\le C/R$, while
\[
 \sum_i\chi_i[D^\xi,\chi_i]
                 =-\tfrac12\sum_i[[D^\xi,\chi_i],\chi_i]
\]
has norm at most $C\xi/R^2$.
Expanding the squared localized norms therefore gives
\[
 \|D^\xi f\|^2\ge\sum_i\|D^\xi\chi_if\|^2-CR^{-2}\|f\|^2.
\]
In a complete axial gauge on one cube, each link is
a product of at most $6R/\xi$ plaquette holonomies,
so it differs from one by at most $6R\xi\alpha$.
The operator and gradient differ from their free
versions by $CR\alpha$. Apply the free estimate
to each $\chi_if$ and use the gradient localization
identity. Two applications of
$(a-b)^2\ge2^{-1/2}a^2-(1+\sqrt2)b^2$ leave the
coefficient $c_1'/2$ and error
$C(R^{-2}+R^2\alpha^2)\le C(2\alpha+16\ell'^{-2})$.
The antiperiodic seam is absorbed in the local gauge;
it changes no plaquette. This proves the claim.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Averages at the level of the spinor]
\label{C-408-9}
Let $U$ have bare spacing $\xi_j=L^{-j}$ and satisfy
$|\partial U(p)-1|\le c^{\rm SO}_2\xi_j^2$ at every plaquette,
so that all its successive averages are defined. Put
\[
 \alpha=\max_{0\le n\le j}\xi_n^{-2}
          \max_p|\partial(\mathcal M^{j-n}U)(p)-1|,
 \qquad \xi_n=L^{-n}.
\]
Let $R(U)$ be the composite average onto the unit
lattice, normalized by $RR^*=1$. Then
\[
 \begin{split}
 R(U)&=\widetilde R(\mathcal MU)Q(U)\iota^*,\\
 \|\nabla^{\mathcal MU}(Q(U)\varphi)\|
 &\le(1+CL^2\alpha\xi^2)\|\nabla^U\varphi\|
                       +CL^2\alpha\xi\|\varphi\|,\\
 \|\nabla(R\iota\varphi)\|
 &\le C_A(\|\nabla^U\varphi\|+\alpha\|\varphi\|),\\
 \|\varphi-(R\iota)^*(R\iota)\varphi\|
 &\le\tfrac34\|\nabla^U\varphi\|+C_A'\alpha\|\varphi\|.
 \end{split}
\]
The constants are independent of the number of steps.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The composite is formed with the averaged configuration
at each successive level, so its first factor is
$Q(U)\iota^*$ and its remaining factors form
$\widetilde R(\mathcal MU)$. Their normalized adjoints
are isometries, proving the first identity and $RR^*=1$.
Two contour transports in one block differ by at most
$\frac32L^2\alpha\xi^2$: join them by the corresponding
plaquette surface and telescope the product. Thus the
normalized contour mean differs from any chosen contour
by $O(L^2\alpha\xi^2)$. The same comparison holds
between a block link and a chosen joining path.
Taking a covariant difference of the block average
now gives the second inequality. At successive meshes
$\xi_n=L^{-n}$ its errors contain $\xi_n$ or
$\xi_n^2$. Their sums and products are bounded,
which proves the third inequality.

In a unit cube an axial gauge makes each bare link
within $2\alpha\xi_j$ of one. The same gauge makes
each averaged link within $C\alpha\xi_n$ of one,
by \cite[Prop.~14.1]{YMM1}. Summing the contour errors
over the levels shows that $R\iota$ differs from
the ordinary unit-cube mean by at most $C\alpha$.
Also the transformed ordinary gradient differs from
the covariant gradient by at most $C\alpha$.
The cube Poincar\'e inequality has constant
$\sqrt3/\pi<3/4$. Apply it in this gauge and undo
the gauge to prove the last estimate.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Block operators uniformly in the mass]
\label{C-408-5}
There are $\epsilon_S,\varrho_S,\varrho'_S,\delta_0>0$
and $C_{\rm side}\ge1$, depending only on $L,b_F$
and the chamber operator, with the following property.
Suppose $\ell'\ge C_{\rm side}$,
$|\partial U(p)-1|\le\epsilon_S\xi^2$, $m\ge0$,
$a\in[a_-,a_+]=[b_F(1-L^{-1}),b_F]$. Let $J$ be a matrix
field on the bare sites with values in the complex span of
$\mathfrak B$, acting by the same matrix $\widehat J$ on every
chamber at a site, and assume $\sup|J|\le m/2+\varrho_S$. Then
\[
 \mathcal S=(D^\xi[U]+m-\widehat J+aR^*R)^{-1},
 \qquad T=R\mathcal SR^*,\qquad D=a-a^2T
\]
exist, and $|T(y,y')|\le Ce^{-\delta_0|y-y'|}$.
If the target has a next block level, the bare
curvature is at most $\epsilon_S\xi^2/L^2$, and
$\sup|J|\le m/2+\min\{\varrho_S,\varrho'_S/L\}$,
then $\Gamma=D+b_Fq^*q$ has
\[
 \max\left\{\sup_y\sum_{y'},\sup_{y'}\sum_y\right\}
          e^{\delta_0|y-y'|/(2L)}|\Gamma^{-1}(y,y')|\le C.
\]
Here $q=L^{-1/2}Q$ at that level.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
First take $\sup|J|\le m/2$. Put
$G=(D^\xi+m-\widehat J+aR^*R)f$ and
$P=(R\iota)^*(R\iota)$. The penalty lives on
chamber-independent spinors. Pair the equation with
$f$ and take real parts to obtain
\[
 a\|P\varphi\|^2\le\|f\|\|G\|,
 \qquad (m/2)\|f\|^2\le\|f\|\|G\|.
\]
In particular $\sup|J|\|f\|\le\|G\|$.
The energy and averaging estimates give
\[
 \sqrt{c_1'/2}\mathcal N(f)
 \le2\|G\|+a\|P\varphi\|
            +\sqrt{C_{\rm en}(\alpha+\ell'^{-2})}\|f\|,
\]
and
$\|f\|\le\|P\varphi\|+\frac54\mathcal N(f)+C_A'\alpha\|f\|$.
Choose $\epsilon_S\le c^{\rm SO}_2$ and the side floor so that
\[
 \tfrac54\sqrt{2C_{\rm en}(\alpha+\ell'^{-2})/c_1'}
                             +C_A'\alpha\le\tfrac12.
\]
The small-curvature averaging bound of
\cite[Prop.~14.1]{YMM1} gives $\alpha\le2\epsilon_S$
at every level. The inequalities close and give
\[
 \|f\|\le C_{\mathcal S}\|G\|,\qquad
 \mathcal N(f)\le C_\nabla\|G\|,
\]
with
\[
 C_{\mathcal S}=4A^2+10\sqrt2(c_1')^{-1/2},\qquad
 A=(1+5\sqrt2a_+/(4\sqrt{c_1'}))a_-^{-1/2}.
\]
The finite-dimensional operator is therefore invertible.

Take $\varrho_S=(6C_{\mathcal S})^{-1}$.
Split a larger source into a part of norm at most
$m/2$ and a remainder of norm at most $\varrho_S$.
Conjugating by $e^h$, with
$|h(x)-h(x')|\le\delta_0|x-x'|$, changes the
Dirac term by $C\delta_0$, because it has range one
mesh. It changes the penalty by the same order,
because it acts within unit cubes. For sufficiently
small $\delta_0$ the total change is at most
$(2C_{\mathcal S})^{-1}$. The Neumann series bounds
the conjugated inverse uniformly. Smearing by $R,R^*$
then gives the exponential kernel bound for $T$.

For the final assertion set $b_F'=b_F/L$,
$P_1=Q^*Q$, $Y=(a+b_F'P_1)^{-1}$ and
$a'=ab_F'/(a+b_F')$. The resolvent identity gives
\[
 \Gamma^{-1}=Y+a^2YT'Y,\qquad
 T'=R(D^\xi+m-\widehat J+a'(QR)^*(QR))^{-1}R^*.
\]
Indeed $Y=a^{-1}-a^{-2}a'P_1$; multiplication by
$\Gamma$ verifies the identity. The parameter
$La'$ belongs to $[a_-,a_+]$.
Dilate by $L$ so the next block lattice has spacing
one. The curvature is multiplied by $L^2$, the
mass, source and penalty by $L$, and the side is
divided by $L$. Choose $C_{\rm side}$ to include
this extra factor. The stronger curvature and
source hypotheses let the preceding inverse proof
apply. Its decay is $\delta_0/L$ in the old units.
The kernels of $Y$ are supported in blocks of side
$L$. Sum the identity with weight
$e^{\delta_0|y-y'|/(2L)}$ to obtain the assertion.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}\label{C-408-7}
The side floor is used even at zero curvature: the
localization error contains $\ell'^{-2}$. The mass
does not enter the constants. Invertibility at small
mass comes from the block penalty and Poincar\'e
inequality.
\end{remark}

\subsection{Comparing the fermion operators on two meshes}\label{C-420-1}

At the restart level the two cutoffs have the same block lattice.
Their quadratic forms nevertheless use different bare lattices and
different classical backgrounds. We compare the forms in two steps:
first change the background on one bare lattice, and then change the
bare spacing. The mass term carried into the restart is obtained by
differentiating the same quadratic form. A Cauchy estimate therefore
gives its comparison without a separate expansion.

\begin{definition}[The common block lattice]\label{C-420-2}
Use the positive-mass data of \cref{C-418-2}, with chamber fermions,
$r=1/2$, $N_f\ge1$, and $\nu=8N_f$. In particular the constants
are those of \cite[Prop.\ 10.20]{QCDM1}, with its positive lower
mass $\mathsf m_-$ and the source radii chosen there. The two data are
\[
 \mathrm A=(g,\ell,K,\mathsf b,\mathsf m),\qquad
 \mathrm B=(g,\ell,K+1,\mathsf b,\mathsf m).
\]
Their classical comparison uses the hypotheses and constants of
\cite[\S113, in particular eq.\ (2146) and Prop.\ 113.9]{YMM1}.
Thus the blocks and averaging maps agree at partner levels, although
their classical backgrounds can differ. Choose $1\le u<s<K$ and put
\[
 t_0=K-s,\quad t_1=K-u,\quad
 N_{[d]}=\ell^3L^{3d},\quad x_{[d]}=L^d\mathsf b,\quad
 \varepsilon_{\rm r}=2c_\rho\varepsilon(L^s\mathsf b).
\]
Level $t_0$ of $\mathrm A$ and level $t_0+1$ of $\mathrm B$ have
the common lattice $\Lambda_{s,\ell}$. In units where its spacing
is one, the bare spacings are
$\xi^{\rm A}=\xi=L^{-t_0}$ and $\xi^{\rm B}=\xi/L$.
The spinor inner product at spacing $\xi'$ is $\xi'^3\sum f^*f'$.
The common block space $\mathsf H_{[s]}$ has dimension $\nu N_{[s]}$.
The mass and source in these units are
\[
 \mathfrak m_s=L^{-s}\mathsf m,\qquad J_s=L^{-s}J,
 \qquad \operatorname{Lip}_s(J_s)=L^{-2s}\operatorname{Lip}(J).
\]
Here $J$ takes values in the complex span of the permitted bilinear
matrices. This span contains the identity.

For either bare field $U$, let $R=R^\bullet(U)$ be the composite
fermion average, normalized by $RR^*=1$, and set
\[
 a^{\rm A}=\theta_{t_0},\quad a^{\rm B}=\theta_{t_0+1},\qquad
 a_-=b_F(1-L^{-1})\le a^\bullet\le a_+=b_F.
\]
Whenever the inverse exists, define
\begin{align*}
 \mathcal K^\bullet[U;J']
   &=D^{\xi^\bullet}[U]+\mathfrak m_s-\widehat J'
                                      +a^\bullet R^*R,\\
 \mathcal S^\bullet&=(\mathcal K^\bullet)^{-1},\qquad
 \mathsf T^\bullet=R\mathcal S^\bullet R^*,\qquad
 \mathsf D^\bullet=a^\bullet-(a^\bullet)^2\mathsf T^\bullet,\\
 \mathsf M^\bullet[U;J'][N]
   &=\left.\partial_z\mathsf D^\bullet[U;J'-zN]\right|_{z=0}
     =(a^\bullet)^2R\mathcal S^\bullet\widehat N
                                      \mathcal S^\bullet R^*.
\end{align*}
For $\sup|J'|\le\mathfrak m_s/2$ the inverse exists at every
$U$, by accretivity. For
$\sup|J'|\le\mathfrak m_s/2+\varrho_S$ it exists under the
curvature and side hypotheses of \cref{C-408-5}.

For $\sup|w|<8\varrho$ put
\[
 \hat s_w(x)=\frac{F^{\rm UV}}{L^s(\mathsf b-w(x))}.
\]
Suppose $L^s\mathsf b\ge\Theta_\star$ and
$\varpi(W)<\varepsilon_{\rm r}$. Choose
$U^{\rm A}\in\mathcal C(\mathbf B^{\rm A}_{t_0},W)$ and
$U^{\rm B}\in\mathcal C(\mathbf B^{\rm B}_{t_0+1},W)$, and define
\[
 \mathsf D^\bullet_{\rm st}(W)
  =\mathsf D^\bullet[U^\bullet;J_s]
       +\mathsf M^\bullet[U^\bullet;J_s][\hat s_w].
\]
These are the two quadratic forms at the classical restart.
\end{definition}

\begin{corollary}[The discarded mass slices]\label{C-420-3}
Let $F_{<i_0}$, $F^{\rm UV}_{<i_0}$, $F^{\rm UV}$, and $B_5$
be as in \cref{C-398-40}. Then $0\le F^{\rm UV}\le B_F$ and,
for $t_0\le j\le k$ and masses in $[0,1]$,
\begin{align*}
 0\le F^{\rm UV}-F^{\rm UV}_{<t_0}&\le B_5L^{-t_0},\\
 |F_{<t_0}(k;m)-F^{\rm UV}|&\le B_5(L^{-t_0}+3L^{-(k-t_0)}),\\
 |F_{<t_0}(k;m)-F_{<t_0}(j;m')|&\le6B_5L^{-(j-t_0)},\\
 |F_{<t_0}(k;m)-F_{<t_0}(k;m'')|
       &\le B_5|m-m''|L^{-(k-t_0)},\\
 |\sigma_i(k;m)-\sigma_i(j;m')|&\le8LB_5L^{-(j-i)}\quad(i<j).
\end{align*}
At level $t_1$ the second bound is
$3B_5(L^{-(K-s)}+L^{-(s-u)})$.

Here is the corresponding estimate with a complex constant source.
Use the cutoff and levels of the datum under consideration, put
$t_i=L^{K-i}\mathsf b$, $t_k'=L^{K-k}(\mathsf b-c)$, and assume
$|x_i-t_i|\le\bar B$, $|c|<8\varrho$, $i<i_0\le k$, and
$n=k-i_0$. For $x_i'=x_i-L^{K-i}c$,
\begin{align*}
 |\mathsf b-c|&\ge\tfrac34\mathsf b,\qquad |x_i'|\ge\tfrac14t_i,\\
 \left|G_{<i_0,k}(x')-\frac{F_{<i_0}(k;\mathfrak m_k)}{t_k'}\right|
 &\le\frac{16\bar B F(k;\mathfrak m_k)}{3t_k^2}L^{-(n+1)},\\
 |t_k'G_{<i_0,k}(x')-F^{\rm UV}|
 &\le B_5(L^{-i_0}+3L^{-n})
                 +\frac{4\bar B F(k;\mathfrak m_k)}{t_k}L^{-(n+1)}.
\end{align*}
At $c=0$ the constants $16/3$ and $4$ can both be replaced by $2$.
Finally,
\begin{align*}
 \sup|\hat s_w|&\le\frac{4F^{\rm UV}}{3L^s\mathsf b}
