bounded by \(\epsilon_j[\lambda]\).
For \(|\lambda|<R\),
\begin{align*}
 \sum_{j\le n}\omega_{n+1-j}\epsilon_j[\lambda]
     &\le2C_w^{\rm s}\Phi_n
       \le2C_w^{\rm s}C_{\rm pc}S_{1/4}\phi_n,\\
 c_{\rm cs}\sum_{j\le n}\omega_{n+1-j}\epsilon_j[\lambda]
                  +c_{\rm cs}^\Delta|\lambda|\Sigma_n^\psi(s)
     &\le2c_{\rm cs}C_w^{\rm s}\Phi_n,\\
 \epsilon_j[\lambda]&\le2C_w^{\rm s}\phi_{n-1}\quad(j\le t_1),\\
 |\lambda|\Lambda_n^0[\rho(s)]&\le c_0^\Delta.
\end{align*}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Units, moved moments, and mass forms are linear in their
three extraction data. Their sums are therefore the extraction
of the displayed three data, with cell sums \(0+\lambda0\).
Phase invariance preserves the form of their quadratic terms.
Subadditivity proves the summand bounds.
The remaining calculation is \cref{C-422-7}, pointwise in \(z\).
Its extra weighted size is at most
\[
 |\lambda|\Sigma_n^\psi(s)
 \le(c_\psi^\Delta/\omega_1)\Phi_n
 =C_w\frac{c_{\rm cs}}{c_{\rm cs}+c_{\rm cs}^\Delta}\Phi_n.
\]
This is exactly the allowance for both the old-activity sum
and its additional cell contribution. The individual bound
uses \(\omega_{n+1-j}\ge\omega_1\);
the scalar bound uses the decay of \(\Lambda_n^0\).
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[The small-field step for a closed datum]\label{C-424-25}
Let \(t_1\le k<K\). For
\(\mathfrak c'=(\sigma_i)_{t_1\le i\le k}\in2\mathscr D'_k\),
set
\[
 \mathfrak c_\lambda[\mathfrak c']
   =(w_\lambda,-a_KJ,(\sigma_i(s))_{i<t_1},\mathfrak c').
\]
The step is defined at every
\((z,\mathfrak c',\lambda)\in
\mathcal O\times2\mathscr D'_k\times\mathrm P(R)\).
All conclusions of \cref{C-422-8} hold, including its
pointed, reference, infinite-lattice, and source-energy bounds.
The outputs are jointly holomorphic in these variables and
the pair, with values in the stated local domains.
In particular,
\[
 \epsilon_{k+1}^{{\rm s},\psi}
       \le(2C_w^{\rm s}-C_w)\phi_k,\qquad
 \epsilon_{k+1}^{{\rm s},0}
       \le\tfrac{15}8C_w^{\rm s}\phi_k
                             +\tfrac35 C'_{\rm lin}\tau_k^\lambda.
\]
The increment and any restriction of its pieces take values
in \(\mathbb M\), and satisfy
\[
 |\nu_{k+1}-\mu_{k+1}|\le\tfrac12B_\nu\phi_{k+1}.
\]
At fixed \(\lambda\), the locality bound of \cref{C-422-8}
uses only differences of the coordinates
\(\sigma_i\), \(t_1\le i\le k\).
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The embedding \(\mathfrak c_\lambda[\mathfrak c']\) belongs
to \(2\mathscr D_k(\alpha_0)\):
\(\|w_\lambda\|_\sharp\le2\varrho<8\varrho\),
\(L^{k+1}\|a_KJ\|<2r_M\), and the earlier source coordinates
have norm less than \(B_\sigma\phi_i\).
Apply \cref{C-422-8}, by induction on \(k\), to the early
arrays in \cref{C-424-24}. We spell out why this application
also gives the additional parameter assertions.

The early arrays are independent of \(\mathfrak c'\), affine
in \(\lambda\), and holomorphic in \(z\) on the fixed cores.
Their scalar pointers are local terms with zero Wilson
coefficient. Their fermion summands satisfy \cref{C-422-6},
including the torus rule. The preceding newly generated
activities have the same properties by induction.
Thus all hypotheses used for the small-field construction in
\cref{C-422-8} hold jointly on the displayed open set.
No agreement between constructions at smaller pair radii is
needed: this step and its increment are formed at \(\alpha_0\).

The extra scalar localization is at most
\[
 K_\Lambda^{\rm s}\mathsf s_k(\alpha_0)c_0^\Delta
          \le5c_{\rm cl}/144.
\]
Together with the ordinary terms this gives
\((1/4+1/8+13/144+5/144)c_{\rm cl}=c_{\rm cl}/2\).
Its contribution to the new scalar activity is at most
\(C_w^{\rm s}\phi_k/8\), by the last inequality in
\cref{C-424-16}. These are precisely the two scalar
calculations in \cref{C-422-8}.
For the fermion terms, \cref{C-424-24} bounds the ordinary
lag sum and the extra cell sum by their ordinary values.
Consequently the full recurrence and its pointed version
give the stated sizes, also at the reference.

All localizations, Gaussian integrations, and cluster series
are holomorphic in their inputs, with the uniform bounds just
proved on compact parameter sets. Their limits are therefore
jointly holomorphic in \(z,\mathfrak c',\lambda\) and the pair.
Phase invariance gives one barred and one unbarred field in
degree two. Constant colour rotations at the trivial pair
show that every extracted moment lies in \(\mathbb M\),
including an arbitrary subset of pieces.
The locality proof in \cref{C-422-8} varies only
\(\mathfrak c'\); \(w_\lambda,J\), and the earlier coordinates
are fixed. Its same Cauchy disc and absolute moment sum give
the stated increment bounds. Finally the scalar value at the
trivial pair, the Gaussian part at \(w_\lambda\), and the
fermion normalizer at \(m_0-a_K\widehat J\) have the same
bounds as in that proof. This gives its source-energy estimate.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[The parameter window]\label{C-424-26}
For a closed datum the chain in \cref{C-424-8} is defined
and holomorphic on \(\mathcal O\times\mathrm P(R_k)\)
through level \(k\), and
\[
 \|\sigma_k(s,\lambda)-\sigma_k(s)\|
       \le\tfrac12B_\sigma\phi_k,\qquad
 \|\sigma_k(s,\lambda)\|
       \le(B_\sigma-C_{\rm var}/2)\phi_k<B_\sigma\phi_k.
\]
At \(\lambda=0\) it is the source chain.
These assertions include \(k=K\).
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The proof of \cref{C-422-9} applies with the jointly
holomorphic increments of \cref{C-424-25}.
For completeness its two shrinking-disc terms are
\[
 Q_\sigma^{-1}LB_\sigma\phi_k/2,\qquad
 Q_\sigma^{-1}B_\nu\phi_{k+1}.
\]
Their sum is at most \(B_\sigma\phi_{k+1}/2\), since
\(L\phi_k\le2\sqrt L\phi_{k+1}\),
\(B_\nu\le B_\sigma/8\), and
\(Q_\sigma=2\sqrt L+1/4\).
Both differences vanish at \(\lambda=0\), which is the
hypothesis needed for Schwarz's lemma on each successive disc.
The initial bound is the mass condition in
\eqref{eq:closed-datum-lags}.
At \(K\), the coordinate embedding is still admissible:
\(L^{K+1}\|a_KJ\|=L\|J\|_\infty<Lr_J=r_M\).
Composition gives the asserted joint holomorphy.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[History coordinates and the interior]\label{C-424-27}
Let \(h\in\mathcal H_k[t_1]\) and \(|\lambda|<R_k\).
The chain along \(h\) has the estimates in \cref{C-422-10}.
In particular, for \(S_j=\bigcup_{t_1<i\le j}\widetilde Z_i(h)\)
and sites \(x\) where step \(j\) is made along \(h\),
\[
 |\sigma_j^h-\sigma_j|(x)\le
 8B_\nu\phi_j e^{-\kappa_\sigma\operatorname{dist}(x,S_j)/(2L^j)}
 \quad\text{if }\operatorname{dist}(x,S_j)\ge R'_\flat L^j,
\]
and on \(\Omega_j\),
\[
 |\sigma_j^h-\sigma_j|\le16B_\nu\phi_j,\qquad
 |\sigma_j^h|\le2B_\sigma\phi_j.
\]
The history coordinates belong to \(2\mathscr D'_j\)
and are holomorphic on \(\mathcal O\times\mathrm P(R_k)\).
Moreover
\[
 \sum_{X\subset\Lambda_n}
 |e_n(X;\mathfrak c_{n-1})-e_n(X;\mathfrak c^h_{n-1})|
              \le C'_{\mathfrak E}\#_n(\widetilde Z_n).
\]
The conditions \((\mathrm{Int}_i)[s,\lambda;h]\) hold for
\(t_1\le i\le k\), \(i<K\).
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The full and restricted chains agree through the base.
The proof of \cref{C-422-10} therefore starts with zero
coordinate difference. Its only analytic inputs are the
absolute piece bound, the Lipschitz locality estimate, and the
source-energy bound in \cref{C-424-25}. Thus its exponentially
weighted recurrence and its polymer sum apply unchanged.
The bound \(16B_\nu\le B_\sigma\), together with
\cref{C-424-26}, keeps every history coordinate in
\(2\mathscr D'_j\).
Its entries are the history chain on a fixed set \(\Omega_j\)
and the full chain elsewhere; both are holomorphic by induction.
Evaluating \cref{C-424-25} at these coordinates gives every
clause of \((\mathrm{Int}_i)\).
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Regular fermion sums]\label{C-424-28}
For \(h\in\mathcal H_k[t_1]\), \(|\lambda|<R_k\),
the regular activities have total norm at most
\(C_{\rm leg}^{\rm s}\Sigma_{\mathcal L}(h)\).
Their contribution to a cube of \(\mathcal L_n\) is at most
\(C_{\rm leg}^{\square,\rm s}\phi_n\).
The mass member has per-cube bound
\[
 w_0\nu C_H^2h_F^2L(\bar B_M+2B_\sigma)\phi_{n-1}
\]
and the corresponding sum over all layers.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Apply the regular-sum proof in \cref{C-422-11}.
We verify the inputs for all families, including those at a
regular subset of pointers along a history.
The early families have no rim. By \cref{C-424-24} they
have the extraction data, vanishing matrix cell sums, and
summand sizes needed for the unit count in \cref{C-422-16}.
The later families have them by \cref{C-424-25}.
Their moved pieces satisfy, polymer by polymer,
\[
 \sum_p\sum_y\|a_{X,p}(y)\|
           e^{\kappa(d_j(Z_p)-d_j(X))}
 \le CA_\kappa^2h_F^{-2}
                         \bigl(\|F_j(X)\|+\|G_j(X)\|\bigr).
\]
Indeed, the localized-leg count bounds the double row sums of
each piece by the right side. These row sums bound its zeroth
moment; taking the difference of the two data gives the formula.
Thus the count requires no additional symmetry of an early family.

At a later rim, let \(F^h(X)\) be the sum of pointed terms
at the regular pointers of \(X\).
Before extraction its part with generators is the integral,
over the pointing parameter, of the first variation of the
cluster sum. The sum of insertions over any subset of places
has norm at most the original even element's norm.
Hence the pointed estimate in \cref{C-424-25} bounds
\(F^h(X)\) by the activity size. The extraction terms it
retains are a subset of the same summands.
The kernels and forms actually used along the history
therefore satisfy the short-lag version of the unit count.

The terms with summable kernels cost at most
\(2C_w^{\rm s}K_{\rm fin}\phi_{n-1}\).
The cell terms cost at most
\((C_0^{\rm cs}h_F^2+
2c_{\rm cs}C_{\rm pc}S_{1/4}C_w^{\rm s})\phi_n\).
At long lags the units cost at most
\[
 \frac{N_{\rm u}L^{9/2}}{C_\omega L^{1/4}}\,
                 2C_w^{\rm s}C_{\rm pc}S_{1/4}\phi_n;
\]
at short lags they cost at most
\(2N_{\rm u}C_w^{\rm s}S_{\rm lag}\phi_{n-1}\).
These are exactly the four sums proved in \cref{C-422-11},
using the four estimates in \cref{C-424-24}.
The floor \eqref{eq:free-history-leg-floor} bounds their
sum by \(C_{\rm leg}^{\square,\rm s}\phi_n\), and then
by \(C_{\rm leg}^{\rm s}\) after summing over the layers.

The mass coefficient is a convex combination of the two
adjacent scale coefficients, except on the first layer where
it is the base coefficient. The bounds in
\cref{C-424-26,C-424-27}, and
\(L^{-1}\phi_{t_1}\le\phi_{t_1-1}\) on the first layer,
give the same bound in either case.
The ordinary background count proves the assertion for the mass.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[The first seven fermion classes]\label{C-424-29}
For a closed datum, \(|\lambda|<R_k\), and
\(h'=(h,\mathsf o)\in\mathcal H_{k+1}[t_1]\), the first
seven fermion classes together have size at most
\[
 b_k^{\rm tot,s}
   =b_k^{\rm blk,s}+b_k^{\rm lay,s}+b_k^{\rm ms,s}
   \le b^{\rm tot,s}(\gamma).
\]
Thus \((\mathrm{Sh}_k)[s,\lambda;h']\) holds.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The class estimates in \cref{C-422-11} use the old families
through their holomorphy on the fixed cores, the per-cube
bounds, and three sums: the weighted lag sum, the cell sum,
and a summable kernel times the individual current-scale size.
These are supplied by \cref{C-424-24,C-424-28}.
More explicitly, the first two classes use Cauchy's estimate
on the ordinary link polydisc, with the regular sums of
\cref{C-424-28}; all shifted pairs remain in the same cores.
The stored-layer count uses
\[
 \sum_{j\le m}C_\omega L^{(m-j)/4}\epsilon_j[\lambda]
 \le\sum_{j\le m}\omega_{m+1-j}\epsilon_j[\lambda]
 \le2C_w^{\rm s}C_{\rm pc}S_{1/4}\phi_m.
\]
Short lags also satisfy this bound since
\(1\le\omega_{m+1-j}\).
These estimates retain the ordinary \(C_{\rm lay}^{\rm s}\).

The third and fourth classes use the potential bound of
\cref{C-424-25}, followed by the same lag, cell, and
summable-kernel estimates. Apply the individual bound of
\cref{C-424-24} at \(n=k+1\) when its size is read at
the current level \(k\).
The fifth and sixth classes use these estimates at each
stored layer and its per-cube bound.
All pointers of an early polymer are regular; for later
polymers the subset-of-pointers bound was verified in
\cref{C-424-28}. Hence the division of classes by the cell
of a polymer remains valid.
The seventh class contains only later rim and mass forms;
it uses \(|\nu_j^h-\mu_j|\le B_\nu\phi_j/2\).
Each of the three ordinary shares therefore retains its bound.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Induction for a closed datum]\label{C-424-30}
Let a closed datum at radius \(R\) over \(\mathcal O\) be
given. For \(t_1\le k\le K\), \(z\in\mathcal O\), and
\(|\lambda|<R_k\), every \(h\in\mathcal H_k[t_1]\)
satisfies the interior conditions of \cref{C-424-8}.
For \(k<K\), every next step satisfies its share condition.
Moreover
\[
 \mathsf I^{\rm F}(k)[s(z),\lambda]\quad
                      (t_1\le k\le K,\ |\lambda|<R_k).
\]
Thus all the conclusions of \cref{C-424-9,C-424-10,C-424-11,C-424-12,C-424-13,C-424-14,C-424-15} hold at every level
on any common disc \(|\lambda|<r_\lambda\le R_K\).
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The interior and share assertions are
\cref{C-424-27,C-424-29}.
At the base, \cref{C-424-7} gives the exponential
representation with exponent
\(A_{t_1,h_\emptyset}^{\rm F}(s)+\lambda\Delta(s)\).
Its changed weight, mass, arrays, and vacuum constant are
exactly those in \cref{C-424-8}.
There is no piece, stored lower layer, or boundary term.
The weight condition gives the ordinary loss in the action.
The regular and mass bounds follow from
\cref{C-424-9,C-424-28}; these also bound the exponent,
with the ordinary background estimate.
Hence \(\mathsf I^{\rm F}(t_1)\) holds on \(\mathrm P(R)\).

Suppose it holds at \(k\), and restrict to
\(\mathrm P(R_{k+1})\subset\mathrm P(R_k)\).
By the first assertions, \cref{C-424-15} applies to every
prolongation. We check the eight bounds in the resulting
representation.
The kept halves and formed factors have the ordinary bounds
at \(w_\lambda\), since \((w_\lambda,J)\in\mathcal P\).
The action retains the ordinary fraction of its weight.
The stored-factor estimate uses the same fine-mass operators
and the mass coefficient bound of \cref{C-424-28}.
The updated mass and regular sums obey that lemma at \(k+1\).
The early arrays keep their domains; the later pointed
activities have the properties and \(E_0^{\rm s}\) bound of
\cref{C-424-25}.
The generated boundary terms, rejected halves, reblocked linear
term, and sourced strip terms obey the ordinary boundary
bound \(\mathsf B_\natural\), by
\cref{C-424-13,C-424-14}.
Their frame size is \(64b^{\rm tot,s}(\gamma)/51\);
their edge scalar size is \(E_0^{\rm s}\);
their insertion size is at most \(b^{\rm blk,s}(\gamma)\).

For the vacuum label, the discrepancy from the common
\(E_{k+1}(s,\lambda)\) consists of three terms:
source energies at polymers outside \(\Lambda_{k+1}\),
boundary normalizers, and differences between full-chain
and history-chain source energies inside \(\Lambda_{k+1}\).
The first has the polymer-tail bound of \cref{C-424-25}.
For the second, the fermion normalizer is the ordinary one
at the fine mass of \(s\); its Gaussian part at \(w_\lambda\)
has bound \(9e^{-\kappa''d(X)}/32\) outside the regular
region and the ordinary pointer bound inside.
The third is bounded by \cref{C-424-27}.
The ordinary three constants add to \(C'_{\mathfrak E}\).
Thus their sum defines \(g_{k+1}\) with
\[
 |g_{k+1}|\le C'_{\mathfrak E}\#_{k+1}(\widetilde Z_{k+1}).
\]
Finally the exponent bound uses the regular fermion and mass
bounds, the scalar regular bound, \(E_0^{\rm s}\) for edges,
and the ordinary estimate on formal background legs.
These verify all eight clauses.
Induction proves the representation on each shrinking disc.
The last assertion follows from \(R_K\le R_k\).
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Holomorphy along a history]\label{C-424-31}
For \(h\in\mathcal H_k[t_1]\), all its chains, coordinates,
restricted increments, mass field, pointed activities,
source energies, and label corrections \(g_n\) are jointly
holomorphic on
\(\mathcal W_k=\mathcal O\times\mathrm P(R_k)\).
The activity assertion includes joint holomorphy with the pair.
The vacuum energy is holomorphic there, and
\[
 E_k(s,0)=E_k(s),\qquad g_n(h;s,0)=g_n(h;s).
\]
Every coefficient of its measure has a jointly Borel density
holomorphic in \((z,\lambda)\) at every free-coordinate point
on \(\mathcal O\times\mathbb C\).
On \(\mathcal W_k\) this density agrees almost everywhere
with the exponential representation.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The full chain is holomorphic by \cref{C-424-26}.
A restricted increment is the sum of the extracted pieces
whose polymer is inside the fixed region \(\Lambda_j\).
Each piece is a product of holomorphic activity coefficients
and localized background walks at the fine mass.
The absolute moment bound of \cref{C-424-25} sums their
norms uniformly on compact parameter sets.
Thus restriction of the piece sum preserves holomorphy.
The history recurrence and its coordinate assembly then prove
holomorphy of the history chain, restricted increments,
and mass field by composition. Evaluation of
\cref{C-424-25} gives the activity and source-energy assertions;
the vacuum energy is their finite sum.

The three parts of \(g_n\) were described in the proof of
\cref{C-424-30}. Its source-energy parts are holomorphic
by the preceding paragraph. The fermion boundary normalizer
is holomorphic in \(-a_KJ\) on \(L^n\|a_KJ\|<2r_M\).
Its Gaussian part inside the regular region is the pointed
Gaussian path at weight \(w_\lambda\), formed from polynomial
insertions affine in that weight. Outside the regular region,
it is the centered cluster series with origins
\(\mathcal V^{\rm q}\) and
\(\mathbb W^{\rm q}=-F^{v'}_{Y,2}\).
The first is independent of the weight and the second is
complex linear in its values on the polymer.
The uniform bounds in \cref{C-424-13} give locally uniform
convergence of both series on \(\mathcal W_k\).
Their terms are holomorphic, so their sums are holomorphic.
At \(\lambda=0\), induction gives the same early arrays,
reference, subsequent activities, increments, and coordinates
as the ordinary source flow. This also identifies the three
parts of every \(g_n\), proving both identities at zero.

The density assertion, including the common Borel choice and
pointwise holomorphy on the full parameter space, is
\cref{C-424-21}. That proposition uses the positive
zero-source measure and a countable gluing of Cauchy series;
it is independent of the shrinking RG window.
Uniqueness of densities identifies it with the exponential
representation on \(\mathcal W_k\).
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Summing the histories]\label{C-424-32}
For the datum of \cref{C-424-6} and any
\((z,\lambda)\in\mathcal O\times\mathbb C\), its scalar
bare density \(\varsigma^{s,\lambda}\) has a bounded Borel
representative \(\varsigma^\sharp\) invariant under every
bare gauge transformation constant on level-\(t_1\) blocks,
such that
\[
 \mathfrak w_h\varsigma^\sharp
       =\mathfrak w_h\varsigma^{s,\lambda}
                    \quad dU\text{-almost everywhere}
 \qquad(h\in\mathcal H_k[t_1],\ t_1\le k\le K).
\]
For every \(h''\in\mathcal H_{n-1}[t_1]\), \(n>t_1\),
\[
 \sum_{h|_{n-1}=h''}\tau_h[\varsigma^{s,\lambda}]
      =\mathbf T\,\tau_{h''}[\varsigma^{s,\lambda}].
\]
Consequently
\[
 Z_k(z,\lambda)=Z_{t_1}(z,\lambda)
                  \qquad(t_1\le k\le K,\ \lambda\in\mathbb C).
\]
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Let \(\mathcal G_{t_1}\) be the compact group of these
block-constant transformations, and let \(\Upsilon_v\)
be its action on the base Grassmann algebra.
Write
\[
 \mu=\xi_*(\mathfrak w_{h_\emptyset}\,dU),\qquad
 N_1=\mathsf N_0\cup(\mathsf X_{h_\emptyset}^{\rm co}
                                      \setminus\mathsf S_\emptyset).
\]
By \cref{C-424-17,C-424-18}, \(\mu\) is invariant under
\(\mathcal G_{t_1}\) and \(\mu(N_1)=0\).
Where both arguments belong to
\(\mathsf S_\emptyset\setminus\mathsf N_0\),
\[
 \Delta(s)(v\cdot V)=\Upsilon_v\Delta(s)(V).
\]
This identity uses the evaluation-set covariance and the
joint gauge invariance of each array and background, and the
fact that the mass matrix commutes with colour.

Let \(dv\) be Haar probability measure and set
\[
 N^\sharp=\left\{V:\int\mathbf1_{N_1}(v\cdot V)\,dv>0\right\}.
\]
Tonelli and invariance show that \(N^\sharp\) is an invariant
Borel \(\mu\)-null set. Off it define
\[
 \Delta^\sharp(V)=
 \int\Upsilon_v^{-1}\Delta(s)(v\cdot V)
             \mathbf1_{\mathsf S_\emptyset\setminus\mathsf N_0}
                                      (v\cdot V)\,dv.
\]
The integrand is bounded and Borel.
Haar invariance gives
\(\Delta^\sharp(u\cdot V)=\Upsilon_u\Delta^\sharp(V)\);
on
\((\mathsf S_\emptyset\setminus\mathsf N_0)\setminus N^\sharp\)
it equals \(\Delta(s)(V)\).
Put \(G^\sharp(U)=\exp[\lambda\Delta^\sharp(\xi(U))]\)
when \(\mathfrak w_{h_\emptyset}(U)\ne0\) and
\(\xi(U)\notin N^\sharp\), and put \(G^\sharp=1\)
elsewhere.

The unperturbed transported base density \(F(U)\) satisfies
\(F(U^v)=\Upsilon_vF(U)\): the Dirac and block kernels
are gauge covariant, \(J\) commutes with colour, and partial
Berezin integration preserves this covariance.
The base weight and its support are invariant.
Hence
\(\varsigma^\sharp(U)=\operatorname{Ber}[G^\sharp(U)F(U)]\)
is invariant everywhere. On the base support it agrees
with \(\varsigma^{s,\lambda}\) off a set of
\(\mathfrak w_{h_\emptyset}dU\)-measure zero.
Every later weight is this base weight times a bounded Borel
product of tests and gauge-fixing factors. The claimed
agreement follows for all \(h\).

At a step \(n>t_1\), the gauge transformations used to sum
its prolongations are constant on level-\((n-1)\) blocks.
Each such block is a union of level-\(t_1\) blocks, so
\(\varsigma^\sharp\) has precisely the invariance required
by the ordinary history identity.
Its gauge defects vanish for bounded Borel densities by
\cite[Prop.\ 44.1]{YMM1}. Applying the identity to
\(\varsigma^\sharp\) and then using its weighted almost
everywhere agreement gives the displayed measure identity.
Iteration and preservation of total mass give the last formula.
This is also the scalar identity of \cref{C-424-20}.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[The comparison datum]\label{C-424-33}
Take the base data of \cref{C-418-4} at \(t_b\), with
its difference format and lag bounds \((\mathrm L1)\)--\((\mathrm L3)\)
at a number \(\Lambda_b\ge1\). Suppose \(d_b(s)=d_b\)
is constant. Choose \(0<c\le1\) such that
\[
 cE_0^{\rm s}\le2c_0^\Delta,\qquad
 2\sqrt LcC_w^{\rm s}\le c_\psi^\Delta.
\]
On an affine source domain with
\(\|w\|_\sharp\le(2-c)\varrho\), set
\[
 t_1=t_b,\quad w^\Delta=\widehat w_b,\quad
 \delta\sigma=-\delta_{t_b}(s),\quad
 \mathfrak n=d_b,\quad
 \text{early arrays }-\Delta^{(j)}(s).
\]
These give a closed datum at \(R=c\Lambda_b/2\).
Its exponent is
\(\widehat\Phi_s^{(t_b)}-\Phi_s^{(t_b)}\), and
\[
 \tfrac12(3\sqrt L)^{-(K-t_b)}c\Lambda_b<R_K.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The difference format in \cref{C-418-4} supplies local
holomorphic pointed arrays with the common pair domains.
Their extraction data are the negatives of the differences
of the two flows' data, with their common paths.
The infinite-lattice reference cell sums are
\(0-0\) as matrices, since each flow has had its mass
coefficient extracted. Phase invariance and the summand
norm bounds are preserved. The mass difference is a
holomorphic field in \(\mathbb M\); the weight and vacuum
difference are constants. Thus all format and parameter
requirements in \cref{C-424-23} hold.

For the four quantitative conditions, the comparison lag
bounds give, respectively,
\begin{align*}
 R\Sigma_k^\psi
   &\le\tfrac12cC_w^{\rm s}\phi_k
     \le c\sqrt L C_w^{\rm s}\phi_{k-1}
     \le\tfrac12c_\psi^\Delta\phi_{k-1},\\
 R\Lambda_{t_b}^0[\rho]&\le\tfrac12cE_0^{\rm s}\le c_0^\Delta,\\
 |\lambda\widehat w_b|&<\tfrac12c\varrho,\\
 R\|\delta_{t_b}\|&\le\tfrac12cB_\sigma\phi_{t_b}
                         \le\tfrac12B_\sigma\phi_{t_b}.
\end{align*}
The third estimate, and the zero Lipschitz constant of
\(\widehat w_b\), keep \(w+\lambda\widehat w_b\) inside
the source weight ball. Its fermion source is unchanged.
Substituting the four data in
\eqref{eq:free-measure-exponent} gives exactly the stated
difference of exponents, with its signs.
Finally \(Q_\sigma<3\sqrt L\) and \(K-t_b\ge1\)
give the strict comparison of radii.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Application to the restart interpolation}

\begin{lemma}\label{C-424-22}
Use the cutoff-comparison data of \cref{C-418-2}, with
condition \textup{(k0)} and \(u\ge u_*\) from
\cref{C-418-9}.  Fix one of the two cutoffs and a base
\(t_0<t_b\le t_1\), and suppress its superscript.
Let the differences \(\Delta_b^{(j)}\) have the format
and lag bounds \textup{(L1)--(L3)} of \cref{C-418-4}
with \(\Lambda_b>0\), at every \(s\in\mathcal P\).
Assume that \(d_b(s)=d_b\) is independent of \(s\).
Choose
\[
 0<c_\lambda\le\tfrac18,\qquad
 c_\lambda E_0^{\rm s}\le c_0^\Delta,\qquad
 2\sqrt Lc_\lambda C_w^{\rm s}\le c_\psi^\Delta,
 \qquad
 \rho_b=\tfrac12(3\sqrt L)^{-(K-t_b)}c_\lambda\Lambda_b.
\]
Let \(s(z)=(w,J)\) be an affine family on \(\mathcal O\)
as in \cref{C-424-6}, with
\(\|w\|_\sharp\le(2-c_\lambda)\varrho\).
Then the following data satisfy \cref{C-424-6} at base
\(t_b\) and radius \(2\rho_b\):
\begin{equation}\label{eq:free-measure-restart-data}
 w^\Delta=\hat w_b,\qquad
 \delta\sigma=-\delta_{t_b},\qquad
 \mathfrak n=d_b,\qquad
 \Delta^{(j)}=-\Delta_b^{(j)}\quad(j\le t_b).
\end{equation}
Their exponent is \(\hat\Phi_s^{(t_b)}-\Phi_s^{(t_b)}\).
For every complex \(\lambda\), their base measure is
the interpolation measure \(\rho_{s,\lambda}^{(t_b)}\)
of \cref{C-418-4}.  Its later terms are
\(\check\tau_h^{\rm F}[s,\lambda]\), with densities
\(g_h(z,\lambda,\cdot)\) from \cref{C-424-21}, and
\[
 \operatorname{Ber}\rho_{s,\lambda}^{(t_b)}(\mathcal V_{t_b})
   =\sum_{h\in\mathcal H_K[t_b]}
          \operatorname{Ber}\int g_h(z,\lambda,v)
                                          \,d\mathscr M_h^{\rm fr}(v).
\]

These same data form a closed datum in the sense of
\cref{C-424-23}, with
\[
 R=c_\lambda\Lambda_b,\qquad
 R_K=RQ_\sigma^{-(K-t_b)}>2\rho_b,\qquad
 Q_\sigma=2\sqrt L+\tfrac14.
\]
Consequently the integration, shift, and density induction
conditions \(\mathrm{Int}_i\), \(\mathrm{Sh}_k\), and
\(\mathsf I^{\rm F}(k)\) of \cref{C-424-8} hold at all
levels from \(t_b\) through \(K\), on
\(|\lambda|<2\rho_b\), with the indicated conditions
only where the next step exists.  In particular, all the
hypotheses required for the estimates in
\cref{C-424-9,C-424-10,C-424-11,C-424-12,C-424-13,C-424-14,C-424-15}
hold there.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The depth assumptions imply
\(1\le K-t_b<K-t_0<K\), so the base is in the permitted
range.  The constant function
\(\hat w_b=L^{-(K-t_b)}(x_{t_b}-\hat x_{t_b})\)
is real.  The matrix field
\[
 \delta_{t_b}(s)=s_{t_b}-\hat s_{t_b}
                          +\sigma_{t_b}(s)-\hat\sigma_{t_b}(s)
\]
lies in \(\mathbb M\) and is holomorphic on a neighborhood
of \(\mathcal P\), by the original and restarted source
flows.  The scalar \(d_b\) is constant.

The asserted difference format gives locality, core
holomorphy, Borel coefficients, joint gauge invariance,
and vanishing of the scalar part at the trivial pair.
The boundedness condition on the fixed core also holds.
For the two original families it follows from their
activity bounds at \(\alpha_0\); for the full scalar
part one uses the bound
\(E_0^{\rm s}e^{-(\kappa+1)d_j(X)}\), which includes
the normalizers, closed loops, Gaussian part, and constant
family.  Bounding only the scalar fluctuation family
would not suffice here.

The fermionic parts are formed from
\[
 -\bigl(F_j(s)-\hat F_j(s),\ G_j-\hat G_j,\
                                      \mu_j-\hat\mu_j\bigr),
\]
with infinite-lattice family \(-(G_j^\infty-\hat G_j^\infty)\).
The extraction rule is linear.  Common paths, phase
invariance, and the zero matrix cell sums are preserved
by this difference and sign.  Its sizes are exactly
\(r_j^\psi\) and \(\rho_j=r_j^0\) in the lag bounds.

Those bounds give, with \(R=c_\lambda\Lambda_b\),
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 R\sum_{j\le t_b}L^{-(t_b-j)}\rho_j
       &\le c_\lambda E_0^{\rm s}\le c_0^\Delta,\\
 R\sum_{j\le t_b}\omega_{k+1-j}r_j^\psi
       &\le c_\lambda C_w^{\rm s}\phi_k
        \le2\sqrt Lc_\lambda C_w^{\rm s}\phi_{k-1}
        \le c_\psi^\Delta\phi_{k-1},\\
 R\|\delta_{t_b}\|&\le c_\lambda B_\sigma\phi_{t_b}
                           \le\tfrac12B_\sigma\phi_{t_b}.
 \end{aligned}
\]
For \(|\lambda|<R\), the gauge-weight increment has
norm at most \(c_\lambda\varrho\), strictly less if it
is nonzero.  The assumed margin for \(w\) therefore
keeps \((w+\lambda\hat w_b,J)\) in \(\mathcal P\).
This proves all the required inequalities, already at
radius \(R>2\rho_b\).

Substitution of \eqref{eq:free-measure-restart-data} into
\eqref{eq:free-measure-exponent} gives
\[
 a_K^{-1}A(\hat w_b,\mathsf U)
 +L^{-t_b}\mathsf S_1(\delta_{t_b}\psi^{\rm bg})
 -\sum_{j\le t_b}\sum_X\Delta_b^{(j)}(X)+d_b
       =\hat\Phi_s^{(t_b)}-\Phi_s^{(t_b)}.
\]
At zero interpolation parameter the base measure is the
ordinary sourced term.  Multiplication by the exponential
of this difference, using \cref{C-424-7}, gives the
claimed equality at every complex \(\lambda\).
Lemma~\ref{C-424-34} then identifies every later term
from the base measure alone.  Proposition~\ref{C-424-21}
supplies its holomorphic density, and
\cref{C-424-20} gives the equality of total integrals.

For the closed datum, its additional compact-parameter
bounds follow from holomorphy of the difference data at
each core pair.  The preceding inequalities are the
closed inequalities at radius \(R\).
Since \(Q_\sigma<3\sqrt L\) and \(K-t_b\ge1\),
\(R_K>2\rho_b\).  The all-level induction
\cref{C-424-30} therefore applies throughout the required
disc and gives the remaining assertions.
\end{proof}

\section{Pure-gauge coefficients}\label{sec:qcdm2-pure-coefficients}

We identify the order-six coefficient of the pure-gauge source energy with a lattice Gaussian coefficient and compute its continuum limit. The comparison retains the nonlinear constraint, the Haar density, and the gauge-fixing determinant.

The proof has four reductions. The field-scale expansion and its tail bound are given in \cref{C-350-6,C-350-7}. \Cref{C-350-13} identifies the retained coefficient with the Gaussian coefficient under a flat block constraint; the running counterterms cancel in this identity. The comparison estimates \cref{C-350-14,C-350-15} and the box exhaustion then remove the constraint and the finite volume. Finally the lattice graphs are matched with their homogeneous kernels. Their local terms of degree $-4$ cancel, and the six contributions of degree $-5$ give the coefficient $8/(3\pi)$ in \cref{IV-73-100}.

\subsection{The Gaussian coefficient on the lattice}

We compute the pure-gauge coefficient in covariant gauge with
gauge parameter one. The gauge fixing contributes two quadratic
terms in addition to the Haar density. These terms must be kept
when the coefficient is compared with the constrained integral.

Identify the Hermitian traceless matrices with $\mathbb R^3$ by
the Pauli basis, so that $[X,Y]=2iX\times Y$. For an oriented
plaquette $p$, write its four boundary bonds as $b_i$ and their
signs as $s_i$, and put $A_i=A(b_i)$. Define homogeneous polynomials
by
\[
 a_p(e^{itA})=\sum_{j\ge2}t^j\mathsf a_p^{(j)}(A),\qquad
 \frac1i\log\prod_{i=1}^4e^{its_iA_i}
       =t\,dA(p)+t^2\mathfrak z_1(p)+t^3\mathfrak z_2(p)+O(t^4).
\]
The logarithm is taken near the identity. Thus the formulas do
not require a choice of logarithm for an arbitrary configuration.

\begin{lemma}[Wilson, Haar and gauge-fixing terms]
\label{IV-73-9}
The terms needed through order four are
\[
 \begin{split}
 \mathfrak z_1(p)&=-\sum_{i<j}s_is_jA_i\times A_j,\\
 \mathsf a_p^{(2)}&=\tfrac12|dA(p)|^2,\qquad
 \mathsf a_p^{(3)}=\langle dA(p),\mathfrak z_1(p)\rangle,\\
 \mathsf a_p^{(4)}&=\tfrac12|\mathfrak z_1(p)|^2+
       \langle dA(p),\mathfrak z_2(p)\rangle-\tfrac1{24}|dA(p)|^4.
 \end{split}
\]
The negative logarithm of the Haar density in exponential
coordinates has quadratic term $|A|^2/3$ and no odd terms.
For a site function $\lambda$, let
$\bar\lambda(b)=(\lambda(b_-)+\lambda(b_+))/2$. The derivative
of the logarithmic gauge action is
\[
 \left.\frac d{ds}A^{s\lambda}(b)\right|_0
 =-d\lambda(b)+2A(b)\times\bar\lambda(b)
       -\tfrac13A(b)\times(A(b)\times d\lambda(b))+O(A^4)d\lambda(b).
\]
Define the Faddeev--Popov operator by
$\mathsf M(A)\lambda=\left.\frac d{ds}d^*(A^{s\lambda})\right|_{s=0}$.
Its homogeneous terms are
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \mathsf M^{(0)}&=-d^*d,&
 \mathsf M^{(1)}(A)\lambda&=2d^*(A\times\bar\lambda),\\
 \mathsf M^{(2)}(A)\lambda&=-\tfrac13d^*(A\times(A\times d\lambda)),&
 \mathsf M^{(3)}&=0.
 \end{aligned}
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The convergent product of the four exponential series gives
\[
 \mathsf a_p^{(j)}=-\tfrac12
   \sum_{j_1+\cdots+j_4=j}\operatorname{tr}
               \prod_{i=1}^4\frac{(is_iA_i)^{j_i}}{j_i!}.
\]
Comparing its linear and quadratic terms with the exponential
of its logarithm gives $dA(p)$ and
$i\mathfrak z_1=-\frac12\sum_{i<j}s_is_j[A_i,A_j]$.
The logarithm is analytic, and rescaling all four arguments
shows that its next coefficient $\mathfrak z_2$ is homogeneous
of degree three. Expanding $1-\cos|t\,dA+t^2\mathfrak z_1+
t^3\mathfrak z_2+O(t^4)|$ gives the three Wilson terms.
The Haar density is a constant times $(\sin|A|/|A|)^2$;
its negative logarithm is $|A|^2/3+O(|A|^4)$.

For the gauge derivative put $\mathsf a_Y=-2Y\times\cdot$.
Conjugation by $e^{isY}$ is $e^{s\mathsf a_Y}$, and the
derivative of the exponential is
$\mathsf f(\mathsf a_Y)$, where $\mathsf f(z)=(e^z-1)/z$.
Differentiating
$e^{iA^{s\lambda}(b)}=e^{is\lambda(b_-)}e^{iA(b)}e^{-is\lambda(b_+)}$
therefore gives
\[
 \mathsf f(\mathsf a_A)^{-1}
                 (\lambda(b_-)-e^{\mathsf a_A}\lambda(b_+)).
\]
Use $1/\mathsf f(z)=1-z/2+z^2/12+O(z^4)$ and
$\mathsf a_A^2=4A\times(A\times\cdot)$.
There is no cubic term in this expansion. Applying $d^*$
gives the operator formulas.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[The free kernels and the coefficient]
\label{IV-73-15}\label{IV-73-19}
On $\mathbb Z^3$ write $\mathsf k_\mu=e^{ik_\mu}-1$ and
$d^\circ k=(2\pi)^{-3}dk$ on $[-\pi,\pi]^3$. Set
\[
 G(x-y)=\int e^{ik\cdot(x-y)}|\mathsf k|^{-2}\,d^\circ k,
 \qquad C((x,\mu),(y,\nu))=\delta_{\mu\nu}G(x-y).
\]
On a torus of side $N$, replace the integral by
$N^{-3}\sum_{k\in(2\pi/N)\mathbb Z^3/2\pi\mathbb Z^3,\ k\ne0}$.
These are the inverses of $d^*d$ on functions and of
$d^*d+dd^*$ on forms, off their constant modes. On the
lattice their symbols are integrable and positive; hence
they define real positive Gaussian covariances. Let
$\langle\cdot\rangle_0$ denote the centered Gaussian family
with covariance $\delta_{aa'}C(b,b')$ in the Pauli basis.

Define
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 E_p(b)&=\sum_i s_iC(b_i(p),b),&
 \Pi(p,q)&=\sum_js_jE_p(b_j(q)),\\
 g(b)&=G(b_+,b_+)+G(b_-,b_-)-2G(b_+,b_-),\\
 D(b;b')&=\tfrac12\sum_{x\in\{b'_-,b'_+\}}
                         [G(x,b_+)-G(x,b_-)].
 \end{aligned}
\]
Thus $E$ and $\Pi$ are the covariances with one and two
curvature entries. Put
\begin{equation}\label{IV-73-17}
 \begin{split}
 S_3&=\sum_p\mathsf a_p^{(3)},\qquad S_4=\sum_p\mathsf a_p^{(4)},\\
 V_2&=S_4+\tfrac13\sum_b|A(b)|^2
       +\tfrac23\sum_bg(b)|A(b)|^2
       -4\sum_{b,b'}D(b;b')D(b';b)\langle A(b),A(b')\rangle.
 \end{split}
\end{equation}
On the infinite lattice these are formal sums. Their
occurrence in a cumulant means the sum of the corresponding
local cumulants. Absolute convergence for the expressions
below is proved in \cref{IV-73-55}.

The joint cumulant of Gaussian polynomials is defined by
the finite moment--partition formula; no exponential moment
of a polynomial is assumed. Define
\begin{equation}\label{IV-73-24}
\begin{split}
 \mathsf B_1(p,q)={}&\langle\mathsf a_p^{(3)};\mathsf a_q^{(3)}\rangle_0
 +\langle\mathsf a_p^{(2)};\mathsf a_q^{(4)}\rangle_0
 +\langle\mathsf a_p^{(4)};\mathsf a_q^{(2)}\rangle_0\\
 &-\langle\mathsf a_p^{(3)};\mathsf a_q^{(2)};S_3\rangle_0
  -\langle\mathsf a_p^{(2)};\mathsf a_q^{(3)};S_3\rangle_0\\
 &-\langle\mathsf a_p^{(2)};\mathsf a_q^{(2)};V_2\rangle_0
  +\tfrac12\langle\mathsf a_p^{(2)};\mathsf a_q^{(2)};S_3;S_3\rangle_0.
\end{split}
\end{equation}
Use the superscript $\mathrm{lat}$ for the infinite lattice.
Write $x(p)$ for the plaquette barycentre. For compactly supported $f,h$ put
\begin{equation}\label{IV-73-25}
 \mathsf P_1^{\mathrm{lat}}(f,h;a)=
       a\sum_{p,q}f(ax(p))h(ax(q))\mathsf B_1^{\mathrm{lat}}(p,q).
\end{equation}
The factor $a$ is $a^{-2}\beta^{-3}\mathsf b^3$ when
$\beta=\mathsf b/a$: each smeared action observable has
the factor $a^{-1}$.
\end{definition}

The last two terms of $V_2$ follow from the gauge-fixing
Jacobian. On a finite torus, with operators restricted to
the mean-zero site functions,
$(\mathsf M^{(0)})^{-1}=-G$ and
\[
 \begin{split}
 -\operatorname{tr}[(\mathsf M^{(0)})^{-1}\mathsf M^{(2)}]
       &=\tfrac23\sum_bg(b)|A(b)|^2,\\
 \tfrac12\operatorname{tr}[((\mathsf M^{(0)})^{-1}\mathsf M^{(1)})^2]
       &=-4\sum_{b,b'}D(b;b')D(b';b)\langle A(b),A(b')\rangle.
 \end{split}
\]
For the first identity use
$\operatorname{tr}[X\times(Y\times\cdot)]=-2\langle X,Y\rangle$
and cycle $Gd^*$ past a bondwise operator.
For the second put $R=Gd^*(A\times\bar{\,\cdot\,})$.
Its kernel is
\[
 R(x,y)=\tfrac12\sum_b[G(x,b_+)-G(x,b_-)]
       (\delta_{y,b_-}+\delta_{y,b_+})A(b)\times\cdot.
\]
Thus $\operatorname{tr}R=0$ and
$\operatorname{tr}R^2=-2\sum_{b,b'}D(b;b')D(b';b)
\langle A(b),A(b')\rangle$, which proves the claim since
$(\mathsf M^{(0)})^{-1}\mathsf M^{(1)}=-2R$.
In particular the Jacobian has no linear term.
On $\mathbb Z^3$ these are identities for the local
coefficients of the formal sums defining $V_2$;
we do not take a trace over the whole infinite lattice.
Coordinate symmetry gives $g(b)=1/3$ there.

\subsection{Kernel bounds and the comparison with a torus}

Write $\langle x\rangle=\max\{1,|x|\}$ and
$\lg t=1+|\log t|$. A periodic symbol $\sigma$, smooth
off zero, belongs to $\mathcal S^s$ if
\[
 |\partial^\alpha\sigma(k)|\le C_\alpha|k|^{s-|\alpha|}
                       \qquad(0<|k|\le\sqrt3\pi)
\]
for every multi-index $\alpha$. Its kernel is
$K(x)=\int e^{ik\cdot x}\sigma(k)\,d^\circ k$ when $s>-3$.
On a torus of side $N$ use the nonzero-mode sum $K_N$.
The symbols of $C,E,\Pi,D$ above belong respectively to
$\mathcal S^{-2},\mathcal S^{-1},\mathcal S^0,
\mathcal S^{-1}$. This follows by multiplying
$|\mathsf k|^{-2}$ by the displayed difference symbols;
$|\mathsf k|\ge2|k|/\pi$ controls every derivative.

\begin{lemma}[Lattice and torus kernels]
\label{IV-73-39}\label{IV-73-75}
If $s>-3$ and $\sigma\in\mathcal S^s$, then
\[
 |\nabla^\alpha K(x)|\le C_\alpha\langle x\rangle^{-3-s-|\alpha|},
 \qquad |K_N(x)|\le C\langle x\rangle_N^{-3-s}.
\]
Here $|x|_N$ is the least Euclidean norm among the lifts
of $x$ and $\langle x\rangle_N=\max\{1,|x|_N\}$.
The constants involve finitely many symbol bounds and
are independent of $N$. For each fixed $x$, $K_N(x)\to K(x)$.
Moreover,
\[
 |K_N(x)-K(x)|\le C N^{-3-s}
                   \qquad(|x|_\infty\le3N/4).
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
A difference of order $\alpha$ multiplies the symbol by
$\mathsf k^\alpha$ and raises its order by $|\alpha|$,
so first consider $\alpha=0$. At $x=0$ integrability
gives the bound. At $|x|\ge1$, choose a smooth cutoff
$\chi$ equal to one on the unit ball and zero outside
the ball of radius two. The integral of
$\chi(|x|k)\sigma(k)$ is at most $C|x|^{-3-s}$.
The complementary symbol is smooth and periodic, with
derivative bounds $C_\alpha|k|^{s-|\alpha|}$ and support
where $|k|\ge|x|^{-1}$. Choose $j$ with
$|x_j|\ge|x|/\sqrt3$ and integrate by parts $r>s+3$
times in $k_j$. The resulting bound is
\[
 C|x|^{-r}\int_{|k|\ge|x|^{-1}}|k|^{s-r}\,dk
                       \le C|x|^{-3-s}.
\]
This proves the lattice estimate and its difference versions.

For the torus put $h=2\pi/N$. Comparison with the cubes
of side $h$ about nonzero modes gives
\[
 N^{-3}\sum_{0<|k|\le\rho}|k|^t\le C\rho^{3+t}
       \quad(t>-3),\qquad
 N^{-3}\sum_{|k|\ge\rho}|k|^t\le C\rho^{3+t}
       \quad(t<-3).
\]
Indeed $|k'|$ on such a cube lies between
$(1-\sqrt3/2)|k|$ and $(1+\sqrt3/2)|k|$.
Use a lift with $|x|=|x|_N$, so $|x_j|\le N/2$.
The part $\chi(|x|k)\sigma$ has the required bound by
the first sum. For the complementary part $\sigma''$,
summation by parts gives
\[
 (1-e^{ihx_j})^r\sum_ke^{ik\cdot x}\sigma''(k)
 =\sum_ke^{ik\cdot x}\delta_j^r\sigma''(k),
 \quad\delta_jf(k)=f(k)-f(k-he_j).
\]
The left factor has modulus at least $(4|x_j|/N)^r$.
For $|k|\ge2rh$, the integral representation of
$\delta_j^r$ bounds it by $Ch^r|k|^{s-r}$; it vanishes
unless $|k|\ge2/(3|x|)$. The bounded number of modes
with $|k|<2rh$ contribute at most
$Ch^r|x|^{r-s-3}$ after normalization. The second sum
gives the same bound for the other modes. Dividing by
the left factor proves the torus estimate.

For pointwise convergence split the symbol at a fixed
radius $\epsilon$. The part near zero contributes at
most $C\epsilon^{3+s}$ to both the sum and the integral.
The remaining smooth part converges by Riemann summation.
Let first $N\to\infty$ and then $\epsilon\downarrow0$.

Finally the finite Fourier sums give the exact identity
\[
 \sum_{v\in\{0,1\}^3}K_{2N}(x+Nv)=K_N(x).
\]
The sum over $v$ selects the modes of the smaller torus;
the zero mode is omitted on both sides. If
$|x|_\infty\le3N/4$, each of the seven nonzero images
has distance at least $N/4$ on the torus of side $2N$.
Thus $|K_N(x)-K_{2N}(x)|\le CN^{-3-s}$.
Iterate over $2^jN$ and use pointwise convergence.
The geometric series converges because $s>-3$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Scalar convolutions]\label{IV-73-40}
For $a> D$, $D\in\{3,6\}$ and $R\ge1$,
\[
 \sum_{z\in\mathbb Z^D}(R+|z|)^{-a}\le C_aR^{D-a}.
\]
For $a,a'\ge0$ and $a+a'>3$,
\[
 \sum_{z\in\mathbb Z^3}\langle z\rangle^{-a}
                    \langle x-z\rangle^{-a'}
 \le C_{a,a'}\langle x\rangle^{-\min\{a,a',a+a'-3\}}
                    \lg\langle x\rangle.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
On a unit cube the factor $R+|z|$ changes by at most
$1+\sqrt D$. Comparison with the integral and rescaling
by $R$ prove the first assertion.
For the convolution, $|x|<2$ follows from the first
assertion since the two factors are comparable.
Otherwise split into $|z|\le|x|/2$, $|x-z|\le|x|/2$
and their complement. On the first part use
$\langle x-z\rangle^{-a'}\le C|x|^{-a'}$ and sum
the first factor in radial shells. This gives
$C|x|^{-a'}\max\{1,|x|^{3-a}\}\lg|x|$.
The second part gives the symmetric bound. On the
complement $|x-z|$ and $|z|$ are comparable and at
least $|x|/2$, so the tail is bounded by
$C|x|^{3-a-a'}$. These are the three asserted exponents.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Connected pairings and their sums}

For a homogeneous polynomial $F$ of degree $r$, use its
polarization
\[
 F[\![X_1,\ldots,X_r]\!]=
   \left.\partial_{t_1}\cdots\partial_{t_r}
                    F(\textstyle\sum_jt_jX_j)\right|_{t=0}.
\]
Thus $F[\![A,\ldots,A]\!]=r!F(A)$.
An index $i=(b,a)$ specifies a bond and a colour; $\delta_i$
is its coordinate form. Write $C(i,j)=\delta_{aa'}C(b,b')$
and $E_p^a(b)=E_p(b)e_a$.

\begin{lemma}[Connected pairings]\label{IV-73-53}
Let $F_v$, $1\le v\le r$, have degrees $m_v$.
Their joint cumulant is the sum over symmetric matrices
$n=(n_{vv'})$ of nonnegative integers satisfying
\[
 2n_{vv}+\sum_{v'\ne v}n_{vv'}=m_v,
\]
whose graph on the vertices $1,\ldots,r$ is connected.
For each matrix choose one pairing of the slots with these
numbers of lines. Its contribution is
\[
 \frac{\displaystyle\sum_{\text{slot indices}}
       \prod_v F_v[\![\delta_{i(v,1)},\ldots,\delta_{i(v,m_v)}]\!]
       \prod_{\{e,e'\}}C(i(e),i(e'))}
      {\displaystyle\prod_{v<v'}n_{vv'}!
                           \prod_v2^{n_{vv}}n_{vv}!}.
\]
For the scalar cubic Wilson vertex, contraction of any two
slots with a colour-diagonal kernel is zero. In particular
a self-contraction at this vertex vanishes, as do two lines
from one quadratic curvature vertex to that cubic vertex.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Wick's formula expresses a moment as a sum over all pairings.
Each pairing splits uniquely into its connected components
on the polynomial vertices. The moment--partition identity
for cumulants therefore selects the connected pairings.
Expand each polynomial as $1/m_v!$ times its polarized form.
The number of pairings with fixed matrix $n$ is
\[
 \frac{\prod_vm_v!}
      {\prod_{v<v'}n_{vv'}!\prod_v2^{n_{vv}}n_{vv}!}:
\]
choose the slots at each vertex, match the slots at different
vertices, and pair those remaining at each vertex.
The factors $m_v!$ cancel those in the polynomial expansions.

The polarization of $\mathsf a_P^{(3)}$ is the sum over
the six permutations of
\[
 -\left\langle dX(P),
            \sum_{i<j}s_is_jY(b_i)\times Z(b_j)\right\rangle.
\]
If two slots have the same colour, every summand contains
one of $\langle e_a,e_a\times Z\rangle$,
$\langle e_a,Z\times e_a\rangle$ or
$\langle Z,e_a\times e_a\rangle$, all zero.
Two lines from $\mathsf a_p^{(2)}=\frac12\sum_a(dA)^a(p)^2$
identify the two colours and give the same cancellation.
Equivalently every monomial of $\mathsf a_P^{(3)}$ has
three different colours, so these cancellations hold for
each pairing before summing positions.
\end{proof}

For use in the coefficient calculation, define the colour-diagonal
kernel $\Sigma$ by
\[
 \delta_{aa'}\Sigma(b,b')=
  \langle\partial_{b,a}\partial_{b',a'}V_2\rangle_0
       -\langle\partial_{b,a}S_3;\partial_{b',a'}S_3\rangle_0.
\]
The expression is invariant under simultaneous rotations of
the three colours, so its colour matrix is a scalar multiple
of the identity. At fixed positions this is an identity of
finite sums; the convergence assertion below also justifies
the summed expression.

The seven cumulants in \eqref{IV-73-24} give six classes:
\begin{align*}
 \mathsf T_{\rm I}&=-3\Pi(p,q)
                       \sum_{b,b'}E_p(b)\Sigma(b,b')E_q(b'),\\
 \mathsf T_1&=\tfrac12\sum_{P,P',a,a',i,j}
       \mathsf a_P^{(3)}[\![E_p^a,E_q^{a'},\delta_i]\!]
       C(i,j)\mathsf a_{P'}^{(3)}[\![E_p^a,E_q^{a'},\delta_j]\!],\\
 \mathsf T_4&=-\tfrac14\sum_{P,a,a'}
                 \mathsf a_P^{(4)}[\![E_p^a,E_p^a,E_q^{a'},E_q^{a'}]\!],\\
 \mathsf T_{4'}&=\tfrac14\sum_{a,i,j}C(i,j)
     \bigl\{\mathsf a_q^{(4)}[\![E_p^a,E_p^a,\delta_i,\delta_j]\!]
          +\mathsf a_p^{(4)}[\![E_q^a,E_q^a,\delta_i,\delta_j]\!]\bigr\},\\
 \mathsf T_5&=-\tfrac12\sum_{P,a,i,i',j,j'}C(i,j)C(i',j')
     \bigl\{\mathsf a_q^{(3)}[\![E_p^a,\delta_i,\delta_{i'}]\!]
                 \mathsf a_P^{(3)}[\![E_p^a,\delta_j,\delta_{j'}]\!]\\
 &\hspace{44mm}+\mathsf a_p^{(3)}[\![E_q^a,\delta_i,\delta_{i'}]\!]
                 \mathsf a_P^{(3)}[\![E_q^a,\delta_j,\delta_{j'}]\!]\bigr\},\\
 \mathsf T_6&=\tfrac16\sum_{i_1,i_2,i_3,j_1,j_2,j_3}
   \mathsf a_p^{(3)}[\![\delta_{i_1},\delta_{i_2},\delta_{i_3}]\!]
   \mathsf a_q^{(3)}[\![\delta_{j_1},\delta_{j_2},\delta_{j_3}]\!]
                     \prod_{v=1}^3C(i_v,j_v).
\end{align*}
Here $P,P'$ range over plaquettes. In particular
\[
 \mathsf B_1(p,q)=\mathsf T_{\rm I}+\mathsf T_1+
       \mathsf T_4+\mathsf T_{4'}+\mathsf T_5+\mathsf T_6.
\]
We give the enumeration to fix the symmetry factors.
The two cubic observables have three joining lines,
giving $1/3!$. A quadratic and a quartic observable
have two joining lines and one self-contraction at the
quartic vertex, giving $1/4$.
For degrees $(2,3,3)$ the joining multiplicities are
$(1,1,2)$ and give $1/2$.
For two quadratic observables and a quadratic term of
$V_2$, the three joining multiplicities are one; these
terms enter $\mathsf T_{\rm I}$.
With the quartic Wilson vertex the possibilities are
one line joining $p,q$, one from each to $P$, and one
self-contraction at $P$; or two from each to $P$.
Their factors are $1/2$ and $1/4$.
Finally, with two cubic vertices $P,P'$, the degree
conditions give $n_{PP'}=1+n_{pq}$. The case
$n_{pq}=2$ is disconnected. If $n_{pq}=1$, there
are two assignments of the remaining observable legs,
each with factor $1/2$; together with the coefficient
$1/2$ in \eqref{IV-73-24} they give the cubic part
of $\mathsf T_{\rm I}$. If $n_{pq}=0$, two legs
from one observable to one cubic vertex vanish by
\cref{IV-73-53}; the remaining pattern gives
$\mathsf T_1$ with factor $1/2$.

\begin{lemma}[Absolute sums and one weakened line]
\label{IV-73-55}\label{IV-73-56}
Suppose the real kernels are colour diagonal and, with
$c_0\ge1$, satisfy
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 |C(b,b')|\le c_0\langle b_--b'_-\rangle^{-1},\qquad
 |E_p(b)|\le c_0\langle x_p-b_-\rangle^{-2},\\
 |D(b;b')|\le c_0\langle b_--b'_-\rangle^{-2},\qquad
 |\Pi(p,q)|\le c_0\langle x_p-x_q\rangle^{-3},
 \qquad |g(b)|\le c_0.
 \end{gathered}
\]
Write every Wilson vertex using the displayed curvature
factors in \cref{IV-73-9}. The sum of the absolute values
of the resulting connected pairings, over their positions,
is at most $Cc_0^5$, uniformly in $p,q$.
The same bound holds if the decay exponent of any one
line is lowered by $1/2$. It also holds for torus sums
with periodic distances, with a constant independent of
the side. In particular the infinite-lattice coefficient
and the six classes above are absolutely convergent.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
A plain leg is a component of $A$; a curvature leg is
a component of $dA$. A line with $j$ curvature ends
has decay exponent $1+j$. The standard writing of
$\mathsf a^{(3)}$ has one curvature and two plain legs.
The three parts of $\mathsf a^{(4)}$ have respectively
four plain legs, one curvature and three plain legs,
and four curvature legs. Each graph has at most five
lines. The finite numbers of component monomials,
colour sums and pairings can therefore be included in
$C$, leaving only the position sums.
Changes of a base point within one plaquette cost a
fixed factor in each decay bound.

Put $u=x_q-x_p$, and let $z,w$ be the positions of
the summed vertices relative to $x_p$.
For $\mathsf T_1$ the majorant has exponents at least
$(2,2,1,2,2)$ on the lines
$z,w,w-z,u-z,u-w$. Discard the central factor,
which is at most one. The sum factors into two
convolutions. Each has exponents at least $2,2$,
or $3/2,2$ if one outer line was weakened. Their
sums are bounded by \cref{IV-73-40}, since the sum
of the two exponents is strictly greater than three.
Weakening the central line leaves it bounded by one.

The cubic and ghost-loop terms of $\mathsf T_{\rm I}$
are bounded by
\[
 \langle u\rangle^{-3}
  \sum_{z,w}\langle z\rangle^{-n_1}
       \langle w-z\rangle^{-n_3}\langle u-w\rangle^{-n_5},
 \quad n_1,n_5\in\{2,3\},\quad n_3\ge2,
 \quad n_1+n_3+n_5=8.
\]
The four possibilities for $(n_3,n_5)$ are
$(2,3),(3,2),(3,3),(4,2)$.
Apply \cref{IV-73-40} first to $w$. Its remaining
power in $u-z$, added to $n_1$, exceeds three by
at least $1/2$, even if one of the three exponents
was lowered by $1/2$. Absorb the logarithm by a
power smaller than this margin and apply the same
lemma to $z$. This gives a uniform bound. If instead
the fixed line from $p$ to $q$ was weakened, its
factor is still at most one and the argument is
unchanged.

The other terms of $\mathsf T_{\rm I}$ have one
position sum bounded by a convolution with exponents
$2,2$; weakening one line leaves their sum at least
$7/2$. The class $\mathsf T_4$ has exponents $4,4$.
The class $\mathsf T_5$, after bounding its fixed
$p$--$q$ line by $c_0$, has exponents at least
$2,2$. These sums are bounded in the same way.
There are no position sums in $\mathsf T_{4'}$ and
$\mathsf T_6$. Pairings excluded by colour vanish
individually, by \cref{IV-73-53}; their absolute values
therefore also vanish.

For a torus the same convolution proof uses the
nearest images in the three regions of its radial
split. The number of such images is bounded in
dimension three. Extending each positive sum to the
corresponding lattice sum proves the same bound;
the finite number of lines makes the image factor
independent of the side.

For the kernels themselves, \cref{IV-73-39} supplies
the hypotheses. To justify the derivative grouping
in $\Sigma$, first sum the plaquettes containing one
fixed bond. Differentiating $\mathsf a_P^{(3)}$
either leaves one curvature leg and one plain leg,
or puts the derivative on the curvature leg.
The first case has total line degree at least three
between the two differentiated vertices. In the
second case, the two opposite plaquettes in each
direction give a first difference of a product of
two line kernels; the difference bound in
\cref{IV-73-39} again gives total degree at least
three. The resulting majorant is
$C\langle z\rangle^{-2}\langle w-z\rangle^{-3}
\langle u-w\rangle^{-2}$, which is summable by the
same two convolutions. Thus the regrouping into
$\Sigma$ and the formula for $\mathsf T_{\rm I}$
preserve absolutely convergent sums.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The finite-dimensional expansion}

\begin{lemma}[Two coefficients of a covariance]
\label{IV-73-26}\label{C-403-31}
Let $\mathcal W\subset\mathbb R^m$ be bounded and Borel,
and contain a ball about zero. Let $\phi,\theta,X,Y$
be smooth real functions on a neighbourhood of
$\overline{\mathcal W}$. Suppose that $\phi(0)=0$,
$d\phi(0)=0$, its Hessian $H$ is positive definite,
and $\phi$ has a positive infimum on the part of
$\mathcal W$ outside every sufficiently small ball
about zero. Suppose also that $X,Y$ and their
gradients vanish at zero. Write subscripts for
homogeneous Taylor polynomials and set
\[
 W_j=\phi_{j+2}+\theta_j,\qquad
 X_{1,j}=X_{j+2},\quad X_{2,j}=Y_{j+2}.
\]
The covariance for the normalized density
$e^{-\beta\phi-\theta}$ on $\mathcal W$ satisfies
\[
 \operatorname{Cov}_\beta(X,Y)
      =\beta^{-2}\gamma_0+\beta^{-3}\gamma_2+O(\beta^{-4}),
                    \qquad\beta\ge1,
\]
where the cumulants below are Gaussian with covariance
$H^{-1}$, and
\begin{align*}
 \gamma_0={}&\langle X_{1,0};X_{2,0}\rangle,\\
 \gamma_2={}&\langle X_{1,2};X_{2,0}\rangle
          +\langle X_{1,0};X_{2,2}\rangle
          +\langle X_{1,1};X_{2,1}\rangle\\
 &-\langle X_{1,1};X_{2,0};W_1\rangle
  -\langle X_{1,0};X_{2,1};W_1\rangle
  -\langle X_{1,0};X_{2,0};W_2\rangle\\
 &+\tfrac12\langle X_{1,0};X_{2,0};W_1;W_1\rangle.
\end{align*}
The error constant may depend on all the stated data.
In particular the result applies on a sufficiently
small fixed window under the local hypotheses alone.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Choose $\rho>0$ so that $B(0,\rho)\subset\mathcal W$
and $\phi(y)\ge(y,Hy)/4$ on this ball. Outside it,
the integrals of $1,X,Y,XY$ are $O(e^{-c\beta})$.
Set $t=\beta^{-1/2}$ and change variables $y=tz$.
The functions
\[
 \begin{split}
 v(t,z)&=t^{-2}\phi(tz)-\tfrac12(z,Hz)
                                  +\theta(tz)-\theta(0),\\
 x(t,z)&=t^{-2}X(tz),\qquad y(t,z)=t^{-2}Y(tz)
 \end{split}
\]
extend smoothly to $t=0$. Taylor's formula with
integral remainder shows that their first four
$t$ derivatives are bounded by fixed polynomials
in $|z|$ whenever $|tz|\le\rho$. Also
\[
 e^{-(z,Hz)/2-v(t,z)}\le Ce^{-(z,Hz)/4}.
\]
For $f\in\{1,x,y,xy\}$, expand $fe^{-v}$ through
degree three in $t$. Its remainder, multiplied by
$e^{-(z,Hz)/2}$, is bounded by
$Ct^4\langle z\rangle^N e^{-(z,Hz)/4}$ for a fixed
$N$. The same bound applies along the Taylor
segment $0\le s\le t$. Integration and the Gaussian
tail outside $|z|<\rho/t$ therefore give
\[
 \int_{\mathcal W}F e^{-\beta\phi-\theta}
  =Z_t t^{2\nu}
       \left[\sum_{j=0}^3t^j\langle(fe^{-v})_{[j]}\rangle
                                                   +O(t^4)\right],
\]
where $F=1,X,Y,XY$, respectively, $\nu=0,1,1,2$,
and $Z_t=t^m e^{-\theta(0)}\int e^{-(z,Hz)/2}\,dz$.
The exponentially small outer integral is absorbed
in the remainder. For $F=1$ the leading term is
one, so the denominator is at least $Z_t/2$ for
small $t$. Division of the four expansions is
therefore legitimate with an $O(t^4)$ error after
the factors $t^{2\nu}$ have been removed.

To identify the coefficients, introduce formal
variables $u_1,u_2$. The coefficient of $u_1u_2$
in
\[ \log\langle e^{u_1x+u_2y-v}\rangle \]
is the normalized covariance of $x,y$. The moment-partition
formula, grouped by the numbers of blocks of each
size, gives
\[
 \log\langle e^Z\rangle
       =\sum_{r\ge1}\frac1{r!}\langle Z;\ldots;Z\rangle.
\]
Taking that coefficient yields the formal series
\[
 \sum_{r\ge0}\frac{(-1)^r}{r!}
       \langle x;y;\underbrace{v;\ldots;v}_{r}\rangle.
\]
Its constant and quadratic terms are exactly
$\gamma_0,\gamma_2$. Each polynomial $X_{a,j}$ and
$W_j$ has the parity of $j$. At an odd total order,
every term of the moment-partition formula has an
odd Gaussian moment and vanishes. Multiplying by
$t^4$ gives the claimed remainder $O(t^8)$.
For the remaining compact interval of $\beta\ge1$,
enlarge the constant using boundedness of $X,Y$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Gauge fixing in a finite box}

Let $\Lambda_n=\{0,\ldots,n\}^3$, $n\ge2$, and
$\Lambda_n^\circ=\{1,\ldots,n-1\}^3$. A bond is free
if both endpoints lie in the box and at least one
is interior. Write $B_n$ for the positively oriented
free bonds and $P_n$ for all plaquettes in the box.
The configurations $\mathcal U_n$ equal one on all
other bonds. The gauge group $\mathcal G_n$ equals
one on the boundary. Let $\mathsf{Form}_n$ be the
real Lie-algebra-valued forms vanishing on the
nonfree bonds, and let $\mathsf X_n$ be the site
functions vanishing on the boundary. On these
spaces $d^*$ is the adjoint of $d$ for the sums
over bonds and interior sites.
Put
\[
 T_n=\{\langle x-e_1,x\rangle:x\in\Lambda_n^\circ\},
 \qquad S(U)=\sum_{p\in P_n}a_p(U).
\]
A superscript $T$ means that a configuration equals
one, or a form vanishes, on $T_n$.
In exponential coordinates write
$\sigma_1(|A|^2)=(\sin|A|/|A|)^2$ for the Haar
density with its constant factor removed.

\begin{lemma}[A slice in the box]\label{IV-73-12}
The map $(u,V)\mapsto V^u$ is a diffeomorphism
$\mathcal G_n\times\mathcal U_n^T\to\mathcal U_n$
and carries the product of the normalized Haar
measures to the product Haar measure on $\mathcal U_n$.
The only zero of $S$ in $\mathcal U_n^T$ is one.
For every $\tau>0$, the form
\[
 \tfrac12\|dA\|^2+\tfrac1{2\tau}\|d^*A\|^2
\]
is positive definite on $\mathsf{Form}_n$; $d^*d$
is positive definite on $\mathsf X_n$.

For suitable $0<\rho_2,\rho_3\le\rho_1\le1/20$,
the map $\Xi(\lambda,A)=A^\lambda$ is a diffeomorphism
on a neighbourhood of
\[
 \overline{\mathcal D},\qquad
 \mathcal D=\{(\lambda,A)\in\mathsf X_n\times
           \mathsf{Form}_n^T:|\lambda|_\infty<\rho_1,
                              |A|_\infty<\rho_3\}.
\]
Its image $\mathcal W=\Xi(\mathcal D)$ has compact
closure in $\{|A'|_\infty<1\}$, and the
Faddeev--Popov determinant is nonzero there.
For each $|A|_\infty\le\rho_3$, the map
$\lambda\mapsto d^*(A^\lambda)$ is injective on
$|\lambda|_\infty\le\rho_1$, and its open image
contains $|c|_\infty<\rho_2$. For bounded Borel
functions $\Phi,w$, with $w\ge0$,
\begin{equation}\label{IV-73-14}
 \begin{split}
 &\int_{\mathcal W}\Phi(A')w(d^*A')|\det\mathsf M(A')|
                    \prod_{b\in B_n}\sigma_1(|A'(b)|^2)\,dA'\\
 &=\int_{|A|_\infty<\rho_3}
       \prod_{b\in B_n\setminus T_n}\sigma_1(|A(b)|^2)\,dA
       \int_{d^*(A^{\{|\lambda|_\infty<\rho_1\}})}
                         w(c)\Phi(A^{\lambda(c)})\,dc.
 \end{split}
\end{equation}
Here $\lambda(c)$ is the unique solution in that
domain. All Lebesgue measures use the Euclidean
scalar products just specified.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The condition $U^{u'}=1$ on $T_n$ is the recursion
\[
 u'(x)=u'(x-e_1)U(\langle x-e_1,x\rangle),
                         \qquad x\in\Lambda_n^\circ,
\]
starting with $u'=1$ on $x_1=0$. It determines
$u'$ uniquely. Then $V=U^{u'}$ and $u=u'^{-1}$
are the required inverse coordinates. Products
and inverses in the group make both maps smooth.
At fixed $u$, invariance of Haar measure permits
the change $V(b)\mapsto U(b)$ off $T_n$. On each
line parallel to $e_1$, change $u(x)$ to
$u(x-e_1)u(x)^{-1}$ in decreasing order of $x_1$.
Each substitution preserves Haar measure and
leaves the earlier substitutions fixed. This
proves the measure identity.

If $S(V)=0$, every plaquette holonomy is one.
The direction-one bonds with initial coordinate
$x_1\le n-2$ already equal one by the constraint
or the boundary condition. The $1\nu$ plaquettes,
$\nu=2,3$, propagate the boundary value one along
direction one to all direction-$\nu$ bonds.
Finally the $12$ plaquettes at $x_1=n-1$
propagate the value one from $x_2=0$ to the
remaining direction-one bonds. Hence $V=1$.

The additive version proves that $dA=0$ implies
$A=d\lambda$ for a unique $\lambda\in\mathsf X_n$:
choose $\lambda$ recursively along $T_n$ to cancel
$A$ there and use the same plaquette argument.
If also $d^*A=0$, then $\|d\lambda\|^2=0$,
so $A=0$. The same recursion shows that
$d\lambda=0$ implies $\lambda=0$. These facts
prove both positivity assertions.

In exponential coordinates the preceding
diffeomorphism is $\Xi$. Restrict first to
$|\lambda|_\infty,|A|_\infty<1/10$, where
$|A^\lambda|_\infty<1$. Set
$c(\lambda,A)=d^*(A^\lambda)$. Differentiating
the group action gives
\[
 \partial_\lambda c(\lambda,A)
       =\mathsf M(A^\lambda)\vartheta_\lambda,
 \qquad
 \det\vartheta_\lambda
       =\prod_{x\in\Lambda_n^\circ}\sigma_1(|\lambda(x)|^2)>0.
\]
At zero this derivative is $-d^*d$, which is
invertible. Apply the inverse function theorem
to $(\lambda,A)\mapsto(c(\lambda,A),A)$.
Choose a closed product neighbourhood inside its
domain of injectivity, and then smaller radii
$\rho_2,\rho_3$ whose product lies in its image.
Compactness gives the asserted common radii,
the nonvanishing determinant and the closure
property for $\mathcal W$.

The Haar identity in exponential coordinates
contains the product of the site densities
$\sigma_1(|\lambda(x)|^2)$ and the unconstrained
bond densities. The constant Haar factors cancel
because $\#T_n=\#\Lambda_n^\circ$. At each fixed
$A$, change $\lambda$ to $c$. The displayed
derivative identity gives
\[
 dc=|\det\mathsf M(A^\lambda)|
       \prod_x\sigma_1(|\lambda(x)|^2)\,d\lambda.
\]
Fubini's theorem and this substitution give
\eqref{IV-73-14}.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[The box coefficient]\label{IV-73-27}
For the Wilson probability measure on $\mathcal U_n$
with density proportional to $e^{-\beta S}$, and
for $p,q\in P_n$,
\[
 \langle a_p;a_q\rangle_{n,\beta}
  =\beta^{-2}\mathsf B_0^{[n]}(p,q)
   +\beta^{-3}\mathsf B_1^{[n]}(p,q;\tau)+O(\beta^{-4}).
\]
The coefficients are the Gaussian coefficients
\eqref{IV-73-24} on the box, with covariance
$(d^*d+\tau^{-1}dd^*)^{-1}$; the leading coefficient
is $\mathsf B_0^{[n]}=3\Pi^{[n]}(p,q)^2/2$.
The error constant may depend on the box, $p,q$
and $\tau>0$. The coefficient $\mathsf B_1^{[n]}$
is independent of $\tau$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
For $F=1,a_p,a_q,a_pa_q$, use the Haar identity
of \cref{IV-73-12} and gauge invariance to reduce
the integral to $\mathcal U_n^T$. Away from the
window $|A|_\infty<\rho_3$, the action has a
positive minimum by compactness and the uniqueness
of its zero. The omitted integral is therefore
$O(e^{-c\beta})$. The denominator on the window
is at least $c\beta^{-d_1/2}$, where
$d_1=\dim\mathsf{Form}_n^T$: integrate over a ball
of radius $\beta^{-1/2}$ and use $S(e^{iA})\le C|A|^2$.
Thus the same error is exponential after normalization.

In \eqref{IV-73-14}, take
$w(c)=e^{-\beta\|c\|^2/(2\tau)}$ and
$\Phi(A')=F(e^{iA'})e^{-\beta S(e^{iA'})}$.
Gauge invariance makes the latter constant on
each gauge orbit. The inner integral of $w$
equals
\[
 (2\pi\tau/\beta)^{d_0/2}(1-\epsilon(A)),
 \qquad0\le\epsilon(A)\le Ce^{-c\beta},
 \qquad d_0=\dim\mathsf X_n,
\]
uniformly in $A$, because its domain contains
the fixed ball $|c|_\infty<\rho_2$.
Consequently the original normalized expectations,
up to exponentially small errors, have density
$e^{-\beta\phi_\tau-\theta}$ on $\mathcal W$, where
\[
 \begin{split}
 \phi_\tau(A)&=S(e^{iA})+\|d^*A\|^2/(2\tau),\\
 \theta(A)&=-\sum_{b\in B_n}\log\sigma_1(|A(b)|^2)
                                     -\log|\det\mathsf M(A)|.
 \end{split}
\]
These functions are smooth on a neighbourhood
of the compact closure. The Hessian is positive
by \cref{IV-73-12}. A zero of $\phi_\tau\circ\Xi$
would have $S(e^{iA})=0$ and $d^*(A^\lambda)=0$.
The first condition gives $A=0$; injectivity of
the gauge function gives $\lambda=0$. Compactness
therefore supplies the lower bounds away from
zero required by \cref{IV-73-26}.

The chart expansions of \cref{IV-73-9} give
$\phi_{\tau,3}=S_3$ and
$\phi_{\tau,4}=S_4$. Expand the determinant as
$\log\det(1+Z)=\operatorname{tr}Z-\operatorname{tr}Z^2/2+O(Z^3)$,
with $Z=(\mathsf M^{(0)})^{-1}
(\mathsf M(A)-\mathsf M^{(0)})$.
The linear trace is zero. The quadratic Haar
and determinant terms give precisely $V_2-S_4$
in \eqref{IV-73-17}. Thus $W_1=S_3$, $W_2=V_2$,
and \cref{IV-73-26} yields the claimed coefficients.
The leading curvature covariance is independent
of $\tau$. Subtract it, multiply by $\beta^3$
and let $\beta\to\infty$ to see that the next
coefficient is independent of $\tau$ as well.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The pure-gauge coefficient on a constrained fibre}

We need a coefficient determined by the lattice and its
constraint, independently of the intermediate running couplings.
We first define it by a finite-dimensional integral.

For polynomials \(X_{a,j}\), \(a=1,2\), \(j=0,1,2\),
and \(W_1,W_2\), put
\begin{equation}\label{C-350-5}
 \begin{split}
 \gamma_2[\nu]={}&
 \langle X_{1,2};X_{2,0}\rangle_\nu
 +\langle X_{1,0};X_{2,2}\rangle_\nu
 +\langle X_{1,1};X_{2,1}\rangle_\nu\\
 &-\langle X_{1,1};X_{2,0};W_1\rangle_\nu
  -\langle X_{1,0};X_{2,1};W_1\rangle_\nu\\
 &-\langle X_{1,0};X_{2,0};W_2\rangle_\nu
  +\tfrac12\langle X_{1,0};X_{2,0};W_1^2\rangle_\nu.
 \end{split}
\end{equation}
These are joint cumulants.  If \(\nu\) is even,
\(X_{a,0}\) is even, and \(W_1\) is odd, the last
cumulant equals
\(\langle X_{1,0};X_{2,0};W_1;W_1\rangle_\nu\).
Indeed, expanding a cumulant with the product entry
\(W_1^2\) adds only
\(2\langle X_{1,0};W_1\rangle
\langle X_{2,0};W_1\rangle\) and
\(2\langle W_1\rangle
\langle X_{1,0};X_{2,0};W_1\rangle\), both zero by parity.

Let \(\phi,\theta,X,Y\) be real and smooth near zero,
with \(\phi(0)=0\), \(d\phi(0)=0\), and positive
Hessian \(H\).  Assume \(X,Y\) and their gradients
vanish at zero.  Subscripts on these functions denote
homogeneous Taylor polynomials.  Put
\[
 W_j=\phi_{j+2}+\theta_j,\qquad
 X_{1,j}=X_{j+2},\qquad X_{2,j}=Y_{j+2}.
\]
The covariance under the normalized density
\(e^{-\beta\phi-\theta}\) on a sufficiently small fixed
window about zero has expansion
\begin{equation}\label{C-350-31}
 \beta^{-2}\gamma_0^{\rm L}
       +\beta^{-3}\gamma_2^{\rm L}+O(\beta^{-4}),
 \qquad
 \gamma_0^{\rm L}=\langle X_{1,0};X_{2,0}\rangle_{H^{-1}},
 \quad \gamma_2^{\rm L}=\gamma_2[\nu_{H^{-1}}].
\end{equation}
Here \(\nu_{H^{-1}}\) is the centered Gaussian measure
with covariance \(H^{-1}\). This is \cref{IV-73-26};
the last term has the form in \eqref{C-350-5} by
the parity identity above.
We write \(\gamma_{m'}^{\rm L}[\phi,\theta,X,Y]\)
for these two coefficients, \(m'=0,2\).

\begin{proposition}[Composition of the fibre charts]\label{C-350-12}
Let \(N=\ell L^K\), \(\ell=2L^m\), and
\(1\le t\le K\), with
\(2L^{m+K-t+1}\ge C_LM\).  Let \(\mathsf Y\) be
the space of arrays \(y=(\mathcal A_j)_{j<t}\), where
\(\mathcal A_j\) is a real \(\mathfrak{su}(2)\)-valued
one-form on the non-pivot bonds at level \(j\).
There are a neighborhood \(\mathsf O_t\) of one in
\(\mathcal V_t\) and \(\rho_2>0\) such that
\[
 W_t=W,\qquad W_j=V_{W_{j+1}}[\mathcal A_j],\qquad
 \Psi(W,y)=W_0
\]
define a real analytic diffeomorphism from
\(\mathsf O_t\times\mathsf Y_{\rho_2}\) onto an open
neighborhood \(\mathsf U\) of the trivial bare configuration.
Here \(\mathsf Y_{\rho_2}=\{y:|\mathcal A_j|<\rho_2\}\),
and \(V_W[\mathcal A]\) is the one-step fibre chart.
It satisfies \(\mathcal M W_j=W_{j+1}\).
For a real analytic \(\theta\) and \(C_H>0\),
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pure-flat-haar}
 \int H(U)\,dU
   =C_H\int_{\mathsf O_t}\int_{\mathsf Y_{\rho_2}}
                    e^{-\theta(W,y)}H(\Psi(W,y))\,dy\,dW
\end{equation}
whenever \(H\) is bounded Borel and supported in
\(\mathsf U\).

For positive strengths \(\kappa_j\), let
\[
 F_\kappa(U)=A(U)+\sum_{j<t}\kappa_jG_j(\mathcal M^jU),
 \qquad \phi_\kappa(y)=F_\kappa(\Psi(1,y)),
\]
where \(G_j\) is the block gauge-fixing function.
Then \(\phi_\kappa\ge0\), \(\phi_\kappa(0)=0\),
\(d\phi_\kappa(0)=0\), and its Hessian is positive
definite and block diagonal by level.

The coefficients
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pure-flat-coefficients}
 \mathsf g_{m'}[N,t](p,q)
  =\gamma_{m'}^{\rm L}
    [\phi_\kappa,\theta(1,\cdot),
                     a_p\circ\Psi(1,\cdot),a_q\circ\Psi(1,\cdot)],
 \qquad m'=0,2,
\end{equation}
are independent of \(\kappa\) and of the adapted chart.
They depend only on \(N,t,L,p,q\), with plaquettes read
in bare lattice units.

An adapted chart here is a smooth chart \(\Psi'(w,y)\)
near \((0,0)\) with \(\Psi'(0,0)=1\) and
\(\operatorname{Lg}\mathcal M^t\Psi'(w,y)=w\), whose
Haar formula is
\(C'\varrho'(w)e^{-\theta'(w,y)}\,dw\,dy\), with
\(C'>0\), positive continuous \(\varrho'\), continuous
\(\theta'\), and smooth \(\theta'(0,\cdot)\).
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The size assumption makes each lattice through level
\(t\) admissible for the one-step chart.  Choose one
calibration \(\mathsf t_*\) so large that
\(\varepsilon(\mathsf t_*)\le1\) and
\(\delta(\mathsf t_*)\le\delta_{\rm im}\).
It serves at every level.  Near the trivial block field,
the averaged background \(V_j^{\rm bf}(W)\) is analytic,
\(V_j^{\rm bf}(1)=1\), and
\(\mathcal M V_j^{\rm bf}(W)=W\).
The chart has the form
\(V_W[\mathcal A]=e^{iB'}V_j^{\rm bf}(W)\), with
\(B'=\mathcal A\) on the non-pivot bonds.

We first remove the gauge-fixing factor from the one-step
integration formula of \cite[Prop. 52.2]{YMM1}.
On its chart image this factor is
positive and bounded below, and the small-field indicator
is one.  Apply that formula to the bounded function
\(H/\mathfrak G_j[\mathsf t_*]\), and set
\(B=\mathsf t_*^{1/2}\mathcal A\).
The powers of \(\mathsf t_*\) and the gauge normalizers
cancel.  The remaining constant is
\((2\pi^2)^{-\#\mathfrak X_j^+}L^{-3\#\Gamma_j}\),
and the density is the product of the elimination
normalizer and the chart Jacobian.  Iterating downward
and applying Fubini gives \eqref{eq:pure-flat-haar}, with
\[
 C_H=\prod_{j<t}(2\pi^2)^{-\#\mathfrak X_j^+}
                            L^{-3\#\Gamma_j},\qquad
 0<e^{-\theta}\le\prod_{j<t}(27L^9)^{\#\Gamma_j}.
\]
Here \(\mathfrak X_j^+\) denotes the positively oriented
non-pivot bonds at level \(j\), and \(\Gamma_j\) the
positive bonds at level \(j+1\).
Continuity of the charts lets us choose
\(\mathsf O_t\times\mathsf Y_{\rho_2}\) on which every
step lies in this domain.

The map
\[
 U\longmapsto\left(\mathcal M^tU,
  \left(\operatorname{Lg}
    [\mathcal M^jU(b)V_j^{\rm bf}(\mathcal M^{j+1}U)(b)^{-1}]
                      \right)_{j<t,\ b\text{ non-pivot}}\right)
\]
is an analytic left inverse of \(\Psi\).
Its differential is injective.  Indeed, a vector in its
kernel has zero variation at level \(t\).  Descending
one level, it has zero variation on the non-pivot bonds;
the invertibility of the averaging derivative at each
pivot forces its variation there also to vanish.
Induction reaches the bare level.  The dimensions agree,
so the inverse function theorem makes \(\Psi\) a local
analytic diffeomorphism.  The left inverse gives global
injectivity on the chosen domain.  The Haar density
pulled back by this diffeomorphism is positive and
analytic.  It agrees almost everywhere with the
continuous density above, hence everywhere; this also
proves analyticity of \(\theta\).

For the Hessian, let \(E_j(W)\) be the value of the
bare action on the minimal orbit over \(W\), and set
\(E_0=A\).  Along the chain,
\(E_{j+1}(W_{j+1})=E_j(V_{W_{j+1}}[0])\).
Since \(E_t(1)=0\),
\[
 A(W_0)=\sum_{j<t}
     \bigl(E_j(V_{W_{j+1}}[\mathcal A_j])
                         -E_j(V_{W_{j+1}}[0])\bigr).
\]
Each summand and its derivative in \(\mathcal A_j\)
vanish at \(\mathcal A_j=0\), for all higher fields:
the background is critical on the constrained fibre.
Its Hessian at zero therefore has only the \((j,j)\)
block.  The same is true of \(G_j(W_j)\), which is
nonnegative and zero at \(\mathcal A_j=0\).

The Hessian is positive definite.  A vector in its
kernel gives linearized fields \(a_j\) with \(a_t=0\),
\(da_0=0\), and zero linearized contour variables at
every level.  Averaging preserves closed forms, so each
\(a_j\) is closed.  On a simply connected block it
then vanishes on internal bonds, because its contour
variables vanish.  It is constant on bonds crossing
any one adjacent block face, by the plaquette equation.
Its average at that coarse bond is this constant.
Descending from \(a_t=0\) gives \(a_j=0\) at every
level.  The chart differential is invertible, so the
original vector is zero.

To compare adapted charts, their transition map has
the form \((w,y)\mapsto(w,s(w,y))\), with
\(s(0,0)=0\).  Equality of the two Haar formulas yields
\[
 C_H\varrho_H(w)e^{-\theta(e^{iw},y)}
  =C'\varrho'(w)e^{-\theta'(w,s(w,y))}
                                      |\det D_ys(w,y)|.
\]
Both sides are continuous, so this equality holds also
on the fibre \(w=0\), although that fibre has ambient
measure zero.  The change \(y\mapsto s(0,y)\) therefore
identifies the two conditional densities up to a
constant.  Their observable covariances and hence their
Laplace coefficients coincide.

Finally, gauge transformations equal to one on the top
lattice preserve this fibre, the action, and both
plaquette observables.  Integrate the normalized
gauge-fixing factors over their orbits, starting with
the finest sites.  Each integrates to one at every
strength, by \cite[Prop. 6.2]{YMM1}.
Restricting to a fixed small chart changes
this identity only by exponentially small terms in
\(\beta\), because the gauge-fixing phase has a strict
minimum in the gauge directions.  Thus neither
coefficient in \eqref{eq:pure-flat-coefficients} depends
on \(\kappa\).  In bare units all the levels through
\(t\) are \(L^j\mathbb Z^3/N\mathbb Z^3\); the
constraint, Haar measure, action, and observables on
them depend only on \(N,t,L,p,q\).
\end{proof}

\subsection{The pure-gauge flow at a complex field scale}

For the pure-gauge comparison we use the running coefficients
as calibrations. This fixes both the integration boxes and
the Gaussian measures at scale zero. We specify this choice
before identifying any Taylor coefficient with a constrained
integral.

Let $D=(K,\beta)$ be an admitted pure-gauge first-passage
datum at $g$, with physical spacing $a=L^{-K}$ and label
$b=a\beta$. Write $x_0=\beta$ and
$x_{j+1}=L^{-1}x_j-e_{j+1}$ for its running coefficients.
Put
\[
 D_j=L^ja,\quad t_j=L^{-j}\beta=b/D_j,\quad
 \mathfrak b(x)=A_1(\log x)^{p_0},\quad
 \delta(x)=\mathfrak b(x)x^{-1/2}.
\]
The notation $D_j$ denotes a length, while $D$ denotes
the datum. At level $j$ the calibration and the coefficient
of the original action are both $x_j$.
For sources $w_1=f\circ x,w_2=h\circ x$, put
$\eta=\|w_1\|_\infty\|w_2\|_\infty$.
Suppose their supports lie in balls of radius $d$ whose
distance is at least $d$, with $8a\le d$.
Set $r=d/a$ and $l=\max\{1,\log(2b/d)\}$.

\begin{proposition}[Pure-gauge parameters]\label{C-350-6}
There is a threshold $\gamma_s>0$, depending only on
the construction constants, such that every admitted
datum with $g\le\gamma_s$ and $K\ge3$ has the following
properties. Every step lattice is large enough for its
chart and curvature response, and $\ell\ge N_{\mathsf H}$.
Moreover
\[
 x_0>\cdots>x_K>g^{-2},\qquad x_{K-1}>Lg^{-2},\qquad
 \tfrac34t_j\le x_j\le2t_j,\quad
 \tfrac34\le t_j/x_j\le\tfrac43\quad(j<K).
\]
The weighted small-field progression is admitted with
calibrations $x_j$ and coefficients $x_j$.
One can require in addition
\[
 \log x_{K-1}\ge\max\{2p_0,1+\log L\},\qquad
 \delta(x_{K-1})\le\delta_{\rm ch},\qquad
 \delta(x_{K-1})^2\le\tfrac18\rho^2\delta(t_\flat)^2,
\]
where the positive numbers $t_\flat,\rho,\delta_{\rm ch}$
are chosen from the construction constants as in the proof
below. They are independent of the datum and the sources.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The coupling recursion gives $|x_j-t_j|\le\bar B$.
The first-passage condition gives $x_{K-1}>Lg^{-2}$
and $x_K>g^{-2}$. Choose $\gamma_s$ so small that
$x_{K-1}\ge12\bar B$. Then $|t_j/x_j-1|\le1/12$,
which implies the displayed comparisons.
The admitted sides satisfy $LMR(x_K)\le L^m$;
the side conditions in the gauge construction give
the admissibility of all preceding step lattices and
$\ell\ge N_{\mathsf H}$.
The admission lemma \cite[Lem. 126.2]{YMM1} applies
since $MR(x_K)\le L^m$. It supplies the place and
progression hypotheses, including the weighted-array
bound, for \cite[Prop. 122.1]{YMM1}. The weighted
progression uses its one-step coefficient discs and
the diagonal choice of their coefficients.
Its step and chain domains have fixed positive
thresholds, including $\delta_{\rm ch}$.
Once $t_\flat$ and $\rho$ below have been chosen,
all the remaining conditions follow by decreasing
$\gamma_s$: $x_{K-1}>L\gamma_s^{-2}$, and
$\delta(x)$ decreases to zero for $\log x\ge2p_0$.
This order of choices does not use any source norm
or any later comparison depth.
\end{proof}

At a common complex scale $\lambda$, keep the counterterms
$e_j$ and the boxes $|B_j(b)|<\mathfrak b(x_j)$ fixed,
put the field $\lambda x_j^{-1/2}B_j$ into every chart,
and scale the nonlinear action potentials as specified
in the proof below. Set
\[
 \xi_j(\lambda)=t_j+\lambda^2(x_j-t_j),\qquad
 \tau_j(\lambda)=\xi_j(\lambda)/x_j.
\]
Thus $\xi_{j+1}=L^{-1}\xi_j-\lambda^2e_{j+1}$.
At $\lambda=1$ this is the original progression.
At $\lambda=0$ its Gaussian precision on the non-pivot
bonds is
\[
 \mathsf M_j=(t_j/x_j)\mathsf B_j^{\rm cv}+\widehat{\mathsf G},
 \qquad \mathsf M_j\ge\tfrac34\gamma^{\rm tr}.
\]
In particular its Gaussian is conditioned on the stated
box. The parameter $\tau_j(0)$ is $t_j/x_j$.

Let $E_\mu^{(j),\lambda}$ be the resulting local terms,
including the source $\mu_1w_1+\mu_2w_2$, and define
\[
 \mathsf n_j^\lambda=
  \sum_{X,z}\left.\partial_{\mu_1}\partial_{\mu_2}
                   E_\mu^{(j),\lambda}(X,1,z)\right|_{\mu=0},
 \qquad
 \mathsf h_{2m}^{(n)}=\sum_{j\le n}\mathsf n_{j,[2m]},
 \qquad \mathsf H^{(n)}[D]=\beta^3a^2\mathsf h_6^{(n)}.
\]
The sum over $z$ is over the level-$j$ sites in $X$.
The subscript $[2m]$ denotes the coefficient of
$\lambda^{2m}$ at zero.

\begin{proposition}[The coefficient tail]\label{C-350-7}
There are constants $\rho\in(0,1/2]$, $c_0,C_J,C_n,C_R$
and radii
\[
 R_j=\frac{\delta(t_\flat)}{2\delta(x_j)},\qquad
 R_j^{-2}\le c_0(\log x_j)^{2p_0}D_j/b,\qquad
 (\rho R_j)^2\ge2,
\]
such that the progression is holomorphic in its common
field scale on $|\lambda|<R_j$ through step $j+1$.
Its integrated terms are even in $\lambda$.
The source derivatives vanish on domains missing the
corresponding source supports. With
\[
 \begin{gathered}\psi_i=\min\{1,(d/D_i)^3\},\qquad
 \chi_i=\min\{1,(d/D_i)^{5/2}\},\\
 \Pi_{i+1}=\max\{1,(d/D_{i+1})^3\}
                  e^{-[d/(4MD_{i+1})-2]_+},\end{gathered}
\]
their norms at rate $\kappa^+=(1+4\beta_s)\kappa$ obey
\[
 \begin{split}
 \|\dot E_a^{(i+1),\lambda}\|_{\kappa^+}
       &\le C_J|\lambda|^2R_i^{-2}D_i^{-1}\psi_i\|w_a\|_\infty,\\
 \|\ddot E^{(i+1),\lambda}\|_{\kappa^+}
       &\le C_J|\lambda|^2R_i^{-2}D_i^{-2}\chi_i\eta,
