                           \qquad i\le j,\quad |\lambda|\le\rho R_j.
 \end{split}
\]
In particular $\mathsf n_{j+1,[0]}=\mathsf n_{j+1,[2]}=0$ and
\[
 |\mathsf n_{j+1}^\lambda|
       \le C_n|\lambda|^2R_j^{-2}D_j^{-2}\chi_j\Pi_{j+1}\eta.
\]
For $m=2,3$ and $D_n\ge d$,
\[
 \sum_{j=n}^{K-1}|\mathsf n_{j+1,[2m]}|
 \le C_Rb^{-m}l^{2mp_0}d^{m-2}
                   (d/D_n)^{5/2-(m-2)}\eta.
\]
Consequently, for $n\le n'\le K$ and $L^n\ge r$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pure-running-coefficient-tail}
 |\mathsf H^{(n')}[D]-\mathsf H^{(n)}[D]|
       \le C_R l^{6p_0}(r/L^n)^{3/2}r\eta.
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Choose the lower calibration $t_\flat\ge\gamma^{-2}$
so that $\log t_\flat\ge2p_0$,
$K_P\delta(t_\flat)\le w_*/8$,
$\bar B\delta(t_\flat)^2\le\sigma_*A_1^2$, and
\[
 S_\omega(E^\flat+\tfrac32\alpha_0^2B_\sharp)+2
       \le N^\flat(t_\flat)
       :=\frac{w_*\alpha_0}
                    {4K_\Lambda(1+\beta_s)\delta(t_\flat)}.
\]
Here $S_\omega$ is the sum of the localization weights,
and $E^\flat$ bounds the regular local terms and the
terms created by one step. These constants are fixed
by the one-step bounds; the two extra units provide
room for its parameters and for Cauchy differentiation.
Since $\delta$ decreases to zero, this choice exists.
The last condition in \cref{C-350-6} implies
$t_\flat<x_j$ and $(\rho R_j)^2\ge2$.
The comparison $x_j\ge3b/(4D_j)$ proves the stated
bound on $R_j^{-2}$.

The action coefficient remains in its one-step disc:
\[
 |\xi_j(\lambda)-x_j|
   =|\lambda^2-1|\,|x_j-t_j|
   <2R_j^2\bar B\le\tfrac12\sigma_*x_j
                           \qquad(|\lambda|<R_j).
\]
In the normalized fields, the gauge-fixing quadratic
term is $-(1-\tau_j)(B_j,\widehat{\mathsf G}B_j)/2$.
Combining it with the Gaussian of precision
$\tau_j\mathsf A_j^{\rm cv}$ gives exactly
$\tau_j\mathsf B_j^{\rm cv}+\widehat{\mathsf G}$.
We give the scaling of the remaining potentials and
check their domains. Put $t=x_j$ and
$\mu=\lambda(t_\flat/t)^{1/2}$. For the Jacobian,
gauge-fixing, action and localized potentials, respectively,
the formulas are
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 V^{{\rm J},\lambda}(B)&=V^{\rm J}[t_\flat](\mu B),&
 V'^{,\lambda}(B)&=V'[t_\flat](\mu B),\\
 V^{\natural,\lambda}(B)&=\mu^{-2}
                   V^{\natural}[t_\flat](\mu B),
                   &&\natural\in\{{\rm G},{\rm A}\}.
 \end{aligned}
\]
The last two potentials vanish to order at least three
in the fluctuation field. Their quotients therefore
extend holomorphically across $\lambda=0$ and vanish
there. The first and fourth potentials vanish there
as well. These formulas preserve the original potentials
at $\lambda=1$.

To check the bounds, write
$r=\mathsf C_{\mathcal A}\mathfrak b(t)$,
$r_\flat=\mathsf C_{\mathcal A}\mathfrak b(t_\flat)$,
and $R_\flat=\delta(t_\flat)/\delta(t)=2R_j$.
Then
\[
 |\mu|r/r_\flat=|\lambda|/R_\flat.
\]
Thus dilation by $\mu$ maps the fluctuation domain
at $t$ into that at $t_\flat$. Schwarz's lemma applied
to the first and fourth potentials gives a factor
$|\lambda|/R_\flat$. For the cubic-vanishing potentials,
apply it after dividing by the first two powers of
the dilation parameter. Their quadratic growth bound
then gives
\[
 |V^{\natural,\lambda}(Y;B)|
 \le |\lambda|K_P\delta(t)
 (1+M^3r_\flat^{-2})e^{-\lambda_Vd(Y)}(Q_Y(B)-1),
 \qquad\natural\in\{{\rm G},{\rm A}\}.
\]
Here $Q_Y$ is the quadratic fluctuation bound in the
one-step expansion. The lower-calibration inequalities
give $M^3r_\flat^{-2}\le2/9$. All three intrinsic
potentials are consequently bounded by
$|\lambda|k_{\rm int}e^{-\lambda_Vd(Y)}Q_Y(B)$,
and the fourth by
$|\lambda|k_{\rm iv}e^{-\lambda_Vd(Y)}$, where
\[
 k_{\rm int}=2K_P\delta(t),\qquad
 k_{\rm iv}=K_\Lambda s_{\mathfrak a}(t)n_\flat.
\]
The number $n_\flat$ is the norm of the localized
array at the lower calibration, including the two
units of room above; $s_{\mathfrak a}(t)=\delta(t)/a_{0,j+1}$.
The chosen room yields
\[
 R_jk_{\rm int}=K_P\delta(t_\flat)\le w_*/8,
 \qquad
 R_jk_{\rm iv}=\tfrac12K_\Lambda
                 s_{\mathfrak a}(t_\flat)n_\flat\le w_*/8.
\]
Locality and gauge covariance are preserved by dilation.
These bounds verify the hypotheses of the scalar step.

We recall the step estimate with its parameter dependence.
The scalar cluster expansion in \cite[Thm. V]{YMM1},
on these domains, has nonconstant bond contribution bounded by
\[
 K_\Pi|\lambda|(32k_{\rm int}+9k_{\rm iv})
                  e^{-\lambda_{\rm out}d(X)},
 \quad R_jk_{\rm int}\le w_*/8,\quad
 R_jk_{\rm iv}\le w_*/4.
\]
Thus its bound on $|\lambda|<R_j$ is at most
$41K_\Pi w_*/8$. The series converges normally in
the action coefficient, field scale and bare-array
parameters. Its change under
$(\lambda,B)\mapsto(-\lambda,-B)$ is zero after
Gaussian integration. Its value at zero is independent
of the bare-array variation. Evenness, vanishing at
zero and Cauchy's formula therefore bound its
derivative in that variation by $c|\lambda|^2R_j^{-2}$
on the smaller disc. The derivative is taken in the
localized-array seminorm at $t_\flat$; the spare unit
in the preceding room bound supplies its Cauchy disc.
The pointed version differs by the bounded tent sum
$3L^3$. These facts prove holomorphy, evenness and
the uniform step estimate used in the induction.

Here are the localization counts that close its first
and second source derivatives. A source weight at
level $i$ has size at most
$36M^3\alpha_0^2D_i^{-1}\psi_i\|w_a\|_\infty$.
A member from level $i'=i-n$ whose domains meet
that source is read with factor at most
\[
 c'\left[L^{3n}e^{-[2L^{n-1}-2]_+}
       +(n+2)L^{4-4n}\min\{CL^{3n},C'N_{i'}\}\right].
\]
This is the bracket-localization count of
\cite[Prop. 51.16]{YMM1}: the first term counts
the distant domains; in the second, count only
places over a cube meeting the source.
Here $N_{i'}\le77\max\{1,(d/D_{i'})^3\}$.
The current-level reading costs at most two.
Furthermore
\[
 R_{i-n}^{-2}\le\tfrac43(1+n)^{2p_0}L^{-n}R_i^{-2}.
\]
For $D_{i'}\ge d$, one has $N_{i'}\le77$,
$\psi_{i'-1}\le L^{3(n+1)}\psi_i$ and
$\chi_{i'-1}\le L^{5(n+1)/2}\chi_i$.
After the radius and length factors are included,
the first derivative has the summable factor
$77L^{7-n}$, and the second has $L^{7/2-n/2}$,
up to fixed powers of $n+2$.
For $D_{i'}<d$, a domain meeting both supports
has size at least $[d/(4MD_{i'})-2]_+$.
Passing from rate $\kappa^+$ to $\kappa$ supplies
$e^{-4\beta_s\kappa[d/(4MD_{i'})-2]_+}$,
which sums the smaller-scale terms against every
power and logarithm. The product of first derivatives
is controlled by $\psi_i^2\le\chi_i$.

These two finite sums are the constants in the two
derivative recursions. Choose $\rho\le1/2$ so that
$\rho^2$ times each is at most its induction margin.
This choice precedes $\gamma_s$.
Induction proves the two stated derivative bounds.
Each new domain depends only on the old members and
source plaquettes within it, so it also proves the
support assertion. Summing the second derivative
over domains meeting both supports gives $\Pi_{j+1}$
and the bound for $\mathsf n_{j+1}^\lambda$.

At order zero the activity has no source dependence.
At order two its mixed derivative is a covariance
of two linear forms in the field at the trivial
configuration. Each form is invariant under constant
gauge rotations. Averaging the adjoint representation
over $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ gives zero, so both forms
vanish. This proves the two missing low orders.

Finally apply Cauchy's formula on $|\lambda|=\rho R_j$.
The coefficient of order $2m$ is at most
\[
 c b^{-m}(\log x_j)^{2mp_0}
                    D_j^{m-2}\chi_j\Pi_{j+1}\eta.
\]
If $D_j\ge d$, then $\Pi_{j+1}=1$, $\log x_j\le l$
and
$D_j^{m-2}\chi_j=d^{m-2}(d/D_j)^{5/2-(m-2)}$.
For $m=2,3$ the exponent is positive, so summing
the geometric progression gives the tail bound.
Multiply its $m=3$ case by $\beta^3a^2$ and use
$d/D_n=r/L^n$ and $\beta^3a^2b^{-3}d=r$.
This proves \eqref{eq:pure-running-coefficient-tail}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Removing Gaussian restrictions}

\begin{lemma}\label{C-350-10}
Let \(\nu\) be a centered Gaussian measure on
\(\mathbb R^I\), with coordinate variances at most
\(\sigma_i^2\).  Let \(Q\) be open, bounded, convex,
and symmetric, containing \(\prod_i(-c_i,c_i)\).
Set \(t_i=c_i/\sigma_i\) and
\(\epsilon=\sum_i e^{-t_i^2/2}\).
Suppose that \(F_1,\ldots,F_r\), \(r=2,3\), are
complex polynomials of degrees at most \(k_j\), with
\(|F_j|\le S_j\) on \(Q\), and put \(k=\sum_jk_j\).
If \(t_i^2\ge\max\{4,2k\}\) and \(2^k\epsilon\le1\),
then their cumulants in \(\nu\) and \(\nu(\cdot\mid Q)\)
differ by at most
\[
 q_r(1+2^k)\epsilon\prod_jS_j,
 \qquad q_2=5,\qquad q_3=37.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
For \(z\notin Q\), let \(s=\max_i|z_i|/c_i\ge1\).
The segment from \(-z/s\) to \(z/s\) lies in
\(\bar Q\).  The polynomial
\(\tau\mapsto F_j(\tau z/s)\) is bounded by \(S_j\)
on \([-1,1]\), so the Chebyshev bound gives
\(|F_j(z)|\le S_j(2s)^{k_j}\).  On \(Q^c\),
\[
 s^k\le\sum_i(|z_i|/c_i)^k\mathbf1_{\{|z_i|\ge c_i\}}.
\]
The one-dimensional Gaussian tail moment satisfies
\(\mathbb E[(|z_i|/c_i)^k;|z_i|\ge c_i]
\le e^{-t_i^2/2}\) under the assumed bound on \(t_i\).
Consequently
\[
 \nu(Q^c)\le\epsilon,\qquad
 \int_{Q^c}\prod_j|F_j|\,d\nu
                   \le2^k\epsilon\prod_jS_j.
\]
For any subproduct \(F\), write \(S\) for the
corresponding product of bounds and \(m,m^{\rm r}\)
for its full and conditional moments.  Then
\[
 m^{\rm r}-m=m^{\rm r}\nu(Q^c)-\int_{Q^c}F\,d\nu,
 \qquad
 |m^{\rm r}-m|\le(1+2^k)\epsilon S,
 \quad |m^{\rm r}|\le S,\quad |m|\le2S.
\]
Expand the cumulant over partitions.  For a partition
with \(p\) blocks, telescoping its product of moments
costs at most \(p2^{p-1}(1+2^k)\epsilon\prod_jS_j\).
Multiplication by \((p-1)!\) and summation give
\(q_r=\sum_p\mathrm S(r,p)p!2^{p-1}\), which is five
for \(r=2\) and thirty-seven for \(r=3\).
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Coefficients of a logarithm]\label{C-350-22}
If \(G\) is holomorphic on the unit disc,
\(G(0)=0\), and \(\operatorname{Re}G\le E\), then
\(|G_{[m]}|\le2E\) for every \(m\ge1\).
In particular, if \(F(0)=1\), \(F\ne0\), and
\(|F|\le e^E\) there, and
\[
 F=1+\lambda R_1+\lambda^2R_2+O(\lambda^3),
\]
then \(W_1=-R_1\) and \(W_2=R_1^2/2-R_2\)
satisfy \(|W_1|,|W_2|\le2E\).
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
For \(0<r<1\) and \(m\ge1\),
\[
 G_{[m]}r^m=-\frac1\pi\int_0^{2\pi}
       (E-\operatorname{Re}G(re^{i\theta}))e^{-im\theta}\,d\theta.
\]
The nonnegative factor has mean \(E\), since
\(\operatorname{Re}G(0)=0\).  Let \(r\uparrow1\).
For the second assertion use the holomorphic logarithm
\(G=\log F=-\lambda W_1-\lambda^2W_2+O(\lambda^3)\).
\end{proof}

\subsection{The coefficient before and after removing the tests}

Use the pure-gauge progression of
\cref{C-350-6,C-350-7}, calibrated at the running
coefficients \(x_i\). Let \(N=\ell L^K\),
\(\mathsf N=N+\beta\), and write \(a_K=L^{-K}\),
\(b=a_K\beta\).  The admitted coupling window gives
\[
 x_0>x_1>\cdots>x_K>g^{-2},\qquad
 \tfrac34\le\tau_i:=L^{-i}x_0/x_i\le\tfrac43.
\]
The side is large enough for every step and for the
free curvature estimates.  In particular
\(\ell L\ge C_LM\) and \(\ell\ge N_H\).
Take the coupling ceiling small enough that the
background chains at \(|\lambda|\le1\) lie in their
fixed cores.

Let \(\mathsf B_i^{\rm cv}\) and \(\hat{\mathsf G}\)
be the free curvature and gauge-fixing matrices on the
non-pivot bonds at height \(i\).  Both are nonnegative,
and
\[
 \mathsf A_i^{\rm cv}=\mathsf B_i^{\rm cv}+\hat{\mathsf G}
                \ge\gamma^{\rm tr}>0,
 \qquad
 \mathsf M_i=\tau_i\mathsf B_i^{\rm cv}+\hat{\mathsf G}
                \ge\tfrac34\gamma^{\rm tr}.
\]
These are the free-template operators of
\cite[Props.\ 120.3 and 120.6]{YMM1}.
Let \(\nu_i^\circ\) be the centered Gaussian with
precision \(\mathsf M_i\otimes1_{\mathfrak g}\), and
let \(\nu_i^{\rm r}\) be its restriction, normalized
to mass one, to
\(\{|B_i(b)|<\mathfrak b(x_i)\}\), where
\(\mathfrak b(x)=A_1(\log x)^{p_0}\).
The norm here is the Euclidean norm on each copy of
\(\mathfrak g\); these windows are products of balls.

For real bounded sources \(w_a=f_a\circ x\) on
plaquettes, let \(\mathsf n_j^\lambda\) be the mixed
source derivative of the scalar activity sum of
level \(j\) at the trivial configuration and common
field scale \(\lambda\).  Write
\[
 \mathsf h_{2m}^{(n)}=\sum_{j\le n}\mathsf n_{j,[2m]}.
\]
The sources have supports in balls of radius \(d\)
at distance at least \(d\), with \(8a_K\le d\).
No sign or Lipschitz restriction is needed in the
next proposition.

\begin{proposition}\label{C-350-11}
Let \(2\le n\le K\), and let
\(\mathsf{Bx}=\prod_{i<n}\{|B_i(b)|<\mathfrak b(x_i)\}\).
There are bounded functions \(\mathsf O_a^\lambda\)
and \(\mathsf D^\lambda\) on this set, continuous
for \(|\lambda|\le1\) and holomorphic for
\(|\lambda|<1\), such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pure-tested-covariance}
 \sum_{j\le n}\mathsf n_j^\lambda
       =\langle\mathsf O_1^\lambda;
                            \mathsf O_2^\lambda\rangle_{
                                      \mathsf D^\lambda\,dB},
 \qquad \int\mathsf D^\lambda\,dB=1,
 \qquad \mathsf D^0\,dB=\bigotimes_{i<n}\nu_i^{\rm r}.
\end{equation}
The observables have the form
\(\mathsf O_a^\lambda(B)=o_a(\lambda B)\),
with \(o_a\) analytic near zero.  Uniformly on the window,
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \mathsf O_a^\lambda
    &=\lambda^2(X_{a,0}+\lambda X_{a,1}
                              +\lambda^2X_{a,2})+O(\lambda^5),\\
 \mathsf D^\lambda/\mathsf D^0
    &=\exp[-\lambda W_1-\lambda^2W_2+O(\lambda^3)].
 \end{aligned}
\]
Here \(X_{a,m}\) is homogeneous of degree \(m+2\);
\(W_1\) is odd of degree at most three; and \(W_2\),
up to an additive constant, is even of degree at most
four.  Thus
\[
 \mathsf h_4^{(n)}
       =\langle X_{1,0};X_{2,0}\rangle_{\otimes_i\nu_i^{\rm r}},
 \qquad
 \mathsf h_6^{(n)}=\gamma_2^{\rm r}
       :=\gamma_2[\otimes_i\nu_i^{\rm r}].
\]
Put \(\gamma_2^\circ=\gamma_2[\otimes_i\nu_i^\circ]\).
If
\[
 \gamma^{\rm tr}\mathfrak b(x_{n-1})^2\ge80,
 \qquad
 10240N^3e^{-\gamma^{\rm tr}\mathfrak b(x_{n-1})^2/8}\le1,
\]
then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pure-test-removal}
 \beta^3a_K^2|\gamma_2^{\rm r}-\gamma_2^\circ|
 \le C_X\mathsf N^{36}
        e^{-\gamma^{\rm tr}\mathfrak b(x_{n-1})^2/8}
                           \|w_1\|_\infty\|w_2\|_\infty.
\end{equation}
The constant \(C_X\) depends only on the fixed RG constants.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Form the background chain downward from the trivial
point \(v_n^\lambda=0\), inserting
\(\lambda x_i^{-1/2}B_i\) at step \(i\).
Its radius satisfies
\[
 r_n=0,\qquad
 r_i=L^{-1}r_{i+1}+\tfrac{11}{10}c_{\mathfrak h}\delta(x_i)
                \le\tfrac85c_{\mathfrak h}\delta(x_i),
 \qquad \|v_i^\lambda\|\le|\lambda|r_i.
\]
The coupling ceiling keeps these radii inside the
chart domains, for complex as well as real \(\lambda\).
Write \(\tilde U_i^\lambda=\exp(iL^{-i}A_i^\lambda)\)
for its backgrounds.  Define \(\mathsf O_a^\lambda\)
as the action insertion
\(a_K^{-1}\sum_pw_a(p)a_p(\tilde U_1^\lambda)\)
plus the source term in the height-zero step.  Define
\(\mathsf D^\lambda\) as the product of the normalized
step densities along this chain.

Iterating the one-step integral identity gives
\[
 \exp D_n^{\lambda,\mu}
   =\int\exp(\mu_1\mathsf O_1^\lambda
                    +\mu_2\mathsf O_2^\lambda)
                                    \mathsf D^\lambda\,dB,
\]
where \(D_n^{\lambda,\mu}\) is the sourced activity
exponent at the trivial top.  At the bottom step its
value in the chart equals its value at
\(\tilde U_1^\lambda\): the chart triple is in the
level-one core, and its restrictions and the configuration
have the same pairs.  Local terms depend only on those
pairs.  This verifies the bottom step as well as all
later steps.

The identity first follows for real \(0<\lambda\le1\).
Both sides are holomorphic in \(\mu\) and \(\lambda\).
Indeed, the provision gives holomorphic conditioned
covariances and connecting operators; their conditioning
identity gives a holomorphic whole covariance and inverse.
The gauge forms and potentials are holomorphic on the
same cores.  Bounded integration over the windows
preserves this property, and the step normalizers have
no zeros by the scalar step in \cref{C-350-7}, with
the bounds in \cref{C-350-23}. The identity therefore
extends to \(|\lambda|<1\).  At zero sources it gives
normalization of \(\mathsf D^\lambda\); its mixed
logarithmic derivative gives
\eqref{eq:pure-tested-covariance}.

At \(\lambda=0\), the chain is trivial and the
potentials vanish.  The step's two quadratic forms combine
to
\[
 \tau_i\mathsf A_i^{\rm cv}+(1-\tau_i)\hat{\mathsf G}
                     =\mathsf M_i.
\]
At height zero, \(\tau_0=1\) and the whole covariance
is \((\mathsf A_0^{\rm cv})^{-1}\otimes1\), so the
same formula holds there.  This proves the Gaussian
product assertion, including the bottom field.

The action insertions start at quadratic order, and
the chain reads \((\lambda,B)\) through \(\lambda B\).
Their Taylor coefficients have the stated homogeneous
degrees.  To control the degrees in the logarithm of
the density, telescope the activity terms against the
normalizers of adjacent steps.  Their sum leaves a
constant, the running counterterms at the backgrounds,
the localized Gaussian terms, and the determinants of
the whole covariances.  All remaining terms have one
of the forms
\[
 \lambda^{-2}F(\lambda,\lambda B),\quad
             F(\lambda,\lambda B),\qquad
 F(\lambda,\zeta)=O(|\zeta|^2)
                   \text{ in the first case}.
\]
The first class consists of the quadratic forms and
the action and gauge-fixing potentials; the second
contains the other potentials, determinants, localized
Gaussian terms, and counterterms.  Their functions
\(F\) are holomorphic near zero.  Thus the coefficient
of \(\lambda^m\) has degree at most \(m+2\) in the
first class and at most \(m\) in the second.
The simultaneous substitution \((\lambda,B)\mapsto
(-\lambda,-B)\) preserves the density: the moved
coefficient is even in \(\lambda\), and induction
preserves this parity in the earlier activity families.
Hence \(W_1\) is odd and \(W_2\) is even.  Constants
in \(W_2\) disappear from the relevant cumulants.
Expanding the covariance now gives exactly
\eqref{C-350-5} and the two asserted coefficients.

It remains to justify the quantitative removal of
the windows.  The bounds in the next lemma give
\(|X_{a,m}|\le C_S\mathsf N^8\|w_a\|_\infty\)
and \(|W_1|,|W_2|\le2C_S\mathsf N^7\) on
\(\mathsf{Bx}\).  Every coordinate variance is at
most \(4/(3\gamma^{\rm tr})\), and the window contains
the component cube of half-side
\(\mathfrak b(x_{n-1})/\sqrt3\).  Thus the parameters
of \cref{C-350-10} satisfy
\[
 t_i^2\ge\tfrac14\gamma^{\rm tr}\mathfrak b(x_{n-1})^2
                      \ge20,
 \qquad
 \epsilon\le10N^3e^{-\gamma^{\rm tr}\mathfrak b(x_{n-1})^2/8}.
\]
Apply that lemma to the seven cumulants in
\eqref{C-350-5}.  Their total polynomial degrees are
at most ten.  The largest product of their bounds
has power \(\mathsf N^{30}\).  Finally
\(\beta^3a_K^2\le\mathsf N^3\), and the coordinate
count contributes at most \(10\mathsf N^3\).
This gives \eqref{eq:pure-test-removal}.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Bounds on the Gaussian windows]\label{C-350-23}
In the preceding setting, for \(|\lambda|<1\),
\[
 |\mathsf O_a^\lambda|\le C_S\mathsf N^8\|w_a\|_\infty,
 \qquad
 \mathsf D^\lambda\ne0,\qquad
 |\mathsf D^\lambda|\le e^{C_S\mathsf N^7}|\mathsf D^0|.
\]
Consequently
\( |X_{a,m}|\le C_S\mathsf N^8\|w_a\|_\infty\)
and \(|W_1|,|W_2|\le2C_S\mathsf N^7\).
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
There are at most \(3N^3\) plaquettes and
\(a_K^{-1}\le N\).  The backgrounds stay in a fixed
complex neighborhood of one.  These facts bound the
first part of each observable.  The source family at
height zero has size at most \(CL^K\|w_a\|_\infty\)
and at most \(3N^3\) terms.  Its field weight on the
window is at most \(CN^3\mathfrak b(\beta)^2\).
Since \(L^K\le N\) and
\(\mathfrak b(\beta)^2\le C\beta\), this gives the
displayed \(\mathsf N^8\) bound.

For the density, the real-reference comparison of the
whole covariance on a complex core gives
\[
 \|\mathbf C_*^{-1}\|\le c_{\rm r}+\gamma_{\rm r}/2,
 \qquad \operatorname{Re}\mathbf C_*^{-1}
                         \ge\gamma_{\rm r}/2,
 \qquad \|\mathbf C_*\|\le2/\gamma_{\rm r}.
\]
The gauge-fixing operators also have uniformly bounded
row sums.  Thus each quadratic form on a window is
bounded by \(CN^3\mathfrak b(x_i)^2\).
The potential bound has the form
\(Ce^{-\lambda_Vd_i(Y)}Q_Y(B_i)\), where
\(\lambda_V>\kappa_{\mathcal D}+\log2\) and
\(\lambda_V>\kappa_{\mathcal D}+2\).
Summing over polymers, first at a fixed cube or bond,
therefore gives the same bound.  Each step density
is an exponential and has no zero.

Its normalizing integral is
\(\det(2\pi\tau_i(\lambda)^{-1}\mathbf C_*)^{1/2}\)
times the exponential of a sum of local terms.
The latter sum has modulus at most \(CN^3\).
The covariance bounds,
\(1/2<\operatorname{Re}\tau_i(\lambda)
\le|\tau_i(\lambda)|<3/2\), and dimension at most
\(9N^3\) bound the modulus of the determinant factor
between \(e^{-CN^3}\) and \(e^{CN^3}\).
Thus all normalizers are nonzero and have both bounds.
The same estimates at zero bound the reciprocal of
\(\mathsf D^0\).  Multiplying over at most
\(K\le N\) heights, with
\(\mathfrak b(x_i)^2\le C\beta\), proves the claimed
\(\mathsf N^7\) bound.
Cauchy's estimate gives the observable coefficients;
\cref{C-350-22} applied to
\(\mathsf D^\lambda/\mathsf D^0\) gives the logarithmic
coefficients.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Identification with the flat-top coefficient}

Set
\[
 \mathsf T[N,n](w_1,w_2)
   =\sum_{p,q}w_1(p)w_2(q)\mathsf g_2[N,n](p,q).
\]
The next identity is exact.  In particular, no error
depending on the running counterterms enters it.

\begin{proposition}\label{C-350-13}
In the setting of \cref{C-350-11},
\[
 \beta^3a_K^2\gamma_2^\circ=\mathsf T[N,n](w_1,w_2).
\]
The right side depends only on the bare lattice, the
depth \(n\), \(L\), and the two lattice sources.
The identity holds for every size of the integration
windows allowed in \cref{C-350-11}.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
For real \(0<\lambda\le1\), write
\(\zeta_i=\lambda x_i^{-1/2}B_i\).
The background chain used in \cref{C-350-11} depends
only on these fields.  We compare it with the composed
chart of \cref{C-350-12}, keeping track of the gauge
transformations between their backgrounds.

Start at the flat top \(W_n=1\).  At a level \(i+1\),
choose a background \(U_{+,i+1}\) in the minimal orbit
over \(W_{i+1}\), axial on its blocks, and a gauge
transformation \(u_{i+1}\) such that the chain's
background is \(\tilde U_{i+1}^\lambda
=U_{+,i+1}^{u_{i+1}}\).  With this transformation fixed,
put
\[
 \check\zeta_i=\operatorname{Ad}(u_{i+1})^{-1}\zeta_i,
 \qquad W_i=V_{W_{i+1}}[\check\zeta_i].
\]
The background-lowering identity gives an element of
the minimal orbit over \(W_i\) gauge equivalent to
the chain's next background.  Put this element into
the axial gauge and absorb that change into \(u_i\).
The chain bounds keep \(\varpi(W_i)<\varepsilon_{\mathcal W}\alpha_0\)
and all three triples---the axial triple, its transform
by \(u_{i+1}\), and the chain triple---in their cores.
The last two have the same pair.  This construction
works downward for every \(\zeta_i\) in its window,
with \(u_{i+1}\) depending only on higher fields.
At height zero it gives the bare configuration
\(W_0=V_{W_1}[\check\zeta_0]\).

The provision is gauge covariant and depends on a
triple only through its pair.  Therefore the whole
covariance, the gauge-fixing forms, the potentials,
the source terms, and the localized Gaussian terms
can all be read at the axial triple with field
\(\check\zeta_i\).  For the whole covariance this
also follows directly from the conditioning identity
\(\mathbf C_* =\mathbf C+\mathbf C\boldsymbol\Gamma
\boldsymbol\Gamma^{\mathsf T}\mathbf C\): the two
operators on the right transform by the same
orthogonal conjugation.

At the axial triple, the sum rules identify the
whole covariance with \(\mathsf A_W^{-1}\), where
\(\mathsf A_W=\mathsf B_W+\hat{\mathsf G}_W\).
The quadratic form of the step is
\[
 -\frac{\tau_i(\lambda)}2(B_i,\mathsf B_WB_i)
                       -\frac12(B_i,\hat{\mathsf G}_WB_i).
\]
Its second term combines with the gauge-fixing
potential to give \(-\lambda^{-2}x_iG_i(W_i)\).
Its first combines with the action potential to give
\[
 -\lambda^{-2}\xi_i(\lambda)L^i
            [A(\tilde U_i^\lambda)-A(\tilde U_{i+1}^\lambda)].
\]
The Jacobian potential gives the chart Jacobian.
The localized Gaussian family and its determinant
give the elimination normalizer and a constant.
The ordinary activity families telescope against
the normalizing denominators.  Their remaining
counterterms cancel the changes in \(\xi_i\), since
\[
 \lambda^{-2}\xi_j(\lambda)L^j
                     +\sum_{i\le j}L^ie_i=\lambda^{-2}x_0.
\]
Using \(A(\tilde U_n^\lambda)=0\), we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pure-flat-density-cancellation}
 \mathsf D^\lambda(B)=c_n(\lambda)
  \exp\left[-\lambda^{-2}
       \left(x_0A(W_0)+\sum_{j<n}x_jG_j(W_j)\right)-\theta\right],
\end{equation}
where \(c_n(\lambda)\) is independent of \(B\).
The observables become
\(a_K^{-1}\sum_pw_a(p)a_p(W_0)\).
The function \(\theta\) is the composed chart density,
up to a constant.

This comparison does not require a measurable choice
of all the gauge transformations as a function of all
fields.  At a fixed choice of the higher fields,
\(B_i\mapsto\operatorname{Ad}(u_{i+1})^{-1}B_i\)
is one orthogonal map.  It preserves Lebesgue measure
and every product of centered Euclidean balls.
Integrate first in the finest field.  Equality of
the integrands at corresponding fields gives equality
of these integrals by that fixed orthogonal change
of variables.  Repeat upward.  Fubini applies to the
bounded Borel integrands.  Thus the two descriptions
give equal integrals on every sufficiently small
product of such balls, with observables or their
product inserted.  The use of Euclidean balls here
is essential to this change of variables.

For completeness, identify the Gaussian polynomials
in this equality.  Write \((qB)_i=x_i^{-1/2}B_i\).
In the chain variables, let \(\Phi^{\rm ch}\),
\(\Theta^{\rm ch}\), and \(o_a^{\rm ch}\) denote
respectively the phase, the logarithm of the chart
density, and the observable in
\eqref{eq:pure-flat-density-cancellation}.
They are analytic near zero.  The zero-scale
Gaussian identifies their Hessian as
\[
 H^{\rm ch}=\bigoplus_{i<n}x_i(\mathsf M_i\otimes1)>0.
\]
Thus \(q\) maps the full Gaussian product to the
Gaussian with covariance \((H^{\rm ch})^{-1}\).
The polynomials in \cref{C-350-11} are
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 X_{a,m}(B)&=(o_a^{\rm ch})_{m+2}(qB),\\
 W_1(B)&=(\Phi^{\rm ch}_3+\Theta^{\rm ch}_1)(qB),\\
 W_2(B)&=(\Phi^{\rm ch}_4+\Theta^{\rm ch}_2)(qB)
                                      +\text{constant}.
 \end{aligned}
\]
Cumulants of order at least two do not see the
constant.  Hence \(\gamma_2^\circ\) is the Laplace
coefficient for these functions.

Choose the common windows so small that both phases
are bounded below by a positive multiple of the
squared coordinate norm.  The preceding integral
identity gives one covariance for every Laplace
parameter \(\beta'>0\).  In the chain chart its
order-three coefficient is \(\gamma_2^\circ\).
In the composed chart the phase is
\(\beta\phi_\kappa\), with \(\kappa_j=x_j/\beta\),
and the observables carry the factors \(a_K^{-1}\).
Comparing \eqref{C-350-31} for these two descriptions
gives
\[
 \gamma_2^\circ
   =\beta^{-3}a_K^{-2}
                \sum_{p,q}w_1(p)w_2(q)\mathsf g_2[N,n](p,q).
\]
The coefficients do not depend on the chosen windows,
and \cref{C-350-12} removes the gauge strengths.
The bare lattice remains \(\Lambda_N\) on replacing
\((\ell,K)\) by \((\ell L^{K-n},n)\), so the stated
identification follows.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Locality of the constrained coefficient}

\begin{lemma}\label{C-350-24}
The following three elementary facts will be used.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item Suppose \(0<\sigma\le1/120\), and \(F(y,z)\)
is holomorphic for \(\|y\|<\sigma\), \(|z|<\sigma\),
with values in \(\mathfrak g^{\mathbb C}\), satisfying
\(|F|\le1/40\), \(F(0,0)=0\), and \(D_zF(0,0)=1\).
For \(\|y\|<\sigma^3\), the equation \(F(y,z)=0\)
has a unique solution with \(|z|\le\sigma^2\).
It is holomorphic, satisfies
\(|z(y)|\le\|y\|/(15\sigma)\), and is real at real
\(y\) when \(F\) is real there.
\item If a lattice box embeds injectively in a bare
torus, every closed path \(\gamma\) in it that lifts
to a closed path in the box has integer Stokes
coefficients supported on its plaquettes, with
\[
 a(\gamma)=\sum_pk_\gamma(p)(da)(p),\qquad
 |k_\gamma(p)|\le|\gamma|.
\]
If each side of the box has at most \(S-1\) sites,
where the torus has side \(S\), every closed path
in the box has this lifting property.
\item The joint Gaussian cumulant of homogeneous
polynomials \(P_1,\ldots,P_r\) is the sum of Wick
pairings connected on the set of polynomial entries.
If their total degree is \(n\) and the covariance
entries have modulus at most \(c\), its modulus is
at most
\[
 (n-1)!!\prod_a\|P_a\|_1\,c^{n/2},
\]
and it is zero for odd \(n\).  If every connected
pairing has an entry bounded by \(\epsilon\), replace
\(c^{n/2}\) by \(c^{n/2-1}\epsilon\).
For two covariances bounded by \(c\), the difference
of cumulants is at most
\[
 (n-1)!!\frac n2\prod_a\|P_a\|_1\,
                         c^{n/2-1}\sup|C-C'|.
\]
Here \(\|P\|_1\) is the sum of the moduli of its coefficients.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
For (i), set \(g(y,z)=z-F(y,z)\).  Then
\(|g|\le1/30\), \(g(0,0)=0\), and \(D_zg(0,0)=0\).
Cauchy and Schwarz estimates give
\[
 |D_zg(y,z)|\le\frac2{15}\sigma^{-2}
                         \max\{\|y\|,|z|\},\qquad
 |g(y,0)|\le\frac{\|y\|}{30\sigma}
\]
on the half-radius domain.  For \(\|y\|<\sigma^3\),
the map \(z\mapsto g(y,z)\) preserves the closed
ball of radius \(\sigma^2\) and contracts by \(2/15\).
Its iterates give the holomorphic solution and the
bound stated; uniqueness gives the reality assertion.

For (ii), join a corner of the box to each site
by paths running successively in the three coordinate
directions.  For a bond \(e=(z,z+e_\mu)\), the path
to \(z\), followed by \(e\) and the reverse path
from \(z+e_\mu\), is the boundary of a strip of
plaquettes in the box.  Sum these strips along
\(\gamma\); the corner paths cancel and each
plaquette occurs at most \(|\gamma|\) times.
Under the additional size condition, two box sites
joined by a torus bond differ by an actual unit
vector: their coordinate differences have modulus
at most \(S-2\).  This proves the lifting assertion.

For (iii), partition each Wick pairing by the
connected components of its graph on the entries.
The moment--cumulant formula identifies the connected
sum with the cumulant.  Count at most \((n-1)!!\)
pairings.  The comparison bound follows by telescoping
the product of its \(n/2\) covariance entries.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Comparison of two bare tori]\label{C-350-14}
Let \(N=2L^{\mathsf m}\), \(N'=L^sN\), \(s\ge1\),
and \(1\le t<\mathsf m\).  Write
\(\pi:\Lambda_{N'}\to\Lambda_N\) for reduction, and assume
\[
 \nu=N/L^t\ge\nu_W
 =\max\left\{192,
      \frac{48(3\log L+\log2)}{\delta_{\rm tp}L(L-1)},
      \frac{C_LM}{L}\right\}.
\]
If the base points of \(p',q'\) are within \(N/8\)
in the sup metric, then, for \(m'=0,2\),
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pure-box-coefficient}
 |\mathsf g_{m'}[N,t](\pi p',\pi q')
                 -\mathsf g_{m'}[N',t](p',q')|
     \le C'_WN'^{237}e^{-\delta_{\rm tp}L\nu/48}.
\end{equation}
For sources supported in balls of radius \(r\ge8\),
with all their base points within \(N/8\), let
\(\breve w_a\) be their lift on one ball of radius
\(N/4\), extended by zero.  Then
\[
 |\mathsf T[N,t](w)-\mathsf T[N',t](\breve w)|
   \le900r^6C'_WN'^{237}e^{-\delta_{\rm tp}L\nu/48}
                             \|w_1\|_\infty\|w_2\|_\infty.
\]
The constant \(C'_W\) depends only on \(L,C_{\rm tp}\).
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Choose every auxiliary gauge-fixing strength \(\kappa_j=1\),
as permitted by \cref{C-350-12}.
We construct a chart in which its local Taylor
polynomials agree on the two tori.  For
\(S=N,N'\), let \(\mathsf Q_t\) be the linearized
block average and \(Y_S=\ker\mathsf Q_t\).
For a top bond \(c\), let \(\mathbf1_c\) be one
on bare bonds crossing from its first top block to
its second, minus one on their reverses, and zero
elsewhere.  A bare bond either lies inside one
top block or crosses one such interface.  Moreover,
\(\mathsf Q_t\mathbf1_c\) is one at \(c\) and
zero at every other positive top bond.

The average at \(c\) depends only on its double
block.  Solve its constraint independently by writing
\[
 \hat y=y+\sum_{c>0}h_c(y)\mathbf1_c,\qquad
 \mathcal M^t(e^{i\hat y})=1,
 \qquad y\in Y_S.
\]
Use \cref{C-350-24}(i) with
\(\sigma_t=(75L)^{-t}/(60L)\) for the function
\(\operatorname{Lg}\mathcal M^t(e^{i(y+z\mathbf1_c)})(c)\).
Its derivative in \(z\) at zero is one.  To check
its complex domain, one averaging step takes a
configuration whose variables and inverses lie
within \(\epsilon\le1/(200L)\) of one to variables
and inverses within \(75L\epsilon\) of one.
Indeed the contour means are within \(20L\epsilon\),
and the products entering the logarithm are within
\(48L\epsilon<1\).  The average is
\[
 \exp\left(L^{-3}\sum_{x\in B(c_-)}\log W_x\right)U[c],
\]
where \(W_x\) is the contour-transport product divided
by the straight transport \(U[c]\).
This formula is holomorphic.  At real configurations
with \(\epsilon\le1/(1000L^2)\), it agrees with the
given block average, since the contour means are
unique and the averaging plaquette threshold holds.
Starting with \(\epsilon_0=4\sigma_t\), its iterates
satisfy
\(\epsilon_k=(75L)^{k-t}/(15L)\).
Thus \(\epsilon_{t-1}=1/(1125L^2)\), every step is
admitted, and the final logarithm has modulus less
than \(1/40\).  The implicit-function lemma applies.

Each \(h_c\) depends only on the double block of
\(c\), is real at real fields, and satisfies
\(|h_c(y)|\le\|y\|_\infty/(15\sigma_t)\).
Since \(y\in\ker\mathsf Q_t\),
\(\hat y=y+O(y^2)\).  The map
\[
 A\longmapsto\left(\operatorname{Lg}\mathcal M^t(e^{iA}),
             A-\sum_c(\mathsf Q_tA)(c)\mathbf1_c\right)
\]
has invertible differential at zero, with inverse
\((w,y)\mapsto y+\sum_cw(c)\mathbf1_c\).
Its inverse followed by exponentiation is an
adapted chart, so \cref{C-350-12} allows us to compute
the coefficients in it.

The action, gauge-fixing terms, Haar density, and
Jacobian in this chart are sums of local holomorphic
terms.  Each is bounded by one on
\(\|y\|_\infty<\sigma_t^3\), involves at most
\(12L^{3t}\) bonds, and has support diameter at most
\(2L^t\).  The Jacobian is a product of the
derivatives of the top constraints in the directions
\(\mathbf1_c\), since the constraints use distinct
interfaces.  Reduction by \(\pi\) preserves blocks,
contours, and these formulas on sets of diameter at
most \(N/2\).  Thus the local terms are identical
there after renaming variables.

We next estimate the Gaussian covariance in this
chart.  By independence of the gauge strengths,
choose \(\kappa_j=1\).  For a bare site off the
top lattice, let \(j(x)\) be its highest lattice
level, let \(\hat x\) be its parent at level
\(j(x)+1\), and let \(\operatorname{anc}(x)\)
be its successive ancestors below the top.
Put \(\xi_A(x)=(\mathsf Q_{j(x)}A)(\hat x,x)\).
The Hessian form is
\[
 \mathsf H_S(A,A')=(dA,dA')+
                              \sum_x\langle\xi_A(x),\xi_{A'}(x)\rangle.
\]
The gauge directions are \(d\chi\), with \(\chi=0\)
on the top sites, and
\(\xi_{d\chi}(x)=\chi(x)-\chi(\hat x)\).
This is a bijection, with inverse
\(\chi(x)=\sum_{z\in\operatorname{anc}(x)}\xi(z)\).
Consequently
\[
 Y_S=Y_S^{\rm ax}\oplus d\mathcal X_S,
 \qquad
 \mathsf H_S(y,y)=\|dy^{\rm ax}\|^2+\sum_x|\xi_y(x)|^2.
\]
The map \(d\) identifies \(Y_S^{\rm ax}\) with the
curvatures whose order-\(t\) plaquette averages vanish.
For the range assertion, use
\(\mathsf Q_t=\mathbf Q_t^s-d\vartheta_t\), where
\(\mathbf Q_t^s\) is the straight average: a curvature
with zero plaquette average has a potential with
zero straight average, and adding a gradient adjusts
its top values and then its contour variables.
For injectivity, a closed potential is a gradient
plus a constant one-form.  Summing its zero top
average around each period kills the constant;
the zero contour variables then make the gradient
zero.  In particular \(\mathsf H_S>0\) on \(Y_S\).

The Gaussian variables \(\xi(x)\) are independent
with unit variance, and independent of the axial
curvature, whose covariance is \(\Pi_t^{\rm fl}\).
For an axial field, \(y(b)\) is the mean over
closed paths of length at most \(4(4L)^t\) in the
top block or double block of \(b\).  Apply the
Stokes formula in \cref{C-350-24}(ii):
\[
 y(b)=\sum_p\tau(b,p)(dy)(p),\qquad
 |\tau(b,p)|\le4(4L)^t,
\]
with \(\tau\) supported in that box.  There are at
most \(6L^{3t}\) plaquettes there.  The covariance,
diagonal in colour, is therefore
\[
 \begin{split}
 C_S&=C_S^{\rm ax}+C_S^{\rm g},\\
 C_S^{\rm ax}(b,b')&=\sum_{p,p'}\tau(b,p)\tau(b',p')
                                          \Pi_t^{\rm fl}(p,p'),\\
 C_S^{\rm g}(b,b')&=\sum_x\sigma(b,x)\sigma(b',x),\qquad
 \sigma(b,x)=\mathbf1_{\operatorname{anc}(b_+)}(x)
                       -\mathbf1_{\operatorname{anc}(b_-)}(x).
 \end{split}
\]
In particular,
\(\sup|C_S|\le c_\tau^2+2t\le2c_\tau^2\), where
\(c_\tau=24L^{3t}(4L)^t\).
The gauge part is zero unless endpoints of the
two bonds lie in a common top block.

The free-curvature estimate
\cite[Prop.\ 120.6]{YMM1} gives
\[
 |\Pi_t^{\rm fl}(p,q)|
 \le2L^{3-3t}C_{\rm tp}
            e^{-\delta_{\rm tp}L|x(p)-x(q)|_\infty/L^t}
\]
when
\(\delta_{\rm tp}L(L-1)|x(p)-x(q)|_\infty
\ge(3\log L+\log2)L^t\).
For bonds separated by \(R\ge8L^t\), this bounds
their covariance by
\(2L^{3-3t}C_{\rm tp}c_\tau^2
e^{-\delta_{\rm tp}L(R-4L^t)/L^t}\), provided the
same threshold holds for \(R-4L^t\).
At \(R=N/24\), the assumptions on \(\nu\) imply
these conditions and give
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pure-long-line}
 |C_S(b,b')|\le\epsilon_C
 :=2L^{3-3t}C_{\rm tp}c_\tau^2e^{-\delta_{\rm tp}L\nu/48}.
\end{equation}

There is also an exact periodization identity.  With
\(\Gamma=N\mathbb Z^3/N'\mathbb Z^3\),
\[
 C_N(\pi\iota,\pi\iota')
                 =\sum_{\gamma\in\Gamma}C_{N'}(\iota,\iota'+\gamma).
\]
Indeed pullback commutes with \(d,\mathsf Q_t,\xi\)
and multiplies the Hessian form by \(|\Gamma|\).
The summed covariance on the right is the unique
solution of the associated Gaussian variational
equation with a periodized point source.  Uniqueness
makes it \(\Gamma\)-invariant; testing against
pullbacks gives precisely the covariance equation
on \(\Lambda_N\).

Finally use the parity identity following \eqref{C-350-5}
to replace its product entry \(W_1^2\) by the
four-entry cumulant with two entries \(W_1\).
Expand the resulting cumulants into local Taylor
polynomials.  There are at most
\(64N'^6\) tuples of places, with total degree at
most ten.  A place is near if its support lies
within \(N/4\) of the base of \(p'\).  The two
observable places are near, and near tuples have
the same polynomials on both tori.  Their covariance
difference is a sum of fewer than \(|\Gamma|\)
lines of length at least \(N/2\), by periodization.
For a tuple with a far place, every connected
pairing has a line of length at least \(N/24\).
In fact a path from the observable place to the
far place has at most three edges; the diameters
of the intervening supports cost at most \(7L^t\),
and \(N/4-7L^t>N/8\).

Use \eqref{eq:pure-long-line} and the connected
pairing estimates in \cref{C-350-24}(iii).
Cauchy's estimate bounds the coefficient sum of
a degree-\(k\) local polynomial by
\((108L^{3t}\sigma_t^{-3})^k\).
Collecting these factors, the tuple count,
\(|\Gamma|\le N'^3\), and \(L^t\le N'\) gives
\eqref{eq:pure-box-coefficient}, with power \(237\)
and a constant depending only on \(L,C_{\rm tp}\).
A ball of radius \(r\ge8\) contains at most
\(30r^3\) plaquette barycentres.  Sum over the
two supports to obtain the last bound.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Comparison with the unconstrained Gaussian coefficient}

\begin{proposition}\label{C-350-15}
Let $\ell=2L^m\ge N_{\mathsf H}$, $\ell L\ge C_LM$
and $K\ge1$. Put $N=\ell L^K$. If $p,q$ are
plaquettes of the bare torus and their chosen lattice
lifts $\tilde p,\tilde q$ have base points at sup-distance
at most $N/8$, then
\[
 \begin{split}
 |\mathsf g_2[N,K](p,q)-\mathsf B_1^{\rm lat}(\tilde p,\tilde q)|
 &\le C_*\bigl[\ell^{29/2}KL^{-K/2}
                +\ell^{18}L^{-2K}+\ell^{19}K^2L^{-5K}\bigr]\\
 &\le3C_*\ell^{19}KL^{-K/2}.
 \end{split}
\]
If $\ell^3\le L^K$, the bound is
$3C_*\ell^{29/2}KL^{-K/2}$. The constant is independent
of $K$, the side and the plaquettes.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
By \cref{C-350-12}, the coefficient can be computed in
any normalized gauge on the fibre $\mathcal M^KU=1$.
We choose covariant gauge with parameter one. The
linearized constrained covariance differs from the
ordinary torus covariance by the curvature determined
at level $K$. There is a further correction because
the constraint is nonlinear. We separate these two
comparisons.

\subsubsection*{Gauge fixing and the constraint}
Fix a top site $o$. Use bare gauge transformations
equal to one at $o$, and allow the top field to range
over their pure gauges
\[
 w(\mu')(c)=\operatorname{Lg}
       (e^{i\mu'(c_-)}e^{-i\mu'(c_+)}),\qquad\mu'(o)=0.
\]
This gives one representative of each coset of the
constant transformations. Let
\[ \mathsf M_U\epsilon=\left.\frac d{dt}d^*
\operatorname{Lg}U^{\exp(it\epsilon)}\right|_0. \]
Its determinant, from functions vanishing at $o$ to
mean-zero functions, differs from the determinant
on mean-zero functions by a three-dimensional factor.
Indeed, changing a mean-zero $\epsilon_0$ to
$\epsilon_0-\epsilon_0(o)$ and using
$\mathsf M_U\kappa=i[\kappa,d^*a]$ for constant
$\kappa$ gives the factor $\det_3(1-\tau)$, where
\[
 \tau\kappa=(\mathsf M_U'^{-1}i[\kappa,d^*a])(o).
\]
The first-order trace is zero because the adjoint
action is traceless. Every second-order term has
a factor $d^*a$. In its connected cumulant with
the two quadratic observables, that factor must
pair with $da(p)$ or $da(q)$. The covariance below
satisfies $\langle da\,d^*a\rangle=0$, so the factor
changes neither coefficient under consideration.
We may therefore use the mean-zero Faddeev--Popov
terms in \cref{IV-73-15}.

Write the block average in straight frames.
For a one-step field $\omega$, let
\[
 \varphi_\omega(z)=L^{-3}\sum_{x\in B(z)}\bar\omega(z,x),
 \qquad v_\omega(z)=e^{i\varphi_\omega(z)},
\]
where $\bar\omega(z,x)$ is the linearized contour
average. The step
\[
 m^s(\omega)(c)=\operatorname{Lg}
    [v_\omega(c_-)^{-1}\mathcal M(e^{i\omega})(c)v_\omega(c_+)]
\]
has linear part $Q^s$. This follows from the
linearized block formula: its difference from
$Q^s\omega$ is $-d\varphi_\omega$.
Gauge covariance shows that the $K$-fold composition
$s^{(K)}$ differs from $\operatorname{Lg}\mathcal M^K(e^{ia})$
by a top gauge transformation $u(a)$.
Change the top variable by
\[
 e^{i\mu'_s(z)}=u(a)(z)^{-1}e^{i\mu'(z)}u(a)(o).
\]
At each fixed $a$ this preserves the product Haar
measure on the top sites other than $o$, and the
Haar delta function on the top bonds is gauge
invariant. The constraint is therefore exactly
$s^{(K)}(a)=w(\mu'_s)$. Rename $\mu'_s$ as $\mu'$.
Its linearization is $Q_K^sa+d\mu'=0$.

Put
\[
 \widehat E=\{(a,\mu'):Q_K^sa+d\mu'=0,\ \mu'(o)=0\},
 \qquad (e,He')=(da,da')+(d^*a,d^*a').
\]
The form is positive definite on $\widehat E$.
If it vanishes, $a$ is constant. Summing the
constraint around each straight top cycle gives
$a=0$, and then $\mu'=0$.
Let $\widehat R\omega=(a_\omega,\mu'_\omega)$
be the minimum-energy solution of
$Q_K^sa_\omega+d\mu'_\omega=\omega$,
$\mu'_\omega(o)=0$. It is $H$-orthogonal to
$\widehat E$.

Let $\widehat q_2,\widehat q_3$ be the quadratic
and cubic terms of $s^{(K)}-w$. For the centered
Gaussian field $e$ on $\widehat E$, set
\[
 \begin{split}
 \zeta&=\widehat R\widehat q_2(e,e),\\
 \zeta_3&=\widehat R[\widehat q_3(e,e,e)
                              -2\widehat q_2(e,\zeta)],\\
 N_1&=2\widehat q_2(e,\widehat R\,\cdot),\\
 N_2&=3\widehat q_3(e,e,\widehat R\,\cdot)
                              -2\widehat q_2(\zeta,\widehat R\,\cdot).
 \end{split}
\]
Solving the constraint along $\operatorname{ran}\widehat R$
gives $e-\zeta-\zeta_3+O(e^4)$ and the delta-function
factor $\det(1+N_1+N_2+O(e^3))^{-1}$.
Orthogonality gives $(e,H\zeta)=(e,H\zeta_3)=0$.
Also $\operatorname{tr}N_1=0$: $\widehat R$ preserves
a single colour, and a quadratic equivariant term
has no component in the colour of its second argument
when that argument has only one colour.

Write $X_i=\mathsf a_p^{(i+2)}$ and
$Y_i=\mathsf a_q^{(i+2)}$; their derivatives below
are evaluated at $e$. The observable terms become
\[
 X_1-DX_0[\zeta],\qquad
 X_2-DX_1[\zeta]-DX_0[\zeta_3]+X_0(\zeta),
\]
and likewise for $Y$. The first interaction is still
$S_3$. The second gains
\[
 -DS_3[\zeta]+\tfrac12(\zeta,H\zeta)
 +\operatorname{tr}N_2-\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}N_1^2
 +\tfrac13\sum_y|\mu'(y)|^2-\tfrac13\sum_c|d\mu'(c)|^2.
\]
The last two terms are the top-site Haar density and
the inverse top-bond density of the delta function.
Both signs follow from
$-\log(\sin r/r)^2=r^2/3+O(r^4)$.

Substitution in \eqref{C-350-5} gives the exact decomposition
\[
 \mathsf g_2[N,K]=\mathsf B_1^{\widehat E}
                                      +\sum_{i=1}^{11}\mathsf t_i,
\]
where $\mathsf B_1^{\widehat E}$ is \eqref{IV-73-24}
with the Gaussian on $\widehat E$ and the ordinary
mean-zero torus ghost kernels. The corrections are
\begin{align*}
 \mathsf t_1&=-\langle DX_0[\zeta];Y_1\rangle
                  -\langle X_1;DY_0[\zeta]\rangle,\\
 \mathsf t_2&=\langle DX_0[\zeta];DY_0[\zeta]\rangle,\\
 \mathsf t_3&=-\langle DX_1[\zeta];Y_0\rangle
                  -\langle X_0;DY_1[\zeta]\rangle,\\
 \mathsf t_4&=-\langle DX_0[\zeta_3];Y_0\rangle
                  -\langle X_0;DY_0[\zeta_3]\rangle,\\
 \mathsf t_5&=\langle X_0(\zeta);Y_0\rangle
                  +\langle X_0;Y_0(\zeta)\rangle,\\
 \mathsf t_6&=\langle DX_0[\zeta];Y_0;S_3\rangle
                  +\langle X_0;DY_0[\zeta];S_3\rangle,\\
 \mathsf t_7&=\langle X_0;Y_0;DS_3[\zeta]\rangle,\\
 \mathsf t_8&=-\tfrac12\langle X_0;Y_0;(\zeta,H\zeta)\rangle,\\
 \mathsf t_9&=-\langle X_0;Y_0;\operatorname{tr}N_2\rangle,\\
 \mathsf t_{10}&=\tfrac12\langle X_0;Y_0;\operatorname{tr}N_1^2\rangle,\\
 \mathsf t_{11}&=-\left\langle X_0;Y_0;
       \tfrac13\sum_y|\mu'(y)|^2-\tfrac13\sum_c|d\mu'(c)|^2\right\rangle.
\end{align*}

\subsubsection*{The constrained covariance}
Let $C^{\rm tor}$ be the inverse of $d^*d+dd^*$ off
constant forms, and put $S_0=C^{\rm tor}d^*$ on
exact curvatures. Then $dS_0=1$ on that space.
The $a$ components of $\widehat E$ are exactly
$a=S_0F+d\lambda$, with vanishing level-$K$
plaquette averages of $F$. The Gaussian factors
into independent $F,\lambda$ with covariances
$\Pi_0^{\rm tp}-\Pi_K^{\rm tp}$ and $(G^{\rm tor})^2$.
Consequently
\[
 C_{\widehat E}=C^{\rm tor}-S_0\Pi_K^{\rm tp}S_0^{\mathsf T},
 \quad dC_{\widehat E}d^*=\Pi_0^{\rm tp}-\Pi_K^{\rm tp},
 \quad\langle da\,d^*a\rangle=0.
\]
Orthogonality of the response to the gradients first
gives $d^*a_\omega=0$. Orthogonality to $S_0F$
and the constraint then give
\[
 da_\omega=H_K^{\rm cv}\omega,\qquad
 a_\omega=S_0H_K^{\rm cv}\omega+\text{constant form}.
\]
The constant in direction $\nu$ is $L^{-K}$ times
the mean of $\omega$ on top bonds in that direction:
sum the constraint over those bonds. The gradient
term sums to zero, as does $Q_K^sS_0H_K^{\rm cv}\omega$.

The free-template bounds in \cite[Props. 120.3 and
120.6]{YMM1} give
$|\Pi_K^{\rm tp}(p,q)|\le CL^{-3K}$ and curvature
response row sums at most $CL^{-2K}$.
By \cref{IV-73-75}, the kernels $C^{\rm tor},dC^{\rm tor}$
and $dC^{\rm tor}d^*$ have powers $1,2,3$ uniformly
in $N$. The row sum of $S_0$ is at most $cN$.
It follows that the three covariance corrections
are bounded respectively by
$c\ell^3N^{-1},c\ell^3N^{-2},c\ell^3N^{-3}$.
Thus, with $c_0=c\ell^3$,
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 |C_{\widehat E}(b,b')|\le c_0\langle b-b'\rangle^{-1},\qquad
 |dC_{\widehat E}(p,b)|\le c_0\langle x_p-b\rangle^{-2},\\
 |(\Pi_0^{\rm tp}-\Pi_K^{\rm tp})(p,q)|
       \le\min\{1,c_0\langle x_p-x_q\rangle^{-3}\},\\
 \|a_\omega\|_\infty\le C\ell L^{-K}\|\omega\|_\infty,
 \qquad\|da_\omega\|_\infty\le CL^{-2K}\|\omega\|_\infty.
 \end{gathered}
\]
The bound by one uses that the curvature covariance
is an orthogonal projection. The ghost kernels
satisfy the same bounds as in \cref{IV-73-56}.

\subsubsection*{The Gaussian comparison}
For $|z|_\infty\le3N/4$, \cref{IV-73-75}
and the covariance corrections show that a line
of $\mathsf B_1^{\widehat E}$ differs from its
lattice counterpart by at most $CN^{-1/2}$ times
its majorant with the exponent lowered by $1/2$.
Expand both coefficients into the connected pairings
of \cref{IV-73-53}.
Tuples whose places all lie within $N/4$ of $x_p$
correspond on the two lattices. Telescope their
line products and apply \cref{IV-73-55}; their
total difference is at most $CN^{-1/2}c_0^5$.
Every remaining tuple has a line of length at
least $N/16$ from $p$ or $q$ to a summed place.
Extract its factor $(16/N)^{1/2}$ and use the
same weakened-line bound on each lattice.
Therefore
\[
 |\mathsf B_1^{\widehat E}(p,q)
       -\mathsf B_1^{\rm lat}(\tilde p,\tilde q)|
       \le C\ell^{29/2}L^{-K/2}.
\]

\subsubsection*{The nonlinear vertices}
The one-step straight average is the same holomorphic
map at every level and bond. Its value at a top bond
depends on at most $6L^3$ bonds of the double block.
There is a fixed $\tilde r>0$ on whose sup-norm ball
its modulus is at most one. Cauchy's formula and
polarization therefore bound its homogeneous terms by
\[
 |\tilde c_k(\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_k)|
 \le\frac{k^k}{k!}\tilde r^{-k}
                         \prod_i\sup_{P_c}|\omega_i|.
\]
Writing $\phi_j=Q_j^s\phi$, composition gives
\[
 \begin{split}
 s_2^{(i)}(\phi,\psi)
   &=\sum_{j<i}Q_{j+1\to i}^s\tilde c_2(\phi_j,\psi_j),\\
 s_3^{(i)}(\phi,\psi,\chi)
   &=\sum_{j<i}Q_{j+1\to i}^s
       \left[\tfrac23\sum_{\rm cyc}
        \tilde c_2(\phi_j,s_2^{(j)}(\psi,\chi))
                    +\tilde c_3(\phi_j,\psi_j,\chi_j)\right].
 \end{split}
\]
The required vertices are $\widehat q_k=s_k^{(K)}-w_k$.
The averaging weights are nonnegative, at most
$L^{-2j}$, have row sum $L^j$, and are supported
within $3L^j/2$ of their output bond.

There are three kinds of entries in these vertices:
a covariance line from an external curvature, a
Gaussian field, and a response. Denote them in the
following estimates by $E,A,R$, respectively. At
level $j$ their bounds are
\[
 \begin{split}
 |Q_j^sdC_{\widehat E}(p,\cdot)(c)|
   &\le Cc_0L^j(L^j+|c_--x_p|)^{-2},\\
 \|Q_j^sa(c)\|_{L^2}&\le Cc_0^{1/2}L^{j/2},\\
 |Q_j^sa_\omega(c)|&\le C\ell L^{j-K}\|\omega\|_\infty.
 \end{split}
\]
All moments of the finitely many Gaussian factors
are bounded by their second moments, with constants
depending only on their degree. The corresponding
top-site functions vanish at $o$ and have differences
$-Q_K^sa$ and $\omega-Q_K^sa_\omega$.
Their values are bounded by summing along paths of
at most $3\ell/2$ bonds, or $3\ell$ for a response.

The outer average must be summed with the spatial
profiles of the external lines. In particular, the
product of two inverse-square profiles is summable;
with one such profile its sum over a block of side
$L^i$ is $O(L^i)$. Applying the displayed entry and
row bounds to each term of $s_2^{(K)}$, and summing
over $j<K$, gives the following scale factors:
\[
\begin{array}{c|cccccc}
 \text{entries of }\widehat q_2
   &(E,E)&(E,A)&(E,R)&(A,A)&(A,R)&(R,R)\\ \hline
 \text{factor}
   &KL^{-2K}&L^{-K/2}&L^{-K}&KL^K&L^{K/2}&1.
\end{array}
\]
For $\widehat q_3$, the factors needed below are
$KL^{-2K}$ at $(E,E,R)$ and $KL^{3K/2}$ at
$(A,A,A)$. The products of the powers of $c_0$
from the entries and of the path factors multiply
these scale factors.

For clarity, two path counts needed in the trace
terms can be kept sharper. The quadratic term of
$w$ is, up to its orientation sign,
$\mu'(c_-)\times d\mu'(c)$. It uses only one
undifferentiated top potential. Thus
\[
 \begin{split}
 \|\widehat q_2(E,E)\|_\infty
     &\le C\ell c_0^2KL^{-2K},\\
 \|\widehat q_2(R\omega,R\omega')\|_\infty
     &\le C\ell^3\|\omega\|_\infty\|\omega'\|_\infty,\\
 \|\widehat q_3(E,E,R\omega)\|_\infty
     &\le C\ell^4c_0^2KL^{-2K}\|\omega\|_\infty.
 \end{split}
\]
For the last bound, use the composition formula
for $s_3$. In its two-vertex terms retain the
spatial profiles of the inner quadratic vertex.
The averaging entries and column counts give
\[
\begin{split}
 \sum_c|s_2^{(j)}(E,E)(c)|&\le Cc_0^2jL^{-2j},\\
 |s_2^{(j)}(E,R\omega)(c)|&\le C\ell c_0L^{-K}
 \frac{L^{2j}}{(L^j+|c_--x_p|)^2}\|\omega\|_\infty.
\end{split}
\]
Multiplying by the remaining entry and the outer
average gives $C\ell c_0^2jL^{j-3K}\|\omega\|_\infty$.
Its sum over $j$ is at most
$C\ell c_0^2KL^{-2K}\|\omega\|_\infty$.
The term with one cubic vertex has the same bound
by the product of its two external profiles.
In $w_3$ every monomial contains a difference of
the top potential: this follows also by setting
its two endpoint values equal in the BCH formula.
The two external potentials have bounds
$C\ell c_0L^{-K}$ and differences $Cc_0L^{-K}$;
the response potential and its difference have
bounds $C\ell^2\|\omega\|_\infty$ and
$C\ell\|\omega\|_\infty$. These products are
bounded by the stated $\ell^4$ factor.

One pairing below involves two plain covariance
lines $C_z=C_{\widehat E}(z,\cdot)$ rather than
curvature lines. Averaging the inverse-distance
bound gives
$|Q_j^sC_z(c)|\le Cc_0L^j(L^j+|c_--z|)^{-1}$.
In the quadratic composition, the sum of the
product of these profiles with the outer weights
has scale factor $L^{j-K}$. Its sum over $j<K$
is bounded. The quadratic top-gauge term again
has only one path factor, so
\[
             \|\widehat q_2(C_z,C_z)\|_\infty
                                      \le C\ell c_0^2.
\]
With one curvature line the same sum has factor
$(K-j+1)L^{j-2K}$, whose sum is $O(L^{-K})$.
The top-gauge term has the same single path
factor. Therefore
\[
       \|\widehat q_2(E_z,C_z)\|_\infty
                               \le C\ell c_0^2L^{-K}.
\]

\subsubsection*{The eleven corrections}
Expand a connected cumulant into connected Gaussian
pairings. An entry quadratic in the Gaussian is
equivalently treated by two Gaussian integrations
by parts, in its two curvature directions.
A quadratic vertex with two entries of the same
colour vanishes: both the straight average and
$w$ are odd on a single-colour field. In addition,
contracting two legs of the scalar Wilson cubic
$S_3$ with a colour-diagonal kernel gives zero.
These cancellations remove the pairing patterns
without the decay factors used below.

The resulting estimates are
\[
\begin{array}{c|l}
 \text{term}&\text{upper bound, with a common constant }C\\ \hline
 |\mathsf t_1|&\ell^8KL^{-K}\\
 |\mathsf t_2|+|\mathsf t_5|&\ell^{10}K^2L^{-2K}\\
 |\mathsf t_3|&\ell^{11}L^{-3K/2}\\
 |\mathsf t_4|&\ell^{19/2}KL^{-K/2}\\
 |\mathsf t_6|&\ell^{11}KL^{-K}+\ell^{25/2}L^{-5K/2}\\
 |\mathsf t_7|&\ell^{13}L^{-K/2}+\ell^{15}KL^{-3K}\\
 |\mathsf t_8|&\ell^{16}L^{-2K}+\ell^{19}K^2L^{-5K}\\
 |\mathsf t_9|&\ell^{13}KL^{-2K}\\
 |\mathsf t_{10}|&\ell^{18}L^{-2K}\\
 |\mathsf t_{11}|&\ell^{11}L^{-2K}.
\end{array}
\]
We explain the counts, including the terms with
a sum over an interaction vertex. For $\mathsf t_1$,
the quadratic vertex and curvature response give
$C\ell^2c_0KL^{-K}$. The remaining cubic observable
has bounded moments of size $Cc_0$; hence the
bound is $C\ell^2c_0^2KL^{-K}$. Squaring the first
bound gives $C\ell^4c_0^2K^2L^{-2K}$ for
$\mathsf t_2,\mathsf t_5$. For $\mathsf t_4$,
the two parts of $\zeta_3$ have moments bounded
by $C\ell^5c_0^{3/2}KL^{3K/2}$ before applying
the curvature response $CL^{-2K}$.
These are the first, second and fourth rows.

In $\mathsf t_3$, a surviving contraction puts
one of the external curvature lines in the
quadratic vertex. Its $(E,A)$ rate and the
plain response give $L^{-3K/2}$. The remaining
entry and path factors are bounded by
$C\ell^2c_0^3$, yielding the third row.

For $\mathsf t_6$, sum the position $z$ of $S_3$
after its three colours have been contracted.
If the curl of $S_3$ pairs with the other quadratic
observable and its two plain fields pair with
$\widehat q_2$, use the plain-line estimate just
proved. The remaining curvature sum is at most
$Cc_0\log N$ and the curvature response contributes
$L^{-2K}$. Since $\log N\le C_L\ell K$, this is
bounded by the first term of the sixth row.
There is a second pattern with the same fixed
$p$--$q$ line: the leg of $S_3$ paired with $q$
is a plain field, and its other two legs enter
$\widehat q_2$ as $(E_z,C_z)$. Its bound is
\[
 C\ell c_0^2L^{-K}\cdot c_0N\cdot L^{-2K}
 =C\ell^2c_0^3L^{-2K}
                   \le C\ell^{11}KL^{-K}.
\]
Here $\sum_z|E(q,z)|\le Cc_0N$.
The other surviving patterns put an external
curvature line in $\widehat q_2$. Use its $(E,A)$
rate and sum the remaining two external profiles.
Whenever one is a curvature-curvature line, use
\[
 \min\{1,c_0\langle z\rangle^{-3}\}
                       \le c_0^{1/2}\langle z\rangle^{-3/2}.
\]
Together with an inverse-square line this is
summable in dimension three. The entry and path
counts are bounded by the two terms displayed
for $\mathsf t_6$.
In $\mathsf t_7$, put $R=L^K$, so $N=\ell R$.
A fixed $p$--$q$ line leaves one external direction
in $\widehat q_2$. Its $L^2$ bound is
$C\ell^2c_0^{3/2}R^{-1/2}$; the remaining local
Gaussian factor costs $c_0^{1/2}$, and the
inverse-square position sum costs $Cc_0N$.
Using the larger, plain-response bound $C\ell/R$
gives
\[
 C\frac\ell R(\ell^2c_0^{3/2}R^{-1/2})c_0^{1/2}(c_0N)
 =C\ell^4c_0^3R^{-1/2}.
\]
Without a fixed $p$--$q$ line both directions
in $\widehat q_2$ are external, with bound
$C\ell^2c_0^2K/R^2$. The product of the two
remaining external lines has sum at most $Cc_0^2$.
Thus this case costs
$C(\ell/R)(\ell^2c_0^2K/R^2)c_0^2
=C\ell^3c_0^4K/R^3$.
Substituting $c_0=C\ell^3$ gives the seventh row.

For $\mathsf t_8$, the response energy satisfies
\[
 |(\widehat R\omega,H\widehat R\omega')|
       \le C\ell^3L^{-K}\|\omega\|_\infty\|\omega'\|_\infty:
\]
there are $O(N^3)$ plaquettes and each curvature
response is $O(L^{-2K})$. A fixed $p$--$q$ line
leaves one external direction in each quadratic
vertex. The bound is
$C\ell^3L^{-K}(\ell^2c_0^{3/2}L^{-K/2})^2$.
With no fixed line, each quadratic vertex has
two external directions, giving instead
$C\ell^3L^{-K}(\ell^2c_0^2KL^{-2K})^2$.
The other patterns vanish by the equal-colour
cancellation. Substituting $c_0=C\ell^3$ gives
the two stated terms.

For $\mathsf t_9$, the two external directions
in $N_2$ use the sharper bounds above. Both
$\widehat q_3(E,E,R\,\cdot)$ and
$\widehat q_2(\widehat R\widehat q_2(E,E),
                         \widehat R\,\cdot)$
are bounded by $C\ell^4c_0^2KL^{-2K}$.
Taking the trace costs $9\ell^3$ and gives
$C\ell^7c_0^2KL^{-2K}$. For $\mathsf t_{10}$,
the two entries $\widehat q_2(E,R\,\cdot)$
have bound $C\ell^3c_0L^{-K}$. Summing the two
top indices costs at most $C\ell^6$, which
gives $C\ell^{12}c_0^2L^{-2K}$.
Finally $\mathsf t_{11}$ has $O(\ell^3)$ top
sites and two external potential entries of
size $C\ell c_0L^{-K}$, giving
$C\ell^5c_0^2L^{-2K}$.

Every use of a response on polynomial entries
is justified by its row-sum bound: a real matrix
bounded in the sup norm has absolute row sums
bounded by that norm. Thus no inverse on the
top lattice has been bounded by an operator
norm depending on its side. The constants use
only the fixed one-step radius, the kernel and
response constants, and the bounded polynomial
degrees.

Sum the rows. Since $KL^{-K}\le1$, their sum
is at most
\[
 C[\ell^{13}KL^{-K/2}+\ell^{18}L^{-2K}
                                      +\ell^{19}K^2L^{-5K}].
\]
Adding the Gaussian comparison proves the first
bound. The remaining conclusions follow from
$\ell,K\ge1$, and, for the sharper one,
$\ell^3\le L^K$.
\end{proof}



\subsection{Zero momentum}

Write \(\mathbb T=[-\pi,\pi]^3/(2\pi\mathbb Z)^3\) and
\(d^\circ k=(2\pi)^{-3}dk\).


In this subsection we compute the values at zero momentum of the self-energy and of the vertex function of a plaquette action. Both are expressed through Hessians of the action at constant abelian fields, whose symbols can be computed explicitly.

\begin{definition}[Hessians and zero-momentum coefficients]
\label{IV-73-29}
Write \(\mathsf e_1,\mathsf e_2,\mathsf e_3\) for the Pauli basis.
We work on $\mathbb Z^3$ and fix a gauge parameter $\tau_{\mathrm{gf}}=1$. For a positively oriented bond $b$ and a colour index $a$ we write $\partial_{b,a}$ for the derivative with respect to the variable $A^a(b)$. On a formal sum $\mathsf F=\sum_z\mathsf F_z$ of local terms (\cref{IV-73-19}) the derivative acts term by term, and the terms on which it vanishes are omitted. The derivatives $\partial_{b,a}S_3$, $\partial_{b,a}\partial_{b',a'}S_4$ and $\partial_{b,a}\partial_{b',a'}V_2$ which occur below are then finite sums: a bond is contained in exactly four plaquettes; of a sum over bonds $b''$ only the term with $b''=b$ survives; and of the sum over pairs of bonds in $V_2$ only the terms of the pairs $(b,b')$ and $(b',b)$ survive.

\smallskip\noindent\emph{(1) Hessians.} Let $B$ be a $1$-form on $\mathbb Z^3$ with $\sup_b|B(b)|<1$, and let $q$ be a plaquette. We define real symmetric matrices $\mathsf N(B)$ and $\mathsf h_q(B)$, indexed by the pairs $(b,a)$ of a positively oriented bond $b$ and a colour index $a$, by
\[
\begin{gathered}
\mathsf N(B)_{(b,a),(b',a')}:=\partial_{b,a}\partial_{b',a'}\Bigl[\sum_pa_p(e^{iA})+\frac1{2\tau_{\mathrm{gf}}}\sum_x|\mathrm d^*A(x)|^2\Bigr]_{A=B},\\
\mathsf h_q(B)_{(b,a),(b',a')}:=\partial_{b,a}\partial_{b',a'}\,a_q(e^{iA})\big|_{A=B}.
\end{gathered}
\]
The infinite sums over all plaquettes $p$ and over all sites $x$ are understood as follows: under $\partial_{b,a}\partial_{b',a'}$ only the finitely many terms which depend on $A(b)$ contribute, namely those of the plaquettes containing $b$ and those of the two end points of $b$. Consequently an entry of either matrix vanishes unless $b$ and $b'$ lie in a common plaquette or have a common end point. For fixed $(b,a)$ only finitely many entries $\mathsf N(B)_{(b,a),(b',a')}$ and $\mathsf h_q(B)_{(b,a),(b',a')}$ are different from $0$, and both matrices act on bounded complex $1$-forms $A$ by $(\mathsf N(B)A)^a(b):=\sum_{(b',a')}\mathsf N(B)_{(b,a),(b',a')}A^{a'}(b')$, and likewise for $\mathsf h_q(B)$.

\smallskip\noindent\emph{(2) Constant abelian fields.} For $\gamma\in\mathbb R^3$ with $|\gamma|<1$ let $Y_\gamma$ be the constant $1$-form $Y_\gamma((x,\mu)):=\gamma_\mu\mathsf e_3$. We put $\mathsf e_\pm:=2^{-1/2}(\mathsf e_1\pm i\mathsf e_2)$ and $\mathsf e_0:=\mathsf e_3$. These three vectors form a Hermitian-orthonormal basis of $\mathfrak g\otimes\mathbb C$, and
\[
[\mathsf e_3,\mathsf e_e]=2e\,\mathsf e_e\qquad(e\in\{+1,-1,0\});
\]
we call $e$ the \emph{charge}, and we write $\upsilon:=2e\gamma\in\mathbb R^3$. For $k\in\mathbb R^3$ we define two $3\times3$ matrices $\hat{\mathsf N}_e(k;\gamma)$, $\hat{\mathsf h}_{q,e}(k;\gamma)$ and a number $\hat{\mathsf M}_e(k;\gamma)$ by
\[
\begin{gathered}
\mathsf N(Y_\gamma)\bigl(e^{ik\cdot x}\alpha_\mu\mathsf e_e\bigr)=e^{ik\cdot x}(\hat{\mathsf N}_e\alpha)_\mu\,\mathsf e_e,\\
\bigl(e^{ik\cdot x}\alpha'\mathsf e_e,\,\mathsf h_q(Y_\gamma)\,e^{ik\cdot x}\alpha\,\mathsf e_e\bigr)=\alpha'^*\hat{\mathsf h}_{q,e}\alpha,\\
\mathsf M(Y_\gamma)\bigl(e^{ik\cdot x}\mathsf e_e\bigr)=\hat{\mathsf M}_e\,e^{ik\cdot x}\mathsf e_e
\end{gathered}
\]
for all $\alpha,\alpha'\in\mathbb C^3$. Here $e^{ik\cdot x}\alpha_\mu\mathsf e_e$ stands for the complex $1$-form $(x,\mu)\mapsto e^{ik\cdot x}\alpha_\mu\mathsf e_e$ and $e^{ik\cdot x}\mathsf e_e$ for the complex site function $x\mapsto e^{ik\cdot x}\mathsf e_e$; the bracket $(\cdot,\cdot)$ is Hermitian, and the sum which defines it is finite, since $\mathsf h_q(Y_\gamma)$ has non-zero entries only at bonds of $q$.

The operator \(\mathsf M(A)\lambda\) is \(d^*\) of the derivative
at \(s=0\) of the logarithm divided by \(i\) of
\[e^{is\lambda(b_-)}e^{iA(b)}e^{-is\lambda(b_+)}.\]
It is extended complex linearly. That the left sides have these forms is shown in \cref{IV-73-31}, which also gives explicit formulas.

By these formulas, for fixed $k$, the three objects are real analytic functions of $\gamma$ in $\{|\gamma|<1\}$. 

A second index $j$ denotes the homogeneous polynomial of degree $j$ in $\gamma$ in the Taylor expansion at $\gamma=0$, so that $\hat{\mathsf N}_e=\sum_j\hat{\mathsf N}_{e,j}$, $\hat{\mathsf h}_{q,e}=\sum_j\hat{\mathsf h}_{q,e,j}$ and $\hat{\mathsf M}_e=\sum_j\hat{\mathsf M}_{e,j}$. 

For $k\notin2\pi\mathbb Z^3$ we put $\hat{C}:=\hat{\mathsf N}_{e,0}^{-1}$. By \cref{IV-73-31} at $\gamma=0$ we have $\hat{\mathsf N}_{e,0}(k)=|\mathsf k|^2\mathbf 1-(1-\tau_{\mathrm{gf}}^{-1})\mathsf k\mathsf k^*$ with $\mathsf k=\mathsf k(k)$, so that $\hat{C}$ does not depend on $e$ and is the matrix with the entries
\[
\hat{C}_{\mu\nu}(k)=\frac{\delta_{\mu\nu}}{|\mathsf k|^2}+(\tau_{\mathrm{gf}}-1)\frac{\mathsf k_\mu\overline{\mathsf k_\nu}}{|\mathsf k|^4}
\]
which appears in the formula for $C$ in \cref{IV-73-15}; moreover $\hat{\mathsf M}_{e,0}=-|\mathsf k|^2$.

\smallskip\noindent\emph{(3) Five numbers of the self-energy.} For $k\in[-\pi,\pi]^3\setminus\{0\}$ and $\gamma\in\mathbb R^3$ we put, with all functions taken at $(k;\gamma)$,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathfrak s^{(1)}&:=-\tfrac14\sum_e\operatorname{tr}\bigl[(\hat{C}\hat{\mathsf N}_{e,1})^2\bigr]&&\text{(gluon loop)},\\
\mathfrak s^{(2)}&:=\tfrac12\sum_e\operatorname{tr}\bigl[\hat{C}\hat{\mathsf N}_{e,2}\bigr]&&\text{(gluon tadpole)},\\
\mathfrak s^{(3)}&:=\tfrac12\sum_e\operatorname{Re}\bigl[(\hat{\mathsf M}_{e,1}/\hat{\mathsf M}_{e,0})^2\bigr]&&\text{(ghost loop)},\\
\mathfrak s^{(4)}&:=-\sum_e\operatorname{Re}\bigl[\hat{\mathsf M}_{e,2}/\hat{\mathsf M}_{e,0}\bigr]&&\text{(ghost tadpole)},
\end{aligned}
\]
and $\mathfrak s^{(5)}(k;\gamma):=\frac13|\gamma|^2$ (Haar term). For fixed $k$ each $\mathfrak s^{(i)}(k;\cdot)$ is a homogeneous polynomial of degree $2$ in $\gamma$, bounded by $C|\gamma|^2|k|^{-2}$ (for $i\le4$ by \cref{IV-73-34}(i), for $i=5$ because $|k|$ is bounded on the cube); hence it is integrable over $\mathbb T$, and its integral is a quadratic form in $\gamma$. For $i=1,\dots,5$ we let $c^{(i)}_{\mu\nu}(\tau_{\mathrm{gf}})$, $1\le\mu,\nu\le3$, be the entries of the symmetric matrix with
\[
\frac12\sum_{\mu\nu}c^{(i)}_{\mu\nu}(\tau_{\mathrm{gf}})\,\gamma_\mu\gamma_\nu=\int_{\mathbb T}\mathfrak s^{(i)}(k;\gamma)\,d^\circ k\qquad(\gamma\in\mathbb R^3).
\]
We also need the number
\begin{equation}\label{IV-73-30}
Z_0:=\int_{\mathbb T}\frac{d^\circ k}{|\mathsf k(k)|^2}=\int_{[-\pi,\pi]^3}\frac{dk}{(2\pi)^3}\Bigl(\sum_\mu4\sin^2\frac{k_\mu}2\Bigr)^{-1}.
\end{equation}

\smallskip\noindent\emph{(4) Four numbers of the vertex function of $a_q$.} For a plaquette $q$, $k\in[-\pi,\pi]^3\setminus\{0\}$ and $\gamma\in\mathbb R^3$ we put, again with all functions taken at $(k;\gamma)$,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathfrak v_q^{(1)}&:=\tfrac12\sum_e\operatorname{tr}\bigl[\hat{\mathsf h}_{q,e,2}\hat{C}\bigr],&
\mathfrak v_q^{(2)}&:=-\tfrac12\sum_e\operatorname{tr}\bigl[\hat{\mathsf h}_{q,e,1}\hat{C}\hat{\mathsf N}_{e,1}\hat{C}\bigr],\\
\mathfrak v_q^{(3)}&:=-\tfrac12\sum_e\operatorname{tr}\bigl[\hat{\mathsf h}_{q,e,0}\hat{C}\hat{\mathsf N}_{e,2}\hat{C}\bigr],&
\mathfrak v_q^{(4)}&:=\tfrac12\sum_e\operatorname{tr}\bigl[\hat{\mathsf h}_{q,e,0}\hat{C}\hat{\mathsf N}_{e,1}\hat{C}\hat{\mathsf N}_{e,1}\hat{C}\bigr].
\end{aligned}
\]
These are homogeneous polynomials of degree $2$ in $\gamma$, bounded by $C|\gamma|^2|k|^{-2}$ (\cref{IV-73-36}). For $j=1,\dots,4$ we let $\mathsf g^{(j)}_{q;\mu\nu}(\tau_{\mathrm{gf}})$ be the entries of the symmetric matrix with
\[
\frac12\sum_{\mu\nu}\mathsf g^{(j)}_{q;\mu\nu}(\tau_{\mathrm{gf}})\,\gamma_\mu\gamma_\nu=\int_{\mathbb T}\mathfrak v_q^{(j)}(k;\gamma)\,d^\circ k\qquad(\gamma\in\mathbb R^3).
\]

\smallskip\noindent\emph{(5) Kernels.} Let $\langle\cdot\rangle_0$ refer to the Gaussian family of $\mathbb Z^3$ and $\tau_{\mathrm{gf}}$ (\cref{IV-73-19}), and write $\partial=\partial_{b,a}$, $\partial'=\partial_{b',a'}$. We define
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Sigma(b,a;b',a')&:=\langle\partial\partial'V_2\rangle_0-\langle\partial S_3;\partial'S_3\rangle_0,\\
\Gamma_q(b,a;b',a')&:=\langle\partial\partial'\mathsf a_q^{(4)}\rangle_0-\langle\partial\mathsf a_q^{(3)};\partial'S_3\rangle_0-\langle\partial'\mathsf a_q^{(3)};\partial S_3\rangle_0-\langle\mathsf a_q^{(2)};\partial\partial'S_4\rangle_0+\langle\mathsf a_q^{(2)};\partial S_3;\partial'S_3\rangle_0 .
\end{aligned}
\]
These are means and cumulants (\cref{IV-73-19}) of polynomials in the Gaussian family, and both kernels are symmetric under the exchange $(b,a)\leftrightarrow(b',a')$.

We determine the colour structure of the two kernels. For $g\in G$ the map $\operatorname{Ad}g:X\mapsto gXg^{-1}$ is orthogonal on $(\mathfrak g,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle)$; let $(\operatorname{Ad}g)_{aa'}$ be its matrix in the basis $\mathsf e_1,\mathsf e_2,\mathsf e_3$. The components $(gA(b)g^{-1})^a=\sum_{a'}(\operatorname{Ad}g)_{aa'}A^{a'}(b)$ of the $\mathfrak g$-valued family $(gA(b)g^{-1})_b$ are real linear combinations of the variables of the Gaussian family, so that this family is again centred Gaussian. By \cref{IV-73-19} and the orthogonality of $\operatorname{Ad}g$, its covariance is
\[
\bigl\langle(gA(b)g^{-1})^a\,(gA(b')g^{-1})^{c}\bigr\rangle_0=\sum_{a'}(\operatorname{Ad}g)_{aa'}(\operatorname{Ad}g)_{ca'}\,C(b,b')=\delta_{ac}\,C(b,b'),
\]
which is the covariance of $(A(b))_b$; as a centred Gaussian family is determined in law by its covariance, $(gA(b)g^{-1})_b$ has the law of $(A(b))_b$. By \cref{IV-73-9} the polynomials $\mathsf a^{(m)}_p$ are invariant under $A\mapsto gAg^{-1}$, and so are $S_3$, $S_4$ and, term by term, $V_2$, whose remaining terms involve $A$ only through $|A(b)|^2$ and $\langle A(b),A(b')\rangle$. By the chain rule, each of the two kernels, regarded at fixed $b,b'$ as a matrix $K$ in $(a,a')$, satisfies $K=(\operatorname{Ad}g)^{\mathsf T}K\operatorname{Ad}g$, that is, it commutes with every $\operatorname{Ad}g$. For $g=e^{isY}$, differentiation at $s=0$ shows that $K$ commutes with $\mathsf e_c\times\cdot$ for $c=1,2,3$. Such a matrix is a multiple of $\mathbf 1$: it preserves $\ker(\mathsf e_c\times\cdot)=\mathbb R\mathsf e_c$, so it is diagonal in the basis $\mathsf e_1,\mathsf e_2,\mathsf e_3$, with entries $m_1,m_2,m_3$ say; applying it to $\mathsf e_1\times\mathsf e_2=\mathsf e_3$ and to $\mathsf e_3\times\mathsf e_1=\mathsf e_2$ gives $m_3=m_2$ and $m_2=m_1$. Hence
\[
\Sigma(b,a;b',a')=\delta_{aa'}\,\Sigma(b,b'),\qquad\Gamma_q(b,a;b',a')=\delta_{aa'}\,\Gamma_q(b,b'),
\]
and these identities define the kernels $\Sigma(b,b')$ and $\Gamma_q(b,b')$. Finally, the kernels are covariant under the translations of $\mathbb Z^3$. Indeed, $C((x,\mu),(y,\nu))$ and $G(x,y)$ depend on the sites $x,y$ only through $x-y$ (\cref{IV-73-15}), so that the law of the Gaussian family is invariant under translations; the coefficients of the polynomials $\mathsf a_p^{(m)}$ do not depend on $p$ (\cref{IV-73-9}); and $g(b)=\frac13$ as well as $D(b;b')$, which are built from $G$ (\cref{IV-73-15}), do not change when $b$ and $b'$ are translated together. Hence the formal sums $S_3$, $S_4$, $V_2$ are invariant under translations as well, and $\Sigma(b+y,b'+y)=\Sigma(b,b')$ and $\Gamma_{q+y}(b+y,b'+y)=\Gamma_q(b,b')$ for all $y\in\mathbb Z^3$.
\end{definition}

The symbols of \cref{IV-73-29}(2) can be computed explicitly.

\begin{lemma}[The Hessian at a constant abelian field]
\label{IV-73-31}
Let $\gamma\in\mathbb R^3$ with $|\gamma|<1$, let $e\in\{\pm1,0\}$, $\upsilon=2e\gamma$ and $k\in\mathbb R^3$. Let $j(\vartheta):=(e^{i\vartheta}-1)/i\vartheta$ for real $\vartheta\ne0$ and $j(0):=1$, and put
\[
J:=\operatorname{diag}\bigl(j(\upsilon_1),j(\upsilon_2),j(\upsilon_3)\bigr),\qquad P(k):=|\mathsf k(k)|^2\mathbf 1-\mathsf k(k)\mathsf k(k)^*;
\]
the matrix $J$ is invertible, since $|\upsilon_\mu|<2$ and $j(\vartheta)\ne0$ for $|\vartheta|<2\pi$. For a plaquette $q=p_{\mu\nu}(x)$ let $D_q(k)$ be the $1\times3$ matrix with $D_q(k)\alpha=\mathsf k_\mu(k)\alpha_\nu-\mathsf k_\nu(k)\alpha_\mu$, $\alpha\in\mathbb C^3$. Then the left sides of the three identities in \cref{IV-73-29}(2) have the forms stated there, with
\[
\begin{gathered}
\hat{\mathsf N}_e(k;\gamma)=J^*P(k+\upsilon)J+\tau_{\mathrm{gf}}^{-1}\mathsf k(k)\mathsf k(k)^*,\\\hat{\mathsf h}_{q,e}(k;\gamma)=J^*D_q(k+\upsilon)^*D_q(k+\upsilon)J,\\\hat{\mathsf M}_e(k;\gamma)=-\mathsf k(k)^*J^{-1}\mathsf k(k+\upsilon).
\end{gathered}
\]
Moreover the following hold.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] We have
\begin{equation}\label{IV-73-32}
\det\hat{\mathsf N}_e(k;\gamma)=\tau_{\mathrm{gf}}^{-1}\,|\det J|^2\,|\mathsf k(k+\upsilon)|^2\,|\hat{\mathsf M}_e(k;\gamma)|^2,\qquad\prod_{e}|\det J|=\prod_\mu\sigma_1(\gamma_\mu^2),
\end{equation}
where \(\sigma_1(t)=(\sin\sqrt t/\sqrt t)^2\), continuously extended at zero, and in the second identity $J$ is taken at $\upsilon=2e\gamma$ for each $e\in\{+1,-1,0\}$.
\item[(b)] If $\mathsf k(k+\upsilon)\ne0$ and $\hat{\mathsf M}_e(k;\gamma)\ne0$, then $\hat{\mathsf N}_e(k;\gamma)$ is invertible, and for $q=p_{\mu\nu}(x)$
\begin{equation}\label{IV-73-33}
\operatorname{tr}\bigl[\hat{\mathsf h}_{q,e}(k;\gamma)\hat{\mathsf N}_e(k;\gamma)^{-1}\bigr]=\varpi_q(k+\upsilon),\qquad\varpi_q(k):=\frac{|\mathsf k_\mu(k)|^2+|\mathsf k_\nu(k)|^2}{|\mathsf k(k)|^2}.
\end{equation}
\item[(c)] With $\mathsf k=\mathsf k(k)$,
\[
\hat{\mathsf M}_{e,1}=-\sum_\mu\upsilon_\mu\sin k_\mu,\qquad\hat{\mathsf M}_{e,2}=\frac1{12}\sum_\mu\upsilon_\mu^2|\mathsf k_\mu|^2,\qquad\operatorname{tr}\hat{\mathsf N}_{e,2}=\sum_\mu\upsilon_\mu^2\Bigl[2\cos k_\mu-\frac1{12}\bigl(|\mathsf k|^2-|\mathsf k_\mu|^2\bigr)\Bigr].
\]
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\emph{Second variation.}
Let \(a\) have finite support and \(u_\mu=e^{i\gamma_\mu\mathsf e_3}\).
For small real \(s\) the matrix
\(e^{i(Y_\gamma(b)+sa(b))}e^{-iY_\gamma(b)}\) is near the identity.
Its local logarithm defines a smooth \(\eta_s(b)\), with \(\eta_0=0\).
Termwise differentiation of the exponential series gives
\[
 \left.\frac d{ds}e^{i(Y+sa)}e^{-iY}\right|_{s=0}
 =i\int_0^1e^{itY}ae^{-itY}\,dt
 =i\,\mathsf{dE}(Y)a.
\]
Thus
\[
\eta_s(b)=s\,\mathsf{dE}(Y_\gamma(b))\,a(b)+O(s^2).
\]
Let $p=p_{\mu\nu}(x)$ have the bonds $b_1,\dots,b_4$, and put $\eta_i:=\eta_s(b_i)$. Since $Y_\gamma(b_1)=Y_\gamma(b_3)=\gamma_\mu\mathsf e_3$ and $Y_\gamma(b_2)=Y_\gamma(b_4)=\gamma_\nu\mathsf e_3$, since $u_\mu$ and $u_\nu$ commute, and since $ue^{iX}u^{-1}=e^{iuXu^{-1}}$, we find
\[
\partial\bigl(e^{i(Y_\gamma+sa)}\bigr)(p)=e^{i\eta_1}u_\mu\,e^{i\eta_2}u_\nu\,u_\mu^{-1}e^{-i\eta_3}\,u_\nu^{-1}e^{-i\eta_4}=e^{i\eta_1}\,e^{iu_\mu\eta_2u_\mu^{-1}}\,e^{-iu_\nu\eta_3u_\nu^{-1}}\,e^{-i\eta_4}=e^{iZ},
\]
where $Z\in\mathfrak g$ is the image of this product under $\frac1i\log$; for small $s$ the product is close to $\mathbf 1$, and by the diffeomorphism property recalled above $Z$ is a smooth function of $s$, with $Z=0$ at $s=0$. To first order
\[
Z=\eta_1+u_\mu\eta_2u_\mu^{-1}-u_\nu\eta_3u_\nu^{-1}-\eta_4+O(s^2).
\]
Since $a_p(U)=1-\frac12\operatorname{tr}\partial U(p)$ and $\frac12\operatorname{tr}e^{iZ}=\cos|Z|$, we have $a_p(e^{i(Y_\gamma+sa)})=1-\cos|Z|=\frac12|Z|^2+O(|Z|^4)$. We put $(\mathsf J_\gamma a)(b):=\mathsf{dE}(Y_\gamma(b))a(b)$ and, for a $1$-form $a'$, $(D_\gamma a')(p):=a'(b_1)+u_\mu a'(b_2)u_\mu^{-1}-u_\nu a'(b_3)u_\nu^{-1}-a'(b_4)$; by the expansion of $\eta_s(b)$, $Z=s\,(D_\gamma\mathsf J_\gamma a)(p)+O(s^2)$, and therefore
\[
a_p\bigl(e^{i(Y_\gamma+sa)}\bigr)=\tfrac12s^2\bigl|(D_\gamma\mathsf J_\gamma a)(p)\bigr|^2+O(s^3).
\]
The constant form $Y_\gamma$ satisfies $\mathrm d^*Y_\gamma=0$, so that $\frac1{2\tau_{\mathrm{gf}}}\sum_x|\mathrm d^*(Y_\gamma+sa)(x)|^2=\frac{s^2}{2\tau_{\mathrm{gf}}}\|\mathrm d^*a\|^2$. Taking second derivatives in $s$ at $s=0$ we obtain the quadratic forms of the two Hessians:
\[
\bigl(a,\mathsf h_p(Y_\gamma)a\bigr)=\bigl|(D_\gamma\mathsf J_\gamma a)(p)\bigr|^2,\qquad\bigl(a,\mathsf N(Y_\gamma)a\bigr)=\sum_p\bigl|(D_\gamma\mathsf J_\gamma a)(p)\bigr|^2+\tau_{\mathrm{gf}}^{-1}\|\mathrm d^*a\|^2 ,
\]
the sum over $p$ being finite. A real symmetric matrix of the kind considered in \cref{IV-73-29}(1) is determined by its quadratic form on the forms of finite support; by polarisation, therefore,
\[
\mathsf h_p(Y_\gamma)=(\delta_pD_\gamma\mathsf J_\gamma)^*(\delta_pD_\gamma\mathsf J_\gamma),\qquad\mathsf N(Y_\gamma)=(D_\gamma\mathsf J_\gamma)^*D_\gamma\mathsf J_\gamma+\tau_{\mathrm{gf}}^{-1}\mathrm d\mathrm d^*,
\]
where $\delta_p$ is the evaluation at $p$ and the adjoints are taken with respect to the brackets $(\cdot,\cdot)$.

\emph{Step 2: symbols.} We extend all operators complex linearly. From $[\mathsf e_3,\mathsf e_e]=2e\,\mathsf e_e$ we get $u_\mu\mathsf e_eu_\mu^{-1}=e^{2ie\gamma_\mu}\mathsf e_e=e^{i\upsilon_\mu}\mathsf e_e$, and hence
\[
\mathsf{dE}(\gamma_\mu\mathsf e_3)\,\mathsf e_e=\int_0^1e^{is\upsilon_\mu}\,ds\;\mathsf e_e=j(\upsilon_\mu)\,\mathsf e_e .
\]
So $\mathsf J_\gamma$ maps the form $e^{ik\cdot x}\alpha\,\mathsf e_e$ to $e^{ik\cdot x}J\alpha\,\mathsf e_e$, and for $\alpha'\in\mathbb C^3$
\[
D_\gamma\bigl(e^{ik\cdot x}\alpha'\mathsf e_e\bigr)(p_{\mu\nu}(x))=e^{ik\cdot x}\bigl[\alpha'_\mu+e^{i(\upsilon_\mu+k_\mu)}\alpha'_\nu-e^{i(\upsilon_\nu+k_\nu)}\alpha'_\mu-\alpha'_\nu\bigr]\mathsf e_e=e^{ik\cdot x}D_{p_{\mu\nu}(x)}(k+\upsilon)\,\alpha'\,\mathsf e_e .
\]
Thus $\mathsf J_\gamma$, $D_\gamma$ and $\mathrm d\mathrm d^*$ commute with the translations of $\mathbb Z^3$ and map a plane wave of momentum $k$ and charge $e$ to a plane wave of the same momentum and charge, the coefficient vector being multiplied by $J$, by the $1\times3$ matrices $D_{p_{\mu\nu}(x)}(k+\upsilon)$ ($\mu<\nu$), and by $\mathsf k(k)\mathsf k(k)^*$, respectively; the last symbol follows from the plane-wave formulas of \cref{IV-73-15}. The adjoint of such an operator acts on plane waves through the adjoint matrix. By Lagrange's identity,
\[
\sum_{\mu<\nu}|v_\mu\alpha_\nu-v_\nu\alpha_\mu|^2=|v|^2|\alpha|^2-|v^*\alpha|^2=\alpha^*\bigl(|v|^2\mathbf 1-vv^*\bigr)\alpha\qquad(v,\alpha\in\mathbb C^3),
\]
so that $\sum_{\mu<\nu}D_{p_{\mu\nu}(x)}(k')^*D_{p_{\mu\nu}(x)}(k')=P(k')$ for $k'\in\mathbb R^3$. Together with Step~1 this gives the formula for $\hat{\mathsf N}_e$; for $\hat{\mathsf h}_{q,e}$ only the plaquette $q$ enters, and the factors $e^{ik\cdot x}$ have modulus $1$.

For \(\hat{\mathsf M}_e\), differentiate the defining gauge action in \cref{IV-73-29} and invert the differential \(\mathsf{dE}(Y)\) of the exponential. At $A=Y_\gamma$, $\lambda=e^{ik\cdot x}\mathsf e_e$ and the bond $(x,\mu)$ it gives
\[
\begin{gathered}
\frac d{ds}A^{s\lambda}((x,\mu))\Big|_{s=0}\\
=\mathsf{dE}(\gamma_\mu\mathsf e_3)^{-1}\bigl(e^{ik\cdot x}\mathsf e_e-e^{i\upsilon_\mu}e^{ik\cdot(x+e_\mu)}\mathsf e_e\bigr)\\
=j(\upsilon_\mu)^{-1}\bigl(1-e^{i(\upsilon_\mu+k_\mu)}\bigr)e^{ik\cdot x}\mathsf e_e\\
=-j(\upsilon_\mu)^{-1}\mathsf k_\mu(k+\upsilon)\,e^{ik\cdot x}\mathsf e_e .
\end{gathered}
\]
