Since $\mathsf M(A)\lambda$ is $\mathrm d^*$ of this derivative and $\mathrm d^*$ multiplies plane waves by $\mathsf k(k)^*$ (\cref{IV-73-15}), we obtain $\hat{\mathsf M}_e=-\mathsf k(k)^*J^{-1}\mathsf k(k+\upsilon)$. Here we have used that $j(\vartheta)\ne0$ for $|\vartheta|<2\pi$.

\emph{Step 3: proof of (a).} Let $v:=\mathsf k(k+\upsilon)$ and $\tilde u:=(J^*)^{-1}\mathsf k(k)$. Then
\[
\hat{\mathsf N}_e=J^*\bigl(P(k+\upsilon)+\tau_{\mathrm{gf}}^{-1}\tilde u\tilde u^*\bigr)J,\qquad v^*\tilde u=(J^{-1}v)^*\mathsf k(k)=-\overline{\hat{\mathsf M}_e},
\]
and $P(k+\upsilon)=|v|^2\mathbf 1-vv^*$. For $v,w\in\mathbb C^3$ we have $\det\bigl(|v|^2\mathbf 1-vv^*+ww^*\bigr)=|v|^2|v^*w|^2$: for $v=0$ both sides vanish; for $v\ne0$ we use an orthonormal basis whose first vector is $v/|v|$; in it the matrix is $|v|^2\operatorname{diag}(0,1,1)+ww^*$, the determinant is an affine function of the rank-one summand, and its value is $0+|v|^4|w_1|^2$ with $w_1=v^*w/|v|$. With $w=\tau_{\mathrm{gf}}^{-1/2}\tilde u$ this gives $\det\hat{\mathsf N}_e=|\det J|^2\,|v|^2\,\tau_{\mathrm{gf}}^{-1}|v^*\tilde u|^2$, the first identity in \eqref{IV-73-32}. For the second, $|j(\vartheta)|^2=(2-2\cos\vartheta)/\vartheta^2=\bigl(\sin\frac\vartheta2/\frac\vartheta2\bigr)^2$; since $\det J=\prod_\mu j(2e\gamma_\mu)$, the product over the three charges contributes, for each $\mu$, the factor $|j(2\gamma_\mu)|^2=(\sin\gamma_\mu/\gamma_\mu)^2=\sigma_1(\gamma_\mu^2)$.

\emph{Step 4: proof of (b).} By (a), $\hat{\mathsf N}_e$ is invertible. By the cyclicity of the trace,
\[
\operatorname{tr}\bigl[\hat{\mathsf h}_{q,e}\hat{\mathsf N}_e^{-1}\bigr]=D_q\bigl(P+\tau_{\mathrm{gf}}^{-1}\tilde u\tilde u^*\bigr)^{-1}D_q^*,
\]
with $D_q$ and $P$ taken at $k+\upsilon$. Now $D_qv=v_\mu v_\nu-v_\nu v_\mu=0$, hence $v^*D_q^*=0$ and $PD_q^*=|v|^2D_q^*$; moreover $Pv=0$, and $\tilde u^*v\ne0$ because $v^*\tilde u=-\overline{\hat{\mathsf M}_e}\ne0$. The vector
\[
\mathsf X:=|v|^{-2}D_q^*-\frac{\tilde u^*D_q^*}{|v|^2\,\tilde u^*v}\,v
\]
satisfies $P\mathsf X=D_q^*$ and $\tilde u^*\mathsf X=0$, hence $(P+\tau_{\mathrm{gf}}^{-1}\tilde u\tilde u^*)\mathsf X=D_q^*$. Therefore the trace equals $D_q\mathsf X=|v|^{-2}D_qD_q^*=|v|^{-2}\bigl(|v_\mu|^2+|v_\nu|^2\bigr)=\varpi_q(k+\upsilon)$.

\emph{Step 5: proof of (c).} We expand in powers of $\vartheta$ and of $\upsilon$; the dots stand for terms of degree at least $3$:
\[
j(\vartheta)=1+\frac{i\vartheta}2-\frac{\vartheta^2}6+\dots,\qquad j(\vartheta)^{-1}=1-\frac{i\vartheta}2-\frac{\vartheta^2}{12}+\dots,\qquad|j(\vartheta)|^2=1-\frac{\vartheta^2}{12}+\dots,
\]
\[
\begin{gathered}
\mathsf k_\mu(k+\upsilon)=\mathsf k_\mu+e^{ik_\mu}\bigl(i\upsilon_\mu-\tfrac12\upsilon_\mu^2+\dots\bigr),\\|\mathsf k_\mu(k+\upsilon)|^2=2-2\cos(k_\mu+\upsilon_\mu)\\
=|\mathsf k_\mu|^2+2\upsilon_\mu\sin k_\mu+\upsilon_\mu^2\cos k_\mu+\dots .
\end{gathered}
\]
In $\hat{\mathsf M}_e=-\sum_\mu\overline{\mathsf k_\mu}\,j(\upsilon_\mu)^{-1}\mathsf k_\mu(k+\upsilon)$ the terms of degree $1$ are
\[
-i\sum_\mu\upsilon_\mu\overline{\mathsf k_\mu}\bigl[e^{ik_\mu}-\tfrac12\mathsf k_\mu\bigr]=-i\sum_\mu\upsilon_\mu\overline{\mathsf k_\mu}\,\tfrac12\bigl(e^{ik_\mu}+1\bigr)=-\sum_\mu\upsilon_\mu\sin k_\mu ,
\]
because $\overline{\mathsf k_\mu}(e^{ik_\mu}+1)=-2i\sin k_\mu$, and the terms of degree $2$ are
\[
-\sum_\mu\upsilon_\mu^2\,\overline{\mathsf k_\mu}\bigl[-\tfrac1{12}\mathsf k_\mu+\tfrac12e^{ik_\mu}-\tfrac12e^{ik_\mu}\bigr]=\frac1{12}\sum_\mu\upsilon_\mu^2|\mathsf k_\mu|^2 .
\]
The term $\tau_{\mathrm{gf}}^{-1}\mathsf k\mathsf k^*$ of $\hat{\mathsf N}_e$ does not depend on $\gamma$. Hence $\operatorname{tr}\hat{\mathsf N}_{e,2}$ is the homogeneous polynomial of degree $2$ in the expansion of
\[
\operatorname{tr}\bigl[J^*P(k+\upsilon)J\bigr]=\sum_\mu|j(\upsilon_\mu)|^2\sum_{\nu\ne\mu}|\mathsf k_\nu(k+\upsilon)|^2,
\]
namely
\[
\sum_\mu\Bigl[-\frac1{12}\upsilon_\mu^2\sum_{\nu\ne\mu}|\mathsf k_\nu|^2+\sum_{\nu\ne\mu}\upsilon_\nu^2\cos k_\nu\Bigr]=\sum_\mu\upsilon_\mu^2\Bigl[2\cos k_\mu-\frac1{12}\bigl(|\mathsf k|^2-|\mathsf k_\mu|^2\bigr)\Bigr].
\]
This is the asserted formula for $\operatorname{tr}\hat{\mathsf N}_{e,2}$, and (c) is proved.
\end{proof}

With these formulas we evaluate the self-energy at zero momentum.

\begin{proposition}[The five contributions to the self-energy at zero momentum]
\label{IV-73-34}
Let $\tau_{\mathrm{gf}}=1$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] For $i=1,\dots,4$, all $k\in[-\pi,\pi]^3\setminus\{0\}$ and all $\gamma\in\mathbb R^3$ we have $|\mathfrak s^{(i)}(k;\gamma)|\le C|\gamma|^2|k|^{-2}$, with $C=C(\tau_{\mathrm{gf}})$.
\item[(ii)] $\sum_{i=1}^5c^{(i)}_{\mu\nu}(\tau_{\mathrm{gf}})=0$ for all $\mu,\nu$.
\item[(iii)] At $\tau_{\mathrm{gf}}=1$,
\begin{equation}\label{IV-73-35}
\bigl(c^{(1)}_{\mu\nu},\dots,c^{(5)}_{\mu\nu}\bigr)(1)=\delta_{\mu\nu}\cdot\Bigl(-20Z_0+\tfrac83,\ \ 16Z_0-\tfrac{28}9,\ \ 4Z_0-\tfrac23,\ \ \tfrac49,\ \ \tfrac23\Bigr).
\end{equation}
\end{enumerate}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
\emph{Step 1: bounds.} By the formulas of \cref{IV-73-31}, the entries of $J^{\pm1}$ and of $\mathsf k(k+\upsilon)$ are real analytic functions of $(k,\gamma)$. On $[-\pi,\pi]^3$ we have $P(k)=O(|k|^2)$ and $\partial_kP(k)=O(|k|)$. The terms of degree $1$ in $\gamma$ of $J^*P(k+\upsilon)J$ are terms containing the factor $P(k)$ and the term $\sum_\mu\upsilon_\mu\partial_\mu P(k)$; hence $|\hat{\mathsf N}_{e,1}|\le C|\gamma||k|$, while $|\hat{\mathsf N}_{e,2}|\le C|\gamma|^2$. Every term of $\hat{\mathsf M}_e$ contains the factor $\mathsf k(k)^*$, so that $|\hat{\mathsf M}_{e,j}|\le C|\gamma|^j|k|$. Finally $|\hat{C}|\le C|k|^{-2}$ by the formula for $\hat{C}$ in \cref{IV-73-29}(2), and $|\hat{\mathsf M}_{e,0}|^{-1}=|\mathsf k(k)|^{-2}\le C|k|^{-2}$, as $|\mathsf k(k)|^2\ge\frac4{\pi^2}|k|^2$. Inserting these bounds into the definitions of $\mathfrak s^{(1)},\dots,\mathfrak s^{(4)}$ we obtain $|\hat{C}\hat{\mathsf N}_{e,1}|^2\le C|\gamma|^2|k|^{-2}$, $|\hat{C}\hat{\mathsf N}_{e,2}|\le C|\gamma|^2|k|^{-2}$, $|\hat{\mathsf M}_{e,1}/\hat{\mathsf M}_{e,0}|^2\le C|\gamma|^2|k|^{-2}$ and $|\hat{\mathsf M}_{e,2}/\hat{\mathsf M}_{e,0}|\le C|\gamma|^2|k|^{-1}\le C'|\gamma|^2|k|^{-2}$, which proves (i).

\emph{Step 2: identity of the integrands.} Fix $k\in[-\pi,\pi]^3\setminus\{0\}$, and let $\gamma$ be so close to $0$ that $\mathsf k(k+\upsilon)\ne0$ and $\hat{\mathsf M}_e(k;\gamma)\ne0$ for all $e$. We divide the first identity in \eqref{IV-73-32} by its value at $\gamma=0$, take one half of its logarithm, sum over $e$ and use the second identity in \eqref{IV-73-32}:
\[
\sum_e\Bigl\{\tfrac12\log\det\bigl[\hat{C}\hat{\mathsf N}_e(k;\gamma)\bigr]-\log\bigl|\hat{\mathsf M}_e(k;\gamma)/\hat{\mathsf M}_{e,0}\bigr|\Bigr\}-\sum_\mu\log\sigma_1(\gamma_\mu^2)=\tfrac12\sum_e\log\frac{|\mathsf k(k+2e\gamma)|^2}{|\mathsf k(k)|^2}.
\]
Both sides are real analytic in $\gamma$ near $0$, and we compare their terms of degree $2$. On the left, the expansion $\log\det(\mathbf 1+\mathsf A)=\operatorname{tr}\mathsf A-\frac12\operatorname{tr}\mathsf A^2+\dots$ with $\mathsf A=\hat{C}(\hat{\mathsf N}_{e,1}+\hat{\mathsf N}_{e,2}+\dots)$ yields $\mathfrak s^{(2)}+\mathfrak s^{(1)}$; the expansion $\log|1+z|=\operatorname{Re}(z-\frac12z^2+\dots)$ with $z=(\hat{\mathsf M}_{e,1}+\hat{\mathsf M}_{e,2}+\dots)/\hat{\mathsf M}_{e,0}$ yields, with the sign in front, $\mathfrak s^{(4)}+\mathfrak s^{(3)}$; and by \cref{IV-73-9}, applied to $Y=\gamma_\mu\mathsf e_3$, the term $-\sum_\mu\log\sigma_1(\gamma_\mu^2)$ yields $\frac13|\gamma|^2=\mathfrak s^{(5)}$. On the right, with $\mathsf l(k):=\log|\mathsf k(k)|^2$, the terms of degree $2$ are $\frac12\sum_{e=\pm1}\frac12\sum_{\mu\nu}4\gamma_\mu\gamma_\nu\,\partial_\mu\partial_\nu\mathsf l(k)$. Hence
\[
\sum_{i=1}^5\mathfrak s^{(i)}(k;\gamma)=2\sum_{\mu\nu}\gamma_\mu\gamma_\nu\,\partial_\mu\partial_\nu\mathsf l(k)\qquad(k\ne0),
\]
an identity between homogeneous polynomials of degree $2$ in $\gamma$, valid for all $\gamma\in\mathbb R^3$.

\emph{Step 3: flux argument.} The function $\mathsf l$ is smooth on $\mathbb R^3\setminus2\pi\mathbb Z^3$ and periodic, and on the cube $|\partial\mathsf l|\le C|k|^{-1}$ and $|\partial\partial\mathsf l|\le C|k|^{-2}$. For $0<\varepsilon<1$ we apply Gauss' divergence theorem on the cube $[-\pi,\pi]^3$ less the ball $\{|k|\le\varepsilon\}$; the contributions of opposite faces of the cube cancel by periodicity, and
\[
\int_{[-\pi,\pi]^3\cap\{|k|>\varepsilon\}}\partial_\mu\partial_\nu\mathsf l\,dk=-\int_{|k|=\varepsilon}\frac{k_\mu}\varepsilon\,\partial_\nu\mathsf l\,dS=O(\varepsilon).
\]
Letting $\varepsilon\to0$ we get $\int_{\mathbb T}\partial_\mu\partial_\nu\mathsf l\,d^\circ k=0$. By Step~2 and the definition of the numbers $c^{(i)}_{\mu\nu}$, $\frac12\sum_{\mu\nu}\bigl(\sum_ic^{(i)}_{\mu\nu}\bigr)\gamma_\mu\gamma_\nu=0$ for all $\gamma$; as the matrices are symmetric, (ii) follows.

\emph{Step 4: elementary integrals.} We write $\mathsf k=\mathsf k(k)$. By the symmetry under permutations of the coordinates, $\int_{\mathbb T}|\mathsf k_\mu|^2|\mathsf k|^{-2}d^\circ k=\frac13$. As $\cos k_\mu=1-\frac12|\mathsf k_\mu|^2$, we get $\int_{\mathbb T}\cos k_\mu|\mathsf k|^{-2}d^\circ k=Z_0-\frac16$. Since $\partial_\mu|\mathsf k|^2=2\sin k_\mu$,
\[
\partial_\mu\bigl(\sin k_\mu|\mathsf k|^{-2}\bigr)=\cos k_\mu|\mathsf k|^{-2}-2\sin^2k_\mu|\mathsf k|^{-4};
\]
the function $\sin k_\mu|\mathsf k|^{-2}$ is periodic and $O(|k|^{-1})$, so the flux argument of Step~3 shows that the integral of the left side over $\mathbb T$ vanishes, and $\int_{\mathbb T}\sin^2k_\mu|\mathsf k|^{-4}d^\circ k=\frac12(Z_0-\frac16)$. Finally $\int_{\mathbb T}\sin k_\mu\sin k_\nu|\mathsf k|^{-4}d^\circ k=0$ for $\mu\ne\nu$, the integrand being odd under $k_\mu\to-k_\mu$.

\emph{Step 5: values.} We use \cref{IV-73-31}(c) with $\upsilon=2e\gamma$, and $\hat{\mathsf M}_{e,0}=-|\mathsf k|^2$. For $e=0$ we have $\upsilon=0$, so that $\hat{\mathsf N}_{0,j}=0$ and $\hat{\mathsf M}_{0,j}=0$ for $j\ge1$; the charge $0$ contributes nothing, and for $e=\pm1$ we have $\upsilon_\mu^2=4\gamma_\mu^2$. We write $\delta$ for the matrix $(\delta_{\mu\nu})$.
\begin{itemize}
\item $\mathfrak s^{(5)}=\frac13|\gamma|^2$, whose integral is $\frac13|\gamma|^2$; hence $c^{(5)}=\frac23\delta$.
\item $\mathfrak s^{(4)}=\sum_{e=\pm1}\frac4{12}\sum_\mu\gamma_\mu^2|\mathsf k_\mu|^2|\mathsf k|^{-2}$, whose integral is $\frac29|\gamma|^2$ by Step~4; hence $c^{(4)}=\frac49\delta$.
\item $\mathfrak s^{(3)}=4\bigl(\sum_\mu\gamma_\mu\sin k_\mu\bigr)^2|\mathsf k|^{-4}$, whose integral is $4|\gamma|^2\cdot\frac12(Z_0-\frac16)$; hence $c^{(3)}=(4Z_0-\frac23)\delta$.
\item At $\tau_{\mathrm{gf}}=1$ we have $\hat{C}=|\mathsf k|^{-2}\mathbf 1$ and
\[
\mathfrak s^{(2)}=\tfrac12\sum_{e=\pm1}|\mathsf k|^{-2}\operatorname{tr}\hat{\mathsf N}_{e,2}=4\sum_\mu\gamma_\mu^2\Bigl[2\cos k_\mu-\frac1{12}\bigl(|\mathsf k|^2-|\mathsf k_\mu|^2\bigr)\Bigr]|\mathsf k|^{-2},
\]
whose integral is $4|\gamma|^2\bigl[2Z_0-\frac13-\frac1{12}\cdot\frac23\bigr]=|\gamma|^2\bigl(8Z_0-\frac{14}9\bigr)$; hence $c^{(2)}=(16Z_0-\frac{28}9)\delta$.
\item By (ii), $c^{(1)}=-\sum_{i\ge2}c^{(i)}=-\bigl(20Z_0-\frac{28}9-\frac23+\frac49+\frac23\bigr)\delta=\bigl(-20Z_0+\frac83\bigr)\delta$.
\end{itemize}
This proves (iii).
\end{proof}

The same method applies to the vertex function of a plaquette action.

\begin{proposition}[The vertex function at zero momenta]
\label{IV-73-36}
Let $\tau_{\mathrm{gf}}=1$ and let $q$ be a plaquette. Then $|\mathfrak v_q^{(j)}(k;\gamma)|\le C|\gamma|^2|k|^{-2}$ for $j=1,\dots,4$, all $k\in[-\pi,\pi]^3\setminus\{0\}$ and all $\gamma\in\mathbb R^3$, where $C$ depends on $\tau_{\mathrm{gf}}$ only; and
\[
\sum_{j=1}^4\mathsf g^{(j)}_{q;\mu\nu}(\tau_{\mathrm{gf}})=0\qquad\text{for all }\mu,\nu .
\]
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
\emph{Step 1: bound.} The $1\times3$ matrix $D_q(k)$ is smooth in $k$, satisfies $D_q(k)=O(|k|)$, and depends on $q$ only through the two directions of $q$. In the expansion of $\hat{\mathsf h}_{q,e}=J^*D_q(k+\upsilon)^*D_q(k+\upsilon)J$ in powers of $\gamma$, each term of degree $j\le1$ retains at least $2-j$ factors $D_q(k)$ or $D_q(k)^*$; hence $|\hat{\mathsf h}_{q,e,j}|\le C|\gamma|^j|k|^{2-j}$ for $j=0,1,2$, with $C$ independent of $q$. As in Step~1 of the proof of \cref{IV-73-34}, \cref{IV-73-31} gives $|\hat{\mathsf N}_{e,1}|\le C|\gamma||k|$ and $|\hat{\mathsf N}_{e,2}|\le C|\gamma|^2$, and \cref{IV-73-15} gives $|\hat{C}|\le C|k|^{-2}$. Inserted into the definitions of $\mathfrak v_q^{(1)},\dots,\mathfrak v_q^{(4)}$, these bounds give the asserted bound.

\emph{Step 2: identity of the integrands.} Fix $k\in[-\pi,\pi]^3\setminus\{0\}$. For small $\gamma$ we write $\hat{\mathsf N}_e=\hat{\mathsf N}_{e,0}\bigl(\mathbf 1+\hat{C}(\hat{\mathsf N}_e-\hat{\mathsf N}_{e,0})\bigr)$, and the Neumann series gives
\[
\hat{\mathsf N}_e^{-1}=\hat{C}-\hat{C}\hat{\mathsf N}_{e,1}\hat{C}-\hat{C}\hat{\mathsf N}_{e,2}\hat{C}+\hat{C}\hat{\mathsf N}_{e,1}\hat{C}\hat{\mathsf N}_{e,1}\hat{C}+O(|\gamma|^3).
\]
Hence the terms of degree $2$ in $\gamma$ of $\frac12\sum_e\operatorname{tr}\bigl[\hat{\mathsf h}_{q,e}\hat{\mathsf N}_e^{-1}\bigr]$ are $\sum_{j=1}^4\mathfrak v_q^{(j)}(k;\gamma)$. On the other hand, for small $\gamma$ the hypotheses of \cref{IV-73-31}(b) hold, and by \eqref{IV-73-33} the same expression equals $\frac12\sum_e\varpi_q(k+2e\gamma)$, whose terms of degree $2$ are $2\sum_{\mu\nu}\gamma_\mu\gamma_\nu\partial_\mu\partial_\nu\varpi_q(k)$. Therefore
\[
\sum_{j=1}^4\mathfrak v_q^{(j)}(k;\gamma)=2\sum_{\mu\nu}\gamma_\mu\gamma_\nu\,\partial_\mu\partial_\nu\varpi_q(k)\qquad(k\ne0,\ \gamma\in\mathbb R^3).
\]

\emph{Step 3: flux argument.} The function $\varpi_q$ is smooth on $\mathbb R^3\setminus2\pi\mathbb Z^3$ and periodic, and on the cube $|\partial\varpi_q|\le C|k|^{-1}$ and $|\partial\partial\varpi_q|\le C|k|^{-2}$, since it is a quotient of smooth functions vanishing to second order at $0$ whose denominator is at least $\frac4{\pi^2}|k|^2$. As in Step~3 of the proof of \cref{IV-73-34},
\[
\int_{[-\pi,\pi]^3\cap\{|k|>\varepsilon\}}\partial_\mu\partial_\nu\varpi_q\,dk=-\int_{|k|=\varepsilon}\frac{k_\mu}\varepsilon\,\partial_\nu\varpi_q\,dS=O(\varepsilon),
\]
hence $\int_{\mathbb T}\partial_\mu\partial_\nu\varpi_q\,d^\circ k=0$. By Step~2, $\frac12\sum_{\mu\nu}\bigl(\sum_j\mathsf g^{(j)}_{q;\mu\nu}\bigr)\gamma_\mu\gamma_\nu=0$ for all $\gamma$, and the symmetry of the matrices gives the claim.
\end{proof}

We next record the behaviour of these objects under point reflections.

\begin{lemma}[Point reflections]
\label{IV-73-37}
Let $c\in\frac12\mathbb Z^3$, and let $R_c:x\mapsto2c-x$ on $\mathbb Z^3$ (note that $2c\in\mathbb Z^3$). We let $R_c$ act on bonds by $R_c\langle x,x'\rangle:=\langle R_cx,R_cx'\rangle$, on plaquettes through their corners (the corners of $R_cp$ are the images of the corners of $p$), and on configurations $U$, $1$-forms $A$ and site functions $\lambda$ by
\[
(R_cU)(b):=U(R_cb),\qquad(R_cA)(b):=A(R_cb),\qquad(R_c\lambda)(x):=\lambda(R_cx);
\]
thus $(R_cA)_\mu(x)=-A_\mu(2c-x-e_\mu)$. The following hold.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] For all plaquettes $p$, configurations $U$, $1$-forms $A$ on $\mathbb Z^3$ and $m\ge0$: $a_p(R_cU)=a_{R_cp}(U)$ and $\mathsf a_p^{(m)}(R_cA)=\mathsf a^{(m)}_{R_cp}(A)$. Moreover $\mathrm d^*R_c=R_c\mathrm d^*$ on $1$-forms, and $\mathrm dR_c=R_c\mathrm d$ on site functions.
\item[(b)] For every $\tau_{\mathrm{gf}}=1$ the family $\bigl((R_cA)^a(b)\bigr)_{b,a}$ has the law of the Gaussian family of $\mathbb Z^3$ and $\tau_{\mathrm{gf}}$. Moreover $D(R_cb;R_cb')=D(b;b')$ for all bonds $b,b'$, where $D$ is taken with oriented arguments, that is, it is given by the formula of \cref{IV-73-15} for arbitrary bonds; in particular $D(\bar b;b')=-D(b;b')$ and $D(b;\bar b')=D(b;b')$.
\item[(c)] For a positively oriented bond $b$ let $b^R$ be the positively oriented one of the bonds $R_cb$ and $\overline{R_cb}$, that is, $(x,\mu)^R=(2c-x-e_\mu,\mu)$. Then for all positively oriented bonds $b,b'$ and all plaquettes $q$
\[
\Sigma(b^R,b'^R)=\Sigma(b,b'),\qquad\Gamma_{R_cq}(b^R,b'^R)=\Gamma_q(b,b').
\]
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\emph{Step 1: proof of (a).} Let $p=p_{\mu\nu}(x)$. The loop $\partial p=(b_1,b_2,\bar b_3,\bar b_4)$ passes through $x$, $x+e_\mu$, $x+e_\mu+e_\nu$, $x+e_\nu$. The map $R_c$ carries it to the loop through $y+e_\mu+e_\nu$, $y+e_\nu$, $y$, $y+e_\mu$, where $y:=2c-x-e_\mu-e_\nu$ is the base point of $R_cp=p_{\mu\nu}(y)$; this image loop is $\partial(R_cp)$, traversed in the same sense but started at the opposite corner. Since $\partial(R_cU)(p)$ is the product of the values of $U$ along the image loop, it is conjugate in $G$ to $\partial U(R_cp)$, and the two matrices have the same trace; hence $a_p(R_cU)=a_{R_cp}(U)$. As $R_c(e^{itA})=e^{itR_cA}$, comparison of the Taylor coefficients in \cref{IV-73-9} gives $\mathsf a^{(m)}_p(R_cA)=\mathsf a^{(m)}_{R_cp}(A)$. Next, $(\mathrm d^*A)(x)=-\sum_{b:\,b_-=x}A(b)$, the sum over the six bonds starting at $x$, and $R_c$ maps the bonds starting at $x$ bijectively onto those starting at $R_cx$; therefore $\mathrm d^*R_cA=R_c\mathrm d^*A$. Finally $(\mathrm dR_c\lambda)(b)=\lambda(R_cb_+)-\lambda(R_cb_-)=(\mathrm d\lambda)(R_cb)$.

\emph{Step 2: proof of (b).} The variables $(R_cA)_\mu(x)=-A_\mu(2c-x-e_\mu)$ form a centred Gaussian family, with the same colour structure as $A$. By \cref{IV-73-15} the covariance of $(R_cA)_\mu(x)$ and $(R_cA)_\nu(y)$, for equal colours, is
\[
C\bigl((2c-x-e_\mu,\mu),(2c-y-e_\nu,\nu)\bigr)=\int_{\mathbb T}e^{-ik\cdot(x-y)}\,e^{-i(k_\mu-k_\nu)}\,\hat{C}_{\mu\nu}(k)\,d^\circ k .
\]
Since $e^{-ik_\mu}\mathsf k_\mu(k)=-\mathsf k_\mu(-k)$, and correspondingly $e^{ik_\nu}\overline{\mathsf k_\nu(k)}=-\overline{\mathsf k_\nu(-k)}$, we have $e^{-i(k_\mu-k_\nu)}\hat{C}_{\mu\nu}(k)=\hat{C}_{\mu\nu}(-k)$, also for $\mu=\nu$. The substitution $k\to-k$ shows that the covariance equals $C((x,\mu),(y,\nu))$, and a centred Gaussian family is determined in law by its covariance. Moreover $G(R_cx,R_cy)=G(x,y)$, again by the substitution $k\to-k$ in the formula for $G$; with $(R_cb)_\pm=R_c(b_\pm)$ the formula for $D$ in \cref{IV-73-15} gives $D(R_cb;R_cb')=D(b;b')$. The same formula shows that reversing the first argument changes the sign of $D$, while reversing the second does not change it.

\emph{Step 3: proof of (c).} By (a) and (b), $S_3$ and $V_2$ are invariant under $A\to R_cA$, term by term: the term of a plaquette $p$ is carried to that of $R_cp$, and the terms of a bond $b$ and of a pair $(b,b')$ in $V_2$ to those of $b^R$ and of $(b^R,b'^R)$; here $g(b)=\frac13$ is constant on $\mathbb Z^3$, $|A(R_cb)|=|A(b^R)|$, and the signs coming from reversed arguments of $D$ cancel in pairs. Likewise $\mathsf a_q^{(m)}(A)=\mathsf a^{(m)}_{R_cq}(R_cA)$. Since $(R_cA)(b^R)=A(\bar b)=-A(b)$, the chain rule gives
\[
\partial_{b,a}(\mathsf F\circ R_c)=-(\partial_{b^R,a}\mathsf F)\circ R_c
\]
for every polynomial $\mathsf F$. Each term of the kernels in \cref{IV-73-29}(5) contains exactly two derivatives, so that the signs cancel, and by (b) the means and cumulants do not change under the substitution $A\to R_cA$. Hence $\Sigma(b,a;b',a')=\Sigma(b^R,a;b'^R,a')$ and $\Gamma_q(b,a;b',a')=\Gamma_{R_cq}(b^R,a;b'^R,a')$, which is (c).
\end{proof}

\subsection{Homogeneous parts of lattice kernels}

Fix a smooth function \(\theta:[0,\infty)\to[0,1]\),
equal to one on \([0,\tfrac12]\) and zero on \([1,\infty)\).
Fix a smooth radial function \(\chi\), equal to one on
\(\{|k|\le1\}\) and zero on \(\{|k|\ge2\}\).
Since \(2<\pi\), it also defines a function on the Fourier torus.
An elementary line of degree \(n=s+3\), where \(s\ge-2\)
is an integer, is the Fourier kernel of a symbol
\(\sigma\in\mathcal S^s\) with
\[
 \sigma-\chi\sigma^h\in\mathcal S^{s+1},\qquad
 \sigma^h(tk)=t^s\sigma^h(k),\qquad
 \sigma^h(-k)=(-1)^s\sigma^h(k),
\]
where \(\sigma^h\) is smooth off zero.
Products and translations of line symbols preserve this
definition whenever their resulting order is at least \(-2\);
their leading symbols multiply.
In particular the symbols of \(G,C,E,\Pi,D\) have leading
parts obtained by replacing \(\mathsf k_\mu\) by \(ik_\mu\)
and \(|\mathsf k|^{-2}\) by \(|k|^{-2}\).
Indeed,
\(|\mathsf k|^2-|k|^2\) vanishes to fourth order at zero,
and \(|\mathsf k|^2\ge4|k|^2/\pi^2\).

\begin{lemma}[Homogeneous kernels]\label{lem:pure-homogeneous-kernels}
Let \(s>-3\), and let \(\sigma^h\) be smooth off zero
and homogeneous of degree \(s\). There is a unique smooth
function
\[
 K^h=\mathcal F^{-1}_{\ne0}\sigma^h
\]
on \(\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}\), homogeneous of degree
\(-3-s\), such that for every smooth compactly supported
\(\rho=1\) near zero,
\[
 \int e^{ik\cdot x}\rho(k)\sigma^h(k)\,d^\circ k
                 -K^h(x)=O(|x|^{-N})
 \quad(|x|\ge1)
\]
for every \(N\). The construction preserves parity and
rotations, and multiplication of the symbol by
\((ik)^\gamma\) gives \(\partial^\gamma K^h\).
For an elementary line of degree \(n\),
\[
 |\nabla^\gamma(K-K^h)(x)|
       \le C_\gamma|x|^{-n-1-|\gamma|}
                       \quad(|x|\ge|\gamma|+1).
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Choose \(2N>s+3\), and define
\[
 K_\rho^h(x)=\int e^{ik\cdot x}\rho\sigma^h\,d^\circ k
   +|x|^{-2N}\int e^{ik\cdot x}
              (-\Delta_k)^N[(1-\rho)\sigma^h]\,d^\circ k.
\]
The second integral converges absolutely. Integration by parts
over balls shows that it does not change on replacing \(N\)
by \(N+1\); the boundary terms tend to zero since
\(2N>s+3\). The same argument shows independence of \(\rho\):
the difference of two cutoffs times \(\sigma^h\) is smooth
and compactly supported away from zero.
Taking \(N\) arbitrarily large proves the rapid remainder.
Taking \(2N>s+3+|\gamma|\) permits differentiation under
the integrals, proving smoothness and the derivative rule.
Rescaling \(k\) proves homogeneity. The substitutions
\(k\mapsto-k\) and \(k\mapsto Ok\) prove parity and
rotation covariance.
Uniqueness follows because a homogeneous difference of degree
\(-3-s\) cannot decay faster than every power on every ray
unless it vanishes.

For the lattice line, split its symbol into
\(\chi\sigma^h\) and its remainder of order \(s+1\).
The kernel bound of \cref{IV-73-39} gives
\(K-K^h=O(|x|^{-4-s})\).
Apply the same argument to
\(\mathsf k^\gamma\sigma\), whose leading symbol is
\((ik)^\gamma\sigma^h\).
It gives the estimate with \(\partial^\gamma K^h\)
in place of \(\nabla^\gamma K^h\).
Taylor's formula replaces the former by the latter with
the same error: on the finite difference stencil,
the relevant derivatives of \(K^h\) are bounded by their
homogeneity. This proves the final assertion.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Lines with a leading part]\label{IV-73-38}
For an integer \(n\ge2\), write \(K\in\mathfrak K(n)\) if it is the
Fourier kernel of \(\sigma\in L^1(\mathbb T)\), and has
leading data \((\sigma^h,K^h)\) satisfying
\[
 \sigma^h(tk)=t^{n-3}\sigma^h(k),\qquad
 |\sigma-\chi\sigma^h|(k)\le C|k|^{n-2}\lg|k|,
\]
with \(\sigma^h\) continuous off zero, and
\[
 K^h(tx)=t^{-n}K^h(x),\qquad
 |\nabla^\gamma(K-K^h)(x)|
 \le C_\gamma|x|^{-n-1-|\gamma|}\lg|x|
 \quad(|x|\ge|\gamma|+1),
\]
with \(K^h\) smooth off zero.
The constants include the displayed bounds, \(\|\sigma\|_1\),
and the sphere bounds of \(\sigma^h\) and the derivatives
of \(K^h\). Here \(\lg t=1+|\log t|\).
The leading data are unique: rescale a ray to zero for
\(\sigma^h\), and integer multiples of rational rays to
infinity for \(K^h\), then use continuity.
Every elementary line of degree \(n\ge2\) belongs to
\(\mathfrak K(n)\), by
\cref{lem:pure-homogeneous-kernels}.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Comparing a sum and an integral]\label{lem:pure-riemann-error}
For \(D\in\{3,6\}\), suppose \(F\in C^1(\mathbb R^D)\)
and
\(\sum_{z\in\mathbb Z^D}
\sup_{z+[0,1]^D}(|F|+|\nabla F|)<\infty\).
Then
\[
 \left|\sum_zF(z)-\int F(x)\,dx\right|
       \le\sqrt D\sum_z\sup_{z+[0,1]^D}|\nabla F|.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
On each unit cube the mean value theorem bounds the
difference between \(F(z)\) and its integral by the displayed
supremum times the cube diameter \(\sqrt D\).
The hypotheses permit summation.
\end{proof}

For \(D=3,6\), \(R\ge1\), and \(g:\mathbb Z^D\to\mathbb C\),
put
\[
 \|g\|_{(R)}
 =\max_{|\gamma|\le10}R^{|\gamma|}\sup|\nabla^\gamma g|.
\]
Let \(\mathcal H_s(D)\) denote the nonnegative Borel
functions homogeneous of degree \(s>-D\) and integrable
over the unit ball. If \(s<9-D\), then
\[
 \int H(\kappa)\lg|\kappa|\langle\kappa\rangle^{-10}\,d\kappa<\infty
                         \qquad(H\in\mathcal H_s(D)).
\]
This follows by radial integration.

\begin{lemma}[A kernel against a slowly varying function]\label{IV-73-41}
Suppose \(g\) vanishes outside \(\{|z|\le R\}\), and write
\(\check g(\kappa)=\sum_zg(z)e^{-i\kappa\cdot z}\).
Then
\[
 |\check g(\kappa)|\le CR^D\langle R\kappa\rangle^{-10}\|g\|_{(R)}.
\]
Let \(\widehat T\in L^1(\mathbb T^{D/3})\), \(0<c_0\le1\),
\(-D<s<9-D\), \(H\in\mathcal H_s(D)\), and
\(\iota=0\) or \(1\). If
\[
 |\widehat T(\kappa)|\le H(\kappa)(\lg|\kappa|)^\iota
                              \quad(0<|\kappa|\le c_0),
\]
then
\[
 \left|\int\widehat T(\kappa)\check g(-\kappa)\,d^\circ\kappa\right|
             \le CR^{-s}(\lg R)^\iota\|g\|_{(R)}.
\]
Suppose further that \(s<8-D\), that \(\widehat T^h\)
is homogeneous of degree \(s\), and that
\[
 |\widehat T^h|\le H,\qquad
 |\widehat T-\widehat T^h|\le H'\lg|\kappa|
       \quad(0<|\kappa|\le c_0),\qquad H'\in\mathcal H_{s+1}(D).
\]
If \(G\in C_c^\infty(\{|x|\le1\})\), \(a\in\mathbb R\),
and
\(\|g-R^{-a}G(\cdot/R)\|_{(R)}\le AR^{-a-1}\lg R\), then
\begin{align*}
 &\left|\int\widehat T\check g
       -R^{-a-s}\int_{\mathbb R^D}
                        \widehat T^h(\kappa)\widehat G(-\kappa)
                                                   \,d^\circ\kappa\right|\\
 &\hspace{20mm}\le C(A+\|G\|_{C^{10}})R^{-a-s-1}\lg R.
\end{align*}
In the first integral \(\check g\) is evaluated at \(-\kappa\).
The homogeneous integral is bounded by \(C\|G\|_{C^{10}}\).
Constants depend only on the displayed symbol bounds and \(c_0\).
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Finite differences give
\[
 (e^{i\kappa_j}-1)^N\check g(\kappa)
          =\sum_z\nabla_j^Ng(z)e^{-i\kappa\cdot z}.
\]
For \(N\le10\) the right side has at most \(CR^D\)
terms, each bounded by \(R^{-N}\|g\|_{(R)}\).
Choose \(|\kappa_j|\ge|\kappa|/\sqrt D\), and use
\(|e^{i\kappa_j}-1|\ge2|\kappa_j|/\pi\).
The estimates at \(N=0,10\) prove the Fourier bound.

Outside \(|\kappa|\le c_0\), that bound gives
\(CR^{D-10}c_0^{-10}\|\widehat T\|_1\|g\|_{(R)}\).
Inside, substitute \(\kappa=\kappa'/R\).
Homogeneity and
\(\lg(|\kappa'|/R)\le\lg|\kappa'|\lg R\)
give the second assertion by the integrability stated above.

For the last assertion set \(g^h=R^{-a}G(\cdot/R)\).
Near zero,
\(|\widehat T|\le H+H'/|\kappa|\), since
\(t\lg t\le1\) for \(0<t\le1\).
This majorant belongs to \(\mathcal H_s(D)\).
The preceding estimate applied to \(g-g^h\) therefore
gives the error \(CAR^{-a-s-1}\lg R\).
Apply it again, now at order \(s+1\), to
\(\widehat T-\chi(\cdot/c_0)\widehat T^h\)
and \(g^h\). This costs
\(CR^{-a-s-1}\lg R\|G\|_{C^{10}}\).

Poisson summation gives
\[
 \check g^h(\kappa)
   =R^{D-a}\sum_{m\in\mathbb Z^D}
                 \widehat G(R(\kappa+2\pi m)).
\]
For \(|\kappa|\le2c_0\le2\), every nonzero \(m\)
has \(|\kappa+2\pi m|\ge\pi|m|\).
Since
\(|\widehat G(\xi)|\le C\langle\xi\rangle^{-10}\|G\|_{C^{10}}\),
their total contribution is
\(O(R^{D-a-10}\|G\|_{C^{10}})\), within the claimed error.
The zero term, after rescaling, is
\[
 R^{-a-s}\int
 \chi(\kappa/(c_0R))\widehat T^h(\kappa)\widehat G(-\kappa)
                                                     \,d^\circ\kappa.
\]
Removing \(\chi\) costs at most
\(CR^{-a-s}R^{s+D-10}\|G\|_{C^{10}}\).
The assumption \(s<8-D\) makes this smaller than the
stated error and also proves the absolute bound on the
homogeneous integral.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[One-loop functions]\label{IV-73-42}
Let \(m=2\) or \(3\), \(D=3(m-1)\), and let
\(\sigma_i\) be elementary line symbols of integer orders
\(s_i\ge-2\).
For signs \(\epsilon_i\) and linear maps
\(\lambda_i:\mathbb R^D\to\mathbb R^3\), set
\(l_i=-\epsilon_i\lambda_i\).
Assume the maps \(l_i\) are distinct and, for some \(c_\lambda\ge1\),
\[
 \max_i|l_i(\kappa)|\le c_\lambda|\kappa|
       \le c_\lambda^2\max_{i<j}|l_i(\kappa)-l_j(\kappa)|.
\]
Assume also that
\((l,\kappa)\mapsto(\epsilon_il+\lambda_i(\kappa))_{i=1}^m\)
has an integer matrix of determinant \(\pm1\).
For \(m=3\) require \(s_i+s_j\ge-3\) for \(i\ne j\).
Put
\[
 \omega=3+\sum_i s_i\ge-1,\qquad
 I(\kappa)=\int_{\mathbb T}
          \prod_i\sigma_i(\epsilon_il+\lambda_i(\kappa))\,d^\circ l,
\]
\[
 \Lambda(\kappa)=1+\sum_{i<j}
       \log_+\frac{|\kappa|}{|l_i(\kappa)-l_j(\kappa)|}.
\]
The integral exists almost everywhere and
\(\|I\|_1\le\prod_i\|\sigma_i\|_1\).
Near zero, away from the collision subspaces, there are a
polynomial \(Q\) of degree at most \(\omega\), zero if
\(\omega=-1\), and a homogeneous Borel function \(I^h\)
such that
\[
 I^h(t\kappa)=t^\omega I^h(\kappa),\qquad
 I^h(-\kappa)=(-1)^{\omega+1}I^h(\kappa),\qquad
 |I^h|\le C|\kappa|^\omega\Lambda(\kappa),
\]
\[
 |I-Q-I^h|(\kappa)
        \le C|\kappa|^{\omega+1}\lg|\kappa|\Lambda(\kappa).
\]
Set \(I^h=0\) on the collision subspaces and at zero.
It depends multilinearly only on the leading symbols
\(\sigma_i^h\) and the linear maps. It commutes with simultaneous
rotations whenever the maps do, and is continuous off zero
when \(m=2\).
If \(\omega\ge1\), then
\[
 Q(0)=\int_{\mathbb T}\prod_i\sigma_i(\epsilon_il)\,d^\circ l.
\]
The pair \((Q,I^h)\) is uniquely determined by these
asymptotics and the indicated opposite parities at degree
\(\omega\). Finally
\(|\kappa|^s\Lambda(\kappa)\in\mathcal H_s(D)\) for every \(s>-D\).
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Write \(\varepsilon=c_\lambda|\kappa|\).
For exponents \(t_i>-3\), with pair sums at least \(-3\)
when \(m=3\), the elementary collision estimate is
\begin{equation}\label{IV-73-43}
 \int_{|l|\le2\varepsilon}\prod_i|l-l_i(\kappa)|^{t_i}\,dl
 \le C\varepsilon^{3+\sum t_i}\Lambda(\kappa).
\end{equation}
To prove it rescale to \(\varepsilon=1\).
All centers lie in the unit ball and some pair is separated
by \(c_\lambda^{-2}\). For two centers the singularities
are uniformly separated. For three, let \(d\) be the
smallest pair distance. If \(d\) is bounded below, each
singularity is uniformly isolated. Otherwise the third
center stays a fixed distance from that pair.
Near the third center use its integrable single power.
Near the pair, the ball of radius \(2d\) contributes
\(Cd^{3+t_i+t_j}\le C\); outside it the two distances
are comparable, and radial integration gives at most
\(C(1+\log(1/d))\). This proves the estimate.
For each nonzero linear map \(l_i-l_j\), one of its
linear components bounds a multiple of \(|v\cdot\kappa|\).
The logarithm of the inverse of this component is integrable
on the sphere. This proves the assertion about
\(\mathcal H_s(D)\).

For \(|l|\ge2\varepsilon\), \(|\kappa'|\le|\kappa|\),
periodic distances of all \(\epsilon_il+\lambda_i(\kappa')\)
are comparable to \(|l|\). Hence, for symbols of orders \(t_i\),
\begin{equation}\label{IV-73-44}
 \left|\partial_\kappa^\alpha
       \prod_i\sigma_i(\epsilon_il+\lambda_i(\kappa'))\right|
                    \le C_\alpha|l|^{\sum t_i-|\alpha|}.
\end{equation}
The same estimate holds for the homogeneous symbols on
\(\mathbb R^3\).
The unimodular change of variables on the product torus
proves the \(L^1\) assertion by Tonelli.
The collision estimate and the outer bound prove absolute
convergence at small noncollision \(\kappa\).

We first record a Taylor estimate for arbitrary symbols of
integer orders \(t_i\ge-2\), with \(\omega'=3+\sum t_i\ge0\).
Split at \(2\varepsilon\).
On the inner ball use \eqref{IV-73-43}.
On its complement expand through degrees less than \(\omega'\).
The remainder is bounded by
\(C|\kappa|^{\omega'}|l|^{-3}\), so its integral costs
\(C|\kappa|^{\omega'}\lg|\kappa|\).
Every Taylor coefficient of degree \(j<\omega'\) is
integrable at zero. Restoring its omitted inner ball costs
\(O(|\kappa|^{\omega'})\).
Thus the integral is a polynomial of degree below \(\omega'\)
plus \(O(|\kappa|^{\omega'}\lg|\kappa|\Lambda)\).
When \(\omega'\ge1\), its constant is the integral at zero.

Now put \(A^h(l,\kappa)=\prod_i
\sigma_i^h(\epsilon_il+\lambda_i(\kappa))\).
For \(|l|>2\varepsilon\), expand
\[
 A^h=\sum_{j\le\omega}A_j^h+A_{\rm rem}^h,\qquad
 |A_{\rm rem}^h|\le C|\kappa|^{\omega+1}|l|^{-4}.
\]
Here \(A_j^h\) is homogeneous of degree \(j\) in \(\kappa\)
and \(\omega-3-j\) in \(l\).
Empty sums are understood if \(\omega=-1\).
Define
\[
 I^h(\kappa)=
 \int_{|l|\le2\varepsilon}A^h\,d^\circ l
 +\int_{|l|>2\varepsilon}A_{\rm rem}^h\,d^\circ l
 -\sum_{j<\omega}\int_{|l|\le2\varepsilon}A_j^h\,d^\circ l.
\]
Each integral is absolutely convergent and bounded by
\(C|\kappa|^\omega\Lambda\).
Rescaling, changing signs, and rotating \(l\) prove the
homogeneity, parity, and covariance assertions.
The formula is Borel and multilinear.
For two centers, continuity follows by isolating each
singularity with a fixed smooth partition, translating its
center to zero, and using the integrable majorant
\(C|l|^{s_i}\). The outer remainder has the fixed integrable
majorant \(C|l|^{-4}\), and the subtracted terms are polynomials.

To compare with the cut off homogeneous integral, put
\(X(l,\kappa)=\prod_i\chi(\epsilon_il+\lambda_i(\kappa))\)
and \(\chi_*(l)=\chi(l)^m\).
For small \(\kappa\), \(X-\chi_*\) vanishes near zero
and outside a fixed ball. Its integral against \(A^h\)
therefore has an ordinary Taylor expansion.
For the integral with \(\chi_*\), substitute the preceding
expansion outside \(2\varepsilon\).
The term of degree \(j=\omega\) integrates to zero:
\(A_\omega^h\) is odd in \(l\), whereas the cutoff
and domain are even. The lower terms supply a polynomial;
the omitted outer remainder is \(O(|\kappa|^{\omega+1})\).
Consequently
\(\int XA^h=Q^{(0)}+I^h+O(|\kappa|^{\omega+1})\).

Finally expand every
\(\sigma_i=\chi\sigma_i^h+\sigma_i^\flat\).
Each term containing a remainder has total order at least
\(\omega+1\); the crude Taylor estimate applies to it.
Keeping its polynomial through degree \(\omega\) gives
the stated error and \(Q\). If \(\omega\ge1\), the
constant terms add to the integral at zero.

For uniqueness compare two proposed expansions along
\(t\kappa\), \(t\downarrow0\), on an open cone avoiding
collisions. Successive lower powers of \(t\) identify the
polynomial through degree \(\omega-1\).
At the final degree its polynomial term has parity
\((-1)^\omega\), and the homogeneous term has the opposite
parity. Comparing \(\kappa\) and \(-\kappa\) separates them.
A polynomial vanishing on an open set vanishes identically.
This also proves independence of \(c_\lambda\) and that
replacing \(I(\kappa)\) by \(I(-\kappa)\) replaces its
leading data by the corresponding reflected data.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Differences of a leading term]\label{IV-73-45}
Suppose \(n>0\), and for every multi-index \(\gamma\),
\[
 \nabla^\gamma f(x)=H_\gamma(x)
       +O(|x|^{-n-|\gamma|-1}\lg|x|)
\]
for large lattice \(x\), where \(H_\gamma\) is continuous
off zero and homogeneous of degree \(-n-|\gamma|\).
Then \(H_0\) is smooth, \(\partial^\gamma H_0=H_\gamma\),
and
\[
 \nabla^\gamma(f-H_0)(x)
                 =O(|x|^{-n-|\gamma|-1}\lg|x|).
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Fix a segment \(y+[0,t]e_\mu\) away from zero.
Put \(x_R=\lfloor Ry\rfloor\) and \(N_R=\lfloor Rt\rfloor\).
The telescoping identity
\[
 \nabla^\gamma f(x_R+N_Re_\mu)-\nabla^\gamma f(x_R)
       =\sum_{j<N_R}\nabla^{\gamma+e_\mu}f(x_R+je_\mu)
\]
multiplied by \(R^{n+|\gamma|}\) has, as \(R\to\infty\),
the limit
\[
 H_\gamma(y+te_\mu)-H_\gamma(y)
                =\int_0^tH_{\gamma+e_\mu}(y+se_\mu)\,ds.
\]
The summed remainder is \(O(R^{-1}\lg R)\);
the principal sum is a Riemann sum on a compact set.
The identity also holds for negative small \(t\).
It proves the derivative relation and hence smoothness.
Taylor's formula compares the continuous derivatives and
finite differences of \(H_0\) with error
\(O(|x|^{-n-|\gamma|-1})\), proving the last assertion.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Convolutions and bubbles]\label{IV-73-46}
Write \((X*Y)(u)=\sum_zX(z)Y(u-z)\).
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item Suppose \(X,Y\) have integrable Fourier symbols with
\[
 |\widehat X(k)|\le c|k|^{a_X}\lg|k|,\qquad
 |\nabla^\gamma X(x)|\le c\langle x\rangle^{-n_X-|\gamma|}
                                                    \quad(|\gamma|\le10),
\]
and the analogous bounds for \(Y\), where
\(-3<a_X,a_Y<3\), \(n_X,n_Y\ge0\), and \(n_X+n_Y>3\).
Then the convolution converges absolutely and, for \(r=|u|\ge1\),
\[
 |(X*Y)(u)|\le
 C(r^{-a_X-n_Y}+r^{-a_Y-n_X}+r^{3-n_X-n_Y})\lg r.
\]
\item If \(X\in\mathfrak K(n_X)\), \(Y\in\mathfrak K(n_Y)\),
\(n_X,n_Y\le4\), and \(n_X+n_Y\ge5\), then
\[
 X*Y\in\mathfrak K(n_X+n_Y-3).
\]
Its symbol is \(\widehat X\widehat Y\), its leading symbol
is \(\widehat X^h\widehat Y^h\), and its leading kernel
depends bilinearly and rotation covariantly only on the
two sets of leading data.
\item Let \(K_a,K_b\) be elementary lines of degrees
\(n_a,n_b\in\{1,2,3\}\). The product \(X=K_aK_b\)
has symbol
\[
 I(k)=\int\sigma_a(k-l)\sigma_b(l)\,d^\circ l.
\]
Let \(Q,I^h\) be its data in \cref{IV-73-42}, and let
\(q\) have symbol
\[
 \widetilde Q(k)=Q(0)+\sum_\mu\partial_\mu Q(0)\sin k_\mu.
\]
Then \(q\) is supported on \(0,\pm e_\mu\), and, for
\(n=n_a+n_b\),
\[
 |\nabla^\gamma X(x)|\le C_\gamma\langle x\rangle^{-n-|\gamma|},
 \qquad |I-\widetilde Q|(k)\le C|k|^{\min\{n-3,2\}}.
\]
If \(n\le4\), then \(X-q\in\mathfrak K(n)\), with
leading data \((I^h,K_a^hK_b^h)\).
\item In \(\mathfrak K(n)\), \(n\le6\), the leading
kernel is determined linearly by the leading symbol.
In particular a zero leading symbol gives a zero leading kernel.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For the first two assertions split the convolution into
neighborhoods of its two endpoints and their complement.
Choose a smooth radial \(\theta\), equal to one on
\([0,1/2]\) and zero on \([1,\infty)\), and put
\[
 \theta_1(z)=\theta(4|z|/r),\qquad
 \theta_2(z)=\theta(4|u-z|/r).
\]
Their supports are disjoint. The first endpoint sum is
\[
 T_1=\int\widehat X(k)\check g_1(-k)\,d^\circ k,
       \qquad g_1(z)=\theta_1(z)Y(u-z).
\]
The other has \(X,Y\) interchanged.
The discrete Leibniz rule gives
\(\|g_1\|_{(r)}\le Cr^{-n_Y}\).
The ten additional differences cause only bounded shifts:
on their stencils \(\langle u-z\rangle\ge r/40\).
Thus \cref{IV-73-41} bounds the endpoint sums by the
first two terms in (i).
Away from both endpoints the product is bounded by
\(C(r+|z|)^{-n_X-n_Y}\).
The scalar sum in \cref{IV-73-40} gives its third term.
It also proves absolute convergence and covers bounded \(r\).

For (ii), \(X,Y\in\ell^2\), so Plancherel identifies the
symbol as the integrable product \(\widehat X\widehat Y\).
Multiplying their symbol expansions proves the required
leading-symbol estimate. Put \(n=n_X+n_Y-3\).
For large \(r\), \(\hat u=u/r\), define
\[
 G_1(z)=\theta(4|z|)Y^h(\hat u-z),\qquad
 G_2(z)=\theta(4|z|)X^h(\hat u-z).
\]
Their \(C^{10}\) norms are bounded uniformly in \(\hat u\).
The defining estimates of \(\mathfrak K\) give
\[
 \|g_1-r^{-n_Y}G_1(\cdot/r)\|_{(r)}
                  \le Cr^{-n_Y-1}\lg r,
\]
and likewise for \(g_2\). Apply the final assertion of
\cref{IV-73-41} at symbol orders \(n_X-3,n_Y-3\),
which lie in \([-1,1]\).
In the middle sum replace both kernels by their leading
parts; the error is
\[
 C\sum_z(r+|z|)^{-n_X-n_Y-1}\lg(r+|z|)
                                      \le Cr^{-n-1}\lg r.
\]
The resulting smooth function vanishes near both singular
points. The sum-to-integral estimate
\cref{lem:pure-riemann-error} costs \(O(r^{-n-1})\).
Hence \(X*Y=H_0+O(r^{-n-1}\lg r)\), where
\begin{align*}
 H_0(u)=r^{-n}\biggl[&
 \int\widehat X^h(k)\widehat G_1(-k)\,d^\circ k
 +\int\widehat Y^h(k)\widehat G_2(-k)\,d^\circ k\\
 &+\int
 (1-\theta(4|z|)-\theta(4|\hat u-z|))
                   X^h(z)Y^h(\hat u-z)\,dz\biggr].
\end{align*}
The endpoint integrals are continuous in \(\hat u\) by
the \(C^{10}\) bound in \cref{IV-73-41}.
The middle integrand is dominated by an integrable power
uniformly in \(\hat u\).
Thus \(H_0\) is continuous and homogeneous of degree \(-n\).
The formula proves bilinearity and rotation covariance.

For derivatives, write
\(\nabla^\gamma(X*Y)=X*(\nabla^\gamma Y)\)
and make the same split, taking \(r\ge200+8|\gamma|\).
At the first endpoint replace the smooth factor by
\[
 \theta(4|z|)(\partial^\gamma Y^h)(\hat u-z).
\]
At the second endpoint move all differences onto
\(\theta_2X\) by summation by parts; its rescaled leading
factor is
\[
 \left.
 \partial_y^\gamma[\theta(4|\hat u-y|)X^h(y)]
                                  \right|_{y=\hat u-z}.
\]
In the middle region use \(X^h\partial^\gamma Y^h\).
The same estimates give a continuous homogeneous
\(H_\gamma\) of degree \(-n-|\gamma|\), with remainder
\(O(r^{-n-|\gamma|-1}\lg r)\).
All differentiated kernels are evaluated away from zero
on the indicated stencils. \Cref{IV-73-45} identifies
these functions with the derivatives of \(H_0\).
Enlarging constants on the finitely many remaining lattice
points proves the full \(\mathfrak K(n)\) estimate.

For (iii), Fourier multiplication gives the displayed
one-loop symbol. The maps in \cref{IV-73-42} are
\((l,k)\mapsto(k-l,l)\), with \(c_\lambda=1\),
\(\Lambda=1\), and \(\omega=n-3\).
The discrete Leibniz rule gives the kernel bounds.
Near zero use
\[
 I-\widetilde Q=(Q-\widetilde Q)+I^h
                                      +O(|k|^{n-2}\lg|k|).
\]
Here \(Q-\widetilde Q=O(|k|^2)\), and even
\(O(|k|^3)\) if \(n\le4\).
Away from zero the two integrable singularities are
separated, so \(I\) is bounded.
For \(n\le4\), these are the symbol conditions of
\(\mathfrak K(n)\). The kernel conditions follow by
expanding
\[
 K_aK_b-K_a^hK_b^h
       =(K_a-K_a^h)K_b+K_a^h(K_b-K_b^h)
\]
and using \cref{lem:pure-homogeneous-kernels};
the finitely supported \(q\) changes only finitely many
points in any fixed difference stencil.

Finally suppose \(\sigma^h=0\), and choose
\(G\in C_c^\infty(\{1/2<|x|<1\})\).
The symbol bound and \cref{IV-73-41} give
\[
 \sum_xK(x)G(x/R)=O(R^{2-n}\lg R).
\]
The kernel bound and \cref{lem:pure-riemann-error} give
the same sum as
\[
 R^{3-n}\int K^h(x)G(x)\,dx+O(R^{2-n}\lg R).
\]
Divide by \(R^{3-n}\) and let \(R\to\infty\).
The integral vanishes for every such \(G\), hence \(K^h=0\)
by continuity and homogeneity. Applying this to differences
proves the last assertion.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[The kite graph]\label{IV-73-47}
Let $K_1,\dots,K_5$ be elementary lines with symbols $\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_5$ and degrees $n_1,\dots,n_5$, where
\[
n_1,n_2,n_4,n_5\in\{2,3\},\quad n_3\in\{1,2,3\},\quad n_1+n_2+n_3\le7,\quad n_3+n_4+n_5\le7 ,
\]
and put $\varDelta:=\sum_{i=1}^5n_i-6$. For $u\in\mathbb Z^3$ let $r:=|u|$ and
\[
\mathsf T(u):=\sum_{z,w\in\mathbb Z^3}K_1(z)\,K_2(w)\,K_3(w-z)\,K_4(u-z)\,K_5(u-w).
\]
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] There is a constant $C$, depending on $n_1,\dots,n_5$ only, such that for every $u\in\mathbb Z^3$
\[
\sum_{z,w\in\mathbb Z^3}\langle z\rangle^{-n_1}\langle w\rangle^{-n_2}\langle w-z\rangle^{-n_3}\langle u-z\rangle^{-n_4}\langle u-w\rangle^{-n_5}\le C .
\]
In particular the series defining $\mathsf T(u)$ converges absolutely.
\item[(ii)] For $\kappa=(\kappa_1,\kappa_2)\in\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R^3$ put
\[
\begin{aligned}
\hat{\mathsf T}_{\mathsf p}(\kappa_1,\kappa_2)&:=\int_{\mathbb T}\sigma_1(\kappa_1+l)\,\sigma_2(\kappa_2-l)\,\sigma_3(l)\,d^\circ l,\\
\hat{\mathsf T}_{\mathsf q}(\kappa_1,\kappa_2)&:=\int_{\mathbb T}\sigma_4(\kappa_1-l)\,\sigma_5(\kappa_2+l)\,\sigma_3(l)\,d^\circ l .
\end{aligned}
\]
Both are functions $\mathsf I$ of the kind treated in \cref{IV-73-42}, with $\mathsf m=3$ and with data satisfying the hypotheses of that lemma; their numbers $\omega$ are
\[
\omega_{\mathsf p}:=n_1+n_2+n_3-6\qquad\text{and}\qquad\omega_{\mathsf q}:=n_3+n_4+n_5-6 ,
\]
respectively, and both lie in $\{-1,0,1\}$. For every function $g$ of finite support on $\mathbb Z^6$
\begin{equation}\label{IV-73-48}
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{z,w}K_1(z)\,K_2(w)\,K_3(w-z)\,g(z,w)&=\int_{\mathbb T^2}\hat{\mathsf T}_{\mathsf p}(\kappa)\,\check g(-\kappa)\,d^\circ\kappa,\\
\sum_{z,w}K_4(z)\,K_5(w)\,K_3(z-w)\,g(z,w)&=\int_{\mathbb T^2}\hat{\mathsf T}_{\mathsf q}(\kappa)\,\check g(-\kappa)\,d^\circ\kappa .
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
\item[(iii)] Let $\mathsf Q_{\mathsf p}$ and $\mathsf Q_{\mathsf q}$ be the polynomials of $\hat{\mathsf T}_{\mathsf p}$ and of $\hat{\mathsf T}_{\mathsf q}$ in the sense of \cref{IV-73-42}, let
\[
\tilde{\mathsf Q}_\bullet(\kappa):=\mathsf Q_\bullet(0)+\sum_{j=1}^6\partial_j\mathsf Q_\bullet(0)\,\sin\kappa_j\qquad(\bullet\in\{\mathsf p,\mathsf q\}),
\]
and let $\mathsf q_{\mathsf p},\mathsf q_{\mathsf q}$ be the kernels on $\mathbb Z^6$ with the symbols $\tilde{\mathsf Q}_{\mathsf p},\tilde{\mathsf Q}_{\mathsf q}$, that is, $\mathsf q_\bullet(\zeta)=\int_{\mathbb T^2}e^{i\kappa\cdot\zeta}\,\tilde{\mathsf Q}_\bullet(\kappa)\,d^\circ\kappa$; they vanish off $\{0,\pm e_1,\dots,\pm e_6\}$. There are constants $r_0$ and $C$, depending on $\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_5$ only, and a function $\mathsf U\in C^1(\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\})$, homogeneous of degree $-\varDelta$, such that for every $u$ with $r\ge r_0$
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Bigl|\mathsf T(u)&-\sum_{z,w}\mathsf q_{\mathsf p}(z,w)\,K_4(u-z)\,K_5(u-w)\\
&-\sum_{z,w}\mathsf q_{\mathsf q}(z,w)\,K_1(u-z)\,K_2(u-w)-\mathsf U(u)\Bigr|\le C\,r^{-\varDelta-1}\lg r .
\end{aligned}
\]
\item[(iv)] The function $\mathsf U$ depends only on the leading parts $\sigma_1^h,\dots,\sigma_5^h$, and it is linear in each of them. If every $\sigma_i^h$ is replaced by $\sigma_i^h\circ O^{-1}$, with one and the same rotation $O$, then $\mathsf U$ is replaced by $\mathsf U\circ O^{-1}$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
\emph{Step 1: convergence.} The symbol $\sigma_i$ of $K_i$ is a line symbol of degree $s_i:=n_i-3\ge-2>-3$. \cref{IV-73-39}, applied with $s=s_i$ and $\gamma=0$, therefore gives $|K_i(y)|\le C\langle y\rangle^{-n_i}$ for all $y\in\mathbb Z^3$, and the absolute convergence of the series for $\mathsf T(u)$ follows from the bound in (i). To prove that bound we estimate $\langle w-z\rangle^{-n_3}\le1$; what remains factorises into
\[
\Bigl(\sum_{z}\langle z\rangle^{-n_1}\langle u-z\rangle^{-n_4}\Bigr)\Bigl(\sum_{w}\langle w\rangle^{-n_2}\langle u-w\rangle^{-n_5}\Bigr).
\]
\cref{IV-73-40} applies to the first factor with $(a,a',x)=(n_1,n_4,u)$, since $a,a'\ge2$ and $a+a'\ge4>3$; it bounds that factor by $C\langle u\rangle^{-\min\{n_1,n_4,n_1+n_4-3\}}\lg\langle u\rangle\le C\langle u\rangle^{-1}\lg\langle u\rangle\le C$, because $t^{-1}\lg t=t^{-1}(1+\log t)\le1$ for $t\ge1$. The second factor is bounded in the same way, with $(n_2,n_5)$ in place of $(n_1,n_4)$.

\emph{Step 2: the two one-loop functions.} For $\hat{\mathsf T}_{\mathsf p}$ we take $\mathsf m=3$, $D=6$, the line symbols $\sigma_1,\sigma_2,\sigma_3$ of degrees $s_1,s_2,s_3$, the signs $(\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2,\epsilon_3)=(1,-1,1)$ and the linear maps $\lambda_1(\kappa)=\kappa_1$, $\lambda_2(\kappa)=\kappa_2$, $\lambda_3(\kappa)=0$. The integrand of $\hat{\mathsf T}_{\mathsf p}$ is then $\prod_i\sigma_i(\epsilon_il+\lambda_i(\kappa))$, and $(l_1,l_2,l_3)(\kappa)=(-\kappa_1,\kappa_2,0)$. Up to signs, the pairwise differences of the $l_i(\kappa)$ are $\kappa_1+\kappa_2$, $\kappa_1$ and $\kappa_2$. Hence $\max_i|l_i(\kappa)|\le|\kappa|\le2|\kappa|$ and $|\kappa|\le\sqrt2\max\{|\kappa_1|,|\kappa_2|\}\le2\max_{i<j}|l_i(\kappa)-l_j(\kappa)|$, so that the condition on the $l_i$ holds with $c_\lambda=2$; the three maps $l_i$ are pairwise different. The map $(l,\kappa_1,\kappa_2)\mapsto(\kappa_1+l,\kappa_2-l,l)$ of $(\mathbb R^3)^3$ acts on the three components in $\mathbb R^3$ by the integer matrix
\[
\begin{pmatrix}1&1&0\\-1&0&1\\1&0&0\end{pmatrix},
\]
whose determinant is $1$. Since $n_1,n_2\ge2$ and $n_3\ge1$, we have $s_1,s_2\ge-1$ and $s_3\ge-2$, hence $s_i+s_j\ge-3$ for $i\ne j$. Finally $\omega=3+s_1+s_2+s_3=n_1+n_2+n_3-6=\omega_{\mathsf p}$, and this number lies between $2+2+1-6=-1$ and $7-6=1$. For $\hat{\mathsf T}_{\mathsf q}$ the line symbols are $\sigma_4,\sigma_5,\sigma_3$, the signs are $(-1,1,1)$ and the maps are $\kappa\mapsto\kappa_1$, $\kappa\mapsto\kappa_2$, $\kappa\mapsto0$, so that $(l_1,l_2,l_3)(\kappa)=(\kappa_1,-\kappa_2,0)$; the matrix of $(l,\kappa_1,\kappa_2)\mapsto(\kappa_1-l,\kappa_2+l,l)$ is $\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}-1&1&0\\1&0&1\\1&0&0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$, again of determinant $1$, and the remaining conditions follow as before, now with $n_3+n_4+n_5\le7$.

\emph{Step 3: proof of \eqref{IV-73-48}.} We insert $K_1(z)=\int_{\mathbb T}e^{ik_1\cdot z}\sigma_1(k_1)\,d^\circ k_1$, $K_2(w)=\int_{\mathbb T}e^{ik_2\cdot w}\sigma_2(k_2)\,d^\circ k_2$ and $K_3(w-z)=\int_{\mathbb T}e^{il\cdot(w-z)}\sigma_3(l)\,d^\circ l$. The sum over $(z,w)$ is finite and the three symbols are integrable, so Fubini's theorem gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\sum_{z,w}K_1(z)\,K_2(w)\,K_3(w-z)\,g(z,w)\\
&\qquad=\iiint\sigma_1(k_1)\,\sigma_2(k_2)\,\sigma_3(l)\,\check g\bigl(-(k_1-l),-(k_2+l)\bigr)\,d^\circ k_1\,d^\circ k_2\,d^\circ l ,
\end{aligned}
\]
since $\sum_{z,w}g(z,w)\,e^{i(k_1-l)\cdot z+i(k_2+l)\cdot w}=\check g\bigl(-(k_1-l),-(k_2+l)\bigr)$. For fixed $l$ we substitute $k_1=\kappa_1+l$ and $k_2=\kappa_2-l$, which are translations of $\mathbb T$, and we then carry out the integration over $l$ first; this is the first identity. The function $y\mapsto K_3(-y)$ is the kernel with the symbol $l\mapsto\sigma_3(-l)$, because $K_3(-y)=\int e^{-il\cdot y}\sigma_3(l)\,d^\circ l=\int e^{il\cdot y}\sigma_3(-l)\,d^\circ l$. The derivation of the first identity used only the integrability of the three symbols. Applied to $K_4$, $K_5$ and $K_3(-\cdot)$ in place of $K_1$, $K_2$ and $K_3$, it represents $\sum_{z,w}K_4(z)K_5(w)K_3(z-w)g(z,w)$ by the function $\kappa\mapsto\int_{\mathbb T}\sigma_4(\kappa_1+l)\,\sigma_5(\kappa_2-l)\,\sigma_3(-l)\,d^\circ l$, which becomes $\hat{\mathsf T}_{\mathsf q}(\kappa)$ after the substitution $l\to-l$.

\emph{Step 4: short and long lines.} Let $\varepsilon:=\frac18$ and, for $r>0$, $\theta^r(y):=\theta(|y|/\varepsilon r)$ and $\bar\theta^r:=1-\theta^r$, as functions on $\mathbb R^3$ and, by restriction, on $\mathbb Z^3$. By the choice of \(\theta\), $\theta^r(y)=1$ for $|y|\le\frac12\varepsilon r$ and $\theta^r(y)=0$ for $|y|\ge\varepsilon r$. For the arguments of the five lines we write
\[
(y_1,y_2,y_3,y_4,y_5):=(z,\,w,\,w-z,\,u-z,\,u-w).
\]
For $\mathsf S\subset\{1,\dots,5\}$ let $\mathsf T_{\mathsf S}(u)$ be the series defining $\mathsf T(u)$, with the additional factor $\prod_{i\in\mathsf S}\theta^r(y_i)\allowbreak\prod_{i\notin\mathsf S}\bar\theta^r(y_i)$ in each term; the lines with an index in $\mathsf S$ are called short, the others long. These series converge absolutely by (i), the additional factors taking values in $[0,1]$, and multiplying out $\prod_{i=1}^5\bigl(\theta^r(y_i)+\bar\theta^r(y_i)\bigr)=1$ we obtain $\mathsf T=\sum_{\mathsf S}\mathsf T_{\mathsf S}$.

The arguments satisfy
\[
u=y_1+y_4=y_2+y_5=y_1+y_3+y_5=y_2-y_3+y_4 .
\]
If $\mathsf S$ contains one of the sets $\{1,4\}$, $\{2,5\}$, $\{1,3,5\}$, $\{2,3,4\}$, then a non-vanishing term of $\mathsf T_{\mathsf S}(u)$ requires $|y_i|<\varepsilon r$ for the indices $i$ of that set, hence $r=|u|<3\varepsilon r<r$; thus $\mathsf T_{\mathsf S}=0$. There are three possibilities for $\mathsf S\cap\{1,4\}$, three for $\mathsf S\cap\{2,5\}$ and two for $\mathsf S\cap\{3\}$; of the resulting $3\cdot3\cdot2=18$ sets, two, namely $\{1,3,5\}$ and $\{2,3,4\}$, contain one of the forbidden triples, and $16$ sets remain.

The substitutions $(z,w)\to(w,z)$ and $(z,w)\to(u-z,u-w)$ are bijections of $\mathbb Z^6$; they carry $(y_1,\dots,y_5)$ into $(y_2,y_1,-y_3,y_5,y_4)$ and into $(y_4,y_5,-y_3,y_1,y_2)$, respectively. As $\theta^r$ is even, they show that $\mathsf T_{\mathsf S}$, computed for the lines $(K_1,K_2,K_3,K_4,K_5)$, equals $\mathsf T_{\mathsf S'}$ computed for $(K_2,K_1,\allowbreak K_3(-\cdot),K_5,K_4)$, where $\mathsf S'$ is the image of $\mathsf S$ under the permutation $(12)(45)$, and that it equals $\mathsf T_{\mathsf S''}$ computed for $(K_4,K_5,\allowbreak K_3(-\cdot),K_1,K_2)$, where $\mathsf S''$ is the image of $\mathsf S$ under $(14)(25)$. The new families satisfy the hypotheses of the proposition: $K_3(-\cdot)$ is an elementary line of degree $n_3$, its symbol $\sigma_3(-k)$ being a line symbol with leading part $\sigma_3^h(-k)$ (the cut-off $\chi$ is even), and the conditions on the degrees are invariant under both permutations. Under the group generated by $(12)(45)$ and $(14)(25)$ the sixteen sets fall into seven classes: the set $\emptyset$ alone; the sets $\{1\},\{2\},\{4\},\{5\}$; the set $\{3\}$ alone; the sets $\{1,2\},\{4,5\}$; the sets $\{1,5\},\{2,4\}$; the sets $\{1,3\},\{2,3\},\{3,4\},\{3,5\}$; and the sets $\{1,2,3\},\{3,4,5\}$. We choose the representatives
\[
\emptyset,\quad\{1\},\quad\{3\},\quad\{1,2\},\quad\{1,5\},\quad\{1,3\},\quad\{1,2,3\}.
\]
It therefore suffices to expand $\mathsf T_{\mathsf S}$ for these seven sets, for an arbitrary family of lines obeying the hypotheses; for each of the remaining nine sets we use the expansion of its representative, computed for the transformed family.

\emph{Step 5: long factors.} Let $L_i:=\bar\theta^rK_i$ on $\mathbb Z^3$, let $K_i^h:=\mathcal F^{-1}_{\ne0}\sigma_i^h$, which by \cref{lem:pure-homogeneous-kernels} is smooth on $\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$ and homogeneous of degree $-3-s_i=-n_i$, and let $L_i^h:=\bar\theta^rK_i^h$, extended by $0$ at the origin. Since $\bar\theta^r$ vanishes on $\{|y|\le\frac12\varepsilon r\}$, the function $L_i^h$ is smooth on $\mathbb R^3$, and by homogeneity $L_i^h(y)=r^{-n_i}\,\bar\theta^1(y/r)\,K_i^h(y/r)$. We claim that there are $r_0$ and $C$ such that for $r\ge r_0$, $i=1,\dots,5$ and $|\gamma|\le10$
\begin{equation}\label{IV-73-49}
\begin{gathered}
|\nabla^\gamma L_i(y)|+|\partial^\gamma L_i^h(y)|\le C\,(r+|y|)^{-n_i-|\gamma|},\\
|\nabla^\gamma(L_i-L_i^h)(y)|\le C\,(r+|y|)^{-n_i-1-|\gamma|};
\end{gathered}
\end{equation}
here $y\in\mathbb Z^3$, except in the term $\partial^\gamma L_i^h(y)$, where $y\in\mathbb R^3$. Indeed, \cref{IV-73-39} gives $|\nabla^\gamma K_i(x)|\le C\langle x\rangle^{-n_i-|\gamma|}$, and \cref{lem:pure-homogeneous-kernels} gives $|\nabla^\gamma(K_i-K_i^h)(x)|\le C|x|^{-n_i-1-|\gamma|}$ for $|x|\ge|\gamma|+1$. The derivatives of order $\gamma$ of $K_i^h$ are homogeneous of degree $-n_i-|\gamma|$, hence bounded by $C|x|^{-n_i-|\gamma|}$; the derivatives of order $j\ge1$ of $\bar\theta^r$ are bounded by $Cr^{-j}$ and vanish outside $\{\frac12\varepsilon r\le|y|\le\varepsilon r\}$. The discrete Leibniz rule $\nabla_j(fg)=(\nabla_jf)\,g(\cdot+e_j)+f\,\nabla_jg$ distributes $\nabla^\gamma$ over the two factors, the arguments being shifted by at most $|\gamma|\le10$. Only points $y'$ with $|y'|\ge\frac12\varepsilon r$ contribute, and at such points, for $r\ge r_0$ with $r_0$ large enough, we have $|y'|\ge|\gamma|+1$ and $r+|y|\le C|y'|$ whenever $|y-y'|\le10$. These facts together give \eqref{IV-73-49}.

\emph{Step 6: the scheme for $\mathsf S\ne\emptyset$.} For each of the six non-empty representatives we write
\[
\mathsf T_{\mathsf S}(u)=\sum_{\zeta\in\mathbb Z^D}\mathsf T^{\mathsf S}(\zeta)\,g_{\mathsf S}(\zeta),
\]
where the kernel $\mathsf T^{\mathsf S}$ on $\mathbb Z^D$ collects the short lines, and we let $s$ be the degree of the leading part $\hat{\mathsf T}^{\mathsf S,h}$ of the symbol of $\mathsf T^{\mathsf S}$. The data are as follows.
\begin{itemize}
\item $\mathsf S=\{1\}$, $D=3$, $\zeta=z$: $\mathsf T^{\mathsf S}(z)=K_1(z)$, with symbol $\sigma_1(\kappa)$ and $s=n_1-3$; and
$g_{\mathsf S}(z)=\theta^r(z)\,L_4(u-z)\sum_wL_2(w)\,L_3(w-z)\,L_5(u-w)$.
\item $\mathsf S=\{3\}$, $D=3$, $\zeta=y$: $\mathsf T^{\mathsf S}(y)=K_3(y)$, with symbol $\sigma_3(\kappa)$ and $s=n_3-3$; and
$g_{\mathsf S}(y)=\theta^r(y)\sum_zL_1(z)\,L_2(z+y)\,L_4(u-z)\,L_5(u-z-y)$.
\item $\mathsf S=\{1,2\}$, $D=6$, $\zeta=(z,w)$: $\mathsf T^{\mathsf S}(z,w)=K_1(z)K_2(w)$, with symbol $\sigma_1(\kappa_1)\sigma_2(\kappa_2)$ and $s=n_1+n_2-6$; and
$g_{\mathsf S}(z,w)=\theta^r(z)\,\theta^r(w)\,L_3(w-z)\,L_4(u-z)\,L_5(u-w)$.
\item $\mathsf S=\{1,5\}$, $D=6$, $\zeta=(z,w')$: $\mathsf T^{\mathsf S}(z,w')=K_1(z)K_5(w')$, with symbol $\sigma_1(\kappa_1)\sigma_5(\kappa_2)$ and $s=n_1+n_5-6$; and
$g_{\mathsf S}(z,w')=\theta^r(z)\,\theta^r(w')\,L_2(u-w')\,L_3(u-w'-z)\,L_4(u-z)$.
\item $\mathsf S=\{1,3\}$, $D=6$, $\zeta=(z,y)$: $\mathsf T^{\mathsf S}(z,y)=K_1(z)K_3(y)$, with symbol $\sigma_1(\kappa_1)\sigma_3(\kappa_2)$ and $s=n_1+n_3-6$; and
$g_{\mathsf S}(z,y)=\theta^r(z)\,\theta^r(y)\,L_2(z+y)\,L_4(u-z)\,L_5(u-z-y)$.
\item $\mathsf S=\{1,2,3\}$, $D=6$, $\zeta=(z,w)$: $\mathsf T^{\mathsf S}(z,w)=K_1(z)K_2(w)K_3(w-z)$, with symbol $\hat{\mathsf T}_{\mathsf p}(\kappa)$ (by \eqref{IV-73-48}, applied to $g=\delta_\zeta$) and $s=\omega_{\mathsf p}$; and
$g_{\mathsf S}(z,w)=\theta^r(z)\,\theta^r(w)\,\theta^r(w-z)\,L_4(u-z)\,L_5(u-w)$.
\end{itemize}
In the cases $\{1,5\}$ and $\{1,3\}$ we have substituted $w=u-w'$, resp.\ $w=z+y$, in the sum over $w$; in the cases $\{1\}$ and $\{3\}$ the inner sums converge absolutely by Step~1. Each $g_{\mathsf S}$ vanishes off $\{|\zeta|\le r\}$, since the short factors confine every component of $\zeta$ to $\{|\cdot|<\varepsilon r\}$ and $\sqrt2\,\varepsilon<1$.

Let $g^h_{\mathsf S}$ be the function on $\mathbb R^D$ obtained from $g_{\mathsf S}$ by replacing every $L_i$ by $L_i^h$ and, in the cases $\{1\}$ and $\{3\}$, the inner sum by the integral over $\mathbb R^3$. Since $\theta^r(y)=\theta^1(y/r)$ and $L_i^h(y)=r^{-n_i}(\bar\theta^1K_i^h)(y/r)$, the substitution of $r$ times the variable in the inner integrals gives
\[
g^h_{\mathsf S}(\zeta)=r^{-a}\,G_{\mathsf S}(\zeta/r),\qquad\text{where}\quad a:=\begin{cases}\sum_{i\notin\mathsf S}n_i&\text{if }D=6,\\[2pt]\sum_{i\notin\mathsf S}n_i-3&\text{if }\mathsf S=\{1\},\{3\},\end{cases}
\]
so that $a+s=\varDelta$ in all six cases. Here $G_{\mathsf S}$ is the function $g^h_{\mathsf S}$ computed with $r=1$ and with $\hat u:=u/r$ in place of $u$; it belongs to $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^D)$ and has its support in $\{|\zeta|\le1\}$. We claim
\begin{equation}\label{IV-73-50}
\|g_{\mathsf S}-g^h_{\mathsf S}\|_{(r)}\le C\,r^{-a-1}\qquad(r\ge r_0),
\end{equation}
where $g^h_{\mathsf S}$ is restricted to $\mathbb Z^D$ and $\|\cdot\|_{(r)}$ is the norm used in \cref{IV-73-41}.

In the cases $\{1,2\}$, $\{1,5\}$, $\{1,3\}$, $\{1,2,3\}$ the functions $g_{\mathsf S}$ and $g^h_{\mathsf S}$ are products of the same short factors with the long factors $L_i$, resp.\ $L_i^h$, $i\notin\mathsf S$, evaluated at linear functions of $\zeta$. We write the difference as a sum of terms in each of which one factor $L_i$ has been replaced by $L_i-L_i^h$, and we distribute the differences $\nabla^\gamma$, $|\gamma|\le10$, by the Leibniz rule. By \eqref{IV-73-49} a difference falling on a long factor gains a factor $C(r+|y_i|)^{-1}\le Cr^{-1}$, a difference falling on a short factor gains $Cr^{-1}$, and the factor $L_i-L_i^h$ gains $(r+|y_i|)^{-1}\le r^{-1}$ in comparison with $L_i$; moreover $\prod_{i\notin\mathsf S}(r+|y_i|)^{-n_i}\le r^{-a}$. This gives $r^{|\gamma|}|\nabla^\gamma(g_{\mathsf S}-g^h_{\mathsf S})|\le Cr^{-a-1}$.

In the case $\mathsf S=\{1\}$ let
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathsf w(z)&:=\sum_wL_2(w)\,L_3(w-z)\,L_5(u-w),\\
\mathsf w^h(z)&:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}L_2^h(w)\,L_3^h(w-z)\,L_5^h(u-w)\,dw .
\end{aligned}
\]
For $|z|\le r$ the differences in $z$ fall on $L_3(w-z)$ only. By \eqref{IV-73-49}, by $r+|u-w|\ge\frac12(r+|w|)$ (second assertion of \cref{IV-73-40}, as $|u|=r$) and by the first assertion of \cref{IV-73-40} with $D=3$, $R=r$ and exponent $n_2+n_5\ge4>3$, we obtain
\[
|\nabla^\gamma\mathsf w(z)|\le Cr^{-n_3-|\gamma|}\sum_w(r+|w|)^{-n_2-n_5}\le Cr^{3-n_2-n_3-n_5-|\gamma|}.
\]
Each replacement of an $L_i$ by $L_i^h$ in $\mathsf w$ costs a factor $Cr^{-1}$, by the second inequality of \eqref{IV-73-49}. The replacement of the sum over $w$ by the integral costs a factor $Cr^{-1}$ as well: we apply \cref{lem:pure-riemann-error}, with $D=3$, to $F(w):=L_2^h(w)\,(\nabla_z^\gamma L_3^h)(w-z)\,L_5^h(u-w)$, whose gradient is bounded by $Cr^{-n_3-|\gamma|-1}(r+|w|)^{-n_2-n_5}$ on each cube $w+[0,1]^3$. Since $g_{\{1\}}(z)=\theta^r(z)L_4(u-z)\mathsf w(z)$, since $|\nabla^\gamma L_4(u-\cdot)|\le Cr^{-n_4-|\gamma|}$ on $\{|z|\le r\}$ by \eqref{IV-73-49}, and since the differences of order $\gamma$ of $\theta^r$ are bounded by $Cr^{-|\gamma|}$, the Leibniz rule gives \eqref{IV-73-50} with $a=n_2+n_3+n_4+n_5-3$.

In the case $\mathsf S=\{3\}$ let $\mathsf w(y):=\sum_zL_1(z)\,L_2(z+y)\,L_4(u-z)\,L_5(u-z-y)$, and let $\mathsf w^h$ be the integral over $\mathbb R^3$ of the corresponding product of the $L_i^h$. For $|y|\le r$ the differences in $y$ fall on $L_2$ and on $L_5$ (and, in $g_{\{3\}}$, on the factor $\theta^r(y)$), each difference gaining a factor $Cr^{-1}$. By \cref{IV-73-40} we have $r+|z+y|\ge\frac12(r+|z|)$, $r+|u-z|\ge\frac12(r+|z|)$, and, with $R=2r\ge|u-y|$, also $r+|u-y-z|\ge\frac14(r+|z|)$; the first assertion of that lemma, with exponent $n_1+n_2+n_4+n_5\ge8$, gives $\sum_z(r+|z|)^{-n_1-n_2-n_4-n_5}\le Cr^{3-n_1-n_2-n_4-n_5}$. Hence $|\nabla^\gamma\mathsf w(y)|\le Cr^{3-n_1-n_2-n_4-n_5-|\gamma|}$, and, as in the case $\{1\}$, the replacements $L_i\to L_i^h$ and the replacement of the sum by the integral (\cref{lem:pure-riemann-error}) cost a factor $Cr^{-1}$ each. This proves \eqref{IV-73-50} in all six cases.

\emph{Step 7: symbols, and the pairing with slowly varying functions.} We verify the hypotheses of \cref{IV-73-41} for $\hat{\mathsf T}$, the symbol of $\mathsf T^{\mathsf S}$, and $\hat{\mathsf T}^h:=\hat{\mathsf T}^{\mathsf S,h}$.
In the cases $\{1\}$ and $\{3\}$ ($D=3$, $i=1$, resp.\ $i=3$, $s=s_i$) we take $c_0=1$. On $\{|\kappa|\le1\}$ we have $\chi=1$, so $\sigma_i-\chi\sigma_i^h\in\mathcal S^{s+1}$ gives $|\sigma_i-\sigma_i^h|\le C|\kappa|^{s+1}$ there; the majorants are $\mathsf H:=C|\kappa|^s\in\mathcal H_s(3)$ for $\sigma_i^h$ and $\mathsf H':=C|\kappa|^{s+1}\in\mathcal H_{s+1}(3)$, which belong to these classes since $s>-3$; the required bound $|\sigma_i-\sigma_i^h|\le\mathsf H'\lg|\kappa|$ holds on $\{|\kappa|\le1\}$, as $\lg|\kappa|\ge1$.
In the cases $\{1,2\}$, $\{1,5\}$, $\{1,3\}$ ($D=6$) the symbol is $\sigma_i(\kappa_1)\sigma_j(\kappa_2)$ with $(i,j)=(1,2),(1,5),(1,3)$, its leading part is $\sigma_i^h(\kappa_1)\sigma_j^h(\kappa_2)$, and $s=s_i+s_j$ with $s_i,s_j>-3$. Then $|\sigma_i^h(\kappa_1)\sigma_j^h(\kappa_2)|\le C|\kappa_1|^{s_i}|\kappa_2|^{s_j}$, a function in $\mathcal H_{s_i+s_j}(6)$, and on $\{|\kappa|\le1\}$
\[
\bigl|\sigma_i(\kappa_1)\sigma_j(\kappa_2)-\sigma_i^h(\kappa_1)\sigma_j^h(\kappa_2)\bigr|\le C\bigl(|\kappa_1|^{s_i+1}|\kappa_2|^{s_j}+|\kappa_1|^{s_i}|\kappa_2|^{s_j+1}\bigr),
\]
a function in $\mathcal H_{s_i+s_j+1}(6)$; here we wrote the difference as $(\sigma_i-\sigma_i^h)\sigma_j+\sigma_i^h(\sigma_j-\sigma_j^h)$ and used $|\sigma_j(\kappa_2)|\le C|\kappa_2|^{s_j}$.
In the case $\{1,2,3\}$ we use \cref{IV-73-42}, whose hypotheses hold by Step~2, with the number $c_0$ given there. By the asymptotic assertion of that lemma, $|\hat{\mathsf T}_{\mathsf p}-\mathsf Q_{\mathsf p}-\mathsf I^h_{\mathsf p}|\le C|\kappa|^{\omega_{\mathsf p}+1}\lg|\kappa|\,\Lambda(\kappa)$ for almost every $\kappa$ with $|\kappa|\le c_0$, where $\mathsf I^h_{\mathsf p}$ is the homogeneous part of $\hat{\mathsf T}_{\mathsf p}$. The polynomial $\mathsf Q_{\mathsf p}$ has degree at most $\omega_{\mathsf p}\le1$, so $\mathsf Q_{\mathsf p}-\tilde{\mathsf Q}_{\mathsf p}=\sum_j\partial_j\mathsf Q_{\mathsf p}(0)(\kappa_j-\sin\kappa_j)=O(|\kappa|^3)$, and $|\kappa|^3\le|\kappa|^{\omega_{\mathsf p}+1}\lg|\kappa|\,\Lambda(\kappa)$ for $|\kappa|\le1$. We therefore take $\hat{\mathsf T}:=\hat{\mathsf T}_{\mathsf p}-\tilde{\mathsf Q}_{\mathsf p}$, which is integrable on $\mathbb T^2$: \cref{IV-73-42} bounds the $L^1$ norm of $\hat{\mathsf T}_{\mathsf p}$ by the product of the $L^1$ norms of $\sigma_1,\sigma_2,\sigma_3$, and $\tilde{\mathsf Q}_{\mathsf p}$ is a trigonometric polynomial. We further take $\hat{\mathsf T}^h:=\mathsf I^h_{\mathsf p}$ and the majorants $\mathsf H:=C|\kappa|^{\omega_{\mathsf p}}\Lambda$ (\cref{IV-73-42}) and $\mathsf H':=C|\kappa|^{\omega_{\mathsf p}+1}\Lambda$. They belong to $\mathcal H_{\omega_{\mathsf p}}(6)$ and to $\mathcal H_{\omega_{\mathsf p}+1}(6)$, respectively, since the same lemma asserts that $|\kappa|^{s}\Lambda(\kappa)$ belongs to $\mathcal H_s(6)$ for every real $s>-6$, and since $\omega_{\mathsf p}\ge-1$.
In all cases $-D<s<8-D$, as \cref{IV-73-41} requires: for $D=3$ we have $s\in\{-2,-1,0\}\subset(-3,2)$, and for $D=6$ we have $s\in\{-3,\dots,1\}\subset(-6,2)$.

Inserting the Fourier integrals of the short lines, we have $\mathsf T_{\mathsf S}(u)=\int_{\mathbb T^{D/3}}\hat{\mathsf T}^{\mathsf S}(\kappa)\,\check g_{\mathsf S}(-\kappa)\,d^\circ\kappa$, where $\hat{\mathsf T}^{\mathsf S}$ is the symbol of $\mathsf T^{\mathsf S}$: for the product kernels this follows from Fubini's theorem as in Step~3, and for $\{1,2,3\}$ it is \eqref{IV-73-48}. We apply \cref{IV-73-41} with $R=r$, $g=g_{\mathsf S}$, which vanishes off $\{|\zeta|\le r\}$, $G=G_{\mathsf S}$, the number $a$ of Step~6, and $A=C$, which is admissible by \eqref{IV-73-50} because $\lg r\ge1$. The norm $\|G_{\mathsf S}\|_{C^{10}}$ is bounded uniformly in $\hat u\in S^2$, by the smoothness in $(\zeta,\hat u)$ established in Step~9 and the compactness of $S^2$. In the first five cases, $\{1\}$, $\{3\}$, $\{1,2\}$, $\{1,5\}$, $\{1,3\}$, we obtain
\[
\mathsf T_{\mathsf S}(u)=\mathsf U_{\mathsf S}(u)+O\bigl(r^{-\varDelta-1}\lg r\bigr),\qquad\mathsf U_{\mathsf S}(u):=r^{-\varDelta}\int_{\mathbb R^D}\hat{\mathsf T}^{\mathsf S,h}(\kappa)\,\hat G_{\mathsf S}(-\kappa)\,d^\circ\kappa ,
\]
because $a+s=\varDelta$. In the case $\{1,2,3\}$, where $\hat{\mathsf T}^{\mathsf S,h}:=\mathsf I^h_{\mathsf p}$, the lemma is applied to $\hat{\mathsf T}_{\mathsf p}-\tilde{\mathsf Q}_{\mathsf p}$, and the remaining term is $\int_{\mathbb T^2}\tilde{\mathsf Q}_{\mathsf p}(\kappa)\check g_{\mathsf S}(-\kappa)\,d^\circ\kappa=\sum_{z,w}\mathsf q_{\mathsf p}(z,w)\,g_{\mathsf S}(z,w)$; thus
\[
\mathsf T_{\{1,2,3\}}(u)=\sum_{z,w}\mathsf q_{\mathsf p}(z,w)\,g_{\{1,2,3\}}(z,w)+\mathsf U_{\{1,2,3\}}(u)+O\bigl(r^{-\varDelta-1}\lg r\bigr).
\]
On the support of $\mathsf q_{\mathsf p}$, that is, for $(z,w)\in\{0,\pm e_1,\dots,\pm e_6\}$, we have $|z|,|w|,|w-z|\le1\le\frac12\varepsilon r$ and $|u-z|,|u-w|\ge r-1\ge\varepsilon r$ as soon as $r\ge r_0\ge16$; hence $g_{\{1,2,3\}}(z,w)=K_4(u-z)K_5(u-w)$ there, which produces the first local term in (iii). The image of $\{1,2,3\}$ under $(z,w)\to(u-z,u-w)$ is $\{3,4,5\}$, and the transformed family $(K_4,K_5,\allowbreak K_3(-\cdot),K_1,K_2)$ has, in place of $\hat{\mathsf T}_{\mathsf p}$, the function $\int_{\mathbb T}\sigma_4(\kappa_1+l)\sigma_5(\kappa_2-l)\sigma_3(-l)\,d^\circ l=\hat{\mathsf T}_{\mathsf q}(\kappa)$; its local kernel is therefore $\mathsf q_{\mathsf q}$, and $\mathsf T_{\{3,4,5\}}$ produces the second local term in (iii).

\emph{Step 8: the case $\mathsf S=\emptyset$.} Here $\mathsf T_\emptyset(u)=\sum_{z,w}\prod_{i=1}^5L_i(y_i)$. By \eqref{IV-73-49} with $\gamma=0$, by $(r+|y_3|)^{-n_3}\le r^{-n_3}$ and by \cref{IV-73-40} (as in Step~6, with $r+|u-z|\ge\frac12(r+|z|)$ and $r+|u-w|\ge\frac12(r+|w|)$),
\[
\sum_{z,w}\prod_{i=1}^5(r+|y_i|)^{-n_i}\le C\,r^{-n_3}\,r^{3-n_1-n_4}\,r^{3-n_2-n_5}=C\,r^{-\varDelta}.
\]
Replacing each $L_i$ by $L_i^h$ costs a factor $Cr^{-1}$, by the second inequality of \eqref{IV-73-49}; replacing the sum over $(z,w)\in\mathbb Z^6$ by the integral over $\mathbb R^6$ costs a factor $Cr^{-1}$ by \cref{lem:pure-riemann-error} with $D=6$, applied to $F(z,w):=\prod_iL_i^h(y_i)$, whose gradient is bounded by $Cr^{-1}\prod_i(r+|y_i|)^{-n_i}$ on each cube of side $1$. Hence $\mathsf T_\emptyset(u)=\mathsf U_\emptyset(u)+O(r^{-\varDelta-1})$ with
\[
\mathsf U_\emptyset(u):=\iint_{\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R^3}\prod_{i=1}^5L_i^h(y_i)\,dz\,dw ,
\]
which, after the substitution $(z,w)=r(z',w')$, is seen to be homogeneous of degree $6-\sum_in_i=-\varDelta$.

\emph{Step 9: the function $\mathsf U$.} Let $\mathsf U$ be the sum of the sixteen functions $\mathsf U_{\mathsf S}$, where for a set $\mathsf S$ which is not a representative, $\mathsf U_{\mathsf S}$ is the function of its representative computed for the transformed family (Step~4). By Steps~4, 7 and~8, the inequality in (iii) holds for $r\ge r_0$. Every $\mathsf U_{\mathsf S}$ is homogeneous of degree $-\varDelta$, and so is $\mathsf U$. We let a vector $v\in\mathbb R^3$ take the place of $\hat u$ in the definition of $G_{\mathsf S}$, and we write $G_{\mathsf S}(\zeta;v)$. In the factors $\bar\theta^1K_i^h$ the argument of $K_i^h$ has modulus at least $\frac12\varepsilon$ wherever $\bar\theta^1$ does not vanish, so these factors are smooth on $\mathbb R^3$; the inner integrals in the cases $\{1\}$ and $\{3\}$ may be differentiated under the integral sign, with integrable majorants that are uniform for $(\zeta,v)$ in compact sets. Hence $(\zeta,v)\mapsto G_{\mathsf S}(\zeta;v)$ is smooth, with support in $\{|\zeta|\le1\}$ for every $v$, and $v\mapsto G_{\mathsf S}(\cdot\,;v)$ is of class $C^1$ with respect to the norm $\|\cdot\|_{C^{10}}$. The last bound of \cref{IV-73-41}, $|\int\hat{\mathsf T}^h\hat G(-\kappa)\,d^\circ\kappa|\le C\|G\|_{C^{10}}$, which is linear in $G$, then shows that $\Phi_{\mathsf S}(v):=\int\hat{\mathsf T}^{\mathsf S,h}(\kappa)\,\hat G_{\mathsf S}(-\kappa;v)\,d^\circ\kappa$ is of class $C^1$ in $v$. Since $\mathsf U_{\mathsf S}(u)=|u|^{-\varDelta}\,\Phi_{\mathsf S}(u/|u|)$, the function $\mathsf U_{\mathsf S}$ is of class $C^1$ on $\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$. For $\mathsf U_\emptyset$ we differentiate under the integral sign.

The functions $\mathsf U_{\mathsf S}$ are built from the leading parts $\sigma_i^h$ of the short lines, from the functions $K_i^h=\mathcal F^{-1}_{\ne0}\sigma_i^h$ of the long lines, which depend linearly on $\sigma_i^h$ (\cref{lem:pure-homogeneous-kernels}), from the homogeneous parts $\mathsf I^h_{\mathsf p}$ and $\mathsf I^h_{\mathsf q}$, which depend only on the leading parts and multilinearly on them (\cref{IV-73-42}), and from radial cut-offs; every line enters each $\mathsf U_{\mathsf S}$ exactly once. Hence $\mathsf U$ depends only on $\sigma_1^h,\dots,\sigma_5^h$ and is linear in each of them. If every $\sigma_i^h$ is replaced by $\sigma_i^h\circ O^{-1}$, then $K_i^h$ is replaced by $K_i^h\circ O^{-1}$ (\cref{lem:pure-homogeneous-kernels}), and $\mathsf I^h_{\mathsf p}$, $\mathsf I^h_{\mathsf q}$ are replaced by their compositions with $O^{-1}$ acting on both arguments, since the linear maps $\lambda_i$ of Step~2 commute with this action (\cref{IV-73-42}). The substitutions $\zeta\to O\zeta$ in the continuum integrals defining $G_{\mathsf S}$ and $\mathsf U_\emptyset$, and $\kappa\to O\kappa$ in the integral defining $\mathsf U_{\mathsf S}$, together with the invariance of the radial cut-offs, show that $\mathsf U$ is replaced by $\mathsf U\circ O^{-1}$. This proves (iii) and (iv).
\end{proof}

Write \(p_{[1]}=p_{23}\), \(p_{[2]}=p_{13}\),
\(p_{[3]}=p_{12}\), and \(\lambda(p_{[i]})=i\).
For \(p=p_{[i]}(x_p)\), \(x_p\) is its base point and
\(x(p)\) its barycenter.

\begin{lemma}[The lines of the lattice]\label{IV-73-51}
Let $\tau_{\mathrm{gf}}=1$; we work on $\mathbb Z^3$. For $\iota\in\{1,2,3\}$ write $p_{[\iota]}=p_{\alpha\beta}$ with $\alpha<\beta$, and put
\[
\mathsf c_{\iota,\nu}(k):=\mathsf k_\alpha(k)\,\delta_{\nu\beta}-\mathsf k_\beta(k)\,\delta_{\nu\alpha}\qquad(\nu\in\{1,2,3\},\ k\in\mathbb R^3),
\]
so that for $v\in\mathbb C^3$ the form $(x,\nu)\mapsto e^{ik\cdot x}v_\nu$ satisfies $\mathrm d(e^{ik\cdot x}v_\nu)(p_{[\iota]}(x))=e^{ik\cdot x}\sum_\nu\mathsf c_{\iota,\nu}(k)\,v_\nu$. Let $\hat{C}_{\mu\nu}(k)$ be the bracket in the formula for $C$ in \cref{IV-73-15},
\[
\hat{C}_{\mu\nu}(k)=\frac{\delta_{\mu\nu}}{|\mathsf k|^2}+(\tau_{\mathrm{gf}}-1)\,\frac{\mathsf k_\mu\overline{\mathsf k_\nu}}{|\mathsf k|^4}.
\]
Then for every $x\in\mathbb Z^3$, all directions $\mu,\nu$ and all $\iota,\iota'$, with $p_{[\iota']}=p_{\alpha'\beta'}$, $\alpha'<\beta'$, the following functions of $y\in\mathbb Z^3$ are elementary lines, with the symbols, the degrees $n$ and the leading parts of the symbols listed:
\begin{itemize}
\item $y\mapsto C\bigl((x,\mu),(x+y,\nu)\bigr)$: symbol $\hat{C}_{\nu\mu}(k)$; $n=1$; leading part $\delta_{\mu\nu}|k|^{-2}+(\tau_{\mathrm{gf}}-1)\,k_\mu k_\nu|k|^{-4}$;
\item $y\mapsto E_{p_{[\iota]}(x)}\bigl((x+y,\nu)\bigr)$: symbol $\sum_\mu\overline{\mathsf c_{\iota,\mu}(k)}\,\hat{C}_{\nu\mu}(k)=\overline{\mathsf c_{\iota,\nu}(k)}\,|\mathsf k|^{-2}$; $n=2$; leading part $-i(k_\alpha\delta_{\nu\beta}-k_\beta\delta_{\nu\alpha})|k|^{-2}$;
\item $y\mapsto\Pi\bigl(p_{[\iota]}(x),p_{[\iota']}(x+y)\bigr)$: symbol $\sum_\nu\overline{\mathsf c_{\iota,\nu}(k)}\,\mathsf c_{\iota',\nu}(k)\,|\mathsf k|^{-2}$; $n=3$; leading part $\sum_\nu(k_\alpha\delta_{\nu\beta}-k_\beta\delta_{\nu\alpha})(k_{\alpha'}\delta_{\nu\beta'}-k_{\beta'}\delta_{\nu\alpha'})|k|^{-2}$;
\item $y\mapsto D\bigl((x,\mu);(x+y,\nu)\bigr)$: symbol $\frac12(1+e^{ik_\nu})\,\overline{\mathsf k_\mu(k)}\,|\mathsf k|^{-2}$; $n=2$; leading part $-ik_\mu|k|^{-2}$.
\end{itemize}
If $K(y)$ is an elementary line with symbol $\sigma(k)$ and $y_0\in\mathbb Z^3$, then $K(-y)$ and $K(y+y_0)$ are elementary lines of the same degree, with the symbols $\sigma(-k)$ and $e^{ik\cdot y_0}\sigma(k)$. Consequently, the contraction \cref{IV-73-19} of a leg at a bond or a plaquette with base point $x+\xi$ with a leg at a bond or a plaquette with base point $x+y+\xi'$ equals $\delta_{aa'}$ times an elementary line in $y$ of degree $1+\#\{\text{curl legs among the two}\}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The matrix $\hat{C}(k)$ is Hermitian, and $\hat{C}(-k)=\overline{\hat{C}(k)}$ because $\mathsf k_\mu(-k)=\overline{\mathsf k_\mu(k)}$. By \cref{IV-73-15} and the substitution $k\to-k$,
\[
\begin{aligned}
C\bigl((x,\mu),(x+y,\nu)\bigr)&=\int_{\mathbb T}e^{-ik\cdot y}\,\hat{C}_{\mu\nu}(k)\,d^\circ k\\
&=\int_{\mathbb T}e^{ik\cdot y}\,\overline{\hat{C}_{\mu\nu}(k)}\,d^\circ k=\int_{\mathbb T}e^{ik\cdot y}\,\hat{C}_{\nu\mu}(k)\,d^\circ k .
\end{aligned}
\]
The plaquette $p=p_{[\iota]}(x)=p_{\alpha\beta}(x)$ has the bonds $(x,\alpha),(x+e_\alpha,\beta),(x+e_\beta,\alpha),(x,\beta)$, with the signs $+,+,-,-$. By the formula just proved, $C\bigl((x+\xi,\mu'),(x+y,\nu)\bigr)=\int e^{ik\cdot(y-\xi)}\hat{C}_{\nu\mu'}(k)\,d^\circ k$, and therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
E_p\bigl((x+y,\nu)\bigr)&=\sum_is_i\,C\bigl(b_i(p),(x+y,\nu)\bigr)\\
&=\int_{\mathbb T}e^{ik\cdot y}\Bigl[\hat{C}_{\nu\alpha}(k)\bigl(1-e^{-ik_\beta}\bigr)+\hat{C}_{\nu\beta}(k)\bigl(e^{-ik_\alpha}-1\bigr)\Bigr]\,d^\circ k .
\end{aligned}
\]
As $\overline{\mathsf k_\mu(k)}=e^{-ik_\mu}-1$, the bracket equals $\sum_\mu\overline{\mathsf c_{\iota,\mu}(k)}\,\hat{C}_{\nu\mu}(k)$. In this sum the part of $\hat{C}_{\nu\mu}$ containing $\mathsf k_\nu\overline{\mathsf k_\mu}$ drops out, since $\sum_\mu\overline{\mathsf c_{\iota,\mu}}\,\mathsf k_\nu\overline{\mathsf k_\mu}=\mathsf k_\nu\,\overline{\sum_\mu\mathsf c_{\iota,\mu}\mathsf k_\mu}$ and $\sum_\mu\mathsf c_{\iota,\mu}\mathsf k_\mu=\mathsf k_\alpha\mathsf k_\beta-\mathsf k_\beta\mathsf k_\alpha=0$; what remains is $\overline{\mathsf c_{\iota,\nu}}\,|\mathsf k|^{-2}$. The kernel $\Pi$ arises from $E_p$ by the operation $\mathrm d$ in the second argument (\cref{IV-73-15}). With $q=p_{[\iota']}(x+y)=p_{\alpha'\beta'}(x+y)$, the four bonds $(x+y,\alpha')$, $(x+y+e_{\alpha'},\beta')$, $(x+y+e_{\beta'},\alpha')$, $(x+y,\beta')$ of $q$ contribute, with the signs $+,+,-,-$, the symbols $\overline{\mathsf c_{\iota,\alpha'}}|\mathsf k|^{-2}$, $e^{ik_{\alpha'}}\overline{\mathsf c_{\iota,\beta'}}|\mathsf k|^{-2}$, $e^{ik_{\beta'}}\overline{\mathsf c_{\iota,\alpha'}}|\mathsf k|^{-2}$, $\overline{\mathsf c_{\iota,\beta'}}|\mathsf k|^{-2}$, and their sum is
\[
\bigl(\mathsf k_{\alpha'}\,\overline{\mathsf c_{\iota,\beta'}}-\mathsf k_{\beta'}\,\overline{\mathsf c_{\iota,\alpha'}}\bigr)|\mathsf k|^{-2}=\sum_\nu\overline{\mathsf c_{\iota,\nu}}\,\mathsf c_{\iota',\nu}\,|\mathsf k|^{-2};
\]
that is, $\mathrm d$ in the second argument multiplies the symbol by $\mathsf c_{\iota',\nu}(k)$ and sums over $\nu$. Finally, with $G(x',x'')=\int e^{ik\cdot(x'-x'')}|\mathsf k|^{-2}\,d^\circ k$,
\[
\begin{aligned}
D\bigl((x,\mu);(x+y,\nu)\bigr)&=\tfrac12\sum_{x'\in\{x+y,\,x+y+e_\nu\}}\bigl[G(x',x+e_\mu)-G(x',x)\bigr]\\
&=\int_{\mathbb T}e^{ik\cdot y}\,\tfrac12\bigl(1+e^{ik_\nu}\bigr)\bigl(e^{-ik_\mu}-1\bigr)\,|\mathsf k|^{-2}\,d^\circ k .
\end{aligned}
\]

All four symbols are sums of products of the examples of \cref{IV-73-38}, namely $e^{ik\cdot y}$ (degree $0$, leading part $1$), $\mathsf k_\mu$ and $\overline{\mathsf k_\mu}$ (degree $1$, leading parts $ik_\mu$ and $-ik_\mu$) and $|\mathsf k|^{-2}$ (degree $-2$, leading part $|k|^{-2}$), and no product of degree below $-2$ occurs: the term $\mathsf k_\nu\overline{\mathsf k_\mu}|\mathsf k|^{-4}$ is the product $(\mathsf k_\nu|\mathsf k|^{-2})(\overline{\mathsf k_\mu}|\mathsf k|^{-2})$ of two line symbols of degree $-1$. By the rules for sums and products in \cref{IV-73-38}, the four symbols are line symbols of the degrees $-2,-1,0,-1$, so the kernels are elementary lines of the degrees $1,2,3,2$; their leading parts arise by replacing $\mathsf k_\mu$, $\overline{\mathsf k_\mu}$, $|\mathsf k|^{-2}$, $e^{ik_\nu}$ by $ik_\mu$, $-ik_\mu$, $|k|^{-2}$, $1$, which gives the leading parts listed.

If $K$ has the symbol $\sigma$, then $K(-y)=\int e^{-ik\cdot y}\sigma(k)\,d^\circ k=\int e^{ik\cdot y}\sigma(-k)\,d^\circ k$ and $K(y+y_0)=\int e^{ik\cdot y}e^{ik\cdot y_0}\sigma(k)\,d^\circ k$. The function $\sigma(-k)$ is a line symbol of the same degree, with leading part $\sigma^h(-k)$, as $\chi$ is even; and $e^{ik\cdot y_0}\sigma(k)$ is the product of $\sigma$ with a line symbol of degree $0$ and leading part $1$. For the consequence we recall from \cref{IV-73-19} that the contraction of two plain legs is $\delta_{aa'}C$, that of a curl leg with a plain leg is $\delta_{aa'}E$, and that of two curl legs is $\delta_{aa'}\Pi$. These kernels are invariant under simultaneous translations of their arguments, by their Fourier representations. Hence, by the list above and by the two rules just proved (which take care of the order of the legs and of the shifts $\xi,\xi'$), each contraction is an elementary line in $y$ of degree $1$, $2$, $3$, respectively.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[The vertex insertion]\label{lem:pure-vertex-insertion}
The kernel \(\Gamma_q\) of \cref{IV-73-29} satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{IV-73-54}
 \frac32\sum_{b,b'}\Gamma_q(b,b')E_p(b)E_p(b')
  =\mathsf T_{4'}^{(q)}+\mathsf T_5^{(q)}
       +\mathsf T_4+\mathsf T_1 .
\end{equation}
Here the superscript \((q)\) denotes the first half of the
corresponding expression in \cref{IV-73-53}: the quartic,
respectively cubic, observable is at \(q\).
The identity holds separately for the four groups in the
definition of \(\Gamma_q\), grouping its two mixed derivatives.
Exchanging \(p\) and \(q\) gives the second halves.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Write \(\partial=\partial_{b,a}\), \(\partial'=\partial_{b',a'}\),
\(\delta=\delta_{(b,a)}\), and \(\delta'=\delta_{(b',a')}\).
The connected-pairing formula of \cref{IV-73-53} gives
\begin{align*}
 \langle\partial\partial'\mathsf a_q^{(4)}\rangle_0
