 &=\frac12\sum_{i,j}C(i,j)
       \mathsf a_q^{(4)}[\![\delta,\delta',\delta_i,\delta_j]\!],\\
 \langle\partial\mathsf a_q^{(3)};\partial'S_3\rangle_0
 &=\frac12\sum_P\sum_{i,i',j,j'}C(i,j)C(i',j')
       \mathsf a_q^{(3)}[\![\delta,\delta_i,\delta_{i'}]\!]
       \mathsf a_P^{(3)}[\![\delta',\delta_j,\delta_{j'}]\!],\\
 \langle\mathsf a_q^{(2)};\partial\partial'S_4\rangle_0
 &=\frac12\sum_{P,c}
       \mathsf a_P^{(4)}[\![\delta,\delta',E_q^c,E_q^c]\!],\\
 \langle\mathsf a_q^{(2)};\partial S_3;\partial'S_3\rangle_0
 &=\sum_{P,P',c}\sum_{i,j}C(i,j)
       \mathsf a_P^{(3)}[\![\delta,E_q^c,\delta_i]\!]
       \mathsf a_{P'}^{(3)}[\![\delta',E_q^c,\delta_j]\!].
\end{align*}
For the last line the three vertices are quadratic.
The only connected pairing matrix has one line between each
pair of vertices, with coefficient one.
In each line set \(a'=a\), multiply by
\(\frac12E_p(b)E_p(b')\), and sum over \(b,b',a\).
The colour identity
\(\Gamma_q(b,a;b',a)=\Gamma_q(b,b')\)
gives the left side of \eqref{IV-73-54}.
The first line gives \(\mathsf T_{4'}^{(q)}\).
The second line and its transpose have equal contractions;
their negative sum gives \(\mathsf T_5^{(q)}\).
The negative of the third line gives \(\mathsf T_4\), and
the fourth gives \(\mathsf T_1\), with exactly the coefficients
of \cref{IV-73-53}.
Absolute convergence is supplied by \cref{IV-73-55}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Elementary terms, their expansions, the local parts}

\begin{lemma}[Elementary terms and their degrees]\label{IV-73-57}
Let $\tau_{\mathrm{gf}}=1$, let us work on $\mathbb Z^3$, let $p=p_{[\iota]}(x_p)$ and $q=p_{[\iota']}(x_q)$ be plaquettes, and put $u':=x_q-x_p$. We write every vertex occurring in the formulas of \cref{IV-73-53} in the standard writing (\cref{IV-73-19}, \cref{IV-73-53}), we carry out the sums over the colours, and we write every contraction as an elementary line by \cref{IV-73-51}. Then there are finite index sets $\mathfrak G_\bullet=\mathfrak G_\bullet(\iota,\iota')$, real numbers $c_G$ and elementary lines $K^G_\bullet$, all independent of $x_p$ and $x_q$, such that the following representations hold; every $G$ is called an elementary term. We omit the index $G$ on the lines, and $*$ denotes the convolution of \cref{IV-73-46}.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(1)] $\mathsf T_1=\sum_{G\in\mathfrak G_1}c_G\,\mathsf T^G(u')$, where every $\mathsf T^G$ is a kite as in \cref{IV-73-47}, with degrees satisfying the hypotheses of that proposition and with $\varDelta=5$. Here $K_1$ and $K_2$ are contractions of $(\mathrm dA)(p)$ with legs at $P$ and at $P'$, $K_4$ and $K_5$ are contractions of legs at $P$ and at $P'$ with $(\mathrm dA)(q)$, and $K_3$ is the contraction of a leg at $P$ with a leg at $P'$.
\item[(4)] $\mathsf T_4=\sum_{G\in\mathfrak G_4}c_G\,(X*Y)(u')$, where $X=K_1K_2$ and $Y=K_3K_4$ with $n_i\in\{2,3\}$, and $(n_X,n_Y):=(n_1+n_2,n_3+n_4)\in\{(4,4),(5,4),(4,5),(6,6)\}$, with $(n_X,n_Y)=(4,4)$ for the monomials of $\frac12|\mathfrak z_1|^2$.
\item[(4$'$)] The first half of $\mathsf T_{4'}$ equals $\sum_{G\in\mathfrak G_{4'}}c_G\,K_1(u')\,K_2(u')$, where $n_i\in\{2,3\}$ and $K_1,K_2$ are contractions of $(\mathrm dA)(p)$ with legs at $q$.
\item[(5)] The first half of $\mathsf T_5$ equals $\sum_{G\in\mathfrak G_5}c_G\,K_0(u')\,(X*Y)(u')$ with $Y=K_{\mathrm a}K_{\mathrm b}$. Here $K_0$ and $X$ are contractions of $(\mathrm dA)(p)$ with a leg at $q$, resp.\ at $P$, and $n_0,n_X\in\{2,3\}$; $K_{\mathrm a},K_{\mathrm b}$ are contractions of legs at $P$ with legs at $q$, and $n_{\mathrm a},n_{\mathrm b}\in\{1,2,3\}$; finally $n_0+n_X+n_{\mathrm a}+n_{\mathrm b}=8$, so that $n_Y:=n_{\mathrm a}+n_{\mathrm b}\in\{2,3,4\}$.
\item[(6)] $\mathsf T_6=\sum_{G\in\mathfrak G_6}c_G\,K_1(u')\,K_2(u')\,K_3(u')$, with $n_1+n_2+n_3=5$.
\item[(I)] $\mathsf T_{\mathrm I}=-3\,\Pi(p,q)\sum_{\mu,\nu}\bigl(K^\to_{\iota\mu}*\Sigma_{\mu\nu}*K^\leftarrow_{\nu\iota'}\bigr)(u')$, where $K^\to_{\iota\mu}(y):=E_{p_{[\iota]}(0)}((y,\mu))$ and $K^\leftarrow_{\nu\iota'}(y):=E_{p_{[\iota']}(y)}((0,\nu))$ are elementary lines of degree $2$, and $\Sigma_{\mu\nu}(y):=\Sigma((x,\mu),(x+y,\nu))$, which does not depend on $x$. With $\mathsf s_P(b):=s_i$ if $b=b_i(P)$ and $\mathsf s_P(b):=0$ otherwise,
\begin{equation}\label{IV-73-58}
\begin{gathered}
\partial_{b,a}S_3=\mathsf d_{b,a}+\mathsf u_{b,a},\\
\mathsf d_{b,a}:=\sum_{P\ni b}\mathsf s_P(b)\,\langle\mathsf e_a,\mathfrak z_1(P)\rangle,\qquad\mathsf u_{b,a}:=\sum_{P\ni b}\langle\mathrm dA(P),\partial_{b,a}\mathfrak z_1(P)\rangle ;
\end{gathered}
\end{equation}
the monomials of $\mathsf d_{b,a}$ have two plain legs, those of $\mathsf u_{b,a}$ a curl leg and a plain leg. Moreover
\begin{equation}\label{IV-73-59}
\Sigma_{\mu\nu}=\mathsf q^0_{\mu\nu}+\sum_{G\in\mathfrak G_{\mathrm I}(\mu,\nu)}c_G\,\mathsf f_G(\nabla)\bigl[K_{\mathrm a}K_{\mathrm b}\bigr],
\end{equation}
where $\mathsf q^0_{\mu\nu}$ has finite support (it comes from the line between two slots of the quartic Wilson vertex, from the Haar term and from the ghost tadpole); $\mathsf f_G(k)$ is the product of two trigonometric polynomials, each a line symbol of degree $0$ or $1$, of total degree $d_G\in\{0,1,2\}$; $\mathsf f_G(\nabla)$ is the finite difference operator which multiplies symbols by $\mathsf f_G$; $n_{\mathrm a},n_{\mathrm b}\in\{1,2,3\}$; and $n_{\mathrm a}+n_{\mathrm b}+d_G=4$. The terms $G$ are the ghost loop $-8\,D(b;b')\,D(b';b)$, with $d_G=0$, and the terms of $-\langle\partial S_3;\partial'S_3\rangle_0$ multiplied out by \eqref{IV-73-58}, with $d_G$ the number of entries $\mathsf d$.
\end{enumerate}
The second halves of $\mathsf T_{4'}$ and $\mathsf T_5$ have the same forms, with $p$ and $q$ exchanged and $u'$ replaced by $-u'$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
We use two counting rules: every monomial of $\mathsf a^{(3)}$ has exactly one curl leg and $\mathsf a^{(2)}$ has two (\cref{IV-73-19}); and the degree of a line is $1+\#$(its curl legs) (\cref{IV-73-51}). By the consequence stated in \cref{IV-73-51}, every contraction is an elementary line in the difference of the base points of the two vertices which it joins, its symbol depending only on the two legs; the shifts between the base points of the legs and those of the vertices are absorbed into the lines.

(1) A kite has five lines. There are four curl legs at $p$ and $q$ and one at each of $P$ and $P'$, hence $\sum_in_i=5+6=11$ and $\varDelta=5$. For $i\in\{1,2,4,5\}$ one end of the line $i$ is a curl leg of $p$ or of $q$, so that $n_i\ge2$, and $n_i\le3$. Besides the two curl legs of $p$, the lines $1,2,3$ carry at most two further curl legs, one of $P$ and one of $P'$; hence $n_1+n_2+n_3\le2+2+1+2=7$, and the same count applies to the lines $3,4,5$. With the base points $x_p+z$ and $x_p+w$ of $P$ and $P'$, the sum over $P,P'$ becomes the sum over $z,w$ and over the dual directions of $P,P'$, and the five lines become functions of $z$, $w$, $w-z$, $u'-z$, $u'-w$.

(4) Each of the four lines carries a curl leg at $p$ or at $q$; it has degree $2$, or degree $3$ if its leg at $P$ is a curl leg. The three kinds of monomials of $\mathsf a_P^{(4)}$ (\cref{IV-73-53}) give $(n_X,n_Y)=(4,4)$; $(5,4)$ or $(4,5)$; and $(6,6)$. With the base point $x_p+z$ of $P$, the two lines from $p$ make up $X(z)$, the two lines to $q$ make up $Y(u'-z)$, and the sum over $z$ is $(X*Y)(u')$.

(4$'$) There are two lines from $p$ to $q$, each with its curl leg at $p$; the line between two slots of the vertex at $q$ is a number, independent of the positions, and it is absorbed into $c_G$.

(5) There are four lines, and there are $2+1+1$ curl legs, at $p$, $q$ and $P$; hence $\sum n=4+4=8$. With the base point $x_p+z$ of $P$, the line from $p$ to $P$ is $X(z)$, the two lines from $P$ to $q$ make up $Y(u'-z)$, and the line from $p$ to $q$ is $K_0(u')$.

(6) There are three lines, and there are $1+1$ curl legs, at $p$ and $q$; hence $\sum n=3+2=5$.

(I) In the formula for $\mathsf T_{\mathrm I}$ we write $b=(x,\mu)$ and $b'=(x',\nu)$ with $x=x_p+z$, $x'=x_p+w$. By translation invariance $E_p(b)=K^\to_{\iota\mu}(z)$ and $E_q(b')=K^\leftarrow_{\nu\iota'}(u'-w)$, and by the translation covariance in \cref{IV-73-29}(5) $\Sigma(b,b')=\Sigma_{\mu\nu}(w-z)$; this gives the formula for $\mathsf T_{\mathrm I}$. The functions $K^\to_{\iota\mu}$ and $K^\leftarrow_{\nu\iota'}$ are elementary lines of degree $2$ by \cref{IV-73-51}, the second because $K^\leftarrow_{\nu\iota'}(y)=E_{p_{[\iota']}(0)}((-y,\nu))$. By \cref{IV-73-29}(5) and \cref{IV-73-19}, with $\partial=\partial_{b,a}$ and $\partial'=\partial_{b',a}$,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Sigma(b,b')={}&\Bigl[\langle\partial\partial'S_4\rangle_0+\bigl(\tfrac23+\tfrac43g(b)\bigr)\delta_{bb'}\Bigr]\\
&-4\bigl[D(b;b')D(b';b)+D(b';b)D(b;b')\bigr]-\langle\partial S_3;\partial'S_3\rangle_0 .
\end{aligned}
\]
The bracket has finite range and is translation invariant; it gives $\mathsf q^0_{\mu\nu}$. The middle term is the ghost loop $-8\,D(b;b')\,D(b';b)$, a product of two elementary lines of degree $2$ in $y$ (\cref{IV-73-51}), with $\mathsf f_G=1$. From \cref{IV-73-9} and the Leibniz rule we have
\[
\partial_{b,a}\langle\mathrm dA(P),\mathfrak z_1(P)\rangle=\mathsf s_P(b)\,\langle\mathsf e_a,\mathfrak z_1(P)\rangle+\langle\mathrm dA(P),\partial_{b,a}\mathfrak z_1(P)\rangle ,
\]
which gives \eqref{IV-73-58}. For a function $\mathsf F$ on the plaquettes of one dual direction, the map $b\mapsto\sum_{P\ni b}\mathsf s_P(b)\,\mathsf F(P)$ is a difference operator whose symbol is $\pm\overline{\mathsf k_\alpha}$ up to a factor $e^{ik\cdot y_0}$, a line symbol of degree $1$; this operator yields the factor of $\mathsf f_G$ which belongs to an entry $\mathsf d$. An entry $\mathsf u$ we split into its monomials and treat each of them separately. By the consequence stated in \cref{IV-73-51}, the contraction of a leg with base point $x+\xi$ with a leg with base point $x+y+\xi'$ is an elementary line in $y$ in which the shifts $\xi$ and $\xi'$ are already contained; hence the factor of $\mathsf f_G$ which belongs to an entry $\mathsf u$ is $1$, a line symbol of degree $0$ with leading part $1$, just as for the ghost loop. By \cref{IV-73-53}, the cumulant of two quadratic monomials is a sum of two products of two lines. Hence every term of $-\langle\partial S_3;\partial'S_3\rangle_0$, multiplied out by \eqref{IV-73-58}, has the form $c_G\,\mathsf f_G(\nabla)[K_{\mathrm a}K_{\mathrm b}]$, with $d_G$ the number of entries $\mathsf d$ and with $n_{\mathrm a}+n_{\mathrm b}=2+\#$(curl legs on the two lines). As $\mathsf d$ has no curl leg and $\mathsf u$ has one, $n_{\mathrm a}+n_{\mathrm b}=2+(2-d_G)$. The second halves of $\mathsf T_{4'}$ and $\mathsf T_5$ are treated in the same way, the roles of $p$ and $q$ being exchanged.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Expansions of the elementary terms, with errors]\label{IV-73-60}
Let the setting be that of \cref{IV-73-57}, let $r':=|u'|$ be large, and let $K^h:=\mathcal F^{-1}_{\ne0}\sigma^h$ for every line $K$ with symbol $\sigma$. For the bubbles $X$ and $Y$ let $\mathsf q_X$ and $\mathsf q_Y$ be the kernels $\mathsf q$ of \cref{IV-73-46}(iii), and put $X':=X-\mathsf q_X$, $Y':=Y-\mathsf q_Y$. Then the elementary terms of \cref{IV-73-57} have the following expansions.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(6)] $K_1K_2K_3(u')=K_1^hK_2^hK_3^h(u')+O(r'^{-6})$.
\item[(5)] $K_0(u')\,(X*Y)(u')=K_0(u')\,(\mathsf q_Y*X)(u')+K_0^h(u')\,(X*Y')^h(u')+O(r'^{-6}\lg r')$, where $(X*Y')^h$ is the second component of the leading data of $X*Y'\in\mathfrak K(n_X+n_Y-3)$.
\item[(4)] $(X*Y)(u')=(\mathsf q_X*Y)(u')+(\mathsf q_Y*X)(u')+\mathsf U_G(u')+O(r'^{-6}\lg r')$, where $\mathsf U_G:=(X'*Y')^h$ if $(n_X,n_Y)=(4,4)$ and $\mathsf U_G:=0$ otherwise.
\item[(1)] The expansion of \cref{IV-73-47}(iii) holds, with the error $O(r'^{-6}\lg r')$.
\item[($*$)] In all four cases the function of degree $-5$ in the expansion (that is, $K_1^hK_2^hK_3^h$, $K_0^h(X*Y')^h$, $\mathsf U_G$, resp.\ the function $\mathsf U$ of \cref{IV-73-47}) is determined by the leading parts $\sigma^h$ of the lines alone; it is multilinear in them, it belongs to $C^1(\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\})$, and it is rotation covariant as in \cref{IV-73-47}(iv).
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
(6) By \cref{lem:pure-homogeneous-kernels}, $K_i(u')=O(r'^{-n_i})$, $K_i^h(u')=O(r'^{-n_i})$ and $K_i(u')=K_i^h(u')+O(r'^{-n_i-1})$. As $n_1+n_2+n_3=5$, the product $K_1K_2K_3(u')$ differs from $K_1^hK_2^hK_3^h(u')$ by $O(r'^{-6})$, and $K_1^hK_2^hK_3^h$ is homogeneous of degree $-5$.

(5) The line $X$ is an elementary line of degree $n_X\in\{2,3\}$, so $X\in\mathfrak K(n_X)$ by \cref{lem:pure-homogeneous-kernels}. The bubble $Y=K_{\mathrm a}K_{\mathrm b}$ has $n_{\mathrm a},n_{\mathrm b}\in\{1,2,3\}$ and $n_Y\le4$, so $Y'\in\mathfrak K(n_Y)$ by \cref{IV-73-46}(iii). We write $X*Y=\mathsf q_Y*X+X*Y'$. \cref{IV-73-46}(ii) applies to $X$ and $Y'$, as $n_X,n_Y\le4$ and $n_X+n_Y=8-n_0\ge5$; it gives $X*Y'\in\mathfrak K(n_X+n_Y-3)$, and the spatial estimate in \cref{IV-73-38} with $\gamma=0$ gives $X*Y'=(X*Y')^h+O(r'^{-(n_X+n_Y-3)-1}\lg r')$. Moreover $K_0=K_0^h+O(r'^{-n_0-1})$ by \cref{lem:pure-homogeneous-kernels}, and $K_0$, $K_0^h$, $X*Y'$, $(X*Y')^h$ are bounded by the corresponding powers of $r'$. As $n_0+(n_X+n_Y-3)=8-3=5$, the claim follows.

(4) Multiplying out $X*Y=(\mathsf q_X+X')*(\mathsf q_Y+Y')$ we obtain
\[
X*Y=\mathsf q_X*Y+\mathsf q_Y*X-\mathsf q_X*\mathsf q_Y+X'*Y',
\]
and $\mathsf q_X*\mathsf q_Y$ vanishes off $\{|u'|\le2\}$, because $\mathsf q_X$ and $\mathsf q_Y$ vanish off $\{0,\pm e_j\}$. If $(n_X,n_Y)=(4,4)$, then $X',Y'\in\mathfrak K(4)$ by \cref{IV-73-46}(iii), and \cref{IV-73-46}(ii) gives $X'*Y'\in\mathfrak K(5)$ and $X'*Y'=(X'*Y')^h+O(r'^{-6}\lg r')$. Otherwise we apply \cref{IV-73-46}(i) to $X'$ and $Y'$, with $a_X=\min\{n_X-3,2\}$ and $a_Y=\min\{n_Y-3,2\}$. Its hypotheses hold by \cref{IV-73-46}(iii), which bounds the differences of a bubble of degree $n$ by $C_\gamma\langle x\rangle^{-n-|\gamma|}$ (the kernels $X',Y'$ differ from $X,Y$ at finitely many points only) and the symbol of $X'$, resp.\ $Y'$, by $|\mathsf I-\tilde{\mathsf Q}|\le C|k|^{\min\{n-3,2\}}$. The three exponents in the bound of \cref{IV-73-46}(i) are $-2-4$, $-1-5$, $3-9$ for $(n_X,n_Y)=(5,4)$, the same by symmetry for $(4,5)$, and at most $-8$ for $(6,6)$; so $X'*Y'=O(r'^{-6}\lg r')$ in these cases.

(1) This is \cref{IV-73-47}(iii) with $\varDelta=5$ (\cref{IV-73-57}(1)), so that $r^{-\varDelta-1}\lg r=r'^{-6}\lg r'$.

($*$) In the case (6) this follows from \cref{lem:pure-homogeneous-kernels}. In the cases (5) and (4), \cref{IV-73-46}(ii) shows that the second component of the leading data of a convolution depends only on the leading data of the two factors, bilinearly and rotation covariantly. By \cref{IV-73-46}(iii) the leading data of $Y'$, and of $X'$ in the case (4), are $(\mathsf I^h,K_{\mathrm a}^hK_{\mathrm b}^h)$, where $\mathsf I^h$ depends only on $\sigma_{\mathrm a}^h,\sigma_{\mathrm b}^h$, bilinearly and rotation covariantly, by \cref{IV-73-42}; the leading data of the lines $X$ and $K_0$ are $(\sigma^h,K^h)$ with $K^h=\mathcal F^{-1}_{\ne0}\sigma^h$, by \cref{lem:pure-homogeneous-kernels}. The functions $K^h$ and the second components of leading data are smooth off the origin. In the case (1) the assertions are \cref{IV-73-47}(iii),(iv).
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[A local insertion with vanishing moments]\label{IV-73-61}
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Let $\gamma_{\mu\nu}$, $1\le\mu,\nu\le3$, be functions of finite support on $\mathbb Z^3\times\mathbb Z^3$ whose symbols
\[
\hat\gamma_{\mu\nu}(\kappa_1,\kappa_2):=\sum_{y,y'}\gamma_{\mu\nu}(y,y')\,e^{-i(\kappa_1\cdot y+\kappa_2\cdot y')}
\]
vanish at $\kappa=0$ together with their gradients, and let $K_1,K_2,K_3$ be elementary lines of degree $2$. Then
\[
\Bigl|\sum_{\mu,\nu}\sum_{y,y'}\gamma_{\mu\nu}(y,y')\,K_\mu(u+y)\,K_\nu(u+y')\Bigr|\le C\,|u|^{-6}\qquad(u\in\mathbb Z^3\setminus\{0\}),
\]
where $C$ depends on the $\gamma_{\mu\nu}$ and on the symbols of the $K_\mu$.
\item[(b)] Let $\mathsf q$ be a function of finite support on $\mathbb Z^3$ with $\hat{\mathsf q}(k):=\sum_y\mathsf q(y)\,e^{-ik\cdot y}=O(|k|^2)$ at $k=0$, and let $K_1,K_2$ be elementary lines of degree $2$. Then $|(K_1*\mathsf q*K_2)(u)|\le C\langle u\rangle^{-3}$ for all $u\in\mathbb Z^3$, where $C$ depends on $\mathsf q$ and on the symbols of $K_1,K_2$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
(a) As the $\gamma_{\mu\nu}$ have finite support, only points $y,y'$ in a fixed ball occur; let $|u|$ be large. By \cref{IV-73-39} with $s=-1$, $K_\mu(u)=O(|u|^{-2})$, $\nabla K_\mu(u)=O(|u|^{-3})$, and the second differences of $K_\mu$ near $u$ are $O(|u|^{-4})$. We write $K_\mu(u+y)-K_\mu(u)$ as a sum of first differences along a nearest-neighbour path from $u$ to $u+y$ and compare each of them with $\nabla_jK_\mu(u)$; this gives
\[
K_\mu(u+y)=K_\mu(u)+\sum_jy_j\,\nabla_jK_\mu(u)+O(|u|^{-4}).
\]
We insert this expansion for $K_\mu(u+y)$ and for $K_\nu(u+y')$. The terms of the orders $|u|^{-4}$ and $|u|^{-5}$ then carry the coefficients
\[
\sum_{y,y'}\gamma_{\mu\nu}(y,y')=\hat\gamma_{\mu\nu}(0),\qquad\sum_{y,y'}\gamma_{\mu\nu}(y,y')\,y_j,\qquad\sum_{y,y'}\gamma_{\mu\nu}(y,y')\,y'_j ,
\]
and the last two are $i$ times the derivatives of $\hat\gamma_{\mu\nu}$ with respect to $\kappa_{1,j}$, resp.\ $\kappa_{2,j}$, at $0$. All three vanish by hypothesis, and the remaining terms are $O(|u|^{-6})$. For $u\ne0$ in a bounded set the left side is bounded and $|u|^{-6}$ is bounded below, so the bound holds for all $u\ne0$ after enlarging $C$.

(b) The trigonometric polynomial $\hat{\mathsf q}$ is smooth and vanishes at $0$ together with its gradient, hence $\hat{\mathsf q}\in\mathcal S^2$. The kernel $\mathsf q*K_2$, a finite combination of translates of $K_2$, has the symbol $\hat{\mathsf q}\sigma_2\in\mathcal S^1$, where $\sigma_2\in\mathcal S^{-1}$ is the symbol of $K_2$; by \cref{IV-73-39} it is $O(\langle x\rangle^{-4})$ and lies in $\ell^2(\mathbb Z^3)$, as does $K_1=O(\langle x\rangle^{-2})$. By Plancherel's theorem $K_1*(\mathsf q*K_2)$ is the kernel with the symbol $\sigma_1\hat{\mathsf q}\sigma_2\in\mathcal S^0$, and \cref{IV-73-39} with $s=0$ gives the bound $C\langle u\rangle^{-3}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[The local parts vanish to the second order]\label{IV-73-62}
Let $\tau_{\mathrm{gf}}=1$; we work on $\mathbb Z^3$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] (Self-energy.) In \eqref{IV-73-59} let $\mathsf q_G$ be the kernel $\mathsf q$ of the bubble $K_{\mathrm a}K_{\mathrm b}$ in the sense of \cref{IV-73-46}(iii), and put
\[
\mathsf q^\Sigma_{\mu\nu}:=\mathsf q^0_{\mu\nu}+\sum_Gc_G\,\mathsf f_G(\nabla)\mathsf q_G,\qquad\mathsf W_{\mu\nu}:=\sum_Gc_G\,\mathsf f_G(\nabla)\bigl[K_{\mathrm a}K_{\mathrm b}-\mathsf q_G\bigr],
\]
so that $\Sigma_{\mu\nu}=\mathsf q^\Sigma_{\mu\nu}+\mathsf W_{\mu\nu}$. Then $\mathsf q^\Sigma_{\mu\nu}$ has finite support. Each $\mathsf f_G(\nabla)[K_{\mathrm a}K_{\mathrm b}-\mathsf q_G]$ belongs to $\mathfrak K(4)$, and the first component of its leading data is $\mathsf f_G^h\,\mathsf I_G^h$, where $\mathsf f_G^h$ is the leading part of $\mathsf f_G$ and $\mathsf I_G^h$ is the homogeneous part of the symbol $\mathsf I_G$ of the bubble (\cref{IV-73-46}(iii), \cref{IV-73-42}). Hence $\mathsf W_{\mu\nu}\in\mathfrak K(4)$, and its leading data are functions of the leading parts $\sigma^h$ and of the $\mathsf f_G^h$ occurring in \eqref{IV-73-59} alone. Moreover the symbol of $\mathsf q^\Sigma_{\mu\nu}$ satisfies $\hat{\mathsf q}^\Sigma_{\mu\nu}(k)=O(|k|^2)$ at $k=0$.
\item[(b)] (Vertex.) Let $q=p_{[\iota']}(x_q)$. Let $\gamma_q(b,b')$ be the symmetric kernel of finite range defined below; then, for every plaquette $p$ with $|u'|$ large, $\frac{3}2\sum_{b,b'}\gamma_q(b,b')\,E_p(b)\,E_p(b')$ is the sum of the following terms of \cref{IV-73-60}: the first half of $\mathsf T_{4'}$; the terms $c_G\,K_0(u')\,(\mathsf q_Y*X)(u')$ of the first half of $\mathsf T_5$; the terms $c_G\,(\mathsf q_Y*X)(u')$ of $\mathsf T_4$; and the terms $c_G\sum_{z,w}\mathsf q_{\mathsf q}(z,w)\,K_1(u'-z)\,K_2(u'-w)$ of $\mathsf T_1$. The kernel $\gamma_q$ is defined as follows. Each of $K_0$, $X$, $K_1$, $K_2$, at the points where it is evaluated in these terms, is either a value $E_p(b)$ with $b$ a bond near $q$, or a value $\Pi(p,P)=\sum_is_i\,E_p(b_i(P))$ with $P$ a plaquette near $q$. Substituting this term by term in the four sums we obtain a quadratic expression in the values $E_p(b)$, and $\frac{3}2\gamma_q$ is its coefficient kernel, symmetrised. This kernel does not depend on $p$. Indeed, by the rule for $\mathsf a_p^{(2)}$ in the proof of \cref{IV-73-53}, the plaquette $p$, with its base point and its dual direction, enters the four sums only through the forms $E_p^a$ inserted into the two slots joined to $p$, that is, only through the values of $K_0$, $X$, $K_1$, $K_2$ just described. An elementary term $G$ of these sums is given by the monomials at the vertices at $q$, $P$, $P'$ and by the choice of their legs which are contracted with $p$, with $q$ and with one another, so that the numbers $c_G$ do not involve $p$; and the kernels $\mathsf q_Y$, $\mathsf q_{\mathsf q}$ and the line between two slots of the vertex at $q$ are built from lines among $q$, $P$, $P'$ alone. We define $\gamma_q$ through this way of writing, since the numbers $\sum_{b,b'}\gamma_q(b,b')E_p(b)E_p(b')$ alone would not fix a kernel. Let $\gamma_{q;\mu\nu}(y,y'):=\gamma_q((x_q+y,\mu),(x_q+y',\nu))$. Then the symbols $\hat\gamma_{q;\mu\nu}$, defined as in \cref{IV-73-61}(a), vanish at $\kappa=0$ together with their gradients.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\emph{Step 1: a trace formula.} Let $\mathsf m^1,\dots,\mathsf m^{\mathsf r}$, $\mathsf r\le3$, be real symmetric matrices indexed by $\mathsf i=(x,\mu,a)$, that is, by a bond $(x,\mu)$ and a colour $a$, each with finitely many non-zero entries. For $y\in\mathbb Z^3$ let $\mathsf m_y$ be the translate of $\mathsf m$ by $y$, $(\mathsf m_y)_{(x,\mu,a),(x',\mu',a')}:=\mathsf m_{(x-y,\mu,a),(x'-y,\mu',a')}$, and let $\hat{\mathsf m}(l',l)$ be the $9\times9$ matrix, indexed by $(\mu,a)$ and $(\mu',a')$, with the entries
\[
\sum_{x,x'}e^{-il'\cdot x}\,\mathsf m_{(x,\mu,a),(x',\mu',a')}\,e^{il\cdot x'} .
\]
Then $\hat{\mathsf m}_y(l',l)=e^{-i(l'-l)\cdot y}\,\hat{\mathsf m}(l',l)$, and $\hat{\mathsf m}(l,l)$ is the symbol of the translation invariant matrix $\sum_y\mathsf m_y$, in the sense that $\sum_y\mathsf m_y$ maps $e^{il\cdot x}\alpha$ to $e^{il\cdot x}\,\hat{\mathsf m}(l,l)\,\alpha$. We insert $C(\mathsf i,\mathsf i')=\delta_{aa'}\int_{\mathbb T}e^{il\cdot(x-x')}\,\hat{C}_{\mu\mu'}(l)\,d^\circ l$ and let $\hat{C}(l)$ act on the nine-dimensional space as $\hat{C}(l)$ in the directions and as the identity in the colours. For $\mathsf r=3$ we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{IV-73-63}
\begin{aligned}
&\operatorname{Tr}\bigl[\mathsf m^1C\,\mathsf m^2_{y_2}C\,\mathsf m^3_{y_3}C\bigr]\\
&\qquad=\iint e^{i(\kappa_2\cdot y_2+\kappa_3\cdot y_3)}\Bigl\{\int\operatorname{tr}\bigl[\hat{\mathsf m}^1(l_3,l)\,\hat{C}(l)\,\hat{\mathsf m}^2(l,l_2)\,\hat{C}(l_2)\\
&\qquad\qquad\qquad\hat{\mathsf m}^3(l_2,l_3)\,\hat{C}(l_3)\bigr]\,d^\circ l\Bigr\}\,d^\circ\kappa_2\,d^\circ\kappa_3 ,
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
with $l_2:=l+\kappa_2$, $l_3:=l+\kappa_2+\kappa_3$, all integrals being over $\mathbb T$. Indeed, the sums over the indices are finite and the integrals over the variables $l,l_2,l_3$ of the three covariances converge absolutely; Fubini's theorem allows us to carry out the sums first and then to pass to the variables $\kappa_2=l_2-l$, $\kappa_3=l_3-l_2$. For $\mathsf r=2$ one omits $\mathsf m^3$, the last factor $\hat{C}$ and $\kappa_3$; for $\mathsf r=1$ one has $\operatorname{Tr}[\mathsf m^1C]=\int\operatorname{tr}[\hat{\mathsf m}^1(l,l)\,\hat{C}(l)]\,d^\circ l$. For the quadratic forms $\mathsf F_j:=\frac12(A,\mathsf m^jA)$, \cref{IV-73-53} gives
\[
\begin{gathered}
\langle\mathsf F_1\rangle_0=\tfrac12\operatorname{Tr}[\mathsf m^1C],\qquad\langle\mathsf F_1;\mathsf F_2\rangle_0=\tfrac12\operatorname{Tr}[\mathsf m^1C\,\mathsf m^2C],\\
\langle\mathsf F_1;\mathsf F_2;\mathsf F_3\rangle_0=\operatorname{Tr}[\mathsf m^1C\,\mathsf m^2C\,\mathsf m^3C].
\end{gathered}
\]

The formula \eqref{IV-73-63} also identifies integrands. For a leg $\ell$ of colour $a$ we define $\mathsf v_\ell(k)\in\mathbb C^3$ by $\ell(e^{ik\cdot x}\alpha\,\mathsf e_a)=\mathsf v_\ell(k)\cdot\alpha$, where $e^{ik\cdot x}\alpha\,\mathsf e_a$ denotes the form $(x,\mu)\mapsto e^{ik\cdot x}\alpha_\mu\mathsf e_a$; thus $\mathsf v_\ell(k)=e^{ik\cdot\xi}e_\nu$ for the plain leg at the bond $(\xi,\nu)$, and $\mathsf v_\ell(k)=e^{ik\cdot\xi}\bigl(\mathsf c_{\iota,\nu}(k)\bigr)_{\nu=1,2,3}$ for the curl leg at $p_{[\iota]}(\xi)$. The contraction of $\ell$ with the translate by $y$ of a leg $\ell'$ of the same colour is $\int e^{-ik\cdot y}\,\mathsf v_\ell(k)^{\mathsf T}\,\hat{C}(k)\,\mathsf v_{\ell'}(-k)\,d^\circ k$, and the Hessian $\mathsf m$ of the product $\ell_1\ell_2$ of two legs has
\[
\hat{\mathsf m}(l',l)=\mathsf v_{\ell_1}(-l')\,\mathsf v_{\ell_2}(l)^{\mathsf T}+\mathsf v_{\ell_2}(-l')\,\mathsf v_{\ell_1}(l)^{\mathsf T},
\]
the colour indices being those of the legs. The matrices $\mathsf m^j$ used below are sums of Hessians of monomials in legs. Multiplying out, we find that for all $(l,\kappa)$ the integrand in braces in \eqref{IV-73-63} is a sum of products of the symbols of $\mathsf r$ lines evaluated at $\pm l,\pm l_2,\pm l_3$, and that these products are, term by term, the integrands of the one-loop functions (\cref{IV-73-42}, \cref{IV-73-46}(iii), \cref{IV-73-47}) of the elementary terms of \cref{IV-73-57}, up to substitutions $l\to\pm l+\lambda(\kappa)$ with $\lambda$ linear. At $\kappa=0$ the integrand in braces is the sum of the integrands of these one-loop functions at $\kappa=0$, up to the substitution $l\to-l$ in single terms. We express this by saying that the two sides agree integrand by integrand.

\emph{Step 2: the Hessians at a constant abelian field.} By \cref{IV-73-9} with $t=1$, $a_p(e^{iA})=\sum_m\mathsf a_p^{(m)}(A)$. Let $\mathsf N_j(B)$ and $\mathsf h_q^{(j)}(B)$ be the parts of degree $j$ in $B$ of the Hessians $\mathsf N(B)$ and $\mathsf h_q(B)$ of \cref{IV-73-29}(1). Since $S_3$ is cubic and $S_4$ quartic, $\mathsf N_1(B)$ is the Hessian of the quadratic polynomial $\sum_{b,a}B^a(b)\,\partial_{b,a}S_3$, and $\mathsf N_2(B)$ is that of $\frac12\sum B^a(b)\,B^{a'}(b')\,\partial_{b,a}\partial_{b',a'}S_4$; the matrix $\mathsf h_q^{(j)}(B)$ is obtained in the same way from $\mathsf a_q^{(2+j)}$. Let $\mathsf H_b$ be the Hessian of $\partial_{b,3}S_3$, and let $\mathsf H_b^{\mathsf u}$ and $\mathsf H_b^{\mathsf d}$ be those of $\mathsf u_{b,3}$ and $\mathsf d_{b,3}$ in \eqref{IV-73-58}; these matrices are translation covariant, $\mathsf H_{b+y}=(\mathsf H_b)_y$. For the constant field $Y_\gamma$ of \cref{IV-73-29}(2), with $\mu(b)$ the direction of $b$, we have
\[
\sum_b\gamma_{\mu(b)}\,\mathsf d_{b,3}=\sum_P\langle\mathrm dY_\gamma(P),\mathfrak z_1(P)\rangle=0
\]
(as a quadratic form, every entry of its Hessian being a finite sum), because $\sum_b\gamma_{\mu(b)}\,\mathsf s_P(b)\,\mathsf e_3=\mathrm dY_\gamma(P)$ and $\mathrm dY_\gamma=0$. Hence $\mathsf N_1(Y_\gamma)=\sum_b\gamma_{\mu(b)}\,\mathsf H_b^{\mathsf u}=\sum_\mu\gamma_\mu\sum_y(\mathsf H^{\mathsf u}_{(0,\mu)})_y$, and by Step~1 and \cref{IV-73-29}(2) its symbol is
\[
\sum_\mu\gamma_\mu\,\hat{\mathsf H}^{\mathsf u}_{(0,\mu)}(l,l)=\bigoplus_e\hat{\mathsf N}_{e,1}(l;\gamma)
\]
in the basis $\mathsf e_e$ of the colours.

\emph{Step 3: the structure in (a).} Let $K\in\mathfrak K(n)$ have the symbol $\sigma$ and the leading data $(\sigma^h,K^h)$, and let $y_0\in\mathbb Z^3$. The kernels with the symbols $e^{ik\cdot y_0}\sigma$, $\mathsf k_\mu\sigma$ and $\overline{\mathsf k_\mu}\sigma$ lie in $\mathfrak K(n)$, $\mathfrak K(n+1)$ and $\mathfrak K(n+1)$, respectively, with the leading data $(\sigma^h,K^h)$, $(ik_\mu\sigma^h,\partial_\mu K^h)$ and $(-ik_\mu\sigma^h,-\partial_\mu K^h)$. Indeed, the symbol $\mathsf k_\mu\sigma$ belongs to the kernel $\nabla_\mu K$. For the symbol estimate in \cref{IV-73-38} we write
\[
\mathsf k_\mu\sigma-\chi\,ik_\mu\sigma^h=\mathsf k_\mu(\sigma-\chi\sigma^h)+(\mathsf k_\mu-ik_\mu)\,\chi\sigma^h=O(|k|^{n-1}\lg|k|),
\]
and for the spatial estimate in \cref{IV-73-38}, by Taylor's formula and the homogeneity of the derivatives of $K^h$,
\[
\nabla^\gamma(\nabla_\mu K-\partial_\mu K^h)=\nabla^{\gamma+e_\mu}(K-K^h)+\nabla^\gamma(\nabla_\mu-\partial_\mu)K^h=O(|x|^{-n-2-|\gamma|}\lg|x|);
\]
at the finitely many points with $|\gamma|+1\le|x|<|\gamma|+2$ the left side is a finite number, which is absorbed into the constant. Next, $\overline{\mathsf k_\mu}=-e^{-ik_\mu}\mathsf k_\mu$. For the shift, $(e^{ik\cdot y_0}-1)\,\chi\sigma^h=O(|k|^{n-2})$ and $\nabla^\gamma[K^h(\cdot+y_0)-K^h]=O(|x|^{-n-1-|\gamma|})$. By \cref{IV-73-46}(iii), $K_{\mathrm a}K_{\mathrm b}-\mathsf q_G\in\mathfrak K(n_{\mathrm a}+n_{\mathrm b})$, with the leading data $(\mathsf I_G^h,K_{\mathrm a}^hK_{\mathrm b}^h)$; that lemma applies, since $n_{\mathrm a},n_{\mathrm b}\in\{1,2,3\}$ and $n_{\mathrm a}+n_{\mathrm b}=4-d_G\le4$. A trigonometric polynomial $\mathsf f$ is a finite sum of terms $c\,e^{ik\cdot y_0}$. As a line symbol of degree $0$ it has the leading part $\mathsf f(0)$. As a line symbol of degree $1$ it has $\mathsf f(0)=0$, its leading part is its linear part at $0$, and $\mathsf f$ is a finite sum of terms $c\,e^{ik\cdot y_0}\mathsf k_\mu$: indeed $\mathsf f$ is a linear combination of the functions $e^{ik\cdot y}-1$, and each of these is a telescoping sum, along a nearest-neighbour path from $0$ to $y$, of terms $\pm e^{ik\cdot y_0}\mathsf k_\mu$ (with $\overline{\mathsf k_\mu}=-e^{-ik_\mu}\mathsf k_\mu$ for the steps in the negative direction). Since $\mathfrak K(n)$ is a linear space and the leading data depend linearly on the kernel, multiplication of the symbol by $\mathsf f$ maps $\mathfrak K(n)$ into $\mathfrak K(n)$, resp.\ $\mathfrak K(n+1)$, and multiplies the first component of the leading data by $\mathsf f^h$. Applying this once for each of the two factors of $\mathsf f_G$, we obtain $\mathsf f_G(\nabla)[K_{\mathrm a}K_{\mathrm b}-\mathsf q_G]\in\mathfrak K(n_{\mathrm a}+n_{\mathrm b}+d_G)=\mathfrak K(4)$, with $\mathsf f_G^h\,\mathsf I_G^h$ as the first component of its leading data. Hence $\mathsf W_{\mu\nu}\in\mathfrak K(4)$. The first component of its leading data, $\sum_Gc_G\,\mathsf f_G^h\,\mathsf I_G^h$, depends only on the leading parts $\sigma^h$ (\cref{IV-73-42}) and on the $\mathsf f_G^h$; by \cref{IV-73-46}(iv) the second component is determined by the first, linearly. Finally $\mathsf q^\Sigma_{\mu\nu}$ has finite support, since $\mathsf q^0_{\mu\nu}$ and the $\mathsf q_G$ have and $\mathsf f_G(\nabla)$ is a finite difference operator.

\emph{Step 4: the value of $\hat{\mathsf q}^\Sigma_{\mu\nu}$ at $0$.} The symbol of $\mathsf q_G$ is $\tilde{\mathsf Q}_G$, whose value at $0$ is $\mathsf Q_G(0)$, and $\mathsf f_G(0)=0$ if $d_G\ge1$. Hence
\[
\hat{\mathsf q}^\Sigma_{\mu\nu}(0)=\hat{\mathsf q}^0_{\mu\nu}(0)+\sum_{G:\,d_G=0}c_G\,\mathsf f_G(0)\,\mathsf Q_G(0).
\]
For $d_G=0$ we have $n_{\mathrm a}+n_{\mathrm b}=4$, so that the bubble symbol has $\omega=1$, and \cref{IV-73-42}, with the data of the bubble given in the proof of \cref{IV-73-46}(iii), yields $\mathsf Q_G(0)=\int_{\mathbb T}\sigma_{\mathrm a}(-l)\,\sigma_{\mathrm b}(l)\,d^\circ l$. The terms with $d_G=0$ are the ghost loop and the terms of $-\langle\mathsf u_{b,3};\mathsf u_{b',3}\rangle_0=-\frac12\operatorname{Tr}[\mathsf H_b^{\mathsf u}C\,\mathsf H_{b'}^{\mathsf u}C]$ (Step~1). We compute $\frac12\sum_{\mu,\nu}\gamma_\mu\gamma_\nu$ times each contribution to $\hat{\mathsf q}^\Sigma_{\mu\nu}(0)$.
\begin{itemize}
\item Gluon loop. By \eqref{IV-73-63}, $-\frac12\operatorname{Tr}[\mathsf H^{\mathsf u}_{(0,\mu)}C\,\mathsf H^{\mathsf u}_{(y,\nu)}C]$ is the kernel in $y=b'_--b_-$ with the symbol $\kappa_2\mapsto-\frac12\int\operatorname{tr}[\hat{\mathsf H}^{\mathsf u}_{(0,\mu)}(l_2,l)\,\hat{C}(l)\,\hat{\mathsf H}^{\mathsf u}_{(0,\nu)}(l,l_2)\,\hat{C}(l_2)]\,d^\circ l$, and this symbol is $\sum c_G\,\mathsf f_G\,\mathsf I_G$, summed over the corresponding $G$, integrand by integrand. At zero momentum the integrand is $-\frac12\operatorname{tr}[\hat{\mathsf H}^{\mathsf u}_{(0,\mu)}(l,l)\,\hat{C}(l)\,\hat{\mathsf H}^{\mathsf u}_{(0,\nu)}(l,l)\,\hat{C}(l)]$, and by Step~2
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\tfrac12\sum_{\mu,\nu}\gamma_\mu\gamma_\nu\Bigl(-\tfrac12\int\operatorname{tr}\bigl[\hat{\mathsf H}^{\mathsf u}_{(0,\mu)}(l,l)\,\hat{C}\,\hat{\mathsf H}^{\mathsf u}_{(0,\nu)}(l,l)\,\hat{C}\bigr]\,d^\circ l\Bigr)\\
&\qquad=-\tfrac14\sum_e\int\operatorname{tr}\bigl[(\hat{C}\hat{\mathsf N}_{e,1})^2\bigr]\,d^\circ l=\int_{\mathbb T}\mathfrak s^{(1)}(l;\gamma)\,d^\circ l .
\end{aligned}
\]
\item Gluon tadpole. Let $\mathsf H_{bb'}$ be the Hessian of $\partial_{b,3}\partial_{b',3}S_4$, and let $\mathsf m:=\frac12\sum_{\mu,\nu}\sum_y\gamma_\mu\gamma_\nu\,\mathsf H_{(0,\mu),(y,\nu)}$, a finite sum. By Step~2 and translation covariance $\mathsf N_2(Y_\gamma)=\sum_x\mathsf m_x$, hence $\hat{\mathsf m}(l,l)=\bigoplus_e\hat{\mathsf N}_{e,2}(l;\gamma)$, and Step~1 with $\mathsf r=1$ gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\tfrac12\sum_{\mu,\nu}\gamma_\mu\gamma_\nu\sum_y\langle\partial_{(0,\mu),3}\partial_{(y,\nu),3}S_4\rangle_0&=\tfrac12\operatorname{Tr}[\mathsf m\,C]\\
&=\tfrac12\int\operatorname{tr}\bigl[\hat{\mathsf m}(l,l)\,\hat{C}(l)\bigr]\,d^\circ l=\int_{\mathbb T}\mathfrak s^{(2)}(l;\gamma)\,d^\circ l .
\end{aligned}
\]
\item Haar term: $\frac12\cdot\frac23|\gamma|^2=\frac13|\gamma|^2=\int\mathfrak s^{(5)}$. Ghost tadpole: $\frac12\cdot\frac43\cdot\frac13|\gamma|^2=\frac29|\gamma|^2=\int\mathfrak s^{(4)}$, since by \cref{IV-73-31}(c) $\int\mathfrak s^{(4)}=\sum_{e=\pm1}\frac4{12}\sum_\mu\gamma_\mu^2\int|\mathsf k_\mu|^2|\mathsf k|^{-2}\,d^\circ k$, and $\int|\mathsf k_\mu|^2|\mathsf k|^{-2}\,d^\circ k=\frac13$.
\item Ghost loop. Here $\mathfrak s^{(3)}=4\bigl(\sum_\mu\gamma_\mu\sin k_\mu\bigr)^2|\mathsf k|^{-4}$. By \cref{IV-73-51} the symbols of $y\mapsto D((x,\mu);(x+y,\nu))$ and of $y\mapsto D((x+y,\nu);(x,\mu))$ are $\frac12(1+e^{ik_\nu})\,\overline{\mathsf k_\mu}\,|\mathsf k|^{-2}$ and its image under $\mu\leftrightarrow\nu$, $k\to-k$. Since $(1+e^{ik_\nu})\,\overline{\mathsf k_\nu}=-2i\sin k_\nu$, the ghost loop $G$, for which $c_G=-8$ and $\mathsf f_G=1$, has $\mathsf Q_G(0)=\int\frac14(-2i\sin l_\mu)(-2i\sin l_\nu)\,|\mathsf k(l)|^{-4}\,d^\circ l$, and $\frac12\sum_{\mu,\nu}\gamma_\mu\gamma_\nu\,(-8)\,\mathsf Q_G(0)=\int\mathfrak s^{(3)}$.
\end{itemize}
Summing up, for small $\gamma$ we find\[\frac12\sum_{\mu,\nu}\gamma_\mu\gamma_\nu\,\hat{\mathsf q}^\Sigma_{\mu\nu}(0)=\sum_{i=1}^5\int\mathfrak s^{(i)}=\frac12\sum_{\mu,\nu}\bigl(\sum_ic^{(i)}_{\mu\nu}\bigr)\gamma_\mu\gamma_\nu\] (\cref{IV-73-29}(3)); hence $\hat{\mathsf q}^\Sigma_{\mu\nu}(0)+\hat{\mathsf q}^\Sigma_{\nu\mu}(0)=2\sum_ic^{(i)}_{\mu\nu}$, and this number vanishes, because by \cref{IV-73-34} the five matrices $c^{(i)}$ add up to zero, $\sum_{i=1}^5c^{(i)}_{\mu\nu}=0$ for all $\mu,\nu$. It remains to show that $\hat{\mathsf q}^\Sigma_{\mu\nu}(0)=\hat{\mathsf q}^\Sigma_{\nu\mu}(0)$. Let $\hat\Sigma_{\mu\nu}:=\hat{\mathsf q}^\Sigma_{\mu\nu}+\hat{\mathsf W}_{\mu\nu}$ be the symbol of $\Sigma_{\mu\nu}$. Since $\Sigma$ is symmetric and translation covariant, $\Sigma_{\mu\nu}(y)=\Sigma_{\nu\mu}(-y)$, and the uniqueness of Fourier coefficients gives $\hat\Sigma_{\mu\nu}(k)=\hat\Sigma_{\nu\mu}(-k)$ for almost every $k$. As $\hat{\mathsf q}^\Sigma$ is continuous and $\hat{\mathsf W}(k)\to0$ for $k\to0$, by the symbol estimate in \cref{IV-73-38} for $\mathsf W\in\mathfrak K(4)$, letting $k\to0$ gives the symmetry, and therefore $\hat{\mathsf q}^\Sigma_{\mu\nu}(0)=0$.

\emph{Step 5: the gradient of $\hat{\mathsf q}^\Sigma_{\mu\nu}$ at $0$.} The function $\hat\Sigma_{\mu\nu}$ is integrable on $\mathbb T$, with the Fourier coefficients $\Sigma_{\mu\nu}(y)$. \cref{IV-73-37}(c) with $c=0$, for which $(x,\mu)^R=(-x-e_\mu,\mu)$, gives
\[
\Sigma_{\mu\nu}(y)=\Sigma\bigl((-e_\mu,\mu),(-y-e_\nu,\nu)\bigr)=\Sigma_{\mu\nu}(-y+e_\mu-e_\nu),
\]
hence $\hat\Sigma_{\mu\nu}(k)=e^{-ik\cdot(e_\mu-e_\nu)}\,\hat\Sigma_{\mu\nu}(-k)$ for almost every $k$, by the uniqueness of Fourier coefficients. With $\varphi(k):=\frac12(k_\mu-k_\nu)$ the function $\tilde\Sigma(k):=e^{i\varphi(k)}\hat\Sigma_{\mu\nu}(k)$ is therefore even. By the symbol estimate in \cref{IV-73-38} for $\mathsf W_{\mu\nu}\in\mathfrak K(4)$, $\hat{\mathsf W}_{\mu\nu}=\hat{\mathsf W}^h+O(|k|^2\lg|k|)$ near $0$, where $\hat{\mathsf W}^h=\sum_Gc_G\,\mathsf f_G^h\,\mathsf I_G^h$ is homogeneous of degree $1$ and even: by \cref{IV-73-42} the parity of $\mathsf f_G^h\mathsf I_G^h$ is $(-1)^{d_G}(-1)^{\omega_G+1}$, where $\omega_G=n_{\mathrm a}+n_{\mathrm b}-3$, and $\omega_G+d_G=1$. Consequently the odd part of the smooth function $e^{i\varphi}\hat{\mathsf q}^\Sigma_{\mu\nu}=\tilde\Sigma-e^{i\varphi}\hat{\mathsf W}_{\mu\nu}$ equals the odd part of $-e^{i\varphi}\hat{\mathsf W}^h+O(|k|^2\lg|k|)$, which is $O(|k|^2\lg|k|)$, because $\hat{\mathsf W}^h$ is even and $(e^{i\varphi}-1)\hat{\mathsf W}^h=O(|k|^2)$. So the gradient of $e^{i\varphi}\hat{\mathsf q}^\Sigma_{\mu\nu}$ at $0$ vanishes; as $\hat{\mathsf q}^\Sigma_{\mu\nu}(0)=0$ by Step~4, the gradient of $\hat{\mathsf q}^\Sigma_{\mu\nu}$ at $0$ vanishes as well. Since $\hat{\mathsf q}^\Sigma_{\mu\nu}$ is a trigonometric polynomial, this proves $\hat{\mathsf q}^\Sigma_{\mu\nu}(k)=O(|k|^2)$ and completes the proof of (a).

\emph{Step 6: set-up for (b).} Let $\Gamma_{q;\mu\nu}(y,y'):=\Gamma_q((x_q+y,\mu),(x_q+y',\nu))$. In the rest of the proof $c_G$ denotes $\frac2{3}$ times the number $c_G$ of \cref{IV-73-57}; the reason is that the sums with the numbers $c_G$ of that lemma equal $\frac{3}2\Gamma_q$, by \eqref{IV-73-54}, resp.\ $\frac{3}2\gamma_q$, by the definition of $\gamma_q$ in (b). By the first, second, third and fourth summand we mean the four groups of summands of $\Gamma_q$ as in \eqref{IV-73-54}. In each summand the derivatives $\partial_{b,a}$ and $\partial_{b',a'}$ of \cref{IV-73-29}(5) act on two legs of the vertices at $q$, $P$, $P'$; we call these two legs the outer legs. In the terms on the right of \eqref{IV-73-54} the outer legs are the legs which are contracted with the two curl legs $(\mathrm dA)(p)$, namely the legs at which the lines $K_1$, $K_2$ of \cref{IV-73-57}(4$'$), (4) and (1), resp.\ the lines $K_0$, $X$ of \cref{IV-73-57}(5), end. An outer leg is either plain or a curl leg; in the second case we speak of an outer curl leg. The symbol of a kernel on $\mathbb Z^6$, such as $\Gamma_{q;\mu\nu}$, is defined as in \cref{IV-73-61}(a), so that $\kappa_1$ is the variable dual to $y$ and $\kappa_2$ the variable dual to $y'$; accordingly we say that the outer leg on which $\partial_{b,a}$ acts, $b=(x_q+y,\mu)$, carries the momentum $\kappa_1$, and that the outer leg on which $\partial_{b',a'}$ acts, $b'=(x_q+y',\nu)$, carries the momentum $\kappa_2$. By \eqref{IV-73-54} and \cref{IV-73-57}, $\Gamma_{q;\mu\nu}$ is a finite sum of kernels on $\mathbb Z^6$ with the symbols
\[
c_G\,\mathsf f_{G,1}(\kappa_1)\,\mathsf f_{G,2}(\kappa_2)\,\mathsf J_G(\kappa),
\]
symmetrised under $(\mu,\kappa_1)\leftrightarrow(\nu,\kappa_2)$. Here the $\mathsf f_{G,i}$ are trigonometric polynomials, line symbols of degree $0$ if the corresponding outer leg is plain and of degree $1$ if it is a curl leg. Further, $\mathsf J_G=1$ for the first summand; $\mathsf J_G$ is the bubble symbol $\mathsf I_G(\pm\kappa_2)$ of $Y$ for the second summand, the outer leg at $q$ carrying the momentum $\kappa_1$; $\mathsf J_G=\mathsf I_G(\pm(\kappa_1+\kappa_2))$ for the third summand, both outer legs sitting at $P$; and $\mathsf J_G=\hat{\mathsf T}_{\mathsf q}(\pm\kappa)$ for the fourth summand, the Fourier representation being \eqref{IV-73-48}. By the definition of $\gamma_q$ in (b), the symbol $\hat\gamma_{q;\mu\nu}$ is the same sum with $\mathsf J_G$ replaced by $\tilde{\mathsf Q}_G$, where $\tilde{\mathsf Q}_G:=1$ for the first summand, which is entirely local (the line between two slots of the vertex at $q$ is a number, a factor of $c_G$), and otherwise $\tilde{\mathsf Q}_G$ is the function $\tilde{\mathsf Q}$ of \cref{IV-73-46}(iii), resp.\ $\tilde{\mathsf Q}_{\mathsf q}$ of \cref{IV-73-47}, taken at the argument of $\mathsf J_G$. Indeed, each of the local terms listed in (b) arises from the corresponding full term of \cref{IV-73-57} by replacing a single kernel by its local kernel, while the lines which end at the outer legs are left as they are. In the first half of $\mathsf T_5$ the full term is $K_0(u')\sum_zY(z)\,X(u'-z)$, and the local term has $\mathsf q_Y$ in place of $Y$, in accordance with $X*Y=\mathsf q_Y*X+X*Y'$; in $\mathsf T_4$ the full term is $\sum_zY(z)\,(K_1K_2)(u'-z)$, and again $Y$ is replaced by $\mathsf q_Y$. In $\mathsf T_1$ the substitution $(z,w)\to(u'-z,u'-w)$ turns the full term into
\[
\sum_{z,w}\bigl[K_4(z)\,K_5(w)\,K_3(z-w)\bigr]\,K_1(u'-z)\,K_2(u'-w),
\]
where the bracket, a kernel in $(z,w)$, has the symbol $\hat{\mathsf T}_{\mathsf q}$ by the second identity of \eqref{IV-73-48}; the local term has $\mathsf q_{\mathsf q}(z,w)$, with the symbol $\tilde{\mathsf Q}_{\mathsf q}$, in place of the bracket. The first half of $\mathsf T_{4'}$ is entirely local and is its own local term. In each case the symbol $\mathsf J_G$ of the replaced kernel turns into $\tilde{\mathsf Q}_G$, while the number $c_G$, the factors $\mathsf f_{G,1}$, $\mathsf f_{G,2}$ and the argument of $\mathsf J_G$ remain the same. Let $\hat\Gamma:=\hat\Gamma_{q;\mu\nu}$ be the sum of the symbols of $\Gamma_{q;\mu\nu}$; in $\hat\Gamma-\hat\gamma_{q;\mu\nu}$ the first summand cancels.

\emph{Step 7: counting degrees.} Let $d_{G,i}\in\{0,1\}$ be the degree of $\mathsf f_{G,i}$ and $d_G:=d_{G,1}+d_{G,2}$, the number of outer curl legs; for $G$ in the second, third and fourth summand let $\omega_G$ be the number $\omega$ of $\mathsf J_G$. We use again that the degree of a line is $1+\#$(its curl legs) (\cref{IV-73-51}), and that $\mathsf a^{(2)}$ has two curl legs and every monomial of $\mathsf a^{(3)}$ one (\cref{IV-73-19}). In the second summand the vertices at $q$ and $P$ have two curl legs, of which $2-d_G$ lie on the two bubble lines, so that $\omega_G=2+(2-d_G)-3=1-d_G$. In the fourth summand the vertices at $q$, $P$, $P'$ have four curl legs, of which $4-d_G$ lie on the three lines of $\hat{\mathsf T}_{\mathsf q}$, so that $\omega_G=3+(4-d_G)-6=1-d_G$. In the third summand the bubble lines carry the two curl legs at $q$: for the monomials of $\frac12|\mathfrak z_1|^2$ we get $(d_G,\omega_G)=(0,1)$; for the monomials of $\mathsf a_P^{(4)}$ with one curl leg we get $(1,1)$ or $(0,2)$, according as this leg is outer or not; for those with four curl legs we get $(2,3)$. Thus $d_G+\omega_G=1$, except for these last three kinds, for which $d_G+\min\{\omega_G,2\}\ge2$ and $\omega_G\ge1$.

\emph{Step 8: expansion of $\hat\Gamma-\hat\gamma_{q;\mu\nu}$.} We show that for almost every $\kappa$ with $|\kappa|\le c$, $c$ small,
\[
\begin{gathered}
\hat\Gamma-\hat\gamma_{q;\mu\nu}=\hat\Gamma^h+O\bigl(|\kappa|^2\lg|\kappa|\,\Lambda(\kappa)\bigr),\\
\hat\Gamma^h:=\sum_{G:\,d_G+\omega_G=1}c_G\,\mathsf f_{G,1}^h\,\mathsf f_{G,2}^h\,\mathsf J_G^h,\qquad|\hat\Gamma^h|\le C|\kappa|\,\Lambda(\kappa).
\end{gathered}
\]
Here $\mathsf J_G^h$ is the homogeneous part of $\mathsf J_G$ (\cref{IV-73-42}), taken at the argument of $\mathsf J_G$, and $\Lambda\ge1$ is the function $\Lambda$ of \cref{IV-73-42} for $\hat{\mathsf T}_{\mathsf q}$. The function $\hat\Gamma^h$ is homogeneous of degree $1$ and even, each of its terms having the parity $(-1)^{d_G}(-1)^{\omega_G+1}=1$. Let $\kappa'$ denote the argument of $\mathsf J_G$; then $|\kappa'|\le\sqrt2|\kappa|$. For $d_G+\omega_G\ge2$, \cref{IV-73-46}(iii) gives
\[
\bigl|\mathsf f_{G,1}\mathsf f_{G,2}\,(\mathsf J_G-\tilde{\mathsf Q}_G)\bigr|\le C|\kappa|^{d_G}\,|\kappa'|^{\min\{\omega_G,2\}}\le C|\kappa|^2 .
\]
For the other $G$ we have $\omega_G\le1$, hence $\deg\mathsf Q_G\le1$ and $\mathsf Q_G-\tilde{\mathsf Q}_G=O(|\kappa'|^3)$, and \cref{IV-73-42} gives
\[
\mathsf J_G-\tilde{\mathsf Q}_G=\mathsf J_G^h+O\bigl(|\kappa'|^{\omega_G+1}\lg|\kappa'|\,\Lambda_G(\kappa')\bigr)+O(|\kappa'|^3),
\]
where $\Lambda_G$ is bounded for the bubbles and equals $\Lambda$ for $\hat{\mathsf T}_{\mathsf q}$. Moreover $\mathsf f_{G,i}(\kappa_i)=\mathsf f_{G,i}^h(\kappa_i)+O(|\kappa_i|^{d_{G,i}+1})$, and the functions $t\lg t$ and $t^2\lg t$ are increasing on $(0,1]$, their derivatives being $-\log t$ and $t(1-2\log t)$. We go through the summands.
\begin{itemize}
\item Third summand, $\omega_G=1$, $d_G=0$: $|\mathsf J_G^h|\le C|\kappa'|\le C|\kappa|$, and the errors are $O(|\kappa|^2\lg|\kappa|)$.
\item Fourth summand: $\kappa'=\pm\kappa$, $|\mathsf J_G^h|\le C|\kappa|^{\omega_G}\Lambda$ and $|\mathsf f_{G,1}\mathsf f_{G,2}|\le C|\kappa|^{d_G}$; the leading term is $O(|\kappa|\Lambda)$, and the errors are $O(|\kappa|^2\lg|\kappa|\,\Lambda)$.
\item Second summand: $\kappa'=\pm\kappa_2$, and $\omega_G=-1$ occurs. We take the factor of the outer leg at $P$, which carries the momentum $\kappa_2$, together with $\mathsf J_G$. As $d_{G,2}+\omega_G=1-d_{G,1}\ge0$, we have $|\mathsf f^h_{G,2}(\kappa_2)\,\mathsf J_G^h|\le C|\kappa_2|^{1-d_{G,1}}$ and $|\mathsf f^h_{G,1}\mathsf f^h_{G,2}\,\mathsf J_G^h|\le C|\kappa_1|^{d_{G,1}}|\kappa_2|^{1-d_{G,1}}\le C|\kappa|$. Replacing $\mathsf f_{G,i}$ by its leading part costs a factor $|\kappa_i|$, and
\[
|\mathsf f_{G,1}\mathsf f_{G,2}|\,|\kappa_2|^{\omega_G+1}\lg|\kappa_2|\le C|\kappa_1|^{d_{G,1}}\,|\kappa_2|^{2-d_{G,1}}\lg|\kappa_2|\le C|\kappa|^2\lg|\kappa| .
\]
\end{itemize}
The symmetrised terms are treated in the same way, with the indices $1$ and $2$ exchanged.

\emph{Step 9: the value of $\hat\gamma_{q;\mu\nu}$ at $0$.} We have $\hat\gamma_{q;\mu\nu}(0)=\sum c_G\,\mathsf f_{G,1}(0)\,\mathsf f_{G,2}(0)\,\tilde{\mathsf Q}_G(0)$, the sum extending over the $G$ with two plain outer legs, as an outer curl leg gives $\mathsf f_{G,i}(0)=0$. For such $G$ in the first summand, $\tilde{\mathsf Q}_G=1$, and the line between two slots of the vertex at $q$, contained in $c_G$, is the integral of its symbol (the case $\mathsf r=1$ of Step~1). For such $G$ in the other summands, $d_G=0$, hence $\omega_G\ge1$ by Step~7, and $\tilde{\mathsf Q}_G(0)=\mathsf Q_G(0)$ is the integral of the integrand at $\kappa=0$ (\cref{IV-73-42}). By Step~1 the four summands of $\Gamma_q(b,3;b',3)$ have the trace forms
\[
\begin{gathered}
\tfrac12\operatorname{Tr}[\mathsf m_{bb'}C],\qquad-\tfrac12\operatorname{Tr}[\mathsf m_bC\,\mathsf H_{b'}C]-(b\leftrightarrow b'),\\
-\tfrac12\operatorname{Tr}[\mathsf h_q^{(0)}C\,\mathsf H_{bb'}C],\qquad\operatorname{Tr}[\mathsf h_q^{(0)}C\,\mathsf H_bC\,\mathsf H_{b'}C],
\end{gathered}
\]
where $\mathsf m_{bb'}$, $\mathsf m_b$ and $\mathsf H_{bb'}$ are the Hessians of $\partial\partial'\mathsf a_q^{(4)}$, $\partial\mathsf a_q^{(3)}$ and $\partial\partial'S_4$ ($\partial=\partial_{b,3}$, $\partial'=\partial_{b',3}$), $\mathsf H_b$ is the Hessian of $\partial_{b,3}S_3$ (Step~2), and $\mathsf h_q^{(0)}$ is the Hessian of $\mathsf a_q^{(2)}$. By Step~2,
\[
\begin{gathered}
\sum_{b,b'}\tfrac12\gamma_{\mu(b)}\gamma_{\mu(b')}\,\mathsf m_{bb'}=\mathsf h_q^{(2)}(Y_\gamma),\qquad\sum_b\gamma_{\mu(b)}\,\mathsf m_b=\mathsf h_q^{(1)}(Y_\gamma),\\
\sum_\mu\gamma_\mu\,\hat{\mathsf H}_{(0,\mu)}(l,l)=\bigoplus_e\hat{\mathsf N}_{e,1}(l;\gamma),\\
\sum_{\mu,\nu}\sum_y\tfrac12\gamma_\mu\gamma_\nu\,\hat{\mathsf H}_{(0,\mu),(y,\nu)}(l,l)=\bigoplus_e\hat{\mathsf N}_{e,2}(l;\gamma),
\end{gathered}
\]
the sums in the first line being finite; and $\hat{\mathsf h}(l,l)$ is the matrix of the form $(e^{il\cdot x}\alpha'\mathsf e_e,\mathsf h\,e^{il\cdot x}\alpha\,\mathsf e_e)$, which for $\mathsf h=\mathsf h_q^{(j)}(Y_\gamma)$ is $\bigoplus_e\hat{\mathsf h}_{q,e,j}(l;\gamma)$ by \cref{IV-73-29}(2). The parts of the Hessians which come from an outer curl leg drop out here, since $\mathrm dY_\gamma=0$; they belong to the $G$ with $\mathsf f_{G,1}(0)\,\mathsf f_{G,2}(0)=0$. We use \eqref{IV-73-63} at $\kappa=0$, integrand by integrand, and write $\hat{\mathsf h}_j:=\bigoplus_e\hat{\mathsf h}_{q,e,j}$ and $\hat{\mathsf N}_j:=\bigoplus_e\hat{\mathsf N}_{e,j}$. The four summands contribute to $\frac12\sum_{\mu,\nu}\gamma_\mu\gamma_\nu\,\hat\gamma_{q;\mu\nu}(0)$ the amounts
\[
\begin{gathered}
\tfrac12\!\int\!\operatorname{tr}\bigl[\hat{\mathsf h}_2\hat{C}\bigr],\qquad\tfrac12\cdot2\cdot\bigl(-\tfrac12\bigr)\!\int\!\operatorname{tr}\bigl[\hat{\mathsf h}_1\hat{C}\hat{\mathsf N}_1\hat{C}\bigr],\\
-\tfrac12\!\int\!\operatorname{tr}\bigl[\hat{\mathsf h}_0\hat{C}\hat{\mathsf N}_2\hat{C}\bigr],\qquad\tfrac12\!\int\!\operatorname{tr}\bigl[\hat{\mathsf h}_0\hat{C}\hat{\mathsf N}_1\hat{C}\hat{\mathsf N}_1\hat{C}\bigr]
\end{gathered}
\]
(integrals over $\mathbb T$ with respect to $d^\circ l$), and these are $\int\mathfrak v_q^{(j)}(l;\gamma)\,d^\circ l$, $j=1,\dots,4$, by \cref{IV-73-29}(4). Hence, by \cref{IV-73-29}(4) and \cref{IV-73-36},
\[
\tfrac12\sum_{\mu,\nu}\gamma_\mu\gamma_\nu\,\hat\gamma_{q;\mu\nu}(0)=\tfrac12\sum_{\mu,\nu}\gamma_\mu\gamma_\nu\sum_{j=1}^4\mathsf g^{(j)}_{q;\mu\nu}=0
\]
for all small $\gamma$. Since $\gamma_q$ is a symmetric kernel, $\hat\gamma_{q;\mu\nu}(0)$ is symmetric in $\mu,\nu$, and therefore $\hat\gamma_{q;\mu\nu}(0)=0$.

\emph{Step 10: the gradient of $\hat\gamma_{q;\mu\nu}$ at $0$.} \cref{IV-73-37}(c) with $c=x(q)$, for which $R_cq=q$, gives
\[
\Gamma_{q;\mu\nu}(y,y')=\Gamma_{q;\mu\nu}(\mathsf o-e_\mu-y,\ \mathsf o-e_\nu-y'),\qquad\mathsf o:=2\bigl(x(q)-x_q\bigr),
\]
and the uniqueness of Fourier coefficients gives $\hat\Gamma(\kappa)=e^{-2i\varphi(\kappa)}\,\hat\Gamma(-\kappa)$ for almost every $\kappa$, with the real linear form $\varphi(\kappa):=\frac12[\kappa_1\cdot(\mathsf o-e_\mu)+\kappa_2\cdot(\mathsf o-e_\nu)]$; hence $e^{i\varphi}\hat\Gamma$ is even almost everywhere. Since $\hat\Gamma^h$ is even, the odd part of $e^{i\varphi}\hat\Gamma^h$ is $O(|\kappa|^2\Lambda)$. By Step~8 the odd part of the smooth function $e^{i\varphi}\hat\gamma_{q;\mu\nu}$ is therefore $O(|\kappa|^2\lg|\kappa|\,\Lambda)$ almost everywhere near $0$. The function $\Lambda$ is bounded on an open cone. Indeed, for $\hat{\mathsf T}_{\mathsf q}$ we have $(l_1,l_2,l_3)(\kappa)=(\kappa_1,-\kappa_2,0)$ (Step~2 of the proof of \cref{IV-73-47}), so that the differences $l_i(\kappa)-l_j(\kappa)$, $i<j$, are $\kappa_1+\kappa_2$, $\kappa_1$ and $-\kappa_2$. Let
\[
\mathsf K:=\bigl\{\kappa\in\mathbb R^6:\ \min\{|\kappa_1|,|\kappa_2|,|\kappa_1+\kappa_2|\}>\tfrac12|\kappa|\bigr\}.
\]
This set is open, it is invariant under $\kappa\to t\kappa$ for real $t\ne0$, and it is not empty, since it contains $(v,v)$ for every $v\in\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$: there $|\kappa|=\sqrt2\,|v|$, while $|\kappa_1|=|\kappa_2|=|v|$ and $|\kappa_1+\kappa_2|=2|v|$. On $\mathsf K$ each of the three terms $\log_+\bigl(|\kappa|/|l_i(\kappa)-l_j(\kappa)|\bigr)$ in the definition of $\Lambda$ is at most $\log2$, so that $\Lambda\le1+3\log2$ there. On $\mathsf K$ the odd part is therefore $O(|\kappa|^2\lg|\kappa|)$ almost everywhere near $0$. The odd part of the smooth function $e^{i\varphi}\hat\gamma_{q;\mu\nu}$ differs from its linear part $\kappa\mapsto\kappa\cdot\nabla(e^{i\varphi}\hat\gamma_{q;\mu\nu})(0)$ by $O(|\kappa|^3)$. Hence $|\kappa\cdot\nabla(e^{i\varphi}\hat\gamma_{q;\mu\nu})(0)|\le C|\kappa|^2\lg|\kappa|$ for almost every, and by continuity for every, $\kappa\in\mathsf K$ with $|\kappa|\le c$. Replacing $\kappa$ by $t\kappa$ and letting $t\downarrow0$, we see that this linear function vanishes on $\mathsf K$, a non-empty open set, and hence everywhere: the gradient of $e^{i\varphi}\hat\gamma_{q;\mu\nu}$ at $0$ vanishes. As $\hat\gamma_{q;\mu\nu}(0)=0$ by Step~9, the gradient of $\hat\gamma_{q;\mu\nu}$ at $0$ vanishes as well. This proves (b).
\end{proof}

\subsection{The six terms, the continuum model, the kernel of degree $-5$}

In this subsection we introduce six continuum two-loop integrands and a model built from them, with a smooth ultraviolet cut-off on every line. We show that the model has the same parts of degree $-5$ as the lattice classes of \cref{IV-73-57}, that these parts are multiples of $|u|^{-5}$, and we deduce the large-distance asymptotics of $\mathsf B_1^{\mathrm{lat}}$ and its consequence for smeared plaquette observables.

\begin{definition}[The six two-loop integrands; the model]\label{IV-73-64}
\emph{(1) Tensors and variables.} For $k_1,k_2,k_3\in\mathbb R^3$ we put
\begin{gather*}
v_2(k_1,k_2)_{\mu\nu}:=-(k_1\cdot k_2)\,\delta_{\mu\nu}+k_{1\nu}k_{2\mu},\\
v_3(k_1,k_2,k_3)_{\alpha\beta\gamma}:=\delta_{\alpha\gamma}(k_1-k_3)_\beta+\delta_{\alpha\beta}(k_2-k_1)_\gamma+\delta_{\beta\gamma}(k_3-k_2)_\alpha .
\end{gather*}
The tensor $v_2$ is even and the tensor $v_3$ is odd under the simultaneous change of sign $k_i\to-k_i$ of all arguments, and $|v_2(k_1,k_2)_{\mu\nu}|\le2|k_1||k_2|$ for all $\mu,\nu$. For $k,l,\mathsf p\in\mathbb R^3$ we write
\[
\mathsf x_0:=\mathsf p^2,\quad\mathsf x_1:=k^2,\quad\mathsf x_1':=(k-\mathsf p)^2,\quad\mathsf x_2:=l^2,\quad\mathsf x_2':=(l-\mathsf p)^2,\quad\mathsf x_3:=(k-l)^2 .
\]

\emph{(2) The six integrands.} With summation over repeated tensor indices we define
\begin{equation}\label{IV-73-65}
\begin{aligned}
F_1&:=-\tfrac12\,v_2(k,\mathsf p-k)_{\mu\nu}\,v_2(-l,l-\mathsf p)_{\rho\sigma}\\
&\qquad\qquad\times v_3(-k,l,k-l)_{\mu\rho\alpha}\,v_3(k-\mathsf p,\mathsf p-l,l-k)_{\nu\sigma\alpha}\,/\,\mathsf x_1\mathsf x_1'\mathsf x_2\mathsf x_2'\mathsf x_3,\\
F_2&:=-\tfrac12\,v_2(k,\mathsf p-k)_{\mu\nu}\,v_2(-k,k-\mathsf p)_{\rho\nu}\\
&\qquad\qquad\times v_3(-k,l,k-l)_{\mu\beta\gamma}\,v_3(k,-l,l-k)_{\rho\beta\gamma}\,/\,\mathsf x_1^2\mathsf x_1'\mathsf x_2\mathsf x_3,\\
F_3&:=-\,v_2(k,\mathsf p-k)_{\mu\nu}\,v_2(-k,k-\mathsf p)_{\rho\nu}\,l_\rho(l-k)_\mu\,/\,\mathsf x_1^2\mathsf x_1'\mathsf x_2\mathsf x_3,\\
F_4&:=-\tfrac12\bigl[v_2(k,\mathsf p-k)_{\mu\mu}v_2(l,\mathsf p-l)_{\nu\nu}\\
&\qquad\qquad-\tfrac12v_2(k,\mathsf p-k)_{\mu\nu}\bigl(v_2(l,\mathsf p-l)_{\mu\nu}+v_2(l,\mathsf p-l)_{\nu\mu}\bigr)\bigr]/\,\mathsf x_1\mathsf x_1'\mathsf x_2\mathsf x_2',\\
F_5&:=v_3(\mathsf p-k,l,k-l)_{\alpha\beta\gamma}\,v_3(k,-l,l-k)_{\sigma\beta\gamma}\,v_2(k-\mathsf p,-k)_{\alpha\sigma}\,/\,\mathsf x_1'\mathsf x_1\mathsf x_2\mathsf x_3,\\
F_6&:=-\tfrac16\,v_3(l,k-l,\mathsf p-k)_{\alpha\beta\gamma}\,v_3(-l,l-k,k-\mathsf p)_{\alpha\beta\gamma}\,/\,\mathsf x_2\mathsf x_3\mathsf x_1' .
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
We call $F_1$ the kite, $F_2$ the gluon loop on a line, $F_3$ the ghost loop on a line, $F_4$ the quartic vertex, $F_5$ the term of $\mathsf a^{(3)}$ with $S_3$, and $F_6$ the term of $\mathsf a^{(3)}$ with $\mathsf a^{(3)}$. Each $F_\Gamma$, $\Gamma\in\{1,\dots,6\}$, is a rational function of $(k,l,\mathsf p)$, homogeneous of degree $-4$, even under $(k,l,\mathsf p)\to-(k,l,\mathsf p)$, and invariant under simultaneous rotations of $k$, $l$ and $\mathsf p$. The \emph{lines of $\Gamma$} are the vectors whose squares occur in the denominator of $F_\Gamma$, counted with multiplicity: for $\Gamma=1$ the vectors $k,\mathsf p-k,l,\mathsf p-l,k-l$; for $\Gamma=2,3$ the vector $k$ twice and the vectors $\mathsf p-k,l,k-l$; for $\Gamma=4$ the vectors $k,\mathsf p-k,l,\mathsf p-l$; for $\Gamma=5$ the vectors $k,\mathsf p-k,l,k-l$; for $\Gamma=6$ the vectors $\mathsf p-k,l,k-l$.

\emph{(3) The model.} Let $\rho_0:=\frac\pi{16}$, and let $\rho(\mathsf q):=\theta(|\mathsf q|/2\rho_0)$ for $\mathsf q\in\mathbb R^3$, with the function $\theta$ of \cref{IV-73-38}; thus $\rho(\mathsf q)=1$ for $|\mathsf q|\le\rho_0$ and $\rho(\mathsf q)=0$ for $|\mathsf q|\ge2\rho_0$. Let $R_\Gamma(k,l,\mathsf p)$ be the product of the values of $\rho$ at the lines of $\Gamma$. We define
\[
\Psi_\Gamma(\mathsf p):=\iint R_\Gamma F_\Gamma\,d^\circ k\,d^\circ l\quad(\mathsf p\in\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}),\qquad
\mathsf T^{\mathrm{mod}}_\Gamma(u):=24\int_{\mathbb R^3}e^{i\mathsf p\cdot u}\,\Psi_\Gamma(\mathsf p)\,d^\circ\mathsf p\quad(u\in\mathbb Z^3),
\]
the first integral extending over $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R^3$.

These integrals converge absolutely. Indeed, every entry of $v_3(k_1,k_2,k_3)$ is bounded by $C\max_i|k_i|$; together with the bound on the entries of $v_2$ and with the denominators this gives, on every bounded set of points $(k,l,\mathsf p)$ and with a constant $C$ depending on that set,
\begin{equation}\label{IV-73-66}
\begin{gathered}
|F_1|\le\frac C{|k|\,|\mathsf p-k|\,|l|\,|\mathsf p-l|\,|k-l|^2},\qquad|F_2|,\ |F_3|\le\frac{C(|k|+|l|)}{|k|^2|l|^2|k-l|^2},\\
|F_4|\le\frac C{|k|\,|\mathsf p-k|\,|l|\,|\mathsf p-l|},\qquad|F_5|\le\frac C{|k|\,|\mathsf p-k|\,|l|^2|k-l|^2},\qquad
|F_6|\le\frac C{|\mathsf p-k|^2|l|^2|k-l|^2}.
\end{gathered}
\end{equation}
We integrate these majorants first over $l$ and then over $k$. For $v,w$ in a bounded subset of $\mathbb R^3$, and with integrals over a bounded set of $l$, we have the elementary bounds
\[
\int|l-v|^{-2}|l-w|^{-2}\,dl\le C|v-w|^{-1},\qquad\int|l-v|^{-1}|l-w|^{-2}\,dl\le C\lg|v-w| ,
\]
with constants depending on these sets; moreover $|l|^{-1}|\mathsf p-l|^{-1}\le|\mathsf p|^{-1}\bigl(|l|^{-1}+|\mathsf p-l|^{-1}\bigr)$, since $|\mathsf p|\le|l|+|\mathsf p-l|$, and $|k|+|l|\le2|k|+|k-l|$. For $\Gamma=1$ the majorant is at most $C|\mathsf p|^{-2}\bigl(|k|^{-1}+|\mathsf p-k|^{-1}\bigr)\bigl(|l|^{-1}+|\mathsf p-l|^{-1}\bigr)|k-l|^{-2}$; its integral over $l$ is at most $C|\mathsf p|^{-2}\bigl(|k|^{-1}+|\mathsf p-k|^{-1}\bigr)\bigl(\lg|k|+\lg|k-\mathsf p|\bigr)$, which is integrable over bounded sets of $k$, with a bound uniform for $\mathsf p$ in a bounded set. For $\Gamma=4$ the same argument applies without the factor $|k-l|^{-2}$. For $\Gamma=2,3$ the majorant is at most $2C|k|^{-1}|l|^{-2}|k-l|^{-2}+C|k|^{-2}|l|^{-2}|k-l|^{-1}$, whose integral over $l$ is at most $C|k|^{-2}\lg|k|$, a function integrable over bounded sets of $k$. For $\Gamma=5$ the integral over $l$ is at most $C|k|^{-2}|\mathsf p-k|^{-1}$, and the subsequent integral over $k$ is at most $C\lg|\mathsf p|$. For $\Gamma=6$ the integral over $l$ is at most $C|k|^{-1}|\mathsf p-k|^{-2}$, and again the integral over $k$ is at most $C\lg|\mathsf p|$. Hence, for $\mathsf p$ in a bounded set, the integral of each majorant over a bounded set of $(k,l)$ is at most $C|\mathsf p|^{-2}$, since $1$ and $\lg|\mathsf p|$ are bounded by $C|\mathsf p|^{-2}$ there.

Where $R_\Gamma\ne0$, every line of $\Gamma$ has modulus less than $2\rho_0$. Hence $|l|<2\rho_0$ and $|k|<4\rho_0$ there (by the lines $l$ and $k$, and for $\Gamma=6$ by the lines $l$ and $k-l$), and $|\mathsf p|\le|\mathsf p-k|+|k|<6\rho_0$, by the line $\mathsf p-k$, which occurs for every $\Gamma$. Consequently the integral defining $\Psi_\Gamma(\mathsf p)$ converges absolutely, $|\Psi_\Gamma(\mathsf p)|\le C|\mathsf p|^{-2}$, and $\Psi_\Gamma$ is integrable, radial (by the rotation invariance of $F_\Gamma$ and of $R_\Gamma$, and the substitution $(k,l)\to(Ok,Ol)$), and equal to $0$ for $|\mathsf p|\ge6\rho_0=\frac{3\pi}8$; in particular $\mathsf T^{\mathrm{mod}}_\Gamma(u)$ is well defined.
\end{definition}

In order to compare the model with the elementary terms of \cref{IV-73-57}, we write these terms, too, as integrals over momenta.

\begin{lemma}[Momentum-space forms]\label{IV-73-67}
\textup{(a)} Let $K_1,\dots,K_5$ be elementary lines as in \cref{IV-73-47}, with symbols $\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_5$, and let $\mathsf T$ be their kite. Then, for every $u\in\mathbb Z^3$,
\[
\mathsf T(u)=\int_{\mathbb T}e^{i\mathsf p\cdot u}\Bigl[\iint_{\mathbb T^2}\sigma_1(k)\,\sigma_2(\mathsf p-k)\,\sigma_3(k-l)\,\sigma_4(l)\,\sigma_5(\mathsf p-l)\,d^\circ k\,d^\circ l\Bigr]d^\circ\mathsf p ,
\]
and the triple integral converges absolutely.

\textup{(b)} If two kernels have symbols $\sigma_{\mathrm a},\sigma_{\mathrm b}\in L^1(\mathbb T)$, then their product is the kernel whose symbol is the convolution $k\mapsto\int_{\mathbb T}\sigma_{\mathrm a}(k-l)\,\sigma_{\mathrm b}(l)\,d^\circ l$ of the two symbols. If $X,Y\in\ell^2(\mathbb Z^3)$ are kernels with symbols $\hat X,\hat Y\in L^1(\mathbb T)$, then $X*Y$ \textup{(}\cref{IV-73-46}\textup{)} is the kernel with the symbol $\hat X\hat Y$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
We begin with (b). Let $K_{\mathrm a},K_{\mathrm b}$ be the two kernels. The function $(k,l)\mapsto\sigma_{\mathrm a}(k)\sigma_{\mathrm b}(l)$ is integrable over $\mathbb T^2$; by Fubini's theorem and the substitution $k\to k-l$ on $\mathbb T$,
\[
K_{\mathrm a}(x)\,K_{\mathrm b}(x)=\iint e^{i(k+l)\cdot x}\,\sigma_{\mathrm a}(k)\,\sigma_{\mathrm b}(l)\,d^\circ k\,d^\circ l=\int_{\mathbb T}e^{ik\cdot x}\Bigl[\int_{\mathbb T}\sigma_{\mathrm a}(k-l)\,\sigma_{\mathrm b}(l)\,d^\circ l\Bigr]d^\circ k ,
\]
and the bracket is an integrable function of $k$. For the second assertion we note that $X\in\ell^2(\mathbb Z^3)$ is, by Plancherel's theorem, the sequence of Fourier coefficients of a function in $L^2(\mathbb T)$, which coincides with $\hat X$ by the uniqueness of Fourier coefficients; thus $\hat X\in L^2(\mathbb T)$, and likewise $\hat Y\in L^2(\mathbb T)$. The kernel $z\mapsto Y(u-z)$ has the symbol $k\mapsto e^{-ik\cdot u}\hat Y(-k)$, and Plancherel's theorem in the form $\sum_za(z)b(z)=\int_{\mathbb T}\hat a(-k)\,\hat b(k)\,d^\circ k$, for square summable kernels $a,b$ with symbols $\hat a,\hat b$, gives $(X*Y)(u)=\int_{\mathbb T}e^{ik\cdot u}\hat X(k)\hat Y(k)\,d^\circ k$.

We turn to (a). \emph{Step 1.} For $i\ne3$ the degree $n_i$ is at least $2$, so that $|\sigma_i(\mathsf q)|\le C|\mathsf q|^{-1}$ on $[-\pi,\pi]^3$ (\cref{IV-73-38}); hence $\sigma_i\in L^2(\mathbb T)$ for $i\ne3$, while $\sigma_3\in L^1(\mathbb T)$. The functions
\[
\mathsf A(v):=\int_{\mathbb T}\sigma_1(v+\mathsf q)\,\sigma_4(\mathsf q)\,e^{iu\cdot\mathsf q}\,d^\circ\mathsf q,\qquad
\mathsf B(v):=\int_{\mathbb T}\sigma_2(v+\mathsf q)\,\sigma_5(\mathsf q)\,e^{iu\cdot\mathsf q}\,d^\circ\mathsf q
\]
are bounded, by the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality, and continuous, since translations act continuously on $L^2(\mathbb T)$. Consequently
\[
\Phi(\eta_1,\eta_2):=\int_{\mathbb T}\sigma_3(\mathsf q)\,\mathsf A(\eta_1+\mathsf q)\,\mathsf B(\eta_2-\mathsf q)\,d^\circ\mathsf q
\]
is bounded and continuous on $\mathbb T^2$, by dominated convergence, and the integral over $(\mathsf q_3,\mathsf q_4,\mathsf q_5)\in\mathbb T^3$ which results from inserting the definitions of $\mathsf A$ and $\mathsf B$ (with $\mathsf q_3$ in place of $\mathsf q$ and $\mathsf q_4,\mathsf q_5$ the variables of $\mathsf A,\mathsf B$) converges absolutely.

\emph{Step 2.} Let $\phi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ with support in $\{|x|\le1\}$ and $\phi(0)=1$, and let $\phi_R:=\phi(\cdot/R)$. By \cref{IV-73-47}, the double sum defining $\mathsf T(u)$ converges absolutely; by dominated convergence, $\mathsf T(u)=\lim_{R\to\infty}\mathsf T_R(u)$, where $\mathsf T_R(u)$ denotes the same sum with the additional factor $\phi_R(z)\phi_R(w)$. For fixed $R$ we insert $K_i(y)=\int_{\mathbb T}e^{i\mathsf q_i\cdot y}\sigma_i(\mathsf q_i)\,d^\circ\mathsf q_i$. The sums over $z$ and $w$ are then finite, and by Fubini's theorem they produce the factor
\[
\check\phi_R\bigl(-(\mathsf q_1-\mathsf q_3-\mathsf q_4)\bigr)\,\check\phi_R\bigl(-(\mathsf q_2+\mathsf q_3-\mathsf q_5)\bigr)\,e^{iu\cdot(\mathsf q_4+\mathsf q_5)} .
\]
We pass to the variables $\eta_1:=\mathsf q_1-\mathsf q_3-\mathsf q_4$, $\eta_2:=\mathsf q_2+\mathsf q_3-\mathsf q_5$, $\mathsf q_3$, $\mathsf q_4$, $\mathsf q_5$; this is a linear change of variables with integer matrix of determinant $\pm1$, hence a measure preserving bijection of $\mathbb T^5$, and it gives
\[
\mathsf T_R(u)=\iint_{\mathbb T^2}\check\phi_R(-\eta_1)\,\check\phi_R(-\eta_2)\,\Phi(\eta_1,\eta_2)\,d^\circ\eta_1\,d^\circ\eta_2 .
\]
Here $\int_{\mathbb T}\check\phi_R(-\eta)\,d^\circ\eta=\phi_R(0)=1$, and $|\check\phi_R(\eta)|\le CR^3\langle R\eta\rangle^{-10}$ by \cref{IV-73-41}, applied with $D=3$ to the restriction of $\phi_R$ to $\mathbb Z^3$; this function vanishes off $\{|\zeta|\le R\}$, and its norm $\|\phi_R\|_{(R)}$ is at most $\|\phi\|_{C^{10}}$, a difference being an integral of a derivative. Thus the functions $\eta\mapsto\check\phi_R(-\eta)$ have integral $1$, bounded $L^1$ norms, and integrals over $\{|\eta|\ge\delta\}$ tending to $0$ as $R\to\infty$, for every $\delta>0$. As $\Phi$ is bounded and continuous at $(0,0)$, $\mathsf T_R(u)\to\Phi(0,0)$.

\emph{Step 3.} In the triple integral $\Phi(0,0)$ we change variables to $l=\mathsf q_4$, $k=\mathsf q_3+\mathsf q_4$, $\mathsf p=\mathsf q_4+\mathsf q_5$, again a measure preserving bijection of $\mathbb T^3$. Then $\mathsf q_3=k-l$, $\mathsf q_5=\mathsf p-l$ and $\mathsf q_5-\mathsf q_3=\mathsf p-k$, so that the integrand becomes $\sigma_1(k)\,\sigma_2(\mathsf p-k)\,\sigma_3(k-l)\,\sigma_4(l)\,\sigma_5(\mathsf p-l)\,e^{i\mathsf p\cdot u}$. The triple integral converges absolutely by Step~1, and Fubini's theorem yields the formula of (a).
\end{proof}

The next lemma computes the weights with which the leading parts of the elementary terms add up to the six integrands of \cref{IV-73-64}.

\begin{lemma}[The weights of the six terms]\label{IV-73-68}
Let $\tau_{\mathrm{gf}}=1$, and let $p=p_{[\iota]}(x_p)$, $q=p_{[\iota']}(x_q)$. To an elementary term $G$ of \cref{IV-73-57}, with its lines named as there, we attach its \emph{leading integrand} $\mathsf F_G(k,l,\mathsf p)$, where $\sigma^h$ denotes the leading part of the symbol of the line in question:
\[
\begin{array}{ll}
G\in\mathfrak G_1: & \sigma_1^h(k)\,\sigma_2^h(\mathsf p-k)\,\sigma_3^h(k-l)\,\sigma_4^h(l)\,\sigma_5^h(\mathsf p-l);\\[3pt]
G\in\mathfrak G_4,\ (n_X,n_Y)=(4,4): & \sigma_1^h(k)\,\sigma_2^h(\mathsf p-k)\,\sigma_3^h(l)\,\sigma_4^h(\mathsf p-l);\\[3pt]
G\in\mathfrak G_5: & \sigma_0^h(\mathsf p-k)\,\sigma_X^h(k)\,\sigma_{\mathrm a}^h(k-l)\,\sigma_{\mathrm b}^h(l);\\[3pt]
G\in\mathfrak G_6: & \sigma_1^h(\mathsf p-k)\,\sigma_2^h(k-l)\,\sigma_3^h(l);\\[3pt]
G\in\mathfrak G_{\mathrm I}(\mu,\nu): & \sigma_\Pi^h(\mathsf p-k)\,\sigma^h_{\to,\iota\mu}(k)\,\mathsf f_G^h(k)\,\sigma_{\mathrm a}^h(k-l)\,\sigma_{\mathrm b}^h(l)\,\sigma^h_{\leftarrow,\nu\iota'}(k);
\end{array}
\]
here $\sigma_\Pi$, $\sigma_\to$ and $\sigma_\leftarrow$ are the symbols of $y\mapsto\Pi\bigl(p_{[\iota]}(0),p_{[\iota']}(y)\bigr)$, of $K^\to_{\iota\mu}$ and of $K^\leftarrow_{\nu\iota'}$. Let $\mathfrak G_2=\mathfrak G_2(\iota,\iota')$, resp.\ $\mathfrak G_3=\mathfrak G_3(\iota,\iota')$, be the set of the triples $(\mu,\nu,G)$ such that $G\in\mathfrak G_{\mathrm I}(\mu,\nu)$ is a term of $-\langle\partial S_3;\partial'S_3\rangle_0$, resp.\ of the ghost loop, in \eqref{IV-73-59}; such a triple carries the coefficient $-3\,c_G$, which takes the place of $c_G$ in the sums below. Then, with sums over $\iota,\iota'\in\{1,2,3\}$ and over $G\in\mathfrak G_\Gamma(\iota,\iota')$, where for $\Gamma=4$ only the terms with $(n_X,n_Y)=(4,4)$ are taken,
\[
\sum_{\iota,\iota'}\sum_G c_G\,\mathsf F_G=24\,F_\Gamma\quad(\Gamma=1,2,3,4,6),\qquad\sum_{\iota,\iota'}\sum_{G\in\mathfrak G_5}c_G\,\mathsf F_G=12\,F_5 .
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\emph{Step 1 (Feynman rules).} Let $K(y)=\int e^{i\mathsf q\cdot y}\sigma(\mathsf q)\,d^\circ\mathsf q$ be a line, where $y$ is the base point of its second leg minus that of its first leg; we say that the line carries the momentum $\mathsf q$ from the first vertex to the second. The momentum entering a vertex through this line is then $\mathsf q$ at the second vertex and $-\mathsf q$ at the first. Leading parts of line symbols are additive and multiplicative (\cref{IV-73-38}); hence the sum over the monomials of a vertex may be carried out on the leading parts. By \cref{IV-73-51} at $\tau_{\mathrm{gf}}=1$, every line contributes a factor $\delta_{\mu\nu}|\mathsf q|^{-2}$, where at a plain leg the index of the line is the direction of the bond of that leg; a curl leg at a plaquette $p_{\alpha\beta}$ contributes the factor $i(\mathsf q'_\alpha\delta_{\nu\beta}-\mathsf q'_\beta\delta_{\nu\alpha})$, where $\mathsf q'$ is the momentum entering the vertex; and shifts of base points contribute the factor $1$, the leading part of $e^{ik\cdot y_0}$.

\emph{Step 2 (the vertex $\mathsf a^{(2)}$).} Two curl legs at $p_{[\iota]}$, with entering momenta $k_1,k_2$ and line indices $\mu,\nu$, give after summation over $\iota$, that is, over $\alpha<\beta$,
\[
\begin{aligned}
&i^2\sum_{\alpha<\beta}(k_{1\alpha}\delta_{\mu\beta}-k_{1\beta}\delta_{\mu\alpha})(k_{2\alpha}\delta_{\nu\beta}-k_{2\beta}\delta_{\nu\alpha})\\
&\qquad=-\bigl[(k_1\cdot k_2)\,\delta_{\mu\nu}-k_{1\nu}k_{2\mu}\bigr]=v_2(k_1,k_2)_{\mu\nu} .
\end{aligned}
\]

\emph{Step 3 (the vertex $\mathsf a^{(3)}$).} By \cref{IV-73-53}, $\mathsf a^{(3)}_P[\![X,Y,Z]\!]$ is the sum of $\mathsf t_P$ over the six orders of $X,Y,Z$. Let $P=p_{\mu\nu}$. To leading order, $(Y(b_1),\dots,Y(b_4))$ is replaced by $(Y_\mu,Y_\nu,Y_\mu,Y_\nu)$; hence
\[
\sum_{i<j}s_is_j\,Y(b_i)\times Z(b_j)\to Y_\mu\times Z_\nu-Y_\nu\times Z_\mu-Y_\mu\times Z_\mu-Y_\nu\times Z_\nu ,
\]
and, by the antisymmetry of the cross product,
\[
\mathsf t_P(X,Y,Z)+\mathsf t_P(X,Z,Y)\to-2\bigl\langle(\mathrm dX)_{\mu\nu},\,Y_\mu\times Z_\nu-Y_\nu\times Z_\mu\bigr\rangle .
\]
Both factors are antisymmetric in $\mu\nu$. Summing over $\mu<\nu$ and inserting $(\mathrm dX)_{\mu\nu}\to i(k_{1\mu}X_\nu-k_{1\nu}X_\mu)$, we obtain
\[
-2i\sum_{\mu,\nu}k_{1\mu}\bigl\langle X_\nu,\,Y_\mu\times Z_\nu-Y_\nu\times Z_\mu\bigr\rangle .
\]
For legs of colours $a,b,c$, with indices $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ and entering momenta $k_1,k_2,k_3$, this equals\[-2i\,\epsilon_{abc}\bigl[\delta_{\alpha\gamma}k_{1\beta}-\delta_{\alpha\beta}k_{1\gamma}\bigr].\] We add the terms in which the second, resp.\ the third, leg is the curl leg; they arise by cyclic permutation, under which $\epsilon_{abc}$ is invariant. The leading part of $\sum_\iota\mathsf a^{(3)}_{p_{[\iota]}}[\![\cdot,\cdot,\cdot]\!]$ is therefore
\[
-2i\,\epsilon_{abc}\,v_3(k_1,k_2,k_3)_{\alpha\beta\gamma} .
\]

\emph{Step 4 ($\Gamma=1$).} By \cref{IV-73-67}(a) the five lines $1,\dots,5$ of the kite carry $k$ (from $p$ to $P$), $\mathsf p-k$ (from $p$ to $P'$), $k-l$ (from $P$ to $P'$), $l$ (from $P$ to $q$) and $\mathsf p-l$ (from $P'$ to $q$). The entering momenta are $(-k,k-\mathsf p)$ at $p$; $(k,-l,l-k)$ at $P$, for the legs towards $p$, $q$, $P'$; $(\mathsf p-k,l-\mathsf p,k-l)$ at $P'$; and $(l,\mathsf p-l)$ at $q$. At both cubic vertices the colours are $(a,a',c)$, and $\sum_{a,a',c}\epsilon_{aa'c}^2=6$. With the factor $\frac12$ of $\mathsf T_1$ in \cref{IV-73-53} we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\tfrac12(-2i)^2\cdot6\cdot v_2(-k,k-\mathsf p)_{\mu\nu}\,v_2(l,\mathsf p-l)_{\rho\sigma}\\
&\qquad\times v_3(k,-l,l-k)_{\mu\rho\alpha}\,v_3(\mathsf p-k,l-\mathsf p,k-l)_{\nu\sigma\alpha}\,/\,\mathsf x_1\mathsf x_1'\mathsf x_2\mathsf x_2'\mathsf x_3 ,
\end{aligned}
\]
and $\frac12(-4)\cdot6=24\cdot(-\frac12)$. Since $v_2$ is even, and the product of the two factors $v_3$ is even under the change of sign of all their arguments, this is $24F_1$.

\emph{Step 5 ($\Gamma=6$).} The factor is $\frac16(-2i)^2\cdot6=24\cdot(-\frac16)$. The entering momenta are $-(\mathsf p-k)$, $-(k-l)$, $-l$ at $p$ and the opposite ones at $q$. The tensor $v_3$ is invariant under the cyclic permutations of its arguments together with its indices, and it changes sign under a transposition, like $\epsilon_{abc}$; this gives $24F_6$.

\emph{Step 6 ($\Gamma=5$).} The line $K_0$ carries $\mathsf p-k$ from $p$ to $q$, the line $X$ carries $k$ from $p$ to $P$, and $K_{\mathrm a}$, $K_{\mathrm b}$ carry $k-l$ and $l$ from $P$ to $q$. The factor is $-\frac12(-2i)^2\cdot6=12$, with the factor $-\frac12$ of $\mathsf T_5$, and the tensors are
\[
v_2(k-\mathsf p,-k)_{\alpha\sigma}\,v_3(\mathsf p-k,l,k-l)_{\alpha\beta\gamma}\,v_3(k,-l,l-k)_{\sigma\beta\gamma};
\]
with the factors $|\mathsf q|^{-2}$ of the four lines this is $12F_5$.

\emph{Step 7 ($\Gamma=2$).} By \cref{IV-73-53}, applied to two quadratic polynomials,
\[
-\langle\partial_{b,3}S_3;\partial_{b',3}S_3\rangle_0=-\tfrac12\sum\mathsf a_P^{(3)}[\![\delta_{b,3},\delta_{\mathsf i},\delta_{\mathsf i'}]\!]\,\mathsf a_{P'}^{(3)}[\![\delta_{b',3},\delta_{\mathsf j},\delta_{\mathsf j'}]\!]\,C(\mathsf i,\mathsf j)\,C(\mathsf i',\mathsf j'),
\]
the sum extending over $P,P'$ and over the indices $\mathsf i,\mathsf i',\mathsf j,\mathsf j'$. Here $\sum_{c,c'}\epsilon_{3cc'}^2=2$, and together with the factor $-3$ of $\mathsf T_{\mathrm I}$ the total factor is $-3\cdot(-\frac12)(-2i)^2\cdot2=-12=24\cdot(-\frac12)$. The line $\Pi$ carries $\mathsf p-k$ from $p$ to $q$, and the chain carries $k$. The curl legs give $v_2(-k,k-\mathsf p)_{\mu\nu}$ at $p$ and $v_2(k,\mathsf p-k)_{\rho\nu}$ at $q$, where $\nu$ is the index of the line $\Pi$, and the cubic vertices give $v_3(k,-l,l-k)_{\mu\beta\gamma}\,v_3(-k,l,k-l)_{\rho\beta\gamma}$. With the factors of the five lines, whose squares give the denominator $\mathsf x_1^2\mathsf x_1'\mathsf x_2\mathsf x_3$, and with the parities of $v_2$ and $v_3$, this is $24F_2$.

\emph{Step 8 ($\Gamma=3$).} The ghost loop enters $\Sigma$ through the kernel $-8\,D(b;b')\,D(b';b)$. By \cref{IV-73-51}, the leading parts of the symbols of $y\mapsto D((x,\mu);(x+y,\rho))$ and of $y\mapsto D((x+y,\rho);(x,\mu))$ are $-i\mathsf q_\mu|\mathsf q|^{-2}$ and $+i\mathsf q_\rho|\mathsf q|^{-2}$. With $\mathsf q=k-l$, resp.\ $\mathsf q=l$, and with the factor $-3$ of $\mathsf T_{\mathrm I}$ we obtain
\[
-3\,(-8)\,(k-l)_\mu\,l_\rho\,/\,\mathsf x_3\mathsf x_2=24\cdot(-1)\,l_\rho(l-k)_\mu\,/\,\mathsf x_2\mathsf x_3 ;
\]
together with the factors at $p$ and $q$ and on the lines $\Pi$, $K^\to$, $K^\leftarrow$, as in Step~7, this is $24F_3$.

\emph{Step 9 ($\Gamma=4$).} By \cref{IV-73-57}(4), the terms $G\in\mathfrak G_4$ with $(n_X,n_Y)=(4,4)$ are exactly those which arise from the monomials of $\frac12|\mathfrak z_1|^2$ in the standard writing of $\mathsf a_P^{(4)}$ (\cref{IV-73-53}); here, by \cref{IV-73-9} in \cref{IV-73-9}, with $A_i:=A(b_i(P))$,
\[
\mathsf a_P^{(4)}=\tfrac12|\mathfrak z_1|^2+\langle\mathrm dA(P),\mathfrak z_2\rangle-\tfrac1{24}|\mathrm dA(P)|^4,\qquad\mathfrak z_1=-\sum_{i<j}s_is_j\,A_i\times A_j .
\]
Thus the vertex of the class $\Gamma=4$ is $\frac12|\mathfrak z_1|^2$. At $P=p_{\alpha\beta}$ the replacement of Step~3, $(A_1,\dots,A_4)\to(A_\alpha,A_\beta,A_\alpha,A_\beta)$, gives to leading order
\[
\mathfrak z_1\to-\bigl(A_\alpha\times A_\beta-A_\beta\times A_\alpha-A_\alpha\times A_\alpha-A_\beta\times A_\beta\bigr)=-2A_\alpha\times A_\beta ;
\]
since $\frac12|2A_\alpha\times A_\beta|^2=2|A_\alpha\times A_\beta|^2$ and the terms with $\alpha=\beta$ vanish, the sum over $\iota$, that is, over $\alpha<\beta$, gives $\sum_\iota\frac12|\mathfrak z_1|^2\to\mathsf Q(A):=\sum_{\alpha,\beta}|A_\alpha\times A_\beta|^2$, where $|Z|^2:=\langle Z,Z\rangle$ with the complex bilinear extension of $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$. For $X=\xi\mathsf e_a$ and $Y=\eta\mathsf e_{a'}$ with $\xi,\eta\in\mathbb C^3$, that is, $X_\alpha=\xi_\alpha\mathsf e_a$ and $Y_\alpha=\eta_\alpha\mathsf e_{a'}$, we have, with the bilinear dot product on $\mathbb C^3$,
\begin{gather*}
\mathsf Q(sX+tY)=s^2t^2(1-\delta_{aa'})\sum_{\alpha,\beta}(\xi_\alpha\eta_\beta-\xi_\beta\eta_\alpha)^2,\\
\sum_{\alpha,\beta}(\xi_\alpha\eta_\beta-\xi_\beta\eta_\alpha)^2=2\bigl[(\xi\cdot\xi)(\eta\cdot\eta)-(\xi\cdot\eta)^2\bigr].
\end{gather*}
Polarising, with $X_i=\xi_i\mathsf e_a$ and $Y_j=\eta_j\mathsf e_{a'}$ ($i,j\in\{1,2\}$), we find
\[
\mathsf Q[\![X_1,X_2,Y_1,Y_2]\!]=4(1-\delta_{aa'})\cdot2\bigl[(\xi_1\cdot\xi_2)(\eta_1\cdot\eta_2)-\tfrac12(\xi_1\cdot\eta_1)(\xi_2\cdot\eta_2)-\tfrac12(\xi_1\cdot\eta_2)(\xi_2\cdot\eta_1)\bigr].
\]
Since $\sum_{a,a'}(1-\delta_{aa'})=6$, the factor is $-\frac14\cdot4\cdot2\cdot6=-12=24\cdot(-\frac12)$, with the factor $-\frac14$ of $\mathsf T_4$. The pairs of legs contracted with $p$ and with $q$ give $\xi_{1\mu}\xi_{2\nu}\to v_2(k,\mathsf p-k)_{\mu\nu}/\mathsf x_1\mathsf x_1'$ and $\eta_{1\mu}\eta_{2\nu}\to v_2(l,\mathsf p-l)_{\mu\nu}/\mathsf x_2\mathsf x_2'$, and the result is $24F_4$.
\end{proof}

We now show that the model $\mathsf T^{\mathrm{mod}}_\Gamma$ of \cref{IV-73-64} has, up to a part of degree $-4$, the same part of degree $-5$ as the corresponding lattice terms. For $K\in\mathfrak K(n)$, write $K^h$ for its spatial leading kernel in \cref{IV-73-38}; it is smooth away from zero and homogeneous of degree $-n$.

\begin{lemma}[The model has the degree $-5$ parts of the lattice classes]\label{IV-73-69}
Let $\tau_{\mathrm{gf}}=1$. For $G\in\mathfrak G_1\cup\mathfrak G_4\cup\mathfrak G_5\cup\mathfrak G_6$ let $\mathsf U_G$ be the function of degree $-5$ attached to $G$ in \cref{IV-73-60}. For $(\mu,\nu,G)\in\mathfrak G_2\cup\mathfrak G_3$ let
\[
\mathsf U_G:=\Pi^h\cdot\bigl(K^\to_{\iota\mu}*\mathsf f_G(\nabla)[K_{\mathrm a}K_{\mathrm b}-\mathsf q_G]*K^\leftarrow_{\nu\iota'}\bigr)^h,\qquad\Pi^h:=\mathcal F^{-1}_{\ne0}\sigma_\Pi^h ,
\]
where the chain lies in $\mathfrak K(2)$ by \cref{IV-73-62}(a) and two applications of \cref{IV-73-46}(ii). Let
\begin{gather*}
\mathsf U_\Gamma:=\sum_{\iota,\iota'}\sum_{G\in\mathfrak G_\Gamma}c_G\,\mathsf U_G\quad(\Gamma\ne5),\\
\mathsf U_5(u):=\sum_{\iota,\iota'}\sum_{G\in\mathfrak G_5}c_G\bigl[\mathsf U_G(u)+\mathsf U_G(-u)\bigr],
\end{gather*}
with the coefficients $-3\,c_G$ of \cref{IV-73-68} for $\Gamma=2,3$. Then for each $\Gamma=1,\dots,6$ there are a continuous function $\mathsf l_\Gamma$ on $\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$, homogeneous of degree $-4$, and a pure constant $C$ such that
\[
\bigl|\mathsf T_\Gamma^{\mathrm{mod}}(u)-\mathsf l_\Gamma(u)-\mathsf U_\Gamma(u)\bigr|\le C|u|^{-6}\lg|u|\qquad(u\in\mathbb Z^3\setminus\{0\}).
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\emph{Step 0 (model lines).} For a line whose symbol has the leading part $\sigma^h$, of degree $s$, let $\sigma^{\mathrm{mod}}$ be the periodic continuation of $\rho\sigma^h$, with $\rho$ of \cref{IV-73-64}(3). As $\rho\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$, $\operatorname{supp}\rho\subset\{|k|\le2\rho_0\}\subset\{|k|<\pi\}$ and $\rho=1$ near $0$, the function $\sigma^{\mathrm{mod}}$ is a line symbol with the same leading part (\cref{IV-73-38}), and its parity is exact: $\sigma^{\mathrm{mod}}(-k)=(-1)^s\sigma^{\mathrm{mod}}(k)$. Its kernel $K^{\mathrm{mod}}(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}e^{ik\cdot x}\rho\,\sigma^h\,d^\circ k$ satisfies $K^{\mathrm{mod}}=K^h+O(|x|^{-N})$ for every $N$, with $K^h=\mathcal F^{-1}_{\ne0}\sigma^h$, by \cref{lem:pure-homogeneous-kernels}. For $(\mu,\nu,G)\in\mathfrak G_2\cup\mathfrak G_3$ the elementary term is, by \cref{IV-73-57}(I), the value at $u=u'$ of the function
\[
u\mapsto K_\Pi(u)\,\bigl(K^\to_{\iota\mu}*\mathsf f_G(\nabla)[K_{\mathrm a}K_{\mathrm b}]*K^\leftarrow_{\nu\iota'}\bigr)(u),\qquad K_\Pi(y):=\Pi\bigl(p_{[\iota]}(0),p_{[\iota']}(y)\bigr)\quad(y\in\mathbb Z^3);
\]
here $K_\Pi$ is the elementary line of degree $3$ of \cref{IV-73-51}, with the symbol $\sigma_\Pi$ of \cref{IV-73-68}, and $\Pi(p,q)=K_\Pi(u')$ by translation invariance. For an elementary term $G$ let $G^{\mathrm{mod}}(u)$ be the same expression with every line $K$ replaced by $K^{\mathrm{mod}}$, in particular $K_\Pi$ by $K_\Pi^{\mathrm{mod}}$; for $G$ of type (I) we moreover drop the operator $\mathsf f_G(\nabla)$ and replace $K^\to$ by the elementary line $K_1'$ whose symbol is the periodic continuation of $\rho\,\sigma_\to^h\mathsf f_G^h$; it has degree $2+d_G$.
