\emph{Step 1 (the model in momentum space).} We show that $\mathsf T^{\mathrm{mod}}_\Gamma=\sum c_G\,G^{\mathrm{mod}}$, the sum extending over $\iota,\iota'$ and $G$ as in \cref{IV-73-68}, where for $\Gamma=5$ the term $G^{\mathrm{mod}}(u)$ is replaced by $G^{\mathrm{mod}}(u)+G^{\mathrm{mod}}(-u)$. By \cref{IV-73-67},
\[
G^{\mathrm{mod}}(u)=\int_{\mathbb T}e^{i\mathsf p\cdot u}\Bigl[\iint_{\mathbb T^2}\prod\sigma^{\mathrm{mod}}\,d^\circ k\,d^\circ l\Bigr]d^\circ\mathsf p ,
\]
where the product extends over the lines of $G$ and the arguments of the symbols are those in $\mathsf F_G$. For the kites this is assertion (a) of that lemma, the model lines having the degrees of the lattice lines. For the other types we apply assertion (b) to the products and convolutions of which $G^{\mathrm{mod}}$ is built, one at a time, and we verify its hypotheses. A model line of degree $n$ is bounded by $C\langle x\rangle^{-n}$ (\cref{IV-73-39}), and its symbol is integrable. A kernel in $\ell^2(\mathbb Z^3)$ with an integrable symbol has its symbol in $L^2(\mathbb T)$, as in the proof of \cref{IV-73-67}(b); hence the symbol of the convolution of two such kernels, a product of two functions in $L^2(\mathbb T)$, is integrable, and so is the symbol of the product of two kernels with integrable symbols, a convolution of two integrable functions.
\begin{itemize}
\item For $G\in\mathfrak G_6$, $G^{\mathrm{mod}}$ is a product of three model lines, and the rule for products is used twice.
\item For $G\in\mathfrak G_4$ with $(n_X,n_Y)=(4,4)$, $G^{\mathrm{mod}}=X*Y$, where $X$ and $Y$ are products of two model lines of degree $2$. Their symbols are given by the rule for products, and $|X(x)|,|Y(x)|\le C\langle x\rangle^{-4}$, so that $X,Y\in\ell^2(\mathbb Z^3)$ and the rule for $X*Y$ applies.
\item For $G\in\mathfrak G_5$, $G^{\mathrm{mod}}(u)=K_0(u)\,(X*Y)(u)$ with model lines $K_0$, $X$ and a product $Y$ of two model lines, where $n_X\in\{2,3\}$ and $n_Y\in\{2,3,4\}$. Thus $|X(x)|\le C\langle x\rangle^{-n_X}$ and $|Y(x)|\le C\langle x\rangle^{-n_Y}$ with exponents at least $2$, so that $X,Y\in\ell^2(\mathbb Z^3)$; the kernel $X*Y$ has the symbol $\hat X\hat Y$, and the product with $K_0$ is treated by the rule for products.
\item For $G$ of type (I), $G^{\mathrm{mod}}=K_\Pi^{\mathrm{mod}}\cdot(K_1'*X*K^{\leftarrow,\mathrm{mod}})$ with $X:=K_{\mathrm a}^{\mathrm{mod}}K_{\mathrm b}^{\mathrm{mod}}$; the degrees of $K_1'$, $X$ and $K^{\leftarrow,\mathrm{mod}}$ are $2+d_G$, $4-d_G$ and $2$, all at least $2$. Hence $K_1'*X$ has the symbol $\hat K_1'\hat X$, and \cref{IV-73-40}, with $(a,a')=(2+d_G,4-d_G)$ and $a+a'-3=3$, gives
\[
|(K_1'*X)(x)|\le C\langle x\rangle^{-\min\{2+d_G,\,4-d_G,\,3\}}\lg\langle x\rangle ;
\]
the exponent is at least $2$, so that $K_1'*X\in\ell^2(\mathbb Z^3)$, the logarithm included. The rule for convolutions applies once more to $(K_1'*X)*K^{\leftarrow,\mathrm{mod}}$, and the product with $K_\Pi^{\mathrm{mod}}$ is treated by the rule for products.
\end{itemize}

For $k,l,\mathsf p\in[-\pi,\pi]^3$ the periodic continuations may be replaced by $\rho\sigma^h$. We use the following observation: if $v\in[-\pi,\pi]^3$, $|w|<4\rho_0$ and $|v-w|_{\mathbb T}<2\rho_0$, then $|v-w|<2\rho_0$, because the distance of $v-w$ from any point $2\pi\mathsf m$ with $\mathsf m\in\mathbb Z^3\setminus\{0\}$ is at least $\pi-4\rho_0>2\rho_0$. Let $k,l,\mathsf p\in[-\pi,\pi]^3$, and assume first that every line $\mathsf q$ of $\Gamma$ satisfies $|\mathsf q|_{\mathbb T}<2\rho_0$; this is the case wherever all the factors $\sigma^{\mathrm{mod}}$ are non-zero. Then $|l|=|l|_{\mathbb T}<2\rho_0$, since $l\in[-\pi,\pi]^3$. For $\Gamma\ne6$ we have likewise $|k|<2\rho_0$; then $|k-l|<4\rho_0<\pi$, so that $|k-l|=|k-l|_{\mathbb T}<2\rho_0$ wherever $k-l$ is a line ($\Gamma=1,2,3,5$), and the observation with $v=\mathsf p$ and $w=k$, resp.\ $w=l$, gives $|\mathsf p-k|<2\rho_0$, resp.\ $|\mathsf p-l|<2\rho_0$, wherever these vectors are lines. For $\Gamma=6$ the observation with $(v,w)=(k,l)$ gives $|k-l|<2\rho_0$, hence $|k|<4\rho_0$, and with $(v,w)=(\mathsf p,k)$ it gives $|\mathsf p-k|<2\rho_0$. Thus every line satisfies $|\mathsf q|<2\rho_0$, and $\sigma^{\mathrm{mod}}(\mathsf q)=\rho(\mathsf q)\sigma^h(\mathsf q)$. If, on the other hand, some line satisfies $|\mathsf q|_{\mathbb T}\ge2\rho_0$, then $\sigma^{\mathrm{mod}}(\mathsf q)=0$ and also $\rho(\mathsf q)=0$, since $|\mathsf q|\ge|\mathsf q|_{\mathbb T}$. In either case the product of the factors $\sigma^{\mathrm{mod}}$ equals $R_\Gamma\mathsf F_G$ at $(k,l,\mathsf p)$, the lines of $G$ being the lines of $\Gamma$ (for type (I) the factor $\rho\,\sigma^h_\to\mathsf f^h_G$ of $K_1'$ provides the factors $\sigma^h_\to(k)\,\mathsf f^h_G(k)$ of $\mathsf F_G$). Since $R_\Gamma$ vanishes unless $k,l,\mathsf p\in[-\pi,\pi]^3$ (\cref{IV-73-64}(3)), we obtain
\[
G^{\mathrm{mod}}(u)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}e^{i\mathsf p\cdot u}\Bigl[\iint R_\Gamma\,\mathsf F_G\,d^\circ k\,d^\circ l\Bigr]d^\circ\mathsf p .
\]
By \cref{IV-73-68}, $\sum c_G\iint R_\Gamma\mathsf F_G\,d^\circ k\,d^\circ l=24\Psi_\Gamma$ for $\Gamma\ne5$, whence $\sum c_GG^{\mathrm{mod}}=\mathsf T^{\mathrm{mod}}_\Gamma$. For $\Gamma=5$ the term $G^{\mathrm{mod}}(-u)$ carries the factor $e^{-i\mathsf p\cdot u}$, and $\sum c_G\iint R_5\mathsf F_G\,d^\circ k\,d^\circ l=12\Psi_5$ is even; hence $\sum c_G[G^{\mathrm{mod}}(u)+G^{\mathrm{mod}}(-u)]=12\int(e^{i\mathsf p\cdot u}+e^{-i\mathsf p\cdot u})\Psi_5\,d^\circ\mathsf p=\mathsf T^{\mathrm{mod}}_5(u)$.

\emph{Step 2 (expansions).} \cref{IV-73-60} applies to $G^{\mathrm{mod}}$, the model lines being elementary lines of the same degrees as the lattice lines; the functions of degree $-5$ which it provides are determined by the leading parts of the symbols of the lines alone (\cref{IV-73-60}), and therefore coincide with the $\mathsf U_G$. For $G$ of type (I) let $X:=K^{\mathrm{mod}}_{\mathrm a}K^{\mathrm{mod}}_{\mathrm b}$, of degree $n_X=4-d_G$, and write $X=\mathsf q_X+X'$ with $X'\in\mathfrak K(n_X)$ (\cref{IV-73-46}(iii)). Since $K_1'$ is a line of degree $2+d_G\le4$, two applications of \cref{IV-73-46}(ii) give $K_1'*X'*K^{\leftarrow,\mathrm{mod}}\in\mathfrak K(2)$, and the first component of its leading data is $\sigma_\to^h\mathsf f_G^h\mathsf I^h\sigma_\leftarrow^h$, where the homogeneous part $\mathsf I^h$ of the bubble depends only on $\sigma^h_{\mathrm a}$, $\sigma^h_{\mathrm b}$ (\cref{IV-73-42}). The lattice chain $K^\to_{\iota\mu}*\mathsf f_G(\nabla)[K_{\mathrm a}K_{\mathrm b}-\mathsf q_G]*K^\leftarrow_{\nu\iota'}$ has the same first component of its leading data, by \cref{IV-73-62}(a) and by \cref{IV-73-46}(ii), used for each of its two convolutions. Within $\mathfrak K(2)$ the leading kernel is determined by the first component of the leading data (\cref{IV-73-46}(iv)); hence the two chains have the same leading kernel. Now $G^{\mathrm{mod}}=K^{\mathrm{mod}}_\Pi\cdot(K_1'*\mathsf q_X*K^{\leftarrow,\mathrm{mod}})+K^{\mathrm{mod}}_\Pi\cdot(K_1'*X'*K^{\leftarrow,\mathrm{mod}})$, and the first term is local. In the second term, $K_\Pi^{\mathrm{mod}}=\Pi^h+O(|u|^{-N})$ with $\Pi^h=O(|u|^{-3})$, and $K_1'*X'*K^{\leftarrow,\mathrm{mod}}$ differs from its leading kernel, which is $O(|u|^{-2})$, by $O(|u|^{-3}\lg|u|)$, by the spatial estimate in \cref{IV-73-38}. We obtain in all cases
\[
G^{\mathrm{mod}}=[\text{local terms}]+\mathsf U_G+O(|u|^{-6}\lg|u|).
\]

\emph{Step 3 (local terms).} In this step all lines are model lines, and we omit the superscript $\mathrm{mod}$. Because of the exact parity of the model symbols, every one-loop function $\mathsf I$ built from model lines satisfies $\mathsf I(-\kappa)=(-1)^{\omega+1}\mathsf I(\kappa)$, as one sees by the substitution $l\to-l$; its homogeneous part $\mathsf I^h$ has the same parity (\cref{IV-73-42}). By \cref{IV-73-42} the polynomial $\mathsf Q(\kappa)-(-1)^{\omega+1}\mathsf Q(-\kappa)$, of degree at most $\omega$, is therefore $O(|\kappa|^{\omega+1}\lg|\kappa|\,\Lambda(\kappa))$, hence equal to $0$. Consequently $\mathsf Q=0$ if $\omega\le0$, and $\mathsf Q=\mathsf Q(0)$ if $\omega=1$; in both cases $\mathsf q=\mathsf Q(0)\,\delta_0$. The local terms are thus: $\mathsf Q_{\mathsf p}(0)K_4K_5(u)+\mathsf Q_{\mathsf q}(0)K_1K_2(u)$ for the kites, where $n_4+n_5=4$ if $\omega_{\mathsf p}=1$ and $n_1+n_2=4$ if $\omega_{\mathsf q}=1$; $\mathsf Q_Y(0)K_0X(u)$, with $n_0+n_X=4$, for $\mathfrak G_5$; $\mathsf Q_X(0)Y(u)+\mathsf Q_Y(0)X(u)$, with $n_X=n_Y=4$, for $\mathfrak G_4$; and, for type (I) with $d_G=0$, $\mathsf Q_X(0)K_\Pi(u)\,(K_1'*K^\leftarrow)(u)$, where $K_1'*K^\leftarrow$ is, by \cref{IV-73-67}(b), the elementary line of degree $1$ whose symbol is the periodic continuation of $\rho^2\sigma_\to^h\mathsf f^h_G\sigma_\leftarrow^h$ (a line symbol by \cref{IV-73-38}, with $\rho^2$ in place of $\rho$), $\mathsf f^h_G=\mathsf f_G(0)$ being a number. By Step~0, and by \cref{lem:pure-homogeneous-kernels} with $\rho^2$ in place of $\rho$ for the line $K_1'*K^\leftarrow$, each of these local terms is, up to $O(|u|^{-N})$, its factor $\mathsf Q_\bullet(0)$ times the product of the functions $K^h=\mathcal F^{-1}_{\ne0}\sigma^h$ of its lines, a function homogeneous of degree $-4$ and smooth off $0$. We let $\mathsf l_\Gamma$ be the sum of these functions, each taken with the coefficient with which its term $G^{\mathrm{mod}}$ enters $\mathsf T^{\mathrm{mod}}_\Gamma$ in Step~1. For $\Gamma=5$, where $\mathsf T^{\mathrm{mod}}_5(u)=\sum c_G\bigl[G^{\mathrm{mod}}(u)+G^{\mathrm{mod}}(-u)\bigr]$, the expansion of Step~2 is used at $u$ and at $-u$; accordingly, every such function $\mathsf h$ of a term $G\in\mathfrak G_5$ enters $\mathsf l_5$ together with its reflection $u\mapsto\mathsf h(-u)$, just as $\mathsf U_5$ contains $\mathsf U_G(u)$ and $\mathsf U_G(-u)$. Adding the expansions of Step~2 with these coefficients, we obtain the claimed bound for large $|u|$; for small $|u|$ all terms are bounded. All data being fixed, the constant $C$ is pure.
\end{proof}

The functions $\mathsf l_\Gamma$ and $\mathsf U_\Gamma$ are in fact multiples of $|u|^{-4}$ and $|u|^{-5}$, since $\mathsf T^{\mathrm{mod}}_\Gamma$ is radial.

\begin{lemma}[Rotation invariance of the homogeneous parts; definition of $\kappa_\Gamma^{\mathrm{lat}}$]\label{IV-73-70}
Let $\mathsf t\colon[0,\infty)\to\mathbb C$, let $\mathsf l,\mathsf U$ be continuous functions on $\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$, homogeneous of degrees $-4$ and $-5$ respectively, and assume that for some $C$
\[
\bigl|\mathsf t(|u|)-\mathsf l(u)-\mathsf U(u)\bigr|\le C|u|^{-6}\lg|u|\qquad(u\in\mathbb Z^3\setminus\{0\}).
\]
Then $\mathsf l(u)=c_4|u|^{-4}$ and $\mathsf U(u)=\kappa|u|^{-5}$ with constants $c_4,\kappa$. In particular the functions of \cref{IV-73-69} satisfy $\mathsf l_\Gamma(u)=c_{4,\Gamma}|u|^{-4}$ and
\[
\mathsf U_\Gamma(u)=\kappa_\Gamma^{\mathrm{lat}}\,|u|^{-5}\qquad(\Gamma=1,\dots,6);
\]
this defines the numbers $c_{4,\Gamma}$ and $\kappa_\Gamma^{\mathrm{lat}}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Let $O$ be a rotation with rational entries, $\mathsf N$ a common denominator of these entries, and $\mathsf m\in\mathbb Z^3\setminus\{0\}$. For integers $j\ge1$ the points $j\mathsf N\mathsf m$ and $j\mathsf NO\mathsf m$ lie in $\mathbb Z^3$ and have the same norm $jr_1$, $r_1:=\mathsf N|\mathsf m|$. Let $\hat{\mathsf m}:=\mathsf m/|\mathsf m|$. Subtracting the hypothesis at these two points, at which $\mathsf t$ takes the same value, we obtain by homogeneity
\[
\Bigl|(jr_1)^{-4}\bigl[\mathsf l(\hat{\mathsf m})-\mathsf l(O\hat{\mathsf m})\bigr]+(jr_1)^{-5}\bigl[\mathsf U(\hat{\mathsf m})-\mathsf U(O\hat{\mathsf m})\bigr]\Bigr|\le2C(jr_1)^{-6}\lg(jr_1) .
\]
Multiplying by $(jr_1)^4$ and letting $j\to\infty$ we obtain $\mathsf l(\hat{\mathsf m})=\mathsf l(O\hat{\mathsf m})$; then, multiplying the remaining difference by $(jr_1)^5$, we obtain $\mathsf U(\hat{\mathsf m})=\mathsf U(O\hat{\mathsf m})$. The directions $\mathsf m/|\mathsf m|$ are dense in $S^2$, since $\mathbb Q^3$ is dense in $\mathbb R^3$. The rational rotations are dense in $SO(3)$: the Cayley map $\mathsf A\mapsto(\mathbf 1-\mathsf A)(\mathbf 1+\mathsf A)^{-1}$ is continuous from the real antisymmetric $3\times3$ matrices onto the rotations without eigenvalue $-1$, which are dense in $SO(3)$; the antisymmetric matrices with rational entries are dense among the real ones, and by the formula they are mapped to rotations with rational entries, since the inverse of an invertible matrix with rational entries has rational entries. By continuity, $\mathsf l$ and $\mathsf U$ are invariant under all rotations; as $SO(3)$ acts transitively on $S^2$, they are constant on $S^2$, and homogeneity gives the claim. For the last assertion we note that $\mathsf T^{\mathrm{mod}}_\Gamma$ is the restriction to $\mathbb Z^3$ of a radial function, since $\Psi_\Gamma$ is radial (\cref{IV-73-64}(3)); thus $\mathsf T^{\mathrm{mod}}_\Gamma(u)=\mathsf t(|u|)$ for a function $\mathsf t$, and \cref{IV-73-69} provides the hypothesis.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[The kernel of degree $-5$: large-distance asymptotics of $\mathsf B_1^{\mathrm{lat}}$]\label{IV-73-71}
There are functions $\mathsf U_{ij}\in C^1(\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\})$, $i,j\in\{1,2,3\}$, homogeneous of degree $-5$, and pure constants $C,r_0$ such that for all plaquettes $p,q$ of $\mathbb Z^3$, with $u:=x(q)-x(p)$ and $r:=|u|\ge r_0$,
\begin{equation}\label{IV-73-72}
\begin{gathered}
\bigl|\mathsf B_1^{\mathrm{lat}}(p,q)-\mathsf U_{\lambda(p)\lambda(q)}(u)\bigr|\le C\,r^{-6}\lg r,\\
\sum_{i,j}\mathsf U_{ij}(u)=\kappa^{\mathrm{lat}}|u|^{-5},\qquad\kappa^{\mathrm{lat}}:=\sum_{\Gamma=1}^6\kappa_\Gamma^{\mathrm{lat}} ,
\end{gathered}
\end{equation}
with the numbers $\kappa_\Gamma^{\mathrm{lat}}$ of \cref{IV-73-70}. Moreover $\mathsf B_1^{\mathrm{lat}}$ is bounded.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
We work at $\tau_{\mathrm{gf}}=1$; recall that $\mathsf B_1^{\mathrm{lat}}(p,q)=\mathsf B_1^{\mathrm{lat}}(p,q;1)$ by \eqref{IV-73-25}. Boundedness is contained in \cref{IV-73-55}, which gives $\sup_{p,q}|\mathsf B_1^{\mathrm{lat}}(p,q)|<\infty$ for every $\tau_{\mathrm{gf}}=1$. Let $p=p_{[\iota]}(x_p)$, $q=p_{[\iota']}(x_q)$ and $u':=x_q-x_p$; then $|u-u'|\le\sqrt2$, and we take $r$ large. By \cref{IV-73-53} and \cref{IV-73-57}, $\mathsf B_1^{\mathrm{lat}}(p,q)$ is the sum of $\mathsf T_{\mathrm I}$ and of finitely many elementary terms, to which \cref{IV-73-60} applies.

\emph{Step 1 (local terms at $q$).} These are the first half of $\mathsf T_{4'}$ and the terms with $\mathsf q_Y$ in the first half of $\mathsf T_5$, with $\mathsf q_Y$ in $\mathsf T_4$ and with $\mathsf q_{\mathsf q}$ in $\mathsf T_1$, in the expansions of \cref{IV-73-60}. By \cref{IV-73-62}(b), and since $E_p((x_q+y,\mu))=K^\to_{\iota\mu}(u'+y)$ by translation invariance, their sum equals
\[
\tfrac{3}2\sum_{b,b'}\gamma_q(b,b')\,E_p(b)\,E_p(b')=\tfrac{3}2\sum_{\mu,\nu}\sum_{y,y'}\gamma_{q;\mu\nu}(y,y')\,K^\to_{\iota\mu}(u'+y)\,K^\to_{\iota\nu}(u'+y') .
\]
The kernels $\gamma_{q;\mu\nu}$ have finite support, and their symbols vanish at $\kappa=0$ together with their gradients (\cref{IV-73-62}(b)); the $K^\to_{\iota\mu}$ are elementary lines of degree $2$. \cref{IV-73-61}(a), applied with $\gamma_{\mu\nu}:=\gamma_{q;\mu\nu}$ and $K_\mu:=K^\to_{\iota\mu}$, shows that the sum is $O(|u'|^{-6})=O(r^{-6})$. By the translation invariance in \cref{IV-73-57}, the kernels $\gamma_{q;\mu\nu}$ depend on $q$ only through $\iota'$, so that only finitely many constants occur.

\emph{Step 2 (local terms at $p$).} These are the second half of $\mathsf T_{4'}$ and the terms with $\mathsf q_Y$ in the second half of $\mathsf T_5$, with $\mathsf q_X$ in $\mathsf T_4$ and with $\mathsf q_{\mathsf p}$ in $\mathsf T_1$. We show that they are the local terms at the second plaquette of the ordered pair $(q,p)$; by Step~1, applied to this pair, their sum is then $\frac{3}2\sum_{b,b'}\gamma_p(b,b')\,E_q(b)\,E_q(b')=O(r^{-6})$. For the second halves of $\mathsf T_{4'}$ and $\mathsf T_5$ this holds because they are the first halves for $(q,p)$ (\cref{IV-73-57}). The formulas for $\mathsf T_1$ and $\mathsf T_4$ in \cref{IV-73-53} are symmetric under $p\leftrightarrow q$. An elementary term $G$ of $\mathsf T_1$ or $\mathsf T_4$ is given by the monomials at $P,P'$ and by the choice of the legs contracted with $p$, with $q$, and with one another; taken for the ordered pair $(q,p)$, it becomes a term $\tilde G$ with $c_{\tilde G}=c_G$, and $G\mapsto\tilde G$ is a bijection $\mathfrak G_\bullet(\iota,\iota')\to\mathfrak G_\bullet(\iota',\iota)$. In $\tilde G$ the base points are counted from $x_q$, $u'$ is replaced by $-u'$, and the contractions, which are symmetric in their two legs, are taken from the other end: for the kite
\[
\tilde K_1=K_4(-\cdot),\quad\tilde K_2=K_5(-\cdot),\quad\tilde K_3=K_3,\quad\tilde K_4=K_1(-\cdot),\quad\tilde K_5=K_2(-\cdot),
\]
and for $\mathsf T_4$ we have $\tilde X=Y(-\cdot)$, $\tilde Y=X(-\cdot)$. Since $K(-\cdot)$ has the symbol $\sigma(-k)$, the function $\hat{\mathsf T}_{\mathsf q}$ of $\tilde G$ is
\[
\int_{\mathbb T}\sigma_1(-\kappa_1+l)\,\sigma_2(-\kappa_2-l)\,\sigma_3(l)\,d^\circ l=\hat{\mathsf T}_{\mathsf p}(-\kappa),
\]
and the symbol of $\tilde Y$ is $\mathsf I_X(-k)$, after the substitution $l\to-l$. By the last assertion of \cref{IV-73-42}, whose hypothesis holds here for all $\kappa$, the corresponding polynomials are $\mathsf Q_{\mathsf p}(-\kappa)$ and $\mathsf Q_X(-k)$. The passage from a polynomial $\mathsf Q$ to $\tilde{\mathsf Q}(\kappa)=\mathsf Q(0)+\sum_j\partial_j\mathsf Q(0)\sin\kappa_j$ in \cref{IV-73-47} and \cref{IV-73-46}(iii) commutes with the change of sign of the argument, the sine being odd. Hence the kernel $\mathsf q_{\mathsf q}$ of $\tilde G$ is $(z,w)\mapsto\mathsf q_{\mathsf p}(-z,-w)$, and $\mathsf q_{\tilde Y}=\mathsf q_X(-\cdot)$, so that
\begin{gather*}
\sum_{z,w}\mathsf q_{\mathsf p}(-z,-w)\,\tilde K_1(-u'-z)\,\tilde K_2(-u'-w)=\sum_{z,w}\mathsf q_{\mathsf p}(z,w)\,K_4(u'-z)\,K_5(u'-w),\\
(\mathsf q_{\tilde Y}*\tilde X)(-u')=(\mathsf q_X*Y)(u') .
\end{gather*}
These are the local terms at $p$ in $\mathsf T_1$ and in $\mathsf T_4$.

\emph{Step 3 (the class $\mathsf T_{\mathrm I}$).} By \cref{IV-73-62}(a),
\[
K^\to*\Sigma_{\mu\nu}*K^\leftarrow=K^\to*\mathsf q^\Sigma_{\mu\nu}*K^\leftarrow+K^\to*\mathsf W_{\mu\nu}*K^\leftarrow .
\]
The first term is $O(r^{-3})$ by \cref{IV-73-61}(b), since $\hat{\mathsf q}^\Sigma_{\mu\nu}(k)=O(|k|^2)$. The second lies in $\mathfrak K(2)$, by \cref{IV-73-46}(ii) applied to each of its two convolutions, and it equals its leading kernel, of degree $-2$, up to $O(r^{-3}\lg r)$; by the linearity of the leading data, this leading kernel is the sum over $G$, with the coefficients $c_G$, of the leading kernels of the chains in the definition of $\mathsf U_G$ in \cref{IV-73-69}. Moreover $\Pi(p,q)=\Pi^h(u')+O(r^{-4})$, with $\Pi^h$ homogeneous of degree $-3$ (\cref{IV-73-51}, \cref{lem:pure-homogeneous-kernels}). Therefore
\[
\mathsf T_{\mathrm I}=\sum_{(\mu,\nu,G)\in\mathfrak G_2\cup\mathfrak G_3}(-3\,c_G)\,\mathsf U_G(u')+O(r^{-6}\lg r).
\]

\emph{Step 4 (assembly).} Let
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathsf U_{\iota\iota'}(u):={}&\sum_{\Gamma\ne5}\ \sum_{G\in\mathfrak G_\Gamma(\iota,\iota')}c_G\,\mathsf U_G(u)\\
&+\sum_{G\in\mathfrak G_5(\iota,\iota')}c_G\,\mathsf U_G(u)+\sum_{G\in\mathfrak G_5(\iota',\iota)}c_G\,\mathsf U_G(-u),
\end{aligned}
\]
with the coefficients $-3\,c_G$ for $\Gamma=2,3$; the last sum comes from the second half of $\mathsf T_5$, which is the first half for $(q,p)$ with $u'$ replaced by $-u'$. The function $\mathsf U_{\iota\iota'}$ is homogeneous of degree $-5$ and of class $C^1$ off $0$, by \cref{IV-73-60} and since the leading kernels of the classes $\mathfrak K(n)$ are smooth off $0$. By Steps 1--3 and \cref{IV-73-60}, $\mathsf B_1^{\mathrm{lat}}(p,q)=\mathsf U_{\iota\iota'}(u')+O(r^{-6}\lg r)$. The gradient of $\mathsf U_{\iota\iota'}$ is homogeneous of degree $-6$, and all points $u'+t(u-u')$, $0\le t\le1$, have modulus at least $r/2$; hence $|\mathsf U_{\iota\iota'}(u')-\mathsf U_{\iota\iota'}(u)|\le Cr^{-6}$. With $\mathsf U_{ij}:=\mathsf U_{\iota\iota'}$ for $(i,j)=(\iota,\iota')=(\lambda(p),\lambda(q))$ we obtain the bound in \eqref{IV-73-72}; as $\tau_{\mathrm{gf}}=1$, the finite sets $\mathfrak G_\bullet(\iota,\iota')$, the coefficients $c_G$ and the lines are fixed once and for all, the constants $C,r_0$ are pure. Finally, exchanging $\iota$ and $\iota'$ in the last sum and using Lemmas~\ref{IV-73-69} and~\ref{IV-73-70},
\[
\sum_{\iota,\iota'}\mathsf U_{\iota\iota'}=\sum_{\Gamma=1}^6\mathsf U_\Gamma=\sum_{\Gamma=1}^6\kappa_\Gamma^{\mathrm{lat}}\,|u|^{-5} .
\]
\end{proof}

For the smeared observables of \eqref{IV-73-25} the theorem gives the following rate of convergence on test pairs. Here $\mathfrak T_{\mathbb R^3}(\mathsf d;\vartheta)$ is the set of test pairs at the scale $\mathsf d$ with the shape parameter $\vartheta$ of \cref{def:pure-test-pairs}, taken on $\mathbb E=\mathbb R^3$.

\begin{proposition}[Rate of convergence of $\mathsf P_1^{\mathrm{lat}}$ to $\kappa^{\mathrm{lat}}\mathcal K_5$]\label{IV-73-73}
There is a pure constant $C$ such that the following holds for all $\mathsf d>0$, $\vartheta\in(0,1)$, $(f,h)\in\mathfrak T_{\mathbb R^3}(\mathsf d;\vartheta)$ and $0<a\le\mathsf d$. Recall
\[
\mathcal K_5(f,h)=\iint f(x)\,h(y)\,|x-y|^{-5}\,dx\,dy ,
\]
the integrand being $0$ where $f(x)h(y)=0$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{IV-73-74}
\bigl|\mathsf P_1^{\mathrm{lat}}(f,h;a)-\kappa^{\mathrm{lat}}\,\mathcal K_5(f,h)\bigr|\le C\,\vartheta^{-1}\,a\,\lg(\mathsf d/a)\,\|f\|_\infty\|h\|_\infty .
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}

We recall three properties of a test pair $(f,h)\in\mathfrak T_{\mathbb R^3}(\mathsf d;\vartheta)$: the supports of $f$ and $h$ lie in closed balls $\mathbb B(x_f,\mathsf d)$ and $\mathbb B(x_h,\mathsf d)$ of radius $\mathsf d$; $\mathsf d\le|v-w|\le10\,\mathsf d$ for $v\in\operatorname{supp}f$ and $w\in\operatorname{supp}h$; and $\operatorname{Lip}f\le\|f\|_\infty/\vartheta\mathsf d$, $\operatorname{Lip}h\le\|h\|_\infty/\vartheta\mathsf d$.

\begin{proof}
Let $\varrho:=\mathsf d/a\ge1$, $\mathsf A:=\|f\|_\infty\|h\|_\infty$ and $\varrho_0:=\max\{r_0,8\}$, with $r_0$ of \cref{IV-73-71}. A ball of radius $\varrho+2$ contains at most $C\varrho^3$ points of $\frac12\mathbb Z^3$. The barycentres $x(p)$ lie in $\frac12\mathbb Z^3$, distinct plaquettes have distinct barycentres, and $f(ax(p))\ne0$ implies $x(p)\in\mathbb B(x_f/a,\varrho)$; likewise for $h$.

\emph{Step 1 ($\varrho\le\varrho_0$).} Then the sum defining $\mathsf P_1^{\mathrm{lat}}(f,h;a)$ has at most $C$ non-zero terms, and since $\mathsf B_1^{\mathrm{lat}}$ is bounded (\cref{IV-73-71}), $|\mathsf P_1^{\mathrm{lat}}(f,h;a)|\le Ca\mathsf A$. Moreover $|x-y|\ge\mathsf d$ where $f(x)h(y)\ne0$, whence $|\mathcal K_5(f,h)|\le(\frac{4\pi}3\mathsf d^3)^2\mathsf d^{-5}\mathsf A\le C\varrho_0a\mathsf A$. As $\vartheta^{-1}>1$ and $\lg(\mathsf d/a)\ge1$, \eqref{IV-73-74} holds in this case.

\emph{Step 2 ($\varrho>\varrho_0$, first error).} If $f(ax(p))h(ax(q))\ne0$, then $r=|x(q)-x(p)|\in[\varrho,10\varrho]$ by the separation of the supports; in particular $r\ge r_0$. There are at most $C\varrho^6$ such pairs, and $r^{-6}\lg r\le\varrho^{-6}\lg(10\varrho)$ for these $r$. By \eqref{IV-73-72}, the replacement of $\mathsf B_1^{\mathrm{lat}}(p,q)$ by $\mathsf U_{\lambda(p)\lambda(q)}(x(q)-x(p))$ in $\mathsf P_1^{\mathrm{lat}}(f,h;a)$ costs at most
\[
a\cdot C\varrho^6\cdot C\varrho^{-6}\lg(10\varrho)\,\mathsf A\le Ca\lg\varrho\,\mathsf A .
\]

\emph{Step 3 (second error).} We write $p=p_{[i]}(x)$, $q=p_{[j]}(y)$, so that $x(p)=x+\mathsf o_i$ with $\mathsf o_i:=x(p_{[i]}(0))$, $|\mathsf o_i|=2^{-1/2}$; all terms below are set equal to $0$ where the product of the values of $f$ and $h$ vanishes. After Step~2 we have to compare
\[
\mathfrak R_1:=a\sum_{i,j}\sum_{x,y\in\mathbb Z^3}f(a(x+\mathsf o_i))\,h(a(y+\mathsf o_j))\,\mathsf U_{ij}(y-x+\mathsf o_j-\mathsf o_i)
\]
with
\[
\mathfrak R_2:=a\sum_{x,y}f(ax)\,h(ay)\sum_{i,j}\mathsf U_{ij}(y-x)=a\,\kappa^{\mathrm{lat}}\sum_{x,y}\frac{f(ax)\,h(ay)}{|y-x|^5},
\]
the last equality by \eqref{IV-73-72}. We replace $f$, $h$ and $\mathsf U_{ij}$ one after the other. In every non-zero term, the arguments of $\mathsf U_{ij}$ which occur, and the points between them, have modulus at least $\varrho-2\ge\varrho/2$, and $x,y$ lie in balls of radius $\varrho+1$. By homogeneity, $|\mathsf U_{ij}|\le C\varrho^{-5}$ and $|\nabla\mathsf U_{ij}|\le C\varrho^{-6}$ at these points, and the Lipschitz bound gives $|f(a(x+\mathsf o_i))-f(ax)|\le a\|f\|_\infty/\vartheta\mathsf d$, and likewise for $h$. Therefore
\[
|\mathfrak R_1-\mathfrak R_2|\le a\,C\varrho^6\Bigl[\frac a{\vartheta\mathsf d}\,\varrho^{-5}+\varrho^{-6}\Bigr]\mathsf A\le Ca\vartheta^{-1}\mathsf A .
\]

\emph{Step 4 (third error).} Let $\mathsf F(v,w):=f(v)h(w)|v-w|^{-5}$, equal to $0$ where $f(v)h(w)=0$. Then $\mathfrak R_2=\kappa^{\mathrm{lat}}\sum_{x,y}a^6\mathsf F(ax,ay)$ and $\mathcal K_5(f,h)=\iint\mathsf F$. Let $(v,w)\in(ax,ay)+[0,a)^6$. Unless $\mathsf F$ vanishes at both points $(v,w)$ and $(ax,ay)$, we have $|v-w|\ge\mathsf d-2\sqrt3a\ge\mathsf d/2$ at both points and at all points $(1-t)(ax,ay)+t(v,w)$, $0\le t\le1$ (recall $\varrho>8$), and the Lipschitz bounds for $f,h$ together with the bound $5|z|^{-6}$ for the gradient of $|z|^{-5}$ give
\[
|\mathsf F(v,w)-\mathsf F(ax,ay)|\le\sqrt3a\Bigl[\frac2{\vartheta\mathsf d}\Bigl(\frac{\mathsf d}2\Bigr)^{-5}+10\Bigl(\frac{\mathsf d}2\Bigr)^{-6}\Bigr]\mathsf A .
\]
At most $C\varrho^6$ of the cubes $(ax,ay)+[0,a)^6$, of volume $a^6$, contain points where $\mathsf F\ne0$. Hence
\[
|\mathfrak R_2-\kappa^{\mathrm{lat}}\mathcal K_5(f,h)|\le C\varrho^6a^6\cdot a\vartheta^{-1}\mathsf d^{-6}\mathsf A=Ca\vartheta^{-1}\mathsf A .
\]
Adding the bounds of Steps 2--4 and using $\vartheta^{-1}>1$, $\lg\varrho\ge1$, we obtain \eqref{IV-73-74}.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[The boxes exhaust the lattice]\label{IV-73-76}
Let $\tau_{\mathrm{gf}}=1$, let $p,q$ be plaquettes of $\mathbb Z^3$ and $j\in\{0,1\}$, and write $\mathsf B_0^\Omega(p,q;\tau_{\mathrm{gf}}):=\mathsf B_0^\Omega(p,q)$. The numbers $\mathsf B_j^{[n]}(p+o_n,q+o_n;\tau_{\mathrm{gf}})$ are defined for all $n\ge2$ with $p+o_n,q+o_n\in\mathsf{Pl}_n$, that is, for all but finitely many $n$, and
\begin{equation}\label{IV-73-77}
\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathsf B_j^{[n]}(p+o_n,q+o_n;\tau_{\mathrm{gf}})=\mathsf B_j^{\mathrm{lat}}(p,q;\tau_{\mathrm{gf}}).
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
We use the method of images. Fix $n$ and write $\tau:=\tau_{\mathrm{gf}}$.

\emph{Step 1 (reflections).} We regard forms and functions on the torus $(\mathbb Z/2n)^3$ as $2ne_\nu$-periodic forms and functions on $\mathbb Z^3$, and we write $(\cdot,\cdot)_{\mathsf t}$ for the sums over one period. Let $\varrho_\nu$ be the reflection $z_\nu\to-z_\nu$, acting on bonds by $\varrho_\nu\langle z,z'\rangle=\langle\varrho_\nu z,\varrho_\nu z'\rangle$, and put $(\varrho_\nu^*\tilde A)(b):=\tilde A(\varrho_\nu b)$ and $\varrho_\nu^*\lambda:=\lambda\circ\varrho_\nu$; these maps commute with $\mathrm d$ and $\mathrm d^*$. Let $\mathsf F^{\mathrm{as}}$ and $\mathsf X^{\mathrm{as}}$ be the spaces of real periodic forms $\tilde A$ and functions $\lambda$ with $\varrho_\nu^*\tilde A=-\tilde A$ and $\varrho_\nu^*\lambda=-\lambda$ for all $\nu$; in components, $\tilde A_\mu(\varrho_\nu z)=-\tilde A_\mu(z)$ for $\nu\ne\mu$, and $\tilde A_\mu(\varrho_\mu z-e_\mu)=\tilde A_\mu(z)$. We claim that restriction to the box is a bijection of $\mathsf F^{\mathrm{as}}$ onto $\mathsf{Form}_n^{\mathbb R}$ and of $\mathsf X^{\mathrm{as}}$ onto $\mathsf X_n^{\mathbb R}$. If $z_\nu\in\{0,n\}$, then $\varrho_\nu z\equiv z$ modulo $2n$, hence $\tilde A_\mu(z)=0$ for $\nu\ne\mu$, and $\lambda(z)=0$; by \cref{IV-73-12}(a), $\tilde A$ vanishes on the non-free bonds of the box, and $\lambda$ vanishes on $\partial\Lambda_n$. For $\varepsilon\in\{0,1\}^3$ let $R_\varepsilon:=\prod_\nu\varrho_\nu^{\varepsilon_\nu}$, $|\varepsilon|:=\sum_\nu\varepsilon_\nu$, and $R_\varepsilon(z,\mu):=(R_\varepsilon z-\varepsilon_\mu e_\mu,\mu)$, the positively oriented one among the image bond and its reverse. Every positively oriented bond of the torus has the form $R_\varepsilon(x,\mu)$ with $x_\mu\in\{0,\dots,n-1\}$ and $x_\nu\in\{0,\dots,n\}$ for $\nu\ne\mu$; here $(x,\mu)$ is unique, and $\varepsilon$ is unique if $(x,\mu)$ is free. Hence every $A\in\mathsf{Form}_n^{\mathbb R}$ has the unique continuation $\tilde A(R_\varepsilon b)=(-1)^{|\varepsilon|+\varepsilon_\mu}A(b)$, $b=(x,\mu)$, and every $\lambda\in\mathsf X_n^{\mathbb R}$ the unique continuation $\tilde\lambda(R_\varepsilon x)=(-1)^{|\varepsilon|}\lambda(x)$.

\emph{Step 2 (operators).} The eight boxes $R_\varepsilon[0,n]^3$ cover the torus, and a plaquette lying in two of them lies in a hyperplane $\{z_\nu=0\}$ or $\{z_\nu=n\}$, on whose bonds $\tilde A=0$. The functions $|\mathrm d\tilde A|$ and $|\mathrm d^*\tilde A|$ are invariant under the $\varrho_\nu$, and $\mathrm d^*\tilde A\in\mathsf X^{\mathrm{as}}$ vanishes on these hyperplanes. Hence
\[
(\tilde A,\tilde A')_{\mathsf t}=8(A,A'),\qquad\|\mathrm d\tilde A\|^2_{\mathsf t}=8\|\mathrm dA\|^2,\qquad\|\mathrm d^*\tilde A\|^2_{\mathsf t}=8\|\mathrm d^*A\|^2 .
\]
The operator $\mathsf L_\tau:=\mathrm d^*\mathrm d+\tau^{-1}\mathrm d\mathrm d^*$ on the torus commutes with the $\varrho_\nu^*$ and preserves $\mathsf F^{\mathrm{as}}$. By polarisation, $(\tilde A',\mathsf L_\tau\tilde A)_{\mathsf t}=8(A',\mathsf L_\tau^{[n]}A)$ for all $A,A'\in\mathsf{Form}_n^{\mathbb R}$, where $\mathsf L^{[n]}_\tau$ is the operator on $\mathsf{Form}_n^{\mathbb R}$ of the quadratic form in \cref{IV-73-15}; hence $\mathsf L_\tau\tilde A$ is the continuation of $\mathsf L_\tau^{[n]}A$. The forms in $\mathsf F^{\mathrm{as}}$ have mean $0$, and on periodic forms of mean $0$ the inverse of $\mathsf L_\tau$ is, by the finite Fourier inversion formula, the convolution with
\[
C^{(n)}_{\mu\nu}(z):=(2n)^{-3}\sum_{k\in\mathbb T_n\setminus\{0\}}e^{ik\cdot z}\,\hat{C}_{\mu\nu}(k) .
\]
The continuation of $\delta_{b'}$, for a free bond $b'=(x',\mu')$, is $\sum_\varepsilon(-1)^{|\varepsilon|+\varepsilon_{\mu'}}\delta_{R_\varepsilon b'}$. For functions we have in the same way $(\tilde\lambda,\tilde\lambda')_{\mathsf t}=8(\lambda,\lambda')$ and $\|\mathrm d\tilde\lambda\|^2_{\mathsf t}=8\|\mathrm d\lambda\|^2$, since $\mathrm d\tilde\lambda\in\mathsf F^{\mathrm{as}}$ is the continuation of $\mathrm d\lambda$; the elements of $\mathsf X^{\mathrm{as}}$ have mean $0$, and the continuation of $\delta_{x'}$, $x'\in\Lambda_n^\circ$, is $\sum_\varepsilon(-1)^{|\varepsilon|}\delta_{R_\varepsilon x'}$. By polarisation, as for forms, $\mathrm d^*\mathrm d\tilde\lambda$ is the continuation of $\mathrm d^*\mathrm d\lambda$, and on periodic functions of mean $0$ the inverse of $\mathrm d^*\mathrm d$ is the convolution with $G^{(n)}(z):=(2n)^{-3}\sum_{k\in\mathbb T_n\setminus\{0\}}e^{ik\cdot z}|\mathsf k(k)|^{-2}$. We apply this to $B:=(\mathsf L_\tau^{[n]})^{-1}\delta_{b'}$, whose value at a free bond $b$ is $C^{[n]}_\tau(b,b')$; its continuation $\tilde B$ has mean $0$ and satisfies $\mathsf L_\tau\tilde B=\tilde\delta_{b'}$, the continuation of $\delta_{b'}$, so that $\tilde B$ is the convolution of $C^{(n)}$ with $\tilde\delta_{b'}$. In the same way we treat $(\mathrm d^*\mathrm d)^{-1}\delta_{x'}$ on $\mathsf X_n^{\mathbb R}$, whose value at $x\in\Lambda_n^\circ$ is $G^{[n]}(x,x')$. Consequently, for free bonds $(x,\mu),(x',\mu')$ and for $x,x'\in\Lambda_n^\circ$,
\begin{equation}\label{IV-73-78}
\begin{gathered}
C^{[n]}_\tau\bigl((x,\mu),(x',\mu')\bigr)=\sum_\varepsilon(-1)^{|\varepsilon|+\varepsilon_{\mu'}}\,C^{(n)}_{\mu\mu'}\bigl(x-R_\varepsilon x'+\varepsilon_{\mu'}e_{\mu'}\bigr),\\
G^{[n]}(x,x')=\sum_\varepsilon(-1)^{|\varepsilon|}\,G^{(n)}(x-R_\varepsilon x').
\end{gathered}
\end{equation}
In the first argument the right sides are values of elements of $\mathsf F^{\mathrm{as}}$, resp.\ $\mathsf X^{\mathrm{as}}$, and therefore vanish at non-free bonds, resp.\ on $\partial\Lambda_n$; in the second argument the same follows by symmetry. Since the box kernels vanish there by definition, \eqref{IV-73-78} holds for all bonds and sites of $\Lambda_n$.

\emph{Step 3 (uniform bounds).} The kernels $E^{[n]},\Pi^{[n]},D^{[n]},\mathsf g^{[n]}$ arise from \eqref{IV-73-78} by the differences and means of \cref{IV-73-15}. A difference in the first argument acts on $C^{(n)}$ and $G^{(n)}$. In the second argument, $R_\varepsilon$ maps the four bonds of $q$ onto those of $R_\varepsilon q$, and $\sum_js_j(-1)^{\varepsilon_{\mu_j}}\delta_{R_\varepsilon b_j(q)}=\pm\sum_js_j\delta_{b_j(R_\varepsilon q)}$, with $\mu_j$ the direction of $b_j(q)$, since $\mathrm d$ commutes with the $\varrho_\nu^*$; the same holds for the end points of a bond. Hence each of these kernels is a sum of eight terms $\pm K^{(n)}(x-R_\varepsilon x'+y_0)$ with $|y_0|\le3$, where $x$ and $x'$ are the base points of its two arguments, as in \cref{IV-73-56} (the base point $b_-$ of a bond $b$, the base point $x_p$ of a plaquette $p$; for $\mathsf g^{[n]}(b)$ both are $b_-$), and where $K^{(n)}$ is built as in \cref{IV-73-75} with the symbol of the corresponding line of \cref{IV-73-51}, an element of $\mathcal S^{n_\ell-3}$, $n_\ell$ being the degree of the line. For $x,x'\in\Lambda_n$ we have $|x-R_\varepsilon x'|_n\ge|x-x'|$: if $\varepsilon_\nu=0$, then $|x_\nu-x'_\nu|\le n$, and if $\varepsilon_\nu=1$, then $\min\{x_\nu+x'_\nu,2n-x_\nu-x'_\nu\}\ge|x_\nu-x'_\nu|$. By \cref{IV-73-75}, the kernels of all boxes therefore satisfy the bounds \cref{IV-73-56} with one constant $\mathsf c_0=\mathsf c_0(\tau_{\mathrm{gf}})$.

\emph{Step 4 (pointwise limits).} The arguments are translates by $o_n$ of fixed bonds, sites and plaquettes. For $\varepsilon=0$ the term $K^{(n)}(x-x'+y_0)$ has a fixed argument and converges to the corresponding kernel of $\mathbb Z^3$, by \cref{IV-73-75} and \cref{IV-73-51}. If $\varepsilon_\nu=1$, the $\nu$-th coordinate of the argument is $\tilde x_\nu+\tilde x'_\nu+2\lfloor n/2\rfloor+O(1)$, where $\tilde x=x-o_n$ and $\tilde x'=x'-o_n$ are fixed; its distance from $2n\mathbb Z$ is therefore at least $n-C$, and the term tends to $0$ by \cref{IV-73-75}.

\emph{Step 5 (conclusion).} For $j=0$, $\mathsf B_0^{[n]}=\frac{3}2(\Pi^{[n]})^2$ by \cref{IV-73-19}, which converges by Step~4 to $\frac{3}2(\Pi^{\mathrm{lat}})^2=\mathsf B_0^{\mathrm{lat}}$. For $j=1$, the formulas of \cref{IV-73-53} in the box, which are finite sums, express $\mathsf B_1^{[n]}(p+o_n,q+o_n;\tau_{\mathrm{gf}})$ as a sum, over monomials, pairings and positions, of products of box kernels. We write the positions in the box as translates $P+o_n$, $P'+o_n$, $b+o_n,\dots$ of plaquettes $P,P'$ and bonds $b,\dots$ of $\mathbb Z^3$, and we index the terms by the monomial, the pairing and the positions $P,P',b,\dots$ in $\mathbb Z^3$; this set of indices does not depend on $n$, and a term whose positions do not all lie in the box is set equal to $0$. For fixed $P,P',b,\dots$ all positions lie in the box for every large $n$, and by Step~4 the term converges, as $n\to\infty$, to the term of the formulas of \cref{IV-73-53} on $\mathbb Z^3$ with the same monomial, the same pairing and the positions $P,P',b,\dots$. By Step~3, the box kernels satisfy \cref{IV-73-56} with one constant $\mathsf c_0$; these bounds depend only on differences of base points, which the translation by $o_n$ does not change, and the uniform form of \cref{IV-73-55}, valid for any kernels with these bounds, therefore dominates the moduli of the terms, uniformly in $n$, by a family of majorants over the same set of indices whose sum is at most $C\mathsf c_0^5$. By dominated convergence, $\mathsf B_1^{[n]}(p+o_n,q+o_n;\tau_{\mathrm{gf}})$ tends to the sum of the terms on $\mathbb Z^3$, which converges absolutely and equals $\mathsf B_1^{\mathrm{lat}}(p,q;\tau_{\mathrm{gf}})$ by \cref{IV-73-55}. This is \eqref{IV-73-77}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Evaluating the coefficient}
We extract the coefficient of \(|p|^2\log|p|\) from the six
continuum integrals. In this calculation
\((\mathcal F^{-1}\phi)(p)=\int e^{ip\cdot x}\phi(x)\,d^\circ x\).
Write \(\Gamma_{\mathrm E}\) for Euler's gamma function.

\begin{lemma}[Two Fourier constants]\label{IV-73-80}
Let $\phi\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^3)$ vanish near $0$.

\textup{(a)} For $s\in\mathbb C$ with $\operatorname{Re}s>-3$,
\begin{equation}\label{IV-73-81}
\begin{gathered}
\int_{\mathbb R^3}|p|^s\,(\mathcal F^{-1}\phi)(p)\,dp=c(s)\int_{\mathbb R^3}|x|^{-3-s}\,\phi(x)\,dx,\\
c(s):=\frac{2^s\,\Gamma_{\mathrm E}(\frac{3+s}2)}{\pi^{3/2}\,\Gamma_{\mathrm E}(-\frac s2)},
\end{gathered}
\end{equation}
where $1/\Gamma_{\mathrm E}$ is entire. Moreover $c(s)=0$ for $s=0,2,4,\dots$, and $c(1)=-\pi^{-2}$.

\textup{(b)} We have
\begin{equation}\label{IV-73-82}
\int_{\mathbb R^3}p^2\log|p|\,(\mathcal F^{-1}\phi)(p)\,dp=c'(2)\int_{\mathbb R^3}|x|^{-5}\,\phi(x)\,dx,\qquad c'(2)=\frac3{2\pi}.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\emph{Step 1.} Let $\psi:=\mathcal F^{-1}\phi\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^3)$, and assume first $-3<\operatorname{Re}s<0$. The substitution $t\to t/p^2$ in Euler's integral gives $\int_0^\infty t^{-s/2-1}e^{-tp^2}\,dt=\Gamma_{\mathrm E}(-\frac s2)\,|p|^s$ for $p\ne0$. Since
\[
\iint t^{-\operatorname{Re}s/2-1}e^{-tp^2}\,|\psi(p)|\,dt\,dp=\Gamma_{\mathrm E}\bigl(-\tfrac12\operatorname{Re}s\bigr)\int|p|^{\operatorname{Re}s}|\psi(p)|\,dp<\infty ,
\]
Fubini's theorem yields
\[
\int|p|^s\psi(p)\,dp=\Gamma_{\mathrm E}\bigl(-\tfrac s2\bigr)^{-1}\int_0^\infty t^{-s/2-1}\Bigl[\int e^{-tp^2}\psi(p)\,dp\Bigr]dt .
\]
By Fubini's theorem and the Gaussian integral $\int_{\mathbb R^3}e^{-tp^2+ip\cdot x}\,dp=(\pi/t)^{3/2}e^{-x^2/4t}$,
\[
\int e^{-tp^2}\psi(p)\,dp=\int\phi(x)\Bigl[\int e^{-tp^2+ip\cdot x}\,d^\circ p\Bigr]dx=\int(4\pi t)^{-3/2}e^{-x^2/4t}\,\phi(x)\,dx .
\]
For $x\ne0$ the substitution $t\to x^2/4t$ gives
\[
\int_0^\infty t^{-(s+3)/2-1}e^{-x^2/4t}\,dt=\Gamma_{\mathrm E}\bigl(\tfrac{s+3}2\bigr)\Bigl(\frac{x^2}4\Bigr)^{-(s+3)/2},
\]
as $\operatorname{Re}s+3>0$. The same identity with $\operatorname{Re}s$ in place of $s$,
\[
\int_0^\infty t^{-(\operatorname{Re}s+3)/2-1}e^{-x^2/4t}\,dt=\Gamma_{\mathrm E}\bigl(\tfrac{\operatorname{Re}s+3}2\bigr)\Bigl(\frac{x^2}4\Bigr)^{-(\operatorname{Re}s+3)/2},
\]
together with $\int|x|^{-\operatorname{Re}s-3}|\phi(x)|\,dx<\infty$, which holds as $\phi$ vanishes near $0$ and lies in $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^3)$, shows that the modulus $(4\pi)^{-3/2}t^{-(\operatorname{Re}s+3)/2-1}e^{-x^2/4t}|\phi(x)|$ of the integrand $t^{-s/2-1}(4\pi t)^{-3/2}e^{-x^2/4t}\phi(x)$ is integrable over $(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R^3$. Hence Fubini's theorem applies once more, and
\[
\int|p|^s\psi(p)\,dp=\Gamma_{\mathrm E}\bigl(-\tfrac s2\bigr)^{-1}(4\pi)^{-3/2}\,2^{s+3}\,\Gamma_{\mathrm E}\bigl(\tfrac{s+3}2\bigr)\int|x|^{-s-3}\phi(x)\,dx ,
\]
with $(4\pi)^{-3/2}2^{s+3}=2^s\pi^{-3/2}$. This is \eqref{IV-73-81} for $-3<\operatorname{Re}s<0$.

\emph{Step 2.} The left side of \eqref{IV-73-81} is holomorphic in $s$ on $\{\operatorname{Re}s>-3\}$, since $|p|^{\operatorname{Re}s}|\psi|$ provides integrable majorants locally uniformly in $s$; the function $s\mapsto\int|x|^{-3-s}\phi(x)\,dx$ is entire, since $\phi$ vanishes near $0$ and lies in $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^3)$; and $c$ is holomorphic on $\{\operatorname{Re}s>-3\}$, since $\Gamma_{\mathrm E}$ is holomorphic on the right half plane and $1/\Gamma_{\mathrm E}$ is entire. Both sides agree for $-3<\operatorname{Re}s<0$, hence on the connected set $\{\operatorname{Re}s>-3\}$ by the identity theorem. The entire functions $1/\Gamma_{\mathrm E}(z)$ and $z/\Gamma_{\mathrm E}(z+1)$ agree for $\operatorname{Re}z>0$, hence for all $z$; therefore $1/\Gamma_{\mathrm E}$ vanishes at $0$, and then successively at $-1,-2,\dots$, which gives $c(s)=0$ for $s=0,2,4,\dots$. Moreover $1/\Gamma_{\mathrm E}(-\frac12)=-\frac12/\Gamma_{\mathrm E}(\frac12)=-\frac1{2\sqrt\pi}$, whence $c(1)=\frac{2\,\Gamma_{\mathrm E}(2)}{\pi^{3/2}}\cdot\bigl(-\frac1{2\sqrt\pi}\bigr)=-\pi^{-2}$.

\emph{Step 3.} For (b) we differentiate \eqref{IV-73-81} with respect to $s$ at $s=2$. On the left we obtain $\int p^2\log|p|\,\psi(p)\,dp$, by differentiation under the integral; on the right \[c'(2)\int|x|^{-5}\phi-c(2)\int|x|^{-5}\log|x|\,\phi,\] where $c(2)=0$. From $1/\Gamma_{\mathrm E}(z)=z(z+1)/\Gamma_{\mathrm E}(z+2)$ the derivative of $1/\Gamma_{\mathrm E}$ at $z=-1$ is $(2z+1)/\Gamma_{\mathrm E}(z+2)|_{z=-1}=-1$; with $z=-\frac s2$ this gives $\partial_s\bigl[1/\Gamma_{\mathrm E}(-\frac s2)\bigr]_{s=2}=\frac12$. As $1/\Gamma_{\mathrm E}(-1)=0$, only this derivative contributes, and $c'(2)=2^2\,\Gamma_{\mathrm E}(\frac52)\,\pi^{-3/2}\cdot\frac12$ with $\Gamma_{\mathrm E}(\frac52)=\frac32\cdot\frac12\sqrt\pi=\frac34\sqrt\pi$; thus $c'(2)=\frac3{2\pi}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Two Fourier series: Epstein-type sums near $\mathsf p=0$]\label{IV-73-83}
For $n\in\{4,5\}$ and $\mathsf p\in\mathbb R^3$ let $\mathsf s_n(\mathsf p):=\sum_{u\in\mathbb Z^3\setminus\{0\}}|u|^{-n}e^{-i\mathsf p\cdot u}$. There are functions $\mathsf e_4,\mathsf e_5\in C^\infty(\{|\mathsf p|<1\})$, invariant under the $48$ signed permutations of the coordinates, such that
\[
\mathsf s_4(\mathsf p)=-\pi^2|\mathsf p|+\mathsf e_4(\mathsf p),\qquad\mathsf s_5(\mathsf p)=\tfrac{2\pi}3\,\mathsf p^2\log|\mathsf p|+\mathsf e_5(\mathsf p)\qquad(0<|\mathsf p|<1).
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
We treat the two cases $(\varpi,n,\mathsf c)=(|p|,4,-\pi^{-2})$ and $(\varpi,n,\mathsf c)=(p^2\log|p|,5,\frac3{2\pi})$ together. The function $\varpi$ is continuous, radial and smooth off $0$, and its derivatives of order $j$ are $O(|p|^{2-j}\lg|p|)$ at infinity. For an integer $\mathsf N\ge3$ let
\[
\mathsf K(x):=\int e^{ip\cdot x}\chi(p)\,\varpi(p)\,d^\circ p,\qquad E(x):=|x|^{-2\mathsf N}\int e^{ip\cdot x}(-\Delta_p)^{\mathsf N}\bigl[(1-\chi)\varpi\bigr](p)\,d^\circ p\quad(x\ne0).
\]

\emph{Step 1.} The integrand of $E$ vanishes for $|p|\le1$ and is $O(|p|^{2-2\mathsf N}\lg|p|)$, with $2\mathsf N-2>3$; hence the integral converges absolutely. The value of $E(x)$ does not depend on $\mathsf N$: we write $|x|^2e^{ip\cdot x}=-\Delta_pe^{ip\cdot x}$ and integrate by parts twice over balls (Gauss' theorem); the boundary terms on the sphere of radius $\mathsf r$ are $O\bigl((1+|x|)\mathsf r^2\cdot\mathsf r^{2-2\mathsf N}\lg\mathsf r\bigr)$, which tends to $0$ as $\mathsf r\to\infty$ because $\mathsf N\ge3$; hence $\mathsf N$ and $\mathsf N+1$ give the same value. Consequently $E$ is continuous off $0$ and radial, and $|E(x)|\le C_{\mathsf N}|x|^{-2\mathsf N}$ for every $\mathsf N\ge3$.

\emph{Step 2.} We show $\mathsf K+E=\mathsf c\,|x|^{-n}$ on $\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$. Let $\phi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\})$. By Fubini's theorem, $\int\mathsf K\phi\,dx=\int\chi\varpi\,\mathcal F^{-1}\phi\,dp$. Let $\phi_{\mathsf N}:=|x|^{-2\mathsf N}\phi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\})$. By Fubini's theorem and $2\mathsf N$ integrations by parts, which are permitted as $\mathcal F^{-1}\phi_{\mathsf N}\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^3)$, and by $(-\Delta_p)^{\mathsf N}\mathcal F^{-1}\phi_{\mathsf N}=\mathcal F^{-1}(|x|^{2\mathsf N}\phi_{\mathsf N})=\mathcal F^{-1}\phi$,
\[
\int E\phi\,dx=\int(-\Delta_p)^{\mathsf N}\bigl[(1-\chi)\varpi\bigr]\,\mathcal F^{-1}\phi_{\mathsf N}\,dp=\int(1-\chi)\varpi\,\mathcal F^{-1}\phi\,dp .
\]
The sum is $\int\varpi\,\mathcal F^{-1}\phi\,dp=\mathsf c\int|x|^{-n}\phi\,dx$, by \cref{IV-73-80}(a) at $s=1$ in the first case and by \cref{IV-73-80}(b) in the second. As $\mathsf K+E-\mathsf c|x|^{-n}$ is continuous on $\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$, it vanishes there.

\emph{Step 3.} The periodic continuation of $\chi\varpi$, whose support lies in $\{|p|\le2\}$ and thus in the interior of $[-\pi,\pi]^3$, is continuous, and its Fourier coefficients are the numbers $\mathsf K(u)$, $u\in\mathbb Z^3$. By Steps 1 and 2, $\sum_u|\mathsf K(u)|<\infty$; hence the continuous function $\sum_u\mathsf K(u)e^{-i\mathsf p\cdot u}$ has the same Fourier coefficients and, both functions being continuous, coincides with the periodic continuation of $\chi\varpi$. For $|\mathsf p|<1$ we have $\chi(\mathsf p)=1$, and therefore
\[
\varpi(\mathsf p)=\mathsf K(0)+\mathsf c\,\mathsf s_n(\mathsf p)-\sum_{u\ne0}E(u)\,e^{-i\mathsf p\cdot u} .
\]
We put $\mathsf e_n(\mathsf p):=\mathsf c^{-1}\bigl[\sum_{u\ne0}E(u)e^{-i\mathsf p\cdot u}-\mathsf K(0)\bigr]$. This function is smooth, by the rapid decay of $E$, and invariant under the signed permutations of the coordinates, since $E$ is radial. Finally $\mathsf c^{-1}=-\pi^2$, resp.\ $\mathsf c^{-1}=\frac{2\pi}3$, which gives the claim.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Coefficient of $\mathsf p^2\log|\mathsf p|$ in $\Psi_\Gamma$; scaling of the cut-off]\label{IV-73-84}
Let $\Gamma\in\{1,\dots,6\}$.

\textup{(a)} There are numbers $\mathsf a_0,\mathsf a_1,\mathsf a_2$ and a function $\mathsf o$ on $\{|\mathsf p|<1\}$ with $\mathsf o(\mathsf p)/\mathsf p^2\to0$ as $\mathsf p\to0$, depending on $\Gamma$ only, such that for almost every $\mathsf p$ with $|\mathsf p|<1$
\[
\Psi_\Gamma(\mathsf p)=\mathsf a_0+\mathsf a_1|\mathsf p|+\mathsf a_2\mathsf p^2+\tfrac\pi{36}\,\kappa_\Gamma^{\mathrm{lat}}\,\mathsf p^2\log|\mathsf p|+\mathsf o(\mathsf p).
\]

\textup{(b)} For real $\Lambda>1$ let $R_\Gamma^\Lambda(k,l,\mathsf p):=R_\Gamma(k/\Lambda,l/\Lambda,\mathsf p/\Lambda)$. Then $\iint R_\Gamma^\Lambda F_\Gamma\,d^\circ k\,d^\circ l=\Lambda^2\Psi_\Gamma(\mathsf p/\Lambda)$ for every $\mathsf p\ne0$, and for almost every $\mathsf p$ with $|\mathsf p|<1$
\[
\begin{aligned}
\iint(R_\Gamma^\Lambda-R_\Gamma)F_\Gamma\,d^\circ k\,d^\circ l={}&(\Lambda^2-1)\mathsf a_0+(\Lambda-1)\mathsf a_1|\mathsf p|-\tfrac\pi{36}\,\kappa_\Gamma^{\mathrm{lat}}\log\Lambda\;\mathsf p^2\\
&+\Lambda^2\mathsf o(\mathsf p/\Lambda)-\mathsf o(\mathsf p).
\end{aligned}
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\emph{Step 1.} By Lemmas~\ref{IV-73-69} and~\ref{IV-73-70},
\begin{gather*}
\mathsf T_\Gamma^{\mathrm{mod}}(u)=c_{4,\Gamma}|u|^{-4}+\kappa_\Gamma^{\mathrm{lat}}|u|^{-5}+\mathsf r(u),\\
|\mathsf r(u)|\le C|u|^{-6}\lg|u|\qquad(u\in\mathbb Z^3\setminus\{0\});
\end{gather*}
we put $\mathsf r(0):=\mathsf T^{\mathrm{mod}}_\Gamma(0)$. Hence $\sum_u|\mathsf T_\Gamma^{\mathrm{mod}}(u)|<\infty$. The function $\Psi_\Gamma$ is integrable and vanishes for $|\mathsf p|\ge\frac{3\pi}8$ (\cref{IV-73-64}(3)), that is, outside a ball contained in $[-\pi,\pi]^3$. Therefore the periodic function which equals $24\Psi_\Gamma$ on $[-\pi,\pi]^3$ has the Fourier coefficients $24\int_{[-\pi,\pi]^3}e^{i\mathsf p\cdot u}\Psi_\Gamma(\mathsf p)\,d^\circ\mathsf p=\mathsf T_\Gamma^{\mathrm{mod}}(u)$, which are also the Fourier coefficients of the continuous function $\sum_u\mathsf T_\Gamma^{\mathrm{mod}}(u)e^{-i\mathsf p\cdot u}$. By the uniqueness of Fourier coefficients the two periodic functions agree almost everywhere; as the first one coincides with $24\Psi_\Gamma$ on $[-\pi,\pi]^3$, we obtain, for almost every $\mathsf p\in[-\pi,\pi]^3$,
\begin{gather*}
24\,\Psi_\Gamma(\mathsf p)=c_{4,\Gamma}\,\mathsf s_4(\mathsf p)+\kappa_\Gamma^{\mathrm{lat}}\,\mathsf s_5(\mathsf p)+\hat{\mathsf r}(\mathsf p),\\
\hat{\mathsf r}(\mathsf p):=\sum_u\mathsf r(u)\,e^{-i\mathsf p\cdot u} .
\end{gather*}

\emph{Step 2.} Since $\sum_u|u|^2|\mathsf r(u)|<\infty$, the function $\hat{\mathsf r}$ is of class $C^2$. As $\mathsf T_\Gamma^{\mathrm{mod}}$ is the restriction to $\mathbb Z^3$ of a radial function, $\mathsf r$ and $\hat{\mathsf r}$ are invariant under the signed permutations of the coordinates. A function $\mathsf f$ of class $C^2$ near $0$ with this invariance has vanishing gradient at $0$ (invariance under $-\mathbf 1$), a Hessian at $0$ with vanishing off-diagonal entries (change of sign of one coordinate) and equal diagonal entries (permutations); hence $\mathsf f(\mathsf p)=\mathsf f(0)+\mathsf a\,\mathsf p^2+o(\mathsf p^2)$. We apply this to $\hat{\mathsf r}$, $\mathsf e_4$ and $\mathsf e_5$ and insert \cref{IV-73-83}; this gives (a), the coefficient of $\mathsf p^2\log|\mathsf p|$ being $\frac1{24}\cdot\frac{2\pi}3\,\kappa_\Gamma^{\mathrm{lat}}=\frac\pi{36}\,\kappa_\Gamma^{\mathrm{lat}}$, and $\mathsf o$ being $\frac1{24}$ times the sum of the remainders $o(\mathsf p^2)$ of $c_{4,\Gamma}\mathsf e_4$, $\kappa_\Gamma^{\mathrm{lat}}\mathsf e_5$ and $\hat{\mathsf r}$.

\emph{Step 3.} For (b) we substitute $k\to\Lambda k$, $l\to\Lambda l$ and use $F_\Gamma(\Lambda k,\Lambda l,\Lambda\mathsf q)=\Lambda^{-4}F_\Gamma(k,l,\mathsf q)$ with $\mathsf q=\mathsf p/\Lambda$; this produces the factor $\Lambda^{6-4}=\Lambda^2$ and gives the first assertion. For the second we insert (a) at $\mathsf p/\Lambda$ and at $\mathsf p$, both of modulus less than $1$. The terms with $\mathsf a_2$ cancel, the terms with $\mathsf a_0$, $\mathsf a_1$ give $(\Lambda^2-1)\mathsf a_0+(\Lambda-1)\mathsf a_1|\mathsf p|$, and
\[
\Lambda^2\,\tfrac\pi{36}\,\kappa_\Gamma^{\mathrm{lat}}\Lambda^{-2}\mathsf p^2\bigl(\log|\mathsf p|-\log\Lambda\bigr)-\tfrac\pi{36}\,\kappa_\Gamma^{\mathrm{lat}}\,\mathsf p^2\log|\mathsf p|=-\tfrac\pi{36}\,\kappa_\Gamma^{\mathrm{lat}}\log\Lambda\;\mathsf p^2 .
\]
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Finite parts (analytic regularisation); cut-offs vanishing near the origin]\label{IV-73-85}
Let $\mathbb D:=\{\mathsf z\in\mathbb C:\operatorname{Re}\mathsf z>-\frac12\}\setminus\{\frac12,\frac32,\frac52,\dots\}$; this set is open and connected, and it contains $0$.

\emph{(1) One variable.} A \emph{homogeneous factor of degree $d\in\mathbb Z$} is a function $\mathsf h\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\})$ with $\mathsf h(tk)=t^d\mathsf h(k)$ for $t>0$ and $\mathsf h(-k)=(-1)^d\mathsf h(k)$. Let $\mathfrak P$ be the set of functions on $\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$ of the form $\mathsf g=\sum_\iota\mathsf h_\iota\mathsf g_\iota$, a finite sum, with homogeneous factors $\mathsf h_\iota$ of degrees $d_\iota$ and with $\mathsf g_\iota\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$. For such $\mathsf g$ the integral $\int|k|^{2\mathsf z}\mathsf g(k)\,dk$ converges absolutely and is holomorphic in $\mathsf z$ for $2\operatorname{Re}\mathsf z+\min_\iota d_\iota>-3$; it has a holomorphic continuation to $\mathbb D$ (\cref{IV-73-86}(a)), which is unique. The \emph{finite part} $\operatorname{f.p.}\!\int\mathsf g\,dk$ is the value of this continuation at $\mathsf z=0$; it depends on $\mathsf g$ only, and it is linear in $\mathsf g$.

\emph{(2) Two variables.} Let $c>0$ and $\eta_c(k):=\theta(4|k|/c)$, so that $\eta_c(k)=1$ for $|k|\le\frac c8$ and $\eta_c(k)=0$ for $|k|\ge\frac c4$. Let $\mathfrak P_2(c)$ be the set of Borel functions $\Phi$ on $\{(k,l):k\ne0,\ l\ne0,\ k\ne l\}$ for which there is a constant $C_\Phi$ with the following properties.
\begin{itemize}
\item[($\Phi$0)] $\Phi(k,l)=0$ if $|k|+|l|<c$ or $|k|+|l|>C_\Phi$.
\item[($\Phi$1)] For $0<|k|<\frac c3$, $\Phi(k,l)=\sum_\iota\mathsf h_\iota(k)\Phi_\iota(k,l)$, a finite sum with homogeneous factors $\mathsf h_\iota$ and with functions $\Phi_\iota\in C^\infty(\{|k|<\frac c3\}\times\mathbb R^3)$ which vanish where $|k|+|l|<c$ or $|k|+|l|>C_\Phi$.
\item[($\Phi$2)] For $0<|l|<\frac c3$, $\Phi(k,l)=\sum_\iota\mathsf h'_\iota(l)\Phi'_\iota(k,l)$, with the same properties after the exchange of $k$ and $l$.
\item[($\Phi$3)] $|\Phi(k,l)|\le C_\Phi|k-l|^{-2}$ for $|k|,|l|\ge\frac c8$.
\end{itemize}
For $\Phi\in\mathfrak P_2(c)$ the function
\[
k\mapsto\eta_c(k)\int\Phi(k,l)\,dl=\sum_\iota\mathsf h_\iota(k)\,\eta_c(k)\int\Phi_\iota(k,l)\,dl
\]
lies in $\mathfrak P$, since $\eta_c$ vanishes for $|k|\ge\frac c4$ and the $\Phi_\iota$ are smooth and vanish for $|l|>C_\Phi$; likewise $l\mapsto\eta_c(l)\int\Phi(k,l)\,dk$ lies in $\mathfrak P$. We define
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{f.p.}\!\iint\Phi\,dk\,dl:={}&\iint\bigl(1-\eta_c(k)-\eta_c(l)\bigr)\Phi\,dk\,dl\\
&+\operatorname{f.p.}\!\int\Bigl[\eta_c(k)\!\int\Phi(k,l)\,dl\Bigr]dk+\operatorname{f.p.}\!\int\Bigl[\eta_c(l)\!\int\Phi(k,l)\,dk\Bigr]dl .
\end{aligned}
\]
On the support of $\Phi$, $|k|<\frac c8$ implies $|l|>\frac78c$, hence $\eta_c(k)=1$ and $\eta_c(l)=0$; the same holds with $k$ and $l$ exchanged. Therefore the first integrand vanishes unless $|k|,|l|\ge\frac c8$, and the first integral converges absolutely, by ($\Phi$0) and ($\Phi$3): its integrand is bounded by $C_\Phi|k-l|^{-2}$, which is integrable over bounded sets of $(k,l)$, and it vanishes for $|k|+|l|>C_\Phi$. This finite part is linear on $\mathfrak P_2(c)$ and symmetric under the exchange of $k$ and $l$.

\emph{(3) Cut-offs.} Let $\mathcal Y(c)$ be the set of functions $\Upsilon\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R^3)$ for which there is a constant $C_\Upsilon$ with the following properties.
\begin{itemize}
\item[(Y1)] $\Upsilon(k,l,\mathsf p)=0$ if $|\mathsf p|<c$ and ($|k|+|l|<c$ or $|k|+|l|>C_\Upsilon$).
\item[(Y2)] $\Upsilon(-k,-l,-\mathsf p)=\Upsilon(k,l,\mathsf p)=\Upsilon(Ok,Ol,O\mathsf p)$ for every rotation $O$.
\end{itemize}
Then $\mathcal Y(c')\subset\mathcal Y(c)$ for $c<c'$. For $\Lambda>1$ and a function $\Upsilon$ of $(k,l,\mathsf p)$ or of $(k,l)$, let $\Upsilon^\Lambda$ denote $\Upsilon$ evaluated at the arguments divided by $\Lambda$; if $\Upsilon\in\mathcal Y(c)$, then $\Upsilon^\Lambda\in\mathcal Y(\Lambda c)\subset\mathcal Y(c)$. For a function $G(k,l,\mathsf p)$ which is of class $C^2$ in $\mathsf p$ near $0$ we put
\[
\overline{G_2}(k,l):=\tfrac16\,\Delta_{\mathsf p}G(k,l,\mathsf p)\big|_{\mathsf p=0} ;
\]
this is the mean over the directions of $\mathsf p$ of the term of second order in the Taylor expansion of $G$ in $\mathsf p$, divided by $\mathsf p^2$, since the mean of $\mathsf p_i\mathsf p_j$ over $\{|\mathsf p|=t\}$ is $\frac13t^2\delta_{ij}$. Finally, for $\Upsilon\in\mathcal Y(c)$ and $0<|\mathsf p|<c$ we put
\[
\Xi_\Gamma[\Upsilon](\mathsf p):=\iint\Upsilon F_\Gamma\,d^\circ k\,d^\circ l ;
\]
this integral converges absolutely by \eqref{IV-73-66} and the estimates following it in \cref{IV-73-64}(3), since by (Y1) the integrand vanishes for $|k|+|l|>C_\Upsilon$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Properties of finite parts]\label{IV-73-86}
\begin{enumerate}
\item[\textup{(a)}] \textup{(}Continuation with a parameter.\textup{)} Let $\mathsf h$ be a homogeneous factor of degree $d$, and let $\mathsf g\colon\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb C\to\mathbb C$ have the following properties: for every $\mathsf z\in\mathbb C$ the function $\mathsf g(\cdot;\mathsf z)$ is smooth, and its support lies in a compact set which does not depend on $\mathsf z$; for every multi-index $\alpha$ the derivative $\partial_k^\alpha\mathsf g$ is continuous on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb C$ and, for each fixed $k$, an entire function of $\mathsf z$. Then the function
\[
\mathsf z\longmapsto\int|k|^{2\mathsf z}\,\mathsf h(k)\,\mathsf g(k;\mathsf z)\,dk ,
\]
which is defined for $2\operatorname{Re}\mathsf z+d>-3$, has a holomorphic continuation to $\mathbb D$, and the value of this continuation at $\mathsf z=0$ is $\operatorname{f.p.}\!\int\mathsf h\,\mathsf g(\cdot;0)\,dk$.
\item[\textup{(b)}] If $\mathsf g\in\mathfrak P$ is integrable, then $\operatorname{f.p.}\!\int\mathsf g\,dk=\int\mathsf g\,dk$.
\item[\textup{(c)}] Let $\mathsf h$ be a homogeneous factor of degree $d\le-4$, and let $\eta(k)=\theta_1(|k|)$, where $\theta_1\in C^\infty([0,\infty))$ has compact support and is equal to $1$ near $0$. Then
\[
\operatorname{f.p.}\!\int\eta\,\mathsf h\,dk=-\int(1-\eta)\,\mathsf h\,dk .
\]
\item[\textup{(d)}] \textup{(}A soft line.\textup{)} Let $\mu_0>0$ and $\eta(k):=\theta(|k|/2\mu_0)$. Let
\[
S(k,\mathsf p)=\mathsf P(k,\mathsf p)\,|k|^{-2\mathsf a}\,|k-\mathsf p|^{-2\mathsf a'} ,
\]
where $\mathsf a,\mathsf a'\ge0$ are integers and $\mathsf P$ is a polynomial, homogeneous of degree $2\mathsf a+2\mathsf a'-2$, and assume that $|S(k,\mathsf p)|\le C_S\bigl(|k|^{-2}+|k-\mathsf p|^{-2}\bigr)$. Let $J\in C^\infty\bigl(\{|k|<3\mu_0\}\times\{|\mathsf p|<\mu_0\}\bigr)$ satisfy $J(-k,-\mathsf p)=J(k,\mathsf p)$, and for $k\ne0$ and $i\in\{0,1,2\}$ put
\[
[SJ]_i(k;\mathsf p):=\sum_{|\alpha|=i}\frac{\mathsf p^\alpha}{\alpha!}\,\partial_{\mathsf p}^\alpha(SJ)(k,0).
\]
Then $\eta\,[SJ]_i(\cdot;\mathsf p)\in\mathfrak P$. Moreover, there are a Borel function $\mathsf h_S$ on $\mathbb R^3$, which depends on $S$ only, is bounded on the unit sphere and satisfies $\mathsf h_S(t\mathsf p)=t\,\mathsf h_S(\mathsf p)$ for $t>0$, and a constant $C=C(\mu_0,S,J)$, such that for $0<|\mathsf p|\le\frac12\mu_0$
\[
\Bigl|\int\eta SJ\,dk-\operatorname{f.p.}\!\int\eta\,[SJ]_0\,dk-\operatorname{f.p.}\!\int\eta\,[SJ]_2(k;\mathsf p)\,dk-J(0,0)\,\mathsf h_S(\mathsf p)\Bigr|\le C\,|\mathsf p|^3\lg|\mathsf p| .
\]
\item[\textup{(e)}] \textup{(}Two variables.\textup{)} Let $\Phi\in\mathfrak P_2(c)$ and $(\epsilon,\epsilon')\in\{(1,1),(1,0),(0,1)\}$. If $\epsilon=0$, assume that all degrees of the homogeneous factors in \textup{($\Phi1$)} are $\ge-2$; if $\epsilon'=0$, assume that all degrees of the homogeneous factors in \textup{($\Phi2$)} are $\ge-2$. Then the integral
\[
\iint|k|^{2\epsilon\mathsf z}\,|l|^{2\epsilon'\mathsf z}\,\Phi\,dk\,dl
\]
converges absolutely for large $\operatorname{Re}\mathsf z$, and it has a holomorphic continuation to $\mathbb D$ whose value at $\mathsf z=0$ is $\operatorname{f.p.}\!\iint\Phi\,dk\,dl$. If $0<c'<c$, then $\mathfrak P_2(c)\subset\mathfrak P_2(c')$, and every $\Phi\in\mathfrak P_2(c)$ has the same finite part whether it is regarded as an element of $\mathfrak P_2(c)$ or of $\mathfrak P_2(c')$. If $\Phi\in\mathfrak P_2(c)$ is integrable, then $\operatorname{f.p.}\!\iint\Phi\,dk\,dl=\iint\Phi\,dk\,dl$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\emph{Proof of \textup{(a)}.} Put $m:=\max\{0,-d-3\}$; then $d+m+1\ge-2$. For the proof of (a) let $\eta(k):=\theta(|k|)$, with the function $\theta$ of \cref{IV-73-38}, so that $\eta=1$ for $|k|\le\frac12$ and $\eta=0$ for $|k|\ge1$, and let
\[
T\mathsf g(k;\mathsf z):=\sum_{|\alpha|\le m}\frac{k^\alpha}{\alpha!}\,\partial_k^\alpha\mathsf g(0;\mathsf z)
\]
be the Taylor polynomial of degree $m$ of $\mathsf g(\cdot;\mathsf z)$ at $k=0$. For $2\operatorname{Re}\mathsf z+d>-3$ we decompose
\begin{equation*}
\int|k|^{2\mathsf z}\mathsf h\,\mathsf g\,dk=\int|k|^{2\mathsf z}\mathsf h\,\bigl[\mathsf g-\eta\,T\mathsf g\bigr]\,dk+\sum_{|\alpha|\le m}\frac{\partial_k^\alpha\mathsf g(0;\mathsf z)}{\alpha!}\int|k|^{2\mathsf z}\,\eta(k)\,\mathsf h(k)\,k^\alpha\,dk .
\end{equation*}
The integrand of the first integral on the right vanishes outside a compact set which does not depend on $\mathsf z$. For $|k|\le\frac12$ we have $\eta=1$, and Taylor's formula, together with the continuity of the derivatives of order $m+1$ of $\mathsf g$ on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb C$, bounds the modulus of the integrand by $C|k|^{2\operatorname{Re}\mathsf z+d+m+1}$, with a constant $C$ that stays bounded as long as $\mathsf z$ ranges over a compact set. Since $d+m+1\ge-2$, the exponent is larger than $-3$ as soon as $\operatorname{Re}\mathsf z>-\frac12$. For each $k\ne0$ the integrand is an entire function of $\mathsf z$; differentiating under the integral sign, we see that the first integral is holomorphic on $\{\operatorname{Re}\mathsf z>-\frac12\}$.

In the integrals of the sum we pass to polar coordinates and integrate by parts once. With
\[
\mathsf m_\alpha:=\int_{S^2}\mathsf h(\omega)\,\omega^\alpha\,d\omega
\]
we obtain, for $2\operatorname{Re}\mathsf z+d+|\alpha|>-3$,
\[
\int|k|^{2\mathsf z}\,\eta\,\mathsf h\,k^\alpha\,dk=\mathsf m_\alpha\int_0^\infty\theta(s)\,s^{2\mathsf z+d+|\alpha|+2}\,ds=-\frac{\mathsf m_\alpha}{2\mathsf z+d+|\alpha|+3}\int_0^\infty\theta'(s)\,s^{2\mathsf z+d+|\alpha|+3}\,ds .
\]
As $\theta'$ is supported in $[\frac12,1]$, the last integral is an entire function of $\mathsf z$. If $d+|\alpha|$ is odd, then $\omega\mapsto\mathsf h(\omega)\omega^\alpha$ is odd and $\mathsf m_\alpha=0$. If $d+|\alpha|$ is even, the denominator vanishes only at $\mathsf z=-\frac12(d+|\alpha|+3)$, which is half an odd integer and hence not a point of $\mathbb D$. Consequently the right side of the decomposition is holomorphic on $\mathbb D$; it is the asserted continuation, which is unique because $\mathbb D$ is connected.

The value of this continuation at $\mathsf z=0$ involves $\mathsf g$ only through $\mathsf g(\cdot;0)$: it contains the function $\mathsf g(\cdot;0)-\eta\,T\mathsf g(\cdot;0)$ and the numbers $\partial_k^\alpha\mathsf g(0;0)$. It is therefore equal to the value at $0$ of the same expression built with the function $\mathsf g(\cdot;0)$, which does not depend on $\mathsf z$. By the argument just given, applied to this function, that expression continues $\mathsf z\mapsto\int|k|^{2\mathsf z}\mathsf h\,\mathsf g(\cdot;0)\,dk$ to $\mathbb D$, and by \cref{IV-73-85}(1) its value at $0$ is $\operatorname{f.p.}\!\int\mathsf h\,\mathsf g(\cdot;0)\,dk$.

\emph{Proof of \textup{(b)}.} Let $\mathsf g\in\mathfrak P$ be integrable. Like every element of $\mathfrak P$, the function $\mathsf g$ vanishes outside a bounded set; hence for every $\mathsf N>0$ there is $C_{\mathsf N}$ with $|k|^{2\operatorname{Re}\mathsf z}|\mathsf g(k)|\le C_{\mathsf N}|\mathsf g(k)|$ whenever $0\le\operatorname{Re}\mathsf z\le\mathsf N$. By differentiation under the integral sign and by dominated convergence, $\int|k|^{2\mathsf z}\mathsf g\,dk$ is holomorphic on $\{\operatorname{Re}\mathsf z>0\}$ and continuous on $\{\operatorname{Re}\mathsf z\ge0\}$. The open set $\mathbb D\cap\{\operatorname{Re}\mathsf z>0\}$ is connected, and on it this function coincides with the continuation of \cref{IV-73-85}(1), because the two functions agree for large $\operatorname{Re}\mathsf z$ (identity theorem). Letting $\mathsf z\downarrow0$ along the real axis, we obtain $\operatorname{f.p.}\!\int\mathsf g\,dk=\int\mathsf g\,dk$.

\emph{Proof of \textup{(c)}.} Let $\mathsf m_0:=\int_{S^2}\mathsf h\,d\omega$. For $2\operatorname{Re}\mathsf z+d>-3$, polar coordinates and one integration by parts give
\[
\int|k|^{2\mathsf z}\,\eta\,\mathsf h\,dk=\mathsf m_0\int_0^\infty\theta_1(s)\,s^{2\mathsf z+d+2}\,ds=-\frac{\mathsf m_0}{2\mathsf z+d+3}\int_0^\infty\theta_1'(s)\,s^{2\mathsf z+d+3}\,ds .
\]
The support of $\theta_1'$ is a compact subset of $(0,\infty)$, so the last integral is an entire function of $\mathsf z$. As in the proof of (a), either $d$ is odd and $\mathsf m_0=0$, or the zero of the denominator is half an odd integer and lies outside $\mathbb D$. Hence the right side is the continuation of the left side to $\mathbb D$, and its value at $\mathsf z=0$ is
\[
\operatorname{f.p.}\!\int\eta\,\mathsf h\,dk=-\frac{\mathsf m_0}{d+3}\int_0^\infty\theta_1'(s)\,s^{d+3}\,ds .
\]
On the other hand, $1-\theta_1$ vanishes near $0$ and $d+3<0$; an integration by parts without boundary terms therefore yields
\[
\int(1-\eta)\,\mathsf h\,dk=\mathsf m_0\int_0^\infty\bigl(1-\theta_1(s)\bigr)\,s^{d+2}\,ds=\frac{\mathsf m_0}{d+3}\int_0^\infty\theta_1'(s)\,s^{d+3}\,ds .
\]
Comparing the last two displays, we obtain (c).

\emph{Proof of \textup{(d)}: preparation.} The function $S$ is smooth on $\{k\ne0,\ k\ne\mathsf p\}$, homogeneous of degree $-2$ in $(k,\mathsf p)$ jointly, and even, since the polynomial $\mathsf P$ is homogeneous of even degree. The set $\{(k,\mathsf q):|k|=1,\ |\mathsf q|\le\frac12\}$ is compact, and $S$ is smooth in a neighbourhood of it; together with homogeneity this gives, for every multi-index $\alpha$,
\[
|\partial_{\mathsf p}^\alpha S(k,\mathsf q)|\le C_\alpha\,|k|^{-2-|\alpha|}\qquad\bigl(|\mathsf q|\le\tfrac12|k|\bigr).
\]
For every multi-index $\beta$ the function $\partial_{\mathsf p}^\beta S(\cdot,0)$ is a homogeneous factor of degree $-2-|\beta|$: it is smooth off $0$, homogeneous of this degree, and of parity $(-1)^{|\beta|}$ because $S$ is even. By the Leibniz rule, $\eta\,[SJ]_i(\cdot;\mathsf p)$ is a finite sum of products of such factors with the functions $\eta\,\partial_{\mathsf p}^\gamma J(\cdot,0)$; these belong to $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$, since $\eta$ vanishes for $|k|\ge2\mu_0$. Hence $\eta\,[SJ]_i(\cdot;\mathsf p)\in\mathfrak P$.

Since $J$ is even, the terms of odd degree in its Taylor expansion at $(0,0)$ vanish, and its Taylor polynomial of degree $3$ is $J(0,0)+J_2$ with a quadratic form $J_2$ in $(k,\mathsf p)$. Thus $J=J(0,0)+J_2+J_4$, and Taylor's formula with integral remainder, applied to $J$ and to its derivatives, gives
\[
|\partial_{\mathsf p}^\alpha J_4(k,\mathsf p)|\le C\,(|k|+|\mathsf p|)^{4-|\alpha|}\qquad(|\alpha|\le3)\quad\text{on }\{|k|\le2\mu_0,\ |\mathsf p|\le\tfrac12\mu_0\}.
\]
Each of the four expressions inside the modulus in the asserted estimate, namely $\int\eta SJ\,dk$, $\operatorname{f.p.}\!\int\eta\,[SJ]_0\,dk$, $\operatorname{f.p.}\!\int\eta\,[SJ]_2(k;\mathsf p)\,dk$ and $J(0,0)\,\mathsf h_S(\mathsf p)$, depends linearly on $J$, because $J\mapsto[SJ]_i$ and the finite part are linear. We insert $J=J(0,0)+J_2+J_4$. The quadratic form $J_2$ and the function $J_4$ are even and vanish at $(0,0)$, so that for them the last of the four expressions is $0$. It therefore suffices to consider, in place of $SJ$, the three functions
\[
N:=S,\qquad N:=SJ_2,\qquad N:=SJ_4 ,
\]
and to show that the difference $\int\eta N\,dk-\operatorname{f.p.}\!\int\eta\,[N]_0\,dk-\operatorname{f.p.}\!\int\eta\,[N]_2\,dk$ is equal to $\mathsf h_S(\mathsf p)+O(|\mathsf p|^3)$ for $N=S$, the case which enters with the factor $J(0,0)$, and that it is $O(|\mathsf p|^3\lg|\mathsf p|)$ for $N=SJ_2$ and for $N=SJ_4$. For each of the three functions we write $N_i:=[N]_i$ ($i=0,1,2$), and for $|k|\ge2|\mathsf p|$ we put $N_{\mathrm r}:=N-N_0-N_1-N_2$; moreover, $\mathsf B:=\{|k|\le2|\mathsf p|\}$. Since $|\mathsf p|\le\frac12\mu_0$, we have $\eta=1$ on $\mathsf B$. In all three cases $N(-k,-\mathsf p)=N(k,\mathsf p)$, as $S$, $J_2$ and $J_4$ are even; differentiating with respect to $\mathsf p$ at $\mathsf p=0$, we see that $N_1$ is odd in $k$ while $N_0$ and $N_2$ are even.

\emph{The case $N=S$.} By the bound on the derivatives of $S$, $|N_i|\le C|\mathsf p|^i|k|^{-2-i}$. On the complement $\mathsf B^c$ of $\mathsf B$, Taylor's formula in $\mathsf p$, applied at the points $t\mathsf p$ with $0\le t\le1$, all of which satisfy $|t\mathsf p|\le\frac12|k|$, gives $|N_{\mathrm r}|\le C|\mathsf p|^3|k|^{-5}$. We write
\[
\int\eta N\,dk=\int_{\mathsf B}N\,dk+\int_{\mathsf B^c}\eta\,(N_0+N_1+N_2+N_{\mathrm r})\,dk
\]
and consider the four terms of the second integral one after the other. First, $\int_{\mathsf B^c}\eta N_0=\int\eta N_0-\int_{\mathsf B}N_0$. Second, $\int_{\mathsf B^c}\eta N_1=0$, because $N_1$ is odd and integrable over $\mathsf B^c\cap\operatorname{supp}\eta$, while $\eta$ and $\mathsf B^c$ are invariant under $k\to-k$. Third, $N_2(\cdot;\mathsf p)$ is a homogeneous factor of degree $-4$; assertion (c), applied with $\theta_1(s):=\theta(s/2\mu_0)$, and the vanishing of $1-\eta$ on $\mathsf B$ give
\[
\int_{\mathsf B^c}\eta N_2=\int_{\mathsf B^c}N_2-\int(1-\eta)N_2=\int_{\mathsf B^c}N_2+\operatorname{f.p.}\!\int\eta N_2 .
\]
Fourth, $\int_{\mathsf B^c}\eta N_{\mathrm r}=\int_{\mathsf B^c}N_{\mathrm r}-\int(1-\eta)N_{\mathrm r}$, and
\[
\Bigl|\int(1-\eta)N_{\mathrm r}\Bigr|\le C|\mathsf p|^3\int_{|k|\ge\mu_0}|k|^{-5}\,dk\le C|\mathsf p|^3 .
\]
Collecting the terms, we arrive at
\[
\begin{gathered}
\int\eta S\,dk=\int\eta N_0\,dk+\operatorname{f.p.}\!\int\eta N_2\,dk+\mathsf h_S(\mathsf p)+O(|\mathsf p|^3),\\
\mathsf h_S(\mathsf p):=\int_{|k|\le2|\mathsf p|}(S-N_0)\,dk+\int_{|k|>2|\mathsf p|}(N_2+N_{\mathrm r})\,dk .
\end{gathered}
\]
Both integrals in the definition of $\mathsf h_S$ converge absolutely, because $|S|+|N_0|\le C(|k|^{-2}+|k-\mathsf p|^{-2})$, and $|N_2+N_{\mathrm r}|\le C|\mathsf p|^2|k|^{-4}$ on $\mathsf B^c$. The substitution $k\to tk$, together with $N_i(tk;t\mathsf p)=t^{-2}N_i(k;\mathsf p)$, yields $\mathsf h_S(t\mathsf p)=t\,\mathsf h_S(\mathsf p)$ for $t>0$; the same bounds, taken at $|\mathsf p|=1$, show that $\mathsf h_S$ is bounded on the unit sphere $\{|\mathsf p|=1\}$, so that $|\mathsf h_S(\mathsf p)|\le C|\mathsf p|$; and $\mathsf h_S$ is a Borel function by Fubini's theorem. By its definition $\mathsf h_S$ depends on $S$ only. Finally, $\eta N_0\in\mathfrak P$ is integrable, so that $\int\eta N_0\,dk$ is its finite part by (b).

\emph{The case $N=SJ_2$.} Now $N$ is homogeneous of degree $0$ in $(k,\mathsf p)$, and as above $|\partial_{\mathsf p}^\alpha N(k,\mathsf q)|\le C|k|^{-|\alpha|}$ for $|\mathsf q|\le\frac12|k|$. Hence $|N_i|\le C|\mathsf p|^i|k|^{-i}$, which is integrable near $k=0$ for $i\le2$; further $|N_{\mathrm r}|\le C|\mathsf p|^3|k|^{-3}$ on $\mathsf B^c$, and $|N|\le C|\mathsf p|^2(|k|^{-2}+|k-\mathsf p|^{-2})$ on $\mathsf B$. Therefore
\[
\int\eta N\,dk=\sum_{i\le2}\int\eta N_i\,dk+\Bigl[\int_{\mathsf B}(N-N_0-N_1-N_2)\,dk+\int_{\mathsf B^c}\eta N_{\mathrm r}\,dk\Bigr],
\]
and the bracket is bounded in modulus by
\[
C|\mathsf p|^3+C|\mathsf p|^3\int_{2|\mathsf p|\le|k|\le2\mu_0}|k|^{-3}\,dk\le C|\mathsf p|^3\lg|\mathsf p| .
\]
The term with $i=1$ vanishes because $N_1$ is odd, and the terms with $i=0$ and $i=2$ are finite parts by (b).

\emph{The case $N=SJ_4$.} By the Leibniz rule and the bounds on the derivatives of $S$ and of $J_4$,
\[
|\partial_{\mathsf p}^\alpha N(k,\mathsf q)|\le C|k|^{2-|\alpha|}\qquad\bigl(|\alpha|\le3,\ |\mathsf q|\le\tfrac12|k|,\ |\mathsf q|\le\tfrac12\mu_0,\ |k|\le2\mu_0\bigr).
\]
Hence $|N_i|\le C|\mathsf p|^i|k|^{2-i}$, $|N_{\mathrm r}|\le C|\mathsf p|^3|k|^{-1}$ on $\mathsf B^c\cap\operatorname{supp}\eta$, and $|N|\le C|\mathsf p|^4(|k|^{-2}+|k-\mathsf p|^{-2})$ on $\mathsf B$. Arguing as in the previous case, we find $\int\eta N\,dk=\int\eta N_0\,dk+\int\eta N_2\,dk+O(|\mathsf p|^3)$, and the two integrals on the right are finite parts by (b).

Adding the three cases, the first one multiplied by $J(0,0)$, and using $|\mathsf p|^3\le|\mathsf p|^3\lg|\mathsf p|$, we obtain the estimate of (d), with a constant depending on $\mu_0$, $S$ and $J$.

\emph{Proof of \textup{(e)}.} We split $1=\bigl(1-\eta_c(k)-\eta_c(l)\bigr)+\eta_c(k)+\eta_c(l)$ and treat the three resulting integrals separately; each of them converges absolutely for large $\operatorname{Re}\mathsf z$, as the following discussion shows.

On the support of $\Phi$, $|k|<\frac c8$ implies $|l|>\frac78c$ by \textup{($\Phi0$)}, hence $\eta_c(k)=1$ and $\eta_c(l)=0$; the same holds with $k$ and $l$ exchanged. Therefore the first integrand, which contains the factor $1-\eta_c(k)-\eta_c(l)$, vanishes unless $|k|,|l|\ge\frac c8$, and by \textup{($\Phi0$)} it vanishes unless $|k|+|l|\le C_\Phi$. On this bounded set the factor $|k|^{2\epsilon\mathsf z}|l|^{2\epsilon'\mathsf z}$ is an entire function of $\mathsf z$, bounded for $\mathsf z$ in compact sets, while $|\Phi|\le C_\Phi|k-l|^{-2}$ by \textup{($\Phi3$)}. Hence the first integral is an entire function of $\mathsf z$, whose value at $\mathsf z=0$ is $\iint\bigl(1-\eta_c(k)-\eta_c(l)\bigr)\Phi\,dk\,dl$.

In the second integral, $\eta_c(k)\ne0$ forces $|k|\le\frac c4<\frac c3$, so that \textup{($\Phi1$)} applies, and Fubini's theorem turns this integral into
\[
\sum_\iota\int|k|^{2\epsilon\mathsf z}\,\mathsf h_\iota(k)\,\mathsf g_\iota(k;\mathsf z)\,dk,\qquad\mathsf g_\iota(k;\mathsf z):=\eta_c(k)\int|l|^{2\epsilon'\mathsf z}\,\Phi_\iota(k,l)\,dl .
\]
Since $\Phi_\iota$ vanishes where $|k|+|l|<c$ or $|k|+|l|>C_\Phi$, the integrand defining $\mathsf g_\iota$ vanishes unless $\frac34c\le|l|\le C_\Phi$; consequently $\mathsf g_\iota$ has the properties required in (a). If $\epsilon=1$, assertion (a) provides a holomorphic continuation to $\mathbb D$ whose value at $\mathsf z=0$ is $\operatorname{f.p.}\!\int\mathsf h_\iota\,\mathsf g_\iota(\cdot;0)\,dk$. If $\epsilon=0$, all degrees of the $\mathsf h_\iota$ are $\ge-2$; the $k$-integral then converges absolutely for every $\mathsf z$ and defines an entire function, whose value at $0$ is again the finite part, by (b). Summing over $\iota$, we obtain at $\mathsf z=0$ the number $\operatorname{f.p.}\!\int\bigl[\eta_c(k)\int\Phi(k,l)\,dl\bigr]dk$.

The hypotheses of (e) are symmetric under the exchange of $k$ with $l$, of $\epsilon$ with $\epsilon'$ and of \textup{($\Phi1$)} with \textup{($\Phi2$)}: the set $\{(1,1),(1,0),(0,1)\}$ is invariant under $(\epsilon,\epsilon')\mapsto(\epsilon',\epsilon)$, conditions \textup{($\Phi0$)} and \textup{($\Phi3$)} do not change when $k$ and $l$ are interchanged, and the assumptions on the degrees in \textup{($\Phi1$)} and \textup{($\Phi2$)} are interchanged. Under this exchange the third integral, which contains the factor $\eta_c(l)$, becomes the second one, and the argument just given applies to it. In detail: $\eta_c(l)\ne0$ forces $|l|\le\frac c4<\frac c3$, so that \textup{($\Phi2$)} applies, and Fubini's theorem turns the third integral into
\[
\sum_\iota\int|l|^{2\epsilon'\mathsf z}\,\mathsf h'_\iota(l)\,\mathsf g'_\iota(l;\mathsf z)\,dl,\qquad\mathsf g'_\iota(l;\mathsf z):=\eta_c(l)\int|k|^{2\epsilon\mathsf z}\,\Phi'_\iota(k,l)\,dk .
\]
Since $\Phi'_\iota$ vanishes where $|k|+|l|<c$ or $|k|+|l|>C_\Phi$, the integrand defining $\mathsf g'_\iota$ vanishes unless $\frac34c\le|k|\le C_\Phi$, and $\mathsf g'_\iota$ has the properties required in (a). If $\epsilon'=1$, assertion (a) provides a holomorphic continuation to $\mathbb D$ whose value at $\mathsf z=0$ is $\operatorname{f.p.}\!\int\mathsf h'_\iota\,\mathsf g'_\iota(\cdot;0)\,dl$. If $\epsilon'=0$, all degrees of the $\mathsf h'_\iota$ are $\ge-2$; the $l$-integral then converges absolutely for every $\mathsf z$ and defines an entire function, whose value at $0$ is the finite part, by (b). Summing over $\iota$, we obtain at $\mathsf z=0$ the number $\operatorname{f.p.}\!\int\bigl[\eta_c(l)\int\Phi(k,l)\,dk\bigr]dl$. The sum of the three values at $\mathsf z=0$ is the right side of the definition of $\operatorname{f.p.}\!\iint\Phi\,dk\,dl$ in \cref{IV-73-85}(2).

\emph{Change of the parameter $c$.} Let $0<c'<c$ and $\Phi\in\mathfrak P_2(c)$. Conditions \textup{($\Phi0$)}, \textup{($\Phi1$)} and \textup{($\Phi2$)} at $c'$ follow from the same conditions at $c$ by restriction. For \textup{($\Phi3$)} at $c'$, let $|k|,|l|\ge\frac{c'}8$ and $\Phi(k,l)\ne0$. If $|k|,|l|\ge\frac c8$, \textup{($\Phi3$)} at $c$ applies. Both $|k|$ and $|l|$ smaller than $\frac c8$ is impossible by \textup{($\Phi0$)}. If $\frac{c'}8\le|k|<\frac c8$, we use $\Phi=\sum_\iota\mathsf h_\iota\Phi_\iota$ from \textup{($\Phi1$)}: the $\mathsf h_\iota$ are bounded on $\{\frac{c'}8\le|k|\le\frac c8\}$, the $\Phi_\iota$ are bounded there as well (they are continuous on $\{|k|\le\frac c8\}\times\mathbb R^3$ and vanish for $|l|>C_\Phi$), and $|k-l|\le|k|+|l|\le C_\Phi$; hence $|\Phi|\le C\le C\,C_\Phi^2|k-l|^{-2}$. The case $\frac{c'}8\le|l|<\frac c8$ is symmetric, with \textup{($\Phi2$)}. Thus $\mathfrak P_2(c)\subset\mathfrak P_2(c')$. The integral with $(\epsilon,\epsilon')=(1,1)$ does not involve $c$, so the value at $\mathsf z=0$ of its continuation, which is the finite part with respect to $c$ and also the finite part with respect to $c'$, is the same.

Finally, let $\Phi$ be integrable. By Fubini's theorem the functions $k\mapsto\eta_c(k)\int\Phi(k,l)\,dl$ and $l\mapsto\eta_c(l)\int\Phi(k,l)\,dk$ are integrable elements of $\mathfrak P$, so by (b) their finite parts are their integrals, and the definition of $\operatorname{f.p.}\!\iint\Phi$ reduces to $\iint\Phi\,dk\,dl$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Expansion by regions of $\Xi_\Gamma{[\Upsilon]}$ at small $\mathsf p$]\label{IV-73-87}
Let $\Gamma\in\{1,\dots,6\}$, $c>0$ and $\Upsilon\in\mathcal Y(c)$. Then $\overline{(\Upsilon F_\Gamma)_2}\in\mathfrak P_2(c)$, and there are numbers $\alpha$, $\beta$ and $C$, depending only on $\Gamma$, $c$ and $\Upsilon$, such that
\[
\bigl|\Xi_\Gamma[\Upsilon](\mathsf p)-\alpha-\beta\,|\mathsf p|-\mathfrak f_\Gamma[\Upsilon]\,\mathsf p^2\bigr|\le C\,|\mathsf p|^3\lg|\mathsf p|\qquad\bigl(0<|\mathsf p|\le\tfrac c{16}\bigr),
\]
where
\[
\mathfrak f_\Gamma[\Upsilon]:=(2\pi)^{-6}\operatorname{f.p.}\!\iint\overline{(\Upsilon F_\Gamma)_2}\,dk\,dl .
\]
The map $\Upsilon\mapsto\mathfrak f_\Gamma[\Upsilon]$ is linear on $\mathcal Y(c)$, and $\mathfrak f_\Gamma[\Upsilon^\Lambda]=\mathfrak f_\Gamma[\Upsilon]$ for every $\Lambda>1$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
\emph{Step 1: two factorisations of $F_\Gamma$.} We write the integrand $F_\Gamma$ of \eqref{IV-73-65} in two ways,
\[
F_\Gamma=\sum S\cdot H=\sum S'\cdot H' ,
\]
where the sums extend over the tensor indices carried by $S$, resp.\ by $S'$, the factor $S$ depends on $(k,\mathsf p)$ and $S'$ on $(l,\mathsf p)$ as in the following table, and $H$, resp.\ $H'$, denotes the product of all the other factors of $F_\Gamma$:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
\Gamma&S(k,\mathsf p)&S'(l,\mathsf p)\\\hline
1&v_2(k,\mathsf p-k)_{\mu\nu}/\mathsf x_1\mathsf x_1'&v_2(-l,l-\mathsf p)_{\rho\sigma}/\mathsf x_2\mathsf x_2'\\
2,\ 3&v_2(k,\mathsf p-k)_{\mu\nu}v_2(-k,k-\mathsf p)_{\rho\nu}/\mathsf x_1^2\mathsf x_1'&1/\mathsf x_2\\
4&v_2(k,\mathsf p-k)_{\mu\nu}/\mathsf x_1\mathsf x_1'&v_2(l,\mathsf p-l)_{\mu\nu}/\mathsf x_2\mathsf x_2'\\
5&v_2(k-\mathsf p,-k)_{\alpha\sigma}/\mathsf x_1\mathsf x_1'&1/\mathsf x_2\\
6&1/\mathsf x_1'&1/\mathsf x_2
\end{array}
\]
For $\Gamma=4$ this means
\[
H_{\mu\nu}=-\tfrac12\bigl[\delta_{\mu\nu}v_2(l,\mathsf p-l)_{\lambda\lambda}-\tfrac12v_2(l,\mathsf p-l)_{\mu\nu}-\tfrac12v_2(l,\mathsf p-l)_{\nu\mu}\bigr]/\mathsf x_2\mathsf x_2',
\]
and $H'$ has the same form, with $v_2(k,\mathsf p-k)$ and $\mathsf x_1\mathsf x_1'$ in place of $v_2(l,\mathsf p-l)$ and $\mathsf x_2\mathsf x_2'$. Every component of $S$ has the form required in \cref{IV-73-86}(d): it is a homogeneous polynomial divided by $|k|^{2\mathsf a}|k-\mathsf p|^{2\mathsf a'}$, with $(\mathsf a,\mathsf a')=(1,1)$ for $\Gamma\in\{1,4,5\}$, $(2,1)$ for $\Gamma\in\{2,3\}$ and $(0,1)$ for $\Gamma=6$, and since $|v_2(k_1,k_2)|\le2|k_1||k_2|$ its modulus is at most $2/|k||k-\mathsf p|\le|k|^{-2}+|k-\mathsf p|^{-2}$ for $\Gamma\in\{1,4,5\}$, at most $4|k|^{-2}$ for $\Gamma\in\{2,3\}$, and equal to $|k-\mathsf p|^{-2}$ for $\Gamma=6$. The same holds for the components of $S'$, as functions of $l$. The factor $S$ contains all factors $\mathsf x_1,\mathsf x_1'$ of the denominator of $F_\Gamma$, and $S'$ all factors $\mathsf x_2,\mathsf x_2'$. Hence $H$ is a polynomial divided by powers of $\mathsf x_2,\mathsf x_2',\mathsf x_3$, and $H'$ a polynomial divided by powers of $\mathsf x_1,\mathsf x_1',\mathsf x_3$; in both, $\mathsf x_3$ occurs at most to the first power. Moreover, $H$ and $H'$ are even under the reflection of all their arguments: they are quotients of homogeneous polynomials of even degree, because besides factors $v_2$ each of them contains two factors $v_3$, or the factor $l_\rho(l-k)_\mu$, or neither.

\emph{Step 2: where the lines are long.} Put $\mu_0:=\frac c8$ and $\eta:=\eta_c=\theta(|\cdot|/2\mu_0)$. Let $|\mathsf p|<\mu_0$. By \textup{(Y1)}, $\Upsilon(k,l,\mathsf p)\ne0$ implies $|k|+|l|\ge8\mu_0$. If, in addition, $|k|<3\mu_0$, then
\[
|l|>5\mu_0,\qquad|l-\mathsf p|>4\mu_0,\qquad|k-l|>2\mu_0 ;
\]
these are the lengths whose squares $\mathsf x_2,\mathsf x_2',\mathsf x_3$ occur in the denominator of $H$. Consequently the product $\Upsilon H$, extended by $0$ where $\Upsilon=0$, is smooth on $\{|k|<3\mu_0\}\times\mathbb R^3\times\{|\mathsf p|<\mu_0\}$: this set is covered by the open set $\{|k|+|l|<8\mu_0,\ |\mathsf p|<c\}$, on which $\Upsilon$ vanishes identically, and by the open set $\{|k|<3\mu_0,\ |l|>5\mu_0,\ |\mathsf p|<\mu_0\}$, on which $H$ is smooth. Symmetrically, if $\Upsilon(k,l,\mathsf p)\ne0$ and $|l|<3\mu_0$, then $|k|\ge8\mu_0-|l|$, and
\[
|k|>5\mu_0,\qquad|k-\mathsf p|>4\mu_0,\qquad|k-l|>2\mu_0 ;
\]
